News.title: Stepdad GUILTY of murdering student, 19, in her uni halls after making life-size effigy of her to fulfil sexual fantasy
News.content:
Next

A STEPDAD has been found guilty of murdering a student in her uni accommodation after developing a sexual obsession with her.

Carla Georgescu, 19, was discovered dead on what would have been her 20th birthday at the University of Lancashire campus in Preston.



Her stepdad Nathan Owens, 34, had driven 100 miles from the family home to strangle Carla to death after becoming “consumed by jealousy”.

He has now been convicted of murder following a trial at Preston Crown Court.



Jurors heard how Owens had become “sexually fixated” with his stepdaughter and made a life-size effigy of her to fulfil his sexual fantasy.

He had also manipulated innocent selfies of Carla into sexual images and had filmed himself having sex with her anime dolls and a stuffed cat she had bought him.

Just days before the horror, Carla had spent the weekend shopping for presents with her mum Janina and watching TV together.

On February 1, Owens drove from the family home in Hartlepool and joined his wife and stepdaughter for a meal at the Kimji Korean restaurant.

Footage showed him and Carla left alone together at one point during the meal.

Following the dinner, Owens and Janina were filmed dropping Carla back off at her accommodation, it was said.



Just three days later, he drove through the night before parking up in his Ford Puma outside Carla’s university residence.

Footage showed him shrouding himself in a blanket before making his towards Ribble Hall to murder Carla.

The court was told he left 90 minutes later – “shielding” himself with an umbrella and wearing a face-mask and Carla’s trainers, while carrying two bags.



Owens then returned home to Hartlepool where wife Janina said he was his “normal self”.

The mum told the court the couple later went for their regular walk at a nearby beach together and also shopping at an Asda store.

At the time, Carla’s body was lying slumped against a wardrobe door with injuries to her face and a belt tied around her.

Janina raised the alarm when her daughter failed to respond to her messages and phone calls.

After Carla was found on what would have been her 20th birthday, two officers went to the family home and told her she had been found hanged.



Janina told the court she was left “shaking” while Owens “started crying”.

He had hugged and comforted her, she said, but at that point he still didn’t reveal he had travelled to see Carla the day before, she said.

Janina told jurors it was only when she contacted a hospital mortuary and learned more details about her death that he admitted he had been at the flat.

Owens claimed Carla had wanted him to take incontinence pants to her and help her tidy her room but the prosecution say this was attempt to “cover his tracks”.

When asked by Mr Lumley if she had any reason to “doubt” Owen, Janina replied she didn’t because “it wasn’t inconsistent with his behaviour” and if Carla had wanted him to come he would have.



A post mortem also revealed Carla had been subjected to two heavy blows to her head, slash marks on her cheek and cuts and bruises to her mouth and nose.

Carla’s hands were covered in blood after she attempted to defend herself and she had sexual injuries, the court heard.

The jury was told sex toys and Owens’ DNA were found at the scene.

Mr Lumley said “some form of grievous sexual activity” had taken place which was “hardly surprising” given Owens’ sexual obsession with her.

Jurors were told the killing was possibly driven by “sexual jealousy” after discovering his stepdaughter was due to meet up with a new lover.



In the months leading up to Carla’s murder, Owens had been collecting photos of her taken without her knowledge.

Owens had also filmed himself having sex with her dolls and toys – including one that was a life-sized “effigy” dressed in Carla’s nightie.

He was also said to have manipulated innocent selfies of Carla into sexual images which he viewed in the week before she died.

“The only possible reason for looking at those images is that Nathan Owens had a wholly improper and dangerously entrenched sexual obsession with his stepdaughter,” Mr Lumley told the court.

He continued: “Her death was the culmination, the end point, of weeks, months and perhaps years of a one-sided sexual obsession.



“And it was the beginning of a complex murder investigation, which led to his door in Hartlepool.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“For it was he who was sexually fixated on Carla and it was he, Nathan Owens, who had killed Carla.”

Owens will be sentenced on a later date.

News.title: How windy will it be this week? Where 80mph winds will hit as Storm Austen AND Boelo target UK
News.content:
Next

STORM Austen, the first named storm of the season, is set to batter the UK bringing gale-force winds and torrential rain.

The Met Office has issued amber and yellow weather warnings, saying gusts could cause power cuts, travel delays, and a danger to life along coastal areas.



Here is everything you need to know about the incoming storm, the weather warnings in place, and how windy it will get.

What is Storm Austen?

Storm Austen is a fast-developing Atlantic low-pressure system that the jet stream is pushing towards Britain.



Forecasters say the storm will rapidly intensify before it makes landfall along the southern coast of the country.

Met Office meteorologist Alex Burkill said: “Storm Austen will rapiwdly deepen as it approaches the UK, undergoing a process known as explosive cyclogenesis.



“The most rapid deepening is expected during Thursday.

“As Storm Austen gets closer to the UK, it will reach maturity, meaning it will remain a deep area of low pressure but will no longer be strengthening at the same rate.”

How windy will it get?

When Storm Austen arrives, wind speeds are expected to vary across the country, though south-west England will bear the brunt.

An amber warning for wind is in place between 3am and 10am on Friday for Cornwall, Devon, Plymouth, and the Isles of Scilly.



Gusts of 60 to 70mph are expected there, while exposed coastal headlands could see winds up to 80mph.

A wider yellow wind warning covers parts of the South West, South East, Wales, and Herefordshire between midnight and 2pm on Friday.

These regions face inland gusts of 50 to 60mph, with coastal stretches seeing 70mph.

Persistent heavy rain will accompany the winds, and a yellow rain warning has also been issued for parts of Scotland from 6am Friday until 3am Saturday.

Met Office Deputy Chief Forecaster Chris Bulmer said residents should prepare for potentially severe conditions.



He said: “Storm Austen is expected to bring a spell of impactful weather to parts of the UK from Thursday night and through Friday.

“While there remains some uncertainty in the exact track of the storm, there is increasing confidence in the potential for disruptive winds across parts of southwest England, which is why an amber warning has been issued.

“Wind gusts could potentially reach 60-70mph for a time, and these strong winds will be combined with spells of heavy rain.

“People in affected areas should keep up to date with the latest forecast and warnings as the event develops.”

What disruption can be expected?

The Met Office has warned that flying debris, damaged buildings, power cuts and fallen trees may be possible.



Commuters could face disruption on exposed roads, bridges, and railways, while rough seas are likely to affect ferry crossings in the English Channel.

Safety chiefs have urged the public to stay away from the shoreline.

Ross Macleod, RNLI water safety manager, said: “If you plan to visit the coast or a waterside location, we urge you stay a safe distance from the water as conditions could knock you off your feet or wash you into the sea.”

What happens after Storm Austen?

Once the peak of Storm Austen has passed, winds will begin to gradually ease through Friday afternoon, offering a brief respite early on Saturday.

But the calm may be short-lived.



The Met Office has named the second storm to hit the UK in just 24 hours.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Storm Boelo is due to bring more rain and wind to the nation when it arrives later on Saturday.

Boelo is expected to mostly affect northern parts of the UK as the weekend continues.

News.title: Schoolboy, 6, rushed to hospital after being struck by car as ‘drug driver’, 45, arrested
News.content:
SMASH HORROR Schoolboy, 6, rushed to hospital after being struck by car as ‘drug driver’, 45, arrested







Next

A SCHOOLBOY, aged six, has been rushed to hospital after he was struck down by a “drug-driver”.

The young boy remains in hospital in a serious condition with a head injury.

The child was hit by a Toyota Yaris in Kings Norton, Birmingham around 3:30pm yesterday.

A 45-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of “drug-driving” following the collision.





Officers are reviewing the CCTV and speaking to witnesses to the crash on Monyhull Hall Road, while the driver has been released on suspicion.

West Midlands Police said: “We are investigating after a boy was hit by a car in Kings Norton yesterday.

“Officers were called at around 3.30pm to Monyhull Hall Road after a six-year-old boy was hit by a Toyota Yaris.

“The child was taken to hospital with a head injury and remains in a serious condition.

“The driver of the vehicle, a 45-year-old man, was arrested at the scene on suspicion of drug driving.

“He has been released under investigation pending further enquiries.

“Officers are reviewing CCTV footage and speaking to witnesses.

“As part of our investigation, we would like the public’s help. If you were in the area at the time and have any information, then please speak to us.



“You can do this by calling 101 or email the Serious Collision Investigation Unit at SCIU@westmidlands.police.uk quoting 3145 of 21 Oct.”

News.title: I went to pick up my little girl from nursery – but she wasn’t there…then I got a chilling text that destroyed my world
News.content:
Next

IT’S every parent’s worst nightmare – going to pick up your child from nursery only to be told they’re not there.

Eight years ago, Tom Toolan arrived to collect his five-year-old daughter from nursery after her holiday in Poland – only for her mum to destroy his whole world with a text – “we are not coming back”.



The 63-year-old has spent every waking moment fighting to see Rhian ever since, spending £165,000 on legal fees and campaigning against parental child abduction.

Rhian was five years old when her mum took her to Poland on a three-week holiday in 2018 and never came back. Next August, she’ll turn 13.

Tom, a retired NHS worker and teacher, was about to leave his home in Little Bradley in Suffolk, to pick Rhian up from nursery, when his ex Edyta Sonta texted him.



The message read: “Tom. For now we are not coming back to the UK. Rhian is safe and happy. I will let you know any further information later. Edyta.”

This was in August – a few months after a court ordered Polish national Edyta, a gardener, to let Tom see his daughter in April.

“My whole world changed,” Tom told The Sun.

“I didn’t want to take her away from her mum, I just wanted a relationship with my daughter. But from the beginning it was difficult.”

The dad had grown fearful that his ex might take Rhian away from him, but said he didn’t have enough evidence to bring to court.



He said: “When Rhian would come to see me on the weekend she would say things like ‘we are going to get a house in Poland’ and ‘when we move to Poland’.

“Then Edyta’s house went up for rent. She wouldn’t tell me where Rhian was.”

Tom went to Suffolk police, and the CPS agreed to bring charges and Edyta was ordered to bring Rhian back to the UK.



But she refused, and when the Polish courts also demanded she bring their daughter back, Edyta went into hiding.

It took two years for a yellow Interpol notice to go out with Rhian’s picture.

An extradition warrant and European Arrest Warrant were also put out for Edyta.

This is a fast-track judicial process used across all European Union member states to arrest and transfer a criminal suspect or convicted person from one country to another.

But Tom says it wasn’t circulated in Poland, only the neighbouring countries in case she tried to flee.



In the last eight years, there have been nine recovery attempts to bring Rhian back.

Five years after she vanished, Tom saw a photo of his daughter online as she’d won a school competition and it took a moment to recognise her.

It was only last year that Tom managed to see Rhian in person, and only for half an hour. What she said to him was “absolutely devastating” and her dad will never forget it.



“Thirty minutes to overturn years of lies. She told me she hated me and didn’t want to see me again,” Tom said.

“The words that came out of her mouth… They were her mother’s lies. I don’t want to make her life a misery.

“I was her primary carer from when she was six weeks old. I left her photos of our time together but she wasn’t interested.”

Rhian used to “do everything” with her dad, from walking the dogs to going shopping and swimming – everything was an adventure.

He said: “You don’t recover from something like this. I feel like I’ve lost everything.”



When asked what the next steps are and if he hopes Rhian will contact him when she is older, Tom replied: “Alex Batty came back. But I’m 63. My fear is… I’m healthy at the moment but I’m worried I will die and I will never see her again. It keeps me up at night.

“Not a day goes by without me thinking about her. I have got nowhere to go now. There’s nothing else I can do – I don’t have the money to go back to court again.”

Tom, who lives in Witham, Essex, is now happily married with two sons, but he’s devastated they didn’t get to grow up with their big sister.



“It’s not just me either, it impacts my new family. My stepchildren and Rhian – they all loved each other.

“Rhian was besotted with my wife and I’s firstborn. She just wanted to cuddle him all the time. I feel so sad they don’t have that bond.

“Alex and Thomas are her half-brothers – they’re her brothers. She probably doesn’t even remember Thomas.

“It’s just wrong. It’s not just ruining the parent’s life but the child’s life.

“How will she feel when she realises that everyone around her has lied to her and betrayed her?”



On top of fighting to see his daughter again, Tom also had to fight accusations of being drunk, violent and abusive – all of which were dismissed in court.

He has met 30 other dads in similar situations, all of whom he says have had to fight similar claims.

Government data shows nearly one thousand kids were taken out of the UK illegally by a parent between 2019 and 2023.

Tom continued: “Not one child has been returned from Poland since Rhian was taken. I only know of two, and the dads had to go and get them themselves.

“Children disappear all over the place and the dads are vilified. The parent is running away from the English courts.



“All of the dads I know have won their cases in the UK but still don’t have their child back.”

The European Commission launched infringement proceedings against Poland in 2023 for failing to return abducted children – as parents in the UK face spiralling costs amid a lack of action.

Priti Patel, who raised Tom’s case in the Commons, described it as the “most tragic and appalling”.



“This case has been going on for too long—for many, many years. There are hundreds of other cases of children being abducted that are specific to Poland.

“His life is being destroyed by this, and it cannot go on. It is not sustainable any more, and he has been let down by Polish court orders again and again.”

Edyta previously told a Polish newspaper she didn’t see a future in the UK for her or for Rhian.

She claimed Tom abused her and she moved to Poland for work that would be less physically demanding.

“If I had returned to England, the court would have taken Rhian away from me,” she said.



Suffolk Police said: “Suffolk Police have has charges approved against the mother by the Crown Prosecution Service and an extradition warrant and European Arrest Warrant are in place for her.

“However, she is currently protected from extradition by virtue of her nationality whilst she remains in Poland.”

A Foreign Commonwealth and Development Office spokesperson said previously: “The Government takes international parental child abduction very seriously and our staff stand ready to support those affected 24/7.

“The UK Government has consistently raised this issue with the Polish government and will continue to use every appropriate opportunity to do so.”

The Polish Embassy were contacted for comment.

News.title: Four contenders in running for UK City of Culture 2029 mercilessly mocked as a ‘joke’ – do you agree with shortlist?
News.content:
'CITY IN NEED' Four contenders in running for UK City of Culture 2029 mercilessly mocked as a ‘joke’ – do you agree with shortlist?







Next

THE four contenders in the running for the UK City of Culture 2029 have been mercilessly mocked – but do you agree with the shortlist?

Blackpool, Milton Keynes, Sheffield and Wrexham have all made the list for the coveted accolade which is due to be announced in May next year.



The prestigious City of Culture title is awarded to a city every four years with previous holders including Derry, Kingston-upon-Hull, Coventry and Bradford.

Each location shortlisted receives at least £125,000 from the government for their continued bid while the winner will receive a prize fund of £10million.



However, this year’s shortlist has come under fire with many questioning and poking fun at the choice of cities making the cut.

One online user commented: “Why are cities of culture always cities I don’t want to visit?



“Should be called the City in Need award.”

Another took to X and ridiculed the decision as a “joke” with others commenting the panel had “run out of cities”.



A third added: “None of the listed cities really deserve the accolade in all honesty.”

But others were thrilled their city had made the shortlist with others saying they “all seem like worthy candidates” and the winner would benefit from the funds.

The seaside-city of Blackpool is best known for its iconic 518-foot Tower, Pleasure Beach and Illuminations as well as the home of Strictly Come Dancing.

Council leader Lynn Williams said the city had been “entertaining people for generations” saying: “We have always been a town that entertains the country, and there is nowhere quite like Blackpool.”

Second on the list is Milton Keynes – the new-town built in the 1960s and 70s – which first gained city status in 2022.



It’s famous for its modern urban design, grid-road system and, of course, it’s huge number of roundabouts in addition to landmarks including Bletchley Park.

The council leader, Jane Carr, said it was a “huge honour” adding: “We’re now on the cusp of the 60th anniversary of our founding and have so much to look forward to during this landmark year and beyond.”

Sheffield also made the list with its industrial heritage – known worldwide as the “Steel City” – as well as its musical exports and sporting history.

Councillor Fran Belbin, leader of the city council, said the city was “absolutely thrilled”.

She added: “It’s a tribute to the wonderful creative people of Sheffield, in our world class theatres and museums, our thriving music venues and across our communities and neighbourhoods.



And Wrexham – the largest city in North Wales – is the only city outside England to make the shortlist.

It’s another city with industrial heritage but is also home to Wrexham FC, one of the oldest football clubs in the world, which hit global headlines after it was purchased by Hollywood actors Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney.

Welsh Secretary of State Stephen Kinnock, said the city has a huge amount to offer in heritage, culture and sport” and wished “every success with the next stage of their bid”.

The shortlist was determined by the UK City of Culture expert advisory panel chaired by Sir Phil Redmond.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

It was narrowed down from a longlist of nine cities which included Inverness-Highland, Ipswich, Middlesbrough, Portsmouth and Swindon.



Each city’s bid required them to explain how they would “use culture as a catalyst to transform their place and the lives of communities through boosting growth, opportunities and pride“.

News.title: Will it be darker in the mornings when the clocks go back?
News.content:
Next

CENTRAL heating systems are rumbling back to life as the autumn chill kicks in, and millions of Brits are bracing for the end of British Summer Time.

Later this week, the nation’s clocks will go back by one hour, signalling the return of Greenwich Mean Time (GMT).



While an extra hour tucked under the duvet is always welcome, the change often triggers an annual wave of confusion.

“Will it be darker or lighter in the mornings once the clocks change?”



Why do the clocks go back?

The UK changes the clocks twice a year to make better use of natural daylight.

In the spring, the clocks go forward by one hour to mark the start of British Summer Time (BST), which gives people lighter summer evenings.



In the autumn, the clocks go back by one hour to return the country to Greenwich Mean Time (GMT), the UK’s standard time zone.

When does the time change happen?

The clocks always go back on the last Sunday of October.

In 2026, the change takes place on Sunday, October 25. At exactly 2am, the clocks turn back one hour to 1am.

This means anyone asleep at that time gets an extra hour in bed.



Most smartphones, computers and other internet-connected devices will update their times automatically, but manual clocks and watches will need to be changed by hand.

Will it be darker in the mornings?

No, it will not be darker in the mornings immediately after the clocks go back.

Turning the clocks back by one hour actually makes the mornings lighter.

The shift does not literally create extra daylight, but it does change when the sun rises and sets according to the clock.

For example, on the Saturday before the change, the sun will rise in London at 7.39am. On the Sunday, it will rise at 6.41am.



This gives people more light when they first wake up or travel to work in the morning.

But do remember that the days will continue to shorten as the UK heads towards the winter solstice in December, so the mornings will eventually get darker again.

Will the evenings be darker?

While we’ll initially gain an extra hour of morning light after the clocks go back, the shift also means evenings will become darker earlier.

After the change, sunset will occur an hour earlier on the clock, meaning darkness will fall during the afternoon commute.

In London, sunset on the Saturday before the switch occurs at 5.49pm. On the Sunday, the sun will set an hour earlier at 4.47pm.



Why does the UK still change the clocks?

The concept of daylight saving time in Britain was first introduced and championed by builder William Willett – who also happens to be the great-great-grandfather of Coldplay frontman Chris Martin.

In 1907, while on an early horseback ride in Kent, Willett noticed that most houses still had their blinds drawn despite the sun being high in the sky.

Frustrated by the wasted daylight, he published a pamphlet titled The Waste of Daylight.

Although Willett spent years lobbying Parliament to change the clocks, he died in 1915 without seeing his idea realised.

The UK government officially introduced daylight saving during the First World War under the Summer Time Act 1916.



The goal was to conserve coal supplies by reducing electricity and gas consumption for domestic lighting during wartime.

Germany had implemented a similar measure just weeks prior.

The main argument for keeping the system today is that it prevents people from commuting in pitch darkness during the winter.

But extra evening light also boosts local tourism, encourages outdoor recreation, and cuts evening road accidents by improving commuter visibility.

Despite this, calls to scrap the twice-yearly clock shift pop up almost every year. But in Britain, geography complicates things.



Keeping BST year-round would mean lighter winter evenings in London, but parts of northern Scotland wouldn’t see sunrise until almost 10am.

How can you adjust to the clocks changing?

Even though the autumn change gives people an extra hour of sleep, shorter afternoons and earlier evenings can feel bleak, and the sudden sleep disruption can upset body clocks and natural circadian rhythms.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

To help your body adjust, experts recommend getting plenty of natural light in the morning as soon as you wake up.

It can also help to keep your wake-up time consistent and to make small adjustments to your bedtime in the days leading up to the change.

News.title: Age you can legally leave children home alone in England as October half-term nears
News.content:
Next

AS schools close for half-term, thousands of kids will be at home for the break.

Busy parents may be wondering if they can leave their child at home alone – but what age must they legally be?

The majority of UK schools will be closed from the 26th to 30th October for the autumn half-term.



A number of areas across the country get a slightly longer break, with half-term running from the 19th of October.



For many parents, it can make even a quick trip to the shops difficult with kids running around the house, leaving many wondering at what age can you legally leave your child at home in England.

According to the government website, there is no exact age given for parents who intend to leave their child on their own at home.

However, it is “an offence to leave a child alone if it places them at risk”.

You can be fined or sent to jail if caught doing this as it is a crime to leave a child unsupervised “in a manner likely to cause unnecessary suffering or injury to health“.

Parents are advised to reserve their own judgement about whether their child is mature enough to be left home alone.

The National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children (NSPCC) offers a more comprehensive guide to the query.

“Every child matures differently, so it would be almost impossible to have a “one size fits all” law,” details the NSPCC website.



It advises that children under 12 are rarely considered mature enough to be left by themselves at home for long periods of time, and recommends leaving them in the care of an adult.

Children under 16 years of age should also not be left alone at a property overnight.

For secondary school children, NSPCC advises talking with your child first to see if they feel comfortable being left alone at home, as no matter what age, “there might be reasons that they don’t feel safe in the house alone”.

Babies, toddlers, and very young children should never be left alone.

News.title: Moment out of breath cop sprints up to kid and borrows his bike before chasing down suspected drug dealer
News.content:
Next

THIS is the dramatic moment an out of breath cop commandeered a youngster’s bike to chase down a suspected drug dealer.

Two Cambridgeshire Constabulary officers were initially pursuing the alleged crook on foot down the pavement of Coldhams Lane after spotting him riding an illegal electric bike.



The chase appeared to swing in the fleeing man’s favour when he suddenly ditched his e-bike and made a run for it down a track, outpacing the officers.

But dramatic bodycam footage shows the moment one breathless cop spotted a young boy with a bicycle and asked to take it for the pursuit.



The policeman can be heard urgently asking the lad: “Can I borrow your bike? Can I borrow your bike?

“Please, just to catch a guy, quickly.”



After shouting, “Cheers, we’ll be back,” the officer hopped into the saddle.

Footage showed how the added speed boost meant the cop rapidly closed the distance on his target.



Pedalling furiously, it took the officer just 54 seconds to catch up with the suspect.

He cornered the man around Norman Way, Cambridge, last Friday shortly after 5:30pm.

The suspect, who had been tiring after the chase, came to a stop and put his hands out.

Moving in to make the arrest the officer told the man: “Mate, stay there. Give me your hands. Detained.”

Cops confirmed that the man was arrested on suspicion of possession with intent to supply drugs, failing to stop and dangerous driving.



The 18-year-old man has been bailed until 16 January, said Cambridgeshire Police.

Following the successful capture, the two cops cycled back to the exact spot where they had left the young owner waiting for his property.

Safely handing over the borrowed wheels, the grateful policeman told the boy: “Thank you, thank you very much. See you later.”

A Cambridgeshire Constabulary spokesperson said in a statement: “Can we borrow your bike?”

“Not a question many teenagers expect to hear from a police officer.



“But when a suspected drug dealer abandoned his illegal e-bike in Cambridge and ran off, one boy came to the rescue by lending an officer his bike to continue the chase.

“The suspect was caught, the bike was safely returned, and the young owner received a well-deserved thank you from the officer.”

This isn’t the first time an officer has used a member of the public to help catch a suspect.

In June, one armed police officer was helped by a van driver in the middle of a police chase before they catch the suspect fleeing on foot.

The officer clutching a firearm can be seen approaching a mini-roundabout after the suspect evaded attempts to arrest him.



Standing in the middle of the road, he then turns to a passing motorist in a van who stops and urges the officer to “get in the back, get in the back”.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

In another amusing clip an out of breath bobby is picked up by a driver as he is chasing down two thieving boys.

The woman who filmed the incident said she and her friend were driving home when they saw the chase unfold.

News.title: What is PHP and why did it spark an international cyber-security alert?
News.content:
For more than a decade, serious flaws had gone undetected in the technology underpinning much of the internet.

It took AI to bring them to light and caused a global cyber-security alert.

The vulnerabilities lie within a programming language called PHP, which has been used internationally since the 2000s to build websites.

Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world are scrambling to contain the fallout of the discovery on Wednesday, and have urged website operators to install a new emergency fix or consider taking their platforms offline.

Cyber-security firm Wiz - one of the companies whose researchers uncovered the vulnerabilities - described the flaws as the "most severe" ever detected by AI.

OpenAI, whose technology was used to find the flaws, called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory".

News.title: Barclays cutting 5,000 jobs as it increases reliance on AI
News.content:
Barclays is cutting its staff by around 5,000 as it introduces more artificial intelligence (AI) into its work processes.

The banking group said 1,000 posts had already been closed and it expects a further reduction of 4,000 to be complete by the end of this year, amounting to around 5% of its global workforce.

The bank's cost reductions are focused on its UK retail bank, but some back office functions for the UK are done in India, where a significant proportion of the job cuts are expected to fall.

Barclays said the changes were the result of an ongoing modernisation plan, with the use of AI being the "icing on the cake" of its strategy.

The banking group is reaching the end of a three year cost-cutting programme focused primarily on its UK retail banking arm, although the investment banking division is also affected.

Barclays also revealed it made Â£2.3bn profit in the three months to September, higher than the same period a year ago, but slightly less than forecast.

Economists have been watching companies' results carefully for signs that investment in new technology, and AI specifically, is making a difference in their day-to-day operations, leading to greater efficiency and lower employment.

Barclays Group chief executive CS Venkatakrishnan said the job cuts were the result of significant investment it is making in technology to simplify and improve its business.

"AI has an important role to play and may have a more important role to play in the future.

"We will employ the AI at scale," he said. "But AI is the icing on the cake not the cake.

"Because you need to do the infrastructure build to get the benefits of AI."

Barclays said around 60% of the job cuts will fall within its support functions, including among developers.

Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, said Barclays was "reaching for the AI lever, expecting to cut a decent chunk of its workforce as it expands the use of artificial intelligence", but had failed to match expectations with its financial results.

Will Howlett, financials analyst at Quilter Cheviot said the cuts illustrated "how significantly AI and automation could reshape the banking industry over the next few years".

"Banks have spent heavily on technology for years, but we are increasingly reaching the point where that investment translates into fewer people being required to run the business," he said.

Barclays said it expects its efficiency measures to deliver a further Â£1.1bn of savings in 2027.

News.title: Russell Brand accuser said alleged rape 'really hurt', court hears
News.content:
Warning - this report contains graphic content

The friend of a woman claiming to have been raped by Russell Brand told a jury the complainant had told her after the alleged attack that it had "really, really hurt".

The witness who spoke via video link at his trial said she had attended the Hammersmith Apollo theatre in London with the alleged victim in 2009, where they had been invited to the defendant's dressing room after his comedy show.

She said the woman had told her she had visited Brand's house in London soon after meeting at the theatre.

Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to all seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.

The allegations span a 10-year period from 1999 to 2009 and involve six female complainants.

The witness said Brand had sent a car to collect the woman, which took her to his place in Hampstead.

She said when they spoke about it "quite soon after", she said she "was just crying - really upset".

"He was quite aggressive," she said her friend had told her.

"He forcibly put it in my bum and "it really really hurt".

The witness says she remembers specifically asking the complainant if she had said no to Brand when the alleged attack started.

News.title: Tougher punishments for criminals who refuse to attend sentencing backed by victim's family
News.content:
Tougher punishments for offenders who refuse to attend their sentencings will "rebalance the power" in the justice system, the aunt of murder victim Zara Aleena has said.

From next year, prisoners could be blocked from prison visits and confined to their cells for weeks on end if they do not follow orders to go to court.

This builds on an existing law that orders criminals to attend sentencing or face being fined or jailed for another two years.

"A year or two added to a life sentence wouldn't make any difference to an offender. But taking away these privileges would," Farah Naz said.

Naz said the refusal of the man who murdered her niece to go to his sentencing "left a sense that justice was not quite complete".

Aleena, an aspiring lawyer, was murdered by Jordan McSweeney as she walked home from an east London bar in June 2022.

McSweeney remained in his cell when he was sentenced to life in prison at the Old Bailey later that year.

He was jailed for at least 38 years, which was later reduced to 33 years after he won a Court of Appeal challenge.

Naz said Zara's Aleena's family had hoped that by reading their victim impact statement in front of her murderer, he would see "the consequence of his actions, of what he'd done, the devastation that he had caused".

She added that the new measures would "bring accountability and rebalance the power in the justice system from offender to victim."

Offenders who refuse to attend sentencing can already face a fine or up to two years additional imprisonment for contempt of court.

But the Ministry of Justice has acknowledged that longer jail time alone is unlikely to deter those already behind bars.

The new measures mean offenders could be confined to cells for up to three weeks, while social visits could be banned for 27 days and other prison privileges revoked for longer.

Judges will also be able to restrict social visits further to once every four weeks for a period of almost three months.

For criminals aged 18-20, similar restrictions could be handed down, but for shorter periods of time, the Ministry of Justice said.

However, visits from prisoners' children will be exempt from the new sanctions.

"Criminals should not be able to pick and choose when they face justice," Prisons Minister Catherine McKinnell said.

"Refusing to turn up to sentencing is an insult to victims and their families, and offenders must face the consequences," she added.

News.title: Two storms in two days as Austen and Boelo head for UK
News.content:
Gusts of wind will widely reach 60-70mph, and perhaps 80mph in exposed locations.

Winds of this strength will blow some trees over, bringing a significant risk of transport disruption and there may also be some power cuts.

Some buildings could potentially be damaged by the strongest winds, leading to a risk of flying debris at the height of the storm.

Yellow wind warnings cover most of England and Wales with gusts of wind on Friday forecast to reach 45-60mph, with 70mph gusts likely in some places.

As strong as these winds are, the most damaging winds will run to the south of the low pressure centre.

That puts north-west France firmly in the firing line and parts of Brittany could see gusts close to 90mph.

The Channel Islands are also expecting severe gales with gusts up to 80mph forecast, and some ferry services have already been cancelled.

Heavy rain in Scotland may cause some localised flooding with a Met Office yellow warning for 20-40mm of rain forecast with up to 80mm accumulating in a few areas through Friday.

News.title: Rosenberg: Russia agrees to Ukraine talks but sees little to talk about in new peace push
News.content:
After two days of diplomacy â in Norway's capital and Russia's St Petersburg â is the war in Ukraine any closer to ending?

"Good and constructive" is how Norway's prime minister described Tuesday's talks between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, US President Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and European representatives.

In Oslo, the idea of a trilateral meeting at leaders' level was floated. The hope was that Steve Witkoff's trip to Russia would pave the way for President Vladimir Putin, Zelensky and Trump to meet and agree an end to the fighting.

But Putin has shown little desire to share a table with Zelensky - unless that table is in Moscow.

The Kremlin says it may be willing to resume trilateral talks next month in Abu Dhabi, but only at the technical level.

In a post on X, Steve Witkoff himself conceded that "there is still important work to do", though he claimed "President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end..."

News.title: Dame Judi Dench: 'I can't do a play, a film or read any more'
News.content:
Oscar-winning actress Dame Judi Dench says her eye condition has left her unable to perform on stage or read, more than a decade after she was diagnosed.

Dame Judi was diagnosed with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) in 2012, a condition that affects her vision and has made it incredibly difficult to even recognise faces.

Speaking to Emma Barnett on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, she said: "I can't be on stage. I can't do a play any more. I can't do a film any more. I can't read any more."

She also revealed how her condition can lead to awkward encounters, saying she sometimes approaches the wrong people "and give them an almost hug" before realising her mistake.

When asked about ageing, Dame Judi, who's 91, replied: "There's nothing to say for it at all. [I] don't think about it too much."

News.title: Airbnb hosts can no longer make guests strip beds and wash dishes under new rules
News.content:
Airbnb has changed its rules to limit what property hosts may ask guests to do - including when it comes to cleaning.

The updated guidelines state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules and can also add other "reasonable" requests.

Airbnb states that guests - who are required to pay a cleaning fee - should not be asked to complete tasks normally done by a cleaner, including washing dishes and stripping beds.

The new rules will apply to all reservations booked on or after 20 November on the accommodation marketplace.

"House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we've heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage," Airbnb told the BBC.

"So, we've redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises."

According to the new requirements on the Airbnb website, hosts are generally not allowed to ask guests to complete tasks that "require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner, including stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes".

The company said it may grant exceptions in some circumstances. For example, guests can be asked to limit shower time if there are local drought-related water restrictions.

A property's rules will be displayed to guests more prominently moving forward and will appear in the guests' reservation reminders.

Contracts will only be allowed in limited circumstances, including when required by law or homeowners association rules.

While a host will not be able to impose fines, they remain in control of their house rules and requests, the company said.

If a host's request does not follow Airbnb policies, the issue will be flagged and the owner can appeal if they disagree.

Guests have for years complained about unreasonable tasks they we required to complete before departure, especially as they are required to pay cleaning fees.

TikTok videos from Airbnb hosts Cassie and Jon that show them closely inspecting their rental property in the US state of Georgia after guests leave have gone viral recently for their attention to detail.

One video from the couple, for example, accuses guests of "disrespecting the house rules" for leaving a television remote out of place.

They have been criticised for their strict rules and high standards but said in response that their content had been misinterpreted

Their videos have inspired other content creators to parody stringent hosts.

News.title: UK's gaps in Arctic defence leave it open to Russian attacks, committee warns
News.content:
The UK has "glaring gaps" in its ability to defend the Arctic region, leaving it vulnerable to potential Russian attacks, a report by MPs has warned.

The Commons Defence Committee said a shortage of Royal Navy warships and submarines was leaving the country's critical infrastructure in the High North, including undersea cables and energy supplies, exposed.

In the event of a conflict, the report added that Russia could threaten the UK's population, civilian and military infrastructure and vital supply routes across the Atlantic from the US.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) said it is "clear-eyed about the threat Russia posed" and is investing heavily to protect Britain's undersea cables.

Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer previously warned that Russia could attack Nato by the end of the decade.

The High North - which includes the Arctic circle and areas adjacent to it - has become central to the UK's defence concerns in recent years.

Earlier this year, the MoD said Russian submarine activity in the North Atlantic is now back to the same levels as the Cold War era.

In the new report, MPs highlighted a "shockingly low availability" of submarines and said there was a temporary loss in ability to operate them beneath Arctic ice.

"Russia can then use the ice to conceal and protect its own submarines while threatening Nato sea lanes, UK critical infrastructure and the UK's nuclear deterrent," it added.

Chair of the Defence Committee, Tan Dhesi, said: "This is a demanding, hostile environment, and one that our greatest adversary, Russia, is seeking to dominate for military advantage."

The work to address these gaps "cannot start soon enough," he added.

In light of uncertainty over US support for Nato, the report said the UK should consider whether the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force (Jef), a UK-led military coalition of northern European nations, should focus more on the High North.

An MoD spokesperson said the Jef was already "strengthening Nato's northern flank and increasing our ability to respond rapidly to emerging threats".

Conservative shadow minister for war readiness Stuart Anderson said: "If Nato could be at war with Russia as soon as 2030, as the former prime minister warned, that means time is just as important as money.

"To deter war we must be ready for it, that means spending money now, not kicking the can down the road until it's too late".

News.title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study
News.content:
A clinical trial has been launched in the UK which scientists hope could cut years from the search for new treatments for Alzheimer's disease.

It will test multiple drugs simultaneously, starting with two repurposed medicines already used to treat type 2 diabetes and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).

The study will examine whether the drugs can lessen symptoms such as memory and thinking problems, and help people maintain their quality of life.

Angela Bucksey, 67, from Cambridgeshire, was diagnosed with Alzheimer's in January and is the first person to begin treatment on the trial, called AD-SMART.

"We have Alzheimer's in the family," she told the BBC.

"My mother had it and my aunts, so it was a disappointment rather than a shock when I was diagnosed because I knew it would restrict my life.

"But I was determined that it wasn't going to define me."

Angela said she felt empowered joining the trial because "at least you are doing something".

"Instead of just sitting there, you're standing up and saying, I will fight back."

Alzheimer's is the most common type of dementia, affecting around 600,000 people in the UK.

News.title: Four locations in the running to be UK City of Culture 2029
News.content:
Blackpool, Milton Keynes, Sheffield and Wrexham have been shortlisted to become the UK's City of Culture in 2029.

The winning location will be announced in May and will be the fifth holder of the title - following Derry-Londonderry, Hull, Coventry and Bradford.

A different location is given the City of Culture title every four years. Each shortlisted city will now receive at least Â£125,000 from the government to do further work on their bid.

The eventual winner will receive Â£10m to deliver a year of cultural events and activities drawing on its "local strengths and stories".

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said the shortlisted cities "have shown the pride that exists in their places with the incredible culture on their doorsteps".

Three of the contenders are in England and one in Wales. They were chosen from a longlist of nine, which also included Inverness, Ipswich, Middlesbrough, Portsmouth and Swindon.

News.title: Only one female scientist named in GCSEs, research finds
News.content:
Rosalind Franklin is the only female scientist named in GCSE and National 5 science exam specifications in the UK, according to new research.

A Cambridge study found that of the 86 scientists named by UK exam boards, the English chemist, whose work in the 1950s helped reveal the structure of DNA, was the only woman.

Exam specifications set out the skills and knowledge students are expected to have gained by the end of their course and how they will be assessed.

Exam boards said there was "a clear need for greater representation in science qualifications".

Academics from the University of Cambridge, along with institutions in the US and Australia, examined how many women were mentioned in specifications for biology, chemistry, physics, environmental science, geology and astronomy.

Their work, published in the British Educational Research Journal, looked at six exam boards in the UK:

AQA

Cambridge OCR

Pearson Edexcel

WJEC

CCEA

Qualifications Scotland

At Key Stage 4 and equivalent, including GCSEs and National 5s in Scotland, Franklin was the only woman among the 86 scientists mentioned.

She was also one of three women mentioned at Key Stage 5 and equivalent - including A-levels, AS-levels, National Highers and National Advanced Highers - out of a total of 181 scientists.

Marie Tharp, an American cartographer who created the first map of the floor of the Atlantic ocean in the 1950s, and Inge Lehmann, a Danish seismologist who discovered the existence of the Earth's inner core in the 1930s, both feature in the Cambridge OCR's A-Â­level Geology.

Franklin, who was named in Cambridge OCR's GCSE Biology and Scottish Highers Biology, produced a famous DNA image known as Photograph 51.

Cambridge scientists Francis Crick and James Watson used the image to work out the following year that DNA has a double-helix structure.

Watson, Crick and Franklin's colleague Maurice Wilkins received the 1962 Nobel Prize for the discovery. Franklin had died four years earlier.

Academics who wrote the paper found that "several major scientific breakthroughs" in specifications were made by women, but they were not explicitly mentioned.

The paper said: "Many of the scientific discoveries and explanations were developed in the 1800s and early 1900s, a period when scientific and mathematical practice was largely, but not solely, dominated by men.

"Our findings confirm that the UK science specifications reflect this historical imbalance: although women made significant contributions to major scientific breakthroughs, this fact is rarely acknowledged."

The academics recommended that Franklin should be included "in all specifications when teaching DNA structure".

They also said specifications should refer to Marie Curie, who discovered radium and polonium and coined the term radioactivity, and nuclear physicist Lise Meitner, who discovered nuclear fission, among others.

Stephanie Buttigieg, one of the authors, said: "Relatable role models can help keep more girls in STEM by strengthening their sense of belonging in science and fostering positive attitudes towards scientific careers."

A spokeswoman for the Joint Council for Qualifications, which represents AQA, Cambridge OCR, CCEA, WJEC and Pearson, said: "Exam boards recognise that there is a clear need for greater representation in science qualifications, and this is an area they will be focusing on as these qualifications are reformed."

Qualifications Scotland said the Curriculum Improvement Cycle offered "an opportunity to consider gender representation within our future qualifications and assessments".

The Department for Education in England said "girls should see the contribution women have made in STEM", adding it was "committed to improving the school curriculum over the coming years, and as part of that will make sure every girl can see where their learning can take them".

The Scottish Government said it was "committed to closing the gender gap in STEM and will carefully consider the findings of this research".

Additional reporting by Marthe de Ferrer and Rahib Khan

News.title: Claims 'stabbed' woman tried to drive to hospital because of ambulance wait time denied
News.content:
The Welsh Ambulance Service has denied that a woman who died after crashing a car into a wall after suffering "stab wounds" was driving because of ambulance wait times.

Eleanor Barnfield, 47, died in hospital after police were called to the crash in Bridgend on Monday, where they found she had "puncture wounds unrelated to the collision", which the BBC understands were sustained in a stabbing.

A 61-year-old man from Bridgend, who has been arrested on suspicion of murder, remains in custody.

The ambulance service said it was aware of "misleading rumours" circulating online but said medics were called to the crash in Coity Road at about 12:44 BST and a response unit arrived seven minutes later.

Reports in some media had claimed Eleanor had crashed her car while driving herself to hospital.

News.title: Man Utd captain Fernandes rounds on boss Carrick after Champions League humiliation
News.content:
Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes turned on head coach Michael Carrick following one of the most humiliating nights in the club's European history.

A 4-1 Champions League hammering at Como led to Carrick fielding questions about his future.

He apologised to the 700 travelling fans, having ignored his beaten players after the final whistle to march across the pitch and repeatedly hold his hands up - in a manner similar to Ole Gunnar Solskjaer following a 4-1 defeat at Watford in November 2021 which led to his dismissal as United boss 24 hours later.

However, Fernandes - widely accepted as a football obsessive who watches games regularly and understands the tactical side as well as any player in the United squad - inflicted more damage when he spoke to TNT Sports afterwards.

"It's a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, but sometimes when you give too much the ball to these teams they get confidence," he said.

Asked directly whether Carrick got his tactics wrong, Fernandes added: "That's on the manager and staff to see it, not me. Sometimes you have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable."

Told of Fernandes' comments in his post-match press conference, Carrick offered a curt response: "There's a little bit of whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don't run, and you don't run forward, and you don't run back, you aren't going to win."

News.title: Retired decorator's Pokémon cards sell for £1.5m
News.content:
A retired decorator has become a millionaire after selling a collection of PokÃ©mon cards at auction.

The man, from Woking, said he had no idea the cards had any value until he read in his local newspaper about a single card fetching more than Â£6,000.

His collection, which had been in an attic for 15 years, was auctioned off at Ewbank's on Wednesday for Â£1.56m.

The Surrey auction house claimed it was the UK's most valuable trading cards auction ever and suggested it could be a European record.

"I know people always talk about finding treasure in the attic, but in my case that is literally true," said the man, who asked not to be identified.

"When my son was young, in the late 1990s, he started getting cards and swapping them at school.

"I thought they looked nice and wondered whether they might be a good investment.

"He had his own cards, but he never got to touch these, I'm glad to say."

PokÃ©mon is a Japanese franchise best known for its trading cards, video games and animated television series.

The man said he had bought some complete sets of the cards from someone in Malaysia on eBay.

One set which cost him Â£300 at the time went for Â£75,000 at Wednesday's auction.

The cards, all filed into bespoke PokÃ©mon binders while still sealed, were stored in the attic after his son lost interest in the Japanese gaming and film franchise.

News.title: Angry scenes and protests at Senedd as Reform call for ban on Muslim face coverings
News.content:
Sioned Williams, deputy first minister, said the debate was a "shameful" end to a "sad day" that began with the commemoration of the Aberfan disaster.

Looking at the Reform members, she accused them of "conflating the intimidating behaviour of thugs and those whose protest can descend into disorder and violence, often in demonstrations directed against migrants or Muslims, with the very people who are targeted by that intimidating behaviour".

"I do not accept that a face covering worn by an individual for religious reasons means they don't share British or Welsh values," she said.

"Nor should we suggest that someone belongs any less, because their religious practice differs from that of others."

Williams added: "The Jewish people of 1930s Germany were subject to the Nuremberg Laws, which stated they were no longer German, laws which led to their persecution and extermination by the state that stripped them of the Germaness.

"Who decides that a woman who [has] a face covering is less British or less Welsh?"

The comments led to angry protests and finger-pointing from the Reform benches. A point of order was raised by a member of the party asking the presiding officer if the comments were appropriate.

The presiding officer Huw Irranca-Davies said he was "always happy" to review the record of proceedings, but did not make a ruling. Williams said she was making a "statement of fact".

Carrie Harper, Plaid MS for Fflint Wrecsam, told Reform: "How on earth can you claim to stand up for women when you are trying to dictate what Muslim women can and cannot wear?"

Plaid MS Kiera Marshall, for Caerdydd Penarth, said a Muslim woman in her constituency was subject to a "physical, violent attack in broad daylight".

"The attacker shouted at her about removing her headscarf and continued to do exactly this while physically assaulting her," she said.

"This is just one example of an increasingly common occurrence when Muslim women are being targeted.

"This is exactly what the rhetoric that Reform is peddling is doing."

Labour's Huw Thomas said he had not heard Reform condemn "the masked mobs who stormed RNLI stations across of South Coast, last month".

A lifeboat station in Portsmouth went out of service in September, following anti-migrant protests.

Following the debate, Dr Abdul Azim Ahmed of the Muslim Council of Wales said: "This debate demonstrated the disturbingly authoritarian attitudes members of Reform UK hold, coupled with dangerously ultra nationalist attitudes about culture and belonging."

News.title: UK government services temporarily offline amid PHP cybersecurity threat
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Some “limited” government services may temporarily be offline while work is carried out to address potential PHP cyber security issues, Downing Street has said.

No major public-facing critical services in the UK have been impacted by a severe vulnerability identified in the PHP programming language, Downing Street has confirmed.

Organisations around the world have been scrambling to address the flaw in PHP, which powers almost 70 per cent of websites according to cybersecurity firm Cloudflare. UK cybersecurity chiefs alerted organisations to the "critical security issue" on Wednesday.

A No 10 spokeswoman said on Thursday: "Work has already taken place across government to identify and fix potential exposures to our systems, and our experts are continuing to work closely with both OpenAI and international partners on this issue.

"No large public-facing critical services are being affected by the exercise, but some limited services may temporarily be offline while security work is carried out.

"But this does not mean they were hacked, and work continues to resolve any issues."

The spokeswoman noted it was not "standard practice" to detail which specific government services had been affected.
