He further highlighted the acquisition of 730 electric vehicles, comprising inter-city and metropolitan buses, tricycles and motorcycles, to reduce commuting costs and support cleaner transportation. On the maritime front, he said the Bakassi Deep Seaport had secured the federal government’s approval and Certificate of Compliance, and was awaiting the commencement of construction, with anticipated private investment of approximately $3.5 billion.

He also cited the federal government’s formal re-accreditation of Cross River as a littoral state, describing it as a strategic development for the state’s maritime ambitions. “Our overall target in this sector is to transform our aviation business model into a highly profitable and self-sustaining revenue asset for the state,” he said.

Infrastructure receives the largest explicitly listed sectoral allocation of N246.1 billion, followed by education with N99.6 billion, health with N85.4 billion, agriculture with N28.2 billion and aviation with N21.8 billion. Other provisions include N20.2 billion for the House of Assembly, N19.1 billion for the judiciary, N16.6 billion for power and N11.3 billion for tourism. The governor said the budget would continue to align with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, ensuring continuity in unfinished projects and directing resources towards the state’s strategic priorities.

He pledged continued investment in forest conservation and the green economy, judicial infrastructure, security and youth empowerment.

In education, the governor reaffirmed the policy of free and compulsory education from primary to junior secondary school, alongside the payment of WAEC fees for public-school students. On the judiciary, he promised adequate funding for ongoing court projects and further improvements in the working conditions of judicial officers, while urging the institution to pursue reforms that would strengthen public confidence in justice delivery.

Concluding his presentation, Otu pledged to sustain a government that is responsive to the needs of citizens, prudent in the management of public resources and accountable to the electorate. He emphasised the importance of harmonious relations among the executive, legislature and judiciary, describing institutional cooperation as indispensable to peace, stability and shared prosperity. The governor formally sought the Assembly’s consideration and timely passage of the proposed N987.8 billion Appropriation Bill, expressing confidence that its implementation would accelerate economic growth and improve the welfare of Cross Riverians.

World.title: APC Deploys Diaspora Network to Fight Anti-Tinubu Narratives
World.content:
Michael Olugbode in Abuja

The All Progressives Congress (APC) has unveiled an international mobilisation and media offensive to defend President Bola Tinubu’s economic policies, counter negative narratives about his administration, and rally support for his re-election in 2027, targeting Nigerians living across major countries in Africa, Europe, Asia, the Middle East and North America.

Under the plan, the party intends to activate its overseas chapters, deploy coordinated digital advocacy, establish a rapid-response mechanism to challenge misinformation, mobilise diaspora funding and encourage voter participation at home as it seeks to shape public perception of Tinubu’s first term ahead of the presidential election.

The Director of the PBAT/APC 2027 Presidential Campaign Council (PCC) Directorate of Diaspora Mobilisation, Hon. Abike Dabiri-Erewa, unveiled the strategy at a press briefing in Abuja, describing Nigerians abroad as an influential constituency whose financial contributions, professional expertise and international networks could be harnessed to support the administration.

The initiative signals the APC’s determination to make the diaspora an organised component of its re-election campaign, using Nigerians’ connections with relatives, communities and professional networks abroad to communicate the government’s position on its economic reforms and development agenda.

Dabiri-Erewa said the directorate would not limit its mobilisation to party members, but would also reach out to Nigerians abroad who were willing to participate in the campaign.

“Nigerians abroad are not outsiders. They are stakeholders. They are our doctors, nurses, engineers, students, traders, innovators and community leaders, who send over $20 billion annually back home in remittances,” she said.

She identified the mobilisation of APC diaspora chapters in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, South Africa, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, France, Germany, Australia, Turkey, India and Kazakhstan as a priority, alongside engagement with diaspora associations and community leaders.

At the centre of the strategy is a digital advocacy campaign tagged: ‘Operation Tell Your Story’, through which supporters would receive short videos, infographics and other communication materials promoting the administration’s policies and achievements.

The campaign would address the foreign exchange reforms, foreign reserves, support for small businesses, housing programmes and opportunities for students, while seeking to counter claims the directorate considers misleading.

Dabiri-Erewa also announced plans for a rapid-response hub to provide data, fact-check claims and promote what she described as credible information about Nigeria’s investment climate, economic stabilisation and prospects under Tinubu.

“Our directorate will serve as a rapid-response hub in case of misinformation about Nigeria and the administration. We will provide credible data, fact-check and positive narratives about Nigeria’s investment climate, stabilisation of the economy and the future under President Tinubu,” she said.

The move comes amid continuing public debate over the administration’s economic reforms, particularly the removal of the petrol subsidy and changes to the foreign exchange system, which have had significant implications for households and businesses.

Dabiri-Erewa acknowledged the hardship associated with the subsidy removal but defended the policy as a necessary intervention to address structural weaknesses in the economy.

“President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has decided not to manage our feelings, but to fix the system. And it takes a bold leader to do that,” she said.

She argued that Nigerians living abroad could help explain the rationale behind the reforms to their families and communities, particularly because of their understanding of the challenges associated with the previous foreign exchange arrangements.

However, the directorate’s strategy will face the challenge of persuading voters at home that the administration’s policies are delivering sufficient benefits to justify the economic sacrifices they have experienced. The effectiveness of the campaign will therefore depend not only on the reach of its messaging but also on the credibility of its claims and the administration’s record against measurable economic outcomes.

Beyond digital advocacy, the APC plans to mobilise diaspora contributions through structured fundraising platforms to finance campaign activities, voter education materials, town hall meetings and grassroots mobilisation.

Dabiri-Erewa said the proposed fundraising arrangements would emphasise transparency and accountability, but did not disclose the amount the directorate hopes to raise or provide details of the proposed platforms.

The fourth strand of the strategy would focus on voter education and homecoming mobilisation, with diaspora Nigerians encouraged to remind eligible relatives and community members to register, collect their Permanent Voter Cards and participate in the election.

The directorate also intends to use its overseas networks to encourage Nigerians abroad to return home, engage their communities and take part in the political process.

In a related appeal, Dabiri-Erewa called on the National Assembly to consider constitutional amendments that would allow Nigerians living abroad to vote in Nigerian elections.

She acknowledged that diaspora voting remained a subject of debate but expressed hope that lawmakers would address the issue, potentially expanding the formal participation of Nigerians abroad in the country’s electoral process.

Dabiri-Erewa, who also heads the Nigerians in Diaspora Commission (NiDCOM), said the commission had established a portal for registering Nigerians living outside the country and put the estimated diaspora population at more than 17 million.

She also urged Nigerians to monitor how state and local governments utilise increased allocations following the removal of the petrol subsidy, arguing that greater public revenue should be accompanied by accountability in spending.

Other members of the directorate backed the administration’s economic policies, acknowledging the hardship associated with the reforms while arguing that the intended benefits would take time to materialise. They highlighted investment, skills transfer, business partnerships and collaboration with government institutions as additional ways Diaspora Nigerians could contribute to national development.

Dabiri-Erewa urged the media to support the directorate’s communication efforts, saying the campaign would focus on continuity, national development and Tinubu’s stated ambition to move Nigeria from reforms to prosperity.

With the 2027 election approaching, the APC’s strategy places diaspora mobilisation, digital communication and the battle over the interpretation of the administration’s economic record at the heart of its re-election effort. Whether the initiative translates into broader electoral support will ultimately depend on how Nigerians judge the government’s performance and whether the campaign can substantiate its claims with credible evidence.

World.title: Kogi Monarch Tasks FG on Technical Education to Tackle Unemployment
World.content:
Ibrahim Oyewale in Lokoja

A first-class traditional ruler and the Chairman of Lokoja Traditional Council in Kogi State, the Maigari, Alhaji Ibrahim Kabir, Maikarfi IV, has appealed to the federal government to revert to the era of technical education and Technical Colleges to tackle youth unemployment.

The royal father, who made this call while speaking at the opening ceremony of the National Agency Science and Engineering Infrastructure NASENI Training and Empowerment programme in Lokoja yesterday, pointed out that in those days, the technical colleges were producing middle-level manpower as technicians, noting that the graduates were at best against the backdrop of the present-day graduates of higher institutions who solely relied on the certificate and remained unemployed for several years.

The Maigari, who was represented by a high chief, the Mattawalli of Lokoja, Alhaji Adamu Mohammed, recalled that the students of Lokoja Technical College were helping to repair cars, were good at carpentry and electrical works, and other skills.

He, therefore, urged the federal government to revive technical education, which he said did not require higher qualifications, to reduce the high tide of youth unemployment in the country.

The traditional ruler added that it is high time the federal government and the Ministry of Education reassigned technical education in the curriculum to ignite skill acquisition.

He tasked the beneficiaries to take advantage of the NASENI training and the empowerment programme to learn the skill and become self-reliant in the future.

Earlier, the Executive Director/Chief Executive Officer of the National Agency for Science and Engineering Infrastructure (NASENI), Dr. Khalid Halilu, explained that the federal government has reinforced its commitment to eradicate youth unemployment through skill acquisition interventions to bridge the gap in the ongoing global innovations and technologies.

Halilu made this known while speaking at the official flag-off of the training of 120 electricians in modern electrical installation and maintenance in Lokoja yesterday.

He stated that this has become imperative with a view to ensuring that the teeming youths acquire skills which will fortify their future rather than looking for unavailable white-collar jobs, stressing that skill acquisition is the in-thing now.

The Executive Director/Chief Executive Officer of NASENI, who was presented by a Research Director in the agency, Professor Abdulmaliki Ibrahim, noted that the programme is an instance of the Renewed Hope Agenda of President Bola Tinubu, “who has magnanimously approved the training of the teeming youth in skill acquisition in various fields through NASENI to bridge the gap in global innovations and technologies.”

He explained that the youths must take advantage of the presidential/NASENI training programme to acquire skills and help themselves in the near future.

The executive director pointed out that the programme is simultaneously taking place across the country, noting that Kogi State is the 27th state in Nigeria, noting that the first phase is about to end and the second will start immediately across the country.

World.title: Donald Duke: Nigeria’s Vanishing Middle Class Exposes Deepening Economic Crisis
World.content:
Ayodeji Ake

The presidential candidate of the Peoples Redemption Party (PRP), Donald Duke, has said the disappearance of Nigeria’s middle class reflects the deepening economic crisis in the country, warning that widespread poverty, unemployment and insecurity are pushing the nation towards state failure.

Duke, who spoke in an interview, said many Nigerians who previously considered themselves financially stable, were now struggling to meet their basic needs, leaving them vulnerable to economic shocks and emergencies.

He argued that the country’s economic difficulties had been compounded by shrinking businesses, inadequate job opportunities and a rapidly expanding population that the economy could no longer adequately support.

“The so-called middle class does not really exist anymore. Many of those we call middle class are only surviving from day-to-day. Let there be one serious emergency and they crumble,” he said.

The former Cross River State governor said the widening gap between the wealthy and the poor was an indication that Nigeria’s economy was failing to provide the conditions necessary for a decent standard of living.

“You have perhaps one per cent who are genuinely wealthy and then a huge number of people struggling around or below the poverty line,” he said.

Duke explained that the situation had become a major motivation for his decision to contest the 2027 presidential election, arguing that Nigeria could not afford to continue on its present path for another four years.

“I talk about the urgency of now because I don’t think we can go on like this for another four years,” he said.

He explained that his decision to seek the presidency was driven by the need to move beyond criticism of successive governments and offer solutions to the country’s worsening economic and social challenges.

“You get to a point in your life where you say, ‘Either I walk away or I do something.’

“There is no guarantee that you will win. But I don’t want to look back and say that all these things happened and I did nothing,” he said.

The PRP candidate said his campaign would focus on the substantive issues affecting Nigerians, including poverty, unemployment, economic decline and insecurity, rather than political personalities.

“What I want to do is focus on those who aspire to lead this nation on addressing the issues that affect us and how we can resolve them.

“I talk about the options. I talk about the real issues. I don’t want to talk about personalities,” he said.

Duke linked the country’s economic difficulties to the growing insecurity, including kidnapping, banditry, terrorism and other violent conflicts, arguing that the government must address the underlying causes of these problems.

He described the security crisis as evidence of the state’s inability to protect citizens and create an environment in which they could live productive lives.

“If we don’t address these issues squarely and fundamentally, we’re already a failed state. There’s no question about it. Look at what is happening, banditry, terrorism, kidnapping and all sorts of conflicts. These are symptoms of a state that is unable, not only to properly articulate its challenges, but to deal with them,” he said.

According to him, the existence of government institutions does not necessarily mean that the state is fulfilling its responsibilities to citizens.

“What is the definition of a failed state? Fundamentally, it is a state that fails to meet the aspirations of its people.

“You may still have a government and institutions, but if the state cannot protect the people and provide the environment in which they can live productive lives, then it is failing them,” he said.

Duke added that the experiences of victims of kidnapping illustrated the consequences of the state’s failure to guarantee security.

“Talk to someone who has been kidnapped. That person does not need you to explain the definition of a failed state. His experience has already told him what failure of the state means,” he said.

He maintained that poverty and unemployment were among the underlying factors contributing to banditry and kidnapping, warning that security responses would remain inadequate if the economic conditions driving criminality were ignored.

“When it comes to banditry and kidnapping, poverty and unemployment are at the bottom of much of it.

“We keep reacting to these crises instead of asking what is producing them. We are too reactive in our governance. Governance is not just about today; it is about laying the foundation for tomorrow,” he said.

The former governor expressed concern that Nigeria was not generating businesses and employment opportunities at a rate sufficient to accommodate its growing working-age population.

He said the annual influx of graduates into the labour market, coupled with the difficulties confronting existing businesses, was worsening the country’s employment challenge.

“Businesses are contracting. New ones are not springing up the way they should. At the same time, we are turning out graduates every year and adding more people to the working population, but there is no work for them to do,” he said.

Duke also questioned whether Nigeria’s economy had expanded sufficiently to support its population, comparing the country’s crude oil production with figures from more than four decades ago.

He recalled that Nigeria produced approximately 2.5 million barrels of crude oil daily in 1980, compared with about 1.7 million barrels at the time of his remarks, despite substantial population growth.

“In 1980, Nigeria was producing about 2.5 million barrels of oil a day. Forty-six years later, we are producing around 1.7 million barrels, while our population has tripled.

“So you have to ask: has the economy expanded enough to carry the population? Clearly, it has not,” he said.

He argued that Nigeria’s large population should serve as an economic advantage rather than a source of instability, provided the government invested adequately in education, employment and productivity.

“Our numbers ought to be an asset. But a large population is an asset only when you can educate the people, employ them and make them productive,” he said.

Duke warned that the failure to create sufficient opportunities would continue to encourage Nigerians with the resources to seek better prospects abroad, while those remaining in the country would face mounting economic pressure.

The PRP candidate said his presidential ambition was rooted in his longstanding belief that Nigeria could become a successful nation if its resources and population were properly managed.

He recalled that he had the opportunity to remain in the United States after studying and working there in his twenties but chose to return to Nigeria because he believed he had a role to play in the country’s development.

“I had the opportunity in my twenties to remain in America. I went to school there and worked there for a while.

“But I voluntarily decided that was not where I wanted to be. I believe the Almighty put me in Nigeria for a reason. I believe in this country’s possibilities, and this is where I believe I should contribute,” he said.

He said that conviction had informed his decision to contest the Cross River governorship in 1999 and now underpinned his bid for the presidency ahead of the 2027 election.

“I wanted to prove then that we were better than what we were putting forward. From experience, I know Nigeria can be a very successful nation,” Duke said.

World.title: Udenta Proposes Sovereign Commission to Prevent Post-election Crisis
World.content:
Chuks Okocha in Abuja

A pro-democracy activist and founding National Secretary of the Alliance for Democracy (AD), Professor Udenta O. Udenta, has proposed the establishment of a Sovereign Commission for Democratic Sustainability and National Stability to address Nigeria’s political tensions and prevent elections from triggering national crises.

In a statement, Udenta argued that the challenge ahead of the 2027 general election goes beyond who emerges president, stressing that the country must prioritise national unity and democratic stability over individual political ambitions.

For example, he said that while he is a fervent Peter Obi supporter and will vote for him, there are other players who will drive this project with him that are supporters of President Tinubu, former Vice President Atiku Abubakar, Gov Seyi Makinde, and the other presidential candidates.

He further asserted that “elections cannot, by themselves, build trust or guarantee stability,” adding that the critical question is “what becomes of the nation the day after?”

He stressed that “Nigeria’s survival must matter more than the fortunes of any politician,” because “Nigeria is not temporary.”

The proposed commission would bring together the sitting president, all certified presidential candidates, national leaders and chairmen of political parties, leaders of the Nigeria Labour Congress (NLC) and Trade Union Congress (TUC), the Academic Staff Union of Universities (ASUU), the Nigerian Union of Journalists (NUJ) and civil society representatives.

Udenta stressed that the initiative was designed to be a practical platform for dialogue rather than “another committee of former officeholders or political elders issuing communiqués that gather dust.”

He proposed that all political parties and their presidential candidates make seven pre-election commitments, including participating in the commission regardless of electoral outcome.

According to Udenta, membership would be based on candidacy, declaring that it “only derives from one’s status as a presidential candidate. Period!”

Other proposals, he said, include a commitment by the winner to convene the commission after the election, establish a time-bound 18-month Government of National Unity based on competence, and pursue reforms to reduce the winner-takes-all nature of presidential politics.

The proposed reforms also include legislation for audited public funding of eligible political parties, proportional executive representation, a national dialogue on an Afrocentric democratic model and the restoration of cabinet-level Special Advisers for Inter-Party Matters and Civil Society Relations.

On political party financing, Udenta cited Germany, Sweden, South Africa, Kenya, Malawi and Tanzania as countries with public subsidy arrangements for political parties.

He argued that transparent funding tied to verified electoral thresholds would “reduce parties’ dependence on wealthy patrons, encourage stronger organisation and help credible opposition parties survive between elections.”

The professor maintained that such funding must be governed by disclosure requirements, independent audits and penalties for abuse, rather than left to the discretion of the ruling party.

Udenta also outlined a timeline for the proposed commission, calling for all presidential candidates to “jointly urge calm and direct disputes through lawful channels” within 72 hours of the declaration of election results. He proposed that the commission hold its first formal meeting within 30 days and publish substantive recommendations within 100 days, requiring a public response from the president.

Udenta warned against confusing national stability with the suppression of dissent, declaring: “A stable country is not one in which citizens are afraid to speak.”

According to him, genuine democratic stability requires citizens to disagree peacefully, journalists to investigate without intimidation, courts to operate without political interference,e and peaceful protests not to be criminalised as treason.

He also insisted that opposition parties must retain their freedom to criticise the government, noting that “a voter who supported the losing candidate does not become less Nigerian when the results are announced.

Beyond electoral reforms, Udenta called for stronger federating units and subnational institutions to reduce the concentration of power and resources at the centre. He argued that excessive centralisation makes control of the Federal Government an all-or-nothing political contest.

In his concluding challenge to political leaders, Udenta asked: “Will you help build a democracy that belongs to the whole country, or preserve a system in which every election threatens to divide it?”

He stressed that although political rivalry and competition were necessary in a democracy, they must not undermine national institutions, adding that “only our collective commitment to the national interest can determine whether Nigeria endures and thrives.”

World.title: China, Nigeria Target Billion-Dollar Opportunities As Filmmakers Push Co-production, Market Access
World.content:
Michael Olugbode in Abuja

Nigeria and China are seeking to turn their growing cultural relationship into a stronger commercial partnership in film, with filmmakers from both countries exploring co-production, technology transfer and distribution opportunities that could open up two major audiences to each other’s creative industries.

The push gained momentum at the Chinese Film Screening in Nigeria 2026 in Abuja, where industry stakeholders identified the combination of Nigeria’s storytelling strength and China’s cinema infrastructure, capital and distribution expertise as a potential pathway to expanding the global reach of their productions.

The discussions also highlighted a major challenge facing the proposed partnership: translating cultural exchanges and diplomatic goodwill into concrete business arrangements that enable filmmakers to secure investment, distribute their works across borders and earn sustainable returns.

The Director of the China Cultural Centre in Nigeria, Mr Yang Jianxing, said film remained an important bridge for strengthening understanding between the two countries, whose creative industries offered considerable scope for collaboration.

“China and Nigeria share a deep-rooted traditional friendship and close people-to-people exchanges, and film serves as an important bridge for fostering mutual understanding between our peoples,” he said.

Jianxing said cooperation had expanded through reciprocal film screenings, professional exchanges, festivals and the distribution of productions across national borders.

The partnership involving the Chinese Embassy, the China Cultural Centre and StarTimes Nigeria has helped bring Chinese film and television productions to Nigerian audiences through initiatives including a month-long showcase, the Chinese Women’s Film Festival and screenings of works dubbed or subtitled in local languages, including Hausa.

“StarTimes has successfully brought outstanding Chinese productions and knowledge series to a broader audience,” he said.

He added that Nigerian films had also reached mainstream Chinese digital media platforms, exposing audiences there to Nigerian stories, characters and experiences.

The commercial potential of the relationship was underscored by Fidelis Duker, founder of the Abuja International Film Festival, who said discussions with the Chinese delegation had focused on production, distribution and co-production opportunities, including engagements with Nigerian film institutions and plans to meet distributors and cinema operators in Lagos.

Duker argued that the population sizes of the two countries presented an opportunity to expand the reach of their film industries, provided that investment, technology and distribution networks were developed to support the exchange of content.

“What we found out today, or what we’ve known over the years, is that China has technology,” he said, adding that the Chinese delegation had told participants that China sold 1.3 billion cinema tickets in the previous year.

China’s film market provides an indication of the scale of the opportunity. According to figures released by the China Film Administration, the country generated ¥51.832 billion in box-office revenue in 2025, while cinema attendance reached 1.238 billion.

Domestic productions accounted for nearly 80 per cent of total box-office receipts, and the country ended the year with 93,187 cinema screens.

The figures illustrate the scale of China’s production and exhibition ecosystem, offering Nigerian filmmakers potential access to a market where locally produced content commands a substantial share of cinema revenue.

For Nigeria, the opportunity extends beyond exporting completed films. Collaboration could also create avenues for joint productions, technical training, improved post-production capacity and the development of distribution arrangements that give Nigerian stories a wider international audience.

Duker said the combination of Nigerian creativity and Chinese industrial capacity could be particularly valuable to both sides.

“When you marry Nigerian narrative vitality with China’s technical infrastructure, capital, and unparalleled distribution expertise, you can imagine the possibilities,” he said.

The Chinese delegation, led by the Chairman of Huaxia Film Distribution Company Limited, Bai Yimin, also emphasised the contribution of cinema to bilateral relations.

Bai said cooperation between the countries had produced results through reciprocal film festivals, professional exchanges, and the translation and broadcasting of films.

“In recent years, cooperation in the film industry has become a brilliant chapter in China-Nigerian cultural and people-to-people exchanges,” he said.

He added that the Chinese Embassy and the China Cultural Centre would continue to support initiatives using cinema to connect audiences and strengthen relations between the two countries.

The screening coincided with the 23rd Abuja International Film Festival, which received 10 Chinese film entries this year, five of which were nominated for awards.

Duker said Chinese films had featured in 22 of the festival’s 23 editions, reflecting a longstanding relationship between the event and China’s film industry.

He also credited StarTimes with supporting the festival over the years, saying the relationship had contributed to its growth.

Three films were screened at the event: The Shadow’s Edge, Blades of the Guardians: Wind Rises in the Desert and The Lychee Road.

The screening comes against the backdrop of broader efforts to deepen Nigeria-China cooperation in the creative sector.

In August 2026, the Nigerian Television Authority (NTA) and China Movie Channel signed a strategic cooperation agreement aimed at promoting film co-production, technology transfer, professional training and wider distribution of creative content.

The agreement, announced at the China-Nigeria Film and Literature Symposium in Abuja, signalled an interest in moving cultural relations beyond the exchange of finished productions towards more structured industry collaboration.

The latest engagements at the film festival could build on that momentum by bringing filmmakers, distributors, cinema operators and production institutions into discussions about the practical requirements of cross-border business.

However, access to a large audience does not automatically translate into commercial success. Nigerian and Chinese productions seeking to enter each other’s markets will need effective distribution partners, appropriate subtitling and dubbing, marketing support, clear licensing arrangements and investment structures that protect the interests of participating filmmakers.

Differences in audience preferences, language, production practices and market regulations will also need to be addressed if joint projects are to attract viewers and generate revenue.

For Nigeria, the immediate priority is to ensure that its creative talent benefits commercially from international partnerships rather than limiting participation to festival appearances and cultural showcases.

For China, deeper engagement with Nollywood offers an avenue to broaden the international reach of its productions while building relationships with one of Africa’s most prominent film industries.

The success of the partnership will ultimately depend on whether the two countries can turn screenings and professional exchanges into financed co-productions, regular content distribution and lasting commercial relationships.

With both sides signalling interest in closer collaboration, the emerging challenge is to build an industry-to-industry framework capable of converting shared cultural interests and large populations into tangible opportunities for filmmakers, distributors and audiences.

World.title: Pa Fasoranti: Exit of a Titan of Awolowo’s Political Tradition
World.content:
Fidelis David writes that the demise of the Leader of Pan Yoruba socio-political group, Afenifere, Pa Reuben Fasoranti, has marked the fading of one of the last living links to a political generation whose convictions were forged before independence and tested through the turbulence of the First Republic, Civil War, military dictatorship, the June 12, 1993 election struggle and nearly three decades of uninterrupted civil rule.

When Afenifere leader, Pa Reuben Famuyide Fasoranti died peacefully at his Akure residence on Tuesday, at the age of 100, Nigeria lost more than an elder statesman.

Born on May 11, 1926, in Uso, Ondo State, Fasoranti lived through virtually every defining chapter of modern Nigerian history. Yet, while the country’s political landscape underwent repeated transformations, he remained associated with a tradition of politics rooted in the philosophy of late sage, Chief Obafemi Awolowo: disciplined leadership, social welfare, educational advancement, justice and a federal structure that accommodates the country’s diversity.

His death, therefore, is not simply the loss of a centenarian. It is the departure of a custodian of Awoism whose political influence extended from Ondo State to the wider Yoruba nation and the national struggle for democratic governance.

The head of the Awolowo family and Chairman of African Newspapers of Nigeria Plc, Ambassador Olatokunbo Awolowo- Dosumu, captured the historical significance of his passing when she described him as one of the last titans of the political tradition established by her father.

“With his departure, we have lost, in a very real sense, the last of the titans of the Awolowo political tradition,” she said.

Fasoranti’s political story did not begin in a party office or government house. It began in the classroom, where he developed the discipline and commitment to public service that would later define his political career.

After his early education in Uso, he attended Ondo Boys’ High School and Yaba Higher College before proceeding to the University College, Ibadan. His academic journey later took him to the University of Hull in the United Kingdom, where he obtained a postgraduate diploma in education, and Macquarie University in Australia, where he earned a master’s degree in education administration and school management.

As a teacher and principal, Fasoranti served in institutions including Ondo Boys’ High School, Oyemekun Grammar School and Iju/Itaogbolu Grammar School. He subsequently established Omolere Nursery and Primary School and Akure High School, extending his contribution to education beyond formal public service.

Former Secretary to the Government of the Federation, Chief Olu Falae, who described Fasoranti as an in-law and a close associate of more than 60 years, recalled his generosity towards children from disadvantaged backgrounds.

As founding principal of Iju/Itaogbolu Grammar School, Falae said, Fasoranti admitted pupils whose parents could not afford their fees and allowed them to complete their education on credit, with the opportunity to repay later.

That commitment offers a window into the philosophy that shaped his public life: education was not merely a personal achievement but a social instrument for expanding opportunity.

Fasoranti’s political identity was inseparable from Awolowo’s progressive tradition. From the Action Group to the Unity Party of Nigeria, he remained committed to a political philosophy that placed education, healthcare and social welfare at the centre of governance.

His most prominent executive assignment came between 1979 and 1983, when he served as Commissioner for Finance under the administration of the late Governor Michael Adekunle Ajasin in the old Ondo State.

The period was associated with the implementation of Awolowo-inspired social programmes, particularly free education and free healthcare, which sought to make essential services accessible regardless of social status.

Fasoranti’s role in the administration placed him at the intersection of ideology and public finance, where the ideals of progressive governance had to be translated into policies and expenditure decisions.

His political relevance was not necessarily built on occupying the highest elective offices. Rather, it rested on his place within a network of ideological actors who helped sustain the progressive tradition across successive political generations.

Former Ondo State Governor, Dr Olusegun Mimiko, described him as a man whose politics was defined by fidelity to principle rather than personal ambition.

“Never for once were personal ambition or greed markers of his leadership philosophy or direction; it was all about fidelity to principle and an abiding concern for the future of the nation,” Mimiko said.

That assessment captures the central paradox of Fasoranti’s political life: he exercised considerable influence without becoming a president, governor or elected legislator.

Fasoranti’s place in Nigeria’s political history extended beyond the administration of public institutions. During the struggle against military rule, particularly following the annulment of the June 12, 1993 presidential election, he became associated with the pro-democracy movement and the resistance to military dictatorship.

His involvement in the National Democratic Coalition (NADECO) placed him within a broad coalition of political leaders and activists demanding the restoration of democratic rule.

The period was dangerous for those who challenged the military establishment. Fasoranti reportedly survived an assassination attempt in 1996 during the dictatorship of General Sani Abacha. His significance in that struggle lie in the continuity he represented between Awolowo’s generation of political activism and the campaign to restore civilian government.

For a man who had witnessed independence and the collapse of the First Republic, the return to democracy was not an abstract constitutional ideal. It was part of a lifelong engagement with the question of how Nigeria should be governed.

Fasoranti’s influence reached another defining phase in November 2008, when he emerged as leader of Afenifere following the death of Pa Abraham Adesanya.

For 18 years, he occupied the organisation’s most influential leadership position, navigating disagreements over leadership, political alliances and the direction of Yoruba politics.

Under his leadership, Afenifere continued to advocate restructuring, true federalism, devolution of powers, resource control and a governance system that would give federating units greater responsibility over their affairs.

Yet his tenure was not without controversy. The organisation experienced deep divisions, particularly over leadership and political alignments, culminating in rival tendencies associated with Fasoranti and Chief Ayo Adebanjo.

In 2021, Fasoranti appointed Adebanjo as acting leader and Oba Oladipo Olaitan as deputy leader while retaining his position as substantive national leader.

The divisions became more politically consequential during the 2023 presidential election, when Fasoranti’s endorsement of former Lagos State Governor, Asiwaju Bola Tinubu exposed differences within the Yoruba socio-political establishment over whether to support the eventual president or maintain a different political position.

His relationship with Tinubu was rooted in the broader progressive political family, but the endorsement demonstrated that ideological affinity did not automatically translate into consensus within Afenifere.

President Tinubu, in his condolence message, recalled visiting Fasoranti in Akure in 2022 to inform him of his presidential ambition.

“Pa Fasoranti told me I would be President in his lifetime, and God answered his prayer,” Tinubu said.

The president described him as one of the last great titans of Awolowo’s progressive family, praising his discipline, integrity and commitment to true federalism. The relationship reinforced Fasoranti’s standing as a political patriarch whose counsel carried weight beyond Ondo State.

However, it also illustrated the delicate balance between preserving ideological traditions and navigating the practical realities of electoral politics.

In July 2019, Fasoranti suffered a devastating personal tragedy when his daughter, Mrs Funke Olakunrin, was killed by gunmen along the Ondo-Ore Expressway.

The killing provoked widespread outrage and renewed national debate about insecurity, particularly attacks on travellers and the vulnerability of communities across the country.

For Fasoranti, the tragedy brought the national security crisis into his immediate family. It also sharpened public attention on concerns about the protection of citizens and the effectiveness of Nigeria’s security architecture.

His advocacy for restructuring and a more responsive federation acquired renewed urgency amid national conversations about state policing, regional security arrangements and the distribution of constitutional powers.

The incident became one of the most painful chapters in a life otherwise celebrated for longevity, discipline and public service.

Fasoranti’s death now raises an uncomfortable question for Afenifere and the wider Yoruba political establishment: who now possesses the moral authority, historical experience and political reach to occupy the space he’s leaving behind?

The challenge is not simply to identify a successor to an organisational title. It is to rebuild cohesion in a movement that has experienced divisions over leadership and electoral choices, while preserving its historic commitment to restructuring and social justice.

His long tenure gave him a stature that cannot easily be transferred through an appointment. The next generation of leaders will have to earn legitimacy through their conduct, ideological consistency and capacity to unite competing interests.

In Ondo State, his influence also formed part of the political inheritance of a state whose progressive tradition has shaped its identity for decades. His son, Dr Taiwo Fasoranti, who serves as Secretary to the State Government, represents a continuing family connection to public service, although the elder statesman’s broader legacy extends well beyond his family.

Lagos State Governor, Babajide Sanwo-Olu described the late leader as a symbol of wisdom, integrity and selfless service, noting his longstanding commitment to truth, equity, justice and good governance.

Ondo State Governor, Lucky Aiyedatiwa similarly described him as a patriarch whose contributions to the state, Yorubaland and Nigeria would remain indelible.

“He lived a fulfilled life and left indelible footprints in the sands of time,” Tinubu said of the centenarian.

Therefore, Fasoranti’s death closes a remarkable chapter, but whether it ends the political tradition he represented depends on what happens next.

Awoism cannot survive merely as a slogan invoked during anniversaries or political campaigns. Its enduring relevance rests on whether leaders can translate its ideals into accessible education, affordable healthcare, accountable government, social justice and a federal structure that responds to the needs of Nigeria’s diverse communities.

Fasoranti’s life offered an example of ideological continuity across generations, even as the political environment around him changed dramatically. His record was not without controversy, and his leadership did not resolve every division within Afenifere.

Nevertheless, Pa Fasoranti’s longevity, discipline and association with the progressive tradition gave him a distinctive place in Nigeria’s political history. At 100, he had witnessed the rise and fall of political movements, the triumphs and disappointments of democratic government, and the persistent struggle to define the Nigerian federation.

His departure leaves a void in Ondo State and Yorubaland, but also a test for those who inherit the institutions and ideals he defended. The ultimate measure of his legacy will not be how long his name remains attached to Afenifere, but whether the principles he spent a century representing continue to influence how Nigeria is governed. For the generation that follows him, the question is no longer what Fasoranti stood for. It is whether they possess the conviction to stand for it themselves

World.title: When Shettima Remembers: A Lesson in Unscripted Humanity
World.content:
Rahma Abdulmajid captures the carefully managed armour of Vice President Kashim Shettima, stripping away sterile state protocol, partisan politics, and grandstand podiums to expose the raw human anatomy beneath the leader during his encounter with a longtime friend in New Delhi, India.

History is obsessed with the theatre of power. It immortalizes the roaring stadiums, the blinding camera flashes, and the hollow majesty of choreographed handshakes—but real control operates in the shadows.

True, transformative leadership is never born on a brightly lit stage. It is forged in the shadows, deep within the quiet, unscripted margins where teleprompters go dark and the roaring crowds fall silent. When the glittering costume of power is violently stripped away, only two things can remain: a hollow, echoing emptiness, or the raw, unvarnished force of pure humanity.

New Delhi was buzzing on day two of the BRICS summit. Inside the Nigerian Embassy, the energy turned electric as Vice President Kashim Shettima arrived for a brief courtesy visit. A roaring, joyous crowd of resident Nigerians had gathered, transforming the venue into an impromptu homecoming. Excitement hung thick in the air, punctuated by rising chants and the endless, rapid-fire click of camera shutters capturing every handshake and smile.

Yet beneath that surface warmth, a subtle tension shifted the room. While everyone else basked in the moment, the Vice President’s gaze fractured. His eyes darted from face to face with a sharp, urgent intensity, searching for something vital that the rest of us had completely overlooked.

It was contagious. Soon, it wasn’t just his security detail on high alert. Even those of us in his inner circle found ourselves scanning the room, hunting for whatever phantom danger our principal was so desperately trying to find. Even inside the private quarters meant for his rest, there was no escape from the search.

The moment the commotion outside died down, his voice sliced through the polite small talk. “Where is Mr. Prakash?” The embassy officials froze, trapped in a heavy, bewildered silence. They traded blank stares, hunting for the name in their memories. Then, understanding clicked. He spoke again, steady and firm. “Mr. Prakash,” he said. “The embassy driver. Is he still here?”

Within minutes, Mr. Prakash appeared. He was an elderly, humble Indian man, his weathered face and traditional mourning haircut bearing the unmistakable scars of a life battered by time. Though he held nothing more than a modest driver’s job at an African embassy, he carried a crushing mountain of obligations alone on his narrow shoulders. He approached, his fragile gaze holding the look of someone who had just stumbled upon long-lost family.

The Vice President had just sat down to his welcome meal when he spotted Prakash. In an instant, protocol and plate were forgotten. He stood straight back up, greeting Prakash with a deep reverence that hushed the entire room. “Mr. Prakash, how have you been?” he said warmly. “Thank you for everything.”

Then, turning to the rest of us as if to permanently etch the man’s dignity into our minds, he explained, “He drove me around years ago during my visit to India as governor.” What followed was uniquely disarming: he began inquiring about Mr. Prakash’s family by name. He remembered vivid details from a brief encounter years ago—the kind of trivial history most leaders cast aside.

When Prakash, with trembling hands, pulled out a worn-out phone, desperate for a photograph to mark the improbable reunion, my principal left his meal once more and threw an arm around him like an old, dear friend. In that moment, he posed not as a Vice President, but simply as a man with his brother.

But it wasn’t the cameras that stole my breath that afternoon. It was what happened after the lenses lowered—away from the flashing lights and prying eyes. Without announcement or applause, Shettima slipped a hand into his pocket, scooped out a generous wad of cash, and tucked it quietly into Mr. Prakash’s coat.

No aides were instructed. No media were invited. It was an act born purely out of kindness, deep empathy, and raw humanity. When language threatened to build a wall—because Prakash speaks little English and the Vice President speaks no Hindi—compassion found its own dialect.

He switched effortlessly to Hausa, a Nigerian local language, not for Prakash to understand literally, but to universalise the moment, to say in a tongue he knows best what the heart knows in every language: “Mene ne amfanin nasarar rayuwa idan baka taimaka wa wanda yake bukatar taimakonka ba?” Translated in English, this means, “What is the benefit of success in life if you do not help those who need your help?”

What I witnessed did not surprise me, but it deeply enriched my soul. You see, I too am a Prakash in the Vice President’s world. Over the past three years of working by his side, no living soul has recognised the heavy reality of my life like he has. When my husband died serving our nation, I was left to carry the immense weight of raising our children alone. Yet, His Excellency truly sees that sacrifice, honouring the burden I bear every single day.

To speak the absolute truth, Kashim Shettima’s quiet, unwavering remembrance of my grief over the past three years has outshone even my closest blood relatives across the 11 long years since my husband passed away. He remembers the dates others forget. He asks the questions others avoid. He carries burdens that are not constitutionally his to bear.

Seeing Vice President Shettima evokes the presence of transformative leaders. He reminds me of Uruguay’s President, José Mujica, who chose a modest farmhouse over a palace, and Nelson Mandela, whose profound friendship with Christo Brand transcended prison walls.

Their stories remind us that true leadership is never about titles, offices, or protocols. It lives in an unshakeable refusal to walk past someone in need—a stubborn conviction that every human being, no matter how small their station, is worthy of being remembered.

This noble, compassionate heart is precisely why President Bola Tinubu chose Kashim Shettima as his running mate—to gift Nigeria a leadership defined not by noise, but by empathy; not by showmanship, but by deep, genuine service. In a world where many leaders remember only those who can repay them, it is truly revolutionary to find one who remembers a driver.

-Abdulmajid, a media assistant to the Vice President, writes from Abuja.

World.title: Throwback: The day a South African town recorded a scorching 48.4°C
World.content:
Vredendal in the Western Cape recorded a scorching 48.4°C on 27 October 2015. Image: Wikimedia Commons

On 27 October 2015, temperatures in Vredendal, Western Cape, soared to 48.4°C, marking one of the hottest days in South Africa’s recorded history.

Setting a new maximum temperature record for the town.

According to the South African Weather Service (SAWS), it was also the highest temperature recorded anywhere in the world during October 2015.



A day of extraordinary heat

Vredendal is no stranger to hot weather, but the temperatures recorded that Tuesday were far beyond what residents would normally expect in October.

The town’s previous October temperature record stood at 42.5°C, set in 1999.

The 2015 reading exceeded that record by almost 6°C.



Several other weather stations across the Western Cape and Northern Cape also recorded unusually high temperatures that day.

These included Paarl, Wellington, Clanwilliam and Calvinia.

What caused the extreme heat?

Berg winds can cause temperatures to rise sharply in parts of South Africa.



These hot, dry winds blow from the country’s interior towards the coast.

As the air moves downhill, increasing atmospheric pressure compresses and warms it.

This can push temperatures much higher than usual, particularly when the air is already hot and dry.



South Africa was already battling a drought

The record-breaking October heat came during one of South Africa’s most difficult drought periods.

SAWS later confirmed that 2015 was the country’s driest year on record since 1904.

The drought, together with repeated periods of extreme heat, placed enormous pressure on water supplies, agriculture and communities.



Nearly 11 years later, Vredendal’s extraordinary October temperature remains a reminder of just how intense heat can become in South Africa.

World.title: Ex-Sharks coach: Hyron Andrews was a special person, player
World.content:
This week it was confirmed that experienced lock Hyron Andrews had died from ‘a tear in the aorta (due to natural causes)’, after being found unresponsive at the team hotel while on tour with the Lions.

There has been an outpouring of tributes ever since the tragic death came to light last Friday, and Edinburgh coach Sean Everitt – who previously coached Andrews at the Sharks – has spoken poignantly about the person and player he remembers so fondly.

“He was a motivated young man, with a lot of talent and skills,” Everitt told IOL Sport. “With us preparing for the Lions on Friday night with Hyron in it, he would have been a massive threat.



“He was one of those guys who every week gives his best, whether on the training field or on match day. He was very diligent in his preparation, which is required of a guy who runs a lineout.

“Hyron was an unassuming character, well-mannered, respected by every member of his team, and very humble.

“He had great potential, and he was part of the Junior Springboks, but you would never say so. He just went about his work every day.



“He was incredibly polite and very popular. He was called Ice Man for a reason – he was always chilled and relaxed. He was a good man.”

Hyron Andrews remains in the thoughts of the Lions

Speaking to the media this week, Lions assistant coach Julian Redelinghuys said the team were just taking it day by day.

“We’ve been saying this since it happened: there’s no manual for this. We don’t know how the players are going to respond,” Redelinghuys commented.



“We can only do what we can to support the guys as much as we can and do what we think will be best for the weekend.

“I don’t think there’s any team that has had to go through a thing like this, where a player died in camp a day before a game and then they were on tour for another two weeks.”

FULL STATEMENT

Following Andrews’ autopsy, the Lions released the following statement.



“The French authorities, who conducted the autopsy and, in whose care Hyron’s body currently remains, described the cause of death as ‘a tear in the aorta (due to natural causes), which led to a significant accumulation of blood within the sac surrounding the heart’,” the statement continued.

“The Andrews family asks for respect, privacy and patience during this difficult time as the repatriation process begins.

“A timeline for the return of Hyron’s body to South Africa has not yet been determined. Further information will be communicated when it becomes available and under the guidance of the family.”

World.title: Eskom shares great Koeberg electricity news
World.content:
Eskom has confirmed that Koeberg Nuclear Power Station’s Unit 1 has returned to service following an unexpected shutdown. Image: X @Eskom_SA

Eskom has confirmed that Koeberg Nuclear Power Station’s Unit 1 has returned to service following an unexpected shutdown triggered by an electrical disturbance during planned maintenance activities on Unit 2.

The power utility announced on Thursday that the necessary recovery activities had been completed and Unit 1 was stable and synchronised to the national electricity grid.

The incident occurred on 16 October during testing associated with the planned maintenance outage of Unit 2 at the Western Cape nuclear power station.



According to Eskom, an electrical disturbance exceeded the predefined tolerance limits of a protection system associated with Unit 1, causing the automatic opening of the unit’s 400 kV and 24 kV breakers.

Eskom explains what happened

An investigation found that a conservative protection relay setting contributed to the system’s response.

Eskom said the protection system operated as designed, safely shutting down Unit 1 and ensuring the continued safe operation of the plant.

The utility also stressed that there was no impact on nuclear safety.

“The successful return of Unit 1 reflects the coordinated efforts and commitment of the Koeberg teams responsible for the recovery and restoration activities,” Eskom said in a post on social media platform X.

Unit 2 remains in planned maintenance

While Unit 1 has returned to service, Unit 2 remains offline as part of its planned maintenance programme.



Eskom did not provide a return-to-service date for Unit 2 in its latest update.

Koeberg Nuclear Power Station is located near Cape Town and supplies electricity to South Africa’s national grid.

The latest development means Unit 1 has been restored following the electrical disturbance, while planned maintenance work on Unit 2 continues.

World.title: SASSA announces October 2026 SRD grant payment dates
World.content:
The South African Social Security Agency (SASSA) has confirmed the payment dates for the COVID-19 Social Relief of Distress (SRD) grant for October 2026.

The agency released the schedule in an official notice shared across its social media platforms, giving millions of grant recipients clarity on when to expect their money this month.

SRD payments roll out over two days

According to SASSA, SRD payments for October 2026 take place on Thursday, 22 October, and Friday, 23 October 2026.



Recipients whose applications SASSA approved for October can expect their funds to reflect within this window. However, the time it takes for money to appear may differ depending on the recipient’s bank or chosen payment method.

SASSA encourages applicants to check their application status on the official SRD website before heading to a pay point or retailer. This helps recipients avoid unnecessary trips and long queues if their payment has not yet been reflected.

SASSA SRD grant reaches millions of South Africans

In the same notice, SASSA shared several facts about the impact of the grant since its introduction during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The agency says the SRD grant reached close to 10 million beneficiaries at its peak. It currently supports approximately eight million recipients across South Africa.

SASSA describes the grant as one of the country’s largest social assistance programmes. The agency adds that it continues to provide a vital source of income for vulnerable individuals and households who have little or no other financial support.

For many unemployed South Africans, the monthly payment helps cover basic needs such as food, transport and airtime for job searching.



Grant extended until March 2027

SASSA also reminded South Africans that the government has extended the SRD grant until 31 March 2027.

The agency says the extension aims to ensure continued support for those in need while the grant remains in place.

Recipients should keep their personal and banking details up to date to avoid delays or interruptions to their payments. SASSA also urges applicants to rely only on its official channels for information and to remain alert to scams, especially messages asking for personal details or payment in exchange for faster approval.

Win R2 000 in the South African SASSA grant survey

If you receive a SASSA grant and want to share your story, we want to hear from you.

Take part in our survey and stand a chance to win R2 000. Your responses help us tell the stories that matter.

World.title: What will Durban’s new beachfront amusement park actually look like?
World.content:
Durban’s long-awaited new amusement park is starting to look less like a proposal on paper and more like a future reality.

The R980 million Durban Amusement Park has completed its design phase and secured approval for project development funding, with technical planning now under way.

And while construction has not yet started, concept renders released by the eThekwini Municipality give a colourful glimpse of what the new attraction could eventually look like.



The park is planned for the former Durban Funworld site along the Golden Mile and is expected to bring a permanent, ride-led attraction back to the beachfront after Funworld closed in 2023.

A colourful AMUSEMENT park right on the beachfront

Durban beachfront is getting their own amusement park valued at R1 billion – they are redeveloping the old Funworld Site🎪🎢🎡



I have been waiting forever for this announcement. The eThekwini Municipality shared renders with me earlier today, and they look incredible.



•⁠… pic.twitter.com/BBfmAK37Hq — Ash Müller (@Askash) December 10, 2025

If the renders are anything to go by, the new attraction will be a dramatic change from the largely empty former Funworld site.



The concept designs show a bright, colourful amusement park stretching along the beachfront, with large rollercoaster tracks weaving through the site, numerous rides, landscaped areas, pedestrian walkways and entertainment zones.

The park has been designed to make use of its beachfront location, with views towards the ocean and the Durban skyline forming part of the experience.

The designs also show extensive open areas, palm trees, seating spaces and brightly coloured pathways connecting the various attractions.



A giant rollercoaster will dominate the skyline

One of the most noticeable features in the renders is the large rollercoaster.

The previously released plans include a Lightning Roller Coaster, alongside other major rides including Disko 24 and a Vertical Swing.

The concept images show multiple sections of rollercoaster track, including dramatic loops and elevated sections running through the centre of the park.



This is a deliberate move away from a small-scale children’s funfair towards a larger amusement attraction designed to appeal to families, teenagers and adults.

There will be more than just rides

Despite the focus on rollercoasters and thrill rides, the planned development is not simply a collection of amusement rides.

The park is expected to include an extended-reality and digital entertainment zone, a curated retail offering and an upgraded amphitheatre designed for events.



Earlier plans also included a 1 500-square-metre Virtual Reality Theme Park featuring more than 160 interactive games and global e-sports activations.

That means visitors could potentially spend several hours at the attraction without necessarily going on a single traditional ride.

The aerial concept gives perhaps the clearest idea of the scale of the development.



The render shows the proposed attraction occupying a sizeable section of the beachfront, with rollercoaster tracks, large rides, landscaped areas and colourful activity zones arranged across the site.

The design also incorporates pedestrian areas and spaces where visitors can move between attractions rather than simply queueing for individual rides.

Viewing decks and beachfront walkways

The development is also intended to connect more closely with the surrounding Golden Mile.



Previous plans released by eThekwini included pedestrian walkways, panoramic viewing decks and themed food courts, as well as leisure areas.

The municipality has described the park as a family-oriented, alcohol-free environment, with different zones intended to cater for children, teenagers, adults and older visitors.

Another important part of the design is that the park isn’t intended to be a daytime-only attraction.



The combination of indoor and outdoor facilities is expected to allow it to operate throughout the year, including during wet weather and in the evenings. This could be particularly significant for Durban.

The city’s beachfront already attracts large numbers of visitors, but traditional outdoor attractions can be heavily affected by rain. Adding indoor digital entertainment and other covered facilities could help the development continue operating when the weather turns.

The concept plans also show a significant emphasis on lighting and colourful public spaces, supporting the city’s ambition to make the Golden Mile more of a day-and-night destination.



When will THE new amusement park be built?

The project has now completed its design stage, but construction has not yet started.

The latest update from eThekwini Municipality says technical planning is under way, while statutory development work is expected to continue until the end of the first quarter of 2027.

Construction is expected to follow those processes. The municipality has not yet announced a confirmed opening date.

World.title: Your luggage is most likely to be stolen at this SA airport
World.content:
OR Tambo International Airport recorded the highest number of theft cases among South Africa’s three major international airports. Image: RawPixel

OR Tambo International Airport recorded the highest number of theft cases among South Africa’s three major international airports, according to figures released by Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia.

More than 2 300 criminal and security-related incidents were reported at OR Tambo, Cape Town and King Shaka international airports over three financial years, with theft accounting for the majority of cases.

The figures were revealed by Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia in response to parliamentary questions from DA MP Lisa Schickerling, who requested details of crime and security incidents at the three airports.



OR Tambo records highest number of theft cases

According to Cachalia’s response, 2 339 incidents were reported across the three airports during the period under review.

OR Tambo International Airport recorded the highest number, with 1 487 incidents. Cape Town International Airport followed with 579, while King Shaka International Airport recorded 273.

Theft made up a substantial proportion of the reported cases.



OR Tambo recorded 1 369 theft cases, compared with 305 at Cape Town International Airport and 148 at King Shaka International Airport.

The figures highlight the scale of reported theft at the country’s busiest airport, although they do not establish the precise likelihood of an individual passenger having their luggage stolen.

Cachalia explained that the South African Police Service (SAPS) records incidents that are formally reported and registered as case dockets.



Unreported incidents, matters handled internally by airport operators or airlines, and intelligence that does not result in a registered case are excluded from the figures.

Baggage theft and security breaches

The parliamentary response also highlighted incidents involving baggage handling and baggage pilfering.

At least 346 such incidents were recorded at Cape Town and King Shaka international airports.



At OR Tambo, baggage handling and pilfering incidents were classified under theft-related dockets in the crime administration data. These were included in the theft figures to avoid double counting.

Aviation security breaches were recorded at Cape Town and King Shaka airports, with 21 cases at Cape Town and 11 at King Shaka, bringing the total to 32.

No robbery incidents were reported at OR Tambo or Cape Town international airports during the period. King Shaka, however, recorded nine incidents.



OR Tambo also recorded eight vehicle hijacking cases over the three financial years. Two were reported in 2023/24, followed by six in 2024/25, with none recorded in the financial year ending in March 2026.

Narcotics smuggling cases

The figures further showed that 106 cases involving narcotics smuggling were registered at OR Tambo International Airport, while Cape Town International Airport recorded 11.

Cachalia also clarified that the absence of a case classified as syndicate-related meant that no case had been formally registered under that specific description for the relevant airport and financial year.



The figures provide a snapshot of formally registered airport crime, rather than a complete account of every incident experienced by travellers.

For passengers, the theft totals underline the importance of keeping valuables secure and remaining alert to their belongings while travelling through South Africa’s major international airports.

World.title: ‘You became a beast’: Teko Modise gives Khune ‘his flowers’
World.content:
Former Orlando Pirates and Mamelodi Sundowns midfielder Teko Modise has paid tribute to Kaizer Chiefs legend Itumeleng Khune, revealing how a setback at the 2008 Africa Cup of Nations helped shape the goalkeeper’s career.

Modise, who played alongside and against Khune, believes the former Amakhosi captain used his lack of game time at the tournament as motivation to establish himself as Bafana Bafana’s number one goalkeeper.

The two former teammates represented South Africa at the 2008 AFCON, the 2009 FIFA Confederations Cup and the 2010 FIFA World Cup, which was hosted on home soil.



Speaking on a Soccer Laduma podcast alongside Khune, Teko reflected on the goalkeeper’s journey and explained why his rise to prominence did not surprise him.

“I’ve played against you many times. There was a stage in our career where brands were fighting for us, right? And I remember when we went to the first AFCON, I think it was 2008, you never got an opportunity to play.

“At the time, the coach didn’t believe in you that much. But what I did for you not playing in that AFCON, you became a beast after coming back. You became the number one keeper in the country,” Modise said.



The former midfielder also highlighted Khune’s passion and technical ability, revealing that the goalkeeper enjoyed playing outfield during training sessions.

Teko on how Khune became Mzansi’s no.1

“For me, when I saw you become the number one, it was not a surprise because we saw you coming up. We saw the passion you had. You could also play inside; people do not know that at training you loved playing inside, you loved taking free kicks,” he added.

Modise went on to describe Khune as one of the best goalkeepers he had seen in South Africa, praising the standard he set for others in the position.



“I say it proudly, and I say you’re one of the best I’ve ever seen in the country. You’ve set a standard for goalkeepers within the country itself as to the way it should be.

“I just hope with the career you have had, we can see many more, not just goalkeepers but footballers that will be loyal to teams, and teams that can be loyal to players as well, regardless of what happened at the end,” Teko told Khune.
