World.title: Pensioners make up 100% of buyers in these low-crime small towns
World.content:
If there’s any indication South Africa’s seniors are searching for safety, it’s the sales data from two small towns.

In both towns, where crime is trending downward, pensioners make up 100% of buyers.

Safe South African towns loved by a senior community

In Hattingspruit, on the banks of the Tom Worthington Dam, and Hekpoort, at the foot of the Magaliesburg Mountains, crime is the least of residents’ concerns.



In Hattingspruit, properties rarely go on the market. The town of 10 078 people records, on average, 5 sales a year.

Yet of the 3 sales this year, every buyer has been over 65.

The area is safe. Last year, crime dropped to its lowest levels since the South African Police (SAPS) began reporting its crime statistics.



The town only recorded 28 crimes in the first quarter of the year; of these, 1 was a residential burglary.

The town currently boasts a 1.47% crime rate.

Besides safety, retiree-age buyers also benefit from living beside the dam and the lifestyle that it brings.



There’s carp and bass fishing. A nighttime hiking trail allows for excellent stargazing.

Then in Hekpoort, a farming community on the foothills of the Magaliesburg Mountains and only 60 kilometres from Pretoria, every buyer this year is over 65.

As in Hattingspruit, property sales in Hekpoort remain in the single digits.



Last year, Hekpoort also recorded its lowest crime rate since SAPS began publishing data in 2013.

In the first quarter, 64 crimes were recorded; 3 were residential burglaries.

Safety in Quiet Small Towns

Not every small town is safe.



But South Africa has a handful of low- and no-crime towns.

These include towns like Rhodes in Barkly East, where no crimes were recorded in the first quarter of this year, down from two crimes recorded over the same period last year.

In Coffee Bay on the Wild Coast, 36 crimes were recorded in the first quarter.



In the Western Cape, pensioners have Nuwerus as a low-crime option. The town recorded 17 crimes in the first quarter.

Finding a Safe Community

Pensioners looking to sell up and move to a safer community should think strategically about the areas they find attractive.

This is what you should consider if safety is important.



Count the thoroughfares.

In a suburb like Melkbosstrand, one of Cape Town’s safest suburbs, only a handful of roads link the suburb to its surrounds.

Fewer entry points mean you can station a security patrol at key points to monitor who enters and exits the suburb.



Assess the boundaries.

Boundaries matter as much as thoroughfares. If it’s easy to scale a wall to enter or exit a suburb, criminals will use that.

Consider the surrounding suburbs.

Crime will always leak into a suburb bordering a high-crime community. So, when looking for property, consider the crime statistics of the neighbouring areas.



Look into the unemployment and drug data.

South African crime has been linked to the country’s high unemployment rates. In areas with higher rates of unemployment, desperate residents may turn to crime for money. The same is true of drugs. When users become reliant on drugs, to support that habit, they may commit heinous acts.

World.title: Joburg Water warns of possible contamination in Bezuidenhout Valley
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Johannesburg Water has warned of possible water contamination in Bezuidenhout Valley following repairs to a damaged pipeline.

The pipeline was repaired on Wednesday after a tree stump fell onto it during excavation work by a contractor replacing a sewer pipe.

The bulk water supplier said it was collecting water samples for laboratory testing to ensure the water met the required quality standards.

Residents have been advised not to use the water until further notice.



“An alternative water supply will continue to be provided while restrictions remain in place. Johannesburg Water will notify affected customers once laboratory tests have confirmed that the water meets the required quality standards and normal water supply can safely resume,” it said.

The affected areas include 8th Avenue and the intersections of 4th, 5th, 6th and 7th streets.

World.title: England and France face do-or-die clash at Rugby League World Cup
World.content:
LONDON - England hooker Brad O'Neill says there is a "real belief" the team can pull off a convincing victory over France on Saturday to keep their Rugby League World Cup hopes alive.

After being stunned 30-12 by Tonga in their tournament opener, the world number three must beat the French in Perth and by a big margin.

Only two of the six nations across Pools B and C from the 10-team tournament in Australia, Papua New Guinea and New Zealand progress to the final four.

"Despite the result, I feel like the way that we wanted to play was on show," said Wigan star O'Neill. "There was just maybe a bit of lack of execution, and credit to Tonga's defence as well.

"But I felt like the way we wanted to play was shown and we've just got to keep working on that.

"There is a real belief in our team."

On paper, England should have little problem, winning their last 23 meetings with France.

Coach Brian McDermott has kept faith with the squad that faced Tonga, naming an unchanged side for the Pool B clash.

France, who also need a big win to stay alive after crashing 78-4 to Samoa in an abysmal display, appear to have little hope.

But fullback Arthur Mourgue is adamant they can improve.

"We do have speed and some great forwards but compared with top-quality nations we are still a bit under them," he said. "But we're not going away."

After a mid-week pause, round two of the World Cup gets underway on Friday in Sydney with Tonga looking to build on their England upset when they face Lebanon.

Tonga playmaker Isaiya Katoa said the result might have surprised outsiders, but not within the squad.

"Within our four walls, we had that belief already," he told reporters.

"We understand the potential of this group and I think internally we've just got a bit of a quiet confidence about us."

Papua New Guinea take on Samoa at home in the other Pool B clash with confidence high after thrashing Lebanon 42-18 to get their tournament started.

Holders Australia face Fiji in Brisbane on Saturday, with the Pacific islanders currently topping Pool A after a dominant 40-12 win over the Cook Islands.

The 12-time champion Kangaroos are fresh from a thrilling 24-22 win over New Zealand in the World Cup's opening game, and coach Kevin Walters has shuffled his starting side with James Tedesco, Bradman Best, Sam Walker, Blayke Brailey and Lindsay Smith all coming in.

New Zealand are looking to bounce back against the Cook Islands in Christchurch without star fullback Kalyn Ponga who has a broken arm, opening the door for Keano Kini to start.

World.title: Tesla profits fall on higher spending as 'Elon Inc.' talk builds
World.content:
NEW YORK - Tesla reported lower third-quarter profits as near-trillionaire Elon Musk's electric vehicle maker ramped up huge investments in artificial intelligence and other envelope-pushing technologies.

Besides marginally lower car sales, Tesla saw a drop in revenues from regulatory credits and energy and storage, while spending on research and development more than doubled as the company engages in a spending binge on AI, robotics and autonomous transport.

The earnings were arguably upstaged by Musk's disclosure Tuesday that special committees of independent directors at both SpaceX and Tesla have been set up to discuss a merger of the two companies. Musk, who leads both companies, declined to offer further details Wednesday.

The potential merger -- which some have dubbed "Elon Inc." -- boosted shares of both companies on Wednesday, lifting Musk's wealth back near $1 trillion at $989 billion, according to Forbes' real-time billionaires index.

In the third quarter, Tesla reported profits of $787 million, down 42.7 percent from the year-ago period. Revenues were essentially flat at $28 billion.

Analysts had been cautious about Tesla's latest results heading into Wednesday's release.

While third-quarter auto sales topped estimates, due in part to an uptick in European markets amid high gasoline prices, better sales have not always translated to Tesla's bottom line.

The company has faced questions about the rollout of Tesla's robotaxi venture that has progressed much more slowly than hoped.

Musk has repeatedly made overly rosy forecasts about self-driving technology, as in 2019 when he predicted there would be more than a million robotaxis the following year.

In Texas, where Tesla has focused its robotaxi launch, there are currently about 800 robotaxis, according to FSD Database.

Tesla's release highlighted the September 3 launch of robotaxi service in Austin and said "cumulative unsupervised Robotaxi miles grew eightfold quarter over quarter."

Company officials said Wednesday that if the current pace of robotaxi growth continues, the venture could be meaningful financially as early as next year. The ramp-up is guided by a strong desire to avoid safety problems, company officials said.

For much of this year, Tesla has also encountered scrutiny over swelling capital spending to fund ambitious programs in artificial intelligence, robotics and autonomous driving.

Capital spending more than doubled in the third quarter to $4.7 billion, but the company lowered its capital spending plans compared with earlier in the year.

Chief Financial Officer Vaibhav Taneja, who in July had projected 2026 spending of more than $25 billion, said Wednesday the company expects to spend $20 billion, adding that the company managed "our capital deployment efficiently."

That is still more than double Tesla's 2025 capital budget of $8.5 billion.

Besides robotaxi and AI, Tesla is heavily investing in Musk's "Optimus" humanoid robots as well as the buildout jointly with SpaceX of a large chip factory in Austin.

The chip factory, called Terafab, was the object of some of Musk's most effusive and self-boosting language on Wednesday.

"Terafab I think will be the most valuable building in the world, and will probably have an economic value that will place it in the top 20 of countries," he said.

Musk is also eyeing auto growth, projecting production of five million in 2030 compared with 1.7 million in 2025.

"After many years of sort of grind and things being fairly flat, I think we're now headed for a lot of fun and significant growth," Musk said.

- Looming SpaceX merger? -

But questions about Tesla's future loomed larger with talk of the potential SpaceX tie-up. The companies have a combined equity value of more than $3.5 trillion.

"We think it's a matter of when, not if" the two companies combine, said CFRA Research equity analyst Garrett Nelson.

"That's the whole issue," Nelson said of a potential megadeal. "Tesla as we know it today may not exist in six to 12 months."

On SpaceX's conference call Tuesday night, Musk said the committees have not agreed on the terms of any deal and there is no guarantee they will.

Musk said the two companies could gain from working together on AI software, chip design, robotics and space-based computing.

Talk of the deal heaps additional attention on Musk as the billionaire's latest cash infusion into US political elections fuels fresh criticism. Musk has steered at least $276 million to allies of President Donald Trump in the Republican Party.

Musk is also under scrutiny over a report he ordered a reduction in Starshield telecom services for Ukraine, adding to pressure on the country at the same time Trump has criticised Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and called for him to be replaced.

Shares of Tesla initially rose in after-hours trading, but were down 3.3 percent near 0050 GMT.

World.title: In the Mexican town that makes emblematic Day of the Dead garlands
World.content:
MEXICO CITY - In a workshop in the Mexican town of San Salvador Huixcolotla, three men use small hammers and chisels to punch holes in thick sheets of tissue paper ahead of the Dia de Muertos (Day of the Dead) festival.

The multicoloured paper perforated with intricate folk art designs is known as "papel picado" (pecked paper).

It is a central element in the lavish altars erected to the deceased on November 1-2 and is also used to festoon homes and streets.

Papel picado originated in this small central Mexican town in the late 19th century.

More than a century later, three-quarters of the town's 17,000 inhabitants are employed in producing the paper, which is exported worldwide.

Despite the advent of AI and 3D printing, many people here continue making the paper by hand.

"We get satisfaction from the idea that our craftsmanship is recognised in other countries and that people see value in handmade things," Miguel Reynoso, a 58-year-old papel picado producer, told AFP.

Reynoso has been in the business for 40 years.

He and his wife employ over a dozen people, including their four daughters, making decorative banners for clients as far away as South Korea and Japan.

World.title: Foreign national beaten to death in Durban CBD
World.content:
DURBAN - A foreign national has been beaten to death in Durban’s CBD, with police using CCTV footage to help identify possible suspects.

The man, estimated to be in his late 30s or early 40s, was allegedly assaulted by a group of people on Thursday morning.

According to police, CCTV cameras monitoring the CBD captured a group of marchers moving along Dr Pixley kaSeme Street towards Maud Mfusi Street.

READ | March and March to challenge Constitutional Court asylum ruling

Footage showed two men breaking away from the group and approaching another man standing on the roadside. The pair appeared to engage him in conversation.

When the cameras returned to the area some time later, the man was lying on the ground and the marchers had left.

The victim had swelling at the back of his head.

Police have not established what was used in the assault, and the motive for the attack remains unknown.

Investigators say they are following several leads to identify possible suspects.

World.title: 'I want him to rot in jail' | Soweto mother speaks after alleged rape of daughter
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The mother of a nine-year-old Grade 4 pupil who was allegedly raped by a teacher at a Soweto primary school says her daughter told her it was not the first time she had been raped.

The alleged incident happened at Busisiwe Primary School last Thursday.

The teacher has since handed himself over to police and is expected to appear in the Protea Magistrate’s Court on Friday.

Gauteng Education officials visited the school earlier this week as angry parents protested, demanding the teacher’s removal. He has since been placed on precautionary suspension.

The mother, who cannot be named to protect her daughter’s identity, said she was relieved that the teacher had been apprehended but remained uncertain about whether he had been formally arrested.

READ | Soweto teacher accused of raping Gr 4 pupil hands himself over

“I’m feeling relieved that he has now been apprehended, but I’m here to make sure because, with the way everything unfolded, I don’t even trust that he is arrested for sure,” she said.

She also expressed anger that the teacher had continued working after she reported the alleged incident to the school.

“That killed me because I thought as I went and reported the matter, he would be removed from the school so that my daughter could go to school. But then my daughter was the one sitting at home while the alleged suspect was still going to work as per usual,” she said.

The mother said she believed her daughter’s account and wanted the teacher to remain behind bars.

"I want him to rot in jail. I trust whatever my daughter has said is true, even if some people are trying to say it's not true. I'm standing with my daughter 100%."

She also called for greater awareness of sexual abuse and more support for children who experience it.

The mother said she noticed a change in her daughter’s behaviour last week. The child, who is usually talkative, had become unusually quiet.

“At first, I thought it was bullying. I asked her if there was something wrong happening at school, and she said nothing until she mentioned it on Friday morning, saying that there is something that has been happening in school. And apparently, it’s not the first time,” she said.

The mother said the alleged incident was particularly distressing because it happened on school premises during school hours.

“It’s very sad that it happened on the school premises, during school hours. When you take your child to school, you expect that that’s the safest place. I consider educators as second parents when you are not there,” she said.

World.title: Godongwana confident of 3% economic growth despite downgraded forecast
World.content:
CAPE TOWN - Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana remains optimistic that South Africa’s economy can grow by more than 3 percent over the next three years, despite a downward revision to the country’s growth forecast.

The minister has lowered the economic growth projection for this year to 1.2 percent, from the 1.6 percent forecast in February.

Speaking at a post-mini budget breakfast in Cape Town, Godongwana said stronger economic growth could help absorb more unemployed South Africans, particularly young people.

However, he stressed the need to invest in skills development now to ensure the country is prepared for future opportunities.

He said the government needed to train young people to avoid a skills crisis when growth accelerates.

“We need to train our young people now so that when we reach such growth levels, we don't have a skills crisis,” Godongwana said.

He also believes the country is turning the corner on a fiscal crisis driven by state capture, sluggish economic growth and rising debt.

READ MORE | Godongwana cuts GDP growth forecast to 1.2% for 2026

He attributed the progress to cautious government spending, limits on bailouts and a stronger focus on investment.

Meanwhile, motorists are set to receive some relief from rising fuel prices following the government’s announcement of a R10-billion fuel levy reduction in the mid-term budget.

The temporary relief amounts to a reduction of R1.50 per litre for petrol and R3 per litre for diesel, offering some respite to consumers and businesses facing higher transport and operating costs.

World.title: What's holding up Washington's $14bn arms sale to Taiwan?
World.content:
TAIPEI - Taiwan has been waiting months for US President Donald Trump to approve a $14 billion sale of weapons and equipment, which the island democracy would use to fend off a potential Chinese attack.

Washington -- Taipei's most important security backer -- has sold many billions of dollars' worth of arms to Taiwan, most recently in December when it approved a record $11.1 billion package.

China opposes American military support for Taiwan, which Beijing claims is part of its territory and has threatened to seize with force.

Trump, who last month hailed his "great friendship" with Chinese President Xi Jinping, has resisted US political pressure, including from Republican lawmakers, to give the green light for the current arms package.

AFP takes a look at what's in it and why it's being held up:

- Why is Taiwan buying US arms? -

Taiwan is spending huge sums upgrading its defence capabilities and expanding its domestic weapons production capacity, but it still needs US arms to deter China.

Since Washington switched diplomatic recognition from Taipei to Beijing in 1979, the United States has stuck to its commitments under the Taiwan Relations Act to provide weapons to Taiwan for its defence.

But Trump said in May that US arms sales to Taiwan could be a bargaining chip with China, setting off alarm bells across the world.

Taipei has reminded Trump of US commitments, and US officials including Secretary of State Marco Rubio have insisted American policy on Taiwan has not changed.

The sale would signal US support for Taiwan and send a message to Beijing that if it launched an attack, it would not face "Taiwan alone", said Wang Ting-yu, a senior lawmaker in President Lai Ching-te's Democratic Progressive Party.

- What's in the package? -

Taiwan is developing a multi-layered air defence system, known as the T-Dome, that it hopes could counter a potential Chinese attack.

Patriot missiles, an automated command and control system and a 360-degree air defence radar system are seen as critical components of this system and are among the items in the $14 billion package.

"Together these systems can strengthen the resilience of Taiwan's strategic air defences," said Su Tzu-yun, a military expert at the Taipei-based Institute for National Defense and Security Research.

Money for the weapons system is expected to come from a $25 billion defence spending bill passed by Taiwan's parliament in May after months of political wrangling.

- Why has it been delayed? -

Trump and Xi met in Beijing in May -- the first of four expected meetings for 2026 -- as the rival leaders sought to ease trade tensions between their countries.

Xi issued a blunt warning to Trump that missteps on Taiwan could push the US and China into "conflict".

A record $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan could threaten the US-China trade truce.

"I'm going to make a determination. I'm going to see," Trump said after the summit in response to a question about whether he would go ahead with arms sales to Taiwan.

Rubio said in June that the proposed package was "under review", while officials said in May they were assessing whether American weapons stockpiles were sufficient for its Iran operations.

A US official said recently that the chances of the package being split into smaller chunks "have gone way up".

Some Taiwanese officials have said they do not care if the US bundles the arms into a single package or multiple -- they just want the weapons.

"Militarily... Taiwan is racing against time," said the analyst Su.

"Acquiring weapons is not like ordering at a drive-through. Production, delivery and training all take time before the systems can enter service and become effective."

World.title: Judge certifies fresh bid to jail Sakaja, Charles Kerich over Sh76.7m debt as urgent
World.content:
Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja. [File, Standard]

The High Court has certified as urgent a fresh application seeking to have Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja, former Finance Executive Charles Kerich and two other county officials jailed over an alleged breach of a court-approved payment plan in a Sh106.7 million legal fees dispute.

Justice Francis Gikonyo certified the application by Kwengu & Company Advocates seeking to reinstate a three-month jail sentence previously imposed on Kerich and hold Sakaja, current Finance County Executive Committee Member Ibrahim Auma Nyangoya and Chief Officer for Finance Asha Abdi accountable for the alleged failure to pay Sh76.7 million.

World.title: Kenya confirms third Ebola case
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Kenya has confirmed a third case of Ebola involving a 65-year-old woman who is a close relative of the first two patients.

The Ministry of Health, in a statement, said the woman developed a fever, sore throat and malaise while in quarantine, prompting her isolation and testing.

Her samples tested positive for Ebola at both the National Virology Reference Laboratory and the Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI).

According to the Health Director-General Patrick Amoth, the patient has been transferred to an infectious disease unit, where she is receiving supportive care and being monitored.

“Having been in quarantine, she was diagnosed early and is currently receiving supportive care, improving her chances of recovery while limiting the risk of further spread of the disease,” the statement read.

The second patient, on the other hand, is in stable condition and responding well to supportive care.

The latest case brings the number of confirmed Ebola infections in Kenya to three.

According to the Ministry, of the 130 contacts identified so far, 127 had been traced and placed in quarantine, with efforts ongoing to trace the remaining three.

World.title: Motorists, households face fresh fuel price hikes
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

EPRA attributed the price increases to the escalating conflict in the Middle East. [FIle, Standard]

The Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA) has increased fuel prices, raising the cost of super petrol by Sh12.93 per litre, diesel by Sh9.90, and kerosene by Sh28.49.

The new prices, effective from October 15 to November 14, 2026, will see motorists in Nairobi pay up to Sh226.96 per litre for super petrol, Sh227.76 for diesel, and Sh219.85 for kerosene.

EPRA Director-General Edward Mwirigi Kinyua attributed the price increases to the escalating conflict in the Middle East, which has disrupted petroleum supply chains and driven up the cost of importing fuel.

The rise in kerosene prices is likely to hit low-income households that rely on the fuel for cooking and lighting.

Meanwhile, higher diesel prices could raise the cost of transporting goods and operating public service vehicles, potentially driving up fares and commodity prices.

Diesel is a key fuel for the country's freight transport sector and a significant portion of public service vehicle operations, meaning the increase could have a ripple effect across the economy.

The latest review comes after EPRA maintained pump prices during the September 15 to October 14 pricing period, despite a decline in the cost of importing petrol.

World.title: Oburu Oginga to leave hospital soon - ODM
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

ODM SG Catherine Omanyo criticised bloggers spreading unverified information about the veteran politician.

ODM Secretary General Catherine Omanyo has dismissed social media reports about the health of party leader Oburu Oginga, saying he is recovering well and is expected to be discharged from hospital either today or tomorrow.

Omanyo criticised bloggers spreading unverified information about the veteran politician, accusing them of exploiting his health condition to attract online attention and increase engagement.

“It's unfortunate what I've been reading on social media. Those people who are seeking to have more likes or viewers, they will be disappointed because he's up, he's well, he's fine. In fact, he's headed home either today or tomorrow,” she said.

Omanyo insisted that the reports had exaggerated his situation, dismissing claims of his death and assuring the public that he was doing well.

She noted that health conditions could fluctuate, saying Oburu's position as ODM party leader had made his well-being a subject of heightened public interest.

“Everybody, everybody, including you and me, our health is not static. You can be under the weather any time. It's just that he's a party leader, and it makes breaking news,” Omanyo said.

She urged social media users to exercise restraint when discussing the health of public figures, warning against spreading unverified reports, particularly claims of death, before confirmation from credible sources.

Her remarks come amid growing speculation on social media about Oburu's health, with some users circulating unverified claims about his condition.

World.title: Kenya declares Ebola a formidable epidemic disease, sets new rules
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale, who declared Ebola caused by the Bundibugyo virus a formidable epidemic disease under the Public Health Act. [File,Standard]

Kenya has declared Ebola virus a formidable epidemic disease, introducing new rules governing screening, isolation, quarantine, contact tracing and the handling of bodies.

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale issued the declaration through a legal notice published in the Kenya Gazette on Monday, October 12, under Section 35 of the Public Health Act.

The declaration follows Kenya’s confirmation of its first imported case of Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease on October 6, after a Kenyan citizen who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo travelled through Uganda to Nairobi. The patient died despite receiving supportive treatment.

The case prompted health authorities to trace people who may have come into contact with the patient and strengthen screening at points of entry.

In an update on October 12, the World Health Organization (WHO) said Kenya had listed 127 contacts, with 94 in quarantine, and screened more than 665,000 travellers at points of entry.

WHO also supplied protective equipment and testing materials worth about US$70,000 to support the response.

The government published two legal notices on October 12. Legal Notice No. 203 declares the disease a formidable epidemic, while Legal Notice No. 204 establishes the Public Health (Ebola Disease) Rules, 2026.

The regulations provide for screening at points of entry, medical assessment, isolation, referral, quarantine and monitoring.

They also assign responsibilities to transport operators, health facilities, medical practitioners and laboratories.

Health authorities will conduct investigations and contact tracing, while designated health facilities will manage suspected and confirmed cases. The rules also provide for the inspection and decontamination of premises.

The regulations cover the safe and dignified disposal of bodies, burial procedures, record-keeping, transportation and repatriation. They also address public communication, media houses’ responsibilities in public sensitisation and assistance from enforcement agencies.

The rules provide for offences and penalties, although the Gazette extract does not specify the penalties for individual violations.

What the declaration means

Bundibugyo virus disease is a form of Ebola that spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person or contaminated materials.

Contact with the body of someone who has died from the disease can also expose people to infection during unsafe burial practices.

Symptoms can include fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache and sore throat, followed by vomiting and diarrhoea. The incubation period ranges from two to 21 days.

WHO says no approved vaccine or specific treatment currently exists for the Bundibugyo strain, making early detection, isolation, supportive care and contact tracing central to controlling its spread.

The health agency has advised against travel or trade restrictions on Kenya, Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo based on the information available.

The new rules establish a legal framework for managing the disease, from identifying suspected infections and monitoring contacts to caring for patients and preventing exposure during burials.

World.title: Egypt condemns attack on King Fahd Airport in Saudi Arabia
World.content:
Egypt strongly condemned the Wednesday evening attack on the King Fahd Airport in Dammam, Saudi Arabia.

In an official statement published on its Facebook page, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs stated: “The Arab Republic of Egypt expresses its strongest condemnation and denunciation of the attack that targeted King Fahd Airport in the city of Dammam in the brotherly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. The attack resulted in two civilian casualties and several injuries, in a continued violation of international law and a indiscriminate, irresponsible targeting of air navigation, facilities, and civilians.”

“Egypt stresses its absolute rejection of such practices that inflame the crisis, escalate tension, and destabilize the region. Egypt reaffirms its full solidarity and stand alongside the brotherly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and its leadership in defending its territory and citizens, as the Kingdom’s security is an integral part of Arab and Egyptian national security,” the statement added.

Death toll at 2, 8 injured

The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) announced on Thursday that the death toll from the attack rose to two following a confirmed additional fatality, while the number of injured remains at eight people.

According to the Saudi Press Agency (SPA), quoting the authority’s statement: “Further to the statement issued by the General Authority of Civil Aviation regarding the brutal attack that targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam on Wednesday evening, Jumada Al-Awwal 10, 1448 AH (corresponding to October 21, 2026); the Authority reports that the death toll from the attack has risen to two following a confirmed additional fatality.”

The authority stated that the deceased were a Saudi citizen and an Indian resident.

The list of injured includes a Saudi citizen, two Indian residents, two Yemeni residents, two Bangladeshi residents, and a Nepalese resident.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Egypt to see falling temperatures and heavier autumn rains
World.content:
Meteorological authorities have issued a warning regarding weather conditions during late-night and early-morning hours, as lower minimum temperatures are expected across all regions, alongside winds that will heighten the coldness.

Authorities advised taking a jacket when going out during this time of the year —especially for the elderly and children— in order to prevent catching colds.

El Niño strikes Egypt

According to meteorologists, Egypt is currently being affected this year by the El Niño phenomenon, which impacts countries surrounding oceans, particularly the central and eastern areas of the Pacific Ocean, leading to altered weather patterns.

El Niño leads to a rise in global average temperatures, and the overall warming of the Earth contributes to increased climate shifts.

Meteorologists forecast that the phenomenon’s impact will intensify during November and December, causing a clear climatic shift during the autumn season.

They explained that Egypt is among the countries indirectly affected by this phenomenon, noting that the Meteorological Authority announced autumn rainfall rates this year will be higher than average due to rising sea surface temperatures in the Mediterranean Sea and the impact of climate change.

World.title: Two killed and eight injured in attack targeting King Fahd Airport in Saudi Arabia
World.content:
The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) disclosed the casualties from the attack targeting King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, Saudi Arabia.

In a post on its official X (formerly Twitter) account, GACA reported that the death toll from the attack rose to two following confirmation of an additional fatality.

The deceased were a Saudi citizen and an Indian national.

The Authority noted that eight people were injured, with conditions ranging from minor to severe.

The injured include a Saudi citizen, two Indian nationals, two Yemeni nationals, two Bangladeshi nationals, and one Nepalese national.

GACA indicated that: “They are receiving the necessary medical care in several hospitals. We pray for mercy for the deceased and a speedy recovery for the injured.”

The statement concluded by emphasizing the “ongoing work—in full coordination and integration with relevant security authorities—to assess the damages, take all necessary measures to ensure the safety of passengers and workers, and maintain the security and safety of the Kingdom’s civil aviation ecosystem.”

According to GACA, operational activities at the airport have resumed and air traffic has returned to normal.

World.title: Petroleum Minister, Total Energies discuss fast tracking Cyprus gas link
World.content:
Minister of Petroleum and Mineral Resources Karim Badawi said Egypt is keen to accelerate the connection of Cypriot gas to its infrastructure and strengthen cooperation with French energy company Total Energies to advance exploration, development and production activities in the Mediterranean.

Badawi made the remarks during a meeting with Julian Bouguet, the company’s Senior Vice President for Exploration and Production in North Africa and the Middle East, on the sidelines of the Mediterranean Petroleum Conference and Exhibition in Alexandria.

The meeting, attended by Total Energies Executive Director for Egypt, Lebanon and Cyprus Leila El Hares, reviewed natural gas projects, progress on linking Cyprus’ Cronos gas field to Egypt in cooperation with the petroleum sector, Eni and Total Energies, and opportunities to boost investment in gas exploration and production in Egypt’s Mediterranean waters.

Badawi said progress on the project highlighted the importance of partnerships between governments and global energy companies.

He noted that high-level political support from the Egyptian and Cypriot leaderships had advanced implementation and strengthened coordination among stakeholders.

He said the project would enable Cyprus to export its natural gas using Egypt’s infrastructure for reception, processing and re-export, strengthening Egypt’s role as a regional gas trading hub and delivering mutual economic benefits.

Badawi also expressed interest in expanding Total Energies’ investments in Egypt’s natural gas sector, reaffirming the ministry’s readiness to support projects and explore technical and commercial solutions to cut costs, improve economic viability and accelerate investment decisions.

For his part, TotalEnergies Senior Vice President for Exploration and Production in North Africa and the Middle East Julian Bouguet praised cooperation with the Ministry of Petroleum and Mineral Resources, saying the company was continuing to assess promising exploration prospects and identify areas with strong gas potential.

He added that access to more technical data would improve the assessment of exploration opportunities, noting the company’s intention to continue evaluating prospects in the coming period.

World.title: Sisi: Strong state institutions, public confidence essential to protecting Egypt
World.content:
President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said Wednesday, October 21, 2026, that preserving strong state institutions and public confidence in them is essential to protecting Egypt against attempts to undermine the state.

Speaking at a session titled “National and Citizen Security” on the third day of Egypt Forum 2026, Sisi stressed the need for stronger communication between state institutions and citizens to convey facts and maintain domestic cohesion.

He also said Arab national security is indivisible and that the stability of Gulf states is an integral part of Egypt’s national security.

The session addressed efforts to develop the security system, manage crises and emergencies, and respond to regional and international challenges.

It was attended by Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly and Minister of Defense and Military Production Ashraf Salem Zaher, with Interior Minister Mahmoud Tawfiq, Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty, and Armed Forces Operations Authority chief and National Authority for Crisis and Emergency Management head Mohamed Abdelrahman Rabie also taking part.

Sisi said the Interior Ministry had developed a comprehensive plan to modernize security operations in response to evolving methods of crime.

The plan rests on five pillars: upgrading police facilities and equipping them with modern technology; adopting a scientific approach that uses artificial intelligence and early detection to identify crime patterns and develop appropriate responses; investing in personnel and specialized capabilities; raising public awareness; and modernizing correctional policies for convicted offenders.

He said efforts to strengthen state institutions were essential to preventing state collapse, citing the events of 2011 as a warning.

The Armed Forces and Interior Ministry constitute the two pillars of national security, he said, adding that efforts to undermine the police and portray its practices negatively had continued, sometimes reinforced unintentionally through everyday public reactions to events.

Sisi said the Interior Ministry had a responsibility to introduce initiatives to improve and maintain public perceptions of its work. He urged the Armed Forces and the ministry to develop further initiatives to communicate regularly with citizens and provide accurate information, helping build public confidence and prevent a divide between the people and state institutions.

Referring to the events of 2011, Sisi called for keeping public memory of that period alive to prevent a recurrence. He cited attacks on security forces, the storming of police stations and prisons, and the escape of 33,000 prisoners, saying such events had serious consequences.

Attempts to undermine the police and Armed Forces also sought to cast doubt on their competence and capabilities, he added, arguing that a state with strong institutions trusted by its people is difficult to bring down.

Sisi said the development and modernization of correctional and rehabilitation centers stemmed from ethical, religious and humanitarian principles.

He said the aim was to ensure that offenders were not punished twice for the same crime, with greater emphasis on rehabilitation and helping inmates reintegrate into society. He called for visits to these centers to showcase the work undertaken.

He added that the extensive damage inflicted before 2011 had prompted a rethink of detention facilities as part of the broader security system, and said the defense and interior ministries should continue developing initiatives to strengthen communication with the public.

Sisi also highlighted the role of the National Authority for Crisis and Emergency Management as a supporting arm of the state and government in managing crises and emergencies nationwide.

Its database and capabilities had made it an additional source of support for state agencies, helping improve government performance and effectiveness, he said.

Turning to foreign policy, Sisi said Egypt’s principles since 2014 had included non-interference in other countries’ internal affairs, rejecting conspiracies against states, preserving national unity and state institutions, refusing to engage with armed militias, supporting reconstruction and development, and maintaining balanced relations with all countries.

He stressed the importance of strategic balance and cautioned against taking state decisions under public pressure.

Sisi concluded by calling for continued efforts to strengthen Egypt and maintain a resilient public opinion, warning that the country faced multiple risks beyond the Ethiopian dam issue.

Arab national security, he said, was indivisible, and the stability of Gulf states was a matter of direct concern to Egypt’s national security.

He also called for restoring stability across Arab countries, including Sudan, Libya and Somalia, describing Egypt’s support for Gulf states as an extension of shared Arab national security.

Sisi further said Egypt’s military efforts were intended to defend Saudi territory and borders, not to launch attacks on Yemen.

He said Egypt would defend the territory of Saudi Arabia or any other Arab country if requested to do so, adding that Egyptian military operations would not extend beyond Egypt’s borders or those of a fellow Arab state whose security and stability Egypt sought to protect.

World.title: Al-Azhar warns of ‘Imminent Death’ facing patients in Gaza hospitals, calls for urgent global action
World.content:
Al-Azhar warned on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, of an imminent humanitarian catastrophe and certain death facing hundreds of patients, the wounded, and infants in intensive care units and incubators across Gaza Strip hospitals.

This warning follows alarming statements issued by the Palestinian Ministry of Health regarding the depletion of fuel and oil reserves required to power hospital generators.

Al-Azhar emphasized that deliberately severing the energy lifeline from medical facilities constitutes a collective death sentence for innocent civilians and a full-fledged war crime that violates all international laws and conventions.

In a statement released on Wednesday, Al-Azhar called on the international community, as well as UN and humanitarian organizations, to assume their full responsibilities in the face of silence over this suffocating siege.

It cautioned that turning hospitals from life-saving sanctuaries into mass graves represents a stain on the conscience of humanity and explicit complicity.

Al-Azhar urged swift international action to compel the occupation to open humanitarian corridors and allow the unconditional entry of vital supplies.

Al-Azhar appealed to the Arab and Islamic worlds, the international community, and all living consciences worldwide to act urgently and exert all forms of pressure to rescue the enclave’s healthcare system and break this unjust siege.

It commended the resilience of the valiant medical staff and paramedics in Gaza, who continue to display extraordinary courage and sacrifice in the face of the machine of death and destruction.

World.title: PM: Egypt priorities social protection amid global crisis
World.content:
Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly announced that securing new financial resources for social protection programs remains the Egyptian government’s top priority over the next three years, despite unprecedented global economic challenges.

Speaking at the “Egypt 2026 Forum” during a session on market regulation and effective social safety nets, Madbouly explained that structural economic reforms address decades-old issues while explicitly shielding vulnerable social groups from negative financial impacts.

Highlighting key initiatives, Madbouly noted that the “Takaful and Karama” program has aided 8.2 million families since inception.

Operating on a three-year rotational model designed to transition households into sustainable employment, the initiative currently supports 4.7 million families and will continue to adapt to economic shifts.

Addressing the planned commodity cash-support system, the Prime Minister emphasized that the government is not cutting funding or beneficiaries—who currently represent nearly 60 percent of Egyptian households. Instead, the model offers flexible cash allocations for essential goods tailored to individual family needs while factoring in inflation.

Budget allocations for food and bread subsidies have grown from LE32.8 billion in 2013–2014 to LE178 billion this year.

Additionally, healthcare and education budgets increased by 30 percent and 20 percent year-over-year, respectively, as the government seeks expanded fiscal space to accelerate nationwide rollout of comprehensive health insurance.

World.title: A small but powerful African nation is bringing Formula 1 back to the continent. Not everyone is celebrating
World.content:
Formula One is to return to Africa for the first time in more than three decades, with Rwanda granted a 10-year contract to host a Grand Prix from the early 2030s – a deal described by F1 chief Stefano Domenicali as a “landmark” moment.

For Rwandan President Paul Kagame, the race offers a chance to attract more visitors and investment to the East African nation and raise its global profile. Kagame has led the country for decades, and his government has long been accused of abuses over its treatment of political opponents, journalists and other critics.

The race will be branded the Formula 1 African Grand Prix, presented by Visit Rwanda, the country’s tourism-promotion brand. But while Domenicali says F1 is “showing the world what it means to be a country that has a vision,” Rwanda’s use of sports to promote itself internationally has drawn criticism from human rights groups. Meanwhile, allegations of its support for M23 rebels in neighboring Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) have also raised questions about the image it hopes to project.

Rwanda has spent years building its international profile through sports. Its Visit Rwanda campaign has partnered with prominent European soccer clubs, including Arsenal, Paris Saint-Germain, Atlético Madrid and Bayern Munich, though the arrangements have varied. Arsenal’s eight-season partnership ended in June 2026, while PSG’s agreement runs through 2028. Bayern shifted its deal toward youth development in Kigali, the Rwandan capital, after facing criticism over the partnership.

In July, English Premier League side Aston Villa signed a multi-year Visit Rwanda sponsorship agreement reportedly worth around £20 million (roughly $26.8 million) a year. Human rights campaigners, including Amnesty International UK, have spoken out against the deal, arguing that it could improve Rwanda’s international image despite concerns about repression at home and its alleged role in the conflict in eastern DRC.

Critics have described such partnerships as “sportswashing.”

Hosting a Grand Prix, one of the world’s most prominent sporting events, would take that strategy beyond soccer sponsorships. The race would bring teams, corporate partners, international media and spectators to Rwanda, creating opportunities to promote tourism and attract business. The government hopes it will create jobs, develop local skills and deliver lasting economic benefits.

Itamar Dubinsky, a senior lecturer in African studies and politics at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev in Israel who researches sports and politics in Africa, told CNN that hosting a race differs from paying for visibility through soccer club sponsorships. It would bring the sport’s international network directly into the country.

A worker looks at a display of the Bugesera circuit on the site where it will it be constructed, following the announcement of the deal for a new African Grand Prix, in Bugesera, Rwanda, October 13, 2026. Jean Bizimana/Reuters

The race is planned for a new circuit in Bugesera, about 40 kilometers (25 miles) south of Kigali, as part of a wider development project led by the Rwanda Development Board. The circuit must be completed before the race can take place, and F1 has not announced an inaugural date. Its public announcement does not specify how the project will be financed or what returns it is expected to generate.

Questions remain about the cost, potential public investment and how the venue will be used outside race weekends.

The image Rwanda wants the world to see

Rwanda wants to be seen as a country that attracts tourists and investors and can host major international events. But that image contrasts with criticism of the government’s human rights record. Human Rights Watch (HRW) has documented restrictions on political opposition, independent media and dissent under Kagame. In a report this month, the organization warned that the Grand Prix could put journalists and vulnerable communities at risk.

Lewis Mudge, HRW’s Central Africa director, said F1 had yet to explain how it would assess the agreement’s human rights implications.

“The F1 talks only about the social and economic impact of this deal but, to date, we’ve seen no language with regard to what effect this could have on the human rights outlook in Rwanda,” he told CNN.

Mudge said Rwanda had barred three HRW staff members from entering the country because of their work. He also cited the organization’s documentation of authorities detaining homeless people and street vendors ahead of major events. Before an international conference in Kigali in 2021, some of the city’s poorest residents were detained in a warehouse described as a transit center until foreign visitors had left, according to HRW.

The organization has urged Formula One to assess human rights risks, consult civil society and establish measurable protections for journalists covering the event. F1 has not publicly confirmed that it will adopt those recommendations.

F1 defended its decision to hold the race in Rwanda, telling CNN it had a “long track record of delivering significant economic, social and cultural value to our host nations.” A spokesperson said the race could inspire the sport’s more than 100 million fans across Africa and that F1 believed sport could be “a positive force for good.”

Commuters line up for buses and motorcycle taxis during afternoon rush hour in the center of the Rwandan capital Kigali on April 05, 2024. J. Countess/Getty Images

F1 also referred CNN to comments by Domenicali, its president and CEO, who highlighted the potential for tourism, investment, skills development and business growth. The organization said it had spent years searching for the right partner for its return to Africa and that several parties had expressed interest.

However, F1’s announcement does not explain how potential hosts were assessed or how human rights concerns factored into Rwanda’s selection. CNN asked follow-up questions about its human rights safeguards and due diligence but has not received a response.

Kate Hixon, Africa advocacy director for Amnesty International USA, said Formula One should investigate whether money it receives from Rwanda could be linked to minerals procured from abusive operations in eastern DRC.

Amnesty has reported abuses against miners in areas taken over by M23 and alleged that gold and coltan are smuggled into Rwanda. Hixon urged F1 to publish its due diligence findings.

“Racing fans deserve assurances that money generated from the M23’s abuses is not funding the Grand Prix,” she told CNN.

CNN contacted the Rwanda Development Board and the Rwandan government spokesperson for comment but has not received a response.

The war next door

United Nations experts have documented Rwandan military support for M23 rebels, which have seized territory in eastern DRC. Rwanda disputes allegations about its involvement. The conflict has displaced communities and caused widespread civilian suffering.

A human rights observer in the DRC, known as Healing and Rebuilding our Communities (HROC RDC), described Rwanda’s international image as mixed, with recognition for development and infrastructure alongside allegations of involvement in the conflict. It told CNN that the contrast with civilian suffering in eastern DRC had fueled frustration and called for civilian protection, transparency and accountability.

A displaced family returns toward the village of Togota after seeking refuge elsewhere following a lull in fighting in South Kivu, eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, on December 13, 2025. Jospin Mwisha/AFP/Getty Images

That frustration was also reflected in criticism from DRC Foreign Minister Thérèse Kayikwamba Wagner, who called F1’s decision to hold a Grand Prix in Rwanda “morally indefensible” and said it “would help polish the image of an authoritarian leader.”

Jacques Issongo, from the Congolese civil society movement LUCHA, said Rwanda’s sporting partnerships were intended to divert attention from the conflict.

“By multiplying major partnerships with global sporting giants such as F1, Arsenal and Paris Saint-Germain, Rwanda is creating a media and diplomatic diversion,” he told CNN.

Beyond the spectacle

Africa’s last Formula One World Championship race was held in South Africa in 1993. South Africa hosted 23 championship races, while Morocco held one in 1958. The 1985 South African Grand Prix took place during apartheid, and French teams Renault and Ligier did not attend amid opposition to the country’s racial policies.

Formula One did not return to South Africa in 1986, as international protest over apartheid hardened. It returned in 1992 and 1993 as the apartheid regime was dismantled, but financial problems then ended the South African Grand Prix again. Since then, the high cost of hosting a Grand Prix, infrastructure requirements, and competition for a place on the calendar have blocked an African return.

Drivers including Ayrton Senna and Damon Hill race in the final Grand Prix of South-Africa, Kyalami, 14 March 1993. Paul-Henri Cahier/Hulton Archive/Getty Images

Rwanda now hopes to overcome those barriers, but hosting the race is only part of the challenge.

Formula One may bring visibility, tourism and international prestige, but Dubinsky, the African Studies researcher, says the question is what remains after the cameras leave. If Rwanda builds an expensive circuit that sees limited use, he warned, it could become a “white elephant.”

The race’s success, he said, will depend on whether it delivers lasting economic and social benefits and whether those benefits outweigh the negative attention that the deal may bring.

For Mudge, the bigger concern is whether Rwanda’s pursuit of international recognition will overshadow the country’s human rights record and undermine efforts to improve it.

“Rwanda is run by a government that is very protective of its global image no matter the cost,” he said.

World.title: Liberians in Rwanda Back Push for Direct Kigali–Monrovia Flights
World.content:
LIBCOR leaders meet travel agency, RwandAir representatives

KIGALI, Rwanda – Leaders of the Liberian Community in Rwanda (LIBCOR) have pledged to support an initiative to establish a direct air link between Kigali and Monrovia. They gave the pledge after meeting a Liberian travel agency working on the effort with Rwanda’s national carrier, RwandAir.

The LIBCOR delegation met Tuesday evening with Gbomai Bestman, chief executive officer of Easy Continental Travel Agency, and two senior members of her team. Bestman is in Rwanda on a working visit.



According to a statement from LIBCOR, the talks focused on the agency’s ongoing initiative with RwandAir, its objectives, and what it could mean for Liberians living in Rwanda.

Seleke Kromah, LIBCOR’s Vice Chairman for Administration, led the delegation. Other members of the community’s National Administrative Council attended, including the Vice Chairman for International Affairs, the Financial Secretary and the Treasurer.

The statement said the council took part on the instructions of LIBCOR Chairman James Edgar Denia. Members discussed how the community’s leadership could support the initiative.

Speaking for the delegation, Kromah thanked Bestman for what he called her continued cooperation, partnership and support for Liberians in Rwanda. He said LIBCOR would work with her team to explain the initiative’s goals and benefits to community members.

LIBCOR said it would share details of a planned engagement with the wider Liberian community in Rwanda beginning Thursday.

“LIBCOR remains committed to building meaningful partnerships that promote connectivity, strengthen relationships, and create opportunities for Liberians in Rwanda and back home,” the statement said.

The statement did not say when direct flights might begin, what routes or schedules are being considered, or what role RwandAir has formally committed to.

World.title: Liberia: Final Arguments Set in Peter Bon Jallah Case
World.content:
After months of contested proceedings, prosecution and defense are expected to present their closing arguments as Criminal Court ‘E’ prepares to conclude the trial phase.

By Victoria G. Wesseh

MONROVIA — Criminal Court “E” is scheduled to hear final arguments on Thursday, October 22, in the high-profile case involving Peter Bon Jallah, who is facing multiple felony charges, including gang rape, statutory rape and kidnapping.



The case has reached a critical stage following months of evidentiary proceedings in which the prosecution and defense presented witnesses and sought to establish their respective positions.

The closing arguments will give both sides an opportunity to summarize the evidence, address disputed facts and advance their legal interpretations before the court determines the next steps toward a verdict.

Prosecution and Defense Rest Cases

According to court records, the trial has been vigorously contested, with both sides presenting witnesses in support of their respective cases.

The Government of Liberia, represented by prosecutors from the Ministry of Justice, presented 13 general witnesses and six rebuttal witnesses before resting its case.

The defense, representing Jallah, called eight general witnesses and three subpoenaed witnesses to challenge the prosecution’s allegations and advance its position.

The testimony presented by both sides is expected to feature prominently in their closing arguments as they seek to persuade the court on the strength of the evidence and the applicable law.

Trial Reaches Critical Stage

The case is being heard under Liberia’s legal framework governing rape and other serious criminal offenses. The charges against Jallah include gang rape, statutory rape and kidnapping, each of which carries significant legal consequences if established in accordance with the law.

The final arguments are an important stage of the proceedings, allowing prosecutors to explain why they believe the evidence supports a conviction and enabling the defense to challenge the prosecution’s case.

Presiding Judge Wesseh A. Wesseh will be responsible for considering the evidence and legal arguments presented before the court.

The outcome will depend on the evidence admitted during the trial and the court’s application of the relevant legal standards.

Public Scrutiny and the Fight Against Sexual Violence

The proceedings come amid continued public concern over sexual and gender-based violence in Liberia and calls from civil society organizations and women’s rights advocates for accountability in cases involving sexual offenses.

The administration of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has pledged to uphold the rule of law and strengthen protections for vulnerable people, including minors.

The handling of high-profile cases such as the one involving Jallah is likely to draw continued public attention to the justice system’s response to allegations of sexual violence and the importance of ensuring that criminal proceedings are conducted fairly and without undue delay.

As the court prepares to hear the final arguments, the prosecution and defense will have the opportunity to make their closing submissions before the matter advances toward a determination.

The defendant is presumed innocent until proven guilty by a court of competent jurisdiction.

World.title: Liberia: Supreme Court to Hear Final Appeal in Dennis Estate’s 200-Acre Property Case
World.content:
After earlier rulings affirmed the estate’s ownership, the Supreme Court is set to review a fresh appeal challenging lower court judgments over land in Paynesville’s 72nd Community, with the timeliness of the appeal emerging as a key issue.

By Victoria G. Wesseh

MONROVIA — The Supreme Court of Liberia is set to hear arguments in a decades-long dispute over approximately 200 acres of land in Paynesville’s 72nd Community, as it considers an appeal challenging judgments affirming ownership by the Estate of the late Wilmot F. Dennis.



The appeal was filed by Mark Dennis, also known as Mack Dennis, and Henry Dennis, who are challenging lower court rulings in favor of Madam Estella Dennis-Turay, administratrix of her late father’s intestate estate.

The dispute dates back to 1963 and has passed through multiple judicial proceedings, including earlier appeals to the Supreme Court. The latest proceedings could determine whether the challenged lower court judgments will stand, although the outcome remains in the hands of the justices.

A Dispute Dating to 1963

According to court records, the dispute began in 1963 when four children of Wilmot F. Dennis—Estella Dennis-Turay, Sam Ford Dennis, Mabel Dennis Mann and Jeannette Dennis-Pratt—filed an action before the Sixth Judicial Circuit seeking to cancel deeds they alleged had been improperly obtained by distant relatives to properties belonging to their father, who died before 1954.

After 16 years of litigation, the Civil Law Court ruled in 1979 in favor of the siblings, voiding the disputed deeds and ordering the approximately 200-acre property restored to them.

Subsequent disputes involving boundaries and alleged encroachment by adjoining landowners led to two separate appeals before the Supreme Court.

In 1988 and 1989, the Supreme Court affirmed the 1979 judgment, according to the case history presented in the court records.

Those rulings form a central part of the estate’s position in the latest proceedings.

Dispute Resurfaces After Civil War

The dispute resurfaced during the period surrounding Liberia’s civil conflicts, when Dennis-Turay was reportedly outside the country.

According to subsequent court findings, the defendants began asserting ownership claims over the property during her absence.

On August 30, 2005, then-Civil Law Court Judge Emery Paye issued a writ of possession placing the defendants in possession of the land. The estate later challenged the writ, arguing that it had been issued without notice to the parties previously adjudged to be the rightful owners.

In a ruling dated August 26, 2025, Judge George W. Smith of the Civil Law Court revisited the matter. The decision was subsequently reaffirmed by then-presiding Judge Boima Kontoe on February 25, 2026.

According to the rulings described in the court records, the lower court found that the defendants had misrepresented their status in the proceedings that led to the 2005 writ.

The court characterized their conduct as involving alleged deception, fraud, perjury and contempt, and described them as impostors in relation to the ownership claims.

Those findings form part of the judicial history now before the Supreme Court.

Estate Relies on Probate and Earlier Judgments

Probate records cited by the estate indicate that between 2005 and 2012, Dennis-Turay petitioned the Probate Court to administer her late father’s estate.

The records reportedly included original deeds and certified copies of the 1979 Civil Law Court judgment and the Supreme Court’s 1988 and 1989 decisions.

In 2012, Dennis-Turay was reportedly deeded the property as the sole surviving heir. The deed was subsequently probated and registered.

The estate is relying on these records, together with the earlier judgments, to support its position that ownership of the property has already been judicially determined.

The defendants’ latest appeal has nevertheless brought the matter back before the country’s highest court.

Timeliness of Appeal Becomes a Key Issue

Following Judge Kontoe’s February 25, 2026 ruling, the defendants filed a Bill of Exceptions on March 23, 2026, challenging the judgment.

The estate contends that the filing was made outside the statutory deadline and has asked the Supreme Court to dismiss the appeal on procedural grounds.

According to the estate’s filing, the Bill of Exceptions was submitted 28 days after the judgment, rather than within the 10-day period it says the law requires.

On March 31, 2026, the estate filed a motion seeking dismissal of the appeal for untimely filing.

The case record has since been transmitted to the Supreme Court for consideration.

The justices will have to determine the procedural issues raised by the parties and consider any substantive questions properly before them. Whether the appeal can proceed will depend on the court’s assessment of the applicable legal requirements and the arguments presented.

Earlier Supreme Court Rulings at the Center of the Case

The estate’s position rests substantially on the Supreme Court’s 1988 and 1989 decisions affirming the 1979 judgment.

The doctrines of res judicata and stare decisis may be relevant to the dispute. Res judicata generally concerns the finality of matters already adjudicated between parties, while stare decisis addresses the authority of judicial precedents.

However, the application of these doctrines depends on the specific facts, parties, issues and procedural circumstances before the court.

The Supreme Court’s earlier decisions and the subsequent probate proceedings are therefore likely to feature prominently in the estate’s arguments as it seeks to preserve the lower court judgments.

The defendants’ appeal, meanwhile, will give the justices an opportunity to consider the challenges raised against the latest ruling.

For Dennis-Turay and the estate, a dismissal of the appeal or a decision affirming the lower court judgment would reinforce the existing rulings in their favor.

After more than six decades of litigation, the Supreme Court’s determination could mark a significant development in the long-running dispute over the 200-acre property in Paynesville’s 72nd Community.

The final outcome, however, will depend on the court’s ruling.

World.title: Liberia’s Billion-Dollar Budget: 0.58% for the Capital’s Public Schools
World.content:
Monrovia — Thousands of students in school uniforms marched on Liberia’s legislature on Tuesday, chanting “We want to learn too.” They were protesting months of disruption in the public schools of the capital, Monrovia, where unpaid teachers have repeatedly walked out of classrooms.

By Rodney D. Sieh

The students’ anger has a paper trail. Liberia’s own 2026 budget documents show that the Monrovia Consolidated School System (MCSS), which runs the city’s public schools, receives US$7.23 million. That is 0.58 percent of a national budget the government celebrates as the largest in the country’s history.



The same documents show that schools in the system get US$65,000 a year for educational materials — less than they get for stationery. They also show that three-quarters of the money recorded as the system’s capital spending last year was booked against an airport, a Finance Ministry headquarters and electoral reform.

A billion-dollar milestone

Liberia, a West African nation of about 5.2 million people, is still rebuilding from 14 years of civil war that ended in 2003. Its national budget crossed US$1 billion for the first time this year. Lawmakers approved US$1.25 billion for 2026, up 41.9 percent from the year before, according to an analysis by the budget-monitoring group BudgIT.

President Joseph Boakai’s development plan, known as the ARREST Agenda, names six priorities. The “E” stands for education. The “A” stands for agriculture, which receives about 1.19 percent of the budget even though the Agriculture Ministry’s own target is 10 percent.

The Monrovia Consolidated School System was created by law in 1964 to run public schools in the capital and surrounding communities. Families who cannot afford private fees depend on it. It is where the gap between budget promises and classroom reality is easiest to see.

“Our patience must not be mistaken for weakness”

Tuesday’s march, organized by the MCSS Students Union, lasted more than two hours. It followed a 24-hour ultimatum that expired the same day. Students gathered between the University of Liberia and the Capitol, the seat of the legislature, and handed lawmakers a petition with four demands.

They want the government to carry out a March 27 agreement with the school system on teachers’ pay and status. They want an investigation into alleged intimidation of student leaders. They want the dismissal of an assistant superintendent, Emmanuel Kyne Robertson, whom they accuse of disrupting classes and threatening students. And they want a bigger school budget and more transparency in how it is spent. The allegations have not been independently verified.

“Our patience must not be mistaken for weakness,” the union wrote, “and our commitment to peace must not be used to justify continued inaction while students’ education remains at risk.”

The House of Representatives read the petition in plenary and gave its education and petitions committees one week to report back.

Hours after the march, the government said it would add the remaining 201 volunteer MCSS teachers to the national payroll from October. That brings the number of verified MCSS volunteers absorbed to 409. Back pay is promised one week after October salaries. Teachers’ demands for higher pay were deferred to a government-wide salary reform, for which no date was given.

Where the money goes instead

Education receives US$136.3 million in 2026, or 10.9 percent of the budget. Security and rule of law receive US$154.9 million, about US$18.6 million more than education. Debt service takes US$230 million, 1.7 times the entire education sector.

Capital spending tells a similar story. Of the US$289.7 million set aside for investment projects, education gets 5.3 percent. Roads and energy together take about 61 percent.

Then there is the legislature. The draft budget gave lawmakers US$51.7 million, up from US$41.3 million in 2024. Their travel, goods and services line alone rose to US$14.6 million.

Put differently: the legislature’s running costs for travel and supplies are 38 times what the capital’s public schools get to run their classrooms for a year.

Stationery over science

The school system’s own pages in the 2026 budget book show how little reaches the classroom.

Salaries take 67 percent of the MCSS budget. Capital projects take 28 percent. Everything needed to actually run schools — books, chalk, cleaning, repairs, fuel — gets 5.3 percent, or US$380,000 for a whole year.

Within that sliver:

• Educational materials: US$65,000, down 35 percent from US$100,000 in 2025. That is less than the US$70,000 budgeted for stationery.

• Laboratory supplies: US$5,000 for every science lab in the system, cut from US$25,000.

• Generator fuel: US$54,500, up from US$2,000 — a 27-fold increase. It now nearly equals the entire budget for learning materials.

• ⁠

The outlook gets worse, not better. The government’s own projections cut the system’s operating budget by another 44 percent in 2027, to US$212,112. Educational materials would fall to US$36,282.

The budget also files every dollar of the school system under a single program: “Administration and Management.” There is no separate line for teaching.

The system’s payroll of US$4.85 million covers 1,088 staff, an average of about US$372 a month. That figure includes non-teaching staff. The budget keeps that headcount frozen through 2028, even as hundreds of volunteer teachers are added to the payroll.

An airport, a ministry and an election law

The most striking entry is on page 294 of the budget book. It lists the school system’s estimated capital spending for 2025 at US$388,691.

Only US$94,320 of that — 24 percent — is labeled as school renovation. The remaining US$294,371 is recorded under projects with no apparent link to schools: electoral legal reform (US$117,865), support for small and medium enterprises (US$84,306), a new Finance Ministry headquarters (US$82,135) and an upgrade of Robert International Airport (US$10,065).

The budget book contradicts itself. Elsewhere it records the system’s 2025 capital spending as US$320,150, all on furniture and fixtures, and none under the investment plan at all.

The entries may reflect a coding error rather than diverted money. But either way, the official record of what Liberia spent on its capital’s schools cannot be trusted as published.

For 2026, the budget promises US$2 million for renovating and furnishing MCSS schools. The system’s own list of 2025 achievements, however, claims only that it completed the procurement process to renovate four campuses — not the renovations themselves.

A school system running on volunteers

In December, Finance Minister Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan returned to his old school in Monrovia and announced a 60 percent increase for the capital’s schools, including a US$2 million fund to fix them. On paper, the promise holds: the MCSS budget rose from US$4.52 million to US$7.23 million. Take out the US$2 million capital line, much of it not yet delivered, and the increase is about 16 percent.

The teacher shortage the students are protesting is national. The Education Ministry says Liberia relies on 6,198 volunteer teachers who work without government salaries. In October, the ministry said it had removed more than 1,000 teachers who had abandoned their classrooms from the payroll. Lawmakers have also pressed officials over the U.S.-dollar portion of teachers’ salaries, unpaid since October 2025.

A mid-year supplementary budget, approved in May, added US$7.25 million for education. About 73 percent of it goes to closing payroll gaps and absorbing volunteers — paying for the past rather than building classrooms. MCSS received US$514,510. That includes US$200,000 for its volunteer teachers, roughly US$995 for each of the 201 now being added.

That money is fragile. About nine of every ten dollars in the supplementary package came from the World Bank, not Liberian revenue. BudgIT warned that moving volunteers onto the payroll creates permanent salary costs a one-off top-up cannot sustain. Meanwhile, the government projects total spending will fall to US$1.02 billion in 2027.

The largest share of that mid-year package — 27.8 percent — went not to schools or clinics but to public administration. It included an ambassador’s residence lease in Accra and Independence Day celebrations.

Who lives on the budget

The students did not cite budget codes on Tuesday. But their demands — pay the teachers, fix the classrooms, show where the money goes — line up closely with what the government’s own figures reveal.

The pattern echoes agriculture. A government that puts farming first in its slogan gives it about 1 percent of the budget. A government that puts education among its pillars gives the capital’s public schools less than 1 percent, and less for learning materials than for stationery.

The House committees have until next Tuesday to report on the students’ petition. The salary reform teachers were promised has no start date. The 2027 budget, now being prepared, is projected to be smaller.

For the students who marched, the question is simpler than any budget table. When a country spends US$1.25 billion in a year, why are they still waiting for a teacher to show up?
