World.title: Liberia: More Than 23 Years After Civil Wars, Survivors Begin Receiving Reparations Through Civil Society Initiative
World.content:
Rufus Kartee, 65, says he has lived with a bullet wound to his left hip since surviving the St. Peter’s Lutheran Church massacre in July 1990, 36 years ago. Credit: Anthony Stephens/New Narratives.

Summary:

A coalition of civil society institutions has begun providing medical assistance to Liberians injured during the country’s civil wars, marking an initial step toward reparations.

The initiative comes more than 17 years after Liberia’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission recommended the Liberian government establish a US$500 million (equivalent to US$781 million in today’s dollars) reparations program, which has yet to be implemented.

Advocates say it is the first step towards developing a national victims’ trust fund, funded by donations by Liberians matched by government funds, as survivors grow older and Liberia moves toward establishing a War and Economic Crimes Court.

By Anthony Stephens, senior justice correspondent with New Narratives

JOHN F. KENNEDY HOSPITAL, Monrovia— For 36 years, Rufus Kartee has lived with a bullet wound he says he suffered at the hands of troops of the Armed Forces of Liberia at St. Peter’s Lutheran Church in 1990, where one of Liberia’s deadliest wartime massacres took place. Now 65, he walks with a crutch, struggles to find shelter and sometimes begs for food. He lives with chronic pain and poverty long after the country’s civil wars ended.



On a recent afternoon here at the country’s largest hospital, Kartee holds his medical records and appointment card. A bullet struck his left hip during the massacre, he says, damaging the bone and leaving him unable to walk without assistance. After decades of unsuccessful appeals for medical care, he is finally receiving treatment.

“I am very happy,” Kartee says. “I am in serious pain. From the wound and the damaged bone, it has me breathing fast, fast.”

Kartee is among five civil war survivors receiving medical care through an initiative by the Liberia Massacre Survivors Association, the Independent National Commission on Human Rights and the Women’s NGOs Secretariat. Organizers call it Liberia’s first effort to provide medical treatment as reparations, more than 23 years after the wars ended.

Two beneficiaries are in Montserrado County, two in Nimba and one in Bomi.

The Commission contributed US$55 and LRD 22,000 toward treatment for two survivors at JFK, covering half the cost of a woman’s X-ray and treatment for neck wounds, as well as four pints of blood for Kartee.

The Ministry of Health paid the remaining JFK costs and treatment for the three survivors elsewhere. The Commission also covered transportation, says Commissioner Partmellia Doe Paivey. Kartee was the only patient to undergo surgery.

The survivors were treated for injuries to their arms, ribs, backs and other body parts. A woman from Bomi said forces loyal to former President Charles Taylor threw her into the Mayeh River in 2003, leaving her wounded.

The other four beneficiaries remain unidentified. Paivey said the Commission could not “disclose their names for other purposes,” without elaborating.

The new initiative grew from a proposal by human rights lawyer Tiawan Gongloe for a National War Victims Relief Fund supported by public contributions and government matching funds.

In an opinion piece in August, Gongloe proposed annual contributions of at least US$1 from employed Liberians and those abroad, L$100 from unemployed Liberians who could afford it, and US$5 in government matching funds for every US$1 raised.

At the survivors association’s 17th anniversary gathering in August, Jallah Barbu, head of the office establishing Liberia’s war and economic crimes court, made a public display of his support for the idea by donating the first dollar during his keynote address. Paivey accepted it and pledged to launch the fund within days.

The effort follows a longstanding recommendation of Liberia’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which proposed a US$500 million reparations program over 30 years in its 2009 final report , covering medical care, counseling, education and financial assistance.

More than 17 years later, the recommendations remain largely unfulfilled. In August 2024, then-Justice Minister Oswald Tweh pledged at the United Nations that the Boakai administration was “committed to establishing a reparation trust fund to support conflict victims.” No comprehensive program has emerged.

Kartee’s hardship has deepened with the loss of his wife and two daughters. His wife died of a stroke in July. His eldest daughter, Brenda, the family’s breadwinner, died in 2019 at 35. Another daughter, Kathy, died of tuberculosis that year at 27.

His surviving children also struggle financially. Enes, 40, is a farmer, while Rufus Kartee Jr., 36, is unemployed but helps his father with errands and medical visits.

Kartee describes his circumstances simply: “Very, very poor. Life is tough.”

Government militia fighters advance during fighting for control of a key bridge in Monrovia in 2003, as forces loyal to President Charles Taylor battled rebels of the Liberians United for Reconciliation and Democracy (LURD). Photo: Chris Hondros.

For survivors still living with injuries, trauma and poverty decades after Liberia’s civil wars, advocates say prosecutions alone are not enough.

“We feel that reparations cannot be left out of transitional justice,” says Paivey, a lawyer, arguing that criminal accountability alone cannot address the lasting suffering of war victims.

A memorial at St. Peter’s Lutheran Church honoring those killed in the July 1990 massacre.

But the Commission lacks funds even for Kartee’s nutrition during recovery. It is seeking US$250,000 in the 2026/2027 budget for a victims’ trust fund.

A proposed national reparations framework, potentially headed to the Legislature, would cover medical care, psychological support and economic assistance. Survivor consultations are planned for November. Peterson Sonyah, head of the Liberia Massacre Survivors Association, said his coalition also hopes to provide counseling.

Human rights advocate Adama Dempster has recenly called for an independent reparations body, arguing that compensation could aid reconciliation despite being unable to undo wartime suffering.

Paivey warns that survivors are aging, and some may be needed as witnesses in future war crimes trials.

Surgery has eased Kartee’s pain, but hopes to see those responsible for wartime atrocities face justice.

“So, we that are alive today, if I will survive, I will still be happy to see the people going through court process.”

This story was a collaboration with New Narratives as part of the Investigating Liberia project. Funding was provided by the U.N. Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights and the European Union. The funders had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: Liberia Steps Up Screening as Nigeria Confirms Case
World.content:
MONROVIA — Liberian health authorities are stepping up preparedness measures against Ebola following the confirmation of a case in Nigeria, ordering health facilities, border entry points, public buildings and other institutions nationwide to strengthen screening and immediately enforce infection prevention and control protocols.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

The latest measures come a day after the National Public Health Institute of Liberia (NPHIL) assessed preparedness at Roberts International Airport (RIA), as concerns grew over reports of eight new Ebola cases in Kenya and the potential for the disease to spread across borders.



The developments have prompted authorities to intensify efforts to strengthen surveillance, review emergency response arrangements and ensure that frontline institutions are prepared to identify and respond to suspected cases.

A senior Liberian health official told FrontPage Africa on Wednesday that health authorities were convening an emergency meeting to assess the country’s readiness and coordinate the next steps in the national response.

“We are convening a situation meeting … to start with our office before we first move to inform the various ports to prepare for the national response,” the official said. “We agree to convene … to plan for the eventuality, as NPHIL will obviously step up.”

NPHIL, which leads Liberia’s public health surveillance and outbreak response, is expected to play a central role in coordinating preparedness activities alongside the Ministry of Health and other relevant institutions.

The Ministry of Health has also issued a circular directing institutions across the country to immediately strengthen infection prevention and control measures.

NPHIL Assesses RIA Preparedness

Before Nigeria confirmed its Ebola case on Tuesday, October 20, NPHIL Interim Director General Dr. Sia Wata Camanor toured Roberts International Airport to assess the country’s preparedness to prevent and respond to a potential Ebola threat.

According to a release from NPHIL, the assessment focused on screening measures, infection prevention and control protocols, emergency response arrangements and other public health safeguards at the airport.

The visit formed part of the institute’s ongoing efforts, in collaboration with the Ministry of Health and relevant partners, to strengthen surveillance and ensure that Liberia can promptly detect and respond to public health emergencies.

During the tour, Camanor emphasized the importance of vigilance, effective coordination and strict adherence to established public health protocols at all points of entry.

NPHIL also urged travelers, airport authorities and the general public to remain alert and follow official public health guidance as Liberia strengthens its preparedness measures.

The airport assessment took place against the backdrop of reports of additional Ebola cases in Kenya, raising concerns about the potential regional spread of the disease.

The subsequent confirmation of a case in Nigeria has added urgency to regional surveillance and preparedness efforts.

Nationwide IPC Measures Ordered

In its circular, the Ministry of Health directed all health facilities, border entry points, public buildings and other institutions to strengthen screening and strictly enforce infection prevention and control protocols with immediate effect.

The directive requires institutions to ensure that functional handwashing stations, supplied with soap and water, or appropriate hand sanitizers are available at entrances.

Facilities must also screen individuals for symptoms and relevant travel or exposure histories in accordance with national guidance.

The Ministry emphasized that temperature checks alone are insufficient, underscoring the need for a more comprehensive approach to screening.

Other priority measures include strict adherence to hand hygiene, the appropriate use of personal protective equipment, environmental cleaning and the safe disposal of waste.

The circular further directs health facilities to immediately separate suspected cases from other patients and report them to the relevant County Health Teams and NPHIL. Suspected cases must be referred safely through designated channels.

Authorities have also been instructed to ensure adequate supplies of infection prevention materials and refresher training for frontline personnel.

Facility heads, county health authorities, border officials and institutional managers are responsible for ensuring compliance and promptly reporting shortages or other gaps requiring support.

The Ministry has urged the public to remain vigilant, observe recommended preventive measures and cooperate with health authorities.

Members of the public seeking additional information can contact the Ministry of Health hotline at 5888 or the NPHIL hotline at 4455.

Nigeria Case Raises Regional Concerns

The preparedness measures follow the reported confirmation of a Bundibugyo Ebola case in Nigeria, where the patient is receiving treatment in isolation in Abuja, the country’s capital.

According to information provided by Nigerian authorities and international health agencies, the woman had recently traveled to the Democratic Republic of Congo and Uganda before developing symptoms in Nigeria.

The case was laboratory-confirmed on October 20, according to the information supplied for this report.

Nigerian authorities have initiated contact tracing to identify and monitor people who may have been exposed to the patient. The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention has also activated its emergency response arrangements.

The World Health Organization has urged countries in the region to strengthen surveillance, laboratory readiness and screening at points of entry.

For Liberia, the developments underscore the importance of maintaining effective disease surveillance and ensuring that health authorities can quickly identify and respond to suspected cases.

However, the confirmation of a case in Nigeria does not, by itself, mean Ebola has spread to Liberia.

Challenges Posed by the Bundibugyo Strain

The Bundibugyo strain presents particular challenges because there is no licensed vaccine specifically approved for it.

The Ervebo vaccine, which has been used to control outbreaks caused by the Zaire ebolavirus, targets a different Ebola virus species and cannot be assumed to provide protection against the Bundibugyo strain.

In the absence of a specifically approved vaccine, early detection, isolation, contact tracing and strict infection prevention measures remain critical components of outbreak response.

Adequate protective equipment, trained personnel, and effective coordination among health institutions are also essential to protecting frontline workers and limiting potential transmission.

Liberia’s decision to reinforce preparedness measures reflects the importance of strengthening these safeguards before a potential emergency develops.

Lessons From Liberia’s Ebola Crisis

Liberia’s experience during the 2014–2016 West African Ebola epidemic remains a stark reminder of the consequences of delayed detection, inadequate infection prevention and weak emergency response capacity.

The epidemic devastated communities, overwhelmed health facilities and disrupted economic and social activities across Liberia, Guinea and Sierra Leone.

The current developments place renewed emphasis on the need to translate lessons from that crisis into practical preparedness measures.

The priorities include strengthening surveillance at airports and other points of entry, ensuring that frontline personnel can recognize and report suspected cases, maintaining adequate infection prevention supplies and improving coordination between national and county health authorities.

The effectiveness of the response will depend not only on the issuance of directives but also on their consistent implementation, the availability of resources and the timely communication of accurate information to the public.

With NPHIL having assessed preparedness at Roberts International Airport before Nigeria’s confirmation and the Ministry of Health now ordering nationwide enforcement of infection prevention protocols, Liberia’s immediate challenge is to ensure that preparedness measures are implemented consistently across the country.

Authorities said they will share further updates through official channels as the situation develops.

World.title: Liberia: LAA MD Seeks Board Probe Into Alleged Administrative Irregularities Involving James Spriggs Payne Airport Port Manager Abner Yonly
World.content:
Liberia Airport Authority (LAA) Managing Director Ernest R. Hughes has formally requested a review by the Authority’s Board of Directors into alleged administrative, financial and governance irregularities involving the Port Manager of James Spriggs Payne Airport, Abner Yonly, according to sources familiar with the correspondence.

In a letter dated Oct. 19, 2026, addressed to the Board chairman and members, Hughes outlined several concerns involving Yonly’s management of the airport, including alleged unauthorized financial transactions, personnel decisions and failure to comply with directives from the Authority’s senior management.

A source familiar with the developments, who requested anonymity because of the sensitivity of the matter, said the communication raises questions about administrative oversight, accountability and adherence to established management procedures at the airport.



Yonly did not respond to FrontPage Africa’s inquiry up to the time of publication. He did not respond to FPA’s letter sent to his WhatsApp, as well as text messages and calls.

Among the most significant concerns is a reported request for approximately US$40 million submitted to the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning to support operations and development at James Spriggs Payne Airport.

According to the letter, the request was allegedly made without the prior knowledge, review or authorization of the LAA managing director or senior management.

The letter also raises concerns about reports that bank accounts may have been opened or maintained on behalf of the airport without approval from the Authority’s senior leadership.

Additionally, Hughes cited reports of funds allegedly solicited or received from external entities outside established financial management and reporting procedures.

The allegations, if substantiated, could raise questions about financial accountability and the extent of authority exercised by airport management.

The managing director also identified several personnel-related concerns, including the reported removal of an employee identified as Mr. Bosco from his office assignment without authorization from senior management.

In another incident, Hughes said Yonly allegedly refused to implement a July 6 directive transferring three security officers from Roberts International Airport to James Spriggs Payne Airport.

The letter further referenced an Oct. 14 communication posted in an official LAA forum during discussions about the launch of the Authority’s Strategic Plan. Management reportedly considered the communication inappropriate in tone and inconsistent with expected standards of professional conduct.

Taken together, the concerns outlined in the correspondence point to possible disagreements over management authority, institutional reporting structures and compliance with the LAA’s administrative procedures.

Hughes requested that the Board examine the matters and determine whether additional administrative review, investigation or corrective action is warranted.

The letter does not announce disciplinary action against Yonly or establish that the allegations have been proven.

It also does not indicate whether the Board has initiated a formal investigation or reached any conclusions.

The development comes as LAA continues efforts to strengthen institutional governance, operational efficiency and administrative accountability across the country’s airports.

The outcome of the Board’s consideration could have implications for management oversight and the relationship between the Authority’s central administration and individual airport managers.

The Board had not made its position public up to the time of publication.

World.title: Liberia: AFL Discharges Two Soldiers Over Viral Assault Video
World.content:
MONROVIA — The Armed Forces of Liberia (AFL) has dishonorably discharged two soldiers assigned to the 23rd Infantry Brigade following the circulation of a viral video showing one of them assaulting a young woman while the other stood nearby.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

The soldiers were identified as Sergeant Robert P. Menyon, service number EN/2008-05/1505, and Sergeant Abu S.B. Sheriff, service number EN/2008-05/1646. The discharge ceremony took place at the Barclay Training Center in Monrovia on Wednesday, October 21, 2026.



AFL Chief of Staff Major General Davidson F. Forleh condemned the soldiers’ conduct, describing them as “bad apples” within the military and likening their presence to an “Ebola virus,” remarks that underscored his disapproval of their alleged actions.

The disciplinary action followed public outrage over the video, which showed a soldier physically assaulting a woman while another soldier was present.

Victim Recounts Incident

The woman, identified as Blessing, said the confrontation began when soldiers pursued a group of boys who were playing football in her community.

According to her account, the soldiers chased the boys after a disagreement at the football field. Her younger brother, who was among the boys, ran into their family’s home as the soldiers pursued him.

Blessing said she intervened and pleaded with the soldiers to leave her brother alone. However, she alleged that one of the soldiers began beating her while she held her baby in her arms.

She said the second soldier attempted to persuade his colleague to stop the assault but failed to prevent the beating.

Blessing further explained that the soldiers had later apologized for their conduct and that she had accepted their apology and forgiven them.

Despite the public controversy surrounding the incident, she expressed sadness over the decision to dismiss the two men from the military.

She said she wanted the soldiers to face punishment for their actions but had not wanted them to lose their military careers.

Blessing also indicated that the soldiers had been invited by a woman in the community, although further details about the circumstances surrounding the invitation were not immediately available.

Her account presents a personal dimension to the AFL’s decision, highlighting the difference between her willingness to forgive the soldiers and the military’s responsibility to enforce its standards of conduct.

Forleh Orders Further Action

Following the discharge, the two former soldiers were publicly presented at the Barclay Training Center.

According to accounts of the event, General Forleh instructed officers of the Liberia National Police to handcuff the men.

He also ordered the removal of their families from AFL barracks and directed that they be taken to the area around the Samuel Kanyon Doe Sports Complex to find their way home.

The circumstances surrounding the order, including the arrangements made for the affected families, were not immediately clear.

The AFL’s announcement described the action as a response to unprofessional conduct involving a woman and emphasized the importance of accountability among members of the military.

The dishonorable discharges represent a significant disciplinary response to an incident that has attracted public attention and raised concerns about the conduct of personnel entrusted with maintaining discipline and protecting the public.

The incident also places renewed focus on the standards of behavior expected of members of the armed forces, particularly when they interact with civilians.

Accountability And Military Conduct

The AFL operates under the motto “A Force for Good,” a principle that places public trust and professional conduct at the center of its institutional identity.

The incident has generated debate over the appropriate disciplinary response to alleged misconduct by military personnel. While Blessing said she had forgiven the soldiers following their apology, the AFL proceeded with their dismissal.

Her decision to forgive the men does not, in itself, determine the military’s disciplinary response. The armed forces maintain responsibility for enforcing professional standards and addressing conduct considered inconsistent with military service.

At the same time, the circumstances surrounding the incident, the soldiers’ respective roles and the measures taken against them remain important considerations in assessing the proportionality and fairness of the disciplinary action.

The AFL has not, in the information available for this report, provided further details about the specific disciplinary procedures followed before the discharges.

The incident serves as a reminder that military personnel are expected to exercise restraint and professionalism in their dealings with civilians, and that alleged abuses of authority can carry serious consequences.

For Blessing, the outcome is bittersweet: although she says she forgave the soldiers, their dismissal has left her saddened by the loss of their careers.

World.title: Copper Princesses lose to Venezuela
World.content:
Zambia’s U-17 Women’s National Team, the Copper Princesses, suffered a heartbreaking second defeat at the ongoing FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup in Morocco after losing 2-1 to Venezuela on Wednesday night.

Andrea Suarez scored on the last kick of the game to give 10-player Venezuela a dramatic victory in the Group D encounter.

Zambia started strongly with an excellently worked goal, with Taonga Mubanga’s pass finding Grace Phiri who crossed for Precious Mwewa to tap in.

But Venezuela responded with Orliany Duran blocking an attempted clearance and hammering home the equaliser.

There was late drama in stoppage time when Venezuela goalkeeper Valeria Rebanales was sent off, forcing defender Abril Alejo into goal. Suarez then fired home the winner in the dying moments.

Zambia Coach Carol Kanyemba is yet to comment on the defeat.

The loss leaves Zambia bottom of Group D with no points after losing the opening game 5-0 to Japan.

Japan now top the group with six points after beating France 2-0 on Wednesday.

France and Venezuela have three points each.

Zambia’s last Group D match is against France on Saturday, 24 October 2026 in Rabat.

Venezuela Coach Dayana Frias said her team’s courage made the difference.

“I’m just grateful to God. You should never lose faith. The key was courage. We fought until the very end,” Frias said.

World.title: Mpulungu Kapenta traders hail Solar-powered dryer support
World.content:
Women involved in drying Kapenta in Mpulungu District have thanked the Fish for African Caribbean and Pacific Countries Project (FISH4ACP) for supporting them with a solar-powered dryer, saying it will help improve the quality of their Kapenta.

Twazwane Women’s group chairperson Callen Nakazwe said the equipment will provide a more reliable and hygienic way to dry Kapenta, a small fish that is an important source of food and income in the area.

Mpulungu, Ms Nakazwe said traditional drying methods have for a long time left the Kapenta exposed to dust, insects and changing weather conditions, which may affect its quality.

She disclosed that the solar-powered dryer is expected to help protect the fish during the drying process and produce a cleaner, more consistent product.

‘’We are very grateful for the welcome support because it is a practical investment in our work and livelihoods as improved drying will reduce losses and help us preserve more of the Kapenta as we process it,’’ she disclosed

Ms Nakazwe explained that better-quality fish will also attract buyers and strengthen the women’s ability to compete in local markets especially during the rainy season periods when weather conditions make open-air processing difficult.

She added that the dryer will make their work more efficient while helping them maintain better standards for the Kapenta fish they sell.

The women also expressed hope that the equipment will encourage more people in their communities to adopt improved fish-handling practices.

Ms Nakazwe said they were grateful for the support and pledged to use the dryer responsibly and also called for continued training and support to help them operate and maintain the equipment effectively.

The women said the solar-powered dryer offers an opportunity to improve Kapenta quality, increase the value of their work and support their livelihoods.

FISH4ACP supports sustainable and inclusive development in fisheries and aquaculture value chains.

Its assistance to the women is intended to strengthen Kapenta processing in Mpulungu District.

World.title: Government prioritises tailings Dam safety
World.content:
The Government has identified tailings dam safety as a priority, calling for increased training of regulators and mining operators to strengthen the management of these facilities.

Minerals Regulations Commission Director Mine Inspections and Audits Elite Mhone warned that climate change and increasingly heavy rainfall heighten the risk of tailings dam failures.

Mr Mhone was speaking during a plenary session at the Mining and Investment Insaka in Lusaka.

He said that unlike conventional water dams, tailings facilities continue to grow as mining waste accumulates, requiring ongoing monitoring, stronger safety measures and improved regulatory oversight to protect surrounding communities and the environment.

“The size of rainfall we receive now is not the same as rainfall that was being received in 1964, right now we have got a lot of rainfall,” Mr Mhone

Mr Mhone further said that Zambia’s tailings dam management and safety standards remain inadequate, raising concerns as the country targets annual copper production of three million tonnes.

He has since called for stricter regulatory inspections, independent engineering oversight, a national tailings dam registry and greater accountability for mining companies.

And Zambia Environmental Agency (ZEMA) Acting Director Licensing and Compliance Constantino Mweembela said mining companies should strengthen water quality monitoring and engage communities to protect shared water resources in increasingly water-stressed areas.

“Environmental impact assessments must go beyond regulatory compliance to include practical measures for preventing pollution, monitoring groundwater and surface water, and detecting contamination early,” he said.

Mr Mwembela has also urged mining operators to invest in real-time monitoring systems and adhere to international tailings management standards to safeguard water resources and surrounding communities.

Meanwhile, Seed Global Health Country Director, Chikusela Sikazwe has urged mining companies to integrate health considerations into environmental and social impact assessments from the earliest stages of mining projects.

Dr Sikazwe said this will help to ensure that their investments align with government priorities.

He warned that uncoordinated investments can lead to duplication and underutilised health facilities, calling for stronger collaboration between mining companies and the Ministry of Health.

“The approach should strengthen Zambia’s health system throughout the mining lifecycle, including emergency care and preparedness for disease outbreaks, climate-related health risks and future pandemics,” Dr Sikazwe said.

World.title: President Hichilema attends SADC extraordinary meeting virtually
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema participated in the Extraordinary Summit of the Southern African Development Community (SADC) Heads of State and Government virtually.

President Hichilema’s participation underscores Zambia’s resolve and commitment to supporting discussions and decisions that strengthen the SADC Secretariat, advance regional integration and promote peace, security and stability among Member States.

The Extraordinary Summit was chaired by SADC Chairperson and President of South Africa, Cyril Ramaphosa.

In his opening remarks, President Ramaphosa said the strength of SADC rests not only on political commitments but on strong institutions with the leadership, capacity and resources to translate decisions into tangible improvements in people’s lives.

He said regional integration must be measured by the extent to which it creates jobs, attracts investment, reduces poverty and improves citizens’ livelihoods, while peace and stability remain indispensable foundations for development.

Meanwhile, the Summit has elected Lesotho as the new Chairperson of the SADC Organ Troika on Politics, Defence and Security Cooperation, taking over the leadership of the Organ charged with promoting peace and security in the region.

The Organ plays a central role in preventive diplomacy, mediation, conflict resolution and addressing security challenges, including the situation in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the threat of terrorism and violent extremism in northern Mozambique.

The Summit also appointed and swore in Treasure Maphanga as Deputy Executive Secretary responsible for Regional Integration.

Ms Maphanga’s appointment fills a key treaty position expected to accelerate implementation of the Regional Indicative Strategic Development Plan (RISDP), drive cross-border infrastructure development, expand electricity generation and transmission, and deepen regional value chains and intra-regional trade.

President Ramaphosa congratulated both Lesotho and Ms Maphanga and urged the strengthened SADC institutions to work towards building a region where peace prevails and economic opportunities expand.

Eelier, Southern African Development Community (SADC) Executive Secretary, Elias Magosi said the Extraordinary Summit was convened to conclude two matters deferred from the Durban Summit in August this year.

The first is the election of the incoming Chairperson of the SADC Organ on Politics, Defence and Security Cooperation, after two member states expressed interest in the position in Durban.

He said the Summit had referred the decision pending further consultations, and consultations have since been concluded with a common position for approval today.

Mr Magosi said the Organ remains indispensable in advancing peace, security, stability, democracy and good governance in the region, as well as in providing an enabling environment for accelerating regional integration and sustainable development.

“The second item is the appointment of the Deputy Executive Secretary for Regional Integration, following a recruitment process, he added

Mr Magosi said the Deputy Executive Secretary for Regional Integration is a key pillar and driver of regional integration, overseeing progress on regional integration as guided by the Regional Indicative Strategic Development Plan (RISDP) and relevant protocols.

Meanwhile, Mr Magosi congratulated President Daniel Francisco Chapo of Mozambique for successfully hosting the inaugural International Conference on Disaster Risk Reduction and Resilience in Africa in Maputo from 13th to 15th October, 2026, under the theme on strengthening governance and strategic investment for disaster resilience.

He said the conference called for accelerated implementation of disaster risk reduction commitments, strengthened partnerships and increased investment in resilience-building initiatives across Africa.

Mr Magosi also congratulated Dr Navanethem Pillay of South Africa on being awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize in recognition of her distinguished contributions to peace, justice, human rights and international law, describing it as a source of pride for South Africa, the SADC region and the international community.

World.title: Chinsali Council engages businesses on 2027 budget
World.content:
The Chinsali Municipal Council has engaged the business community in the preparation of its 2027 Output-Based Budget (OBB) to ensure that proposed projects and programmes reflect the development priorities of the district.

Council Public Relations Manager Lolavye Simukoko said the engagement provides a platform for stakeholders to contribute ideas and propose projects for consideration in the 2027 financial year.

Mr Simukoko said the meeting is part of the Council’s efforts to promote public participation in the budgeting process.

The council public relations manager said this in a statement released to ZANIS in Chinsali district.

He said the meeting also featured presentations on services provided by the local authority, the performance of the 2026 Council budget and the role of the Council’s Integrity Committee.

He said the engagement is also intended to ensure that proposed projects aligns with the Chinsali Integrated Development Plan (IDP), the Eighth National Development Plan (8NDP) and the national Grow Zambia Agenda.

During the meeting, stakeholders proposed the construction of an ablution block and fencing of the Council sports facility near the Zambia Army Mess, as well as the provision of waste bins in the Central Business District (CBD) to improve sanitation.

Other proposals include the construction of a transit bus station at Nambuluma Junction, additional Council houses and the rehabilitation of the community hall at the old market in Chinsali CBD.

He explained that the business community also proposed the establishment of parks and recreational spaces near Nkakula Guest House and Bread of Life Church, alongside the development of modern market infrastructure at Choshi, Mishishi and Chinsali Main Market.

Mr Simukoko said stakeholders further proposed the introduction of fire extinguisher supply and refilling services to strengthen fire safety and emergency preparedness in the district.

He said the Council will consider the submissions as part of the budgeting process, with the aim of identifying priority interventions that respond to the needs of the local community.

Mr Simukoko said stakeholder participation is important in promoting transparency, accountability and collaboration between the Council and the business community in advancing development in Chinsali District.

World.title: Kaputa health Director calls for cholera vigilance
World.content:
Kaputa District Health Director Jonathan Bwalya has urged members of the public to remain vigilant against cholera and take extra precautions to prevent the spread of the disease.

Dr Bwalya told the media in an interview that it is important for residents to observe preventive measures and remain alert to the risks posed by cholera, a waterborne disease that can spread through contaminated water and food.

He said his medical team is on the ground and working to ensure that cholera does not spread to Kaputa District.

Dr Bwalya emphasised the importance of public cooperation in preventing the disease, urging residents to take personal hygiene and sanitation seriously.

He further encouraged the public to practice proper hand washing, drink safe water, eat properly handled food and maintain clean surroundings as part of efforts to protect communities from cholera.

Residents were also urged to seek immediate medical attention if they developed symptoms such as acute watery diarrhea and vomiting, which may indicate cholera.

Dr Bwalya’s call comes as health authorities continue to emphasise the importance of vigilance and preventive measures in protecting communities from cholera outbreaks in the wake of reports of a cholera outbreak.

World.title: How long will Kalampa stay top?
World.content:
Nkana’s perfect start to the transitional Super League season is no accident.

Three games, three wins, nine points. Top of Stream A. At Nkana Stadium in Wusakile on Sunday, Elijah Tana’s side did not just beat Nchanga Rangers 2-0, they sent a statement about what a balanced team can achieve.

What is most impressive about this Nkana side is not just the results, but the method.

On one hand, there is Lazarous Kambole, a seasoned striker who knows where the goal is. His opener against Rangers, created by Kedrick Mumba’s vision from his own half, was a reminder that experience still matters in Zambian football. On the other, there is Patrick Gondwe, alert and hungry to pounce when Captain Harrison Chisala’s effort was parried by keeper Victor Chabu.

Nkana are deservedly top. Tana has blended young, energetic players with experienced heads like Kambole and Chisala, and for now, the chemistry is working. But the perfection of nine points masks a lack of clinical edge that better opponents will exploit.

This blend of youth and experience that Coach Tana has spoken about is beginning to produce results. The young, energetic players provide pace and hunger, the experienced heads provide guidance and composure. It is a formula that has served Nkana well throughout its decorated history, and it is working again.

Tana deserves credit for his honesty. “We won’t relax,” he said after the win. “We will continue pushing until the end.” That is exactly the mentality Kalampa needs. Too many times in recent seasons, Nkana have started well only to fade when pressure mounts. This transitional league is short, but it is competitive, and consistency will be key.

Now, spare a thought for Nchanga Rangers. Assistant Coach Israel Mwanza was candid enough to admit his side is under pressure after three straight defeats. Conceding early goals has become a worrying habit for Brave. Yet Mwanza insists their system is fine. Football, however, is a results business. Systems mean little if they cannot stop early setbacks.

For the league as a whole, Nkana’s resurgence is good news. A strong Nkana makes a strong Super League. When Kalampa are firing, attendances improve, rivalry intensifies, and the standard goes up. Their next test away to Konkola Blades will tell us whether this perfect start is a false dawn or the beginning of a genuine title charge in the transitional campaign.

For now, Kalampa are showing the way. The challenge is to stay there.

World.title: Zambia, Botswana, DRC recommit to strengthening regional cooperation
World.content:
Zambia, Botswana and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) have reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening regional cooperation through infrastructure connectivity, integrated value chains and cross-border industrial development.

Botswana’s Minister of Minerals and Energy, Bogolo Kenewendo, says the three countries have an opportunity to transform their mineral wealth into shared prosperity through investment, partnerships and coordinated implementation of agreed initiatives.

Ms Kenewendo adds that the African continent possesses some of the world’s most valuable minerals, as well as the talent and partnerships required to unlock their full economic potential.

The Minister was speaking in Lusaka last evening during a networking cocktail party held on the sidelines of the 2026 Zambia Mining and Investment engagement.

Ms Kenewendo stressed that the continent must move beyond discussions and translate commitments into tangible projects that would benefit its people.

She said the focus should now be on implementation to ensure that the mineral resources of Zambia, Botswana, the DRC and other African countries contribute to sustainable economic growth and prosperity.

Ms Kenewendo said the discussions and engagements held over the past few days had opened up opportunities for stronger collaboration and a brighter future for African mining.

She further stressed that the continent must move beyond discussions and translate commitments into tangible projects that would benefit its people.

And Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) Minister of Mines, Louis Kabamba says African countries must take responsibility for their own development by strengthening leadership and cooperation.

Mr Kabamba said the Insaka has demonstrated the importance of African countries drawing on their own strengths, sharing experiences and exchanging best practices to accelerate development.

He said all stakeholders, including government officials, mining investors and industry leaders, had a responsibility to contribute to the continent’s development.

Mr Kabamba urged African countries to take ownership of their development aspirations and work together to build prosperous economies.

Passing a vote of thanks, Zambia’s Acting Minister of Mines and Mineral Development, Gilbert Siame, said the Insaka has come at an opportune time to showcase the mineral wealth and investment opportunities available in Zambia, Botswana and the DRC.

Dr Siame said the participation of Botswana and the DRC demonstrated the growing importance of the Insaka as a platform for regional trade and investment.

He said the meeting is also expected to facilitate business deals and joint ventures while supporting the Government’s Grow Zambia Agenda, particularly the target of increasing annual copper production to three million metric tonnes by 2031.

President Hakainde Hichilema officially opened the Insaka on October 19, 2026, with business expected to conclude on Friday, October 23.

The event has attracted more than 1,500 participants, including representatives of the World Bank, European Union, African Development Bank and business communities from Australia, China and the United Arab Emirates.

The cocktail party was held at the Mulungushi International Conference Centre in Lusaka, and brought together government officials, investors, mining companies and development partners to explore investment opportunities and strengthen regional cooperation in the mining sector.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 22, 2026
World.content:
Cameroon Train Disaster Survivors Still Await Justice 10 Years Later

Ten years after Cameroon's deadliest rail disaster killed 79 people and injured more than 500, survivors are still dealing with serious injuries, while some victims have not received compensation and legal proceedings remain unresolved. The Camrail train derailed near Eseka on 21 October 2016 while travelling from Yaoundé to Douala. An investigation found that it was travelling at 96km/h in a section with a 40km/h speed limit. Overloading, defective brakes and the addition of extra carriages also contributed to the crash. Survivors continue to suffer from chronic pain and lasting disabilities. In 2018, Camrail and 11 employees were convicted of involuntary manslaughter and causing unintentional injuries. The company's former managing director received a suspended sentence, while other officials were also given suspended sentences. The train driver was sentenced to five years in prison. However, Camrail appealed the ruling, and the appeal has yet to be heard. Victims' lawyers say compensation has been inadequate, with some payments still outstanding.

Burkina Faso Restores Death Penalty Amid Crackdown on Critics

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Burkina Faso's unelected parliament has unanimously adopted a new penal code restoring the death penalty for offences including high treason, terrorism, espionage, parricide and importing expired or prohibited products. The death penalty for ordinary crimes was abolished in 2018. Human Rights Watch warns that reinstating capital punishment could further threaten civil liberties under the military junta, which took power in a 2022 coup. Authorities have restricted media outlets, suspended civil society organisations and unions, and targeted critics through arrests and enforced disappearances. The government said that the measure will help combat terrorism. Rights advocates argue that weaknesses in the justice system increase the risk of wrongful convictions and irreversible injustice.

Nearly 200,000 Zimbabweans Returned From South Africa

Nearly 200,000 Zimbabweans have returned home from South Africa amid anti-migrant protests and attacks targeting foreign nationals, according to the government. Cabinet was told that 197,294 people had returned, including 42,553 repatriated through government assistance and 154,741 who returned independently. The government deployed buses to collect stranded nationals, including those in Cape Town. The protests, involving groups such as Operation Dudula and March and March, have targeted Zimbabweans and other African migrants. Authorities said the number of returnees has declined but are continuing to monitor the situation. Zimbabwe is also screening deportees arriving from South Africa, including 700 people received from the Lindela Repatriation Centre.

Gambia to Compensate Victims With Proceeds From Jammeh's US Mansion

The Gambia's Reparations Commission has received more than US$2.57 million from the sale of a Maryland mansion belonging to former president Yahya Jammeh. The funds will be used to compensate victims of abuses committed during his more than two decades in power. US authorities secured the right to sell the property in 2022, arguing that it had been acquired using criminal proceeds and misappropriated public funds. Jammeh seized power in a 1994 coup and was accused of overseeing torture, forced disappearances, rape and extrajudicial killings. He lost the 2016 election to Adama Barrow but initially refused to step down. He eventually left office in 2017 and went into exile in Equatorial Guinea. A national inquiry found that he had amassed hundreds of properties and misappropriated more than US$300 million.

Latin American Drug Cartels Expand Operations Across Africa

Latin American drug trafficking organizations are expanding into Africa, using the continent as a transshipment point for cocaine and as a new production base for methamphetamine. Global demand is rising, and enforcement efforts are harder to maintain in the Americas, so criminal groups have tried to link up with African networks. Methamphetamine labs have been found in South Africa, Nigeria, Kenya, and Mozambique. It is still common for cocaine to travel through West Africa on its way to Europe. They generate revenue by engaging in money laundering and drug trafficking. They achieve this by capitalizing on corruption, porous borders, and a scarcity of police officers. Nevertheless, the drug trade is gaining popularity, which is a cause for concern as it undermines government institutions and results in a rise in crime, addiction, and violence. The authorities have increased the number of arrests and seizures. Experts warn that criminal networks will continue to thrive where oversight and law enforcement remain weak.

Close 

Kagame Urges Rwanda's Youth to Put Health Before Ambitions

Rwandan President Paul Kagame has called on the youth to prioritise their health and well-being as they chase their personal and professional aspirations. Speaking at a youth engagement event at BK Arena on October 21, he stressed the importance of developing healthy habits from childhood. Kagame warned against alcohol and drug abuse, saying such behaviours can worsen personal difficulties rather than solve them. He also encouraged young people to exercise, continue learning, work hard and make responsible decisions. He called on them to challenge harmful practices in their communities instead of allowing them to become normalised. Kagame said young people should recognise their potential, distinguish right from wrong and take responsibility for shaping their futures.

World.title: South Africa: Govt Welcomes Mid-Term Budget - South African News Briefs - October 22, 2026
World.content:
press review

Govt Welcomes Mid-Term Budget

Minister in the Presidency Khumbudzo Ntshavheni has welcomed the 2026 Medium-Term Budget Policy Statement, reports EWN. She said that it seeks to ease the cost of living. She also welcomed the temporary fuel levy reductions announced by Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana. Ntshavheni highlighted the allocation of R3.8 billion to recruit more than 3,500 social workers to strengthen the fight against gender-based violence. The social workers will help improve prevention efforts and support women reporting abuse at police stations. Discussions are continuing on measures to reduce the impact of fuel costs on consumers.

DJ Warras Murder Case Returns to Court



Two people accused of murdering Warrick "DJ Warras" Stock are set to appear in the High Court in Johannesburg for pre-trial proceedings, reports SABC News. Hlengiwe Buthelezi and Victor Majola face charges of premeditated murder and conspiracy to commit murder. The case was previously delayed while they sought legal representation. Stock was shot dead outside the Zambesi Building in Johannesburg on 16 December last year. Armando Pacula, a Mozambican national accused of shooting Stock, has pleaded guilty. He was sentenced to 25 years in prison.

Businessman Suliman Carrim Faces Additional Charges

North West businessman Suliman Carrim is set to appear in the Musina Magistrates' Court after additional charges of theft and fraud were brought against him, reports EWN. The charges relate to an alleged attempt to smuggle two vehicles from Mahikeng to Musina, with Malawi as their intended destination. Police allege that Carrim and two others tried to obtain bank authorisation documents to transport the vehicles across the border into Zimbabwe. When they allegedly failed to secure the documents, they arranged fraudulent ones. Police arrested two suspects in July after they intercepted the vehicles at the Beitbridge border post.

World.title: Africa: Are Bilateral Ties the Route to Renewed West African Security Cooperation?
World.content:
analysis

Pending the outcome of ECOWAS-AES talks, cooperation between neighbouring states offers a starting point for rebuilding regional security ties.

Despite tensions between the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) and the Confederation of Sahel States (AES), recent advances reflect a broader regional trend. In August, Ghana and Burkina Faso signed a defence agreement, while Mali and Côte d'Ivoire agreed to delimit their shared border.

The withdrawal of Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger from ECOWAS in January 2025 deeply fragmented West Africa's institutional architecture, but did not end cooperation between individual states. Instead, relations are being pragmatically reorganised around countries' security priorities, mainly through bilateral deals. This shift has been underway since 2025 and offers a concrete way to manage divisions without waiting for ongoing ECOWAS-AES negotiations to produce a political agreement.

Across several ECOWAS-AES fault lines, states are reactivating or deepening bilateral cooperation frameworks, agreements, joint commissions, or operational mechanisms, some of which predate the current regional crisis.



Joint patrols launched by Senegal and Mali in the Kayes region in 2025 build on a cooperation framework established in 2021. Mali and Guinea's shared military commission met in April 2025 and June 2026, producing a memorandum of understanding that provides for intelligence sharing. And in August 2026, Ghana and Burkina Faso signed a defence pact after relaunching their Permanent Joint Commission for Cooperation and signing seven cross-border cooperation agreements.

These initiatives show that institutional fragmentation has not paralysed security cooperation altogether, even if the effectiveness of agreements is yet to be demonstrated. They also challenge the notion of a standstill, as bilateral mechanisms play an increasingly prominent role, enabling states to maintain or rebuild relations around their immediate security interests.

This window of opportunity should be maximised while ECOWAS and the AES negotiate a framework for future security cooperation. Talks could drag on, or even stall, given how politically and symbolically charged relations between the two blocs remain. Meanwhile, armed groups continue to exploit gaps in cooperation.

Rather than waiting for a new institutional agreement, regional actors and their partners could reverse the sequence. They could encourage states to cooperate where their interests converge, facilitate rapprochement where political tensions stand in the way, and over time, connect bilateral arrangements through flexible regional mechanisms.

Two of West Africa's border areas need priority attention.

The first is northern Benin, where jihadist groups exploit gaps in neighbouring countries' collaboration. Around the W-Arly-Pendjari complex, where Benin, Burkina Faso and Niger meet, violence remains intense. Further east, in the Benin-Niger-Nigeria triangle, weak coordination is enabling armed groups to expand. Discussions between Nigeria and Benin remain incomplete without Niger, and the rapprochement launched by Beninese President Romuald Wadagni during his June visit to Niamey has yet to reopen the border.

The second is the Sikasso-Korhogo-Bobo-Dioulasso (SKBo) cross-border area, where Mali, Côte d'Ivoire and Burkina Faso meet. Political distrust between Abidjan and Ouagadougou continues to hinder cooperation on the ground, and progress between Côte d'Ivoire and Mali has yet to translate into joint security efforts commensurate with the risks.

Other regional actors could help unblock cooperation in these priority border areas. The Conseil de l'Entente, which brings together Benin, Burkina Faso, Côte d'Ivoire, Niger and Togo, with Mali as an observer, already has a dialogue framework on security and border management. It could discreetly facilitate rapprochement among its members, particularly around the W-Arly-Pendjari complex and the SKBo area, in a format less exposed to ECOWAS-AES political tensions.

In the Benin-Niger-Nigeria zone, the African Union (AU) Mission for Mali and the Sahel (MISAHEL) could offer a complementary entry point. Its mandate, which will extend to Benin and Togo from 2027, and its AU affiliation independent of both ECOWAS and AES, make it well placed to facilitate dialogue among the three countries. The aim would be to gradually restore trust and help states identify concrete ways to restart joint security initiatives.

MISAHEL could share lessons from the Nouakchott Process, launched by the AU in 2013 to strengthen security cooperation in the Sahelo-Saharan region, with the priority border areas. Although the process is largely inactive, the mechanisms it promoted - intelligence sharing, cross-border coordination, joint patrols and regular exchanges between security officials - are precisely those that several states want to revive on an ad hoc basis in their bilateral cooperation.

This approach should remain flexible enough to adapt to the needs that states themselves identify. On one border, the main requirement may be restoring contact between military officials; on another, establishing intelligence-sharing protocols. Elsewhere, political conditions might allow states to go further, with more frequent joint patrols or more formal coordination between countries.

Close 

The goal would not be to replicate a regional mechanism, but to tailor these tools to the needs and possibilities specific to each border area. This variable-geometry approach is increasingly taking shape through the 'coalition of the willing' proposed by Ghana. Rather than waiting for a regional consensus that would require countries to progress at the same pace, the approach is moving towards implementation among states ready to move forward.

In the long run, an ECOWAS-AES framework could develop from working relations established on the ground, rather than from the top down through an institutional agreement. The resulting regional architecture may be less orderly than before, but more solid - precisely because it would be anchored in states' concrete security interests and their need to cooperate.
