Djiby Sow, Senior Researcher, ISS Regional Office for West Africa and the Sahel

World.title: Zimbabwe: Mnangagwa, Angel Caught Up in Another Al Jazeera Investigation That Reveals Zimbabwean Govt Paid UK Terrorist Groups to Force Lifting of Sanctions
World.content:
President Emmerson Mnangagwa's advisor Uebert Angel has been caught up in another Al Jazeera investigation that reveals as much as US$13,000 was paid for a fake rally on the sidelines of COP26, seeking to portray British people's support for a UK-Zimbabwe relationship.

Titled 'Contract Killers and the Far Right', the investigation sees hired Britons packed in a hall, being coached on how to react and what to say at the rally, which was attended by Angel in November 2021.

Mnangagwa joined other world leaders in Glasgow for COP26, a climate conference which seeks to promote net-zero emissions by mid-century and keep the 1.5°C global warming limit within reach for earth's sustainability.

Other than climate issues, Mnangagwa sought to re-sell himself as the rightful leader of Zimbabwe, clean his regime's bad-boy tag and open financial opportunities for the country.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

He was on a public relations charm offensive as he met then UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson and others while Angel sought fake pressure groups that would portray Zimbabwe as a viable friend and trade partner.

"I'm also doing a job up in Glasgow. The President of Zimbabwe is coming to Glasgow for some big pan-African British crap," says Jack Ross, a former election candidate for the UK's Conservative Party.

"He wants me to organise a crowd there for his little project, British Friends of Zimbabwe."

"I am arranging a crowd of 100 to greet him when he arrives, which is a big thing to ask because it is Zimbabwe, but it is being done.

"They are paying me a lot to organise that, again, not necessarily to me personally but to my friends who are community leaders up there."

Ross, who is identified as having been asked by the Zimbabwean government to act on its behalf, has since been suspended following AIU's expose'.

At the rally, a hall is filled with 'actors' whose performances were choreographed to make Mnangagwa seem popular and to show how the British look forward to trade with Zimbabwe.

Although most had to be reminded of their lines and why they were in attendance cheers, a standing ovation, whistles, waving of the Zimbabwean and British flags follow Angel's entrance and exit.

Angel can be seen with far-right activists linked to some of the UK's violent, terrorist groupings such as Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF), Turning Point UK and Patriots of Britain (POB), whom he pays for the staged rally.

The money which was paid to the proscribed terrorist groups by Angel, on video, was likely used to purchase arms in Northern Ireland for use in Scotland, according to the investigation.

Close 

"Any evidence of the funding of terrorist operations will give rise to a potential criminal investigation. It is very serious when a line is crossed between legitimate political debate and meddling or dabbling in paramilitary activity," said

This is not the first time Angel has been caught up in Al Jazeera investigations. He was central to its earth-shattering Gold Mafia investigation that revealed his central role in smuggling Zimbabwe's gold to Dubai and other countries.

World.title: South Africa: Black Market Weight-Loss Drug Sellers Are Moving Fast. South Africa's Regulators Are Struggling To Keep Up
World.content:
Why is South Africa struggling to stop the sellers of illegal weight-loss injections, and how can consumers tell whether the medicines they're buying are safe?

South African regulators have won an important court battle against a pharmacy making its own versions of popular weight-loss injections. But illegal and experimental drugs are still being sold openly, while new rules to crack down on the trade are months away. Why is the country struggling to stop the sellers — and how can consumers tell whether the medicines they're buying are safe?

South African pharmacies are allowed to make up medicines for patients with specific needs. But some are producing weight-loss injections in large quantities without the licences required to manufacture medicines.

In June, the Gauteng High Court ordered Tshwane-based compounding pharmacy iDexis to stop producing medicines containing semaglutide, the substance that makes Ozempic work.

Yet experimental weight-loss drugs such as retatrutide, which are still being studied and haven't been approved for sale anywhere in the world, are still being sold openly in South Africa.

Regulators say clearer rules for pharmacies that make their own medicines are on the way, but these are only expected by February or March 2027. The pharmaceutical industry warns that the delay gives illegal sellers more time to operate.

Australia has banned pharmacy compounding of weight-loss jabs, citing such drugs as "potentially unsafe and dangerous". So why are South African so-called compounding pharmacies still making their own versions of blockbuster weight-loss drugs such as Ozempic and Mounjaro , and selling them to the public?

The reality is that such activity is illegal in South Africa as well, at least in instances where the pharmacies make up copycat weight-loss jabs — which dampen appetite and make people feel full for longer — in large quantities, or use unregistered or illegally imported ingredients to make them.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

But as demand has soared, some pharmacies have turned the niche practice of compounding into a lucrative business. In June, the Gauteng High Court ordered iDexis, a compounding pharmacy in Tshwane, to stop producing medicine containing semaglutide — the active ingredient of Ozempic — after large quantities of compounded weight-loss jabs had been confiscated on its premises.

The court order was an important legal victory for the country's regulators, including the South African Health Products Regulatory Authority (Sahpra), Stavros Nicolaou , chairperson of the Pharmaceutical Task Group , an umbrella organisation for the pharmaceutical industry in South Africa, said during a panel discussion held in Sandton last week.

But he said the momentum built by the court order could be lost if Sahpra and the South African Pharmacy Council (SAPC) don't follow up on it quickly with clearer guidelines for compounding pharmacies about what they can, and cannot legally do. "You can go and win these court cases, and have people on the back foot, but all of that can unravel because we're just not acting swiftly enough as a country," he said.

Illegal drugs in plain sight

The panel gathered representatives from Sahpra and the SAPC, as well as the police service, border control, revenue service and the pharmaceutical industry, to explain to the public how they are working together to stop the trade in fake drugs.

Sahpra says it has received around 600 complaints so far this financial year relating to illegitimate and fake medicines being sold through informal supply chains, reaching the public via online portals, gyms, or even local hairdressers.

"We are worried that the scourge is getting out of control," said Daphne Fafudi , the body's head of regulatory compliance. And it's the public that can pay the ultimate price, she added. "People do die, and it doesn't even come to our attention," she said.

Some fake or illegitimate drugs are sold covertly. Others are traded in plain sight. One of them is retatrutide , a weight-loss injection that is still being tested in studies and therefore hasn't been licensed for sale by a drug regulatory anywhere in the world. Yet, it is sold "openly and brazenly" around the world, including in South Africa, said Nicolaou.

In the July episode of Bhekisisa 's TV programme, Health Beat, we reported how a Johannesburg woman's doctor sold her retatrutide, telling her it's safe because he "had it tested", while making her sign a waiver to release him of any responsibility for what might go wrong .

Earlier this year, a man reportedly died in the United States after taking injections sold as retatrutide on the black market — although the British Medical Journal said the evidence for the drug causing the fatality was "less clear cut" than media reporting suggested.

Nicolaou urged the police service and the Hawks to make an example of those who sell retatrutide in South Africa, as a deterrent to others. "The public needs to know that our enforcement agencies are actually enforcing the law," he told the meeting last week.

Vincent Tlala , CEO of the SAPC , said revised guidelines for compounding pharmacies were underway, a process Sahpra is leading, with input from the SAPC. However, Tlala said, these were not expected to be ready until February or March next year.

According to Nicolaou, this is too late. "The regulations are taking too long," he says. Regulators in other countries have introduced bans and restrictions on compounding pharmacies specifically for weight-loss jabs, to prevent the kind of products that have flooded South Africa. "Why are we not doing the same thing?"

What South African law says about compounding

Compounding medicines is lawful in South Africa, but only under specific conditions . Compounding requires a healthcare professional's prescription, generally for a formulation that is not available as a registered medicine — for instance, if a patient requires a medication as an oral liquid that is only normally sold as a pill.

As for compounding in bulk, the law says that a pharmacy may prepare stock in advance if they can show that patients regularly need the medicine — such as repeat prescriptions for the same person.

But some pharmacies produce large quantities without that evidence, Sahpra chief executive Boitumelo Semete-Makokotlela told Bhekisisa. This means "you're not compounding, you are manufacturing", which requires a good manufacturing practice licence that compounding pharmacies do not hold.

A good manufacturing practice licence shows that a company has met the safety and quality standards required to manufacture medicines.

A second concern is where ingredients come from. Active pharmaceutical ingredients — the substances in medicines that make them work — must be registered in South Africa and imported by a licensed entity, says Semete-Makokotlela. A pharmacy's operational licence does not authorise it to import unregistered ingredients, she says, yet some have arrived in travellers' luggage.

Another loophole that needs to be closed, Semete-Makokotlela notes, is where people sell experimental drugs (meds still being studied) or medicinal products directly to the public that are authorised for "research purposes" only. This includes some peptide products that are neither registered medicines nor experimental drugs in formal trials (like retatrutide), yet are still widely bought and sold as lifestyle or wellness drugs to do things like lower inflammation and boost energy.

Peptides are short chains of amino acids — small building blocks that the body uses to make proteins. Insulin is a peptide , as is semaglutide , the active ingredient in Ozempic. Both are registered medicines in South Africa.

However, there are other peptides, such as BPC-157 , which are being sold online and in gyms as solutions to specific health problems, such as tissue repair. These peptides aren't technically medicines, nor are they actively being studied in drug trials. Yet, they are sold as healthcare products, without evidence that they are safe or effective at treating humans.

Then there is the battle for public opinion, which is proving to be another hurdle. Semete-Makokotlela admits regulators are "on the back foot" when consumers see people losing weight while official warnings struggle to compete.

Close 

The answer, she believes, includes offering people registered alternatives at different prices — including cheaper generics — and working with healthcare professionals to steer patients towards safe, registered medicines.

South Africa's first generic weight-loss drug, containing semaglutide, hit the shelves in August .

How the public can keep safe

During the panel discussion, South African Revenue Service official Gene Ravele called the lack of coordination between enforcement agencies "the number one problem that organised crime is taking advantage of", and that this is also true for counterfeit and illegitimate drugs.

Border Management Authority head Nakampe Masiapato added that police detectives and prosecutors are often generalists, ill-equipped for specialised pharmaceutical cases. "They have no idea what this is about," he said.

For consumers, the advice from regulators is to use authorised channels and check that medicines are registered. Common signs that a drug is not legitimate is that it has unusual or blank packaging, no printed expiry date on the box or container, or that it doesn't have a normal insert detailing how to take it and the common side effects. Broken or dented packaging is another big 'tell', the Sandton meeting heard last week.

The bottom line is that a product's online availability, or a seller's claim that it is equivalent to a registered medicine, is not proof that it has been assessed or approved, said Fafudi. "If you cannot trust the source, do not trust the medicine."

This story was produced by the Bhekisisa Centre for Health Journalism.

World.title: Nigeria: Ebola Outbreak - Lawmakers Move to Amend Nigeria's 100-Year-Old Quarantine Act
World.content:
A tent used to isolate Ebola patients is disinfected in Bunia, DR Congo (file photo).

The senators resolve to treat the proposed amendment as an urgent matter to strengthen the country's response to the Ebola outbreak and prevent further spread of the disease.

The Senate on Wednesday resolved to engage the presidency on the review of Nigeria's Quarantine Act to bring it in line with modern public health legislation and the International Health Regulations.

The Senate President, Godswill Akpabio, directed the Senate Committee on Judiciary to liaise with the executive arm of government and relevant health agencies to develop proposals for amending the law.

Mr Akpabio gave the directive during Wednesday's plenary while lawmakers debated a motion on the need to enforce mandatory health screening at all international airports and other entry points to prevent the spread of Ebola and other epidemic-prone diseases.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The motion was sponsored by Francis Faduyile (APC, Ondo South).

Mr Akpabio said the proposed amendment should be treated as an urgent matter to strengthen the country's response to the Ebola outbreak and prevent further spread of the disease.

"We should take the issue very seriously and we should invite the Senate Committee on Judiciary to start contact with the health authorities in view to amending this Quarantine Act of 1926. This should be immediate, we should consult with the executive arm of government and all relevant agencies.

"We should not attempt to wait for them to bring an Act to us, we should go to them to get their inputs. That is what I think we should do in order to be able to nip this in the bud. Otherwise, if it spreads, there'll be a major problem."

Ebola case in Nigeria

Nigeria confirmed an Ebola case on Tuesday. The patient, a woman who recently arrived in the country on an international flight from Uganda, is receiving medical care in isolation at a private hospital in Abuja.

The Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Muhammad Pate, said 44 people had been identified as contacts of the patient and that authorities were tracking them for monitoring and possible isolation.

Senate's resolutions

After Mr Akpabio's remarks, the lawmakers rejected a proposal for senators to visit the entry points through which the woman travelled before being isolated in Abuja.

Instead, the upper chamber urged the federal government to immediately release emergency funds from the Service Wide Vote to prevent the spread of the Ebola virus.

The Senate also urged the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) and the Port Health Services to make health screening compulsory for all international arrivals at airports, seaports and designated land borders.

Close 

The lawmakers called for enhanced screening of passengers who had been in or transited through affected areas within the preceding 21 days, regardless of their nationality or country of departure.

They further urged the Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria (FAAN) and the Nigeria Immigration Service (NIS) to ensure that all entry points were adequately staffed and equipped with trained port health officers, thermal scanners, protective equipment and isolation rooms.

World.title: Zimbabwe: 200,000 Zimbabweans Have So Far Fled South Africa's Anti-Migrant Protests - Cabinet Told
World.content:
Just under 200,000 Zimbabweans have so far fled South Africa's anti-migrant protests, according to the government.

Cabinet was on Tuesday told that a total of 197,294 people had been repatriated and reintegrated since vigilante groups started hunting foreigners in some of South Africa's cities.

South Africa's anti-migrant protests have been led by pressure groups such as Operation Dudula, March and March and former South African President Jacob Zuma who have made it public that Zimbabweans, Somalis, Nigerians, Ethiopians, Malawians and other African nationals in their country illegally should leave.

Although efforts to flush out foreigners peaked around June 30 when the vigilante groups made a national call to chase them out, lootings, acts of violence and displacement have continuously been noted, with Durban being the latest city to do so.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Foreigners are being told to identify the nearest border from wherever they are and flee.

Of Zimbabwe's 197,294 returnees 42,553 had been repatriated through government efforts which saw buses being dispatched as far as Cape Town to collect stranded nationals at its consulate.

The other 154,741 self-repatriated.

"The nation is advised that the repatriation and re-integration of Zimbabwean nationals from South Africa has significantly declined, for both Government-supported returnees and self-repatriates," reads Tuesday's briefing.

"As at 6th October 2026, a total of 42,553 returnees had been repatriated through Government arrangements. The nationals comprise 10,475 male adults, 13,631 female adults, 9,001 male minors and 9,446 female minors.

"In addition, a cumulative total of 154,741 self-repatriations have been recorded to date."

Government has involved the Joint Operations Command (JOC) in the screening of returnees, some of whom had been serving time in South African prisons.

Some 700 deportees were received from Lindela Prison Repatriation Centre in South Africa.

Added the Cabinet brief: "As at 24th September 2026, a total of 700 deportees from Lindela Prison Repatriation Centre in South Africa were received at the Beitbridge Reception and Support Centre.

"The involvement of the Joint Operations Command (JOC) remains paramount in the screening and handling process, given that some of the deportees are convicts who were serving sentences in South African prisons and are required to complete the remainder of their sentences in Zimbabwe.

"Government continues to monitor the situation and is ready to respond to any possible influx of returnees in the future."

World.title: Rwanda: 'Be Healthy First' - Kagame Tells Youth
World.content:
President Paul Kagame has urged young people to prioritise their health and well-being before pursuing other ambitions, warning that poor health can undermine their ability to develop themselves, support their families and contribute to the country.

Speaking during the #MeetThePresident engagement at BK Arena on Wednesday, October 21, Kagame said young people should take care of themselves from an early age and make choices that protect their health as they work towards their personal goals.

ALSO READ: Use social media to build skills, ICT minister tells youth

"First, take care of yourself. The other things can come afterwards, but you need to be healthy, from childhood to adulthood, so that you can achieve everything else," he said.



Kagame linked personal well-being to discipline, saying young people should develop healthy habits and learn to distinguish between practices that benefit them and those that put their lives at risk.

He cited alcohol and drug abuse as examples of harmful behaviours that society should not accept simply because they have become common, urging young people to question such practices and understand their consequences.

"Some people say they turn to alcohol to cope with difficulties or help them sleep, but drinking will cause you more problems," he said.

ALSO READ: Kagame meets 10,000 youth at BK Arena

Kagame also encouraged young people to build themselves through learning, work and responsible decision-making, without losing sight of their health in the process.

"The Minister of Health always talks to you about exercise, and you should take that advice seriously, because exercise is essential for maintaining good health and keeping your body active," he said.

He urged young people to take an active role in challenging harmful practices within their communities, saying society should be clear about behaviours that put people at risk rather than allowing them to become normalised.

Kagame said young people should be able to discuss such issues openly, understand the difference between acceptable and harmful behaviour, and make informed choices about their lives.

He added that personal responsibility should come before expecting others to solve one's problems, encouraging young people to build their own capacity before relying on outside assistance.

"Don't waste time, learn, work and develop the ability to distinguish right from wrong. You should recognise your own potential and take responsibility for deciding who you want to become," he said.

World.title: Trump pushback, Biden 'disaster' and gender surprise: 5 key moments from Kansas Senate debate
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., and Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton sparred over President Donald Trump, immigration, Iran, transgender athletes, artificial intelligence and personal controversies during a contentious Kansas Senate debate Wednesday night.

The hour-long showdown came less than two weeks before Election Day as Marshall seeks a second term and Hamilton, a longtime pastor, tries to become the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Kansas since 1932.

The race has drawn increased national attention as Republicans and Democrats battle for control of the Senate, with Trump traveling to Kansas earlier this week to campaign for Marshall â a topic touched on during the debate.

Here are five moments that stood out from Wednesday night's debate.

SLEEPER SENATE RACE EMERGES AS UNEXPECTED HEADACHE FOR REPUBLICANS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS

Debate opens with candidates confronted over personal controversies

The debate wasted little time getting contentious, opening with questions about controversies that have fueled attacks against both candidates.

Marshall was confronted with a New York Times review that found his former medical practice sued more than 700 patients over unpaid bills.

"Every year we gave away $3 to $4 million of charity, but we also had a business," Marshall responded. "We had 300 employees, we had a mortgage payment, we had electric."

Hamilton, meanwhile, was questioned about his handling of allegations involving a volunteer at his church's summer camp who was accused of sexual abuse.

Hamilton acknowledged that he should have ensured the individual did not return to the camp following an initial investigation.

FROM 'THIRD REICH' TO âNOT THAT INFORMEDâ: SENATE DEBATES DELIVER FIREWORKS BEFORE MIDTERMS

"I should have checked to make sure that he wasn't going back," Hamilton said. "That was a mistake on my part."

Marshall says 'President Trump is not always right'

Trump became part of the debate after moderators played footage from the president's campaign appearance for Marshall in Kansas earlier in the week.

"And at this election, I'm asking you to pretend, please, that I'm on the ballot. Just pretend," Trump told the crowd.

Marshall was then asked whether Trump's support meant Kansans should expect him to back every part of the president's agenda.

"No," Marshall responded, saying there had been "multiple times" when he objected to Trump.

Pressed to identify a specific disagreement, Marshall pointed to recent immigration enforcement in southwest Kansas and Trump's approach to beef imports.

"Just like with my wife, I can disagree with her. My wife is always right," Marshall joked. "And President Trump is not always right."

Marshall nevertheless urged Trump voters to turn out for him, arguing that electing Hamilton could help Democrats capture the Senate.

Both candidates say there are 'two genders'

The two rivals found themselves in agreement when the moderator asked each candidate how many genders there are.

"There's two. There's a boy and there's a girl," Marshall said. "I delivered 5,000 of them and almost half were boys and half were girls."

"There are two genders, male and female," Hamilton responded.

TOP TAKEAWAYS FROM JD VANCE TOWN HALL: COSTLY GAS, DC CORRUPTION, IMMIGRATION HOT TAKES AND THE WAR

The candidates then turned to the debate over transgender participation in women's sports.

Hamilton said decisions over athletic eligibility should generally be made locally but was unequivocal about whether biological males should compete against females.

"I have a 12-year-old granddaughter. I don't want biological men or boys competing against her that could harm her," Hamilton said. "It's not a fair, fair fight."

Marshall argued that by high school, "boys need to be in boys sports, girls in girls sports," while accusing national Democrats of pushing "transgender ideology."

Hamilton later accused Marshall of using the issue to "pick on" and "bully" people.

Hamilton calls AI an 'existential threat' â but can't name regulations he'd support

Hamilton called for greater federal oversight of artificial intelligence and compared the emerging technology to the development of nuclear power and nuclear weapons.

"We developed a Nuclear Regulatory Commission. We need to do the same thing with AI," Hamilton said.

But when the moderator pressed him to identify specific federal regulations he would support, Hamilton acknowledged he did not yet have an answer.

"You know what? I'm not sure, to be honest," Hamilton said, arguing that even experts are struggling to understand the technology's potential dangers.

Marshall advocated a "light touch" approach focused on national security, transparency, protecting children and privacy, while slamming a one-size-fits-all global order for artificial intelligence advancement.

Hamilton pushed back sharply.

"This is an existential â potential existential threat to the human race," Hamilton said. "We can't just go with a light touch and hope everybody does their best."

BIDEN CONSPICUOUSLY ABSENT FROM CAMPAIGN TRAIL AS OBAMA, HARRIS STEP UP FOR MIDTERM PUSH

Hamilton calls Biden's border policies a 'disaster'

Hamilton sought to put distance between himself and former President Joe Biden when moderators challenged the Democrat over his claim that he would "lead from the middle."

The moderator pointed to Hamilton's past donations to Democrats, including Biden, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Rep. Sharice Davids, D-Kan., before asking him to identify a progressive policy he opposed.

"The Biden policies when it came to the border were a disaster," Hamilton responded. "I believe in strong and secure borders."

"I'm not somebody who favors the Socialist Party," Hamilton added. "I'm somebody who stands in the middle."

Hamilton also reiterated during the debate that he would not support Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer for majority leader if Democrats capture control of the chamber.

World.title: Ex-SJSU volleyball coach alleges trans player failed testosterone test, result was kept 'secret' from team
World.content:
Former San Jose State University (SJSU) volleyball coach Melissa Batie-Smoose alleges a school official told her transgender player Blaire Fleming could not compete at one point during the 2023 season because Flemingâs testosterone level exceeded the eligibility limit.

In a new interview with OutKick, Batie-Smoose, who is now the head volleyball coach at Cisco College, claimed SJSU associate athletics director Laura Alexander informed her of Fleming's failed test before the womenâs volleyball team left for its first conference match.

"So it was told to me by our associate AD, confirming to me that Fleming was not showing up for the test, the blood test," Batie-Smoose said.

INSIDE THE FALLOUT OF THE SJSU VOLLEYBALL SCANDAL: âTHIS IS AN OBVIOUS PROBLEMâ

"And that Fleming had one day left before we were going to leave for our first conference match, and that he needed to come in and test. And then, then she proceeded to tell me the next day that after the test, that the testosterone levels were too high, and Fleming is ineligible to play and will not be going on the trip that day."

The coach added that the alleged failed test was kept "a secret" from the rest of the team.

The allegation also appears in Batie-Smooseâs Oct. 13 federal lawsuit against the California State University (CSU) trustees and 11 SJSU employees.

Fleming then missed a long stretch of the 2023 season. SJSUâs athletics website claimed the player had not competed since Sept. 16 of that year "due to injuries," in a November 2023 game recap.

Batie-Smoose said, "The injury happened the day that Fleming went to go get tested, and it was very questionable."

Batie-Smoose believes the injury explanation helped keep the alleged eligibility issue secret. Her lawsuit also describes that conclusion as her belief.

EX-SJSU VOLLEYBALL PLAYER SPEAKS OUT ON ALLEGED SCHOLARSHIP DECEPTION BY COACH DURING TRANS SCANDAL

"Around the same time the testosterone results were revealed, Fleming thereafter missed conference matches because of a reported hand injury, which Plaintiff believes was an excuse to hide his ineligibility to play because of his hormone level," the lawsuit states.

SJSU's own game records confirm that Fleming missed matches, but they do not establish whether a testosterone test result played a role in the absence.

In 2023, NCAA rules allowed transgender women to play on womenâs teams, but they had to meet requirements for hormone treatment and testosterone levels. The NCAA kept that policy, known as Phase Two, in place through the 2023â24 school year.

Under that framework, transgender women had to complete at least one year of testosterone suppression treatment before competing on a womenâs team. They also had to provide blood-test results that met the NCAAâs limit for their sport. For womenâs volleyball, the Phase Two limit was below 10 nanomoles per liter of total testosterone in the blood.

The requirements applied before an athleteâs first competition in each season segment, including nonconference games. Schools had to submit eligibility documents for an NCAA medical panel to review before the athlete competed. The requirement did not begin only when conference play started.

Schools also had to certify athletesâ eligibility before allowing them to compete. If an athlete became ineligible, NCAA rules required the school to immediately keep that athlete out of competition.

SJSU WAS TOLD OF DECADES-OLD ALLEGATIONS AGAINST VOLLEYBALL COACH DURING CONTROVERSIAL 2024 SEASON

Batie-Smooseâs account does not establish that Fleming played while ineligible. Fleming did return in November of that season, missing 17 matches.

SJSU has declined to respond to a request for clarification.

"Due to pending litigation, San Jose State is unable to respond to your inquiry," a university spokesperson told OutKick.

OutKick also reached out to Fleming, the NCAA, the Mountain West and the CSU for comment, but did not receive a response.

Batie-Smooseâs allegations extend beyond Flemingâs eligibility. She also says her relationship with head coach Todd Kress unraveled as their political views grew apart â and accuses him of using her support for Trump to turn players against her.

She described Kress as a longtime friend who once shared her conservative beliefs.

"Todd was a conservative Republican, and we shared the same views on a lot of things. And thatâs why we were friends for so long," she said. "And then somewhere in the craziness, he went left and really extreme left."

Asked when she noticed that change, Batie-Smoose said it happened "before the first Trump election."

The two continued discussing politics, she said. But she alleges Kress began raising their differences in front of athletes, crossing a boundary she wanted to keep between their personal disagreements and their coaching jobs.

"Oh, yeah. We talked about politics all the time," she said. "You know, once he turned, it was more, um, he would bring it up in settings that I felt like it was very inappropriate."

"We can talk and debate on those subjects when weâre in a room together, but not in front of student athletes. I feel like that is not the time and the place to speak on that."

Batie-Smoose said the treatment intensified after they arrived at SJSU in 2023. She believes Kress brought up her political and religious views to mock her and weaken her relationships with the team.

"Especially once we arrived at San Jose State, and Iâve referred to this before, this man was unrecognizable," she said.

She alleged that Kress knew which players would object to her views and raised the subject in front of them to create division.

Asked whether Kress told those players that he had once held similar conservative beliefs, Batie-Smoose replied: "Oh, no way. No way. He would never state that."

She said she did not share his past political views with the athletes herself.

"I do not talk about those things in front of athletes ever," she said.

Her lawsuit alleges that Kress called her a "Trump lover." It also says she repeatedly expressed her religious belief that "God made man and woman," and that she believes his treatment reflected hostility toward her faith.

She further alleges that he cornered and berated her during an office confrontation in about August 2023, after a canceled recruiting visit. The complaint says he threatened that he could get her fired.

Batie-Smoose says she reported the encounter to administrators and human resources. She alleges they told her Kress was her boss and she needed to listen to him.

Her attorney, Vernadette Broyles, described what she sees as a broader effort to silence her client.

"There was a watchdog that was assigned to be at every practice and to travel with Melissa to watch what she said, to watch what she did," Broyles said.

The lawsuit identifies a university administrator in connection with that allegation. The complaint presents the claimed purpose as Batie-Smooseâs belief.

CSU has defended its handling of Batie-Smoose in its March lawsuit against the U.S. Department of Education.

The employment dispute grew as the volleyball controversy spread.

During the 2024 season, former SJSU co-captain Slusser publicly challenged Flemingâs participation, and several opponents refused to play against SJSU. Batie-Smoose filed a Title IX complaint Oct. 29 alleging unequal treatment and failures to address concerns inside the program.

SJSU placed Batie-Smoose on paid leave days later. Its suspension letter cited several grounds, including alleged disclosure of private student information, differential treatment of athletes and unprofessional conduct. Batie-Smoose disputes those grounds.

On Jan. 31, 2025, the university told her it would not renew her temporary appointment. Batie-Smoose then filed an employment lawsuit against SJSU last September.

Then, this year, on Sept. 4, Judge NoÃ«l Wise dismissed her second amended complaint in an earlier employment case. Wise found that her allegations did not adequately show that SJSU punished her because of her sex or for raising complaints protected by law. The judge emphasized the complaintâs account that SJSU acted after she shared student information with the media despite instructions to keep it confidential.

Wise allowed her to amend. The ruling addressed whether that complaint stated a valid legal claim. It did not decide the dispute after a trial.

The October filing accuses officials of violating her rights to speak, practice her faith and hold political beliefs. It also alleges unequal treatment under the law. Batie-Smoose seeks reinstatement or a comparable job, compensation and correction of adverse personnel records.

Federal investigators have separately challenged SJSUâs handling of the volleyball program.

In January, the Education Departmentâs Office for Civil Rights concluded that the school violated Title IX over athletic participation, facilities and its response to complaints. The agency also raised concerns about unequal treatment in employment, while acknowledging that incomplete records limited its conclusions.

CSU disputes the federal findings. The system sued the Education Department in March, arguing that SJSU followed the law and NCAA rules that governed the seasons under review.

Batie-Smoose says legal advice shaped how much she shared publicly as the dispute unfolded.

"When this all began, I did not have legal representation," she said.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOWâUNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"I mean, we have a lawsuit here and we want to win, and we also want to make change."

She has since returned to coaching. Cisco College in Texas announced her hiring as head volleyball coach in April.

"This is what God intended me to do," she said.

She described the new job as a chance to lead young women again while her case moves forward.

"God put me here. I have a purpose, and Iâm so blessed that I get to lead these young women again, and Iâm having a lot of fun at it."

World.title: Macron has one more chance to save the country or ‘it’s lost for France,’ business owner warns
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

FIRST ON FOX: A French business owner who had five of her family's stores wrecked by looters last week said this coming Saturday's protest could be a watershed moment for France.

Her message to President Emmanuel Macron: "Next Saturday is your last chance to save France," Michele Teboul, the business owner, said in an interview with Fox News Digital.

Addressing both Interior Minister Laurent Nunez and Macron, she said, "If they donât do whatâs necessary to do next Saturday, I think itâs lost for France."

Teboul lost more than merchandise when looters ransacked 15 of her familyâs stores, leaving five completely destroyed. She also lost faith in her governmentâs ability to protect them.

REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: FRANCE BRACES FOR MORE UNREST AFTER PARTS OF PARIS SPUN OUT OF CONTROL

Teboul accused authorities of failing to provide enough police to protect businesses, leaving families like hers facing destroyed stores and a costly recovery. She demanded that they protect the population before another Saturday.

Her familyâs retail operations include stores in Paris, Bordeaux, Lyon, Marseille and Montpellier. Her sons work within the same company and operate their own brand, she said.

For her family, protections put in place before the violence proved insufficient. Attackers used axes to break through boarding, she said, leaving her sons facing a difficult recovery.

"We can say that five of the most important stores have been looted," she said, describing those locations as "completely destroyed."

Now, her family needs to pay for additional protection while trying to meet insurersâ security requirements.

Teboul said it would take at least two months to repair and secure the stores to the required standards. She described those requirements as a condition for obtaining insurance coverage, adding another obstacle to reopening and recovering the business.

"I think the winter season is dead," she said.

VIOLENCE ERUPTS AT FRANCE PROTESTS AS MACRON WARNS UNREST IS BEING EXPLOITED

Companies with established operations and financial reserves may be able to absorb the disruption, she said. Younger businesses face a more difficult path.

"The government said they would help us," Teboul said. "Weâre going to see."

Her sons have hired security guards with dogs. She also said she had heard of other shopkeepers obtaining weapons or tear gas, emphasizing that her sons had not purchased weapons.

"Some have bought weapons," she said. "You know, we are not used to weapons in France."

The concern extends beyond damaged merchandise and storefronts. Teboul, who is Jewish, said that many Jews are considering leaving France and warned that further disorder could deepen that uncertainty if things don't get better.

SOME SYNAGOGUES CANCELED PRAYERS AS FRENCH JEWS FACED WARNINGS AMID VIOLENT PROTESTS

"Itâs going to be very hard to imagine a future in France for us, especially for Jews," she said of her hope that the coming Saturday would be different.

Teboul said Jewish schools, synagogues and community businesses have dedicated security arrangements. Teboul is a former director of CRIF is the umbrella organization representing French Jewish institutions.

She stressed, however, that the weekendâs violence was a national problem affecting people beyond the Jewish community.

"The specific problem of last Saturday is not a problem of Jews," she said. "The whole of France is concerned by this problem."

Teboul said looters sought street-wear and expensive merchandise. She accused police of failing to protect businesses during Saturdayâs unrest, saying officers were overwhelmed as large crowds descended on city centers, particularly in Marseille and Lyon.

She cited an estimate she had heard being talked of as being around 30,000 young people arriving in central Marseille, a figure Fox News Digital could not independently verify. French October 17:

Leading French broadcaster BFM reported on its X account that "Between 1,800 and 3,000 people" engaged in "the ransacking of the city center of Marseille, according to the prosecutor's estimates."

MACRON JETS OUT OF RIOT-TORN FRANCE FOR GULF TRIP AS POLITICAL PRESSURE MOUNTS

"They were not enough," she said of the police.

The French government has acknowledged failures in its response to the unrest.

She said that authorities had mistaken the threat for an ordinary demonstration. "Of course they could prevent it," she added.

Teboul distinguished between students protesting over grievances and those who used the demonstrations as cover to steal.

"There were two events on Saturday," she said. "The looters, they took the opportunity that there were many people downtown, and then they came."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

For Teboul, the next test is whether authorities can protect what remains of her familyâs livelihood and everyone else in the country and restore their sense of security in France.

"We have to feel secure," she said. "We donât feel secure for the moment."

Teboul warned that another failure to protect the population could also have consequences for the countryâs leadership.

"The government may fall down," she said.

Fox News Digital's Sydney Finver contributed to this report.

World.title: House Dem leader's attack on voter ID comes back to haunt him after election fraud bust in his home state
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

House Democrats' No. 3 leader is under fire for his opposition to voter ID in his home state of California.

House Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., spoke at a press conference earlier this month criticizing a measure on Californians' ballot this Election Day that, if passed, would mandate that voters show government-issued photo ID at the polls.

He made the comments just weeks before the Department of Justice (DOJ) announced a crime bust that saw several U.S. permanent residents accused of registering to vote despite not being citizens.

MAP IT: DOJ ILLEGAL VOTING CRACKDOWN SWEEPS 17 STATES AS RAZOR-THIN ELECTIONS FACE SCRUTINY

Rep. Ken Calvert, R-Calif., hammered Aguilar's opposition to voter ID and argued the DOJ's recent actions made it "obvious" that the ballot measure, called Proposition 39, was needed.

"Give me a break," Calvert told Fox News Digital. "You have to show an ID to board an airplane, cash a paycheck, rent an apartment, or even buy cold medicine at the grocery store. Democrats claiming that requiring photo ID before casting a ballot is somehow 'racist' or 'voter suppression' is complete nonsense and an insult to every voter's intelligence."

NEW YORK CITYâS LONE REPUBLICAN IN CONGRESS ACCUSES MAMDANI, SCHUMER OF 'HYPOCRISY' IN VOTER ID FIGHT

Rep. Vince Fong, R-Calif., said voter ID "is basic election security that the vast majority of Americans support, and 36 states already require."

"While opponents are resorting to lies and fearmongering, Proposition 39 is commonsense reform in a world where you need an ID to rent a car, stay at a hotel, open a bank account, or board a flight," Fong told Fox News Digital. "The DOJâs recent voter fraud bust in California is exactly why these safeguards matter."

Rep. Young Kim, R-Calif., similarly said showing photo ID is a "simple standard we already require to board a plane, purchase alcohol, or pick up a prescription."

"This isn't controversial and it shouldn't be complicated. Our elections deserve at least as much consideration as a beer or a bottle of wine," Kim told Fox News Digital.

Aguilar, meanwhile, criticized Proposition 39 during a press conference with Democratic gubernatorial candidate and former Biden administration Cabinet Secretary Xavier Becerra earlier this month.

"We will not stand for this, because we will not stand for people to lose an opportunity to exercise their ability to vote. In Arizona, they tried this. They wanted folks to put their driver's license numbers on their ballots. Think about that. What if you miss one digit? Your vote doesn't count?" Aguilar proposed. "What if you're married in California? What if you're married, and you haven't changed your name and you go to vote? No longer will you be able to vote. That is what is at stake for Californians."

SCHUMER SAID 'DEMOCRATS SUPPORT VOTER ID' â THEN EVERY SENATE DEMOCRAT VOTED AGAINST GOP BILL

He called it a "voter suppression effort" pushed by Republicans.

"Republicans can win only when they suppress the vote. Donald Trump and MAGA Republicans know that they are bankrupt of ideas and solutions, and so they have to change the rules of the game," Aguilar said.

NEWSOM SPARS WITH TRUMP-APPOINTED PROSECUTOR OVER 20,000 SUSPECTED NONCITIZENS ON VOTER ROLLS

Meanwhile, the California government criticized the DOJ's operation while pointing to reports that said more of those charged were registered as Republicans rather than Democrats.

"For nearly a decade, Trump has baselessly alleged mass voter fraud rings were employed by Democrats and utilized 'illegal immigrants' to sway elections across the country â often pointing to California," a release on Gov. Gavin Newsom's state website read. "Courts at all levels have rejected the claims of vast voter fraud or that elections were rigged against the President."

Voter ID laws currently exist in 36 states and polls have shown they have a majority of Americans' support.

But in Congress, several efforts to pass federal voter ID legislation have been thwarted by Democrats in recent years.

Fox News Digital reached out to Aguilar's campaign for a response to his GOP House colleagues' comments.

World.title: Americans are making costly grocery mistake even before entering the store, expert warns
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A grocery shopping mistake that could be costing Americans money starts even before they get to the store, according to cookbook author Jenn Lueke.

"The No. 1 biggest mistake is just not taking the time to plan ahead," Lueke, Boston-based author of "Don't Think About Dinner," told Fox News Digital.

Making a grocery list and deciding what to cook for the week ahead can help shoppers save money and stress less about meals, she said.

SCIENTISTS SAY YOU'VE BEEN THROWING AWAY PERFECTLY GOOD MEAT BECAUSE OF ONE COMMON MISTAKE

Another source of overspending may be the pressure to make a different, impressive dinner every night of the week.

Social media can offer inspiration but Lueke, known online as Jenn Eats Goood, said home cooks can lean on familiar meals and switch them up with ingredients already in their pantries.

CELEBRITY CHEF SAYS IF YOU CAN DRIVE TO MCDONALD'S, YOU CAN COOK HEALTHY MEALS AT HOME

"You really can repeat meals," she said, adding that a "base recipe" can also be tweaked seasonally or depending on what is in your freezer at the moment.

One example from her cookbook is a one-pot chicken thighs and rice dish. Lueke said cooks can swap in different proteins or add seasonal ingredients such as squash in the fall or asparagus and peas in the spring.

NEW PROTEIN RANKING NAMES UNEXPECTED WINNER OVER BEEF, SALMON AND EGGS

A bowl-style meal or vegetable frittata can also serve as a flexible starting point for using up any food that is about to go bad, she said.

Keeping pantry and freezer staples on hand can give shoppers more options during the week, Lueke also said.

CLICK HERE TO 

She recommends ingredients such as canned beans, rice, pasta and quinoa, which can be bought in bulk or picked up on sale. Frozen proteins can also help cut down on weekly shopping trips.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

For shoppers trying to stretch a $50 to $75 grocery trip, Lueke suggests bulking meals up with hearty, lower-cost produce such as carrots, onions, potatoes and sweet potatoes, along with proteins like chicken thighs, tofu and chickpeas.

She also recommends getting more than one use out of an ingredient. If a recipe calls for only part of a can of artichokes, for example, use the rest in another meal, she said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

Spice blends and homemade sauces can also change the flavor of a protein, allowing shoppers to prepare the same ingredient in different ways.

"The biggest thing is having that plan, but also using one ingredient in more than one way, if you can," she said.

World.title: France's riot chaos fuels Farage's warning that mass immigration failures could haunt another country next
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

As violent riots grip France, British political leader Nigel Farage warned Americans against repeating what he described as Europe's mass immigration failures, arguing that years of unchecked migration have transformed European cities and fueled unrest that could eventually spread elsewhere.

"People like me who were warning about this years ago have sadly been proven right, but the problems are gonna be here for a very, very long time," Farage told Fox News Digital in an interview. "Please, please don't make the same level of mistakes that we have," he said in his message to Americans.

Violent riots have erupted across parts of Europe in recent weeks, particularly in France, with Farage pointing to years of mass migration and failed political leadership as key factors fueling the unrest. The Reform UK leader singled out Emmanuel Macron, arguing that the French president should have mobilized the military to confront the violence, after education protests spiraled into riots, destruction and theft.

MACRON JETS OUT OF RIOT-TORN FRANCE FOR GULF TRIP AS POLITICAL PRESSURE MOUNTS

"Macron was asleep at the wheel, and it isn't just that he was at a concert," Farage said. "And whilst the French do have effective police forces, the scale of the uprising, I mean the mass looting, the mass looting and violence that took place in Paris was genuinely horrendous."

"Meloni's reaction was swifter and a better sign of leadership," Farage said, referring to the Italian leader deploying 500 military troops to Milan in response to recent riots. "But the problem is, for people like Macron, who have always said, any criticism of immigration, whether legal or illegal, makes you racist, they psychologically find it hard to face up to their own failures of policy."

Farage warned that the unrest he described in France and elsewhere in Europe could eventually erupt in Britain, pointing to demonstrations in London and questioning whether British leaders would respond more forcefully than Macron.

ITALY UNLEASHES MILITARY RESPONSE TO VIOLENT RIOTS AS FRANCE FACES A RECKONING OF ITS OWN

"You know, my real worry is they can happen in this country too," Farage said. "We've got the same hard left here. We've the same hate mobs that march, chanting in the streets of London, from the river to the sea."

"I'm concerned that these things could happen here. And I wonder whether a British Prime Minister has got any more courage than President Macron in France," he added.

Farage contrasted Europe's failure to control its borders with President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown in the United States.

TRUMP, WALTZ LINK FRANCE RIOTS TO MASS IMMIGRATION AS THOUSANDS ARE ARRESTED

"Look, whatever you think of President Trump's current policies, one thing he has done, and he promised he'd do. He's closed the southern border," Farage said.

Trump vowed Tuesday to treat potential rioters in the U.S. "very rough," pointing to the unrest in France," he said at a rally in Greenville, North Carolina before being interrupted by a protestor in the crowd.

"They're crazy, these people. Look at that guy. He's a nutjob," Trump said, in reference to the protester.

He warned that he would crack down on potential threats, saying he would not allow similar unrest to take hold in the U.S.

FRANCE COULD FACE EVEN WORSE DESTRUCTION WITH SECOND WEEKEND OF PLANNED RIOTS, STATE DEPT WARNS

"That's what you witness over the last three or four days. You watch nutjobs like him in France ruining their country," Trump said. "We're not going to put up with it by the way."

FOILED TERROR PLOT AT BOMBER BASE SIGNALS WIDER THREAT TO US MILITARY INSTALLATIONS: EXPERT

Farage said he has foreshadowed such criminal acts, alleging that Iran has exploited illegal crossings of the English Channel to move operatives into Britain.

World.title: El-Sayed, Rogers clash over Muslim Brotherhood, Trump and guns: 5 fiery debate moments
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Former Rep. Mike Rogers and his Democratic opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, tore into each other at their second Michigan Senate debate Wednesday evening.

Rogers, a former FBI special agent and the Republican U.S. Senate candidate, clashed with El-Sayed over the personal barbs, accusations and fierce divides that have defined one of the countryâs most anticipated Senate elections.

Here are some of the most noteworthy moments from the fiery faceoff.

El-Sayed accuses Rogers of backing Trumpâs war with Iran

As evidence of Rogersâ alignment with President Donald Trump, El-Sayed accused him of backing the war in Iran, a conflict El-Sayed himself described as "aimless."

"He's got a war for everything, and he won't back off the war now. He supports this war," El-Sayed said.

"If you don't believe me, I want you to pay attention. On Sunday, when Donald Trump comes here at the invitation of Mike Rogers to remind you that, in fact, Donald Trump is on the ballot through Mike Rogers. They are hip to hip on this war, and you are paying the cost," he added, referring to one of Rogers' upcoming campaign events.

Rogers quickly fired back, reiterating a moment from their first debate when El-Sayed refused to answer whether Israel or Iran posed a greater threat to the U.S.

"My opponent can't even condemn the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps], which is the terrorist enforcement arm of Iran, and doesn't believe Iran is any more dangerous than Israel. This is an absolute nonstarter," Rogers said.

THE MEDICARE FOR ALL TRADE-OFFS SOCIALISTS AREN'T TALKING ABOUT, ACCORDING TO EXPERTS

Rogers sparks explosive moment with resurfaced Muslim Brotherhood accusations

At one point during the debate, Rogers accused El-Sayed of deleting social media content about defunding the police â a progressive stance that circulated among far-left Democrats in 2020 after the death of George Floyd.

"I will tell you this: he did call for defunding the police â¦ [and] he deleted all of this material. Why would you do that? Why would you go through and take all of that time to delete all of the material? X videos, comments, podcast. Why? Because he was passionate about defunding the police," Rogers said.

"As a matter of fact, he asked the Muslim Brotherhood head, Morsi, in Egypt to defund the police there, too," Rogers added, referring to the former Egyptian president associated with the group.

The last remark triggered a fierce reaction from El-Sayed, who has fended off questions about ties to the Muslim Brotherhood throughout his campaign.

"He keeps raising this question about this association with the organization," El-Sayed said. "It's really quite beneath you."

Although Fox News Digital has not discovered any links between El-Sayed and the Muslim Brotherhood, critics have pointed to El-Sayed's ties to the Muslim Students Association (MSA), a group listed as part of a strategy memorandum for North America written by one of the Muslim Brotherhoodâs members, Mohamed Akram.

El-Sayed served as the vice president of the MSA chapter at the University of Michigan during his time there as a senior in 2007, according to College Fix.

ABDUL EL-SAYED'S ALLEGED FAMILY TIES TO MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD SURFACE AFTER DENYING ANY LINK DURING NBC INTERVIEW

Rogers blasts hidden costs of expanding government promises

Throughout the night, El-Sayed doubled down on promises to expand government programs like Medicaid and measures to "put money in your pocket," a refrain that has been a cornerstone of his campaign.

But Rogers made sure to cast doubt on those commitments, arguing that the policies would carry with them a heftier price tag than the Democratic nominee would acknowledge.

"So think of all of the three things he just talked about. Put money in your pockets. It's a great slogan. There's nothing behind it. Matter of fact, when his Democratic socialist-aligned policies are engaged, you'll be lucky to have a d--- pair of pants when you're done," Rogers said.

"Medicare for all. He doesn't tell you how much taxes you have to get charged, and you lose your private health insurance. These aren't real solutions. These are solutions that are going to make your life more miserable. And it's going to take away your choices in healthcare."

Rogers claims El-Sayed said âquiet part out loudâ on AI regulation

When asked about AI regulation, Abdul El-Sayed briefly mentioned he would support having "democratically appointed folks on the board of these AI corporations," citing what he described as an existential threat to the workforce.

Rogers seized on the moment, accusing El-Sayed of verbalizing a desire to exercise public control of private companies.

"He said the quiet part out loud," Rogers said.

"He wants government to go into these businesses. That is the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). [They] come in for your business and your future. And so, you need to really stop for a minute and think about, do you want somebody who wants the government involved in these companies?" Rogers added.

Notably, Abdul El-Sayed has not officially received an endorsement from the DSA, nor has he affirmed the groupâs platform. Even so, he has endorsed and received endorsements from a number of candidates who have received the DSAâs backing. Among them, El-Sayed supported New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a self-proclaimed socialist, in his bid for office last year.

ROGERS WARNS MICHIGAN VOTERS AGAINST EL-SAYEDâS âEXTREMEâ AGENDA AHEAD OF ELECTION

El-Sayed gets heat in rapid-fire round over Second Amendment

At the close of the debate, Rogers fired back at El-Sayed when the Democratic candidate needled him for refusing to answer yes or no to a question about implementing universal background checks for gun purchases.

"It all depends. It all depends," Rogers said.

"Itâs not hard. Look at that. So dependable," El-Sayed quipped.

Rogers fired back, noting that El-Sayed had once called for doing away with the Second Amendment in comments he had made before he launched his Senate bid.

"You want to ban the Second Amendment. Why donât you talk about that?"

Rogers was alluding to a video published on YouTube in 2023 in which El-Sayed had compared the right to bear arms to a right to healthcare.

"What if we tweaked the Constitution, amended the amendment, and instead of the right to bear arms, we change it to the right to have healthcare?" El-Sayed said.

He claimed altruism in the proposal, saying more people would live and arguing against individuals owning firearms, instead suggesting that only designated community-based groups like police forces should be issued firearms.

The video has since been made private.

With their second debate now in the rearview mirror, El-Sayed and Rogers have closed out their scheduled debates and are unlikely to meet again until after the election. Having cleared their respective primaries and secured their parties' nominations, the pair will face off in Michiganâs general election on Nov. 3.

After the debate, MIGOP Chairman Jim Runestad said in a statement to Fox News Digital: "Mike Rogers demonstrated yet again why he is the commonsense, steady hand Michiganders want to see in the U.S. Senate. We cannot afford Abdul El-Sayed's far-left, big-government policies, and we cannot risk electing a person who campaigns with the likes of Hasan Piker and seemingly justified the horrific terrorist attack targeting children and the Jewish community in Bloomfield Hills."
