World.title: On Main Street, Goldman Sachs makes a bet on AI
World.content:
Artificial intelligence is already a huge business for Wall Street. But how is it playing on Main Street?

Goldman Sachs, as part of a philanthropic effort, is spending big in an attempt to help ensure smaller employers get in on it. The bank announced Thursday that it has launched the Small Business AI Institute as part of a $500 million expansion of its 10,000 Small Businesses, a program geared toward educating and supporting entrepreneurs. It said it would partner with Google, Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta to provide AI training and tools to entrepreneurs.

“You’ve got to embrace new technology always, because if you’re not embracing it, trying to figure out how it can make your businesses better, there’s a real chance that you can fall behind,” Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon said in an exclusive interview for NBC News’ Business in America series.

It’s a pivotal moment for the AI wave and its financial backers, including Goldman. The technology is broadly available to consumers, and U.S. economic growth increasingly depends on the buildup of data centers.

“We believe AI will create the greatest boom in entrepreneurship and small businesses that the world has ever seen,” Sam Altman, CEO and co-founder of OpenAI, said in an announcement from Goldman Sachs. “This is an incredible moment for anyone with an idea for a new endeavor because the gap between imagining it and bringing it to life is getting much smaller.”

Yet the growth that AI is already driving has also helped push up prices for inflation-weary Americans. Anger at data centers is a rare point of bipartisan agreement among voters, and the midterm elections are days away.

In the finance world, critics say AI is an investment bubble that could burst and potentially wipe out companies and jobs. Cracks are forming in the AI trade in markets after Big Tech firms drove much of stocks’ recent surge to record highs.

Goldman Sachs, like much of Wall Street, is in the thick of it all.

The bank’s share price has approximately tripled over the past three years while AI-related companies pushed the stock market to record highs. Goldman helped lead the much-ballyhooed, record-breaking initial public offering for Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which counts xAI and Grok among its core businesses. Goldman is also reportedly working on the IPO of Anthropic, the startup behind the AI chatbot Claude.

“There is going to be a lot of financing to do,” Solomon said last week on an earnings call, “and we’re going to be in the middle of that.”

Goldman and other big firms are counting on small businesses, which make up more than 90% of all U.S. companies and drive most of America’s job growth, to buy in. It won’t be easy getting everyone on board, though.

A recent NBC News poll found that 79% of respondents believe the government isn’t doing enough to regulate AI use. Sixty-seven percent disapprove of how President Donald Trump is handling the technology. Trump has said he favors lax AI regulation from the government.

Meanwhile, some small businesses that already embraced AI have faced backlash from the public, including restaurants that used AI-generated images of food that critics denounced as “slop.”

Still, according to Goldman, entrepreneurs are adopting the technology at a fast clip. A survey this year of more than 2,400 graduates of the company’s small business program found that 86% of respondents were using AI in their businesses, up from just 56% in 2024.

Rechelle Balanzat, founder of the laundry services app Juliette and an alumna of the 10,000 Small Businesses program, told NBC News she sees AI as a tool to help her gin up more business with limited resources.

Rechelle Balanzat, founder of the laundry services app Juliette. Kayla Steinberg / NBC News

“I really treat my AI as my consigliere,” Balanzat said. “They are not there to replace your accountant and lawyer. They are not there to replace humans. However, it does help prep me to have much more meaningful questions when I am meeting with my accountant and with my lawyer.”

Despite the widespread use of AI among the Goldman program alumni, just 15% of them said they had fully integrated AI into their core operations, according to Goldman.

Mike DiMarino, who heads Linda Tool in Brooklyn, New York, was part of the inaugural class of Goldman’s program in 2010. The company makes precision machine components for the military and aerospace industries, and DiMarino thinks AI can help with planning, management and processes.

“I’m sure there’s a lot more it can do that I don’t know yet,” he said.

But DiMarino is also cautious about how Linda Tool uses the technology, especially given how much sensitive information the company handles for its work in defense, aerospace and manufacturing.

Mike DiMarino heads Linda Tool. Kayla Steinberg / NBC News

His concerns mirror broader cybersecurity fears about AI. In July, a swarm of about 700 AI agents created by OpenAI hacked into the open-source platform Hugging Face. Last month, Google said Chinese hackers are using AI to automate their attacks.

In addition to the security risks, company leaders are also increasingly raising concerns about the cost of AI, especially relative to its concrete impact on the bottom line. After spending on AI tokens exploded in the past year, companies from Uber to Microsoft to Meta have all taken steps to limit or re-evaluate how their employees use AI compute power.

Americans are also concerned about what AI will do to the job market. A recent Gallup Poll found that a growing number of workers are worried that technology will make their jobs obsolete. Small businesses employ fewer people than large firms, which makes their workforces especially vulnerable to potential losses.

Balanzat and DiMarino told NBC News they want to use AI to support employees at their businesses, not replace them.

“Machines are expensive,” DiMarino said. “People are priceless.”

World.title: Rep. Ilhan Omar details federal search of her D.C. home, says she’ll have to move for safety
World.content:
Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., on Wednesday described in detail for the first time the early-morning search of her home last week by federal agents, revealing in the process that she can no longer live there because of safety concerns.

In an interview with MS NOW, Omar said she and her husband were initially startled and confused by the arrival of agents with Homeland Security Investigations, who began banging on their doors and yelling at 6 a.m. Oct. 12.

“Well, I mean, you don’t show up to somebody’s house that early in the morning unless you were trying to freak them out, and, you know, it obviously did freak all of us out,” Omar said.

Federal agents searched Omar’s home as part of a criminal investigation that has alarmed Justice Department veterans who cited its proximity to the midterm elections. A person familiar with the investigation has told NBC News that the possible charges against Omar include conspiracy and making false statements in immigration paperwork.

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., in January. Tom Williams / CQ-Roll Call via Getty

Omar told MS NOW she had “only had 2½ hours of sleep” when the agents arrived since she had returned home from a trip in the early morning.

“It was, you know, trying to figure out, like you’re dreaming, this weird thing that’s happening,” Omar said. “But they basically, like, surrounded the house. They were pounding, pounding on the back door and the front door.”

She said she and her husband yelled down to try to communicate that they were coming downstairs momentarily as they rushed to get dressed. Omar added that one of her three children, her 20-year-old son, was also at the residence.

“I thought something was on fire. I thought something was happening to the neighbor,” Omar said, adding that she was particularly confused when she saw HSI agents at the door, since they often focus on issues like human trafficking, drugs, cybersecurity and terrorism.

“The fact that they were at my house that early in the morning, you know, was so, so bizarre,” she said. “I was like, ‘Why are you here?’”

Omar said the agents presented her with a warrant at the door after she asked to see one. They then asked her to sign a paper that would waive certain rights she has as a member of Congress, Omar said, adding that she declined to sign it.

Under the Speech or Debate Clause of the Constitution, members of Congress are protected from civil and criminal liability relating to their legislative acts.

Omar said in the interview that the agents took 17 items from her home, including old phones belonging to her and one of her daughters. Seizing the phone of a sitting member of Congress typically triggers a set of law enforcement protocols to ensure the Speech or Debate Clause is upheld.

The search took “four or five hours,” Omar told MS NOW.

“I don’t think I was able to call my attorney until about an hour into the search,” she said. Asked what she was doing during that time, she said, “I sat on the couch, staring at the warrant, trying to make sure that they were staying within the bounds of what the warrant allowed them to do.”

The Department of Homeland Security referred NBC News to the Justice Department, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Omar’s account of the search.

In addition to the phones, Omar said, agents took multiple items belonging to her husband, Tim Mynett, including a camera that was passed down by his uncle, a Somali phrase book that he was using to learn the language and his notebooks.

Omar said that according to the receipt she was given after the search, she does not believe the agents took anything with her DNA. She also said she was not asked to provide a DNA sample.

Overall, Omar said, the agents “mostly conducted themselves in a decent way.”

“They did a really good job in putting everything back in its place,” Omar said. “They actually even folded some of my clothing that were not folded.”

Still, Omar criticized the federal investigation.

“The people who knocked on my door, searching for papers, literally have his papers,” Omar said, referring to the paperwork filed by her late father. “They are the ones who processed us to come to the United States.”

She said that after the search, she can no longer live at her Washington home.

“Obviously, I can’t continue to live there, because our address has been public,” Omar said. “And with the death threats that I deal with, it’s not, it’s no longer going to be feasible to be in that house and have my kids, like, visiting off and on having people track them.”

Omar rejected President Donald Trump’s insistence that he had “nothing to do” with the investigation.

“I mean, he’s got everything to do with it,” she said. “You know, this goes back to 2019 when he was screaming about the fact that, you know, I, I need to be sent back, I need to be deported.”

Omar has been a frequent target of Trump since his first term. He has called her “garbage,” accused her of fraud and called for her deportation.

Omar said she feels “confident in my truth” as she again denied the allegations against her.

“How more obvious could these people be? You know, it’s, like, you could at least have the appearance of not having this be fictitious,” Omar said. “But they’ve chosen to blatantly have every character that has been involved be someone who has expressed explicitly that they don’t want me to be in the United States.”

World.title: Wisconsin governor candidates tangle over the economy, Trump and the 2020 election
World.content:
Democrat David Crowley and Republican Tom Tiffany sparred Wednesday night in their sole debate in Wisconsin’s race for governor, sniping at each other on affordability, President Donald Trump, abortion and the 2020 election.

Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, and Tiffany, a member of Congress representing a northern Wisconsin district, are in a close race to succeed retiring Democratic Gov. Tony Evers — the first open governor’s race in the state since 2010.

The debate most prominently focused on economic issues, with each candidate taking aim at the other over whose policies would best bring down prices. Tiffany vowed to undo various tax increases and return surplus dollars to residents, while Crowley advocated for a “fair tax system” that would fund education, infrastructure and transportation.

Throughout Wednesday’s hourlong debate, Crowley frequently linked Tiffany to Trump and his policies — including the “big, beautiful bill,” tariffs and the war with Iran — that he said have raised prices in the state and nationally. He also accused Tiffany of “doing the bidding” of “the billionaire class,” pointing to the donations he has received from Republican megadonors.

“When Congressman Tom Tiffany says he’s focusing on affordability, let’s be very clear: He voted for the big, ugly bill that [helped] some of the highest earners here in the state of Wisconsin,” Crowley said, referring to the 2025 tax cut and spending bill that reduced funding for healthcare and food assistance programs in many states.

“We don’t need what is happening in Washington, D.C., coming into the state of Wisconsin. It is very clear that he is working for Donald Trump and the billionaires who are funding his campaign,” Crowley added.

Tiffany retorted that “while my opponent” was “consistently focused on being against Donald Trump, I’m for Wisconsin — and rather than creating a bunch more programs that are going to end up taxing the people of Wisconsin more, I want to put more money in the taxpayers’ pockets.”

Later, he accused Crowley of sounding “like a socialist.” Following a competitive primary this summer in which he beat state Rep. Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist, by fewer than 4,000 votes, Crowley had sought to downplay the policy differences between them as part of an effort to unite Democrats.

“I think it’s really important to know that he said there’s very little difference between me and Francesca Hong,” Tiffany said of his opponent Wednesday night. “That sounds like a socialist to me.”

Later in the debate, Tiffany was pressed about his votes to overturn the 2020 presidential election results as a member of Congress. Responding to questions from the moderators, Tiffany said, “One of the reasons that I did that is Zuckerbucks.”

After the 2020 election, Trump allies falsely claimed that the millions of dollars Facebook co-founder Mark Zuckerberg donated to groups helping election administration offices was a front by Zuckerberg to help Joe Biden win the election. Wisconsin voters banned the use of private funds in election administration by ballot measure in 2024.

“Let’s be very clear — the congressman just said that the only reason why he was willing to throw away hundreds of thousands of votes here in the state of Wisconsin is because he disagreed on how somebody spent money,” Crowley said.

“He has shown us that because of one disagreement, he’ll throw [votes] out,” Crowley added.

Abortion also emerged as a contentious topic. Tiffany said he would uphold the state law allowing abortion access through 20 weeks of pregnancy.

But in the House, Tiffany has supported so-called heartbeat bills that would ban abortion care at about six weeks of pregnancy. He said Wednesday that he would not sign legislation that would restrict abortion access at six weeks.

Crowley has said that as governor he would work with the Legislature to enshrine abortion rights in the state constitution. He reiterated that plan Wednesday and declined to say whether he’d sign a bill that would legalize abortion with no gestational limits.

“I don’t believe a law like that would ever actually reach my desk,” he said.

World.title: Idaho mom who blamed vaccines for twins' deaths facing death penalty
World.content:
An Idaho prosecutor is seeking the death penalty against a woman charged with murder in the 2025 deaths of her twin toddlers.

Andrea Shaw, 23, has pleaded not guilty and has said the 18-month-old twins became sick and died after receiving flu shots and routine childhood vaccinations. But Payette County Prosecutor Mike Duke wrote in court documents that an autopsy revealed symptoms consistent with smothering and wrote that suffocation "is the only conceivable explanation" for their deaths.

In July, a grand jury indicted Shaw, on two counts of first-degree murder, according to court records and a statement from the Payette Police Department.

Deputy prosecuting attorney Ryon Sirucek notified the court of his intent to seek the death penalty last week.

In the court document, Sirucek said the state would try to show that four aggravating factors make capital punishment appropriate in the case: That more than one murder was committed at the time; that the killings were especially heinous, atrocious or cruel; that the defendant showed "utter disregard" for human life; and that she would likely pose a continuing threat to society.

"That's outrageous," said Shaw's attorney, Joseph Filicetti. "They're not going to be able to prove the underlying case beyond a reasonable doubt, so there's not a chance the death penalty is going to come into play."

Filicetti requested the court drop the indictment against Shaw due to alleged improprieties in front of a grand jury, CBS affiliate KBOI-TV reported.

In this image taken from court video, Andrea Shaw attends a court hearing remotely via video, on July 2, 2026, in the Payette County District Court in Payette, Idaho. KIVI-TV via AP

He said the grand jury that indicted Shaw wasn't told that the county coroner found the cause of death to be undetermined but consistent with hyperthermia, or overheating. The pathologists who examined the twins also said their causes of death were undetermined, Filicetti said.

"A prosecutor has a duty of candor, meaning that they have to be truthful in front of [the grand jury] and they have a duty to provide exculpatory evidence, which is evidence giving [the grand jury] any reason to believe that this person's not guilty - some other reason that these deaths could have occurred outside of murder - and the prosecutor did not do that," Filicetti told KBOI.

The prosecutor's office wrote in court documents that the temperature in the twins' room would often reach 100 degrees, but that the children had survived high temperatures before and that their time of death didn't correlate to the peak temperature of the day.

"They don't have any motive, they don't have any backstory, they don't have any confession ... She didn't do any of that, and they can't prove she did any of it," Filicetti said.

The twins were found dead in their shared bed May 1, 2025, according to court records. They had been vaccinated eight days earlier, and the day after their vaccinations Shaw took them to the emergency room, reporting that they were lethargic and felt feverish. The doctor felt the symptoms were a reaction from the vaccinations, and the twins were given Tylenol and a popsicle and sent home, according to the court records.

KBOI reported in May

of 2025 that after the bodies of 18-month-old twins had been discovered, police said at the time, "Foul play is suspected, and the incident is being handled as a homicide at this time," but did not identify any suspects.

A few days after the twins' deaths, Shaw went on an internet show produced by Children's Health Defense, an anti-vaccine group founded by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. He has not been affiliated with the group since December 2024, when he formally resigned as chairman to join President Donald Trump's administration.

Medical experts point out that the childhood vaccines at issue - hepatitis A, influenza and DTaP - are safe and effective for kids and recommended by various medical groups.

Shaw is also a plaintiff in a federal lawsuit brought by Children's Health Defense and others against the American Academy of Pediatrics, accusing the organization of racketeering and lying about the safety of vaccinations. The American Academy of Pediatrics has asked the court to dismiss the lawsuit, calling it the "latest missive in a campaign targeting" the academy and its "use of science-backed evidence in vaccine policy."

Shaw is being held without bond. A trial has been set for January.

World.title: Trump rallying with Hinson in Iowa as she pledges to push back on White House
World.content:
Sioux City, Iowa — President Trump is set to rally Thursday with Rep. Ashley Hinson in Iowa as he seeks to boost Republican candidates in a political environment that has dimmed for the party — prompting modest pushback from the very candidates he's supporting.

Hinson, who is running for Iowa's open Senate seat, initially pledged to be the president's "top ally" in the upper chamber. But as she faces off against Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek in a contest that, like several in the Hawkeye State, has grown more competitive than expected, she's adjusted that commitment in recent weeks.

When she and Turek went head-to-head at a debate earlier this month, the former local news anchor said she would be Mr. Trump's ally when it's "important for Iowa." But she said she would "push back on him" when it's needed — as she said she would regardless of who's in the White House.

Last week, Hinson told Fox News: "If he's going to say something that's wrong, I'm going to challenge him on it."

"I'm not afraid to say, 'hey, I disagree with you on this,'" she said. "But I'll be an ally to somebody when they're with me."

For Republicans, the Senate race in Iowa is just one of several in which Democrats appear competitive despite Mr. Trump winning the state by double digits in 2024. Iowa has been hit hard by high energy prices and last year's U.S.-China trade war, which led Beijing to boycott American soybeans. It's a picture that appeared unthinkable at the outset of the cycle — and puts Republicans' Senate majority on the line.

Hinson, who's represented the state in the House since 2021, said she would be at the rally on Thursday to welcome Mr. Trump to Iowa, "because I think this is a contrast election."

As the nation experiences challenges, she posed the question: Who do Iowans want at the helm?

"You want a mom, a minivan-driving mom who's common sense, who's driving that common sense back into Washington, D.C.," she said. "I think that's what Iowans want as their U.S. senator."

Hinson has made the minivan motif central to her campaign. She connected the image to her emphasis on working with Mr. Trump for Iowans earlier this week, describing a recent call with the president.

"I had just finished dropping off the boys, I was ready to run an errand," Hinson said at an event in Des Moines geared toward moms, alongside Sen. Katie Britt. "And I see pop up on my caller ID in my minivan, 'DJT.'"

She continued, "'Ashley, it's your favorite president,' that's how he introduced himself."

Hinson said the call lasted five minutes and that Mr. Trump was "just checking in on us here in Iowa." She said she thanked the president for his efforts to move forward on trade with China and asked about a deal for China to buy more soybeans.

At the event, Hinson also delivered her latest break with the president, according to Semafor, telling reporters, "I don't think we need to be making any more deals with Russia," regarding Mr. Trump's waiver of sanctions against Moscow.

The criticism follows Hinson's move to separate herself from the president's handling of the war with Iran late last month. Tucked within a post expressing support for methods to combat high prices, such as a pause on diesel exports, Hinson made one of the first splits by a GOP Senate candidate with the president over the war, writing: "The war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end."

The statement appeared in contrast to Hinson's vote earlier in September, when the House considered a resolution aimed at reining in the president in Iran. While two other Iowa Republicans locked in tight races supported the resolution, Hinson opposed it.

At the debate a couple weeks later, Turek pressed Hinson over those votes, saying during a discussion on energy costs: "We are in this situation because of this unnecessary war in Iran that Ashley Hinson voted in favor of continuing."

Hinson clarified during the debate that she believes the war must be brought to an "immediate and successful end" by not allowing Iran to have a nuclear weapon and by making sure that U.S. allies in the region are protected. Asked why she doesn't support the efforts to pass war powers resolutions in Congress, Hinson said, "I don't think we need another resolution."

"And I certainly don't want to see the president not be able to do a orderly end to this war," she added.

Thursday's rally marks the president's second visit to Iowa this year, after he kicked off campaigning in the midterms with a trip to the Des Moines area in January. Mr. Trump also announced plans last month for the largest steel plant in U.S. history to be built in Iowa, in an Oval Office event with Hinson in attendance. During the announcement, the president pledged to visit the state for a "great rally" to help get the Republican candidates elected.

"We'll save you a good Iowa pork chop, sir," Hinson replied.

World.title: Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield, and what they mean to Ukraine
World.content:
Over the past week, Ukraine has received a stark reminder of its growing dependence on uninterrupted access to Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield networks in its drone-heavy war against Russia, now in its fifth year.

Ukraine has a fraction of Russia's resources, but its aggressive development of drone warfare on defensive and offensive fronts has helped it endure an onslaught from its much bigger adversary, which invaded Ukraine in early 2022. That was true until last week, when Ukraine reported a throttling of the Starshield network that was causing its drones to stop midflight and fall out of the sky.

The two SpaceX networks operate on a constellation of thousands of low-Earth satellites — Starlink is the commercial version, while Starshield is a military product licensed to the U.S. government and its partners, among them Ukraine.

Kyiv's reliance on drones has made Starlink and Starshield nearly indispensable to its arsenal. When Ukraine experienced a disruption to those networks, it lost the shield of interceptors and drones that offered some protection against Russian drone and missile strikes.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy believes Musk throttled Starshield at the request of U.S. officials, though the world's richest man has denied any role and said it's the U.S. government that controls the military-grade network. President Trump has also denied he's responsible for slowing the network. However, CBS News reported Tuesday that Musk was behind the disruption, though a number of questions remain unanswered.

There has also been conflicting information about whether full access to the networks has been restored. As of Wednesday afternoon, Starlink remained throttled, Zelenskyy's office confirmed.

Here's what's known about Starshield and Starlink — and their role in the Ukraine war.

What happened in Ukraine?

On Oct. 13, Ukraine's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment, making it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones, officials and soldiers told CBS News.

Ukrainian soldiers said they noticed "speed limits" had been imposed on their use of SpaceX's Starshield internet dishes, the military-grade Starlink dishes that Ukrainians strap onto their drones so remote pilots can maintain their connection with the unmanned aircraft as they fly toward Russian targets.

Access was restricted by turning off dishes on Ukrainian drones flying above a certain speed, causing them to fall out of the sky. Ukraine's Ministry of Defense sources said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions without informing them beforehand.

Zelenskyy said Saturday the speed limits had prevented Ukraine from using Starshield to shoot down Russian Shahed attack drones.

What are Starshield and Starlink?

Starshield, the military-grade satellite network, runs on the same constellation of satellites as its civilian sister, Starlink, but has fewer technical limitations and more advanced security features. Both are operated by Musk's company SpaceX.

The U.S. government pays SpaceX to license the use of Starshield and controls who can access the technology. Its use has been limited to Ukraine and occupied territories. It is not available in Russia.

There is no working alternative to Starlink, as no direct competitor approaches Starlink's coverage of 11,150 satellites. Amazon Leo aims to compete, but at this point, it has under 400 satellites in low Earth orbit and has been hampered by the launchpad explosion of a Blue Origin rocket in May.

Regular Starlink terminals have a 70 km/hr (43.5 mph) speed cap, which is the speed at which internet can be used in a vehicle in motion. At rates exceeding the cap, the internet degrades and is no longer usable.

Starshield has no artificial speed cap and is known to work at speeds of at least 160 km/hr (99.4 mph). Starshield-equipped strike drones cruise at 160 km/h or more, and they're the backbone of Ukrainian mid-range strikes.

During the throttling over the last week, Ukrainian units reported link drops at speeds as low as 90 km/hr (55.9 mph), making those drones inoperable. The degradation of Starshield is estimated to have cost Ukraine tens of millions of dollars in losses, according to an analysis by Dimko Zhluktenko, a drone pilot and analyst in the Armed Forces of Ukraine.

On Oct. 15, some Ukrainian officials said that the Starshield restrictions had been lifted. But Zelenskyy told NBC News on Sunday the maximum speed was still 161 km/hr.

Zelenskyy told Fox News on Wednesday that the service was "still limited," but he added that Secretary of State Marco Rubio told him he would "work with his team on this to unblock" it.

Members of a National Police of Ukraine battalion set up a Starlink satellite communication terminal at a combat position in the Donetsk region of Ukraine on Oct. 16, 2026. Photo by Dmytro Smolienko/Ukrinform/NurPhoto via AP

Is Ukraine using Starshield or Starlink?

It uses both. Starlink has been providing internet service to Ukrainian civilians and military forces since 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, according to Reuters.

Initially funded by private donors and a U.S. foreign aid contract, SpaceX won a Pentagon contract to pay for Starlink for Ukraine in 2023, along with a contract for 500 Starshield terminals.

In August 2024, SpaceX signed another Defense Department contract to expand Starshield usage to 3,000 terminals for the front lines, Bloomberg reported.

Beyond communicating with and guiding drones over long distances, Starshield also serves another function: It connects every sensor and weapon system on the battlefield. Disruptions to the service have an impact that can be compared to an office having to function without being able to connect to Wi-Fi.

Ukraine's military uses Starlink for general battlefield communications, and Ukrainian civilians rely on it for communications needs, too.

On the Russian side, the Kremlin had also been using Starlink until February, when SpaceX cut off its access. As a result, Ukraine gained more than 150 square miles of territory.

Musk and throttling Ukraine's access to Starshield

CBS News reported Tuesday that a decision by Musk led to restrictions on Ukraine's use of SpaceX's satellite communications network, though it remains unclear how Musk's order to curtail service was executed.

Musk had spoken with administration officials multiple times, seeking clarity on the president's thinking on the matter. He has in the past expressed distaste for the perception that his company could be seen as profiting from the Ukraine war.

The temporary restrictions came as a surprise to some Trump administration officials, who said neither Mr. Trump nor the Pentagon had specifically ordered any limits meant to deliberately disrupt drone operations and battlefield communications.

The president said Monday he was seeking information about who had ordered the slowdown. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday denied the Pentagon had manipulated the service, saying, "We haven't made any directives or anything like that."

Can Elon Musk stop the use of Starlink and Starshield?

Musk has not admitted to imposing restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starshield.

"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," the world's richest person wrote on X.

He added that Starlink is a "commercial service," writing that it is "limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action."

Rubio, however, seemed to attribute the network constraints to Musk.

"The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr. Musk," Rubio told reporters in Mumbai on Wednesday.

Within a few minutes, though, he seemed to concede that Starshield was different: "We don't control what a private company — how they decide their product can be used. Now, if they're in a contract with the United States military, like Starshield, that's a different matter, because that's something we are purchasing and using for our use."

Intelligence-sharing

At around the same time as the Starlink and Starshield disruptions, Ukraine also did not receive warnings from U.S. intelligence about major Russian strikes.

Ukraine relies on a mixture of American sensors, aircraft, surveillance and human intelligence to map Russian positions and launch sites.

The early warning system, which is distinct from the SpaceX products, notifies Ukraine when Russia has launched a ballistic missile in its direction. It failed in at least two instances, on Oct. 13 and Oct. 18.

On Oct. 13, Zelenskyy said Ukraine "received no advance warning" when Russia launched a ballistic missile barrage. That overnight attack targeted energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv and Kharkiv, killing six people and leaving some 600,000 without power.

Ukrainian sources said U.S. officials said the warning system had failed due to "bad weather." Ukrainian officials expressed doubt about that explanation and accused the U.S. of "playing" with the system. By 3 a.m., that system seemed to have been restored.

Then on Monday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had been hit by another wave of Russian missile and drone strikes, "and again, there was no warning from partners."

A senior Pentagon official told CBS News Monday there had been "no change to Department of War policy regarding intelligence sharing or any capabilities we are enabling Europeans to provide to Ukraine."

By Wednesday, however, the warning system appeared to have been restored: "Now intelligence works. Thank you so much. That was crucial for us," Zelenskyy said on Fox News.

Rising pressure to end the war

Deliveries of key Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine have also slowed, Ukraine has said.

Rubio on Tuesday called interceptors the "most in-demand product right now in the defense field," and said that "when a country doesn't get interceptors from the United States, it's not because we're denying. We have our own needs, too."

"There's nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine," he said. "It's simply a balance between our obligations."

Mr. Trump has grown impatient with the more than four-year-long war. He has sought to portray the ongoing Ukraine war as the reason for high energy prices and has vented his frustration with Zelenskyy more frequently in recent weeks, accusing him of not doing enough to end it.

He waived restrictions on buying Russian diesel earlier this month in an effort to ease pressure on the price of the commodity, a move Zelenskyy argued could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin. And Mr. Trump also waived sanctions on Russia last week.

Mr. Trump said earlier this month that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop striking each other's energy infrastructure — announcing an "energy ceasefire." Zelenskyy initially said Ukraine was willing to abide by such an agreement, but that Russia's strikes never ceased, and several days later he told the Financial Times his country would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries because Russia was still attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

The Russian government never confirmed that it had agreed to a ceasefire.

Mr. Trump told reporters Tuesday that Russia keeps "grinding away" and is more capable of sustaining casualties than Ukraine, arguing "it's time" for Zelenskyy to make a deal.

World.title: Chemical leak in Toledo forces evacuations, shelter-in-place
World.content:
A massive chemical leak in Toledo, Ohio, is forcing some people out of their homes while others have been told to shelter in place.

A plume of smoke full of chemicals erupted from the MC Tank terminal.

One injury has been reported so far. According to officials, a Lucas County sheriff's deputy who responded to the scene wasn't feeling well and drove himself to a hospital.

Toledo Fire and Rescue ordered everyone within a 1-mile radius of 1266 Progress Ave. to evacuate, and everyone within a 3-mile radius to shelter in place due to a hazardous materials release.

In an update Wednesday, Toledo officials say the evacuation and shelter-in-place zone has been reduced to half a mile. The orders beyond that zone have been lifted.

"There is still concern that the tank is emitting this chemical, and it has the potential within 12 hours of the incident to be explosive," said Toledo Mayor Wade Kapszukiewicz. "As a result, our first responders and hazmat teams and safety teams are not approaching the tank."

The evacuation orders were issued at 10:48 p.m. Tuesday, and the shelter-in-place orders were issued at 4:24 a.m. Wednesday.

Those within the shelter-in-place area were asked to stay indoors, close windows and doors and turn off ventilation that draws in outside air. They were also asked to keep pets inside.

MC Tank Transport Inc. said in a statement that equipment associated with its operations is involved in the incident.

According to the statement and as the City of Toledo confirmed, the chemical involved in this incident is glycidyl methacrylate, an industrial chemical used to make certain plastics, paints and coatings perform better.

Who is in the evacuation zone?

According to the City of Toledo, the zone is a 1-mile radius around 1266 Progress Ave. Those living or working within 1 mile of that address were asked to evacuate and can go to:

Shoreland Elementary School — temporary shelter.

Meijer parking lot (off East Alexis) — Red Cross and TARTA buses are stationed to provide shelter as needed.

City of Toledo

The shelter-in-place zone is a 3-mile radius around 1266 Progress Ave. No injuries have been reported.

Toledo public schools were closed on Wednesday.

World.title: Candidates clash over Trump policies, Senate control in debate
World.content:
The candidates in Kansas' surprisingly competitive Senate race faced off in a debate Wednesday evening, as Republicans fight to head off the possibility of their first loss in a Kansas Senate contest in nearly a century.

Incumbent GOP Sen. Roger Marshall hammered away at what it would mean if he were to lose — that it could help hand control of the Senate to Democrats: "My opponent's going to say anything he can to lie to get into that office and give control to Chuck Schumer."

Marshall's Democratic challenger, megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton, tried to convince voters that he's not too progressive for Kansans and went on the offensive against Marshall over the impact of tariffs, the Iran war and other Trump administration policies on the state.

Marshall hewed closely to many of President Trump's views, and like him, blamed rising diesel costs on the war in Ukraine, rather than the Iran war.

"The real problem with the cost of diesel, in particular, is No. 1, is the Ukraine war, and because of that, diesel production has gone down," Marshall said. But at the same time, he said of Mr. Trump's recent announcement that the U.S. would purchase Russian diesel, "it doesn't sound like a great idea to me." He added, "If this brings Russia to the bargaining table and it ends the war, then I'm all for it right now."

While Marshall implored Trump voters to come out and vote for him, he said he does not always align with the president and has "objected" to him multiple times before, specifically citing the ICE raids in Kansas and Mr. Trump's short-term waiver on beef imports, both of which have hurt Kansas farmers.

Hamilton described himself as a "moderate or independent-minded Democrat" and vowed to "work across the aisle to try to bring people together to solve problems."

Hamilton largely sought to distance himself from mainstream Democrats. He promised not to vote for Schumer to be majority leader if Democrats win the Senate, called the Biden administration's border policies a "disaster" and said during a discussion on transgender participation in sports: "I have a 12-year-old granddaughter. I don't want biological men or boys competing against her that could harm her."

Marshall argued Hamilton leans further to the left than he has let on. The Republican senator also questioned how independent Hamilton would be.

"He's going to say he's going to vote against these things, but every Democrat stands up, and when Schumer tells them to jump, they say, 'how high?'" Marshall said during the sports discussion. "So why is he going to be any different once he gets to Washington? He can tell us one thing, but let's see what his actions would be like."

Hamilton said he would try to "force" Mr. Trump to end the Iran war. High gas prices and tariffs are putting many farms in the state in dire economic straits, with many voters telling CBS News that they aren't sure if they will survive past next year if conditions continue.

"It was not a good decision to go to war in Iran, and we need to get out," said Hamilton.

Marshall said he "want[s] this war to be over … as soon as possible, but we cannot let Iran have a nuclear weapon." He described Hamilton's views as "war through weakness, as opposed to peace through strength."

Hamilton slammed Mr. Trump's tariffs, arguing they have led to chaos and uncertainty. Marshall said the president's tariffs have led to a "manufacturing renaissance."

Mr. Trump's immigration policies have also drawn scrutiny in Kansas, including a string of Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids that agricultural leaders warned could cause workforce disruptions. Marshall pushed back last month, saying in a post on social media that ICE "needs to coordinate with our local law enforcement."

During Wednesday's debate, Hamilton called ICE's practices "militarized" and "politicized." Marshall said "all this discussion starts with a secure border," arguing Democrats could loosen border enforcement.

Polling suggests a tight race, and millions of dollars have gushed into Kansas, flooding the state's airwaves with anti-Marshall and anti-Hamilton ads.

The debate's moderator wasted no time in asking both candidates about their biggest controversies. For Marshall, that's the New York Times report about how the OB/GYN aggressively pursued his former patients — many of whom struggled economically — for medical debts and in some cases had them arrested.

Hamilton faced questions regarding his church's response to an incident of child sex abuse at a youth summer camp in 2005.

Marshall said "we did everything possible to take good care of people" and that many of his patients got free care. He conceded that some patients were turned over to collections agencies, which he called a fairly rare occurrence that is standard in the medical industry.

At his rally in Wichita on Monday, Mr. Trump defended Marshall against these allegations, saying he was required by law to report the debt, and that he's been unfairly "made out to be some kind of Shylock character." (The Anti-Defamation League later said the term "Shylock," a reference to a Jewish moneylender in William Shakespeare's "The Merchant of Venice," is "rooted in a longstanding antisemitic stereotype.")

On the abuse scandal, Hamilton said his church subsequently changed its policy on handling allegations of abuse, and "ultimately, we helped get this man put behind bars." Still, Hamilton admitted, "I should have checked to make sure that he wasn't going back (to the youth camp). That was a mistake on my part."

Cathy Bien, a spokesperson for Hamilton's United Methodist Church, told CBS News on Wednesday that the incident was "handled the best way [they] knew how 20 years ago."

Kansas could decide which party controls the Senate, and even before the debate, early voting numbers were skyrocketing in the state. Election officials say that they are fielding numbers that rival the 2024 presidential election.

The race could hinge on how many Republicans cross party lines to vote for Hamilton. At least 100 Kansas Republican leaders have endorsed Hamilton, including former governors, state officials and Mr. Trump's own former White House press secretary, Stephanie Grisham.

But many are voting early to ensure Republicans maintain control of the Senate. One early voter in Wichita, Tim Higgins, told CBS News that he's backing Marshall because "it's important to keep the progress that the nation is currently on since the presidential election."

However, for many, the race is about state issues.

"Rural Kansas is struggling, urban Kansas is struggling," said former Republican state Rep. Terrie Huntington, who is voting for Hamilton. "I think people are looking for change."

World.title: Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers clash in final Michigan Senate debate
World.content:
Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed clashed onstage Wednesday during the second, and final, debate in the increasingly bitter Michigan Senate race. El-Sayed repeatedly argued his opponent is and would be a "sock puppet" for President Trump in the Senate, while Rogers cast his opponent as untrustworthy and trying to run from past, further-left positions.

The neck-and-neck race is one of the nation's most closely watched contests in the November midterms and could help determine which party wins control of the Senate. Democrats hope to take advantage of Mr. Trump's unpopularity and voters' frustration with inflation and the Iran War. Republicans have sought to capitalize on divisions between progressives like El-Sayed and more moderate Democrats on Middle East policy and Medicare for All.

Senate candidates Abdul El-Sayed, left, Mike Rogers shake hands after their debate on Oct. 21, 2026, at WXYZ-TV in Southfield, Michigan. Robin Buckson-Pool / Getty Images

El-Sayed called Rogers' platform a "MAGA vision" and argued the former congressman "stand[s] hip-to-hip with Donald Trump on all of his worst policies, the policies that are raising the price of your gas, making it impossible to afford your groceries." The Democratic former health official responded to attack lines by inviting the audience to play "MAGA bingo."

"He's going to bend to Donald Trump because he is a sock puppet for the man," said El-Sayed.

Rogers pushed back at one point, saying: "He wants to make this about Donald Trump. The bingo game ought to be: 'How many times can he put Trump in any answer?'"

Asked by reporters after the debate if he's planning to attend Mr. Trump's Michigan rally on Sunday, which El-Sayed brought up, Rogers said he'd go but didn't know all the final details yet.

During the debate, Rogers argued El-Sayed has not been honest about his platform, accusing him of engaging in a "pattern of deception."

"Think about this: there are so many Democrats who are coming out today and saying they can't vote for Abdul El-Sayed because he's too extreme," Rogers said. He also claimed he's "doing exceptionally well with Jewish Democrats who are literally afraid," alluding to some community members' reluctance to support El-Sayed, a frequent critic of the Israeli government.

The debate was somewhat tamer than the two candidates' first faceoff earlier this month, which featured insults and interruptions in virtually every answer. But it was still testy.

One of the more contentious moments came after Rogers tried to link El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood and suggested he had the same supporters as terror groups like Hamas — allegations El-Sayed has vehemently pushed back against.

Earlier this month, several news outlets reported on social media posts by El-Sayed's half sister suggesting the Democratic candidate's mother had supported the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist group and political movement founded in her home country of Egypt.

El-Sayed has disavowed any connection to the organization, and has noted that he wasn't raised by his birthmother since his parents divorced when he was young. Rogers said El-Sayed was trying to make himself look like "a victim."

"You can grin and you can smile and you can talk real pretty, but I'm going to tell you what, that is a risk to our national security," Rogers said. He told reporters after the debate that he questions whether El-Sayed can get a security clearance if elected.

El-Sayed called the allegations "shameful."

"He keeps raising this question about this association with an organization I've never been a part of, because [of] my mom, who's a nurse in Missouri?" the Democrat said. "It doesn't make any sense, and it's actually really quite beneath you, Mike."

El-Sayed pressed Rogers on the Iran war, pointing to the conflict as the cause of high consumer prices and casting the Republican as a hawk who has "a war for everything."

"We need a War Powers Resolution, rather than a senator who is going to stand hip-to-hip with Donald Trump on this war that made no sense when it started and certainly makes no sense now," El-Sayed said when asked how he would bring costs down.

Rogers has called on the war to end, but also said on the debate stage that if Iran is allowed to control the Strait of Hormuz or build a nuclear weapon that gas could rise even higher.

The moderators asked El-Sayed whether he views Iran as a significant threat to U.S. national security. It was a variation on a question during the first debate, when El-Sayed was asked whether Iran or Israel is a bigger threat, which he called a "ridiculous hypothetical."

El-Sayed said Wednesday that "there's no doubt that Iran has posed a threat," but he argued "that threat had been contained" by the Obama-era deal that limited Iran's nuclear program. Mr. Trump ended that deal during his first term in office.

Rogers said Iran is "absolutely" a threat and argued El-Sayed's previous answers on Iran were "an absolute nonstarter if you're going to send somebody … to the United States Senate."

Meanwhile, Rogers pushed El-Sayed on some of his progressive policy views, including his support for Medicare for All, a single-payer healthcare plan.

"Money in your pocket? You'll be lucky to have a damn pair of pants when you're done," said Rogers, arguing El-Sayed's policies would require significant tax hikes.

El-Sayed responded by saying: "Right now, the folks pulling the money out of your pocket are the big corporations who are buying his campaign." Asked by CBS News after the debate about how much the plan would cost, El-Sayed argued if implemented it'd be less expensive than the costs of healthcare currently, and said the platform has bipartisan support.

On tariffs, El-Sayed criticized Mr. Trump's tariffs but said he is open to some import duties. He said, "You don't give all the chemo all at once, all at the same time."

Rogers called the president's tariffs a "mixed bag," questioning the trade war with Canada but saying the "reshoring of manufacturing is underway."

World.title: Judge curbs DHS efforts to conduct sweeps for possible noncitizen voters
World.content:
A federal judge ruled late Wednesday that the U.S. Department of Homeland Security's practice of knocking on doors and asking people about their immigration status — and whether they have voted in recent elections — likely violates the Voting Rights Act.

The ruling took aim at an operation that was documented by a CBS News investigation earlier Wednesday. Homeland Security Investigations has posted photos and videos of agents approaching homes in multiple states. The Trump administration says the practice is part of an effort to crack down on voting by noncitizens, but critics say it could intimidate legal voters.

In her ruling, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin ordered federal immigration authorities to stop carrying out "elections-related field operations and field interviews" in nine states, including California and New York, if the operations are likely to involve people who government officials "know, suspect, or should reasonably know or suspect are U.S. citizens."

Her order will remain in effect until polls close on Election Day. She stayed the ruling until 5 p.m. on Friday, which will give the government a chance to seek appeal.

Martinez-Olguin sided with groups that sued over the noncitizen voting investigation surge, including the California Nurses Association and National Nurses United. She found the policy likely ran afoul of a section of the Voting Rights Act that makes it illegal to "intimidate, threaten, or coerce" those who assist people with voting or engage in voter mobilization efforts.

"Plaintiffs do not claim, nor does the Court find, that it is unlawful for federal officials to undertake investigations into unlawful voting in federal elections," the judge wrote. "Rather, Plaintiffs seek to stop DHS from continuing to investigate U.S. citizens, who have a legal right to vote, in a way that intimidates and threatens the participation of CNA/NNU members from urging or aiding others to vote."

Martinez-Olguin also pointed to the "high likelihood of error" in the government's process for assembling a list of potential targets, which includes data from government agencies and commercially available data.

Protect Democracy, one of the groups that sued over the policy, celebrated the ruling.

"It was clear from the start that DHS built its lists on bad data, never checked how often it was wrong, and recklessly sent agents to people's homes weeks before an election," Beau Tremitiere, counsel at Protect Democracy, said in a statement to CBS News. "Today's ruling should remind us that American citizens hold the ultimate power in our democracy, not the government–no matter what the administration says otherwise."

CBS News has reached out to DHS for comment.

President Trump has prioritized cracking down on voter fraud during his second term, although there has been little evidence to back up his claims of widespread voting by noncitizens. Just 156 people have been charged with voting-fraud related offenses since the beginning of the Trump administration, according to the Justice Department.

The Justice Department reported earlier this week that it arrested several dozen green card holders in California on allegations they illegally registered to vote in U.S. federal elections.

World.title: On dating apps, men use AI to put their best face forward
World.content:
Marissa, a 31-year-old Boston resident, downloaded dating apps because she is looking for love. But more and more, she finds herself looking for something else: AI-free photos.

The marketing professional said she routinely comes across dating app profiles that appear to be digitally altered. Usually, the changes are minor and can be easily made using tools like Photoshop, such as editing someone out of a photo. Sometimes, however, the photo appears to be completely AI-generated, she told CBS News, citing a photo she came across on Bumble of a man dressed in a suit tiling a bathroom wall.

"AI aside, I'm not sure what the appeal is there," she said (Marissa asked to withhold her surname for privacy reasons).

Numerous women on TikTok also report spotting photos of men on dating apps that appear to be AI-generated. Their accounts demonstrate how AI is blurring the line between what's real and what's fake in the already fraught arena of online dating. They also raise ethical questions about how far is too far when it comes to manipulating your online persona.

"People want authentic connections and conversations," Kathryn Coduto, an assistant professor at Boston University who studies dating apps, told CBS News in an email. "I think AI has made people more wary and skeptical of others, especially people they don't know."

Of course, dating app users have long relied on filters and other editing tools to polish their photos. But AI tools are upping the ante, allowing people to create high-quality images within seconds, and in some cases, fabricate fake scenes.

"A dater has to think about how they're going to capture someone's attention in a few seconds or less," Coduto told CBS News. "This might mean making your photo look a little better than it might have before."

To be sure, this practice isn't exclusive to men. However, they appear more likely to use AI to spruce up their dating profiles than women, Coduto added.

"So far, men are more interested in AI in the dating space, which isn't surprising," Coduto said. "Women tend to receive more matches and messages, so men have a harder time standing out."

The "digital stylist" who helps men AI their photos

AI can create obvious distortions when it generates photos, such as omitting a finger from someone's hand. For Marissa, a telltale sign is the person's face, which sometimes looks "waxy" in AI-generated photos, she said.

Still, as technology improves, it's becoming harder to distinguish a real photo from one created by AI models.

Lana Li, a Brooklyn, New York, dating consultant who runs the Substack "Love Me Like a Robot," calls herself a "digital stylist." She uses AI to help men level up their dating app photos, and defends using the technology as long as the photos still genuinely represent who they are.

"I can take a picture of somebody and then put them in a different outfit or change their hairstyle a little bit, or put different shoes on them," she told CBS News. "Or if I think their body language doesn't look confident in the picture, I will have [ChatGPT] change that."

The 37-year-old also uses FaceApp to change men's facial expressions. She said the edits are subtle, such as slightly lifting the corner of someone's mouth to make them look "friendlier."

Despite her liberal approach to using AI, there are lines Li is unwilling to cross. For example, one client asked her to digitally alter a photo so that his head was on a marathon runner's body — a request she declined.

"I told him, 'I can't work with you if you want to not represent yourself accurately,'" she said.

Two men who spoke to CBS News on the condition of anonymity to maintain their privacy told CBS News they've used AI in their online dating photos, but in ways they feel stop short of being misleading and remain true to who they are.

A ban on Hinge

One man, a 30-year-old tech employee and client of Li's, said she used ChatGPT to digitally clothe him in more professional garb and to tame his frizzy hair.

"It's very subtle," the New York City resident said, saying he still looked like himself, even with the edits. He emphasized that he doesn't want to "catfish" anyone — a concern for singles even in the absence of AI.

Another man is pulling back after one of his AI photos backfired. The 50-something-year-old New York City resident said he fed photos of himself into Aragon.ai, an AI headshot generator, which produced a picture of him standing on a Manhattan roof with a sunset in the background. It immediately drew hits on his Hinge profile.

"This picture generally got the most likes," he told CBS News. "Now that could just be because it was the first thing they saw. But regardless, it was proving to be effective, and women seemed to like it."

That was, until Hinge banned him. He managed to get his account back but ultimately decided to delete the sunset photo, suspecting it was the reason for his removal from the app.

"How much AI am I OK with?"

Most popular dating apps have policies that limit the use of AI-generated images in people's profiles. Hinge emphasizes the importance of authenticity on its website, noting that people should be able to discern "fact from fiction."

"If you decide to include generative AI images, audio, or video in your profile, it should not be used to misrepresent yourself or your intentions," the company says on its AI policy page.

Hinge also uses automated tools and human reviewers to detect and remove "prohibited material," according to the company's terms of service. If users see suspicious AI material, they can confidentially report it through the app or online.

A spokesperson for Match Group, which owns Hinge, Tinder and a handful of other dating apps, told CBS that as generative AI evolves, the company is "watching closely and listening to daters, who tell us they want more transparency, more authenticity, and more confidence that a real person is on the other end."

Bumble also uses tools to detect and weed out AI-generated content, and lets users report profiles that feature such images. A spokesperson said the company prohibits inauthentic profiles, and Bumble's community guidelines bar the use of "artificially generated photos or enhanced photos to deceive others."

"We enforce this through a combination of AI-powered tools, human moderation, verification features and member reporting, and we take action based on the severity of a violation, up to and including permanently banning accounts," the spokesperson said.

Marissa, the 31-year-old who lives in Boston, said that when she sees a person's profile whose photos bear the hallmarks of AI, she chooses to move along.

"The dating pool is already challenging, and this is just another thing we have to grapple with," she said. "How much AI am I OK with?"

World.title: 5 simple ways to relieve the aches and pains of sitting at a desk all day
World.content:
5 simple ways to relieve the aches and pains of sitting at a desk all day

Olga Pankova/Getty Images/Moment RF

Back pain, eye strain, sluggishness, shoulder aches, restlessness.

If you sit in front of a computer for long periods of time, whether it's for work or leisure, you've probably experienced one of these symptoms.

But there are ways to relieve some of this discomfort — and even combat some of the health risks that may come with prolonged sitting. That includes walking breaks, ergonomic solutions and quick, simple stretches.

Here's a roundup of tips that have been previously featured on Life Kit.

If you feel tired and sluggish … go for a five-minute walk (every half hour)

Antonio_Diaz/Getty Images/iStockphoto

We know that a sedentary lifestyle isn't great for human health. Studies have shown it can lead to fatigue, weight gain and back and joint pain — and it's been linked to chronic diseases like obesity, heart disease and cancer. Yet adults in the United States spend an average of 9.5 hours sitting per day, involved in activities tied to computers, laptops and phones.

Sponsor Message

But there may be a way to mitigate its harms. In 2023, researchers at Columbia University Medical Center set out to find the least amount of movement you need to counteract the dangers of prolonged sitting. And they found that walking for five minutes every 30 minutes was the most effective strategy .

In 2023, our colleagues at NPR's Body Electric tested out this five-minute walking exercise on our NPR listeners. Over 20,000 participants joined the challenge — and reported higher productivity and lower fatigue .

Want to give this walking challenge a try? Get instructions from Body Electric — and use this worksheet to keep track of your walking breaks .

If your back aches from slouching over your desk … rotate your spine

Beck Harlan/NPR

Anyone who works at a desk knows how easy it can be to slip into a slouch. If we're not careful, that mid-back rounding can creep into all of our sitting time and create pain by putting stress on the middle section of our spine.

This movement above seeks to relieve that stress and encourage flexibility by mimicking the natural movements of the spine — side bending, bending backward and rotating, says Vinh Pham, a physical therapist. The idea is to get the body comfortable with these motions so that when you encounter them in real life, they're not painful.

Sponsor Message

To do this modified movement, which Pham calls the 3D T-spine rotation, stand up and drop your right foot behind the left, about a foot apart. Starting with the right arm straight up and the left arm behind you, as if you're shaking the hand of the person behind you, simultaneously drop your arms — still in a straight position — and twist toward your right foot. Move them back to their original position and hold for two seconds. Repeat the movement ten times before switching legs and doing the same exercise on the other side.

For more pain-relieving stretches, read this story.

If your eyes hurt from staring at a screen … stretch your eye muscles

When you stare at a screen for long periods of time, your eyes have to work hard. They must first turn inward to look at a close subject, then adjust the focus for short vision and hold that position.

Digital eye strain, as eye doctors call it, can cause eye fatigue, headaches or blurry vision. Try the exercise below to relieve that strain.

LA Johnson/NPR

If you feel fidgety and restless … change your position (and don't worry too much about the "right" posture)

ljubaphoto/Getty Images/E+

Fidgeting is a sign you need to break out of a stagnant posture, says Katy Bowman , a biomechanist and author of Rethink Your Position and Movement Matters. Even a position that feels comfortable at first can begin causing back pain, headaches or stiffness if you hold it long enough .

So listen to your body and mix things up. Alternate between sitting, standing, reclining and moving. That might mean opting to stand in the back of a conference room during a big staff meeting, taking a call while going on a walk or reading a report with your feet propped up in the break room.

The goal is to put yourself in configurations that contort your body in different ways. They should be "adaptive and dynamic" and easy to "change in and out of," says Leada Malek , a physical therapist and author of the book Science of Stretch.

Sponsor Message

Don't worry too much about what is "good" and "bad" posture. Both Malek and Bowman agree on a common phrase among physical therapists: "Your best posture is your next posture."

If sitting at your desk makes you feel uncomfortable … adjust your workspace

LA Johnson/NPR

Your monitor screen should be at eye level so you're not craning your head down to see. And, your keyboard and mouse should be low enough so you're not shrugging your shoulders and lifting up your arms like a praying mantis to type and click.

Meg Honan, a professional ergonomist, says this common "head down and arms up" position sets you up to feel "achy, sore and tired." To combat this uncomfortable and oftentimes painful position, try repositioning your tech. Bring your laptop or desktop monitor screen up to eye level with a stack of books or some other platform.

Place your keyboard and mouse at a lower height where you don't have to shrug your shoulders to use them. If your keyboard is attached to your laptop, consider connecting an external keyboard and mouse so you can have the computer screen at your eye level and lower your arms. External mouses don't just help lower our arms, but they also prevent the constant strain of using a trackpad.

For more ergonomic tips, read our story .

This story includes reporting from Ruth Tam, Sylvie Douglis, Frank Festa, Andee Tagle, Manoush Zomorodi and Margaret Cirino. This story was edited by Meghan Keane. The visual editor is Beck Harlan. We'd love to hear from you. Leave us a voicemail at 202-216-9823, or email us at LifeKit@npr.org.
