World.title: A GOP congressman voted to cut Medicaid. It covers 62% of his district. Can he win?
World.content:
A GOP congressman voted to cut Medicaid. It covers 62% of his district. Can he win?

toggle caption i Jae C. Hong/AP

Ulises Hernandez, of Bakersfield, Calif., has had health coverage through Medicaid for as long as he can remember.

But he had never waited as long for care as he did in September after a dental crown slipped down his throat during a procedure. He spent eight hours in an emergency room waiting for care and more than two days without food.

This story was produced in partnership with KFF Health News.

Sitting in his wheelchair to protest looming federal Medicaid cuts outside Republican U.S. Rep. David Valadao's Bakersfield office, Hernandez described his wait as a foreshadowing of what's ahead.

"I couldn't eat, I couldn't drink, I couldn't do anything, and I was in pain," said Hernandez, who had been discharged from the hospital a few days before. "I'm livid."

Hernandez, 41, said Valadao "should be ashamed of himself" for voting for the Republicans' One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The law is expected to reduce Medicaid spending by more than $900 billion through 2034, with provisions such as stricter Medicaid eligibility rules and reducing federal money to states.

Sponsor Message

Hernandez plans to vote for challenger Randy Villegas in hopes that this Central Valley toss-up district, where roughly 6 in 10 of constituents are enrolled in Medicaid, can help give Democrats control of Congress.

toggle caption i Mario Tama/Getty Images

Villegas, a political science professor, has embraced the progressive rallying cry for "Medicare for All" and called out Valadao for a vote "that is going to rip away healthcare from Valley families," since many working-age adults may not satisfy new work requirements and twice-a-year eligibility checks that, by political design, start after the midterm elections.

Valadao defends his vote on the GOP bill. During a televised Oct. 6 debate, he said "there are no actual cuts" to Medicaid.

toggle caption i Jackie Fortiér/KFF Health News



An estimated 60,000 more residents of his district could be without coverage by 2034 due to the tax and spending bill and the expiration of enhanced premium tax credits for Affordable Care Act insurance plans, according to the left-leaning Center for American Progress think tank.

Researchers estimate that those new rules will push more than 2 million Californians statewide off their coverage and that the state stands to lose about $30 billion a year, more than any other state.

Fertile Ground, High Unemployment

Bakersfield is an oil town, and it wears that identity proudly. Pump jacks nod in the distance. Streets run wide. The Kern River's bed lies dry, its water siphoned to feed the agricultural fields.

Sponsor Message

Sitting partially in the southernmost portion of the contested congressional district, this city produces much from the land, but unemployment is high.

Democrats have outnumbered Republicans in voter registrations by double-digit percentage points in Valadao's district since he was first elected to the U.S. House in 2012, yet he has won six of his seven congressional elections.

toggle caption i Mario Tama/Getty Images

Valadao has survived by focusing on local issues such as water infrastructure and distancing himself from the Trump administration, said Jeffrey Cummins, a political science professor at California State University-Fresno. Valadao is the last remaining Republican House incumbent who voted to impeach Trump after the Jan. 6, 2021, riot at the U.S. Capitol who is running for reelection to Congress.

"This is an area where, even when we see the registration advantage for Democrats, that they are moderate Democrats who tend to be concerned with agricultural issues, and Valadao in the past has successfully appeased those voters," Cummins said.

But California's congressional map was redrawn last year as part of a national mid-decade redistricting fight, and Valadao's Central Valley seat is considered more favorable for Democrats than before. Cummins said a different mix of voters, coupled with anger toward incumbents, could flip the seat.

"Valadao knows that he's on notice," Cummins said.

toggle caption i Jackie Fortiér/KFF Health News



Nationwide, healthcare costs remain a top affordability concern for voters, and they trust Democrats over Republicans by a 2-to-1 margin on the issue, according to a September KFF poll. Valadao lost in 2018, when Democrats targeted his votes to repeal the ACA, as well as his alliance with Trump.

On Nov. 3, he faces Villegas, a populist backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) who favors a single-payer universal healthcare system.

"The system that we have now, we pay twice as much as other countries across the world, despite the fact that we have worse healthcare outcomes," Villegas said during the debate.

Sponsor Message

At campaign event, no mention of healthcare

On Sept. 30, Valadao held a $1,000-a-ticket fundraiser. It was hosted by House Speaker Mike Johnson, who is campaigning across 22 states in six weeks as Republicans try to hold the chamber.

Afterward, press were allowed at an invitation-only reelection event in Bakersfield, held in an office building just outside of the new district Valadao hopes to represent. Arches of red, white, and blue star-shaped balloons framed the small stage.

toggle caption i Mario Tama/Getty Images

Neither lawmaker mentioned Medicaid or the rising cost of healthcare when they spoke to the audience.

After brief speeches, Valadao repeatedly refused to answer KFF Health News' questions about his vote for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and its impact on his constituents' Medicaid coverage, saying, "I think you are distorting the truth."

Of the half dozen attendees KFF Health News approached among roughly 50 in the room, none lived in Valadao's district.

They came anyway. Retired nurse Charlotte Brandt lives in the neighboring Republican-held district but follows Valadao's votes closely. She called him "a hero for the Central Valley," citing his work on water, oil, and agriculture, which she said sustain Kern County as the "breadbasket of the world."

toggle caption i Mario Tama/Getty Images

Her daughter, Allison Brandt Oliver, who also lives in Republican Vince Fong's district, said she favored the stricter Medicaid eligibility rules Republicans put into place, saying her concern is whether spending is going to U.S. citizens who contribute to the economy.

A few days later during the televised debate, Valadao said he was among the negotiators who secured community engagement provisions in the law, which will require certain adults on Medicaid to prove they're working or completing other activities such as job training or volunteering.

"It's not an actual cut," Valadao said. "We need people to actually put in and make a fair effort to try to cover their expenses and be a part of their community. This is not an unreasonable ask."

Sponsor Message

$32 million in campaign ads for one swing district

In a sign of how vital this district is, Republicans and Democrats have each booked more than $16 million in ads here through Election Day, according to data compiled by AdImpact.

"When you start getting over $10 million of spending total in the district, I would say that that's pretty high," Cummins said.

Some of the ads are reaching voters in unexpected ways.

Outside a local library, Seslie Maese, a stay-at-home mom from Bakersfield, said her 7-year-old, who often watches Lego videos on YouTube, runs to her whenever a certain ad plays.

"David Valadago is going on vacation again, Mom," he'll tell her, mispronouncing the congressman's name. Her son doesn't realize the ad, paid for by a Democratic political action committee, means that as a criticism.

Maese is undecided. Even though she's a registered Republican, she said what she has heard about Valadao doesn't sound positive, such as that he went back on his pledge not to cut Medicaid for vulnerable populations by voting for the federal tax-and-spending law.

For Maese, a politician who says one thing and does another is a deal-breaker.

"He just hasn't come through with anything he said," she said, "especially since he cut off a lot of Medicaid."

This story comes from NPR's health reporting partnership with KFF Health News, a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

World.title: Trump's redistricting gave Republicans a head start, now it goes to the voters
World.content:
Trump's redistricting gave Republicans a head start, now it goes to the voters

Voters across much of the South are casting ballots ahead of next month's midterm elections in congressional districts that were redrawn following calls from President Trump. He said it would help the GOP hold the House, where they currently outnumber Democrats 218 to 214.

In state legislatures over the last year, Republicans tilted about eight more seats their way than Democrats did in response. (That's an estimate, shown on the bar graph below.)

Loading...

But it's the voters who will decide whether it works.

Here's the catch: Republicans redrew districts partly on how people voted in the presidential election in 2024. Now the political mood has changed and many who voted for President Trump two years ago could be voting for Democrats, or not voting, in the midterms. The Republicans could lose many of the districts they targeted.

Usually, states redistrict early in each decade after the census. But Trump called on legislatures to do it now. It set off a chain reaction of political crises across the country that threw legislatures into the national spotlight.

Sponsor Message

Texas Republicans issued arrest warrants for Democratic legislators who'd left the state. The Louisiana governor suspended a primary after thousands of votes were already cast so the lines could be redrawn. In Missouri, the state supreme court found the Republican secretary of state in contempt for sticking with a GOP map that was not legally in effect.

In California and Virginia, Democrats won approval in statewide votes for redistricting in response to the Republicans in other states – only to have the courts toss out Virginia's plan. And when the Supreme Court weakened the Voting Rights Act this spring, it fueled rushed legislative sessions to draw maps that often ended up weakening the voting power of minority communities.

In a few places, Republicans rejected Trump's call to redistrict, including dramatic votes in the Indiana and South Carolina legislatures. But overall, Trump prompted a cycle of mid-decade redistricting unlike any since the 1960s, when courts set the current rules.

Here's where states redistricted - or didn't.

World.title: How long does it take to save up for a starter home? Twice as long as it did in 2019
World.content:
How long does it take to save up for a starter home? Twice as long as it did in 2019

toggle caption i Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

Mortgage rates topping 7% is the latest sign of how hard it has gotten to buy a first house, with aspiring owners already facing sky-high prices. A new analysis out Thursday shines a light on yet another growing obstacle: the amount needed to close a home loan.

"Over the last seven years, the time to save up that down payment and closing costs has doubled," said Mike Calhoun, president of the Center for Responsible Lending, a research nonprofit that promotes economic opportunity. The report was released by the center's Julian Bond Institute.

Since 2019, the last time the center made the same calculation, home prices have shot up, inflation spiked and has remained stubbornly high, and the rising cost of food, gas, healthcare and more has strained family budgets. Closing costs on a home loan have also ticked up, driven in part by rising homeowners insurance.

Sponsor Message

Amid all this, renters' incomes have not kept pace, and personal savings rates have dropped.

Today, the center calculates that for a median-income renter household, it would take a "staggering 16 years" to save up a down payment and closing costs for a starter home. That's twice as long as in 2019. And it would take even more time — 21 years — for a median-income Black renter household.

That kind of time frame upends a main reason that many look to buy in the first place. As the analysis notes, "young children at the time the family starts saving may have left the household — for higher education or the workforce — before the family will have saved enough to purchase their first home."

The report also narrows its calculations to middle-income households — making roughly $50,000 to $120,000 — whose members are more likely to be viable homeowners. For them, the savings time has also doubled, to 12 years.

For front-line workers, such as police officers, firefighters, EMTs, nurses and teachers, the researchers find that "the years to save has at least doubled and now ranges from 10 to 13 years."

As stark as those numbers are, Calhoun said they're likely an undercount.

The center's calculations are for a 3.5% down payment, since that's what the Federal Housing Administration requires for first-time buyers. The median first-time buyer actually puts down about 10%. The report also assumes families are really "stretching their savings," he said, even though many can't save at all, are forced to eat into savings or take on debt.

Sponsor Message

The divide in the housing economy has widened

The Center for Responsible Lending's report highlights a sharp divide in the housing economy, exacerbated when the COVID-19 pandemic triggered a spike in inflation, mortgage rates and home prices.

"If you look at the last seven years, they have been extraordinarily good to homeowners," Calhoun said. Those who bought when prices were far lower have accumulated enormous equity as home values have shot up. Some were also able to lower their monthly payments by refinancing, as mortgage rates hit historic lows of around 2% or 3% before they spiked.

Many homeowners with low rates have decided they can't afford to move and see their mortgage payments double. That has meant fewer older adults downsizing and fewer overall putting their homes on the market, intensifying a national housing shortage.

Meanwhile, rising rents have consumed an increasing share of family incomes, according to a recent report by the Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies. "From 2001 to 2024, renter incomes rose by 9 percent in real terms while rents rose by 30 percent," it says. This has left a quarter of renters paying more than half their income on rent and utilities.

Despite a recent softening in rental markets, a record number of renters are still considered cost burdened. Lower-income households are also hit harder by inflation, since basic goods and services make up a larger portion of their budgets.

The center calculates a starter home cost of $335,574, which is 80% of the median sales price of existing homes. And the center finds that it takes less time to save a down payment and closing costs for that in some major metropolitan areas than others — from 11 years in Houston to 24 in Los Angeles.

The report also notes that housing costs have outstripped incomes pretty much everywhere and that "the problem is even more acute in the fastest-growing rural areas than in urban areas." A recent analysis by center-left think tank Third Way found that housing construction has been unable to keep up with rural growth, creating severe pressure on affordability.

Sponsor Message

Many buyers rely on help from family

The widening housing wealth gap leaves a more privileged share of Americans who are able to buy a home. "Cash purchases are way up," Calhoun said. For younger buyers, "the overwhelming way people come up with the money is from assistance from family, the 'bank of mom and dad' and friends."

Far fewer buyers get help from down payment assistance programs, even though there are thousands of them. "The programs often run out of money," Calhoun said. "A lot of these are very small, idiosyncratic."

He'd like to see more assistance programs "to reach a broader array of people who don't have intergenerational wealth."

The center's report also calls for zoning and other reforms to boost the supply of smaller, cheaper starter homes, including duplexes, townhomes and manufactured housing. A sweeping new law passed by Congress this year aims to promote that, but the onus is on states and cities to follow up, and creating new supply will take time.

Despite all this, a related survey from the center finds that millennials and Gen Zers aspire to homeownership at the same rate as earlier generations — a "testament to the resilience of the American dream," according to Thursday's report.

It's the main way "most families generate wealth that they can pass on to the next generation," said report co-author David Silberman. "I think the case for homeownership remains really strong, despite all the trends we're pointing to in the challenges of getting there."

World.title: Trump merchandise stores are closing: 'He has peaked'
World.content:
Trump merchandise stores are closing: 'He has peaked'

toggle caption i Frank Langfitt/NPR

BENSALEM, Pa. – When the Trump merchandise store here announced it was closing earlier this year, Wes Alker, a Trump superfan and retired auto mechanic, came by for some nostalgia and the going-out-of-business deals. They included everything from "Trump Won" caps for $9.99 to Trump pool floats for $19.99.

Trump stores first emerged during the 2016 campaign. But with the president now in his second and final term, store owners say there isn't as much to fire up the consumer fan base and sales have softened.

At least four stores have closed this year. The MAGA Mall , a big online retailer and wholesaler, reports sales of MAGA gear are down 30% compared to a presidential election year when Trump is on the ballot.

toggle caption i Frank Langfitt/NPR

"He's no longer a viable business model for entrepreneurs because he has peaked," said Alker, who wore a gray T-shirt with a photo of former President Joe Biden and former Vice-President Kamala Harris which read, "Dumb and Dumber."

Sponsor Message

Trump's lame duck status isn't the only drag on demand. When the Bensalem store closed – it still maintains an online presence – Trump's average approval rating had already fallen from 50 % when he took office to 44 %.

Nine months later, when Bill Hays shut down his Trump super store outside of Knoxville, Tennessee, the president's approval rating had fallen five more points.

toggle caption i Frank Langfitt/NPR

Hays said unpopular policies – such as DOGE's massive government staff cuts – have had an impact. He noticed that instead of immediately putting on their new Trump gear, more buyers asked for bags.

"People were not wearing their colors, so to speak, like they did before the (2024) election," said Hays, 80.

toggle caption i Frank Langfitt/NPR

When Hays opened his store in April 2024, business boomed. One day, he said, there was a line of 80 people out the door and sales hit $200,000 a month. By the time it closed in September, sales had fallen to just $20,000 a month.

"After the inauguration, I think a lot of people felt that their job was done," said Hays. "They didn't have to promote MAGA or Trump."

Hays still has a Trump store in the Tennessee tourist town of Gatlinburg. He's waiting to see how Christmas sales go before deciding its future.

Trump stores are a phenomenon. Other charismatic presidents such as Ronald Reagan and Barack Obama developed ardent followings, but didn't inspire brick-and-mortar merch outlets in red and blue states. Hays says Trump created such demand because he's a salesman - and he tells people what they want to hear.

Sponsor Message

toggle caption i Frank Langfitt/NPR

Ron Solomon, president of the MAGA Mall, says there are about 20 stores that specialize in Trump merchandise still in operation.

In Myrtle Beach, Rick Kligman sells items out of two stores, but he's trying to get rid of older material, stuffing $40 worth of merchandise into a grab bag that he sells for $9.99. He's concerned about the mid-terms and thinks a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate could turn off the more casual Trump consumer.

"I don't want to be sitting holding thousands and thousands of dollars of Trump merchandise and absolutely no possibility of selling it," said Kligman, 69.

Given term limits and Trump's age, retailers are diversifying beyond the Trump brand and embracing more patriotic products, including hats that say "We the People."

Solomon says this is a natural progression.

Eventually, Trump will leave the national stage. Unless a family member picks up the mantle, Solomon says the Trump merchandise business "will fade away."



Research by NPR's Susie Cummings.

World.title: Farm country has beef with Trump as midterms approach
World.content:
Farm country has beef with Trump as midterms approach

toggle caption i RONALDO SCHEMIDT/AFP for Getty Images

Driving around his farm in a four-wheeler, Scott Birker warned that his cattle were in a bad mood.

"They're a little grumpy with me right now," he said.

When asked why, he said matter-of-factly: "We just got done weaning."

Birker should know his herd well, given that he's been raising beef cattle outside the Eastern Iowa town of Garrison since 2001. His operation has about 150 "mama cows" and sells feeder calves, as well as some cattle for meat. And Birker is also the northeast regional vice president for the Iowa Cattlemen's Association.

All of which is to say that since August, when Trump announced that his administration would raise the quota on beef imported under lower tariffs – temporarily suspending tariffs on up to 300,000 metric tons of imported beef – Birker knows it when he says: that hurt people.

Sponsor Message

"That surprise, with a very volatile market already, with a tight supply, hurts us really, really fast and really, really hard," Birker said.

It's not that raising beef cattle was easy before that new import policy. Margins are always tight, says Zach Raff, incoming livestock economist at Iowa State University. But there have also been other challenges – for example, drought in much of the western U.S. made hay much more expensive and shrank the nation's beef herd.

"The beef herd size is at an all time low – a 75-year-low," said Raff. "So you couple that with very strong demand. And that's going to make prices what you see at the store right now."

Ground beef currently costs around $6.80 a pound – a fact of which the Trump administration is keenly aware. But the administration's attempts to bring those prices down have backfired politically and possibly economically..

Multiple Trump administration policies have made life tougher for beef producers. Last year, amid the trade war between the two countries, China cut its US beef purchases. In February, Trump signed an executive order to subject some Argentinian beef to fewer tariffs.

And in August, he signed the executive order to suspend tariffs on 300,000 metric tons of beef imports – specifically, lean beef trimmings, with the goal of lowering the price of ground beef. The order added that the imported beef was to be sold at 25% below market prices.

Sponsor Message

That helped push U.S. cattle prices lower, but the far bigger challenge, according to Raff, was the amount of uncertainty it introduced.

"If I'm a producer, I think, well, look what's happening – perhaps next year they're going to import even more. The year after, there's going to be a different policy," said Raff. "And I'm going to say, 'Well, these prices for my cattle right now are at record highs and projected to be high. So I'm just going to send my heifers to be processed.' I'm not going to decide to replace the beef herd when I know that there's a lot of uncertainty."

This means the beef imports can have an added downside, disincentivizing producers from keeping breeding stock around that could grow the beef herd, which would lower beef prices in the long run.

Big picture

From an economics 101 perspective, the Trump decision to import more beef does make sense as a way of bringing down consumer prices. But the 300,000 metric tons that could be exempted from tariffs is equivalent to around 2% of total US beef consumption.

That made for a lose-lose situation: the policy was enough to rattle beef producers, but not enough to help consumers. Indeed, the average ground beef price per pound in September was only about 13 cents lower than it was in August.

All of this looms over the 2026 midterm elections, especially in farm states such as Iowa. Iowa Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson, who's running for the state's open Senate seat, made news when she publicly broke with the Trump administration on its decision to lower tariffs on beef imports.

"We need to focus on affordability, but I think this isn't the way to do that," she said on Fox News. "I think we need to focus on helping our cattlemen grow their herd."

Sponsor Message

Her opponent, Democratic state legislator Josh Turek, has in turn been stressing that Hinson has supported some Trump policies that have hurt farmers writ large.

"She's been in favor of all this five times in favor of the tariffs," he said in an interview with NPR. "Farmers rely on markets, on free trade, more than any other group."

In the governor's race, similarly, Democratic state auditor Rob Sand has sharply criticized Trump's trade policies, while Republican businessman Zach Lahn has avoided that kind of criticism.

Iowa Republican strategist David Oman says that in either race, the beef policy could be a deciding factor.

"Both of them will be two- or three-, four-point races in my view," he said. "So any one element like this topic that cuts against you hurts."

Indeed, the administration has been playing defense on the beef policy from the beginning. Speaking in Iowa just days after the beef executive order, Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins acknowledged that the August order lifting the beef tariff rate quotas, or TRQs, might not be popular.

"I believe everyone will look back on this time and say, okay, didn't love the three month lift of the TRQ, but we're so grateful to a president that is willing to listen, willing to make big, bold decisions, and willing to put it all out there for our American producers," she said at the Iowa Farm Progress Show.

How it plays

Seth Watkins, who has his own cattle herd in southwestern Iowa, outside the town of Clarinda, says that these trade decisions make him upset not only with Trump, but with all of Washington.

"As much as what the president does frustrates me, I think I'm more frustrated with Congress, who should be exercising the checks and balances we learned about in high school civics," he said.

Sponsor Message

He's a Democrat and going to vote blue in this election, though he says he doesn't blame other farmers who have supported Trump.

"They honestly were told that tariffs were going to make markets better," he said. "They were told that we were going to enter this new golden era. I just filled up my pickup with $6.30 diesel fuel."

This is not just about Iowa. Several states with some of the tightest races this year – Texas, Nebraska, Montana, and Kansas – are also major beef-producing states, meaning lots of people weighing these particular trade policies as they vote.

Back on his farm, Birker knows how he'll vote, too: "I'll vote Republican."

Birker stresses that this is purely a personal decision, and that the Iowa Cattlemen are a non partisan group. But for his part, he generally votes Republican, and getting to talk personally to Hinson also reinforced his choice.

As for Trump, Birker approves of how he's doing as president.

"I do, I do," he said. "I just think it's a long putt. He's a businessman, and I think we've got to stick it out with him."

Trump will have the opportunity to convince more Iowans when he travels to Sioux City this week as part of his pre-midterm push.

World.title: See how Big Tech is transforming Spain's landscape
World.content:
See how Big Tech is transforming Spain's landscape

Loading...

ZARAGOZA, Spain — Aragon's rugged plains stretch out under a clear blue sky, the buildings visible as "a few tiny cubes sprawled like a throw of dice" across the terrain — as George Orwell wrote in Homage to Catalonia, of his time here during the Spanish Civil War in the 1930s. Today, excavators eat the earth, carving huge chunks of the landscape in the race to build the behemoths of the AI boom.

This drought-stricken region of northeast Spain has become the focus of American companies searching for locations to place their energy- and water-intensive data centers. In Aragon, Amazon Web Services promises to spend almost $40 billion to build multiple vast complexes — one alone as large as 600 American football fields. Microsoft and the asset management firm Blackstone are among those following suit, signing agreements to build data centers that will transform this region and the livelihoods of its inhabitants.

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

Even as other countries enact regulations to curb the expansion of data centers (and Spain's national government weighs new restrictions), Aragon's regional government is welcoming the companies with open arms. Touting themselves as the "Virginia of southern Europe" after the U.S. state with the largest concentration of data centers, they are taking the bet that hosting data centers will bring jobs and prepare the region for the economic shifts they believe AI will bring.

Sponsor Message

"This is a new economy that is evolving, and it's very difficult to foresee how many activities are going to be coming around it," said Eva Valle, the economic counsellor for the regional government. "But they are coming."

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

The companies were drawn to the region with promises of large tax breaks and fast-tracked planning permissions that give these data centers a special status usually reserved for the general interest of the local population. This order gives them the power to expropriate land, strips local mayors of veto powers, and restricts the time the public has to object to 23 working days. (For the recent Amazon Web Services development, the regional government opened the window to oppose the project over the Christmas period. Opponents of the project believe they did this to try to push it through at a time when people would be paying less attention, though the government denies this.)

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

The rapid approval process for these large and hyperscale facilities has left many in Aragon feeling excluded from decisions that will profoundly impact their region and lives.

"It's going to be like living beside a prison"

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

The first time Silvia Baselga and her family learned of the data center soon to tower over their home was when they noticed the survey markers poking out of the ground on the other side of their garden wall. "When we saw this, we went to the city hall and said, 'OK, we want information. This is really close to our house.'" But the local council told them they had no information. Only when the planning documents were later made public did they learn that the outer perimeter of the data center is to be built within 300 feet of their home in the hilltop village of Botorrita. The plans showed that the complex will be larger than the village itself.

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

Baselga's parents retired here for the tranquility of a life spent in a tight-knit village community. Their home looks out over fields and gently rolling hills. To try to block the noise the data center will emit, Baselga believes the company will build a 20-foot-high wall, as happened in a nearby village. "We're going to open the window and see nothing," she said. Friends regularly visit at night to gaze at the stars in this rural setting. Baselga said the center's 24-hour security lights will block out the night sky. "It's going to be like living beside a prison."

Sponsor Message

Centers like these are set to be built across Aragon — 27 in total, according to official documents — some by Spanish and other firms, but most by American companies, taking up about 7 square miles of land. At least one is built partly on ground originally classified as protected for natural ecosystems. The companies promise employment. Amazon Web Services told NPR it will create 6,200 permanent jobs once these centers are built. But many residents fear they will also deliver an environmental crisis.

Economic development "at the cost of the environment"

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

The data centers will consume many times the current electricity needs of the region and require large amounts of water to cool their servers in one of Spain's driest regions, one that's been repeatedly blighted by drought.

Julio Enfedaque drives across the parched land his family has farmed for generations. This year it barely rained for four months, and the government cut the amount of water available for irrigation by two-thirds. "Even if they say the data centers won't take the water that we need for agriculture, I am sure it's going to become very complicated to farm like my ancestors used to." Enfedaque has advised his nephews to find different careers and leave the land.

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

Amazon Web Services says its data centers will draw water only after temperatures hit 86 degrees Fahrenheit and that they are investing millions of dollars to help fix leaking water pipes and working with farmers to use AI technology to make their water use more efficient. "We're trying to not only use as less [sic] water as possible, but also to help those communities where we operate have the best infrastructure," David Blázquez, Amazon's head of public policy for Spain and Portugal, told NPR.

But the company remains opaque about how much water each center will use. Blázquez said it's "a company policy not to publish water usage per site." Regional figures show Amazon's three existing data centers, which are much smaller than what is planned, used 68 million liters — 48% more than the company had originally told regional officials they would need.

Sponsor Message

Endangering valuable habitat for rare and migratory birds

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

Perhaps an even bigger problem is the energy these centers need to run. Unlike many data centers in the U.S., which are powered by natural gas, companies in Aragon say they will rely mainly on renewable sources (though they also have diesel generators on site). Blázquez says Amazon Web Services has secured "a hundred renewable projects in Spain," including 17 in Aragon.

While that energy is carbon-free, ecologists and biologists warn that additional wind projects could have their own devastating consequences for the environment.

The region is full of hunting grounds for vultures and other birds of prey and an important stop for migrating birds.

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

"The vultures look for the thermal air currents to lift them. But they run straight into the windmills — for them it's like flying through knives," explained José Antonio Pinzolas, an ornithologist.

Aragon's own environmental agency has warned that wind farms in this area pose a high risk of collision to the endangered red kite and other protected raptors, and has documented an increase in bird and bat deaths in recent years as the renewable sector expands.

"I've collected ospreys, golden eagles, kestrels by the dozen, black vultures," said Juan Ballesteros, a nature protection officer for the local government.

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

Ballesteros used to love his job for its access to wildlife. Now, he said, he spends his days placing the corpses of birds killed by turbine blades into body bags. Ballesteros met NPR as he arrived to collect the body of a young Eurasian black vulture that lay dead on the ground, its wings splayed in the dirt at the foot of a wind turbine.

Blázquez told NPR, of the damage to this important habitat that the expansion of wind and solar farms causes, that Amazon Web Services "definitely shares those concerns." He said they work with renewable energy companies that comply with environmental legislation. But Pinzolas said the growing number of bird deaths shows the current protections in place are not working.

Sponsor Message

Environmental groups say the overall impact of wind turbines on birds isn't being properly assessed.

Several groups have crowdfunded together to mount a legal action to try to stop Amazon Web Services' expansion in Aragon. The court case challenges the Aragon government's fast-tracked approvals of the plans. "We have concerns about water consumption, about energy consumption, the impact on some other industries and on the environment," said Luis García,, an activist with Ecologistas En Accion, one of the organizations involved in the case. He said the economic benefits of data centers are not great enough to justify the "huge damage they do to the environment."

Locals fight to preserve nature for future generations

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

One recent weekend in the region's capital, Zaragoza, an avenue filled with demonstrators protesting against a new data center to be built at the edge of a forest by the city. Residents fear the heat and noise of the complex will destroy a tranquil space that is a haven during the hot summer months.

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

"This is a worthy fight as all the worlds invades us, to save this pine forests, to save the environment, against this voracious capitalism that thinks only of economic interests and not of people," said Marian Rams, a local resident with white hair dyed in hues of pink, green and blue. "They want to swap nature for data centers."

toggle caption i Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR

Nearby, a little girl no older than 5 chanted along with the demonstrators. Her mother, Ana Domezian, walked alongside her with her second child, a baby, nestled in a carrier against her chest. "If we don't fight now for what we have," she asked, "what are we going to leave to them in the future?"

World.title: Can a dream help you solve a problem? Here's how to try tonight
World.content:
Can a dream help you solve a problem? Here's how to try tonight

toggle caption i Michele Spatari / AFP via Getty Images

We spend about two hours every night making home movies in our minds. Over a lifetime, that adds up to about seven years of dreaming.

For most of human history, those movies were considered sacred. Many early civilizations believed dreams were messages from the gods. In ancient Greece, people slept in temples hoping a dream would bring guidance or healing.

By the 1970s, scientists took a far less romantic view. A few psychiatrists likened dreams to the brain's attempt to make sense of random signals , and their theory threw cold water on the idea that dreams were meaningful.

Sponsor Message

Psychologist Rosalind Cartwright, known to colleagues as the "Queen of Dreams," pushed back. She believed dreamwork could be a form of therapy and made her case in books including Crisis Dreaming, co-written with Lynne Lamberg and The Twenty-Four Hour Mind. She published many studies from her lab experiments.

Today there's a resurgence of interest and new research. And one ancient practice is getting a fresh look: dream incubation, planting a question in your mind before sleep in hopes your dreams will offer insights.

It may sound mystical, but there's research behind it. In a small study from the 1990s an instructor at Harvard Medical School asked college students to focus on a problem at bedtime. About half reported a dream related to it, and many felt the dream contained a solution.

Jungian analyst Lisa Marchiano uses the practice with people navigating challenges and midlife transitions. The first step, she says, is asking a good question, and that takes time. "You want to ask a question that could be answered," Marchiano says. Skip yes-or-no questions. Instead, make it targeted but open-ended. If you're weighing a job offer, ask, "What would it look like if I took this job?" or "What would it look like if I went on another date with this person?"

Sponsor Message

Next, write down what you already know about the problem. "You're looking for the stuff you don't know," she says. "You want to invite your unconscious to fill in the gaps."

In other words, consult your inner "dream maker." As Marchiano puts it, "Instead of going to ChatGPT, try going to your dream maker."

Finally, turn it into a ritual so it doesn't feel like one more chore. You could take a bath as a way to wind down as you set an intention or "ask" for a dream. Marchiano says she writes her question in her journal, then copies it onto a slip of paper, folds it and tucks it into a small velvet bag to put under her pillow.

How to try dream incubation tonight:



Think of a challenge, decision or problem you face. Write it down as an open-ended question.

Review it before lights out. If you can, place a related picture or object by your bed.

As you drift off, tell yourself you'd like to dream about it.

Keep a pen and notebook on your nightstand.

When you wake up, lie still before reaching for your phone. Jot down anything you remember, even a fragment or an emotion.

That last step matters. Many people say they don't remember their dreams, and the window is short. "You only have about three to five minutes to remember," says Dr. Harrison Shong-Wen Chow, a Stanford anesthesiologist. Writing a dream down or telling someone helps move it into long-term memory, he says.

Chow's own research explores something even more surprising: how dreams under anesthesia may help people process fear and trauma. There's also research into how an electronic device may help deliver dream prompts for targeted dream incubation .

Be patient. Dream incubation may not yield anything the first night, and dream recall is subjective. But over time, the practice may lead to a fresh insight, or at least a new way of listening to yourself.

Sponsor Message

World.title: Canadians caught up in Trump voter fraud crackdown as U.S. accuses Canada of election interference
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Robert Harold Corbett was sure he was an American citizen until federal agents showed up at his door with an arrest warrant earlier this month.

Corbett was born in Canada, but raised in the United States, he told reporters outside a federal courthouse in Raleigh, N.C.

"I did not find out I was adopted until I was 51 years old," said Corbett, who has been charged with one count of falsely claiming citizenship to vote and one count of voting by an alien. The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) says he voted in six elections since 1998.

Corbett is among at least 11 Canadians who have been caught up in a crackdown on non-citizen voting by U.S. President Donald Trump's administration ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

Wednesday, the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa drew a direct connection between those prosecutions and what it described as Canadian interference in American politics.

In a statement, the embassy accused Canadian politicians of openly attempting to influence the U.S. election through trade policy, political campaigning and public remarks. It also singled out Canadians for illegally voting, claiming Canada has the second-highest number of its citizens facing fraudulent or illegal voting charges of any country.

"All Canadians should refrain from attempting to participate in or influence U.S. elections in any way. Americans decide America's elections," said the statement, which comes amid heightened tensions between the U.S. and Canada over tariffs and trade.

WATCH | U.S. ambassador to Canada accuses Canadian politicans of interference: Canada 'absolutely not' interfering in U.S. midterms, Joly says | Duration closed caption 1:19 Asked about the United States Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra's comments about watching for Canadian interference in the U.S. midterm elections, Minister of Industry Mélanie Joly says 'we never do that and we never accept that also being done to us in Canada.' She says her recent visits to the U.S. were 'to attract investments' by American companies and she will continue to do so.

Since late last year, federal prosecutors have charged dozens of non-citizens, many of them longtime U.S. permanent residents, with illegally voting in federal elections. But several of those accused say they didn't know they were breaking the law, with some saying they didn't even know they were registered to vote.

Investigations have consistently found that illegal voting by non-citizens is highly uncommon, says David Becker, executive director of the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation and Research.

"This is likely an attempt to sow doubt about the elections in advance of an election in which the president and his administration might fear the voters might reject them," Becker said.

A Reuters investigation published in September found that software glitches and clerical errors across a dozen states could have added more than 30,000 self-declared non-citizens to voter rolls since 2000.

Becker says the DOJ has an "election crimes manual" that cautions prosecutors against taking enforcement actions close to elections because of the potential to influence voters.

"There's no reason these arrests couldn't have been made on Nov. 4 or some time after," he said.

Aaron Cohen, a Florida criminal defence lawyer who represents several non-citizens facing voting-related charges, says some of the confusion among his clients stems from election officials failing to properly verify eligibility when registering voters.

"I feel strongly that it's a policy decision for whatever policy outcomes are that the current administration is seeking," Cohen said of the U.S. efforts to prosecute non-citizens for voter fraud.

Lawyers who spoke with CBC News said U.S. voter registration systems can sometimes catch non-citizens up in errors, and one of them says he has seen an uptick in non-citizens being questioned last month.

Handcuffs, prison time

The DOJ's news release including information about Corbett's arrest features images of people handcuffed with their arms being held by police officers and faces blurred.

A video posted by the department on X Tuesday features a COPS-style montage of masked officers and a man in pajamas being led down a brightly lit hallway, advertising the arrests of 28 people in Californian for non-citizen voting. Two Canadians were among them.

Corbett told WRAL, a North Carolina NBC affiliate broadcaster, that he spent the night in a crowded and dirty jail cell with "people peeing on the floors." He said he was certain he was a dual citizen of Canada and the U.S.

Paige Adamson, a Canadian citizen who has lived in Point Roberts, Wash., as a U.S. permanent resident for 14 years, was accused by U.S. border agents of illegally voting and questioned for several hours in September, CBC previously reported.

Adamson, who was heading back to the States after a birthday dinner in British Columbia, was told t he Department of Homeland Security (DHS) believes she falsely claimed she was a U.S. citizen in order to vote in Washington state.

The department also alleged Adamson voted in Washington state's 2018 general election and cited those allegations as grounds for removing Adamson from the U.S. Adamson says she has no memories of ever voting in the U.S.

A North Carolina Election Integrity Team sign in Spanish, seen Oct. 25, 2024, in Durham, N.C., warns non-citizens not to vote and that doing so could lead to deportation — a notice that advocacy groups say could intimidate legitimate voters who speak Spanish. (Jonathan Drake/Reuters)

The consequences for the accusations can be serious. The Trump administration has sought to deport non-citizens convicted of voting illegally and in June, another North Carolina-based Canadian, Denis Bouchard, was sentenced to two months in federal prison.

Others have successfully challenged their charges. In August, a federal judge in Florida acquitted Gaynell Jeffries, a Canadian citizen accused of illegally voting, after she argued that an election official had mistakenly told her permanent residents were eligible to cast ballots.

Broader implications for democracy

Frédérick Gagnon, a political science professor at the Université du Québec à Montréal and the head of the university's Observatory on the U.S., says the prosecutions in the U.S. are unfolding under a climate of fear and uncertainty for immigrants and other non-citizens living there.

"People are worried about profiling. They're worried of getting arrested and we can see that ICE wants to operate so quickly that sometimes they're proceeding with arrests that aren't justified," Gagnon said.

LISTEN | Political scientist Lucan Way says the U.S. has crossed the line into 'competitive authoritarianism': The Current 16:14 Is the U.S. sliding into competitive authoritarianism? Ever since U.S. President Donald Trump took office for the second time, he's been criticized for eroding democracy and the rule of law. Now, political scientist Lucan Way, argues that the United States has definitively crossed the line into a system of what he calls competitive authoritarianism. Lucan Way, a Distinguished Professor of Democracy in the Department of Political Science at the University of Toronto, explains what that looks like, and whether it can be reversed.

He said Trump's repeated allegations of widespread voter fraud also serve a political purpose by mobilizing his supporters.

Both Becker and Gagnon see no indication Canadians in particular are being singled out.

"They're looking at anybody they can possibly find because they are desperate to make the lie of widespread non-citizen voting look a little better," Becker said.

World.title: He bought a used SUV from a Volvo dealer. He regrets trusting their inspection process
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When Ashton-Vitaly Evdosin bought a certified pre-owned Volvo last fall, he trusted it had gone through a rigorous inspection.

But on the day he drove the SUV home from the dealership, he noticed a clunking noise coming from the rear suspension. When he brought it back, a rear shock was leaking.

A few weeks later, the warning light for the parking brake came on. Evdosin had the 2021 XC60 Recharge towed and the problem was traced to a broken wire.

Most worrying — the check engine light kept coming on.

After having the SUV towed and checked over in April, the light switched back on just as he was leaving Volvo Mont-Royal. He returned it immediately.

In the year since Ashton-Vitaly Evdosin bought his 2021 Volvo XC60, he estimates he's had it towed four times for various issues. (Submitted by Ashton-Vitaly Evdosin)

He was told the electric motor that powers the rear wheels, known as the ERAD, had "catastrophically failed." The repairs took over a month because the dealership was waiting for backordered parts.

Evdosin said none of the problems he's run into were flagged in the dealership's inspection report.

He doesn't understand how Volvo could have certified the SUV in the first place.

"What I want Volvo to do is to take accountability and deem this vehicle unfit to be sold, because I don't think they should have let this vehicle out of the dealership," said Evdosin, who is a university student.

WATCH | 'Certified pre-owned' status gave buyer a sense of security: He bought a certified pre-owned Volvo last year. That's when the problems started | Duration closed caption 3:51 Last fall, Ashton-Vitaly Evdosin purchased a certified pre-owned Volvo for nearly $50,000, trusting it had gone through a rigorous inspection. But over the past year, the 2021 hybrid vehicle has run into a succession of problems — none of which were flagged in the dealership’s inspection report.

What does 'certified' even mean?

A car being advertised as a "certified pre-owned vehicle" means — in theory — it has gone through a detailed inspection at the dealership.

"You're given kind of a health check-up on the car," said George Iny, executive director of the Automobile Protection Association.

The inspection is supposed to spell out what is working on the car, and what needs to be repaired immediately or down the road.

But in some cases, Iny said the inspection is not done.

"Dealers tell us privately, 'We don't want to do the inspection in case we can't sell the car,'" he said. "So in fact, it's smoke and mirrors."

George Iny is the executive director of the Automobile Protection Association. He’s not surprised Volvo hasn’t cancelled Evdosin's sale. "The car would practically have to implode before they would consider taking one back," said Iny. (Toni Choueiri/CBC)

Depending on the manufacturer, certified pre-owned cars are typically less than five years old.

In Quebec, Iny said an auto dealer has to provide a mandatory full-coverage warranty on the vehicle for either one, three or six months after the sale, for all vehicles with less than seven years or 120,000 km.

Iny said franchised dealers also offer warranty coverage that goes beyond the legal warranty, usually for six months to two years after the sale, depending on how much the dealer or consumer pays.

Jesse Caron, who is an automotive expert at CAA Quebec, says this cost isn’t always included in the advertised price, and can cost the consumer up to $2,000, depending on the car.

He recommends consumers ask for the dealership's inspection report and get a CARFAX, which tracks past accidents, ownership changes and the service record.

Caron encourages people to get a second opinion and have the vehicle checked over by another mechanic.

If previously undetected problems are found or the suggested repairs can be done cheaper elsewhere, the consumer can see if the dealership is willing to lower the price.

Owner wants sale cancelled

Evdosin did not get an independent inspection done on his vehicle. He said the fact the car was certified by the dealership gave him a false sense of security.

After he complained to Volvo, the company offered him nearly $1,800 — equivalent to about three monthly vehicle payments. Evdosin bought the SUV for $50,000.

Evdosin declined the offer and sent the company a legal demand letter. His complaint was escalated to Volvo's legal department for review. He hasn't heard from them since July.

After the manufacturer's warranty expired a few months ago, he had to use his extended warranty to repair both hydraulic struts when the tailgate stopped opening.

"They said it was a wiring issue," said Evdosin.

Since then, he’s detected rust on the inside of both back doors, and he had to get a seat repaired after he noticed the leather was peeling.

He wants the dealership to take the car back and refund his money.

"When I'm using it, I worry: when is the next issue going to hit, and am I going to be stranded?" said Evdosin.

He wishes he'd had it inspected by another mechanic.

"I could have avoided this whole headache," said Evdosin.

Anti-lemon law doesn't apply

In Evdosin's case, Iny said the province's consumer protection legislation wouldn't apply because his 2021 vehicle is already too old.

In 2023, Quebec introduced its "anti-lemon" law, which protects consumers against seriously defective vehicles.

It applies to new gas-powered, hybrid and electric vehicles purchased or leased with less than three years or 60,000 kilometres on them.

But for a vehicle to be declared a lemon, it has to meet at least one of the following criteria:

Three unsuccessful repair attempts for the same problem. Twelve repair attempts for separate, unrelated problems. More than 30 days spent at the dealership for one or two repairs — excluding periods where parts were unavailable or on backorder.

Ashton-Vitaly Evdosin is worried about what other problems may pop up on his 2021 XC60 Recharge. Since his extended warranty expired this summer, he's had to use his extended warranty with a $250 deductible to make repairs. (Louis-Marie Philidor/CBC)

Iny understands Evdosin's frustration, but said he's fortunate Volvo stood behind the warranty and did all the repairs.

"He's lucky he's been driving a loaner, because many people in that situation would be paying for a rental somewhere. They'd be out thousands of dollars," said Iny.

Iny said his association is happy the province brought in extra protection for consumers, but he would have liked to see it include getting legal fees reimbursed.

The maximum amount you can claim in small claims court is $15,000. But if the vehicle is more expensive than that, and the customer wants a cancellation of sale, you'll have to hire a lawyer, which many people can't afford.

"Typically if you have to go to trial, it's going to be over $20,000," said Iny.

He's not surprised Volvo hasn't cancelled the sale.

"The car would practically have to implode before they would consider taking one back," said Iny.

Volvo looking into matter

In a statement provided by Volvo Car Canada, the manufacturer said it takes all customer concerns seriously, and that safety is its top priority.

"Certified by Volvo vehicles pass specific inspection requirements and go through a reconditioning process to qualify as a Certified by Volvo vehicle, and also include the applicable warranty," said company spokesperson Jennifer Okoeguale in an email.

She said Volvo is working with the dealership to better understand and review the circumstances around what happened with Evdosin's car, and was unable to provide further comment at press time.

The Corporation des concessionnaires automobiles du Québec — which represents major franchised automotive dealerships that offer certified pre-owned vehicles — did not respond to CBC's questions about the quality of inspections, nor whether it had received complaints about particular dealerships.

Evdosin had hoped for a settlement.

These cases can often be "long and difficult," said Evdosin, who decided to go public with his story to warn other consumers what they should do before buying a certified used vehicle.

He says it will be difficult for him to pursue Volvo in court.

"It's so expensive nowadays to deal with lawyers," said Evdosin. "Every minute costs something."

World.title: Politics is widening U.S. gender divides. In Canada? It's complicated
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Connor Halloran says his last relationship wasn't entirely quashed by a disagreement with his now ex-partner over politics, but it was "almost the last straw."

Halloran said his past partner's contradictory views "made me judge her a little differently in a way that I didn't really want to be around her as much anymore."

He's not alone — at least on the University of Ottawa campus, where most students either said politics is pivotal in their relationships or that they avoid bringing it up altogether.

CBC Radio's The House caught Halloran and his friend and fellow geography major Alex Kelly as they stepped out onto a campus sidewalk after an exam on Wednesday.

Kelly maintains it's best to keep politics out of dating to "avoid conflict and confrontation."

"Is that kind of living in secrecy? Maybe a little bit," Kelly said. "But, I mean, [if] you want a long-lasting relationship, I think sometimes a little bit of secrecy is good — maybe."

Alex Kelly, left, and Connor Halloran, right, spoke to CBC Radio's The House on Oct. 14 at the University of Ottawa. (David Cummings/CBC)

The cautious sentiments are "very familiar" to Daniel Cox, the director of the Survey Center on American Life, who, in his most recent book, looks at how politics has impacted some youths' dating lives as a symptom of a larger social trend.

"There is this incredible wariness about dating someone even with a little bit of a different political take or whose identity didn't quite align," Cox told The House.

In Generation Uncoupled, Cox examines the growing political divide among young American women and men. Cox says he interviewed over 100 people whose personal stories his book relies on.

"It's not necessarily that young men are becoming more conservative, but young women are becoming much, much more liberal," he said.

In his research, Cox said he found social media plays a role in fragmenting young Americans along gender lines.

"When it comes to the algorithms, they are both very, very powerful and they are better able to identify gender than almost any other attribute," Cox said.

"So young men and young women have very different experiences when they're on the same social media platforms, and their realities are shaped by this understanding, this sort of validation machine that is affirming their perspectives, experiences and point of view."

Cox also points to the divisive politics of U.S. President Donald Trump, in a chapter titled The Divider in Chief, and told The House the president serves as the biggest dealbreaker "by a landslide" when it comes to young people's relationships.

"When I talked to a lot of young women who said that they could not date a Trump supporter, his policies never really came up," Cox said. "Rather it was his demeaning comments about women, belittling behaviour, his history of sexual assault allegations."

According to Andrew Parkin, executive director of the Environics Institute For Survey Research, youth aren't feeling the same split north of the border.

"People in the U.S. are reacting to their political developments," Parkin told The House. "We haven't had a leader like Trump to provoke that kind of reaction to see what would happen."

Parkin pointed to a longstanding polling trend of young women tending to lean a bit more toward the left than young men, who generally lean a little more socially conservative, saying the difference has "been there for a while, and it's not growing."

"Men are not generally becoming more conservative," he said.

"To the extent that there's a gender difference among younger people, between young men and young women, it'll be women that are a little bit more dissatisfied" with government and the political system.

Can love really be blind — to politics?

The House also checked in with Melissa and Conrad Muhly, a couple living just outside of Philadelphia.

Since the start of their 25 years of marriage, a once trivial political wrinkle between them has grown in significance: Melissa is a dual Canada-U.S. citizen and has been voting Democrat while Conrad voted for Trump.

LISTEN | Melissa and Conrad's previous appearance on The House: The House 48:48 Elbows up, Canada

Conrad said politics "matters significantly" when it comes to relationships.

Melissa said political differences weren't a big deal when they started dating 26 years ago, adding, "these days it feels almost like your political views become part of your value system and your soul."

"Now, we have a great marriage, a great relationship for both of us," Conrad said. "For someone starting out, I think to have [such] diametric views, it would be very difficult to have a relationship."

"I think that it would be very tough for a couple newly dating to navigate these waters," Melissa said. "We've been able to do it, but it hasn't always been easy."

Asked whether they would end up married had they met today, Melissa didn't mince words: "absolutely not.… In fact, I wouldn't date a Republican, if I'd known what one was 25 years ago."

"I would, you know, try to sway my significant other at the time to see the right side of things, and if she did, we would get along fine," Conrad responded, as they both chuckled.

World.title: Boos, heckling greet Brady Tkachuk at 1st NHL game back in Ottawa
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A chorus of boos awaited former Ottawa Senators captain Brady Tkachuk as he made his return to the ice at Canadian Tire Centre Wednesday night.

It was a packed stadium of vocal Sens fans who did not hold back in letting Tkachuk know how they feel about him.

"He's a traitor, there's not much else to say," said fan Jack Kelso.

"He promised he'd give us the [Stanley Cup], but he left."

Earlier this year, the 27-year-old requested a trade to join the Florida Panthers alongside his older brother and podcast co-host, a move that was unpopular with many fans.

Nearly every time Tkachuk took the ice, or touched the puck, chants, often profane in nature, erupted through the stadium.

"I was expecting it, I just didn't think it would be this much," said fan Lesley Miller.

WATCH | Harsh homecoming for Brady Tkachuk from Ottawa Senators fans: Harsh homecoming for Brady Tkachuk from Ottawa Senators fans | Duration closed caption 2:35 Former Ottawa Senators captain Brady Tkachuk faced off against his former teammates for the first time Wednesday night since requesting a trade to the Florida Panthers in the spring. Fans at the sold-out Canadian Tire Centre booed him throughout the entire game. The CBC's Emma Weller was there.

A number of attendees also altered their Tkachuk jerseys to showcase their new upset with the player, with some replacing his name with that of the team's new captain Thomas Chabot.

Others chose to throw their jerseys onto the ice.

On an episode of his Wingmen podcast, Tkachuk committed to donating any Sens jerseys tossed on the ice by upset fans to the Boys and Girls Club of Ottawa.

Ottawa Senators fans wore altered jerseys of former Senators player Brady Tkachuk at the game between the Senators and the Florida Panthers in Ottawa. (The Canadian Press/Lisa Wallace)

During the game, a video tribute was made to Tkachuk, who waved to the crowd amid the chants.

Shortly after, he scored the first goal of the night in a power-play goal midway through the first period.

The Sens bounced back, winning the game 5-1.

Tkachuk focuses on fun

After the game, Tkachuk said he has no hard feeling towards anyone and just tried to enjoy the experience.

"It's new, those were my teammates not too long ago," he said.

"It was nice to be in front of this passionate fan base," he added when asked about the fan's reaction to his return.

Travis Green, head coach of the Ottawa Senators, said the game felt "as close to a playoff game as you're gonna get."

"It was very emotional, physical, was a hard fought game and I thought our team was excellent tonight," he said.

Tkachuk spent eight seasons with the Senators after being drafted fourth overall in 2018.

He is set to return to the Canadian Tire Centre on March 18.

World.title: MPs moving to restrict gambling ads in Canada amid mounting harms

This story is part of a CBC News series examining the public health impacts of online gambling.

For T.S., a 22-year-old Ontario man recovering from a gambling problem, widespread advertising for online casinos and betting during sports broadcasts is "frustrating."

"Imagine you're an alcoholic and there was a beer ad during every show you watched," he told CBC News.

His gambling started three years ago as a fun Friday night activity with friends, but escalated.

One night last year he found himself locked inside a bathroom, losing it all — having bet away $14,000.

T.S., who CBC has agreed not to name, says he quickly sought treatment and hasn't gambled since. But during his spree, all those ads fuelled him to gamble more.

"It certainly … would trigger me to go back and place another bet."

Politicians in Ottawa are moving to curb the widespread advertising currently seen across sports broadcasts, social media and online video games.

WATCH | Sports gambling ads are everywhere. There's a push to change that: Sports gambling ads are everywhere. There’s a push to change that | Duration closed caption 2:29 Federal MPs are moving forward with a bill to restrict sports betting ads in Canada. It comes as new data shows that the number of problem gamblers is on the rise in Ontario.

The federal standing committee on Canadian heritage meets next week to vote on Bill S-211 , a law that proposes to rein in the ads across the country, amid new findings of increased addiction and gambling-related suicides in Ontario.

2-3 ads per minute

A new analysis for CBC News shows Canadians continue to be bombarded with betting promotions during sports broadcasts.

CBC partnered with the University of Bristol to assess the 2026 NHL playoffs to count the numbers of logos and gambling messages.

Across seven televised games featuring Canadian teams, viewers faced 3,000 gambling messages. Ninety-five per cent of those instances included no information about harm reduction or age restrictions.

Raffaello Rossi, the lead researcher and a senior lecturer in marketing at the University of Bristol, says by reviewing every second of the game, his team found ads or logos appearing two to three times every minute.

Ads appeared on stadium rinks, jerseys, helmets and during commercial breaks.

WATCH | Researcher Rafaello Rossi on his findings: Researcher found thousands of gambling messages in NHL games | Duration closed caption 0:34 Raffaello Rossi of the University of Bristol analyzed seven NHL broadcasts and found two to three gambling messages per minute in the form of logos and banners, which he says are more effective than commercial ads.

"Advertising via logos around the stadium, on the jerseys, on the helmets is much more efficient, because you've got a lot of knock-on effects," he said.

"For example, if a news broadcast shows the highlights of a match, you will see these logos all across the sporting event. If somebody shares something on their social media, you will see those logos."

He says viewers are additionally seeing the emergence of ads for prediction markets.

The new analysis also confirms little has changed since a CBC Marketplace study with Rossi's team in 2024 revealed viewers were bombarded with thousands of ads and product placements in five NHL games (up to three per minute).

Rossi says that's because Canada is behind other countries in passing legislation to curb gambling advertising.

"Multiple countries since then have introduced quite strict regulations and restrictions on gambling marketing in sports. So, for example, in Belgium and Italy and Spain, there's almost entire bans on sponsorship during sports."

Proposed Canadian ad standards

If Bill S-211 is approved at committee next week, the legislation — which has already passed the Senate — would be presented for a third and final reading in the House of Commons.

"It is a national framework around sports betting advertising," says the bill's sponsor, Bardish Chagger, the MP for Waterloo.

She says limits on advertising are a way to address emerging harms, including growing rates of gambling addiction and suicide deaths, like those witnessed in Ontario after the province allowed private online casinos and sports betting in 2022.

MP Bardish Chagger is sponsoring a bill launched by Sen. Marty Deacon to restrict gambling ads. The standing committee on Canadian heritage is set to vote on the bill in late October. (Dave Seglins/CBC)

"People are being impacted in a very harmful way. They are losing their livelihoods, they're losing their homes, they're losing their savings, they're losing their lives," Chagger told CBC News.

Sen. Marty Deacon first spearheaded the bill in the Senate and says it is time Canada tackles some of the negative public impacts of online gambling.

"These ads are ubiquitous across the country, especially in national broadcasts that are sponsored by betting companies, with logos plastered across broadcast desks, arenas and fields; this encourages Canadians in every province to gamble, even in those provinces who have held back," she wrote in an email to CBC News.

"We know where this is going, but we're allowing it to happen anyway."

Sen. Marty Deacon first spearheaded the bill in the Senate, where it has passed. (Twitter)

Current Canadian regulations are supposed to restrict gambling advertising targeting minors, at-risk people and gamblers who have asked to be excluded from the sites.

But the code doesn't go as far as some European countries, which have outright banned televised promotions on sportswear and during events.

Belgium, the Netherlands, the U.K., France and Germany have imposed time-of-day bans on gambling s, restricting them to after 9 p.m.

In France, companies have to get approval for their promotional strategies from the regulatory authority and submit an annual action plan to curb addiction.

While Canada's Bill S-211 isn’t prescriptive, it asks the federal government to acknowledge the harms of online gambling and hold consultations to craft stricter regulations.

Toronto Maple Leafs celebrate a goal flanked by advertising for Jackpot City online casino. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)

Chagger says she hopes her bill will eventually lead to a ban on gambling promotions on sportswear and during live sporting events, outlaw ads during certain hours and prohibit celebrities and athletes from collaborating with gambling companies.

Ontario and Alberta oppose the federal bill.

In a letter to the federal government, Minister of Service Alberta and Red Tape Reduction Dale Nally said the bill creates a two-tier regulatory system and threatens future profits.

Ontario's Attorney General Doug Downey wrote to the federal government earlier this year, saying that the province should be left to regulate ads.

"Ontario has already established comprehensive and modern regulatory framework for online gaming and sports betting, which came into force in 2022. Advertising standards and protections were a central component of this work," he wrote.

Public health response

A coalition of a dozen mental health organizations, including the Canadian Mental Health Association and Public Health Physicians of Canada, alongside 28 prominent addictions researchers, have sent submissions to Parliament asking for national action .

"The entire world is grappling with this in some way," said Matthew Young, a leading gambling researcher and senior research associate at the Canadian Centre on Substance Use and Addiction.

"The real challenge right now is that we have a regulatory regime that is built upon physical borders, but a product that doesn't respect physical borders."

Addictions researcher Matthew Young is lobbying for limits on gambling ads and better monitoring of harms. (Ousama Abdel Rahman/CBC)

"The argument that it's provincial and territorial jurisdiction was all fine and well until ads from Ontario blanketed the nation and then suddenly New Brunswick had to deal with ads from Ontario."

The Canadian Gaming Association (CGA), a national trade group representing 80 companies that run casinos and online sports betting, has filed its own submission opposing the plan to regulate gambling ads across the country.

Instead, the CGA wants the government to spend money on assessing the "underlying health challenges" of gambling addiction, and let provinces decide advertising standards for themselves."

"Unlike alcohol and cannabis, online gambling platforms, both regulated and unregulated, are readily accessible with just a few clicks. In this environment, advertising plays an important role in directing consumers toward regulated operators that are subject to stringent oversight, consumer protection requirements and responsible gambling standards," the CGA submission states.

Recovering gambler T.S. says advertising for online casino games should be banned or require warnings, similar to rules for other addictive substances, like tobacco and alcohol.

"I think similar to cigarettes, you could put labelling on the apps themselves, as well as the ads: 'Here's what happened to Terry when he spent half his life savings on blackjack one night.'"
