World.title: Loved You Can See Everything? Thank Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

If you're aware of Nathan Fielder, you're probably aware he, in his resoundingly patriotic words, "graduated from one of Canada's top business schools with really good grades."

Which — despite the intentionally ridiculous way it's read out in the intro to his show Nathan for You — is true: The Canadian comedian really did get his bachelor of commerce at the University of Victoria, before eventually transitioning to that show, known for its farcically absurd business advice.

It might seem random to connect Canadian business school with obsessive investigations and near-incomparable success. But that background established a pattern for the Vancouver-born Fielder. Since the earliest days of his comedy career, Fielder has built what basically amounts to an entire field of study around the fickle nature of truth.

Practically all his work has been undergirded by this concept, from his early days at CBC's This Hour Has 22 Minutes to the more mind-bendingly bizarre The Curse and The Rehearsal and all the way to the world's hottest documentary right now: the Elizabeth Holmes-focused You Can See Everything, which released last Friday.

But as odd as those releases seem, they have created something of a cottage industry around Fielder, and the belief he is turning the format of documentary on its head. The film's run-and-gun-style employed an incredibly small team of roughly seven on-site crew members, a significant number of which, like Fielder, hail from Canada. And given the tradition of documentary in this country — as well as the fact that this time, he's not doing it alone — the movie's success may not seem so odd after all.

Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes appears in a still from Nathan Fielder's mindbending documentary You Can See Everything. (A24)

Unreal success

The most prominent Canadian of You Can See Everything is, of course, Fielder himself. He first rose to fame with his show, Nathan for You, a Comedy Central expansion of a segment that he established on 22 Minutes.

That series was what led the documentary's co-director, Lance Oppenheim, to approach Fielder about working on a project together in the first place, according to an interview with Vulture.

From there, Oppenheim and Fielder brought in their respective collaborators. On Fielder's end, that included Adam Locke-Norton, the editor with whom he first collaborated for shorts like Morris, Flashback and Eves, released on YouTube in 2006.

Meanwhile, Oppenheim brought in his own team, supported by the Great White North. That included Ottawa-born producer Tatiana Bears, who told CBC News she flew to the location just 24 hours after getting Oppenheim's call to start shooting. There was also director of photography David Bolen, a Toronto native who was the cinematographer for Oppenheim's narrative debut Primetime and his prior, self-styled "documentary fantasy" creations Spermworld and Some Kind of Heaven.

Bolen's camera was a particularly mind-bending aspect of You Can See Everything, fuelling much of its Oscars buzz.

Further down the line, there are more names: Saskatchewan's Katina Danabassis was in charge of costuming. Described by Vogue Philippines as "one of A24’s most radical collaborators," her oeuvre stretches from fellow Canadian Celine Song's Materialists and Past Lives to Fielder's The Curse, as well as this year's The Drama.

And then Ontario filmmaker Stephen Coleman — who previously worked on A24 projects Materialists, The Drama and the upcoming Jesse Eisenberg film The Debut — lent his hand as second assistant director.

They are now among those listed in A24's "for your consideration" Oscars campaign : Danabassis for best costume design, Bolen for best cinematography, Bears for the coveted best picture and Locke-Norton for best editing. Fielder and Oppenheim are submitted for best director.

A24 is also submitting You Can See Everything in the documentary category, but it may be angling for a record with best picture: If successful, it would become the first documentary to garner a nomination in that category.

Canadians in Hollywood

Canadians finding their way into Hollywood productions is by no means a new phenomenon. The United States has offered a fertile and appetizing landing pad to well-trained anglophone Canadian creatives without a thriving homegrown industry of their own. But A24, which funded You Can See Everything, has been establishing itself as both a home for, and source of, Canadian talent.

The distribution studio behind films like Backrooms, Everything Everywhere All at Once and Moonlight is infamously experimental, having enough faith in Fielder's vision that it signed a contract allowing him to cancel the project at any time, consequence-free.

Early this year, the studio released Undertone, the ultra low-budget, Toronto-shot horror from Montreal director Ian Tuason that earned more than $20 million US worldwide. It also nabbed the Anthony Bourdain biopic Tony, directed by Canada's Matt Johnson. That film had a surprisingly strong $5-million US wide debut, following a prior limited release, and eventually grossed nearly $20 million US worldwide.

That incursion hasn't been without friction. Along with a perceived shift away from risk-taking indie fare, A24 was recently in hot water over pulling the Canadian-directed Tony from an independent Toronto theatre over a "clearance issue." That practice, orchestrated and overseen by distributors but kept alive by large cinema chains' superior market share , keeps smaller theatres from being able to play the same film as nearby larger ones.

Still, a supposed turn to Canadian talent could make awards sense. And when it comes to success at the Academy, there is one place Canada has historically shown considerable strength: the world of documentary filmmaking.

The term "documentary" itself was coined by critic John Grierson in 1926, who would go on to create Canada's National Film Board. Meanwhile, the Quebec-set 1922 film Nanook of the North is widely cited as the first feature-length documentary. Though many scenes in the latter were staged , the early connections have bloomed into recurrent Oscars success.

A Canadian documentary feature — producer Guy Glover's The Stratford Adventure — was first nominated at the 1955 ceremony. The country's first documentary feature win came in 1976 with The Man Who Skied Down Everest, followed by CBC's Just Another Missing Kid in 1983 and most recently for a wholly Canadian production with Artie Shaw: Time Is All You've Got. It tied for a win in 1987.

Nominations are more frequent: as recently as Julian Brave NoiseCat's Sugarcane (co-directed with Emily Kassie) for the 2025 ceremony and Nisha Pahuja's To Kill a Tiger at the 2024 awards. Numerous other Canadian-crafted films have also made their way to the Academy Awards, such as Daniel Roher's 2022 film Navalny, or the 2002 Michael Donovan co-produced Bowling for Columbine.

In the best documentary short category, Canadians are even more representative: Since 2011, at least 10 films by Canadians have been nominated. Of those, four have won. Conversely, no wholly Canadian movie has ever been nominated for or won best picture — though Canadian filmmakers James Cameron and Paul Haggis have won for Titanic and Crash, respectively.

In the international category, in which Canada is more routinely competitive, only Denys Arcand has won: for The Barbarian Invasions in 2004 (the category was then called best foreign language film).

World.title: Toronto Crime Stoppers pauses program after CBC investigation reveals more details of data leak
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Toronto Crime Stoppers is pausing its program, effective immediately, said its chair, Sean Sportun, in a statement sent late Wednesday evening.

The news follows an exclusive CBC investigation from earlier in the day revealing that information from more than 1.5 million tips submitted to Canadian Crime Stoppers programs over the last 25 years was exposed in a massive data breach.

It was the first time precise figures were made public showing the severity of the information exposed, as well as how many Canadian tipsters were compromised.

Up until the investigation was published, the Canadian Crime Stoppers Association (CCSA) and individual chapters had not spoken out about the extent of the breach, only saying they awaited a detailed report from Navigate360, the U.S.-based third party company that manages its data through its platform P3.

Toronto Crime Stoppers now says it has removed the "Tip Submit” feature from its website and will no longer accept or process any new information intended for the program. It has also advised Navigate360 to immediately suspend the intake function for the Toronto Crime Stoppers chapter from its platform.

In the statement, the organization advised the public not to send tips by phone, online or through its app "until we have a safer way to protect you."

"People in Toronto have come to Toronto Crime Stoppers because we promised they could stay anonymous. This week’s reporting shows that for some of them, that promise was broken. We are deeply sorry," Sportun said in a statement.

The Toronto Police Service also announced in a statement Wednesday evening that it has "temporarily suspended its use of Crime Stoppers" until further review.

CBC found thousands of unredacted names

According to CBC's investigation, Toronto Crime Stoppers had the most tips represented in the leak of all Canadian chapters, with more than 179,000 tips.

The analysis also revealed that more than half of all Canadian tips included personally identifiable information. CBC could not determine in every instance whether the information belonged to a tipster, a victim or someone accused of a crime.

However, CBC found that in over 4,300 reports, tipsters introduced themselves with a full name, although Crime Stoppers explicitly tells the public to avoid including identifying details . Still, this represented a fraction of reports, at less than one per cent of all entries over 25 years. CBC wasn't able to verify whether all names were legitimate.

Despite hundreds of those tips containing clear staff warnings that a tipster had "self-identified" or had been "exposed," the information still appeared in the database unredacted.

WATCH | More on the investigation: Over a million Canadian tips leaked from Crime Stoppers database | Duration closed caption 1:52 A CBC News investigation found more than a million tips submitted to Crime Stoppers in Canada over the past 25 years were exposed in a massive data breach. About half the leaked Canadian tips obtained by CBC contained personal information.

Toronto Crime Stoppers' Wednesday statement reiterated that the program aims to keep tips anonymous.

"We never ask for your name, and we don’t want it," it said. "But people sometimes include details to explain what they saw. Before a tip goes to investigators, our practice is to remove those details. It has come to light that some of those original tips containing potentially identifying information were stolen from P3."

The Toronto police statement, which was sent at almost the same time, said the news "raises serious concerns regarding the protection of confidential information provided through the Crime Stoppers program."

At the time of publication, CBC could still access a tip form using the main P3 platform.

World.title: Some of Canada's top scientists push for changes to Carney's new major projects bill
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

More than 50 of Canada's leading scholars and scientists are urging Parliament to make major changes to a signature bill from Prime Minister Mark Carney's government in an effort to avoid irreversible environmental harm for the sake of fast-tracking projects.

In an open letter sent Thursday, 56 fellows of the Royal Society of Canada propose six significant amendments to Bill C-39, the Building Canada Strong Act, which is being reviewed by special committees in the House of Commons and Senate for swift passage.

The goal of the 243-page bill is to speed up decisions on projects to give greater certainty to proponents and investors by establishing a one-year review deadline and regions of national interest where certain types of projects can be pre-approved.

The fellows say they support the federal government's decision to create conditions for investment, jobs and economic growth, but they say the bill as written goes too far to endanger nature, wildlife and human health.

"Bill C-39 countermands the environmental protections currently in place in Canadian law, laws written to avoid irreparable harms," the fellows wrote. "We call upon the House and Senate to uphold these laws and to consider our recommendations for the benefit of nature, Canadians and the rest of the world."

The Royal Society of Canada is considered the country's senior national bilingual academy. It recognizes academic, artistic and scientific excellence and its members often advise government. There are more than 2,000 Royal Society of Canada fellows, according to the academy's website.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and Minister of Transport Steven MacKinnon prepare for a committee appearance on Monday. (Justin Tang/Canadian Press)

Bill C-39 proposes to amend more than a dozen pieces of federal legislation, including laws that protect species at risk, fisheries and water quality.

It also intends to eliminate a five-year sunset clause that limited the government's extraordinary powers under initial Building Canada Act, Bill C-5, to exempt certain projects deemed in the national interest from a wide set of environmental regulations and acts of Parliament.

The fellows are asking parliamentarians to keep the sunset clause in place.

They're also looking for regions of national interest to be fully defined, an acknowledgement that additional time may be required to evaluate projects and thorough reviews before shovels hit the ground, among other amendments.

"This is not a build Canada while protecting our environment act," said Sarah Otto, a professor in the department of zoology at the University of British Columbia, who signed the letter.

"It is a build Canada strong while damaging the environment [act]."

Potential long-term consequences

The letter is the latest step by scientists and environmentalists to raise alarms about Bill C-39, as the governing Liberals use their majority to push through the controversial proposed legislation without the usual time allotted for parliamentary debate and review.

"Some of the changes that can be happening are going to affect ecosystems forever," John Smol, a Queen's University biology professor who signed the letter, told CBC News.

"We really have to take into consideration what are the long-term consequences and who's paying for this? It's not going to be the industry, it's going to be our children and grandchildren."

WATCH | Speed over species? Concerns mount over Bill C-39: Critics warn Bill C-39 puts environment at risk | Duration closed caption 2:03 The federal government is pushing Bill C-39 to speed up approvals for major energy and infrastructure projects. Environmental groups warn it could weaken protections for water and wildlife, but Ottawa insists safeguards will remain.

Federal ministers defended Bill C-39 on Monday at the special legislative committee in the House of Commons.

"Clearer timelines do not predetermine outcomes, and responsible developments and robust oversight can and should exist together," said Dominic LeBlanc, minister responsible for Canada-U.S. trade, intergovernmental affairs and one Canadian economy.

All opposition parties say they're planning to suggest amendments to Bill C-39 to address environmental concerns and another contentious proposal to change the Labour Code. Unions warn the bill will limit the right to strike, but the government says the proposed legislation will protect it.
