World.title: Over 2,500 arrested for fuel theft since October 2024: Wednesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

⛽ Mexico targets fuel theft with thousands of arrests: Deputy Energy Minister for Hydrocarbons Juan José Vidal Amaro reported that federal security forces have arrested 2,539 people for huachicol (fuel theft) offenses since October 2024. Authorities have seized 5,572 vehicles and 173.7 million liters of fuel, and 2,224 companies have been shut down for selling fuel without the required permits. He also said that 180 companies have been removed from the registry of approved fuel importers over alleged involvement in fuel smuggling.

Deputy Energy Minister for Hydrocarbons Juan José Vidal Amaro reported that federal security forces have arrested 2,539 people for huachicol (fuel theft) offenses since October 2024. Authorities have seized 5,572 vehicles and 173.7 million liters of fuel, and 2,224 companies have been shut down for selling fuel without the required permits. He also said that 180 companies have been removed from the registry of approved fuel importers over alleged involvement in fuel smuggling. 🔥🇺🇸 Sheinbaum: No commitment to buy more U.S. natural gas: Asked whether buying more U.S. gas would undermine energy sovereignty, the president said Mexico hasn’t entered into any “agreement” or made any “commitment” to do so. She acknowledged that the idea is “something that the United States has put on the table” as Trump seeks to reduce the U.S. trade deficit with Mexico. However, Sheinbaum said that Mexico’s objective is to produce more gas domestically, including to supply new combined-cycle power plants.

Asked whether buying more U.S. gas would undermine energy sovereignty, the president said Mexico hasn’t entered into any “agreement” or made any “commitment” to do so. She acknowledged that the idea is “something that the United States has put on the table” as Trump seeks to reduce the U.S. trade deficit with Mexico. However, Sheinbaum said that Mexico’s objective is to produce more gas domestically, including to supply new combined-cycle power plants. ✈️ Sheinbaum praises Ambassador Johnson despite disagreements: The president said U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson “has helped us on many issues,” including by providing assistance to Mexico to get U.S. restrictions on new flights from Mexico City airports AICM and AIFA lifted. She acknowledged her government has disagreed with some of his public remarks, including his comments on corruption in Mexico, but stressed that Mexico wants “the best possible relationship with the United States.”

Why today’s mañanera matters

At President Sheinbaum’s Wednesday morning press conference, Energy Ministry officials provided an update on the government’s fight against fuel theft (known colloquially as huachicol or huachicoleo) and a fuel smuggle/tax evasion scheme known as huachicol fiscal. Both crimes have cost the federal government and state oil company Pemex huge amounts of money in lost revenue.

Today’s mañanera was also significant as the president told reporters that Mexico has not made any commitment to purchase more natural gas from the United States, as U.S. President Donald Trump has reportedly urged it to do.

Mexico is already heavily reliant on the United States for its natural gas supplies.

On Wednesday morning, Sheinbaum also offered praise for U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ron Johnson, highlighting that he assisted Mexico in its efforts to have U.S. restrictions lifted on new flights to the U.S. from the Mexico City International Airport and the Felipe Ángeles International Airport.

More than 2,500 huachicol-related arrests since Sheinbaum took office

Juan José Vidal Amaro, deputy energy minister for hydrocarbons, reported that federal security forces have arrested 2,539 people for huachicol offenses since the government took office in October 2024.

He said that authorities have seized 5,572 vehicles used to transport fuel as well as 173.7 million liters of fuel.

Vidal said that the data provides evidence of the progress that has been made in combating “illegal activities in the fuel market.”

Earlier in the press conference, he reported that 2,224 companies have been shut down for selling fuel without holding the applicable permits. Vidal also said that 2,032 gas stations have been fined for not having adequate “volumetric controls” on their gas pumps.

In addition, the deputy minister said that 180 companies have been removed from the government’s registry of approved fuel importers due to their alleged involvement in fuel smuggling.

Sheinbaum says Mexico hasn’t agreed to purchase more natural gas from the US

A reporter raised the possibility of Mexico purchasing more natural gas from the United States in order to reduce the U.S. deficit in the bilateral trade relationship. “Wouldn’t this be a backward step for Mexico in the quest for energy sovereignty?” she asked the president.

Sheinbaum responded that Mexico hasn’t entered into any “agreement” or made any “commitment” to purchase more gas from the United States.

Her remarks came almost two weeks after the Financial Times reported that she and U.S. President Donald Trump had “discussed the prospect of Mexico increasing purchases of U.S. natural gas, on which it already depends for about three-quarters of its demand.”

Sheinbaum acknowledged that the possibility of Mexico buying more U.S. gas is “something that the United States has put on the table” as the Trump administration seeks to reduce the U.S. trade deficit with Mexico.

“It’s not that they’re particularly interested in selling more gas,” she said, explaining that what Trump is interested in is reducing the United States’ trade deficit with Mexico, which increased more than 20% year over year in the first eight months of 2026 to reach almost US $156 billion.

Sheinbaum said that her government has told its U.S. counterpart that its objective is to produce more gas in Mexico, in part to ensure sufficient supplies for new combined-cycle power plants.

“If for any reason we can’t produce the gas [needed for new power plants] in Mexico, we’ll have to get the natural gas from somewhere. But the objective is to produce it in the country,” she said.

The government is open to using fracking to boost natural gas production in Mexico, but no clear timeline has emerged for when new projects could begin.

Environment Minister Alicia Bárcena told Congress earlier this month that, “the conditions for proceeding with hydraulic fracturing operations currently do not exist, nor is there any authorization from the president.”

Sheinbaum: Ambassador Johnson ‘has helped us on many issues’

A reporter asked the president about her recent description of U.S. Ambassador Johnson as “a good ally of Mexico” shortly after she called on him to respect Mexico’s laws in light of the United States cooperation with the state of Querétaro on an “international police training academy” project that hadn’t been authorized by the federal government.

Sheinbaum responded that Johnson, ambassador to Mexico since May 2025, “has helped us on many issues.”

She said that Johnson helped her government “a lot” on the issue of “air transport” after the United States last year revoked approval for existing and planned flights to the U.S. from the Mexico City International Airport and the Felipe Ángeles International Airport (AIFA).

The U.S. Department of Transportation last week lifted restrictions on new flights to the U.S. from AICM and AIFA, allowing Mexican airlines to launch new routes to U.S. airports. The lifting of the restrictions — which were imposed due to aviation disputes between Mexico and the U.S. — will allow U.S.-bound passenger flights to depart from AIFA for the first time.

Sheinbaum said that Johnson worked with Mexican and U.S. officials on the “whole process” related to Mexico’s efforts to have the U.S. restrictions lifted.

“We have to say it, and finally the [U.S.] sanction was lifted,” she said.

“[Johnson] helped on this issue,” Sheinbaum said.

“There are other issues on which the ambassador helped us,” she added.

Sheinbaum acknowledged that her government has disagreed with some of Johnson’s public remarks, including those he made about corruption in Mexico during an address in Sinaloa in April. She said that she and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs have expressed their disagreement to the ambassador.

“But there are issues on which he has helped us,” Sheinbaum reiterated.

“… We don’t have any problem in saying it. What do we want? The best possible relationship with the United States, always with respect for our sovereignty and respect for our compatriots in the United States,” she said.

World.title: MND Local Puerto Vallarta: Hurricanes keep coming, golf course disruption, free drinking water fountains
World.content:
It is feeling a little bit like “Groundhog Day” in Puerto Vallarta as we closely watch the trajectory of Hurricane Trudy, the fourth hurricane to come our way in recent weeks. If we are lucky, the storm will follow the path that Polo, Rachel and Simón took and skirt the coast without making landfall. While the storms’ impacts have been relatively moderate in Vallarta, they have caused flooding on the Baja California peninsula and El Niño-linked erosion damage in Southern California, and our hearts go out to communities affected.

Major headlines this month include the ordered demolition of a controversial condo complex in San Pancho, Nayarit; infrastructure issues and the tragic loss of five lives due to recent storms; the rollout of a new program to bring free drinking water fountains to schools, sports, civic and tourist areas throughout the city; and devastating tree culling at the Marina Golf Course.

Recent storms cause beach erosion, flooding and five deaths

Puerto Vallarta is recovering from four back-to-back hurricanes that skirted the city’s southern coast and Banderas Bay. The first hurricane, Polo, rolled in on Sept. 23, followed by Rachel, then Simón and Trudy. The storms brought major tidal surges and pounding waves to Vallarta’s beaches, filling the Malecón with rocks and sand, eroding beaches and leaving just rocks behind.

Impressive photos and videos show waves hitting the Malecón seawall and bouncing many feet into the air. Communities of Yelapa and Boca de Tomatlán were evacuated as a preventative measure as Hurricane Simón approached. Heavy rainfall also caused sewer system backups in the Versailles neighborhood and street flooding in many parts of town. Authorities also closed local beaches, but tragically, one young woman was swept away and is presumed drowned at Playa de Oro during Hurricane Polo. Four people, including two children, were killed when rushing water swept away their home in La Cuesta in the municipality of Talpa de Allende.

Profepa orders demolition of San Pancho beachfront condo

On Oct. 7, the Federal Attorney’s Office for Environmental Protection (Profepa) ordered the demolition of two towers of the Punta Paraíso condo complex in San Pancho, Nayarit. The towers sit directly on the beach in this coastal community and have been the subject of protests by residents for over a decade due to the buildings’ environmental impacts and encroachment into the protected Federal Maritime Terrestrial Zone.

Hurricanes Rachel and Simón pounded the beachfront towers, severely damaging their foundations, causing the towers to lean and necessitating the evacuation of residents.

The developer, Pacific Lifestyle Properties, was also ordered to pay a 96,220-peso (US $5,216) fine for building in the federal zone. Score one for Mother Nature and zero for illegal development.

Seapal rolls out free drinking fountains in public schools, sports fields and tourist spots

Remember to bring your refillable water bottles on your next trip to Puerto Vallarta because visitors and residents alike will soon have access to free, purified drinking water in various locations throughout the city.

This summer, Puerto Vallarta’s municipal water utility, Seapal, launched a program to bring purified drinking water fountains to public schools, civic, sports and tourist spots around Vallarta. The program aims to improve public health, increase access to safe, free drinking water, and reduce plastic pollution.

New fountains have already been installed in several schools and the Emiliano Zapata Municipal Market, and several more are planned for the Unidad Deportiva Agustín Flores Contreras sports complex, Centro Cultural y Módulo Deportivo La Lija, Seapal Vallarta’s central offices, Unidad Municipal Administrativa (UMA), and on the Malecón.

Marina Golf Course culls trees in major remodel, angering residents

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Marina Vallarta Club De Golf (@marinavallartaclubdegolf)

The Marina Golf Course has been systematically cutting down dozens of large, mature trees over the past several weeks, angering residents and displacing wildlife. Golf course administrators claim the culling of trees is part of a comprehensive remodeling project and that they plan to plant more trees than are being removed.

In the meantime, however, residents must wait decades for new trees to grow to the size of the old ones and face the constant sound of chainsaws and the sadness of watching trees being felled for many more days.

The trees being removed are mostly a nonnative species of ficus, but they provide habitat for native birds such as white ibises, great kiskadees, golden-cheeked woodpeckers, chachalacas and more.

The course has been closed most of the summer and fall during the remodeling project. Rest assured, visitors to Vallarta coming to the course this year will see a drastically different landscape.

They say the only constant is change. Let us just hope the next changes coming to Vallarta are less destructive and more positive, like the free drinking water program. But hurricane season is not over yet, so we will just have to wait and see.

Debbie Slobe is a writer and communications strategist based in Puerto Vallarta, Jalisco. She blogs at Mexpatmama.com and is a senior program director at Resource Media. Find her on Instagram and Facebook.

World.title: Beloved Ballet Folklórico announces US tour in celebration of 75th anniversary
World.content:
Amalia Hernández’s Ballet Folklórico de México will celebrate its 75th anniversary with a tour to 24 cities in the United States, beginning Jan. 30 in Northridge, California, and concluding March 23 in Austin, Texas.

The Ballet Folklórico de México was established in 1952 by dancer and choreographer Amalia Hernández. The group revolutionized Mexican dance and laid the foundation for traditional choreographies and costumes to gain prestige in Mexico and abroad.

The company will travel with more than 50 members and present a repertoire of dances from various regions of Mexico, featuring live music, colorful garments and routines that blend folk traditions with theatrical staging.

“Our 75th anniversary is a celebration not only of Ballet Folklórico de México, but of the people, communities, traditions and artists who have kept Mexico’s cultural heritage alive,” Ballet Folklórico de México General Manager Salvador Lopez, who is also Hernández’s grandson, said in a statement.

“It is an honor to bring Amalia Hernández’s artistic legacy to audiences across the United States and to introduce new generations to the beauty and diversity of Mexico,” he added.

Where will the ballet perform?

In California, the company will perform in Northridge, Modesto, Santa Barbara, Los Angeles, Chico, Davis, Berkeley, San Luis Obispo and Costa Mesa; in Arizona, in Tucson and Mesa; and in Texas, in El Paso, Lubbock, Richardson, San Antonio and Austin.

The tour will also reach Las Vegas, Nevada; Carmel, Indiana; East Lansing, Michigan; Milwaukee, Wisconsin; Minneapolis, Minnesota; Chicago, Illinois; Santa Fe, New Mexico; and Denver, Colorado.

Tickets are available through the official channels of the participating venues and, depending on the city, through platforms such as Ticketmaster.

In addition to its international tours, the Ballet Folklórico de México maintains a residency at the Palacio de Bellas Artes in Mexico City, where it has held regular performances since 1959.

With reports from El Universal

World.title: NBA commissioner hints at Mexico City expansion
World.content:
During an appearance on the Pat McAfee Show on Tuesday, NBA Commissioner Adam Silver said that Mexico City could potentially be included among the NBA’s next expansion locations thanks to the growing popularity of basketball in the capital.

However, the expansion wouldn’t be immediate, Silver said.

“We’re still a few seasons away from actual expansion taking place. We’ve been public about the fact that we’re looking at Las Vegas and Seattle. Maybe down the road there’s Mexico City, which is the largest city in North America,” he stated.

One of Silver’s arguments for potentially expanding into Mexico City is its relative proximity to other markets in the league, highlighting that it is actually closer to travel between Mexico City and New York than New York to Los Angeles.

“It’s a shorter flight from New York to Mexico than from New York to Los Angeles, so you can see why we’d be interested,” Silver noted.

Silver also mentioned discussions regarding sports infrastructure in the capital, which would factor into the decision.

“They are talking about building a new arena in Mexico City; it’s not in the immediate plans, but there is great potential there in the long term,” he said.

The possibility of a new arena was previously mentioned in an Oct. 16 ESPN report. According to the outlet, at least one Mexico City-based group approached PJT Partners — the firm advising the NBA on its expansion — with a proposal to establish a franchise and develop a sports complex centered around a new basketball arena.

ESPN said no construction plans have been confirmed or announced yet.

With reports from ESPN and Marca

World.title: Lyon Bans All Protests This Saturday
World.content:
Riot police in Paris after the 17 October protest. File photo; the new ban applies to Lyon. Photo: Jorge Jaramillo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

FRANCE · PROTESTS

Published Thursday, 22 October, 6:40 a.m. ET (12:40 p.m. Paris) · Source: Rhône prefecture order, reported by Le Figaro, Lyon Capitale, Le Monde

Authorities in Lyon, France’s third-largest city, have banned every demonstration there this Saturday, 24 October. The order follows riots and looting a week earlier during a nationwide cost-of-living protest.

Key Facts — What happened Lyon’s prefecture banned all demonstrations in the city for Saturday, 24 October.

— Who decided The Rhône prefect, the national government’s top local official.

— Why Looting and violence marked the 17 October protest a week earlier.

— What happens next Saturday 24 October, when a new protest day, “Acte II”, is called.

— Why it matters for US readers Lyon is a major city for visitors and business. Avoid crowds Saturday.

— Prediction markets Kalshi: last trade 11% for a French state of emergency before 1 November, as of 6:38 a.m. ET.

This story is part of our coverage of the why France is in crisis. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. Latest: Paris Bans Street Protests on Thursday

In plain English France has had weeks of protests over living costs, and riots followed the biggest march on 17 October. Now the government’s local chief in Lyon says no demonstration at all may take place there on Saturday. A prefect is the national government’s top official in a region or department, with power over local policing.

The Rhône prefecture, the state authority that oversees policing in Lyon, announced on Thursday 22 October that all demonstrations are banned in the city on Saturday 24 October. It comes a week after looting and violence on the margins of the 17 October march, part of the unrest we follow in our France protests coverage.

A new call for a protest day against the high cost of living, labelled “Acte II”, is called for the same Saturday by a Yellow Vest coordination, Lyon Mag reported. Our explainer on why France is protesting sets out how the movement began.

What the Ban Covers

The prefecture’s wording, as quoted in French media, is that “any demonstration” is barred in Lyon on Saturday (our translation). The reports available so far did not give hours or a map of the area.

Lyon already has tighter rules. A night curfew from 9 p.m. to 6 a.m. was first imposed for the night of 19 to 20 October in part of the central Presqu’île district, Lyon Mag reported, after gatherings had been banned between 6 p.m. and 9 p.m. Bars, restaurants and public transport were allowed to keep running. The reports we saw did not say whether it still applies.

Paris Meets Over the Unrest

President Emmanuel Macron chaired a security council at the Élysée Palace on Thursday morning, and Le Monde’s live coverage reported that it had ended. Party leaders were due at Matignon, the prime minister’s office, at 2:30 p.m. Paris time (8:30 a.m. ET), Libération reported.

The 17 October march drew 550,000 people by the Interior Ministry’s count and 800,000 by the organisers’ count. Several cities saw riots that evening.

Protest placards in Paris on 17 October. File photo. Photo: FreCha, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

What Prediction Markets Say

On Kalshi, which is regulated in the US by the CFTC (the Commodity Futures Trading Commission), traders put the chance that France declares a state of emergency at 11% before 1 November and 23% before 1 January 2027, with 37,588 contracts traded across the two markets. Prices are as of 6:38 a.m. ET on 22 October and are bets, not polls.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for US Readers

Anyone in Lyon on Saturday should expect a heavy police presence and steer clear of crowds, since even a peaceful march is banned. Check the US Embassy and prefecture notices, and see our guide to travel to France right now.

What Is Not Known

The hours and exact area of the ban were not reported at the time of writing. It is also unclear whether organisers will challenge the order in court or march anyway, and what the Élysée meeting decided.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Lyon banning protests this Saturday?

Yes. The Rhône prefecture announced on Thursday 22 October that all demonstrations in Lyon are banned on Saturday 24 October.

Why did the prefecture ban the protests?

The order comes a week after looting and violence on the edges of the 17 October cost-of-living protest, French media reported.

What is Acte II?

It is the name given to a new protest day against the high cost of living, called for Saturday 24 October by a Yellow Vest coordination.

Is it safe to travel to Lyon this weekend?

The order targets demonstrations, and no travel closure has been reported. Visitors should avoid crowds and follow prefecture and US Embassy advice.

Has France declared a state of emergency?

Not as of this writing. Kalshi traders put the chance of one before 1 November at 11%, as of 6:38 a.m. ET on 22 October.

World.title: Iran Airspace Closure Odds Jump to 41%
World.content:
File photo: the Milad Tower in Tehran, the capital of Iran.

IRAN · AVIATION · PREDICTION MARKETS

Key Facts — Prediction markets Polymarket: 41.0% by 31 December, up 11.5 points in 24 hours (22 October, 6:30 a.m. ET).

— Trigger No single trigger was reported; Gulf shipping attacks and strike talk dominated the day.

— What it measures A “Yes” needs Iran to suspend commercial flights across all of its airspace.

— What counts next Foreign ministers meet in Istanbul on Friday 23 October; the 31 October line expires on 31 October.

— Volume About US$10.4 million traded in all; about US$62,800 in the past 24 hours.

Traders now put the odds that Iran fully closes its airspace by 31 December at 41%. That is 11.5 points higher than 24 hours ago and 13.5 points higher than a week ago, according to Polymarket.

It matters to US readers because a closed Iranian sky would reroute flights between Europe and Asia, push up fuel costs and signal that the war around Iran is widening.

In Plain English Airspace closure: a government order that stops commercial airlines from flying through a country’s sky. Tehran flight region: the block of sky that Iran’s air traffic control manages, which airlines cross on routes between Europe and Asia. Polymarket price: 41% means traders pay 41 cents for a contract that pays US$1 if the closure happens.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket, a crypto-based exchange, asks whether Iran will close its airspace by a set date. The question opened on 25 June 2026 and has one line per deadline.

31 December: 41.0% “Yes”, up 11.5 points in 24 hours and 13.5 points in seven days; about US$24,400 traded in 24 hours.

41.0% “Yes”, up 11.5 points in 24 hours and 13.5 points in seven days; about US$24,400 traded in 24 hours. 31 October: 8.0% “Yes”, up 0.5 points in 24 hours and down 1.0 point in seven days; about US$38,400 traded in 24 hours.

About US$10.4 million has traded on the question in all, and about US$62,800 in the past 24 hours. Each line is modest in size, so a few large orders can move it.

Our own daily snapshots show the December line at 27.5% on 15 October, 29.5% on 21 October and 33.5% at the start of 22 October, before the latest read of 41.0%. Kalshi, which is regulated in the US by the CFTC, showed no comparable Iran airspace contract in a search of its public market list.

Read on 22 October 2026, 6:30 a.m. ET. These are bets, not polls and not a forecast by this newsroom; live prices are on our Prediction Markets page.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Why the Odds Moved

We found no single event that explains the jump. The move came on a day when several war-related reports were published.

Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister, rejected a report that Donald Trump had blocked a planned Israeli offensive. He also said the only way to guarantee the war is over is to “bring down this regime”, according to Iran International’s live coverage on 22 October.

The same coverage quoted Trump as saying on Wednesday that talks with Iran were continuing “to some extent”, with an outcome “one way or the other” fairly soon. Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said Tehran would give diplomacy another chance if Washington showed a sincere wish to build trust.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guard navy said four ships transferring oil cargo in the northern Persian Gulf were hit and burning, and that three more struck mines and caught fire in the western Strait of Hormuz overnight. Iran International also reported an attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, Saudi Arabia, that killed two people and injured eight, with operations resuming afterwards.

Turkey will host foreign ministers from Egypt, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Britain, France and Germany in Istanbul on Friday 23 October. They plan to discuss the US-Iran war, Hormuz and other regional conflicts.

The sky over Iran is already regulated. The EU Aviation Safety Agency’s bulletin, revised on 30 September 2026 and valid to 16 November, tells airlines not to operate in the Tehran flight region at any altitude, citing the risk from weapons and air defences.

That advice is not an Iranian closure order, and the market only counts closures that Iran itself orders. Earlier general closures, such as the one on 28 February 2026, came before the market opened and do not count.

What It Means for US Readers

Airlines already avoid Iran’s sky, so a formal closure would change little for most US travellers directly. It would matter more as a sign that Tehran expects fighting at home, which tends to move oil and shipping insurance first.

Fuel costs reach US drivers and airlines through the oil price, and our report on Brent crude and Hormuz fears shows how sensitive that price already is. US politics is also in play, with midterm elections on 3 November.

For policy, the odds sit beside our earlier coverage of the US-Iran ceasefire market and the Israel-Iran ceasefire market. Together they show traders pricing a harder road than talks alone would suggest.

What It Means for Latin America and Africa

Oil exporters such as Brazil, Mexico, Colombia, Nigeria and Angola gain when war lifts crude prices, while fuel importers across both regions pay more. A wider conflict would also raise shipping and insurance costs on routes through the Gulf and the Red Sea.

We have no market or official data tying this contract to any one country in either region. See our Latin America odds page and Africa odds page for regional markets.

What Is Not Known

It is not known what moved the price, and no Iranian aviation authority has announced a new closure in the reports we found. We could not confirm the current status of Iran’s airspace from an Iranian source.

It is also not known whether the rise reflects fresh information or a thin book. Single lines trade only tens of thousands of dollars a day.

Finally, the ship hits and mine strikes are claims by Iran’s Revolutionary Guard navy, and we have not seen independent confirmation of the number of vessels or their cargo.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are prediction markets saying about Iran closing its airspace?

Polymarket gives a 41% chance that Iran fully closes its airspace by 31 December, up 11.5 points in 24 hours. The 31 October line sits at 8% (22 October, 6:30 a.m. ET).

What counts as a full airspace closure?

A general suspension of commercial flights across all of Iran or the Tehran flight region. Partial closures, such as one covering only western routes, do not count, and earlier closures from before the market opened on 25 June do not either.

Why did the odds move?

No single trigger was reported. The jump came as Netanyahu spoke of bringing down Iran’s government, ships were reported burning in Gulf waters and Trump said talks were continuing “to some extent”.

Is it safe to fly over Iran now?

European regulators say no. The EU Aviation Safety Agency tells airlines not to operate in Iran’s airspace at any altitude, in a bulletin valid until 16 November 2026.

Does a market price mean a closure will happen?

No. Prices are bets by traders, not forecasts by this newsroom or any government, and they can reverse quickly when news arrives.

World.title: São Paulo Nightlife Tonight: Blue Note, JazzB — October 22, 2026
World.content:
São Paulo · Nightlife

Tonight, Thursday 22 October 2026, São Paulo’s best-confirmed music is on and around Avenida Paulista. Blue Note SP hosts the singer Lissa Martins at 8 p.m. and a Phil Collins and Genesis tribute at 10:30 p.m., while JazzB in Vila Buarque presents a jazz quintet at 9 p.m. The evening is cool and dry at about 19°C (66°F), and all times are São Paulo time.

Tonight at a Glance — Date Thursday, 22 October 2026. All times São Paulo time (UTC-3).

— Weather Cool and dry. Open-Meteo shows 20.1°C (68°F) at 6 p.m., 19.1°C (66°F) at 8 p.m. and 18.9°C (66°F) at 10 p.m., with a chance of rain of 8 per cent or less.

— Top pick Prazer, Lissa, the singer Lissa Martins revisiting her career with two guests, at Blue Note SP at 8 p.m.

— Neighborhood in focus Consolação and Avenida Paulista, where Blue Note SP sits on the second floor of the Conjunto Nacional.

— Entry prices The venue pages publish no prices. Blue Note SP sells through Eventim and JazzB through Sympla, where we could not read the amounts.

— Safety note Paulista is busy until late but side streets empty out, so book an Uber or 99 to the door and home again.

If You Only Go to One Place Prazer, Lissa, Blue Note SP, Avenida Paulista Lissa Martins looks back on a career that runs from childhood singing through the pop group Rouge to musical theatre, with the guests Kiara Sasso and Nando Pradho.

Tonight’s Top 4

1. Prazer, Lissa, Blue Note SP Lissa Martins returns to Blue Note after an April show. She revisits her early singing, the big hits of the pop group Rouge, musical theatre and her solo projects, with Kiara Sasso and Nando Pradho as guests. Tonight Thursday 22 October 2026, 8 p.m., Sala 1.

Genre Pop and musical theatre in an intimate club setting, with restaurant service during the show.

Entry Sold through Eventim. We could not read the price. Minors must be accompanied by a legal guardian.

Address Avenida Paulista 2073, second floor of the Conjunto Nacional, Consolação.

Verdict A friendly first night for visitors, because the club is small and the repertoire is pop. For foreigners: Rouge was a Brazilian pop group of the early 2000s, and seating at the tables is first come, first served, so arrive early.

2. Daniel D’Alcantara / Mathias Hindal Quinteto, JazzB A jazz quintet in a small jazz room in the centre. The venue lists two 50-minute sets between 9 p.m. and 11 p.m. Tonight Thursday 22 October 2026, 9 p.m. to about 11 p.m.

Genre Jazz.

Entry Sold through Sympla, where advance tickets guarantee a table, with seats allocated in order of arrival. We could not read the price, and the page does not mark the show as sold out.

Address Rua General Jardim 43, Vila Buarque. The room has tiered seating inside and an open-air terrace.

Verdict The best pick for listeners who want music rather than a night out. For foreigners: book in advance, because the Sympla ticket is what guarantees a table.

3. Popcast: Tribute to Phil Collins and Genesis, Blue Note SP A tribute show that moves through the solo career of Phil Collins and the classics of the band Genesis. The musicians have worked with Leo Jaime, Toni Garrido and Geraldo Azevedo. Tonight Thursday 22 October 2026, 10:30 p.m., Sala 1.

Genre Rock and pop tribute.

Entry Sold through Eventim. We could not read the price.

Address Avenida Paulista 2073, second floor of the Conjunto Nacional, Consolação.

World.title: Rio de Janeiro Nightlife Tonight: Piaf Musical, Audio Rebel — October 22, 2026
World.content:
Rio de Janeiro · Nightlife

Tonight, Thursday 22 October 2026, Rio de Janeiro has one big-ticket show and a handful of smaller rooms. The musical Piaf – Eu Não Me Arrependo, about the French singer Édith Piaf, plays the Teatro Riachuelo Rio at 8 p.m., Audio Rebel in Botafogo hosts the ÀIYÉ show at 7 p.m., and Rio Scenarium opens on Rua do Lavradio at 7 p.m. The evening is mild and dry at about 21°C (70°F), and all times are Rio time.

— Top pick Piaf – Eu Não Me Arrependo, a musical about Édith Piaf starring Laila Garin, at the Teatro Riachuelo Rio at 8 p.m.

Tonight’s Top 3

Genre Musical theatre built around Piaf’s best-known songs. The script is by Newton Moreno and Alessandro Toller, and Sergio Módena directs.

Entry Plateia VIP R$250 (about US$50), Plateia R$220 (about US$44), Balcão Nobre R$150 (about US$30) and Balcão R$50 (about US$10), sold through Ingresso.com. The listing gives an age rating of 12.

2. ÀIYÉ, Audio Rebel, Botafogo Audio Rebel is an independent music room that says it has run since 2005, with a programme centred on Rio’s new independent scene. Tonight’s listing is a “show-experimento” by ÀIYÉ. Tonight Thursday 22 October 2026, 7 p.m.

Genre Experimental and independent music. The venue’s agenda gives no further detail.

Entry R$35 (about US$7), listed on the venue’s agenda.

Address Rua Visconde Silva 55, Botafogo.

Verdict A way to see the local independent scene rather than a tourist show. For foreigners: the 7 p.m. start is early, so you can still head to Lapa afterwards.

3. Rio Scenarium A house of seven rooms on three floors on Rua do Lavradio, presented by the venue as a place for live Brazilian music, from samba de raiz to gafieira and choro. The venue’s site gives Thursday opening hours of 7 p.m. to 1 a.m., and tickets are sold through its Sympla booking page. Tonight Thursday 22 October 2026. Open 7 p.m. to 1 a.m., and we could not confirm tonight’s band.

Genre Live Brazilian music, according to the venue.

Entry We found no published price for tonight.

Address Rua do Lavradio 20, Centro, 20230-070.

Thursday is when Rio’s week turns toward the weekend, but tonight the big rooms are quiet. Vivo Rio and Blue Note Rio list nothing, so the choice is a musical, a small independent venue and the old houses of Lapa.

Édith Piaf was one of the great French voices of the 20th century, and she died in 1963. The Rio production follows her from poverty in childhood to world fame, and covers her love affairs, her role during the Second World War and her health problems.

Botafogo is a residential and bar district in Rio’s South Zone with its own Metro station. Audio Rebel sits on Rua Visconde Silva, so it pairs easily with dinner in the neighbourhood.

World.title: Brazil Grid Loses 191 Towers to Storms
World.content:
BRAZIL · ENERGY

Key Facts — What is happening Brazil’s grid operator ONS said on Wednesday, 21 October, that 191 transmission towers on 230 kV to 500 kV lines have fallen since 26 July.

— Why it matters More than 100 further towers on 138 kV lines also fell, yet the national grid stayed in operation, which matters for US investors in Brazilian power and infrastructure.

— The numbers 191 towers on 230 kV to 500 kV lines and more than 100 on 138 kV lines fell between 26 July and 21 October, a period of about three months.

— Who is who ONS, the Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico, runs Brazil’s national grid; operations director Valter Cardeal spoke at an ONS awards event in Rio de Janeiro.

— What to watch Whether more towers fall as storms continue, and NOAA’s next El Niño update, scheduled for Thursday, 12 November.

— Power Index Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 75.0 points (October 2026 edition).

— What it means for you For US investors in Brazilian power companies and firms in southern Brazil, ONS says the grid stayed operational, though repair work and local outages remain a risk.

Brazil’s grid operator says 191 high-voltage transmission towers have fallen since 26 July. It says the national grid kept operating through the storms.

What the Grid Operator Said

Valter Cardeal, ONS operations director, said 191 towers on 230 kV to 500 kV lines fell between 26 July and 21 October. He said more than 100 towers on 138 kV lines also came down, Agência iNFRA reported.

He spoke on Wednesday, 21 October, at the second ONS operations quality awards in Rio de Janeiro. He blamed weather events for the falls.

Cardeal said the events show the resilience of the national grid, known as the SIN. It kept operating thanks to the work of ONS and the transmission companies, he said.

What NOAA Expects From El Niño

NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center said on Thursday, 8 October, that El Niño continues to strengthen. It sees a strong to very strong event likely through January to March 2027, with chances above 83%.

The center put the chance of a historic event, stronger than any since 1950, at 83% for October to December. Its next update is scheduled for Thursday, 12 November.

What It Means for US Readers

US investors in Brazilian power companies should expect repair work and local outages after storms. ONS says the grid stayed operational, and NOAA’s outlook points to more weather risk into early 2027.

Background is in earlier reports on El Niño, soybeans and the grid, the second emergency grid cut and the yellow tariff flag. Travellers to southern Brazil should expect storm disruption.

What Is Not Known

ONS’s own statement could not be opened, so the tower counts rest on Agência iNFRA’s report of Cardeal’s remarks. The report does not say where the towers fell, how many customers lost power or what the repairs cost.

Agência iNFRA cites weather events, and the sources opened do not tie the falls to El Niño. Whether more towers will fall is not known.

What Comes Next

NOAA’s next El Niño update on Thursday, 12 November will show whether the outlook holds. ONS has not announced any tower redesign in the report reviewed.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many towers have fallen in Brazil since July?

ONS says 191 towers on 230 kV to 500 kV lines fell between 26 July and 21 October. More than 100 towers on 138 kV lines also came down.

Did Brazil suffer blackouts from the fallen towers?

ONS says the national grid kept operating thanks to its work and that of its agents. The report does not give a count of affected customers.

Were the falls caused by El Niño?

Agência iNFRA cites weather events and does not name El Niño. NOAA separately expects a strong to very strong El Niño into early 2027.

What does NOAA expect from El Niño?

NOAA says a strong to very strong El Niño is likely through January to March 2027, with chances above 83%. Its next update is due on 12 November.

What is ONS?

ONS, the Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico, is the operator that runs Brazil’s national interconnected power grid. Its operations director is Valter Cardeal.

World.title: Paraguay Gender Bill Seeks Up to 10 Years
World.content:
PARAGUAY · POLITICS

Key Facts — What is happening On Wednesday, 21 October, parent groups marched through Asunción and gave the Senate a citizen bill, with about 50,000 signatures, that would punish gender content aimed at children with 4 to 10 years in prison.

— Why it matters Paraguay is a close US security partner and its ruling Colorado Party holds a congressional majority, so a bill the Senate president says he backs has a real path, though critics call the wording broad.

— The numbers The bill adds Article 135c to the Penal Code with 4 to 10 years in prison, 10 to 15 years for officials, and 15 to 20 years if an official approved the material.

— Who is who Backers include Miguel Ortigoza, head of a parent federation, and Senator Gustavo Leite of the Colorado Party, while about 50 civil groups reject the bill and the Archdiocese of Asunción keeps its distance.

— What to watch Whether Senate committees take up the bill and how they treat its broad wording, since no debate date has been announced and the proposal is not law.

— Power Index Paraguay ranks 10th of 14 in Paraguay ranks 10th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 36.0 points (October 2026 edition).

— What it means for you For US readers, the bill tests a close Washington partner on speech, schooling and LGBT expression, but nothing changes for visitors today because it is only a proposal.

Parent groups gave Paraguay’s Senate a citizen bill on 21 October that would jail adults for gender content aimed at children. Critics say its wording is broad.

A Paraguay gender bill reached the Senate on Wednesday, 21 October, with about 50,000 signatures behind it. It would punish adults who spread content altering a child’s view of sexuality with 4 to 10 years in prison.

Paraguay is a close US security partner, and its ruling Colorado Party holds a majority in Congress. Senate president Basilio Núñez took the document in person and pledged his support, Última Hora reported.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Paraguay ranks 10th of 14 with 36.0 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (55); weakest: future resources (13). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What the Paraguay Gender Bill Would Change

The initiative amends Article 135 of the Penal Code, which covers sexual abuse of children. It adds Article 135c, titled abuse in other forms, in the text ABC Color published.

The draft covers material or acts that could interfere with, alter or damage a child’s natural perception of sexuality. Anyone who makes, sells, promotes or publishes such material would face 4 to 10 years in prison.

Officials and elected authorities would face 10 to 15 years, said lawyer Dannia Ríos, one of the drafters, to Última Hora. If an official authorised or approved such material, the term would rise to 15 to 20 years.

Backers say the aim is to protect children from confusion about identity. Miguel Ortigoza, president of the parent federation Fenapep, said people may live as they choose but should not confuse other people’s children.

Ortigoza told Hoy in September that the idea grew from public events like a kissing protest, where children were present. He said private conduct is not the concern.

Who Backs the Bill and Who Objects

Senator Gustavo Leite of the ruling Colorado Party, a former Paraguayan ambassador to the United States, spoke at the rally. He said a similar Senate initiative once stayed in the drawer, and that 50,000 signatures make that unlikely now.

The march ran from Plaza de la Democracia to the Congress plaza. Crowd estimates conflict: Última Hora said hundreds attended, while EFE reported about 1,000.

About 50 civil society groups jointly rejected the bill. They say it ignores real child abuse and could limit free expression and teaching.

The groups cite Public Ministry data of 34,001 child abuse victims from 2015 to May 2026, many inside families, RDN reported. SOMOSGAY, a Paraguayan LGBT advocacy group, said treating same-sex public affection as abuse would violate constitutional guarantees.

ABC Color and RDN describe the bill as aimed at such affection. The text they quote does not name same-sex couples.

The Archdiocese of Asunción said it will not join the call institutionally while its experts study the Article 135 change. The bishops’ conference family pastoral office, by contrast, backed accompanying the rally, EFE said.

The Textbook Row Behind the March

The march followed days of protest over Education Ministry books for a sexuality programme known as EASE. Passages called Adolf Hitler a famous politician who “reached very high,” and critics said other passages reproduce gender stereotypes.

Hoy said Education Minister Luis Ramírez acknowledged an error and cited a zonal trial. The Ombudsman’s office asked for withdrawal, while the minister called it a pilot, Última Hora said.

Opposition Senator Esperanza Martínez denounced the books as promoting machismo. A defender of the materials, author María Judith Turriaga, said they were published out of context and misread, Última Hora reported.

How a Citizen Bill Moves Through Congress

Article 123 of Paraguay’s Constitution lets voters propose bills to Congress, with the form and number of signatures set by law. Hoy reported in September that the bill must first pass through committees.

On Wednesday the Senate lost its quorum twice as several senators went out to join the march, Última Hora reported. Fourteen agenda points, mostly requests for information, were left unresolved.

What It Means for US Readers

Paraguay is one of Washington’s closest South American partners. US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau visited Asunción from 19 to 21 October, as this Landau visit report details.

For visitors nothing changes today, because the text is a proposal that has not been debated. Critics call its wording on acts and material broad, so foreign teachers, publishers and charities in Paraguay would watch the final text.

For background, see the guide to Paraguay’s politics, the vote on marriage under 18 and the Paraguay hub. The Chamber of Deputies passed that marriage bill a day before the march.

What Is Not Known

The number of valid signatures is not confirmed. Organisers say more than 50,000, ABC Color says nearly 50,000, and Hoy reported 48,600 certified in September.

No debate date has been reported, and it is unclear how the Senate will treat the text. Whether the ruling party’s leadership backs the bill beyond the Senate president’s pledge is not known.

The reports reviewed contain no comment from the US government or the president’s office. Whether the text would cover same-sex affection is disputed between backers and critics.

What Comes Next

The next step is a committee referral in the Senate, which its president says he backs. The bill would still need to pass Congress, and nothing in the reports says when.

It does not mean anything has become law, and no one can be charged under the draft today. Committees can amend, delay or shelve a citizen initiative.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does the Paraguay bill propose?

It would add Article 135c to the Penal Code. Making or spreading material or acts that alter a child’s perception of sexuality would bring 4 to 10 years in prison.

Who is behind it?

Parent federations led by Miguel Ortigoza and a group of lawyers, including Dannia Ríos, drafted it. Senator Gustavo Leite and Senate president Basilio Núñez publicly back it.

Is it law yet?

No, it is only a proposal. Citizens delivered it to the Senate on Wednesday, 21 October, and it must pass committees and both chambers.

Does it affect tourists or expats?

Nothing in the reports says it would apply to visitors, but critics call the wording broad. Foreigners who live or teach in Paraguay should follow the final text.

Why did the march happen now?

Organisers had said in September they would deliver the bill on 21 October. The march also followed a row over Education Ministry sexuality books.

Sources: Última Hora, 21 October 2026; Última Hora, march report; Última Hora, Senate quorum; Última Hora, Ombudsman and EASE books; ABC Color, 21 October 2026; RDN, 21 October 2026; Hoy, 24 September 2026; Hoy, EASE books; EFE via Infobae, 21 October 2026; Constitution of Paraguay, Article 123 (all accessed 22 October 2026).

World.title: Bolivia Asks US to Back 2 Elite Police Units
World.content:
BOLIVIA · SECURITY

Key Facts — What is happening Bolivia’s Government Minister, Marco Antonio Oviedo, said on Wednesday, 21 October, that he asked US cooperation partners the night before to help create two elite police units in Santa Cruz and Beni.

— Why it matters Oviedo says Bolivia already works with US cooperation bodies against drug gangs, and the request came after three killings in under 24 hours in Warnes and La Guardia, close to Santa Cruz city.

— The numbers Two units are planned, one between San Ignacio de Velasco and San Matías, one near Santa Ana in Beni, and Oviedo put installation at just under a year; 230 trained police joined the plan’s launch.

— Who is who Oviedo runs the police as Government Minister, the Bolivian interior post. General Commander Adrián Álvarez leads the force, and President Rodrigo Paz leads the government.

— What to watch Whether Washington publicly confirms what it will fund, which no source found yet states, and when the first unit opens in San Ignacio, where Oviedo says some infrastructure already exists.

— Power Index Bolivia ranks 12th of 14 in Bolivia ranks 12th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 28.4 points (October 2026 edition).

— What it means for you US travellers to eastern Bolivia should follow State Department advisories, and US agencies and investors should watch how deep Washington’s role in Bolivian policing grows.

Bolivia’s interior minister says he asked US partners on Tuesday night to help build two elite police units. He announced it on Wednesday as a new border security phase began in Santa Cruz.

Bolivia has asked US partners to help build two elite police units, minister Marco Antonio Oviedo said on Wednesday, 21 October. He spoke in Santa Cruz, Bolivia’s largest city, as the government launched a second phase of its border security plan.

The request matters to US readers because Brújula Digital reports that Washington has publicly backed the Paz government’s fight against crime. It also follows three killings in under 24 hours near Santa Cruz city, Los Tiempos said.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Bolivia ranks 12th of 14 with 28.4 points. Strongest pillar: military means (55); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (13). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (CCC+); economy contracting (-1.2%); inflation of 20%. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What Oviedo Announced

Oviedo, who runs the police as Bolivia’s Government Minister, told reporters he sat down with US cooperation officials on Tuesday night. He said he proposed two “super elite” units, according to El Deber and Los Tiempos.

One unit would sit between San Ignacio de Velasco and San Matías in Santa Cruz department, he said. The other would go to Santa Ana “or around there” in Beni, El Deber reported.

Oviedo chose those areas because, he said, narcoterrorism is most frequent there. Narcoterrorism is his government’s term for drug gangs that use armed violence.

The Santa Cruz unit should open faster because “some infrastructure” already exists in San Ignacio, he told El Deber. Los Tiempos quoted him saying the units would be installed in “just under a year”.

Both units would get “all the technological and logistical elements” needed to confront crime, Oviedo said. He gave no cost, no headcount and no US funding figure.

Why Santa Cruz Is Under Pressure

Two Brazilian men were shot dead inside a home in Warnes, Santa Cruz department, on Tuesday, 20 October, Los Tiempos reported. Neighbours described the attackers as tall men in camouflage with Brazilian accents.

In La Guardia, police found a body in the boot of a car without number plates, Los Tiempos added. Santa Cruz police commander Edson Fernández confirmed investigations into the Warnes killings.

Oviedo said Santa Cruz has become a “central objective” for criminal groups. He rejected the idea that police were overwhelmed, saying they were “showing results”, El Deber reported.

He also said narcoterrorism had taken over part of the Attorney General’s Office. Bolivia’s prosecutors have not answered that claim in the sources reviewed.

What Frontera Segura 2.0 Does

Frontera Segura 2.0, or Safe Border 2.0, is the second phase of a plan to put police permanently on the frontier. It was launched on Wednesday on Plaza 24 de Septiembre in Santa Cruz city.

Police commander Adrián Álvarez said 230 officers finished a training course and will join the plan. He promised a fresh contingent every 45 days, El Deber reported.

Álvarez named three aims: a permanent state presence at the border, territorial control there, and security for residents. Santa Cruz will be the hub, with operations in Beni and Pando too.

The training course was called Organised International Networks and Narcoterrorism: Safe Border, Los Tiempos and Opinión reported. Oviedo spoke at its closing ceremony.

Oviedo admitted the police have too few officers. He said numbers would grow “little by little” as the budget allows, Opinión and Los Tiempos reported.

The US Link and Oviedo’s Record

Oviedo told Los Tiempos his ministry also works with the European Union, the United Nations, American cooperation bodies and foreign intelligence. The US has openly backed Paz’s government against crime, Brújula Digital wrote.

Brújula Digital adds that Bolivia belongs to the Shield of the Americas, a Washington-led alliance against narcoterrorism, alongside 13 other countries. The sources do not say whether that alliance would pay for the new units.

Oviedo listed what he calls his results, including the capture of Uruguayan suspect Sebastián Marset and his expulsion to the United States. Oviedo called Marset one of the world’s two biggest traffickers, a claim the sources do not test.

He also cited the arrests of former president Luis Arce and his son Marcelo Arce, who are suspects, not convicted. Former attorney general Roger Mariaca and prosecutor Alberto Zeballos were detained on 30 September over alleged drug links, Brújula Digital reported.

Oviedo warned judges and prosecutors who, he says, shield the criminal network. Mariaca, Zeballos and both Arces are accused or detained, not convicted, and the sources give no reply from them.

What It Means for US Readers

Oviedo says Bolivia already works with US cooperation bodies, so a request for elite units could deepen a security tie. Marset, whom Oviedo says was expelled to the United States, is one reason Bolivia’s drug fight draws US attention.

Travellers to Santa Cruz, Beni and the Brazilian border area should check State Department advisories before they go. Investors in Bolivian debt and mining should note that the government links crime and its prosecutors in public.

Background is in earlier reports on threats against the Paz family, a PCC gang arrest and the Santa Cruz jewellery heist. Another report covers US riot gear for Bolivian police, and the Bolivia hub has more.

What Is Not Known

No US statement on the two units was found, so it is unknown whether Washington has agreed. Oviedo described a proposal made on Tuesday night, not a signed deal.

The cost, the number of officers and the opening dates are not public. Brújula Digital says only Santa Cruz and Beni, while El Deber and Los Tiempos name San Ignacio and San Matías.

The Government Ministry’s own statement could not be opened, so quotes rest on El Deber, Los Tiempos, Opinión and Brújula Digital. Police have not named suspects in the Warnes and La Guardia killings, and the Brazilian attackers’ identity rests on neighbours’ accounts.

Shield of the Americas membership comes from Brújula Digital alone. The same outlet is the only source for US public backing of Paz.

What Comes Next

Police promise new contingents every 45 days, so the first test is whether the next one arrives on time. Any US announcement on funding or training would show whether the elite units are firm.

None of this means US troops or agents will operate in Bolivia, and no source says so. It also does not mean the killings are solved.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Bolivia ask the United States for?

Minister Marco Antonio Oviedo said he asked US cooperation partners on Tuesday night to help install two elite police units. One would sit between San Ignacio de Velasco and San Matías, the other in Beni.

Has the United States agreed?

No US statement was found in the sources reviewed. Oviedo described a proposal, and Washington has not confirmed funding or training in the reports found.

What is Frontera Segura 2.0?

It is the second phase of Bolivia’s Safe Border plan, launched on Wednesday, 21 October, in Santa Cruz. It aims for a permanent police presence on the frontier and territorial control there.

When would the elite units open?

Oviedo told Los Tiempos the units would be installed in just under a year. He said the Santa Cruz unit should be faster because infrastructure already exists in San Ignacio.

Is it safe to travel to Santa Cruz?

Santa Cruz saw three killings in under 24 hours this week, according to Los Tiempos. Travellers should check State Department advice and local news before visiting.

World.title: Honduras Holds 2 Police Agents Over Drugs
World.content:
HONDURAS · SECURITY

Key Facts — What is happening A judge in San Pedro Sula ordered two agents of Honduras’s new anti-extortion police division held on Wednesday, 21 October, on aggravated drug-trafficking charges, and a third agent is wanted.

— Why it matters The case lands inside the DAET, a unit created in May to fight gangs that Washington lists as terrorists, and it tests how clean Honduras’s police partners are.

— The numbers Prosecutors say a raid on 19 October found 114 bags of suspected marijuana and 65 wraps of suspected cocaine, and the first court hearing is set for Monday, 26 October at 10:00 a.m.

— Who is who The DAET is led by police commissioner Jorge Daniel Molina Gálvez, and prosecutors from the Public Ministry’s organised-crime unit, known as FESCCO, bring the case.

— What to watch The hearing on Monday, 26 October in San Pedro Sula, the search for the third agent, and the separate inquiry by the police disciplinary directorate, Didadpol.

— What it means for you For US readers the case shows corruption risk inside a unit that fights Barrio 18, a gang the US lists as a terrorist group, which matters for security cooperation with Honduras.

A judge in San Pedro Sula has ordered two Honduran anti-extortion police agents held on aggravated drug-trafficking charges. A third agent from the same unit is still wanted.

A judge in San Pedro Sula ordered two police agents held in custody on Wednesday, 21 October, on aggravated drug-trafficking charges. A third agent from the same unit has not surrendered and faces an arrest warrant.

The men belong to the DAET, a new Honduran police division created in May to fight extortion and gangs. This Honduras police drug case matters to US readers, since Washington lists the gang Barrio 18 as terrorist.

What Prosecutors Say Happened

The Public Ministry, Honduras’s prosecution service, says police searched a house on Bulevar Mackey in San Pedro Sula on 19 October. It says officers seized 114 small bags of suspected marijuana, 65 wraps of suspected cocaine and several amounts of suspected crack.

Investigators also collected ammunition, magazines, military-style clothing and badges from former police structures, the Public Ministry said. All of the items will be analysed as evidence, and the drugs are described only as suspected.

Prosecutors filed a complaint of aggravated drug trafficking through FESCCO, their special organised-crime unit, against three DAET agents. One of the three also faces a charge of holding prohibited ammunition.

What the Court Decided

Ruy Gabriel Barahona, spokesman of the Judicial Branch, confirmed that a judge ordered custody for two agents. One of them, Ángel Daniel Rodríguez Fuentes, also faces a charge of illegal possession of prohibited ammunition.

Both men surrendered voluntarily after the prosecution filed its complaint, the judiciary said, and arrived at court with other police officers. They are held at the headquarters of the Special Forces Police in Tegucigalpa while the case continues.

The first hearing is set for Monday, 26 October, at 10:00 a.m. in San Pedro Sula. Prosecutors will present their evidence there, and custody is a precaution, not a finding of guilt.

The arrest warrant for the third agent remains in force, the judiciary said. His name has not been released.

What the Police Say

An El Heraldo headline says the DAET chief probed the case for a month and does not rule out a conspiracy. Regional police chief Eduardo Lanza told Proceso Digital the inquiry began with drugs found in a vehicle.

La Prensa reports that DAET authorities say the drugs came from a Los Cabezones gang seizure that the agents allegedly kept unlawfully. The paper also reports that prosecutors are examining whether the drugs were meant to plant evidence on detainees.

The police disciplinary directorate, Didadpol, opened its own inquiry after the arrests of two agents. Security Minister Gerzon Velásquez confirmed the raid and the arrest of two agents, Proceso Digital reported.

On Wednesday morning the regional police chief for the north, Eduardo Lanza, said no officers had been detained. He added that the facilities are police-linked, used as offices or storage; La Prensa reports that the agents lived in the house.

Why the DAET Matters

Honduras created the DAET after closing DIPAMPCO, an earlier police directorate against gangs and organised crime. The National Defence and Security Council ordered it shut after a 21 May raid in Corinto, Omoa, in which five officers died.

The Security Ministry confirmed the new unit on Friday, 29 May, under police commissioner Jorge Daniel Molina Gálvez. Congress had voted on 18 May to treat gangs as terrorist associations and to toughen extortion penalties, Tunota reported.

Earlier anti-gang units failed, said Nelson Castañeda of the civil-society group ASJ, and the DAET must avoid their mistakes. He and the unit’s director both warned about infiltration by criminal intelligence networks, El Heraldo reported.

What It Means for US Readers

The US State Department designated Barrio 18 a foreign terrorist organization on 11 September 2025, with notice published on 24 September. Honduran units that pursue the gang therefore tackle what Washington treats as terrorism.

No US agency is named in this case, and the sources do not say the DAET has US funding. Any security partnership with Honduras still relies on units free of criminal links, so the case will be watched.

Readers can follow related coverage in 80 Honduran soldiers training in Mississippi and Honduran deportees and a US warning. Background is in the guide to Honduras in Latin America and the guide to who runs the economy.

The Honduras hub collects the latest news from the country. San Pedro Sula, where the case is heard, is the country’s industrial centre and the site of its main airport.

What Is Not Known

Reports differ on the second agent’s name, so this article names only Rodríguez Fuentes. The third agent’s identity and whereabouts are not public.

The raid date is unclear: the Public Ministry says 19 October, while the regional police chief spoke of Tuesday. El Heraldo quotes the DAET chief with higher drug counts.

No laboratory result has been published, and the sources do not say where the drugs came from. The agents have not publicly answered the allegations in the reports reviewed, and they are presumed innocent.

What Comes Next

The hearing on Monday, 26 October will show what evidence prosecutors present and whether the judge keeps the two agents in custody. It does not decide guilt, which would need a full trial.

The disciplinary inquiry by Didadpol and the search for the third agent run in parallel. Further complaints against other officers have not been reported.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened in the Honduras police drug case?

A judge in San Pedro Sula held two agents of the DAET police unit on Wednesday, 21 October, on aggravated drug-trafficking charges. A third is wanted.

What is the DAET?

The DAET is the Honduran police division against extortion and terrorist associations, created in May after DIPAMPCO was closed. It is led by commissioner Jorge Daniel Molina Gálvez.

What did police find in the house?

Prosecutors say a 19 October search found 114 bags of suspected marijuana and 65 wraps of suspected cocaine. Crack and ammunition were also found.

When is the next court date?

The first hearing is set for Monday, 26 October, at 10:00 a.m. in San Pedro Sula. Custody is a precaution and does not mean the agents are guilty.

Why does this matter in the United States?

The unit targets gangs such as Barrio 18, which the US lists as a foreign terrorist organization. Clean police partners matter for US security cooperation.

World.title: Bryan Ruiz Named Costa Rica Head Coach After Two Wins as Interim
World.content:
Costa Rica has named former captain Bryan Ruiz head coach of its men’s national team, giving the permanent job to the man who led La Sele on an interim basis this month and tasking him with taking our team back to the World Cup in 2030. The Costa Rican Football Federation (FCRF) announced the appointment today after its Executive Committee met and contract terms were finalized.

The federation said the decision gives continuity to the work Ruiz began in his two matches as interim coach and is intended to consolidate a new stage for the national team. Ruiz, 41, took charge on Sept. 28 after the federation fired Argentine coach Fernando Batista following a run of poor results. In his first match on the bench, Costa Rica beat Nicaragua 3-0, and days later it beat Haiti 2-0 at Estadio Ricardo Saprissa.

Those two wins, with five goals scored and none conceded, kept Costa Rica in League A of the CONCACAF Nations League, the objective the federation had set for the interim period. His record as a coach remains thin. Before October, Ruiz worked as an assistant and in the youth divisions at Liga Deportiva Alajuelense, and he had led the club’s first team in only two games on an emergency basis. The national team is his first permanent post in charge of a senior side.

He will be assisted by former Costa Rica internationals Wílmer López and Christian Bolaños, with Wardy Alfaro also joining the coaching staff, according to the federation. López and Bolaños both represented Costa Rica at World Cups as players. In its statement, the federation said Ruiz was for years one of the leading figures of the national team and wore the captain’s armband with pride. It added that he will now bring that experience, leadership and knowledge of both the domestic and international game to the bench.

As a player, Ruiz was a left-footed attacking midfielder who captained Costa Rica at three consecutive World Cups, in Brazil 2014, Russia 2018 and Qatar 2022. He was the central figure of the 2014 side that reached the quarterfinals, the best finish in Costa Rica’s history.

His club career took him to Twente and PSV Eindhoven in the Netherlands, Fulham in England, Sporting in Portugal and Santos in Brazil before he returned to Alajuelense and retired in 2022. Ruiz inherits a program that is still rebuilding. Costa Rica missed the 2026 World Cup under Mexican coach Miguel Herrera, Batista’s tenure ended after a string of Nations League setbacks, and the team has since slipped in the FIFA ranking.

For the October window, Ruiz had already brought veteran goalkeeper Keylor Navas back into his first squad. His first matches as permanent coach come during the November international window, with away friendlies against Ecuador on Nov. 13 and Argentina on Nov. 17. Those two games will offer the first measure of whether a coach with four matches of senior experience can turn a strong start and deep public goodwill into a team capable of returning Costa Rica to the World Cup.

World.title: Study Finds Costa Rica’s Pesticide Use More Than 10 Times Global Average
World.content:
Costa Rica uses pesticides on its farmland at a rate more than ten times the global average, according to a scientific study that raises new concerns about the potential effects of agricultural chemicals on human health and the environment. The research, published in the September 2026 issue of the scientific journal Environment International, found that pesticide use on Costa Rican cropland averaged 21.91 kilograms of active ingredients per hectare annually.

That compares with a global average of 2.18 kilograms and a Central American average of 7.16 kilograms. The findings highlight our heavy dependence on pesticides, particularly in large-scale banana and pineapple production, two of Costa Rica’s most important agricultural exports.

The study, titled Grounding Pesticide Use Intensity and Hazards with Real-World Data: Toward Correcting Global Models in Tropical Agriculture, was conducted by researchers Soledad Castro-Vargas of the University of Zurich, Santiago Alvarez-Fernandez, an independent researcher in Spain, and Ryan E. Galt of the University of California, Davis.

To determine how much pesticide is used, the researchers examined government import and export records, agricultural production statistics, and information about chemicals approved for use in Costa Rica. They then estimated how those pesticides were distributed across different crops and regions.

Banana plantations recorded the highest estimated use, averaging 78.88 kilograms of pesticide ingredients per hectare annually. Pineapple production followed at 34.07 kilograms, rice at 33.88 kilograms, tomatoes at 32.04 kilograms, and potatoes at 30.42 kilograms. The differences were also apparent across Costa Rica.

Limón, home to extensive banana and pineapple plantations along the Caribbean coast, recorded the highest provincial average at 35.77 kilograms per hectare when farmland and managed pastures were included. Heredia and Cartago followed, while Guanacaste had the lowest estimated levels.

One important distinction involves how pesticide use is calculated. Costa Rica’s Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock has reported a national average of approximately 11 kilograms per hectare, but that figure includes pastures, where pesticide use is much lower. When the researchers included both cropland and managed pastures, their estimate was also approximately 11 kilograms per hectare. The higher figure of 21.91 kilograms applies specifically to cultivated crops.

The research also identified the chemicals most commonly used in Costa Rican agriculture. Mancozeb, a fungicide frequently applied to banana plantations to control fungal diseases, accounted for approximately 36% of the estimated pesticide ingredients used nationally. Other widely used chemicals included glyphosate, diazinon, and ethoprophos.

Beyond the amount of pesticide used, the researchers examined the potential dangers associated with the chemicals. Their findings showed that several health-related concerns, including cancer-causing potential and interference with the body’s hormone systems, did not show statistically significant improvements during the years examined.

The results were particularly troubling for aquatic life. Several measures of potential harm to organisms living in rivers, streams, and other waterways worsened over time, even as some other environmental indicators showed modest improvements. However, the researchers stressed an important limitation. Their study examined the hazardous properties of pesticides, not the actual exposure of individual people or the number of illnesses caused by agricultural chemicals.

The figures were also estimates based on official records and agricultural models, rather than measurements of every pesticide application on individual farms. Nevertheless, the findings challenge the idea that newer agricultural products have consistently made pesticide use less hazardous.

For Costa Rica, the research adds another dimension to a longstanding debate over the environmental costs of intensive agriculture. Costa Rica is internationally recognized for its biodiversity and conservation efforts, but its major agricultural industries continue to rely heavily on chemical treatments to protect crops from pests and disease.

The researchers argue that better reporting of pesticide applications, more detailed information about their use in individual regions, and continued environmental monitoring would help authorities better understand the possible consequences. They also call attention to gaps in scientific knowledge about how agricultural chemicals affect tropical ecosystems, where wildlife and environmental conditions can differ substantially from those in countries where much of the existing research has been conducted.

The study provides a clearer picture of where pesticides are being used most heavily and which chemicals deserve closer examination. It also raises questions about whether current agricultural practices are reducing the potential dangers to people and the environment.

World.title: Will Costa Rica’s New Megaprison Make Life Safer?
World.content:
Leave it to the Frente Amplio (Broad Front) political party to spoil the fiesta. Our sparkling new 34 million dollar megaprison was all ready to be opened. The transfer of the gangbangers and cartel leaders and random violent killers in La Reforma to their new supermax (at least by Tico standards) jail was a done deal. Then the most radical of Costa Rica’s many political parties sued, defending the rights of hardened criminals to not have to endure conditions too hot or uncomfortable.

At this writing the CACCO as it is officially called, for Centro de Alta Contención y Crimen Organizado (High-Security Center and Organized Crime Unit) waits expectantly for its new inhabitants. I am all for putting the worst of the worst in a place where they can no longer control any illicit operations from a jail cell.

Costa Rica has long had a curious mentality toward lawbreakers. Leniency has always been the given. Faith in rehabilitation of the bad guys part of the fabric of crime and punishment. Forgiveness was always an “I’m sorry and I won’t do it again” away. Prisoners are referred to as “Privados de Libertad”, those deprived of liberty. That their actions were what deprived them of liberty in the first place goes unspoken.

Now the pendulum has swung back furiously the other direction. Our president Laura Fernandez made the pilgrimage to El Salvador to tour their famous new megaprison, accompanied by Bukele, the right wing rock star president. The two were accompanied by various officials, all photographed waltzing down the prison corridors like travel agents inspecting a new five star hotel.

The prison in El Salvador is the model for the new one here, albeit with much larger capacity. Which is fitting, given that the crime problem in El Salvador caused by gangs was far greater than anything we have experienced in Costa Rica. The dream of the present government here seems to be that the new prison will bring about change as dramatic as what has happened under Bukele. Build it, fill it and our country will be safer.

There is an important distinction between the criminal elements of our two countries. The MS-13 gangs of El Salvador began among refugees of the long civil war who ended up in the poorer neighborhoods of Los Angeles. By the mid-1990s the gangs had gained notoriety with local and federal law enforcement agencies, and thousands with criminal records were deported back to El Salvador.

Many of the gang members had little previous connection with El Salvador and did not assimilate back into society. Instead they took up locations throughout the country and became a dangerous predatory class. The bulk of their money was made through extortion of local businesses, though they were also involved in human trafficking, and contract killings.

Their influence was much like that of organized crime mobs in the urban US through much of the 20th century. Any place the gangs took up residence became their personal fiefdoms, and they got a piece of any type of financial transaction. When Bukele went after the gangs he throttled the problem at the source.

The difference for Costa Rica is that we are a shipment bridge for international drug transactions, particularly cocaine. The cartels established their territories here over time, relying on force, but also extensive bribery at all levels of law enforcement. There have been a recent number of highly publicized cocaine busts, but even the most optimistic reports from the US Coast Guard and DEA estimate that the amount captured accounts for only about 10 to 15 percent of all coke shipments.

Busting local cartel leaders does not get to the root of the problem. The problem is both the source– the cocaine producers of Colombia, Peru and Bolivia, and the market: Millions of consumers in North America and Europe, all too ready to snort blow and jabber the night away.

Until the unlikely day that there are no more users, the cocaine will flow, and Costa Rica will continue to be a strategic point along the shipment route. The demand is too great and the earnings too lucrative to think that removing those at the top of the chain will solve the problem.

Meanwhile CACCO awaits. Soon it will be full and only time will tell if our new hardline attitude toward organized criminals will make a difference in our overall safety and sanity
