World.title: PM Briceño says Garifuna leaders did not demand apology over population figures during meeting
World.content:
PM Briceño says Garifuna leaders did not demand apology over population figures during meeting

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Prime Minister John Briceño says representatives of the National Garifuna Council did not demand an apology during their recent meeting over his controversial remarks about the size of Belize’s Garifuna population.

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Briceño was asked whether he had apologized to the organization for providing inaccurate population figures in earlier public comments.

“They never did ask for an apology,” the Prime Minister responded.

Briceño said the meeting instead focused on more substantive issues affecting the Garifuna community and efforts to determine how government could address those concerns.

The controversy began after Briceño, during an exchange with Trinidadian soca artist Machel Montano, suggested that Belize’s Garifuna population numbered only approximately 3,000 to 4,000 people.

The figure drew criticism from members of the Garifuna community, who challenged its accuracy and expressed concern about the apparent underestimation of their population.

Briceño subsequently acknowledged the mistake and apologized for the incorrect figures.

National Garifuna Council President Alex Nolberto previously confirmed that the Prime Minister had reached out and acknowledged his error.

The discussions between the government and the council have also involved broader concerns, including cultural preservation, land rights and a proposed Memorandum of Understanding.

Briceño indicated Wednesday that dialogue with the council is continuing and that further consideration is being given to the issues raised by its representatives.

He maintained that the meeting was intended to advance discussions on matters affecting the Garifuna community rather than focus exclusively on the controversy surrounding his remarks.

World.title: Cabinet has still not discussed new cost-of-living relief measures, PM Briceño confirms
World.content:
Cabinet has still not discussed new cost-of-living relief measures, PM Briceño confirms

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Prime Minister John Briceño has confirmed that Cabinet has not yet held substantive discussions on additional measures to ease the rising cost of living, despite mounting pressure on the government to provide further relief to struggling Belizean households.

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Briceño acknowledged that ministers have submitted several proposals for consideration but said Cabinet has not yet had the opportunity to discuss them.

He indicated that discussions on the proposals are expected to begin, although he did not provide a specific timeline for decisions or implementation.

The Prime Minister’s comments come as rising food prices, fuel costs and other household expenses continue to place pressure on Belizean families.

Earlier this month, Briceño acknowledged the need for additional interventions, pointing to existing government programmes intended to help households retain more of their income.

These include educational assistance, expanded free education and adjustments to income tax thresholds.

The government has also introduced electricity relief measures, including an increase in the GST exemption threshold for residential electricity bills from $100 to $200 per month.

However, calls for further action have intensified, with questions also being raised about ministerial allowances and whether elected officials should make financial sacrifices as ordinary Belizeans contend with increasing expenses.

For now, Briceño has not announced any new relief package, leaving Belizeans awaiting Cabinet’s consideration of the proposals already submitted.

World.title: Government still undecided on appealing landmark ruling declaring 2020 states of emergency unconstitutional
World.content:
Government still undecided on appealing landmark ruling declaring 2020 states of emergency unconstitutional

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Prime Minister John Briceño says his government has not yet decided whether it will challenge a landmark Court of Appeal ruling that declared two states of emergency imposed in Belize City in 2020 unconstitutional.

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Briceño said he was still awaiting advice from the Attorney General before determining the government’s next course of action.

“I have not heard yet from the Attorney General,” Briceño said, indicating that he expects to receive an update on the matter by Tuesday.

The Prime Minister’s comments come nearly seven weeks after the Court of Appeal delivered its September 3 judgment, striking down emergency proclamations issued during the height of gang-related violence in Southside Belize City.

According to 7 News’ reporting on the judgment, the appellate court ruled that the emergency declarations and mass detentions carried out under them violated constitutional protections.

The ruling represents a significant legal setback for the use of emergency powers as a crime-fighting strategy, raising questions about the circumstances under which future governments can impose similar measures.

Belize has repeatedly relied on states of emergency to detain suspected gang members without immediately pursuing ordinary criminal charges, arguing that extraordinary measures are necessary to address escalating violence.

However, critics have maintained that such operations undermine fundamental constitutional rights and expose individuals to detention without sufficient judicial safeguards.

Briceño did not indicate whether the government intends to seek further review before the Caribbean Court of Justice, leaving the future of any legal challenge uncertain.

World.title: PM Briceño celebrates historic European flight, says tourists have been avoiding Belize over difficult connections
World.content:
PM Briceño celebrates historic European flight, says tourists have been avoiding Belize over difficult connections

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Prime Minister John Briceño says the announcement of direct air service between Germany and Belize represents a major breakthrough after successive governments spent years attempting to attract a European airline.

Speaking on Wednesday, Briceño welcomed the agreement with Discover Airlines, describing it as an exciting development that could open an important new tourism market.

He explained that many European tourists have expressed interest in visiting Belize but have instead chosen competing destinations because of the difficulty and time involved in reaching the country.

According to Briceño, some European travelers currently face journeys extending over two days when connecting through other international airports.

The new service is expected to make Belize substantially more accessible to visitors from Germany and other European countries.

Briceño said several administrations had attempted to secure such a connection without success, making the agreement an important milestone for Belize’s tourism industry.

According to the airline’s October 20 announcement, flights will begin on December 16, 2027, operating on Thursdays and Sundays until mid-April 2028.

The service will connect Frankfurt, one of Europe’s major aviation hubs, with the Philip Goldson International Airport.

Discover Airlines will become the first European carrier to introduce the scheduled service, giving Belize an opportunity to strengthen its presence in a tourism market that has traditionally relied on connections through North America and other international gateways.

Briceño expressed optimism that the route will attract additional visitors, encourage investment and create opportunities for businesses throughout Belize’s tourism sector.

World.title: PM Briceño defends US$2 million Discover Airlines guarantee: ‘That’s the rule of the game’
World.content:
PM Briceño defends US$2 million Discover Airlines guarantee: ‘That’s the rule of the game’

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Prime Minister John Briceño has defended his government’s decision to commit approximately US$2 million in financial guarantees to secure direct air service between Europe and Belize, arguing that the country had little choice if it wanted to attract the airline.

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Briceño was asked whether he was comfortable with the financial commitment associated with the agreement with Discover Airlines.

“That’s the rule of the game,” the Prime Minister responded.

He explained that the airline would not have agreed to introduce the service without the government’s commitment.

“They would not come if we don’t sign on to it,” Briceño said, arguing that Belize must weigh the cost of attracting the airline against the economic opportunities the route could generate.

Tourism Minister Anthony Mahler previously confirmed that the arrangement involves approximately US$2 million over three years, with the guarantee intended to reduce the airline’s financial exposure as it introduces the new destination.

The arrangement is understood to be a revenue guarantee, rather than a straightforward payment for the airline to operate flights.

Briceño expressed confidence that the resulting increase in European visitors would ultimately justify the government’s investment.

Discover Airlines, part of the Lufthansa Group, has officially announced that its Frankfurt-to-Belize service will begin December 16, 2027, operating twice weekly through mid-April 2028.

The government is banking on increased visitor spending, tourism employment and access to the European market to offset the potential cost of the guarantee.

However, the amount Belize will ultimately be required to pay under the arrangement will depend on the agreement’s terms and the airline’s financial performance.

World.title: PM Briceño says removing Ambassador Alexis Rosado from ICJ case would not be in Belize’s best interest despite active rape case
World.content:
PM Briceño says removing Ambassador Alexis Rosado from ICJ case would not be in Belize’s best interest despite active rape case

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Prime Minister John Briceño has defended his government’s decision to retain Ambassador Alexis Rosado as part of Belize’s legal team before the International Court of Justice (ICJ), despite the serious criminal charges against the veteran diplomat.

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Briceño acknowledged that the allegations against Rosado could raise concerns but maintained that removing him at this critical stage of Belize’s territorial cases would not serve the country’s interests.

“I’m not in any way trying to minimize the severity of the accusations,” Briceño said, emphasizing that Rosado remains innocent until proven guilty under Belizean law.

The Prime Minister pointed to the approaching ICJ hearings involving Guatemala in February and Honduras in March, arguing that continuity and experience are essential as Belize prepares to defend its sovereignty.

He noted that Rosado has spent decades working on the territorial disputes alongside Ambassador Assad Shoman.

“I don’t think it would be in the best interest of the nation to be able to remove him at this time,” Briceño said.

Rosado faces criminal charges arising from allegations of rape, sexual assault and aggravated assault, which he is contesting in court. His trial has experienced delays, including changes to his legal representation.

During court proceedings earlier this month, it was confirmed that Jamaican attorney Deborah Martin had been retained as his lead counsel.

Rosado has continued performing his diplomatic responsibilities while the criminal proceedings remain unresolved.

The ICJ’s official records identify Rosado as Belize’s Co-Agent in the case involving Honduras and the Sapodilla Cayes.

Briceño described the timing of the criminal proceedings as unfortunate but insisted that the government’s priority remains presenting the strongest possible legal case in defence of Belize’s territorial integrity.

World.title: PM Briceño leaves door open to US military operations in Belize as security talks advance
World.content:
PM Briceño leaves door open to US military operations in Belize as security talks advance

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Prime Minister John Briceño has not ruled out the possibility of American military personnel conducting joint security operations in Belize, saying his government is prepared to consider proposals that serve the country’s national security interests.

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday following an event associated with Belize’s US$125 million Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC) compact with the United States, Briceño revealed that he had briefly discussed security cooperation with the United States Ambassador and a senior military official.

He said he has instructed senior Belizean security officials, including the Chief Executive Officer in the Ministry of National Security, the Commander of the Belize Defence Force and the Commandant of the Belize Coast Guard, to hold further technical discussions with their American counterparts.

“We know we need help,” Briceño acknowledged, pointing to Belize’s need for additional equipment, intelligence and training to confront potential threats from powerful Mexican drug cartels.

The Prime Minister was specifically asked whether Belize would permit foreign troops to operate on its territory, particularly as neighboring countries debate the implications of expanded American military involvement.

He declined to make a definitive commitment, saying the technical discussions must first take place before government determines what arrangements would be acceptable.

Briceño maintained that Belize is prepared to cooperate on measures that benefit both the country and the wider region.

The discussions follow regional efforts to strengthen security cooperation under the US-backed Shield of the Americas initiative, which addresses transnational organized crime and other security threats.

For now, the Prime Minister has not announced any agreement authorizing American combat operations or the deployment of foreign troops on Belizean soil.

World.title: PSU responds to PM on Ministerial allowances: Accuses government of politicizing poverty, says ministers’ allowances are being used to justify vote-buying
World.content:
PSU responds to PM on Ministerial allowances: Accuses government of politicizing poverty, says ministers’ allowances are being used to justify vote-buying

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Public Service Union (PSU) President Dean Flowers has accused the Briceño administration of perpetuating a culture of political patronage in which vulnerable Belizeans are forced to depend on elected representatives for basic necessities, arguing that the government’s justification for ministerial allowances exposes deeper failures in the country’s social assistance system.

Speaking with Breaking Belize News, Flowers expanded on concerns raised in a recent PSU statement, which warned that using politicians’ personal assistance to address public needs creates a system of indebtedness, unequal access to assistance and political dependency.

The controversy follows comments by Prime Minister John Briceño, who defended ministerial allowances on the grounds that elected officials regularly receive requests for assistance with medical expenses, funerals, education and other emergencies.

Briceño said ministers frequently give away their allowances and contribute additional money from their own pockets, suggesting that eliminating those benefits would reduce their ability to assist struggling constituents.

However, the PSU’s recent statement questioned whether such assistance should depend on the personal discretion of politicians rather than established government programmes.

The union warned that when assistance is distributed through politicians, recipients can feel personally indebted to those who provide it. It argued that the arrangement encourages political patronage and creates unequal conditions for candidates who do not have access to similar financial resources.

The PSU also raised concerns about the absence of published eligibility criteria, transparent records of assistance provided and independent mechanisms through which citizens can challenge decisions to deny them help.

Instead, the union proposed transparent, institutionalized emergency healthcare and burial assistance programmes that would provide support according to citizens’ needs rather than their political connections.

Its position was summarized in the statement: “Compassion should be policy, not patronage.”

Flowers reinforced those concerns during his interview, but stressed that the PSU’s position should not be misrepresented as a personal confrontation with the Prime Minister or a demand that ministers immediately surrender their allowances.

“The PSU, in essence, said, fix the system. If the roof is leaking, don’t pat yourself on the back because you have people collecting the water in buckets,” Flowers said.

He argued that the Prime Minister’s explanation inadvertently highlighted a much larger problem: the inability of existing government institutions to adequately support vulnerable Belizeans.

According to Flowers, people should not have to visit politicians’ homes, sometimes late at night, seeking assistance to bury relatives, purchase medication or obtain medical treatment.

He maintained that such arrangements undermine citizens’ dignity and create conditions in which politicians can exploit economic hardship for political advantage.

“It is politicizing people’s poverty. It is taking advantage of people’s needs instead of creating a system that is fair, that is open, that is transparent, that people could tap into when they are vulnerable and in need. This is effectively buying votes,” Flowers charged.

He questioned why the government continues to highlight improvements in employment and economic performance while acknowledging that ministers face persistent requests from constituents unable to meet basic expenses.

Flowers argued that the reliance on politicians for assistance is evidence of shortcomings in healthcare, social protection and economic policy that cannot be sustainably addressed through political handouts.

He also challenged Briceño to provide a comprehensive accounting of the $7.2 million that Flowers said is allocated annually to elected representatives through constituency development funding.

“Report to us how you are spending that $7.2 million annually, you and your 30 colleagues in the House,” Flowers demanded.

The PSU president recalled an earlier commitment he attributed to Briceño that the Auditor General would provide annual reports on the use of those funds.

He questioned why ministers would need to justify retaining their personal allowances for charitable purposes if separate taxpayer-funded resources were already available to address constituency needs.

Briceño has rejected allegations that constituency development funds are intended to buy political loyalty, maintaining that they allow area representatives from both major political parties to respond quickly to community needs.

Flowers nevertheless maintained that assistance administered through individual politicians creates an inherently unequal system, particularly when some representatives have access to public resources while others must depend on private financing.

He argued that such arrangements also reinforce the need for campaign finance reform.

When asked whether the PSU was recommending that ministerial allowances be eliminated and redirected to the Ministry of Human Development, Flowers rejected that interpretation.

“I’m not here to say that they should cut their allowances,” he explained.

Instead, he suggested that the compensation packages of ministers should be independently assessed to determine whether their salaries and allowances are justified.

If those benefits form part of a reasonable compensation package, Flowers argued, ministers are entitled to use the money for themselves and their families. The government’s responsibility, however, is to ensure that assistance for vulnerable citizens is provided through properly administered public programmes.

He called for a more accessible and transparent social assistance system, improved healthcare, living wages and economic policies that reduce poverty rather than perpetuating political dependency.

Flowers also urged Belizeans to reconsider the expectation that elected representatives should personally provide for their constituents.

“Nobody is elected to take care of nobody,” he said, arguing that politicians should instead create conditions in which citizens can become economically independent.

The PSU president emphasized that the union’s criticisms were not motivated by partisan politics or personal hostility toward Briceño, but by concerns about a system that has become deeply institutionalized in Belize.

He maintained that meaningful reform requires political will, effective oversight and a fundamental change in the relationship between citizens and elected representatives.

“We have to empower people. Let’s give people an opportunity to thrive, an opportunity to feel good about themselves,” Flowers said.

The union’s position is that vulnerable Belizeans should have access to assistance as a matter of public policy, rather than having to depend on the goodwill or political interests of individual ministers.

World.title: Water pressure
World.content:
Addressing a Jamaica Observer Press Club on Wednesday, Water Minister Matthew Samuda (left) acknowledges the public’s concerns about higher water bills, while NWC Board Chairman Michael Shaw said the utility needs sufficient revenue to keep operating.Naphtali Junior

WATER Minister Matthew Samuda and National Water Commission (NWC) officials are defending the utility’s proposed 51 per cent tariff increase, arguing that rising operating costs, ageing infrastructure, and repeated droughts have made higher revenue necessary to maintain and improve water supply.

Speaking at a Jamaica Observer Press Club on Wednesday, Samuda acknowledged the public’s concerns about higher bills, but argued that the country can no longer postpone major repairs to its water system, while NWC Board Chairman Michael Shaw said the utility needs sufficient revenue to keep operating.

“If we could have asked for one per cent and been okay we would have asked for one per cent. No politician on the planet Earth is interested in increasing the cost of living. This is a necessary step to resolve long-standing issues in our water sector,” Samuda said.

He said Jamaica is “in a race against time” to replace ageing infrastructure and improve the reliability of water supplies, warning that the country’s long history of inadequate investment has left the utility facing mounting challenges.

In the meantime, Shaw noted that the NWC needs to be able to meet the public’s expectations while maintaining its daily operations.

“We need to continue the operations from one day to the next. Our citizenry is expecting that when they go home and turn on that tap, there’s water in it. There can’t be any worse feeling. So if you were to measure when you go home and you turn on [the switch] and there’s no light versus turn on and there’s no water, I think it’s a no-brainer, and as such, this tariff is going to right-size our position to ensure that we continue to deliver, as is our commitment to the citizens of Jamaica,” he said.

Samuda said the proposed increase must be viewed against the economic and environmental challenges Jamaica has faced since the last interim tariff adjustment granted in 2019.

He said the COVID-19 pandemic caused significant revenue losses when hotels and other commercial customers shut down, while disruptions to supply chains and rising prices subsequently increased the cost of operating the utility.

He added that droughts in 2022, 2023 and 2025; along with Hurricane Beryl and Tropical Storm Rafael in 2024; alongside Hurricane Melissa last year, further affected the NWC’s operations and revenue.

The minister argued that the utility continued to incur expenses even when drought reduced the amount of water available to sell.

He also pointed to rising energy costs and changes to staff salaries, saying the NWC’s energy costs were now close to 50 per cent higher than in 2019, while salaries had doubled over the same period.

“Nobody plans for three out of your five worst droughts ever during this period. Nobody plans for the worst El Nino in 200 years, which is what this is becoming, and… when we talk about these things people say, ‘El Nino? Whatever.’ But the last time we had an El Nino like this it triggered global famine. This is not a normal weather phenomenon that we are going through,” he added.

Samuda argued that these pressures had been absorbed while the NWC’s tariffs remained unchanged, but said the utility could no longer defer essential repairs to its ageing infrastructure.

He noted that the NWC had never replaced even one per cent of its asset base in a single year during Jamaica’s independent history — a shortfall he said had contributed to the deterioration of pipes and other infrastructure.

He pointed to repeated breaks in a major pipeline at Coral Gardens in Montego Bay, which he said had broken six times in one month and required a $170-million intervention to safeguard the main supply line serving the city.

“The reality is the capital replacement ratio of a utility is not intended to fall below one per cent of total capital replacement being done on an annual basis. In our independent life that has never happened…we’ve never replaced one per cent of the asset base of the water commission in a single year. We’ve never gotten close, and that is the utility standard globally. So what you have happening in the middle of that seven-year period is also the collapse of ageing infrastructure. I should be changing the third generation of those lines now, not the first generation in that way,” he said.

Samuda said the combination of ageing infrastructure, climate-related pressures, and decades of inadequate investment have left Jamaica with urgent work to do.

“Ultimately, it is our responsibility to do now what should have been done a long time ago. We will do it. And we can have confidence that at the back end of our work and our investment in these varying programmes, they will have the confidence; and I assure them in the coming years we’ll have other things to complain about other than potable water in the pipes,” he said.

The proposed 51 per cent increase has not been approved by the Office of Utilities Regulation (OUR), which is to review the NWC’s application.

Furthermore, Acting NWC President Kevin Kerr separately told the Jamaica Observer that the application includes a significantly lower proposed increase for the utility’s lowest consumers, but said the details could not yet be released because the OUR had not reviewed the application.

World.title: Gully bank relocation
World.content:
From left: K2 developer Richard Lake; Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness; developer Michael Lake; and Phillip Paulwell, Member of Parliament for Kingston Eastern and Port Royal, cut the ribbon to the development. At back is Delano Seiveright, state minister in the Ministry of Industry, Investment and Commerce.(Photo: Andrew Holness on X)

AN initiative by the Government to relocate people whose houses are situated on gully banks, and who are often affected by adverse weather events, is to be piloted in four communities across the Corporate Area.

The disclosure was made by Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness on Wednesday, during his address at the official opening and ribbon-cutting ceremony of the K2 housing development in downtown Kingston.

Although the timeline of the pilot’s execution was not disclosed, Holness said the project will facilitate the construction of new abodes for people who will be relocated, or the provision of grants for them to source other spaces to call home.

One of the communities of concern mentioned by Holness was the flood-prone Burger Gully, situated in the Kingston Eastern constituency.

“We will be selecting maybe four communities across the Corporate Area to start the pilot project to have persons who are living on the gully banks, particularly those that are at risk of an epiphenomenal weather event, to help them to move from the gully banks. We cannot continue this unsafe practice… that must come to an end,” Holness said.

Member of Parliament for Kingston Eastern and Port Royal Phillip Paulwell, who was also at the function, had disclosed in August that close to 150 residents of Burger Gully had signalled their willingness to relocate.

The flooding of the gully, an informal settlement also called 17 1/2 Mountain View Avenue, has been an ongoing problem, but worsened last year as sections of the gully which runs through the community were damaged by flood waters.

At that time, Paulwell said lands were identified in the communities of Mountain View and Rockfort to facilitate the relocation exercise, but a response was being awaited from minister with responsibility for works Robert Morgan.

Holness maintained Wednesday that the issue of communities which are currently irregularly settled “must come to an end”, but underscored that “the success of any government policy is dependent upon the government’s ability… to do what it says it’s going to do”.

“In my own constituency I have demonstrated to the people there how the Government can effectively do a relocation. In the best circumstances, relocation is always disruptive. In the best circumstances, persons are going to feel traumatised by relocation. No one wants to have their house uprooted, their furniture taken and destroyed. Nobody wants to have to move from where they have made their life,” said Holness, who is Member of Parliament for St Andrew West Central.

According to Holness, the National Works Agency will also test a programme that will reclaim the reservations [of buildings] 20 feet away from the gullies in Kingston.

“Whenever I speak like this, immediately everybody starts to get worried [that,] ‘Boy, the Government going to come throw me off [my land].’ That’s not what the Government wants to do. The Government has a right in law to, for the public good, have persons relocate. But the relocation must be done in such a way that the people who are relocated are made no worse off,” Holness said.

The K2 development, located in Bournemouth Gardens, Kingston 2, is a 10-storey residence featuring 119 units. It was developed by Sherbourne Limited, led by Michael and Richard Lake.

World.title: Morgan urges patience amid rehabilitation of Seaview Drive corridor in Lucea
World.content:
Robert Morgan, Minister with responsibility for Works

HANOVER, Jamaica — Noting that a permanent fix has been identified for the long-standing road issues along the heavily trafficked Seaview Drive corridor in Lucea, Hanover, Minister with responsibility for Works, Robert Nesta Morgan, is urging residents, motorists, and tourism stakeholders to remain patient as rehabilitation work gets underway.

The critical arterial thoroughfare serves as a main route into Lucea and a major connector for commuters travelling between Montego Bay and Negril, carrying an estimated 15,000 vehicles daily.

“I just want to ask the tourism interests, residents most importantly, and the business sector — please, I’m asking you to be considerate and patient. We know the challenges, we understand what you’ve been through, we know about the two-hour traffic jams, but we have found a solution, and we’re trying to work with our contractor to implement the solution as quickly as possible,” urged Morgan.

The road is scheduled to be fixed under the Shared Prosperity through Accelerated Improvement to Road Network (SPARK) Programme.

Morgan made the appeal while speaking to journalists on Wednesday afternoon following a site tour of the area. The Hanover leg of the tour followed an earlier inspection of flood-prone areas in neighbouring St James.

Accompanying the minister were technical officers from the National Works Agency (NWA); representatives from the main contractor, China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC) Limited; Member of Parliament for Hanover Western, Heatha Miller-Bennett; and Member of Parliament for Hanover Eastern, Andrea Purkiss.

The deteriorating roadway, which has undergone multiple temporary repairs in recent years, has been severely compromised by poor drainage, rising sea levels, and coastal impacts from Hurricane Melissa in October 2025.

Ackowledging the persistent disruption, Morgan noted that the corridor — which forms part of the primary North Coast Highway — has “proven very challenging and has caused significant inconvenience to both residents and business operators alike.”

“The government made the decision a while back to repair it, and we were going to use a $30 million allocation to concrete it, but then we looked at the extent of the challenge and we decided to put it under the SPARK programme,” explained Morgan.

Providing a brief update on the technical progress made to date following the start of work a few weeks ago, the minister outlined the scope of the ongoing works.

“Currently, we have done over 40 meters of pipes, and we have a significant amount of pipe work to go as we have to replace the pipes that are old and are asbestos pipes. Four hundred meters of concrete; we’re going to be doing sidewalks as well as drains,” advised Morgan.

— Anthony Lewis

World.title: Progress made on lots earmarked for Cooper’s Pen residents
World.content:
Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness (second left) in dialogue with Cooper’s Pen resident Debbie Lewis (second right) during a tour of the community. Looking on are (from left) minister of state in the Office of the Prime Minister Senator Abka Fitz-Henley; Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett; and Member of Parliament for Trelawny Northern Tova Hamilton. (Photo: Horace Hines)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — The procurement of amenities, including water for the lots set aside for displaced residents of Cooper’s Pen, has begun, Prime Minister Andrew Holness said Wednesday.

“We have completed the survey of the land, so the land is now divided up into lots and we have started the procurement of the services to put in place the roads, the water and other basic amenities and so the residents will have access to that,” Holness said.

The prime minister shared the update while speaking at the opening ceremony of the Kingston 2 development in downtown Kingston on Wednesday.

Around 20 homes found to be illegally occupied by residents in Cooper’s Pen Trelawny, based on a court ruling, were demolished in an early morning exercise on August 11, leaving dozens of families without shelter.

READ: ‘Devastating’ demolition

The controversial demolition prompted social assistance from the government, including the provision of tents and the procurement of lots for qualifying families to purchase.

Acknowledging that relocation under any circumstances is, at best, disruptive, Holness said,

“In the best circumstances, persons are going to feel traumatised by relocation. No one wants to have their house uprooted, their furniture taken and destroyed. Nobody wants to have to move from where they have made their life. And I wish to use this platform to say to the people of Cooper’s Pen that we understand this.”

However, the prime minister emphasised that any land utilised in the relocation of residents of Cooper’s Pen will be paid for outright.

“I repeat as I did when I visited the people of Cooper’s Pen in August, it will not be free. So nobody should have that in their minds that the land will be just given freely.”

Instead, Holness said, the government will provide various modalities for residents to get fair and reasonable access, either through outright purchase, lease or other forms of contractual arrangement.

Holness also reiterated that previously announced $9.9 million relocation grants for the affected residents are not compensatory, emphasising that the government would not use taxpayers’ dollars to compensate anyone for an act that was unlawful.

READ: Displaced Cooper’s Pen residents receive humanitarian grants

“What we will do, however, which I think all Jamaicans would agree with, is that we should assist with the relocation exercise.”

Noting that the government is moving forward with an emphasis on dialogue, Holness urged the Cooper’s Pen residents not to be swayed by misinformation but to be led by the respective government agencies.

World.title: NWC seeks 51% hike
World.content:
Acting president of National Water Commission Kevin Kerr (left) speaks during Tuesday’s sitting of the Public Accounts Committee as permanent secretary in the Ministry of Water, Environment and Climate Change Wayne Robertson listens. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

The Office of Utilities Regulation (OUR) will decide within 10 days whether to accept a National Water Commission (NWC) application for a tariff review which could pave the way for higher water and sewerage rates.

The OUR confirmed Tuesday in a release that it received the application on Friday, October 16, covering the five-year period from 2026/27 to 2030/31.

The regulator said it would first assess whether the application meets its requirements and may request additional information from the NWC before deciding whether to formally accept it for review.

The development comes as the NWC seeks a 51 per cent increase in water and sewerage rates amid worsening revenue collection and rising expenses.

The utility wants to raise its annual revenue from about $40 billion to $60 billion to cover operating costs and critical investments over the next five years, while noting it owes the Government approximately $21 billion in General Consumption Tax (GCT).

The disclosures were made by NWC officials on Tuesday during a sitting of the Public Accounts Committee (PAC), where the utility’s unpaid bills and financial difficulties came under scrutiny.

Acting NWC President Kevin Kerr told the committee that the proposed increase was included in a tariff application submitted to the OUR last Friday and noted that the commission is awaiting approval from the regulator.

“So what our submission includes is a 51 per cent increase, and there are some scenarios involved if that is not provided; we will have to revise our investment plan, adjust with the determination made at the end of the process and, as usual, the public will be required to participate in a more consultative process by the OUR over the review period,” Kerr said.

Chief financial officer at the NWC Fabian Christie told the committee that the request reflected the utility’s financial challenges.

“The fact is that our revenues have worsened in terms of paying from our customers, and also the fact that we would require a tariff increase, because our expenses have been increasing dramatically,” Christie told the committee.

He also pointed to the impact of natural disasters and worsening droughts on the commission’s finances. Christie said these events could reduce the utility’s revenue by between 10 and 15 per cent in a given year, depending on their severity.

The proposed increase comes against the background of a sharp rise in the NWC’s unpaid bills.

PAC Chairman Julian Robinson, referring to the Auditor General’s findings, said the commission’s payables rose from $10.6 billion in the 2016/17 financial year to $33.2 billion in 2025/26.

The report also found that the NWC’s net receivables — money owed to the utility — stood at $4.6 billion as at March 2026.

Christie told the committee that the $21-billion owed in GCT accounted for the largest share of the NWC’s $33.2 billion in payables. He explained that the commission withholds GCT when it is billed by suppliers and is expected to pass that tax on to the Government.

Christie also confirmed that the money was being used to support the utility’s day-to-day cash needs.

He revealed that the remaining approximately $12 billion in payables includes approximately $6 billion owed to Central Wastewater Treatment Company, which treats much of the sewage from Kingston and parts of St Catherine at the Soapberry facility. The other roughly $6 billion is owed to contractors and suppliers.

Christie acknowledged that the outstanding payments were affecting the commission’s ability to carry out work.

He gave an approximate breakdown of some payments owed to contractors and suppliers, saying about $1.3 billion was between zero and 30 days overdue, $400 million between 30 and 60 days, $500 million between 60 and 90 days, and $1.6 billion outstanding for more than 90 days.

The proposed tariff increase is not the only measure being pursued to improve the NWC’s finances. Kerr said reducing non-revenue water was a priority.

He said the commission had previously undertaken reduction projects in Kingston, St Andrew and Portmore, and was in the final stage of procurement for an islandwide programme, adding that the NWC hopes to select a bidder or bidders by the end of the current financial period.

The planned programme would be rolled out in stages, beginning in areas including Spanish Town, Old Harbour, May Pen, Mandeville, Montego Bay, Negril, Lucea, Ocho Rios, and Port Antonio, before further work in Kingston and Portmore.

Kerr said the long-term target was to reduce non-revenue water to 30 per cent islandwide within 11 years as the current level averages between 70 and 73 per cent.

The NWC’s financial position was also a concern for Robinson, who questioned how the utility would improve its cash flow beyond seeking higher tariffs. He pointed to the growth in payables and the amount owed to suppliers, while raising the need to reduce losses and improve the collection of money owed to the commission.

Christie said the NWC was working on a plan to improve its working capital management, which he expects to submit to the board at the start of next year. He said the effort would need to improve the amount of cash available to meet the utility’s obligations.

Furthermore, Kerr said, the tariff application was tied to an investment plan designed to ensure that financing could be secured for priority projects. He noted that the NWC received an interim tariff in 2019, before the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 eroded its cash flow.

World.title: $2b reasons for flexi-work
World.content:
A screen shot of a section of the Ministry of National Security and Peace submission to Parliament’s Economy amd Production Committee last Wednesday.

JAMAICA’S approximately 114,000 public servants could save nearly $2 billion annually in transportation costs if more of them are allowed to work remotely under flexi-work arrangements.

This point was emphasised by representatives of the Ministry of National Security and Peace during their appearance last Wednesday before Parliament’s Economy and Production Committee to discuss the progress of flex-work arrangements in Jamaica.

A PowerPoint presentation from the ministry’s team, which was shared with the media afterwards, painted what it called the “big picture” involving public sector workers and the costs associated with their daily commute.

It shows that it costs between $12,000 and $24,000 weekly for each public servant to get to and from work.

With vacation and other days off, it is estimated that each public servant spends between $456,000 and $912,000 annually to get to work.

For all public servants combined, the annual figure is between $1.3 billion and $2.7 billion.

The document argued that if public sector employees were allowed to work from home two days each week, they would each save between $4,800 and $9,600.

Across the entire public service, workers would collectively keep between $547 million and $1.9 billion in their pockets annually.

In terms of the impact at the ministry level, the document showed that 196 or 52 per cent of its 374 employees reside in St Catherine; 160 or 43 per cent live in Kingston and rural St Andrew; and 18 or five per cent live in rural parishes.

It emphasised that each of these workers is spending between $12,000 and $24,000 every week to get to and from work.

The ministry said its embrace of flexi-work arrangements is in response to fuel-price pressures and is aimed at modernising work and strengthening public sector resilience.

The security ministry’s team underscored that more people working from home meant an overall smaller fuel bill.

The document referenced a study which shows that 10 minutes of creeping or idling in traffic burns between 300 and 500 millilitres or more than one to two cups of petrol.

Hourly idling while stuck in gridlock sees an average car wasting 0.5 litres to 1.3 litres of fuel per hour, while larger vehicles burn between 1.5 litres and 2.5 litres.

The ministry team cited the negative effects of gridlock on the economy, climate change, productivity, and mental wellness.

It referenced a 1965 World Bank appraisal which described the Kingston–Spanish Town corridor as “the most heavily travelled highway in Jamaica”.

The ministry noted that in 2008 then Minister of Transport Mike Henry indicated that motorists were taking eight times longer on typical journeys as he pointed to the economic cost of congestion

In 2023, Jamaicans were reportedly spending 90 minutes or 40 per cent of working hours daily in traffic.

This is according to a United Nations Jamaica/UWI Department of Economics panel discussion titled ‘The Economics of Congestion’.

It described the time lost as a massive cost for a small island developing state with enormous economic implications that could affect people’s psychological and physiological well-being.

The ministry said it was making the case for action now on flexi-work arrangement having considered the mental wellness of employees, national cost pressures, workforce realities, and public sector modernisation which together strengthen the case for a Government of Jamaica-wide approach.

In terms of the mental health toll, the document cited an international study of January 2025 published in the Makara Journal of Health Research which stated that a significant proportion of workers experienced stress from their commuting routines.

The study found that approximately 74.5 per cent of workers reported that commuting had a detrimental effect on their mental health, while 82.1 per cent experienced mental fatigue which directly impacted their ability to concentrate and perform effectively at work.

The security ministry said the overall approach is for a structured, phased and monitored Government-led flexible work arrangement framework, informed by its experience.

It said eligibility should be transparent, role-based and subject to operational requirements, not a universal entitlement, and argued that the roll-out should be phased in.

The security ministry pointed to positives such as reduced commuting stress and greater autonomy which, it said, can support productive time and work-life balance.

Additionally, it said flexible work can support talent retention, inclusion and recruitment in a changing workforce.

The ministry said it also maintains operating capacity during fuel shortages, natural disasters, and transport disruptions.

Potential savings include transport, toll, fuel, maintenance, and in-office support resources, alongside reduced absenteeism.

World.title: Twinkle Brothers honoured on home turf
World.content:
Councillor for the Falmouth Division Garth Wilkinson (left) shares a light moment with Twinkle Brothers band member Ralston Grant and his wife Della following the Trelawny Municipal Corporation, in collaboration with the Jamaica Cultural Development Commission, National Heroes’ Day Civic and Awards Ceremony in Falmouth on Monday.

FALMOUTH, Trelawny — There was a flood of emotions as reggae musicians Ralston and Norman Grant, of the Twinkle Brothers, Falmouth natives, were recognised for their contribution to Jamaican music at a National Heroes’ Day awards ceremony in historic Water Square in the parish.

Norman is currently on tour, but for Ralston, the occasion held special significance, as decades ago the siblings operated a record shop almost on the exact spot where the awards ceremony was held, long before their music took them to audiences around the globe.

The recognition came through the Trelawny Municipal Corporation, in collaboration with the Jamaica Cultural Development Commission (JCDC), during its 2026 National Heroes’ Day Civic and Awards Ceremony.

Reflecting on the moment, Ralston said the honour was particularly meaningful because it was his first award in their native Trelawny, despite receiving international recognition for the band’s musical achievements since they started out in 1962.

“It means everything, you know, because I’ve never got one from Trelawny before,” he said.

The musician recalled the brothers’ early accomplishments in the Jamaica Festival Song Competition in 1970, where they placed third behind winner Hopeton Lewis and the Jamaicans.

Their musical journey also includes performances before former Governor General Sir Clifford Campbell during an era when their talent was gaining recognition at home.

The citation accompanying the award praised Norman and Ralston for their outstanding contribution to Jamaican music, cultural heritage, and the country’s representation on the international stage.

It also traced their beginnings on how they fashioned their own musical instruments, demonstrating the ingenuity and determination that would underpin their careers that have spanned more than six decades, with an extensive catalogue of albums and singles.

Through their commitment to independent music production, conscious reggae and roots culture, the brothers helped preserve the tradition of live-band reggae while introducing Jamaican sounds to audiences beyond the island.

Their collaboration with Polish group Trebunie-Tutki was also highlighted as an example of their ability to bridge cultural divides through music.

Despite spending more than four decades living largely overseas, Ralston maintains ties to Jamaica, travelling between the island and California, with his wife Della.

The Twinkle Brothers boast an extensive catalogue of songs which include

Faith Can Move Mountains, Never Get Burn, Jahoviah, Since I Threw the Comb Away, Give Rasta Praise, Rasta Pon Top, Enter Zion, among many others.

World.title: Jamaica braces for cyber stress test
World.content:
JAMAICA’s ability to withstand and recover from major cyberattacks will be put to the test later this month when the Jamaica Cyber Incident Response Team (JaCIRT) stages a national exercise — CyberXJM26 — aimed at identifying weaknesses in the country’s cybersecurity defences and strengthening its response capabilities.

Scheduled for October 28 and 29, the exercise seeks to provide the first full test of the country’s ability to coordinate its response to a major cyber incident.

“CyberXjm26 puts national readiness to a public test, showing how well agencies, security forces, and the private sector can coordinate during an incident, identifying gaps that can be fixed before a real one,” JaCIRT director Lieutenant Colonel Godphey Sterling told the Jamaica Observer during a recent interview.

“The aim is to cut the number of attacks that succeed and to recover quickly when one does,” he added.

Dubbed Operation Sargasso Surge, the exercise seeks to simulate a single, escalating cyber incident, starting with minor activity before progressing through serious disruptions to a multi-sector national crisis.

During the exercise participants will investigate incidents, solve challenges, and make decisions under pressure. The initiative is designed to test existing procedures, strengthen communication and collaboration, and identify weaknesses that need to be addressed before an actual emergency.

It will bring together representatives from government ministries, departments and agencies, private-sector organisations, critical infrastructure operators, financial institutions, telecommunications providers, academic institutions, and other stakeholders. Activities will also extend to schools, universities, cybersecurity enthusiasts and professional incident-response teams.

The initiative forms part of activities planned for National Cybersecurity Awareness Month, observed this October under the theme ‘One Nation, Cyber Strong’. The month-long programme of events includes lectures, webinars, in-person sessions, a social media awareness campaign, and a cyber careers symposium. A national cyber exposé, scheduled for October 29, will also feature demonstrations and exhibits as it recognises contributors and volunteers who have helped to build Jamaica’s national incident-response capabilities for more than a decade.

“The 2026 campaign seeks to change behaviour as it brings more awareness so that the public and organisations can begin to adopt habits that close off the easiest routes for attackers,” he said.

“The cyber careers symposium, the competition tracks, and the Cyber Reserve also strengthen the talent pipeline, giving students and professionals a route into the field while giving the division a pool of skilled people it can call on before seeking outside help,” the lieutenant colonel added.

Providing an update on Jamaica’s cybersecurity posture, Sterling said progress had been made, although significant gaps remain.

“Key foundations are now in place — the Cybercrimes Act was amended in February and the national cybersecurity standards framework and incident response plan are finalised. A national coordinating council is proceeding to Cabinet and a Cyber Reserve is being established to draw on students, professionals, and members of the security forces during national incidents. However, some gaps are remaining,” Sterling said, as he pointed to the more than 35,000 instances of cyberattacks that originated from Jamaica since the start of this year, in addition to approximately 12 million vulnerability instances that have affected local systems and services.

“These continue to be monitored and prioritised for mitigation by the CIRT Division. The principal active threats are ransomware, phishing, and AI-assisted attacks,” he added, while noting that opportunistic fraud, including fraudulent donation websites that emerged following Hurricane Melissa, remains a concern.

Going forward, Sterling said that improving the country’s defences will require greater investment in modern detection and automation tools, stronger vulnerability management, and closer information-sharing arrangements with banks, telecommunications providers, and other critical sectors.

He also underscored the need for stronger legislative authority to empower JaCIRT to require organisations to meet cybersecurity standards and report incidents in a timely manner.

To build long-term capacity, Sterling said the entity is relying on the Strengthening Cybersecurity in Jamaica (SCIJ) Project, supported by the Inter-American Development Bank and implemented through the Office of the Prime Minister. The project, which runs from September 2025 to March 2031, aims to bolster cybersecurity protection across public institutions as it expands the pool of specialised professionals available locally.

“JaCIRT’s work is about shifting from reacting to incidents towards preventing them, building a deeper pool of skilled people and ensuring that the country can withstand and recover from an attack. The SCIJ Project is the long-term engine behind much of this as it aims to turn the completed standards framework and incident response plan into practical protection and a stronger workforce across the public sector,” he said.

Beyond testing national readiness, JaCIRT is stepping up its monitoring of cyberspace as it urges individuals and businesses to remain vigilant ahead of the busy Black Friday and Christmas shopping periods, when financially motivated cybercrimes are expected to intensify.

“The outlook for the rest of 2026 is for high, seasonal threat activity, with the main risk shifting to fraud and financially motivated attacks,” Sterling said.

“Phishing and WhatsApp account takeovers remain the most common routes to harm individuals, while ransomware and credential theft remain the main risks for organisations, especially over the holidays when staffing is reduced and detection is slower,” he further said.

World.title: French budget bill sets aside €2.3M for Macron’s future offices
World.content:
Despite the budget allocation, Macron does not yet appear to have found his next place of work. The Elysée told POLITICO the provision was a “precautionary measure … based on the experiences of previous presidents.”

Nicolas Sarkozy and François Hollande are the only two living former presidents currently benefiting from the arrangements — even though Hollande has since returned to parliament as a lawmaker.

Hollande said last month that he is receiving a monthly pension of €5,000 for his time at the Élysée, on top of pensions from previous roles and his current income.

Macron, the youngest president in modern French history, will be 49 when he leaves office and has pledged not to draw his presidential pension.

He has kept his plans for life after the presidency close to his chest, leaving unclear to what extent he intends to remain involved in politics. Although he is constitutionally barred from seeking a third consecutive term, he will be eligible to run for president again once his successor takes office. He has not ruled out the possibility of doing so.

World.title: Cyprus asks EU to put mutual defense back on the agenda
World.content:
The defense clause article had risen up the agenda because of mounting geopolitical threats, including U.S. President Donald Trump’s undermining of the transatlantic alliance, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and hybrid warfare campaign against the EU, and wars in the Middle East.

“Given the gravity of the challenges we face, Cyprus would welcome the resumption of

discussions at the relevant preparatory bodies. I would therefore appreciate an update on the

proposals under consideration, as well as a timeline for the next steps,” Christodoulides wrote.

The EU gamed out how the clause would work in practice with exercises earlier this year.

Cyprus’ six-month presidency of the European Council, which ended on June 30, prioritized the issue after Iranian drones struck a British base on Cypriot soil in March.

But the topic has largely fallen off the bloc’s radar, as the EU turns its attention to negotiating its seven-year, almost €2 trillion budget and finding more funding for Ukraine.

Article 42.7 is not scheduled to be discussed at any European leaders’ summits in the foreseeable future, confirmed an EU official, granted anonymity to speak freely.

World.title: Hacker starten „Millionen“ von Angriffen, um eine weltweite PHP-Sicherheitslücke auszunutzen
World.content:
Regierungen und Website-Betreiber bemühen sich mit Hochdruck, Sicherheitslücken in einer beliebten Internet-Programmiersprache zu schließen.

Cyberangreifer haben „Millionen“ von Versuchen unternommen, eine kritische Sicherheitslücke in einem Grundbaustein des Internets auszunutzen, teilte ein bedeutender Anbieter von Cyberdiensten am Donnerstag mit.

Cybersicherheitsbehörden weltweit bemühten sich am Mittwoch, auf eine Sicherheitslücke in PHP zu reagieren, einer grundlegenden Programmiersprache, auf der 70 Prozent des Internets basieren.

Matthew Prince, der CEO von Cloudflare, einem Internetdienstleister, der von vielen Websites zur Abwehr von Cyberangriffen genutzt wird – wodurch das Unternehmen einen guten Einblick in die Aktivitäten von Hackern erhält –, erklärte in einem Beitrag auf X, man habe „Millionen“ von „Versuchen, die Sicherheitslücke auszunutzen“ festgestellt.

World.title: Hackers launch ‘millions’ of attempts to exploit global PHP cyber flaw
World.content:
The homepage of the PHP.net website is seen on October 22, 2026 in Singapore. | Yong Teck Lim/Getty Images

Cyberattackers have made “millions” of attempts to take advantage of a critical hole in a building block of the internet, a key cyber service provider said on Thursday.

Cybersecurity agencies worldwide scrambled on Wednesday to respond to a flaw in PHP, a foundational computer programming language used to underpin 70% of the internet.

Matthew Prince, the CEO of Cloudflare, an internet services company that is widely used by websites to block cyberattacks — giving it a high level of visibility over what hackers are doing — said in a post on X that it’s seen “millions” of “attempts to exploit” the flaw.

World.title: Russia launches massive strikes on Ukraine as Trump says peace is closer than ever
World.content:
Ukrainian firefighters work at the site of a shopping centre damaged following a missile strike in Kyiv on October 22, 2026. | Serhii Dilin/AFP via Getty Images

Kyiv also attacked Russia with more than 800 drones, the defense ministry in Moscow said.

KYIV – At least one person was killed and 34 wounded in Kyiv as the Russian army attacked Ukraine with ballistic missiles and attack drones overnight, the capital city’s prosecutor’s office reported on Thursday. Overall, 12 Ukrainian regions were under bombardment, authorities said.

“Russian ‘humanitarians’ have launched three waves of ballistic missile strikes against Kyiv, using a total of 21. Unfortunately, the city has sustained significant damage and multiple hits, affecting residential buildings, energy infrastructure, a railway station and the metro, shopping centers, and industrial enterprises. Even a monastery is among the damaged sites,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on Telegram after the attack.

Ukrainian forces reported shooting down 181 out of 210 Russian drones but none of the ballistic missiles.

World.title: Trump-sanctioned ICC wins EU Parliament’s human rights prize
World.content:
This photograph shows a view of the International Criminal Court in The Hague on September 23, 2026. | Remko de Waal/ANP/AFP via Getty Images

STRASBOURG — The International Criminal Court has won this year's Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought, awarded by the European Parliament, according to two people with knowledge of the decision.

The €50,000 prize honors defenders of human rights and freedom of thought, with past winners including Nelson Mandela, Alexei Navalny, Belarusian journalists, and the people of Ukraine.

The Socialists and Democrats group nominated the ICC following U.S. President Donald Trump's sanctions on the court, announced on Oct. 9.

"We stand by the ICC and its officials, and we are committed to safeguarding its work. We must guarantee that the ICC is able to operate independently, free from pressure or external interference," said S&D vice-chair Yannis Maniatis in early October. "It is a people-based organization, not a political one. If the aggressors become the victims, and if we stand by helplessly as international justice erodes, we risk allowing those who believe themselves above the law to prevail."

The prize is named in honor of Andrei Sakharov, a Soviet physicist and political dissident. Shortlisted candidates are traditionally invited to the Parliament’s award ceremony, which takes place during the December plenary session in Strasbourg.

World.title: Adipositas: Sparen kann für den Staat teuer werden
World.content:
Nach Berechnungen des Gesundheitsökonomen Dr. Tobias Effertz und seiner Kollegen verursacht Adipositas in Deutschland jährlich rund 63 Milliarden Euro an Kosten. Knapp 29 Milliarden Euro entfallen auf direkte medizinische Ausgaben, etwa für Arztbesuche, Behandlungen und Rehabilitation. Rund 34 Milliarden Euro entstehen indirekt durch krankheitsbedingte Fehlzeiten, eingeschränkte Leistungsfähigkeit oder vorzeitige Verrentung. Mit diesen Zahlen stehen die Wissenschaftler nicht allein, auch das WifOR Institut kommt zu einer vergleichbaren Größenordnung. Die Nationale Akademie der Wissenschaften Leopoldina veranschlagt die Belastung für Übergewicht und Adipositas unter Einbeziehung weiterer Kosten sogar deutlich höher. Die Studien unterscheiden sich je nach Methodik. Doch eines zeigen sie übereinstimmend: Die wirtschaftliche Dimension der Erkrankung geht weit über die Ausgaben einzelner Krankenkassen hinaus.

Doch eines zeigen sie übereinstimmend: Die wirtschaftliche Dimension der Erkrankung geht weit über die Ausgaben einzelner Krankenkassen hinaus.

Adipositas ist keine reine Lifestyle-Frage. Die chronische Erkrankung entsteht durch ein komplexes Zusammenspiel biologischer, genetischer, sozialer und umweltbezogener Faktoren. Nach Angaben des Robert Koch-Instituts lebt inzwischen etwa jeder fünfte Erwachsene in Deutschland mit Adipositas. Zu Beginn der 2000er-Jahre lag der Anteil mit etwa 12 Prozent noch deutlich niedriger. Die Leopoldina spricht deshalb bereits von einer „Adipositas-Epidemie“.

Der englische Weg der Adipositas-Versorgung

Das deutsche Gesundheitssystem beschränkt sich auf die Behandlung von Folgeerkrankungen der Adipositas, etwa Typ-2-Diabetes oder Herz-Kreislauf-Erkrankungen. Deren Behandlung ist medizinisch notwendig. Die politische Frage lautet jedoch, ob es auf Dauer wirtschaftlich sinnvoll ist, vor allem die Folgen der Adipositas zu finanzieren, anstatt Adipositas direkt zu behandeln. Das ist vor dem Hintergrund des demografischen Wandels und mangelnder Fachkräfte besonders relevant. Eine vom Institut der deutschen Wirtschaft veröffentlichte Prognose geht davon aus, dass Deutschland bis 2036 rund 4,3 Millionen Arbeitskräfte fehlen könnten. Adipositas ist nicht die Ursache des Fachkräftemangels und auch nicht die alleinige Lösung. Sie ist aber ein Faktor, der die Erwerbsfähigkeit beeinträchtigen kann. Eine Gesundheitspolitik, die Menschen länger gesund im Arbeitsleben halten will, muss solche Zusammenhänge berücksichtigen.

Entscheidend ist nicht allein, ob eine Therapie kurzfristig zusätzliche Kosten verursacht.

Der Blick ins Ausland zeigt, dass die politische Debatte über die Versorgung von Adipositas auch anders geführt werden kann. In England hat der staatliche Gesundheitsdienst NHS mit einem stufenweisen Rollout medikamentöser Therapien begonnen. Vorgesehen ist der Zugang zunächst für Erwachsene mit einem Body-Mass-Index von mindestens 35 kg/m2 und mindestens einer Begleiterkrankung. Die Behandlung erfolgt über spezialisierte Dienste und soll zunehmend auch in Hausarztpraxen angeboten werden. Grundlage sind Empfehlungen des englischen Instituts NICE. Nach dessen Schätzungen könnten in England rund 3,4 Millionen Erwachsene grundsätzlich die Kriterien für eine Behandlung erfüllen.

Das englische Modell setzt auf definierte medizinische Kriterien, einen schrittweisen Zugang und die Einbettung in bestehende Versorgungsstrukturen. Gerade darin liegt der gesundheitspolitische Unterschied zu der Debatte in Deutschland. Hierzulande richtet sich der Blick fast reflexartig auf die Kosten moderner Arzneimittel und Therapien. Das ist angesichts knapper Kassen nachvollziehbar, greift aber zu kurz. Entscheidend ist nicht allein, ob eine Therapie kurzfristig zusätzliche Kosten verursacht. Zu berücksichtigen sind ebenso Kosten unbehandelter oder zu spät behandelter Erkrankungen und demgegenüber mögliche Einsparungen durch vermiedene Folgeerkrankungen, weniger Arbeitsausfälle und einen längeren Verbleib im Erwerbsleben. Für Deutschland stellt sich also die grundsätzliche Frage: Soll die medikamentöse Behandlung von Adipositas weiterhin aus der Regelversorgung ausgeschlossen bleiben oder braucht es, ähnlich wie in England, einen zielgerichteten und stufenweisen Zugang für Menschen mit Adipositas?

Gesundheit als Investition

Eine moderne Adipositas-Versorgung ist eine Investition in die Stabilität von Gesundheitswesen, Arbeitsmarkt und Sozialversicherung zugleich. Zugelassene medikamentöse Therapien sollten dort eingesetzt werden können, wo sie medizinisch angezeigt sind. Ernährungs-, Bewegungs- und Verhaltenstherapie bleiben auch weiterhin wichtige Bestandteile, reichen aber in manchen Fällen nicht aus. Notwendig ist ein Versorgungskonzept, das Prävention, Früherkennung und leitliniengerechte Behandlung verbindet.

Wer nur kurzfristige Ausgaben betrachtet, riskiert, langfristig höhere Belastungen zu finanzieren.

Gerade in Zeiten knapper Kassen verlangt ein verantwortungsvoller Haushalt eine vollständige Kostenrechnung. Die entscheidende Frage lautet daher nicht allein, was eine Behandlung kostet, sondern auch, welche Kosten durch Nichtbehandlung entstehen. Wer nur kurzfristige Ausgaben betrachtet, riskiert, langfristig höhere Belastungen zu finanzieren.
