World.title: Who are the losers from the budget?
World.content:
Can the government find more cuts across Whitehall to fund its NATO defence commitments?

With less than a week to go until the budget, Treasury minister Emma Reynolds says squeezing more efficiency out of the government could free up cash for defence. But with public services already under pressure, where can the cuts be made without making things worse?

Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy crunch the numbers, look at which sectors are already flashing the warning signs, and which policies the prime minister could scrap to score a political win.

Elsewhere, is Education Secretary Lucy Powell planning to changes shifts in the department after a lukewarm response to keeping Sir Martyn Oliver as the chief inspector of Ofsted?

World.title: Palantir says NATO AI system has no ‘kill switch’ after Starlink disruptions in Ukraine
World.content:
US software company Palantir has sought to reassure European allies that its military AI system used by NATO has no “kill switch”.

 

Palantir’s executive vice president for the UK and Europe, Louis Mosley, told Reuters on Wednesday that neither the company nor the US could switch off the Maven Smart System AI platform used by NATO’s military headquarters and several European armed forces.

“What we have seen in the news over the past few days around Starlink is extremely concerning,” Mosley said in an interview in Brussels.

“But as concerns Palantir, I can provide categorical reassurance that where customers have bought our software, they are in full operational control of that software,” he said.

“There are no kill switches. There’s no ability for Palantir or the US government to reach in and switch it off.”

It follows recent disruptions to Ukraine’s Starlink and Starshield services, which raised alarm over the reliance on US tech firms.

On 13 October, Kyiv accused Washington of deliberately slowing Starshield, the SpaceX-operated military communications system that Ukrainian forces depend on at the front, as well as SpaceX’s civilian satellite network Starlink.

Reports later emerged that the White House had ordered Elon Musk’s SpaceX to limit Ukraine’s access to Starshield, the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite network.

Musk defended himself on X, and claimed that the “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.”

To which US President Donald Trump replied, saying, “it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon. I don’t know if it was anybody. From what I understand, it’s the same as it’s always been.”

The lack of clarity over who was responsible for the decision is one concern. But for European leaders, the prospect of the Trump administration using US technology that Europe has become so reliant upon as political leverage against its allies is even more alarming.

Palantir’s Maven system

NATO currently uses Palantir’s Maven system, which relies on AI to process large volumes of battlefield data from satellites, radar, drones and other sensors to speed up decision-making.

Palantir won a €480 million tender with NATO in 2025 to supply Maven to the alliance. It has since been deployed at NATO’s Allied Command Operations at the Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe (SHAPE), and in June this year it achieved “full technical operational capability”.

Some European NATO members, including France and Germany, have opted out of Maven, alarmed at the possibility of a private company having so much control over battlefield operations.

“Allowing industry personnel access to national German datasets is out of the question," German Vice Admiral Thomas Daum said earlier this year.

France has meanwhile developed its own service, Arcadia, in an effort to build its own defence data ecosystem and maintain technological sovereignty.

World.title: Barclays to cut 5,000 jobs as it turns to AI to improve efficiency
World.content:
Barclays shares edged lower in London after the bank said on Thursday it would cut around 5,000 jobs, including around 1,000 already cut in the first half of the year.

 

The announcement came alongside an earnings update that showed Barclays’ net profit grew 13% in the third quarter, helped by surging income in its equities division.

Barclays said in an earnings presentation that it was implementing “organisational simplification and technology change efficiency driven by AI”.

About 60% of the job cuts affect support functions, including developers, as AI makes staff more productive, according to the bank.

Will Howlett, a financial analyst at Quilter Cheviot, said the announcement illustrates "just how significantly AI and automation could reshape the banking industry over the next few years".

"Banks have spent heavily on technology for years, but we are increasingly reaching the point where that investment translates into fewer people being required to run the business," he said, adding that "Barclays expects its efficiency measures to deliver more than £1.1 billion (€1.31bn) of savings, which should help bring down costs and improve profitability."

The bank’s profit attributable to shareholders rose to £1.65 billion (€1.97 billion) in the third quarter from £1.46 billion (€1.74 billion) in the July–September period a year earlier.

Barclays chief executive C. S. Venkatakrishnan said he was pleased with the bank’s operational and financial momentum, and said the investment bank division “delivered strong equities performance”.

Income from equities jumped 47% year-on-year, while total group income for the quarter climbed 3% to £7.37 billion (€8.79 billion).

"The investment bank was weaker, particularly in fixed income trading, but Barclays remains on track against its longer-term targets," said Howlett. He added that "the question is increasingly whether Barclays can turn technological investment and a smaller workforce into sustainably lower costs without compromising growth." If it can, he said, "there is still considerable scope for improved returns.”

The bank also announced a £500 million (€596 million) share buyback.

The AI “announcement comes as the company failed to match expectations with its third-quarter performance — with the unveiling of a healthy share buyback failing to entirely ease investors’ disappointment”, noted AJ Bell investment director Russ Mould.

He added that while costs increased across the wider group, there are two "major clouds over the business".

“The first being a widely expected increase in tax on the sector in next week’s (UK) budget and the other being a reported probe into possible misrepresentation of risks in its private credit portfolio,” Mould said.

According to the FT, the Bank of England was examining claims that Barclays had understated risks linked to financing for private credit funds. The concern is whether Barclays made these exposures look less risky in its books, allowing it to hold less capital to cover potential losses.

Barclays has said its private credit exposure is treated in line with accounting and regulatory capital requirements.

World.title: Australia: Bystanders dive into floodwaters to save trapped driver
World.content:
Australian Broadcasting Corporation reporter Will Murray was covering the floods when a vehicle stalled after entering deep water on Buchanan Road. As it began to sink, Murray handed his phone to camera operator Liz Pickering, called emergency services and waded into the floodwater. Another bystander quickly joined him.

 

The pair first tried to open the nearest door, then climbed onto the vehicle and considered smashing the rear window. Murray eventually forced open the rear passenger-side door, allowing the driver to escape before the ute disappeared beneath the water.

Footage captured the dramatic rescue, followed by an emotional moment as the relieved driver embraced one of the men who helped save him. ABC camera operator Liz Pickering said the two men “undoubtedly saved that man’s life”.

No serious injuries were reported. About 170 millimetres of rain had fallen in Morayfield, where severe flooding forced road closures and left the shopping centre largely inaccessible. Queensland authorities warned motorists not to drive or swim through floodwaters, warning that vehicles can quickly become trapped or swept away.

World.title: EU Parliament awards Sakharov Prize to ICC in rebuke of US sanctions
World.content:
The European Parliament on Thursday awarded the International Criminal Court (ICC) the Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought, signalling opposition to US sanctions threatening the court’s work.

 

The annual prize recognises individuals and organisations defending human rights and fundamental freedoms. Past laureates include South African leader Nelson Mandela and Russian opposition figure Alexei Navalny.

US President Donald Trump’s administration announced sanctions against the ICC on 9 October, following repeated criticism of its arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and its investigation into the conduct of US troops in Afghanistan.

“This is a message of hope and resistance sent to Donald Trump. We will not abandon the rule of law and international justice. We will stand with the ICC for as long as it takes,” said French MEP Chloé Ridel, who nominated the court.

Parliament’s political group leaders chose the ICC over two other shortlisted candidates: Tanzanian lawyer Tundu Lissu, who faces political persecution, and Iranian sisters Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, nominated on behalf of those persecuted by Iran’s authorities.

The Socialists and Democrats (S&D) group put forward the ICC and its officials, with other political groups eventually backing the nomination. The decision surprised some insiders, who had expected Lissu to win.

Last week, MEPs from across the political spectrum urged European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to protect the Netherlands-based court from US sanctions.

They called for the use of “all instruments at our disposal”, particularly the EU’s Blocking Statute, which shields European companies and individuals from the effects of certain foreign sanctions.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas described the threat of sanctions against the ICC as “not acceptable” on 9 October, reaffirming the bloc’s commitment to international law. The EU has yet to take concrete action.

World.title: Six European destinations included in ‘Best of the World’ selection for 2027
World.content:
National Geographic has unveiled its list of the 25 destinations around the world that travellers should add to their 2027 itineraries, with six being in Europe.

 

First launched in 2012, its “Best of the World” selection has showcased where to go if you have “a sense of adventure, a fascination with the past”, or seeking the “simple pleasure of wandering unfamiliar city streets”.

Vestland in Norway was among the European destinations to make the cut. Here, travellers will find “epic fjord adventures and wellness-led travel” in one of Europe’s “most breathtaking landscapes”, the magazine said.

Vestland’s sheer scale of natural wonder was also highlighted. “Wherever you go, big wildness awaits”, including sky-high cliffs, turquoise waters and cascading waterfalls.

Poland’s Tricity area, which combines three adjacent cities – Gdańsk, Gdynia and Sopot – also made the list along with German city Leipzig.

For a musical getaway, Leipzig is recommended for its grand opera, orchestral halls and jazz clubs. The city is set to expand its existing 5.3km-long Music Trail, a route that takes visitors to numerous key historical sites, with a second 7.2km loop.

Also making the list is Normandy in France, especially as the region is set to host "Millenium 2027: European Year of the Normans". The celebration marks the 1,000th anniversary of William the Conqueror’s birth. Throughout 2027, more than 1,000 events will take place, including concerts, medieval feasts and theatrical street performances.

Along Spain’s northern coast, Santander will welcome the opening of two world-class art museums in 2027. The region of Cantabria is “often overlooked”, the magazine said, but its capital city is “poised to change that”. Next year an outpost of the Museo Reina Sofia will open in the city and the Museum of Prehistory and Archaeology will move to a new home.

For quiet trails and dark night skies, Dumfries and Galloway in Scotland is a must-visit – especially for stargazers. Next summer, the Scottish Dark Sky Observatory is set to open amid the “rippling hills” of the Galloway and Southern Ayrshire UNESCO Biosphere.

An elephant at the Majete Wildlife Reserve in Malawi Omar Hakeem/Unsplash

Best of the world beyond Europe

Globally, National Geographic called on travellers to “join the biggest celebration of Afro-Brazilian culture in one of South America’s most historic cities”. For the first time in decades, Salvador in Brazil will host the Salvador Carnival immediately after the Festa de Iemanjá – which is the biggest festival of the Candomblé religion.

In Africa, Malawi is described as the continent’s “best-kept secret” that offers “thrilling nature experiences without the crowds”, especially as the classic safari circuit continues to grow in popularity. Thanks to government initiatives and work by conservation organisations, travellers can see the “big five” – lions, leopards, elephants, rhinos and African buffalo – in Malawi’s top wildlife regions, including Liwonde National Park and Majete Wildlife Reserve.

Other destinations to make the selection include Luxor in Egypt, Chengdu in China, Maya Ka’an in Mexico, and the Pacific Coast Highway in California, United States.

National Geographic’s ‘Best of the World’ list for 2027

Penang, Malaysia

Tricity (Gdańsk, Sopot and Gdynia), Poland

Kuélap, Peru

Gdańsk in Poland Anna Gru/Unsplash

Poland on the international tourism map

The tricity area of Gdańsk, Gdynia and Sopot were included on the National Geographic list. It joins the group of Polish destinations previously distinguished by the magazine: Białowieża Forest in 2019 and Łódź in 2022.

Crucially, the accolade underlines that Poland's Baltic coast has far more to offer than sandy beaches and a traditional summer holiday.

Together the three cities form a region where coastal landscapes blend with historical heritage, culture and a modern way of life.

The authors of the list encourage people to explore the region with the invitation: "Discover revitalised waterfronts and bold Baltic flavours in three seaside cities that are coming into their own."

Three cities, three different stories

Gdańsk draws visitors with its landmarks and centuries-old port history. Among the most important sights are Long Market (Długi Targ), the medieval Crane, the Museum of the Second World War and the European Solidarity Centre. The former Gdańsk Shipyard grounds also attract particular attention.

Significantly, the industrial spaces are being given new functions and are becoming venues for meetings, artistic events and a vibrant food scene.

Gdańsk's mayor Aleksandra Dulkiewicz stressed the importance of the distinction for the local community at the press conference.

"Gdańsk is a city of freedom, solidarity and openness,” she said. “A place where history meets modernity and everyone can find something for themselves. This accolade belongs to the residents of Gdańsk, who every day create the unique atmosphere of our city.”

Sopot stands above all for its spa traditions, seaside atmosphere and closeness to nature.

The city invites visitors to stroll along the beach and hike through the Tricity Landscape Park. Its attractions can be discovered outside the peak summer season as well.

Sopot's mayor Magdalena Czarzyńska-Jachim noted at the press conference: "Experts from all over the world have recognised the resort's exceptional atmosphere and the quality of our tourist offer, which Sopot's entrepreneurs work on every day in cooperation with the Sopot Tourism Organisation."

Gdynia, meanwhile, is distinguished by its modernist architecture and a history linked to the development of Poland's maritime economy.

The city, whose dynamic expansion began in the interwar period, became a symbol of Poland's renewed ambitions on the Baltic.

It is worth emphasising that in 2026 Gdynia's Modernist Centre was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List.

Gdynia's mayor Aleksandra Kosiorek drew attention to the special timing of the accolade.

"This distinction has particular significance for us in the year of the centenary of Gdynia being granted city status,” she said. “A hundred years ago Gdynia was a symbol of a bold look to the future and today it once again shows that it is an open, dynamic and inspiring city. We are pleased that its history and present day have been recognised by one of the world's most recognisable travel publications.”

Gastronomy and events all year round

Local cuisine also plays an important role in the National Geographic recommendation. Tricity chefs use regional products, draw inspiration from Kashubian traditions and give classic dishes a contemporary twist.

Fish from the Baltic are another key element of the offer.

The region also attracts visitors with its cultural and sporting events. Gdańsk hosts St Dominic's Fair and the Shakespeare Festival, while Sopot organises a literary festival.

In turn, in 2027 Gdynia will host the main multi-class regattas as part of the Sailing World Championships. Kolosy, the National Meeting of Travellers, Sailors and Mountaineers, is also planned there.

An additional advantage is the ability to travel conveniently between the three cities without a car. Thanks to this, a single trip can combine sightseeing historic monuments, relaxing by the sea and exploring modernist architecture.

World.title: Refusing to cross, unable to escape: Seafarers recount Hormuz dangers to Euronews
World.content:
The Al Ruwais, a 314-metre liquefied natural gas carrier flying a Bahamian flag, has been sitting adrift off the coast of Pakistan for weeks.

 

Fearing for its safety, its 34-member crew does not want to test the waters and attempt to cross the Strait of Hormuz, despite demands from the ship's owners.

"What strikes me as strange is that this company is willing to risk the ship just to pass through the Strait of Hormuz," an electrician aboard the UAE-owned vessel told Euronews.

"If it were up to the company, we'd go through, but for that to happen, the entire crew would have to agree. And they don't. I am waiting to leave by boat for Pakistan, where I will board another vessel."

Under maritime regulations, the right to refuse transit into a designated warlike area is individual, meaning that one sailor objecting is enough to stop a vessel from moving into a danger zone.

On ships whose crews do agree to cross, companies have offered captains up to $100,000 (€89,000) per month plus $50,000 (€44,500) risk bonuses, while ordinary crew wages have risen four to six times.

"On other ships, they give as much as $10,000 (€8,900), but not everyone gets the same amount, and it depends a lot on the position and base salary," the sailor aboard Al Ruwais told Euronews.

"It's only fair that everyone gets the same amount, otherwise, it would mean that the captain's life is worth more than that of the deckhand."

No passage is safe, sailors say

A vital waterway for the world's energy trade, the Straight of Hormuz has been under two concurrent naval blockades since the outbreak of the Iran war following US-Israeli strikes in late February.

The southern corridor near Oman is patrolled by US forces, while the northern route passes through Iranian-controlled waters. The IRGC Navy has stated that vessels transiting routes it considers unauthorised face what it described as "punitive action".

Traffic through the strait has collapsed as a result. More than 125 vessels passed daily before the war. That figure has fallen to fewer than 10 to 12, a drop of more than 90%, according to ship-tracking firm Kpler.

Drone attacks, sea mines and strikes from unknown projectiles have driven the decline, with UK Maritime Trade Operations recording multiple incidents involving fires, sinkings and power failures aboard tankers and LNG carriers.

Ships that do attempt the crossing have taken to turning off satellite AIS transponders, extinguishing running lights at night and shutting down radio equipment to avoid detection.

IRGC boats navigating the Strait of Hormuz AP Photo

The dangers are somewhat different for Iranian sailors. Hamed, a 50-year-old former captain who now runs a maritime management company in Iran, told Euronews that since March of last year the war has resulted in the deaths of some 95 seafarers in commercial, fishing, passenger, tugboat and offshore platform support roles.

Military vessels have suffered heavy damage and ships undergoing repairs in Bandar Abbas have been struck, he said, although precise casualty figures have not been officially released.

"Nearly 60% of our ships are sanctioned and forbidden from calling at foreign ports such as India, Pakistan, the UAE, Oman, Kuwait, and Iraq," Hamed said. "Even Pakistan's maritime borders, where Iranian vessels used to travel, have now been closed to us."

Around 40% of southern Iranian seafarers have refused sea assignments, he said, with many shifting to the Caspian Sea to handle increased grain imports from the north. Wages in the south have been raised by 30 to 100%.

Sailors now earn between 50 and 80 million tomans (€165 to €265) per month, and captains between $1,200 and $4,000 (€1,100 to €3,700).

US forces have boarded Iranian commercial vessels roughly 15 times since the war began, Hamed said, arriving by helicopter and speedboat to inspect cargo for explosives, with no guarantees of their safety.

“The US has provided no safe-passage guarantees for Iranian commercial ships," Hamed said. "Every week we witness aerial or naval drone attacks on Iranian vessels."

He estimated that roughly 35,000 Iranian seafarers across approximately 2,000 vessels continue operating in southern waters to deliver wheat, corn and medicine to ordinary Iranians.

If the situation deteriorates further, he warned, authorities could be forced to declare a complete shutdown and evacuate coastal facilities.

World.title: France confirms first human case of Shamonda virus, previously found only in animals
World.content:
French authorities have confirmed an infection with the Shamonda virus in a patient in Lyon who died in early October, marking the first time the virus has been reported in a human.

 

Until now, the Shamonda virus was considered not to be transmissible to humans. This case is the first documented and reported detection of the virus in a human.

“This is therefore an exceptional case involving a severely immunocompromised patient,” the authorities said.

The Shamonda virus was detected in Europe for the first time this summer. It belongs to a group of viruses transmitted by biting insects called midges, and until now it has affected mostly cattle, considered the main hosts among infected animal species. Sporadic infections in small ruminants and horses were also reported in France this summer.

The infected patient was a severely immunocompromised patient and had been receiving treatment for a serious illness at the Hospices Civils de Lyon, the French Agriculture Ministry said in a statement.

According to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), the specific midge species involved in transmission in this case is still unknown. French authorities say that the hypothesis is that the patient was infected through an insect bite, specifically from a tiny fly, Culicoides midge, in eastern France.

“According to investigations carried out so far, the brain complications observed in the immunocompromised patient before their death were very likely linked to the Shamonda virus infection,” the Ministry said. “Based on current knowledge of the virus, no health risk to the general population has been identified to date”.

Clinical, laboratory and epidemiological investigations are still ongoing to determine whether the virus caused or contributed to the patient’s death and how the infection was acquired, together with the World Health Organization (WHO) and the ECDC.

In infected adult cattle, the main symptoms are fever, lethargy and diarrhoea. In dairy cows, a significant drop in milk production may also be observed, according to Sciensano, Belgium’s national public health institute.

Shamonda virus was first detected in Nigeria in the mid-1960s and has since been reported sporadically in cattle in West, East and southern Africa and in Japan. This summer, it was detected for the first time in Western Europe, with cases reported in Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland, as well as Jersey island.

This story has been updated to include a comment from the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC).

World.title: EU's Sakharov Prize won by the International Criminal Court
World.content:
The EU has announced the International Criminal Court as the winner of this year's Sakharov Prize. The annual prize is awarded to individuals and organizations for their work in supporting human rights and democracy.

The International Criminal Court (ICC) has won this year's Sakharov Prize, awarded by the European Union to individuals and organizations in recognition of their work to support and protect human rights and democracy.

"This prize recognizes the important work of the court in upholding international law and justice," said European Parliament President Roberta Metsola, who announced the winner at the European Parliament in Strasbourg.

She said the EU was similarly "built on respect for multilateralism and international institutions."

In naming the ICC as the prize winner, Metsola also took time to recognize the two other finalists: Tanzanian jailed lawyer and human rights defender Tundu Lissu and the imprisoned Iranian twin sisters Taraneh and Romina Rahimi.

"This award comes at a time when the Court and its officials face unprecedented challenges, including sanctions aimed at disrupting the Court's judicial mandate," ICC president and top judge Tomoko Akane said.

The prize ceremony will take place in December.

What is the International Criminal Court?

Set up in 2002 in the Hague, the ICC is responsible for prosecuting the most serious of crimes, including genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes.

The ICC has recently come under sanctions from the US government under President Donald Trump in response to what Washington called political bias. The ICC has issued an arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleged war crimes in Gaza.

What's behind the US attempt to shut down the ICC? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The US said it wants to "dismantle" the court.

The awarding of the Sakharov Prize is a further show of support after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.

What is the Sakharov Prize?

The prize, awarded every year by the European Parliament, was set up in 1988 to honor those who defend human rights and basic freedoms.

It is named after Soviet dissident and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Andrei Sakharov.

Previous winners include Nelson Mandela (1988), Aung San Suu Kyi (1990), Mahsa Jina Amini and the Woman, Life, Freedom movement in Iran (2023) and Andrzej Poczobut, a journalist from Belarus, and Mzia Amaglobeli, a journalist from Georgia (2025).

World.title: Can Germany overhaul its economy before AfD grows stronger?
World.content:
Conflicts, rising costs and Chinese competition are testing Germany's economic model like never before. Which new sectors could revive growth and contain the far-right AfD, whose support has grown larger than ever?

Germany's export-led economic model faces unprecedented strain just as support for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party reaches a new peak.

Chinese rivals are steadily eroding the market share of major German industrial players, while persistently high energy prices, elevated labor costs and excessive red tape are adding to the structural crisis.

After two years of contraction, real GDP edged up only 0.2% last year, according to the Federal Statistical Office, Destatis. Exports to China fell 9.7% in 2025, withGerman vehicle and part shipments plunging by a third.

While there are signs the German economy is turning the corner, the government's latest forecast of 1.3% growth in 2026 is still modest compared with the pre-COVID boom years.

The AfD is currently polling ahead of all other political parties in Germany. The country's many economic challenges have been a major factor in the right-wing populists' rise.

Germany's domestic intelligence agency sees reliable indications that the AfD is right-wing extremist in its entirety.

The party has vowed to put Germany back on a growth path by ending the transition to renewable energies, lowering taxes and renegotiating European Union treaties, while also reforming welfare and sharply restricting immigration.

Merz seeks growth via advanced tech

As Chancellor Friedrich Merz's coalition searches for a fresh growth strategy to fend off the rise in populist politics, the government has set out its high-tech agenda focusing on six priority sectors.

These are artificial intelligence (AI), quantum computing, microelectronics, biotechnology, clean energy (including nuclear fusion) and climate-neutral mobility.

Irene Bertschek, head of the Digital Economy research unit at the Leibniz Center for European Economic Research (ZEW), argues that Germany's research in these "key enabling technologies is very strong, particularly in the area of climate-neutral technologies."

Yet, the results are often commercialized abroad, Bertschek told DW, with the United States leading in AI and China closing the gap quickly.

Germany under pressure To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trillions in new investments

A report published Monday by the Made for Germany initiative — a group of 147 companies and investors — builds on the government's plan, estimating that these and other new technologies could attract up to €4.1 trillion ($4.6 trillion) in investment by 2035.

Realizing that potential, however, will depend less on today's industrial giants, like Volkswagen, Siemens and BASF.

"It will not primarily be the established companies that conquer these new fields, but innovative newcomers — startups," Oliver Falck, director of the ifo Center for the Economics of Innovation and Digital Transformation, told DW.

The task, Falck said, is to create the right conditions for startups to emerge, including proximity to top universities, access to private capital and enough freedom to experiment.

He argues for state financing during the early-stage "valley of death" — the risky phase between research and commercial viability when private financing is often scarce.

Investors circle future growth sectors

There are clear signs this shift is already happening. Data from Deutsche Bank and startupdetector, a German startup database and market intelligence platform, show more than 3,000 startups were founded in Germany in the first half of 2026, up 88% from the same period last year. One-third of the new ventures have an AI focus.

Venture-capital investment soared 44% to €5.8 billion in the first half of 2026, with firms such as Neura Robotics and drone manufacturers Stark and Quantum Systems benefiting.

US investors, meanwhile, are increasingly buying up Germany's famed Mittelstand — its traditional small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) — with an eye on their specialized technology.

"The German Mittelstand is highly innovative. Now it is essential to invest in key technologies such as artificial intelligence and to tap into the potential that arises at the intersection with established technologies," Bertschek stressed.

The expert, who is also chair of the German government's Commission of Experts for Research and Innovation (EFI), thinks SMEs should make better use of their huge amounts of production data and collaborate with AI startups to help those young firms grow.

China has built more than 2,000 economic zones and industrial parks (file photo from 2020) Image: Liu Quanle/VCG/MAXPPP/dpa/picture alliance

A case for special economic zones

Another idea for accelerating the shift to new high-tech sectors comes from Sven Gabor Janszky, chairman of the Leipzig-based futures-research institute 2b AHEAD. He argues that Germany needs special economic zones to help catch the next wave of economic growth.

"For a few specific technologies, you lower the regulations, you recruit ambitious workers and pump money into these zones," Janszky told DW.

This, he added, would follow the examples of Silicon Valley and Chinese mega-cities Shenzhen and Shanghai's Pudong district, and echoes the conditions that helped rebuild the German economy after World War II.

In Janszky's view, these zones would help Germany position itself as a first mover in emerging fields rather than remaining tied to older industrial strengths.

"EU regulations may try to prohibit this move, but Germany will have to overcome them so we can grow the economy again," he added.

Defense spending powers tech growth

The sharp rise in Germany's defense spending will also help several of the high-tech sectors now being prioritized.

According to the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), the defense budget is expected to reach around €120 billion in 2026 — roughly 2.6% of GDP. The government wants this figure to hit 3.5% by 2029.

The resulting procurement will provide a major boost to the production of drones, sensors, communications systems and other dual-use technologies that have both civilian and military applications.

How China is upping pressure on German businesses To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The cost gap need not be decisive

Yet, with major rival China benefiting from much lower energy and worker costs, along with huge government subsidies, Germany will continue to face similar price disadvantages when exporting its new high-end tech. But that doesn't have to spell failure, said Falck, the ifo expert.

"Take the semiconductor industry as an example. It is probably unrealistic to aim for leadership along the entire value chain. But it is enough to lead at individual choke points," he pointed out.

"And that is exactly where Germany is strong: as a supplier of equipment for state-of-the-art chip fabs and as a supplier to the world's AI gigafactories, with power semiconductors."

In other words, with a first-mover advantage, decades of high-quality production data and a focus on specialized niches, Germany can remain a major force in advanced industrial and engineering technologies.

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

Police are investigating a possible arson attack after more than 20 MAN trucks were set on fire on Thursday evening in the Sellerhausen-Stünz neighborhood of Leipzig, in eastern Germany, local media reported.

The fire broke out around 2 a.m. (0000 GMT) with several vehicles being completely destroyed. The initial estimate of the cost of the damage reached seven figures, according to Radio Leipzig.

The Police Center for Countering Extremism and Terrorism from the Saxony criminal investigation bureau will take over further investigations since a political motive for the arson cannot be ruled out.

The fire services were able to bring the flames under control by morning and there were no report of injuries.

World.title: Harry Kane: Ballon d’Or for Bayern Munich striker?
World.content:
The most prestigious individual prize in football will be awarded on Monday, with Bayern Munich's English striker Harry Kane the front runner. Kane has developed even more in the Bundesliga despite an uneven league.

To most Bayern Munich fans under the age of 40, Karl-Heinz Rummenigge was the club CEO who regularly spoke his mind. But for those with longer memories, or a better grasp of Bavarian football history, he was one of the club's all-time great players. He was also the last Bayern man to win the Ballon d'Or, in 1981. The last Bundesliga player to win was Borussia Dortmund's Matthias Stammer, in 1996.

That long drought looks set to end on Monday, with Harry Kane, born 12 years after Rummenigge's win, the favorite to pick up the trophy at a ceremony held, as a one off, in his native London.

"It's obviously special for me that the ceremony is taking place in London. "I come from London and lived there for a long time — maybe that's a good omen," Kane told club magazine Säbener51. "The Ballon d'Or would be a massive success for me."

Lamine Yamal, the prodigious Barcelona and Spain forward who won the Euros at 16 looks to be the main competitor. At the end of the 2025-26 season, on which the award is judged, Yamal won the World Cup with Spain as well as the La Liga title.

Kane career not just measured in numbers

Kane's 73 goals for club and country last season make for a strong case, and the Bundesliga's most expensive signing of all time has already racked up 156 goals in 158 games for the serial German champions. But it's not just the numbers that tell the story, according to his club coach.

"People in England saw him as a goalscorer during his time playing there," said Vincent Kompany of his striker last season. "We've seen other qualities too, such as his footballing intelligence. We can appreciate that now – it was perhaps somewhat underestimated in England. He's like a fine wine that improves with age. I also enjoy that aspect of his game."

At 33, Kane continues to improve at a point where many footballers start to regress. While he is helped by being more reliant on guile and technique than pace, Kane's professionalism is key to staying at the top, according to his Bayern teammate Serge Gnabry.

"He always has the right attitude, always leads the way, and sets the tone," Gnabry said ahead of Bayern's 2-2 draw in the Champions Leagueagainst Arsenal on Wednesday. "He never strays from his path, helps the team with his performance, and is a top-tier player."

Kane scored a penalty in that match and provided a sensational pass from which Alphonso Davies scored Bayern's opener, another reminder of his all round game. "The pass was one of my best ones. I knew Phonzy [Davies] would be able to get there with his speed. Whatever I can do to help the team, I'll do. At the moment, it seems to be with assists more than goals," Kane said postmatch.

Leading from the front

That attitude has been with Kane from the start. His first-ever coach Dave Bricknell, from Ridgeway Rovers, an amateur club in northeast London, told DW after he joined Bayern from Spurs in 2023 that: "Harry's mentality is his greatest strength. He doesn't let anything worry him. If he misses a chance, he doesn't care, he will go and score from another chance."

His England coach, Thomas Tuchel, has also emphasized Kane's leadership. "He is the first one to push everyone and that is his mindset and he became a very, very hardworking forward on top of his finishing skills. He is a complete package," he said last month as Kane extended his England goal-scoring record against the Czech Republic.

There are detractors who point to perceived 'stat-padding', scoring against inferior opponents in international qualifiers and in the Bundesliga, where there are fewer elite teams, and a lot less money, than in England. While Kane's ratio of 213 goals in 320 games in the Premier League is a little off his Bundesliga stats, it bears comparison with any other player in the history of the league.

Harry Kane has missed out on international honors with England Image: Odd Andersen/AFP

Should Kane win the award, it will be a boost in profile for the Bundesliga, which has been unable to keep pace, both commercially and on the pitch, with other top European leagues of late, particularly the Premier League and La Liga. Winning it in a league outside of England or Spain would make Kane's feat even greater. Other than Ousmane Dembele, who won it last year after Paris Saint-Germain's Champions League win, and Lionel Messi, a serial Ballon d'Or winner, the last player to take the Ballon d'Or for a season played outside England or Spain was was Kaka at AC Milan in 2007, when Italy's Serie A was considered a stronger league.

Kane's career hasn't been straightforward though. After signing his first senior contract with Spurs in July 2010, he was sent out on various loans to lower league sides between 2011-2013 without ever making a huge impression.

Domestic trophies won but international success eludes

For former teammate Jermain Defoe, who also coached Kane at Spurs, those experiences were formative.

"You have to show a resilience. It's not easy when you go out on loan, it can feel like you're being rejected by the club that you are at, which isn't the case," he told DW in 2023 before adding that Kane's ability was always clear.

"When he joined up with the [Tottenham] first team, you could see the potential. He was always a good finisher, always hit the ball clean… With Harry you already knew, he had that natural instinct and always felt comfortable in front of goal."

Those goals have, after a failure to win a trophy in England, led to two Bundesliga titles and a German Cup. But success with England remains elusive after a 2026 World Cup exit in the semifinals. Kane will be 35 by the time of the next Euros, in the UK and Ireland in 2028, and has a deal with Bayern until the following year. His form since joining Bayern suggest he could get better still.

Edited by: Jonathan Harding

World.title: Bulgaria: Concerns about security in the Black Sea dominate presidential election campaign
World.content:
Bulgaria's presidential election campaign has been shaped by recent drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea and the government's reduced support for Ukraine, making foreign policy a key factor in the first round.

Six months after Bulgaria's parliamentary election, the country is gearing up to choose its next president.

Although the role of president in Bulgaria is largely ceremonial, the election on October 25 — with a potential runoff on November 1 — will serve as a test for the government of former President Rumen Radev, whose party won a landslide victory in April, securing an unprecedented majority — the first in Bulgaria in almost three decades.

Although there are 27 candidates on the ballot, the race has narrowed to a duel between the incumbent president, Iliana Yotova, who served two terms as Radev's vice president and is backed by the prime minister, and former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, who is supported by opposition parties.

The role of the president

According to the Bulgarian Constitution, the Bulgarian president embodies national unity. He or she represents the country at international level (with a few exceptions), is the commander-in-chief of its armed forces, appoints members of the Supreme Judicial Council and various regulatory bodies, including caretaker governments, and has the power to veto legislation.

Sunday's presidential election will serve as a test for the government of Rumen Radev. Pictured here: newspaper headlines on the morning after Radev's landslide victory in April Image: Valentina Petrova/AP Photo/picture alliance

Hristo Panchugov, a political scientist at the New Bulgarian University in Sofia, argued that although the president's powers are formally limited, the office is particularly significant in the current context.

"For the first time in Bulgaria's modern democratic history, we have an absolutely uncontested majority that is not held together by any coalition, but rather by a single political party that faces an opposition that is completely falling apart," he told DW.

Panchugov went on to say that it would have been better if the campaign had focused more on "whether the president could serve as a counterbalance."

Opposition candidate Andrey Gyurov reiterated this point in an interview with DW: "We are seeing a concentration of power that always bears the marks of a slide toward autocracy... A president should know how to say no."

Iliana Yotova declined DW's request for an interview.

Iliana Yotova, president of Bulgaria (left), has the backing of Prime Minister and former President Rumen Radev (right) Image: BGNES

The impact of the war in Ukraine

Initially, the presidential race was characterized by small rallies, a lack of televised debates and numerous personal attacks on the two leading candidates.

In recent weeks, however, following drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea, the two frontrunners' diverging positions on support for Ukraine have come to the fore.

Bulgaria's government initially declined invitations to join the Coalition of the Willing and NATO's anti-drone initiative but changed its position on the latter after the recent drone attacks.

Yotova has advocated for the establishment of a "Coalition of Peace," in which she believes Bulgaria would have a stronger diplomatic voice in the process to endRussia's war in Ukraine.

"There are many warmongers in our country; I am not one of them," she said at a campaign rally this month. "As long as I am president — and if you place your trust in me — not a single Bulgarian soldier will go to Ukraine."

Yotova has sought to reassure voters that no Bulgarian troops will be sent to Ukraine, even though this has not featured in public debate, and has been ruled out by a 2025 parliamentary declaration that reaffirmed that the Bulgarian Armed Forces would not participate in hostilities there.

Nevertheless, the recent drone attacks on commercial ships in the Black Sea have put new pressure on both the president and Rumen Radev's Progressive Bulgaria party.

The effect of the Black Sea drone strikes

"The drone strikes in the Black Sea brought the otherwise abstract geopolitical situation right into the daily lives of every Bulgarian," Boriana Dimitrova, managing partner of the Alpha Research market and social research agency, told DW.

After a second series of drone attacks on ships in waters off the Bulgarian coast, Prime Minister Rumen Radev (center right) summoned the Russian ambassador, Eleonora Mitrofanova (center left), for talks Image: BGNES

Many in Europe, including Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, have laid the blame for the attacks squarely at Russia's door. The fact that Bulgaria's leaders did not clearly attribute blame for the attacks fueled frustration across the country.

After the first drone attack, President Yotova convened the country's Consultative Council on National Security. Its subsequent declaration did not name the source of the threat in the Black Sea.

A week later, after the second attack, Prime Minister Radev said, "We lack solid, clear evidence to level accusations against any specific party; however logic suggests the outcome works to the advantage of Russia." He then summoned the Russian ambassador for talks.

Opposition to an 'ambiguous' foreign policy stance

The stance of the government and president is having an impact on the race.

"We're seeing a slight decline in support for Iliana Yotova, which is not threatening her first-place position by any means in the first round, but there has been a decline given the ambiguity of some of the positions she has taken," said Boriana Dimitrova.

As the issue of security entered the public debate, some Bulgarians took to the streets in Sofia to protest against what they saw as the government's ambiguous foreign policy stance on this matter.

"I think the drone attacks in the Black Sea and the utterly spineless stance of the president, the prime minister, and everyone acting in unison were the last straw, and I believe that, on the eve of the presidential election, this should serve as a catalyst," Vlada Tzenova, one of the protesters, told DW.

All this is reflected in the preliminary results of the latest opinion poll conducted by Alpha Research. While expected voter turnout is up, the gap between the two frontrunners has narrowed: Yotova is still ahead, leading Gyurov by about 12 percentage points in the first round, but the margin is smaller than it was.

Who could be the kingmaker?

Nevertheless, these recent dynamics do not necessarily mean a shift in the balance of power.

Protesters gathered in the Bulgarian capital in late September to voice grievances over the direction of state policies and perceived alignment with Russia Image: Artur Widak/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Panchugov said that Gyurov's campaign has been hampered by his hesitancy to declare his candidacy, a lack of "passion" in his campaign, and the fact that he made few comments on current affairs before he joined the race.

Moreover, supporters of the candidate of the pro-Russian nationalist Vazrazhdane (Revival) party, which ranked third in the Alpha Research poll, would be most likely to support Yotova in a second round.

What could decide the outcome of the election is the fact that both GERB and DPS, two of the established parties that attracted the support of more than 660,000 voters in April, did not field a presidential candidate.

According to Alpha Research, half of GERB's supporters do not intend to vote in the first round. The party dominated Bulgaria's political landscape for 17 years but lost power in December following mass anti-corruption protests backed by opposition parties supporting Andrey Gyurov.

Most of the remaining GERB supporters are expected to back Gyurov, as the party has historically opposed Iliana Yotova's political home, the Bulgarian Socialist Party.

At the same time, both Gyurov's campaign and nationalist parties are seeing increased mobilization, with the latter drawing support from voters disappointed by the government's cautious response to the drone attacks.

"We can view these elections as the first test of confidence in the party that recently won the election," Boriana Dimitrova said. "In peaceful times, the center attracts the most attention; in turbulent times, those candidates who take a clearer stance — regardless of the direction — gain greater visibility."
