World.title: Africa CDC calls crisis meeting as Ebola spreads
World.content:
African health officials will hold a crisis meeting as the Ebola outbreak spreads from Congo to neighboring countries and beyond. The "extraordinary virtual meeting" will convene on October 28.

Africa's Center for Disease Control (CDC) late Wednesday announced that it would convene an "extraordinary virtual meeting" of national health officials as the continent's latest Ebola outbreak continues to spread.

More than 9,500 people have been infected since the virus was first confirmed in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) in May. Nearly half of those infected have died.

The Africa CDC announcement followed news on Tuesday that the virus had spread to Nigeria, arriving with a woman who had returned from Uganda earlier in the month.

Authorities in Nigeria say they are tracing 44 contact persons, with Health Minister Muhammad Pate noting that officials are, "doing everything possible to contain this case."

Uganda, which recorded 20 cases in this latest outbreak and declared itself "Ebola-free" in July, has rejected Nigeria's claims. The World Health Organization (WHO) declared the Uganda outbreak over on August 27.

Did Ebola start spreading before officials even knew? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Virulent Ebola strain with no approved vaccines or treatments

This current outbreak involves the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which no approved vaccines or treatments exist. The strain was also matched to the patient in Nigeria.

"We did three levels of tests, but all molecular. The strain was Bundibugyo," said Olajumoke Babatunde, director of the public health laboratory service at the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention.

Africa CDC Director General Dr. Jean Kaseya billed the October 28 crisis meeting as a chance to "strengthen our collective response."

In all, the outbreak, which the WHO says is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak ever, has spread to four countries in Africa and is active in two of them.

One French national, a doctor doing humanitarian work in transmission zones inside Congo was infected but recovered after treatment at a specialized facility in France.

It has also spread wider than previous outbreaks, reaching central, eastern and western regions across Africa.

Africa CDC's Kaseya made note of this in a post to X late Wednesday, writing: "Ebola is now affecting three regions of Africa. The situation demands urgent action and political leadership at the highest level."

"We must now accelerate our actions, reinforce coordination and mobilize the full strength of our continent," Kaseya's post continued. "Africa has the expertise, the institutions and the capacity to defeat this outbreak. We must act together and we must act now."

For its part, the WHO advised "all countries in the region to sustain a high level of readiness as the DRC outbreak continues to evolve."

World.title: EU moves to loosen rules on pesticide use as experts sound the alarm
World.content:
The European Union wants to relax rules for pesticides, saying it will be easier for farmers to adopt more environmentally friendly options. But health and environmental experts say the risks are far too great.

As part of its drive to "streamline and simplify" EU laws, the European Commission has proposed sweeping changes for agriculture and food safety legislation. These include a move to ease rules controlling the use of pesticides and herbicides, which help fight pests and weeds.

Under current EU rules, which date back to 2011, primary pesticide components, or active substances, are only granted approval for limited periods of no more than 15 years.

The European Commission's proposed revamp of the system would make indefinite greenlighting — including of the controversial glyphosate, which has been linked to cancer and kills almost all plant life — the default. Safety reviews would only be done in exceptional cases, and regulatory authorities, not the industry, would bear responsibility.

The commission has said its goal is to cut costs, simplify work for authorities and help farmers stay competitive. Scientists and doctors, however, warn that concerns over human health and environmental impact from these toxic substances are being brushed aside.

Why does the EU want to deregulate pesticides?

The European Commission has said it's responding to complaints from farmers and the agriculture industry to clarify EU rules that govern pesticide use.

A joint statement released in May by 19 food associations, including CropLife Europe, which promotes pesticides, said complicated administrative procedures and a lengthy approvals process meant farmers were "left without any effective solutions to protect their crops against insects, weeds and diseases," putting food security and livelihoods at risk.

"The existing system of periodic renewal assessment of every active substance has become unsustainable," the commission's press service told DW, citing "chronic delays" and "bottlenecks" in the approval of new, more sustainable products.

In recent negotiations, EU member states said open-ended authorizations should be restricted to "low-risk active substances."

But their stance is still wanting to extend initial approval periods for other substances to up to 15 years, and a maximum of 25 years for renewals.

Herbert Dorfmann, a center-right Italian member of the European Parliament, said there is currently a yearslong delay in approving new pesticides, including more eco-friendly options, meaning farmers are forced to rely on older substances. Or, if these are banned, go without altogether.

The commission wants to "make the system more efficient and responsive," while guaranteeing that "the protection of human and animal health and the environment remain the highest priorities."

Dorfmann, who as co-rapporteur is responsible for interinstitutional negotiations on the issue, backs the commission's stance, saying the EU needs "to open up the system for innovation."

He aims to bring the parliament's proposal on the new pesticide rules to a vote among EU lawmakers before the end of the year.

How do pesticides affect human health, environment?

Ecologists and medical experts, however, have spoken out forcefully against the proposed changes, saying the potential implications for human health and the environment are being downplayed.

In September, more than 500 experts from across the EU signed an open letter calling on the European Parliament to suspend its consideration of the new regulations and conduct an independent investigation into health and environmental impacts.

On October 7, UN rights experts also backed the call for a full review into whether the proposed changes violated the EU's obligations under international human rights law, especially with regard to agricultural workers and children.

Pesticides can persist in the environment, contaminating water and degrading soils. They can also drive biodiversity loss and poison other animals higher up the food chain.

In January 2020, beekeepers in Berlin protested the continued authorization of glyphosate by leaving unsellable tainted honey at the entrance to Germany's Agriculture Ministry Image: Adam Berry/Getty Images

When it comes to humans, the European Environment Agency has said it was "not yet possible to estimate the burden of disease linked to current levels of exposure to all pesticides."

However, exposure to chemical pesticides, including banned substances that still persist in the environment, has been linked to various cancers, chronic respiratory disease, neurological disorders and developmental delays, as well as problems with fertility and behavior.

And exposure is widespread: A survey conducted between 2014 and 2021 found that 84% of urine samples from both children and adults in five European countries contained residue from two or more pesticides.

Martina Vijver, scientific director and ecotoxicology expert at Leiden University in the Netherlands, said experts were "deeply concerned" that the EU's current plan "will weaken rather than strengthen the level of protection for pesticide regulation."

Speaking at the European Parliament in September, she said regular reassessments were key to evaluating the safety of pesticides with new findings, pointing out that the perception of risk changes over time.

"The regulatory system must remain capable of correcting yesterday's decisions with tomorrow's knowledge," she said.

More than 50 substances banned since 2011

Salome Roynel, a policy officer at the Pesticide Action Network Europe, an NGO based in Brussels, said the harmful effects of pesticides aren't often fully understood until years later, when the product is up for reconsideration.

"New science emerges all the time," she told DW, highlighting how 56 active substances have been banned in the EU since 2011 as a result of periodic reviews.

That includes the insecticide chlorpyrifos, previously used in orchards and on vegetable and cereal crops, which has been tied to harmful effects on children's brain development.

Pesticides banned in Europe linked to bees deaths in Kenya To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Roynel said it was "obvious that there was some kind of alignment" between the changes proposed by the EU institutions and the demands of the pesticide lobby.

This echoes a new report by nonprofit research and campaign group Corporate Europe Observatory, which said Dorfmann and other lawmakers had "copy-pasted […] industry demands" into their regulatory proposals.

Dorfmann denied the lobby influence, telling DW he had met with "both sides, industry and environmental associations," in public debates on the issue.

"The main objective is not to keep old products in the market. The main objective is to bring new ones to the market," Dorfmann said.

Part of that plan, he added, would be to help more environmentally friendly "biocontrol" products and low-risk substances to bypass current administrative hurdles and get on the market faster.

Farmers need 'incentive' to switch to safer pesticides

It's an idea previously championed by Vijver, who agrees that the current system means more environmentally friendly pesticides are stuck in an administrative "traffic jam." She told DW that biocontrol products could go in a green "bus lane" to ease the way to approval at the European Food Safety Authority, while maintaining crucial safety reviews to filter out the more dangerous products.

Can we cut down on pesticide use with 'plant vaccines'? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Roynel also supports the plan to speed up approval for biocontrol substances, but said it needs to be part of a wider system change that includes financial support, monitoring and training to use these new products, as well as maintaining the restrictions on more harmful chemical pesticides ― not further deregulation.

"If farmers get easier access to synthetic pesticides tomorrow, they would have no incentive to switch to biocontrol," she said. "It's important to put [biocontrol pesticides] on the market and we fully support that, but… it will not be the silver bullet."

Edited by: Tamsin Walker

World.title: India news: CJP leaders Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka released from Tihar Jail
World.content:
10/22/2026 October 22, 2026 Amit Shah criticizes opposition over 'vote theft' protests

Indian Home Minister Amit Shah accused the opposition of using allegations of "vote theft" to challenge the BJP's electoral victories [FILE: July 6, 2026] Image: Naveen Sharma/ANI

Union Home Minister Amit Shah criticized Congress and the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) on Thursday over allegations of electoral irregularities, saying protests and demonstrations would not help them win elections, the Hindustan Times reported.

Speaking at an event in Delhi, Shah accused the opposition of using allegations of "vote theft" to challenge the Bharatiya Janata Party's (BJP) electoral victories.

Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi has claimed that India's election authority had enabled "vote theft," or manipulation of electoral rolls to favor Modi's BJP in the 2024 general elections.

Currently, the opposition along with the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and other student organizations are demanding the resignation of the country's controversy-hit Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, after more than 130 million names were removed from draft electoral rolls nationwide.

Meanwhile, separately, BJP spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia accused Gandhi of links with foreign-based organizations that he alleged were amplifying protests in India, the Times of India newspaper reported.

Bhatia alleged that the organizations were part of a wider effort to create unrest and undermine constitutional institutions, and demanded that Gandhi disclose details of his meetings with them, the report said.

World.title: Inteligencia artificial y manipulación: nuevas claves para interpretar lo que vemos en internet
World.content:
El avance de la tecnología permite a los estafadores generar fraudes digitales con mayor rapidez y, sobre todo, más convincentes. Frente a esta nueva generación de engaños hay hábitos sencillos que pueden ayudarnos a no caer: parar, pensar y verificar

Si un internauta de 2019 pudiera navegar por las redes sociales de hoy quedaría perplejo ante la dificultad para distinguir algunos vídeos generados por inteligencia artificial (IA) generativa de vídeos reales. En tan poco tiempo la tecnología ha evolucionado tanto, señala Carmen Torrijos, lingüista computacional especializada en este campo, que el ojo humano puede tener grandes dificultades para detectar determinados contenidos creados de manera sintética. Y los estafadores se aprovechan de ello. “Ahora tienen la posibilidad de crear anuncios, webs o de imitar la voz de personas en poco tiempo y con un resultado excelente”, añade.

Ese mismo internauta dudaría ante los sofisticados fraudes que cada día se lanzan a la red, como los anuncios de inversiones en los que se suplanta la identidad de personas conocidas, las tiendas online que venden productos inexistentes o las notas de voz que llegan de repente en forma de mensaje en nombre de un familiar que pide ayuda. “Vivimos un tiempo en el que consumimos contenidos cortos que nos exigen una reacción muy rápida, por eso son el caldo de cultivo perfecto para los engaños digitales”, alerta la experta.

Para luchar contra tanto espejismo existen tecnologías para detectar contenido sintético, pero ninguna ofrece una detección universal y completamente fiable, agrega Torrijos. Solo queda entrenarse en unos hábitos básicos para cambiar nuestra exposición a este tipo de trampas. Siga leyendo.

Anuncios generados con IA, una oferta demasiado buena para ser cierta

En las redes sociales proliferan contenidos creados con IA que utilizan imágenes, sonidos o textos impactantes, a menudo protagonizados por figuras públicas, para difundir contenidos falsos o manipulados y conseguir que el usuario haga clic. Estas son algunas señales para detectarlos:

Suplantan la identidad de personas o entidades conocidas. Recurren a fotos o vídeos generados con IA de famosos, sin su consentimiento, para explotar la confianza que genera un rostro popular. También pueden utilizan la imagen de compañías conocidas o medios de comunicación a través de sus logos y sus colores corporativos.

Prometen un producto o un servicio extraordinario. Lo más común, explica Martín Vigo, fundador de la empresa de ciberseguridad Triskel Security, son las inversiones que ofrecen grandes beneficios en poco tiempo. También se crean anuncios engañosos de videojuegos para el móvil. “Muestran unos gráficos de alta calidad en la publicidad que luego no se corresponden con los reales, mucho más básicos”, agrega el experto.

Crean una falsa sensación de urgencia. Presentan sus ofertas agresivas como una promoción limitada o exclusiva para quien la recibe.

El fraude se produce fuera del anuncio. Llevan al usuario a una página donde se le exige un pago por el supuesto servicio, se le solicitan sus datos personales a través de un formulario de captación, o se le redirecciona a una conversación en una plataforma de mensajería donde se continúa con la estafa.

El mayor engaño tras los anuncios: la estafa de inversión. Las falsas inversiones son uno de los principales usos fraudulentos de los anuncios generados con IA. En este fraude, el delincuente actúa como asesor financiero al frente de una empresa falsa, desde la que promete rentabilidades muy altas si se le confía dinero o criptomonedas. Los estafadores aseguran que la cantidad inicial puede multiplicarse hasta por diez.

Después de realizar el primer pago, el estafador suele mostrar a la víctima los rendimientos a través de una aplicación falseada. Entonces le sugiere una aportación mayor. En el momento en el que el inversor decide recuperar su capital, se le exige más dinero, en concepto de comisión o pago de impuestos. Si paga, la estafa continúa; si no, el estafador se esfuma y con él todo lo invertido.

Comercios ‘online’ falsos, creados al detalle mediante IA

La IA permite a los estafadores dar forma a tiendas digitales con todos los elementos que hoy tienen este tipo de páginas. Ofrece la posibilidad de elaborar textos, imágenes de productos y un diseño coherente, incluso falsas reseñas de usuarios, explica Vigo. “Muchas de las herramientas de IA generativa dan la posibilidad de hacer todo esto en cuestión de horas. También clonar una web de alguna marca conocida”, detalla el experto. “Si, además, se compra un dominio que se parezca mucho al original, pero que no sea exactamente igual, el engaño resulta todavía más difícil de identificar”, completa. Vigo recomienda conocer sus características para estar alerta:

Pueden imitar con gran precisión la apariencia de páginas legítimas. Cuidan al máximo todos los aspectos, como la política de privacidad, las condiciones de compra, entre otros. Incluso pueden disponer de un servicio de atención al cliente mediante un bot de IA.

Ofrecen precios anormalmente bajos. Su principal gancho son los descuentos, especialmente en productos de marcas conocidas, bajo el pretexto de una falsa liquidación, un excedente de existencias o una promoción temporal.

‘Comercializan’ productos atractivos. En muchas ocasiones promocionan artículos con propiedades extraordinarias, como aparatos para eliminar lesiones o cremas antiarrugas que garantizan resultados prodigiosos; también juguetes o electrodomésticos con funcionalidades de ciencia ficción o muebles de formas sorprendentes.

Incorporan sistemas de pago reales. Utilizan plataformas de pago como las de las tiendas legítimas porque su objetivo es obtener el dinero de los compradores; muchas solo aceptan transferencia, Bizum o métodos sin protección al comprador. Existen varios tipos de comercios fraudulentos en línea, describe Vigo: los que no realizan ningún envío una vez se ha realizado el pago, los que despachan un producto de mucha peor calidad que el anunciado y los que su único objetivo es capturar los datos de la tarjeta de la víctima.

Se publicitan en buscadores y en redes sociales. Suelen promocionarse a través de anuncios creados con IA en las principales plataformas.

Aprovechan acontecimientos comerciales. Multiplican sus anuncios en momentos de grandes compras como los periodos de rebajas, Black Friday o Navidad, donde se camuflan entre el aluvión de ofertas.

Tienen una vida muy corta. Suelen desaparecer una vez que han obtenido un determinado número de pedidos o de datos de los usuarios. Lo más habitual es que vuelvan a aparecer con otro dominio y otra identidad.

Pueden fingir la tramitación del pedido. Suelen enviar correos electrónicos falsos sobre el estado del pedido, con órdenes de compra y facturas falsas e incluso información ficticia sobre el seguimiento del envío. Lo hacen para reforzar la apariencia de legitimidad en todos los canales de contacto con el comprador y prolongar el engaño.

Tres segundos para suplantar una voz, el auge del ‘deepfake’

La gran revolución de la IA generativa, señalan los expertos, es la creación de vídeos y audios que imitan la apariencia y la voz de una persona con tal precisión que engañan tanto a algoritmos como a humanos. La palabra deepfake combina los conceptos en inglés deep learning, que significa aprendizaje profundo, y fake, que quiere decir falso.

“Hoy, esta tecnología ha avanzado mucho”, explica Torrijos, lingüista computacional especializada en IA. “Antes se necesitaba hasta una hora de voz para clonar a una persona con garantías. Hoy bastan tres segundos para lograr una reproducción aceptable y 15 para obtener una imitación óptima”. Este es el uso fraudulento más extendido en la actualidad y el que más preocupación genera, añade Torrijos. De esta técnica se valen los estafadores en fraudes tanto en el ámbito familiar como en el empresarial. Y se usa en mensajes cortos, explica la experta, ya que camuflan mejor cualquier fallo de la clonación y no permiten a la víctima pararse a reflexionar.

La estafa del hijo en apuros. El estafador clona la voz de un familiar de la víctima, que suele ser un hijo o un nieto, y le envía, desde un número desconocido, mensajes cortos a través de una plataforma de mensajería instantánea. En esas notas de voz el estafador plantea una emergencia, como que ha perdido el teléfono, y escribe desde el de un amigo, o ha tenido un accidente y se ha quedado sin batería y ha de realizar un pago con urgencia. Se trata de una estafa que con el avance de la IA se produce cada vez más por notas de voz. Los estafadores suelen estudiar a sus víctimas a través de sus redes sociales, en el caso de que no sean privadas, señala el Instituto Nacional de Ciberseguridad (INCIBE). De esta manera pueden recopilar información sobre los miembros de la familia, así como números de teléfono y audios de voz con los que generar la estafa.

La estafa del CEO. En este tipo de fraude, el delincuente suplanta la identidad de un directivo de una empresa, habitualmente un CEO (siglas en inglés de chief executive officer, puesto equivalente a director ejecutivo). El objetivo es engañar a uno de sus empleados para que revele información privada que puede ser utilizada posteriormente o realice una transferencia a una cuenta ajena a la compañía. La Agencia de la Unión Europea para la Cooperación Policial (Europol) señala que cada vez es más común el uso de la IA en esta modalidad de estafa a través del deepfake. La clonación de voz es el uso más extendido, pero la facilidad para clonar la imagen que permiten los programas de última generación está multiplicando los ataques en los que también se suplanta la apariencia física y los movimientos de directivos.

Ante fraudes perfeccionados con IA, ¿qué se puede hacer? El principal recurso de los usuarios de internet para no caer en estafas generadas con IA es la misma que para el resto de fraudes: pararse un segundo a pensar y verificar por otro canal. Una pausa antes de actuar. Muchos fraudes están diseñados para provocar una reacción inmediata, como una supuesta oportunidad de inversión que termina en unas horas, un producto rebajado temporalmente o un familiar que necesita dinero de manera urgente. Esta premura reduce el tiempo que la víctima puede dedicar a pensar y favorece que actúe instintivamente. Al mismo tiempo, señala Vigo, la exigencia de una respuesta inmediata ha de ser un indicador que haga saltar la alerta de que se puede estar frente a un engaño. Verificar por otro canal. Si un contenido genera dudas sobre si es real o ha sido generado con IA, los expertos recomiendan comprobarlo por otra vía. En el caso de un anuncio generado con IA. No clicar en el anuncio. Si promete una inversión extraordinaria, un producto muy rebajado, ponerlo bajo sospecha. Se debe buscar información por otro canal, como los buscadores, o comprobar si la empresa se encuentra en el registro oficial de la Comisión Nacional del Mercado de Valores (CNMV), que cuenta con una sección de Advertencias sobre Entidades No Autorizadas. Se actualiza periódicamente, pero que no aparezca ahí no significa que sea fiable, puede deberse a que aún no la haya detectado.

En el caso de una tienda online. Si se ha llegado a la web a través de un anuncio, conviene realizar una búsqueda por otra vía, como los buscadores. Se puede recabar más información añadiendo al nombre términos como estafa, fraude, reclamaciones... Si se trata de una marca conocida, comprobar la URL, si se parece al nombre de la marca pero no es igual, conviene desconfiar.

En el caso de recibir una petición urgente de un familiar o de un directivo. Comprobar la petición por el número habitual de esa persona, nunca devolver la llamada desde “llamadas recientes o perdidas”. Vigo recomienda acordar de antemano una contraseña familiar: una palabra o una pregunta con una respuesta que solo conozcan los miembros de la familia. Si alguien llama o envía una nota de voz pidiendo dinero con urgencia, basta con pedirle esa palabra. Una voz clonada puede imitar el tono y la forma de hablar, pero no puede saber algo que nunca se ha dicho en público. En el caso del superior, contactar por las vías oficiales o incluso, si fuera posible, confirmar la petición en persona.

World.title: Mi vecina es morosa y ocupa la vivienda de su madre fallecida. ¿A quién reclamamos la deuda?
World.content:
Pregunta. Tenemos una vecina morosa que acumula una deuda de más de 6.000 euros. Los propietarios murieron y la casa está habitada por la hija y la familia de esta. No se adjudicaron la herencia. La hija y los dos hijos mayores de edad trabajan, mientras que el el marido cobra una pensión no contributiva. ¿Cómo podríamos cobrar la deuda? ¿Se podría hacer alguna anotación de la deuda en la finca? F.J. Callejón

Respuesta. Cuando los propietarios de la vivienda han fallecido y los herederos no han aceptado ni rechazado la herencia, los bienes forman una herencia yacente. Las reclamaciones judiciales por impago de cuotas comunitarias deben dirigirse contra la herencia yacente y los herederos desconocidos o potenciales.

Respecto a la ocupación de la vivienda por parte de la hija con su familia, con carácter general, el Tribunal Supremo y las Audiencias Provinciales determinan que no se puede condenar al pago de cuotas comunitarias a un heredero si no se acredita que ha aceptado la herencia, bien de forma expresa o tácitamente. El uso de la vivienda puede ser indicio de aceptación tácita de la herencia, pero esto debe ser valorado y declarado en el procedimiento judicial correspondiente. Por ejemplo, la Audiencia Provincial de Madrid considera que el uso y disfrute de los bienes de la herencia podría constituir un acto de aceptación tácita de la misma (artículo 999 del Código Civil). Si formalmente no se considera aceptada la herencia, la deuda recae sobre la herencia yacente (el patrimonio del fallecido que aún no tiene titular adjudicado). Si se considera aceptada la herencia, entonces el heredero responde de las deudas de la comunidad de forma solidaria con su propio patrimonio.

Respecto a la anotación de la deuda sobre la finca, no se trata de una cuestión sencilla. Para que el Registro de la Propiedad y el juzgado permita una anotación preventiva de embargo sobre los bienes, es necesario acreditar el título sucesorio e identificar quiénes son los herederos concretos titulares de esos derechos.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: Afghans washed up on Texel were human smuggling victims
World.content:
Two Afghan men whose body parts washed ashore on Texel in 2023 were victims of a vast human smuggling network led by infamous migrant smuggler Idriss Ghazi Kareem, according to an investigation by regional broadcaster NH and investigative TV programme Zembla.

The Afghan refugees, Samiullah (20) and Ahmad Jan (27), were only identified this summer. They had boarded a rubber dinghy on the night of August 12, 2023, along with 66 others just north of Calais, in an attempt to cross the English Channel. The boat’s engine failed and, after an explosion, the vessel tore apart.

Although 60 men survived, six were declared dead when found. Samiullah and Ahmad Jan, though, had gone missing.

Two months later, a single foot still in a shoe and a torso washed up on Texel. Dutch detective Fetze Venema worked with the Red Cross to identify the remains, including tracking down the relatives of the missing men in Afghanistan for DNA testing.

Idriss Ghazi Kareem

Following the incident, French authorities dismantled a huge human-trafficking network led by Idriss Ghazi Kareem. He was tried with eight others in Paris last year and sentenced to 15 years in prison for, among other things, procuring boats and other equipment for migrants to cross the English Channel.

The court found he earned hundreds of thousands of euros a year from his people-smuggling operations, which he continued to organise from prison.

Kareem had visited the Netherlands several times, including just three days before the fatal accident. The Marechaussee, the military police force responsible for border control, says the country plays a key role in people-smuggling.

“It involves the import, transit, and storage of nautical equipment that is transported to the French coast, where it is then used to ferry migrants across to Great Britain.”

The Marechaussee has not commented on the latest media investigation, saying it “may be part of an ongoing investigation”.

Additional research by NH and Zembla found that at least 26 people, including eight women and two children, have died this year attempting to cross the English Channel in unseaworthy boats.

“Floating coffins”

Much of the equipment – from the rubber boat to its motor and life vests – was substandard. “These rubber boats are not seaworthy and generally originate from China,” national public prosecutor for migration-related crime Petra Hoekstra told Zembla. “They are imported into the Netherlands via Turkey.”

And, he said, the smugglers knew that. “For us, that is an aggravating circumstance. They believe that the money outweighs a human life. And that means they are deliberately placing people in floating coffins.”

World.title: Rotterdam police arrest AI scammers over €400k thefts
World.content:
Police in Rotterdam have rounded up a gang who ran a sophisticated phishing scam using a fake banking app that stole nearly €400,000 from 170 victims.

The gang set up a bogus bank helpdesk service that targeted customers by phone and asked them to download an app that could read the NFC chip on their bank card.

Police arrested the two men behind the operation, a 23-year-old man from Vaassen, and a 25-year-old man from Ede, on October 4. On Tuesday they appeared in court, where a magistrate extended their detention for 90 days.

The fraudsters made the scam more plausible by using AI-generated voices to read out messages telling their victims to check if Google Pay had been installed on their phones by their bank.

When they saw it had not, they were told to press 1, which connected them straight to the fake helpdesk.

The victims were told to install the app and hold their card to their phone, allowing the criminals to download their details. At the same time accomplices would try to hack into the account using the card’s PIN.

Ruben van Well, head of the Rotterdam cybercrime team, said the victims ranged in age from their twenties to their eighties. “We found a lot of young people had been defrauded,” he said. “The victims also came from all over the country.”

Police confiscated hundreds of thousands of euros in cryptocurrency following the arrests and took the fake app and server offline. “We are not ruling out further arrests,” said Van Well.

World.title: Lost Erasmus book returns to Rotterdam after 400 years
World.content:
A book by Dutch Renaissance philosopher Desiderius Erasmus, which was thought to be lost, has been returned to Rotterdam after being identified by a collector in the US.

La civilité puérile (The Civility of Children) is a short collection of thoughts on good manners in children, printed in French in 1609.

The booklet contains rules such as: “It is downright ridiculous to make trumpet sounds with your nose: leave that to horn players and elephants.”

“If someone else sneezes, you must wish them good health (pay close attention to that)” is another piece of advice, along with “only sit down at the table after you have washed your hands, and cut your nails too.”

John Tholen, a curator at the Rotterdam Library, told regional broadcaster Rijnmond that getting the book back after four centuries was a very special event.

“We have found an unknown piece of the puzzle regarding the history and influence of Erasmus’s ideas,” Tholen said. “This copy is the only one left in the world from a print run of perhaps as many as 1,000.”

The UNESCO Erasmus Collection in Rotterdam holds more than 3,000 editions of the scholar’s works, plus another 3,000 books and articles about him published after 1900.

World.title: Off the rails: a final goodbye to the Apekop train
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The iconic Apekop train, officially known as Mat ’64 (Materieel ’64), made its last journey on Wednesday before heading back into retirement.

Originally retired from service in 2016, the passenger train was brought back by operator Keolis last year, to the delight of train enthusiasts, to run between Amersfoort and Barneveld Zuid after refurbishment work on newer trains led to a rolling stock shortage.

But its 12.25pm departure from Barneveld Zuid on Wednesday is said to be its final trip. The train will now return to Stichting 2454CRW, a volunteer organisation that maintains old trains.

First appearing on Dutch tracks in 1961, the Mat ’64, the last NS train built largely in the Netherlands, came to symbolise Dutch commuter travel. The trains served passengers for more than five decades, with hundreds in service at their peak.

The nickname Apekop, which translates as “monkey head”, comes from the train’s distinctive rounded nose.

World.title: Health insurance could cost you €177 more next year
World.content:
Healthcare premiums are set for their biggest rise in 15 years after insurer DSW announced its premium will go up by €14.75 a month in 2027.

The basic insurance package, which is compulsory for everyone, will cost €173.50 per month, or €2,082 a year.

DSW is traditionally the first Dutch health insurer to publish its rates for the following year, but all companies tend to follow a similar line because the content of the basic package is prescribed by law.

The rise of 9.3% is the largest in percentage terms since 2011, when premiums went up by 10%.

“In the eight years I have worked here I have never seen such a big increase,” Aad de Groot, chair of DSW’s board of directors, told broadcaster NOS.

It is also more than the €12.50 estimated by the health ministry in its budget calculations for next year. The maximum health benefit (zorgtoeslag) is going up by €11 a month for people earning the minimum wage, meaning low earners will have to pay more out of their own pockets for health cover.

The excess, or deductible, on health insurance is also going up for the first time in a decade. From January patients will have to pay the first €400 for treatment covered by the basic plan, up from the current level of €385.

De Groot said the government had not taken into account cuts to mental health care, hospital care and care at home in its calculations. “The effect is that the state is paying less but individuals are paying more through their premiums,” he said.

People whose earnings are just above the threshold for government support will be hit hardest, he added. Some 200,000 people have fallen behind on their insurance payments, according to the CAK, the government agency that handles healthcare bills, up from 172,000 in 2022.

“We see a growing group of people who are struggling to pay their premiums,” De Groot said. “It is a painful increase, but we have no option but to do this.”

Insurers must publish their rates by November 12, after which Dutch residents have until the end of the year to decide whether to switch to a different insurer for 2027.

World.title: European Commission investigates Booking over scams
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The European Commission has launched an investigation into whether Amsterdam-based travel site Booking.com has breached data protection laws by not cracking down on fake adverts.

The Brussels-based commission will also consider whether the company told site users which adverts had been ranked higher in search results because their owners had paid more, as is required under transparency rules.

In a third branch of the investigation, Booking.com is accused of exposing users to phishing scams by hackers who gained access to the company’s reservation and guest data.

Booking.com could be hit with fines amounting to 6% of its turnover if the commission decides it has breached the rules and refuses to change its policies.

The number of scams reported on the website increased by 500% between 2022 and 2024, with fraud totalling €4.2 billion in 2024 alone.

Henna Virkkunen, European commissioner for tech sovereignty, said: “Europeans should be able to book their holidays without fear of being scammed.”

In a statement, Booking.com said it was “cooperating fully” with the investigation, adding: “security, trust and the protection of personal information are top priorities.”

“We remain committed to working with relevant governments, regulators, law enforcement and industry partners to combat cybercrime and online fraud and protect travellers and partners,” the company said.

World.title: Feyenoord second best to Betis as Isco is on the spot for CL win
World.content:
Feyenoord endured a frustrating evening in Spain as a penalty by Real Betis’s outstanding player, Isco, secured a 1-0 win for the La Liga side.

The Rotterdammers were second best for most of the game, but held out until the 59th minute, when Abde Ezzalzouli’s cross hit the arm of Jeremiah St. Juste in front of goal.

Isco, who was at the heart of Betis’s attacks all evening, grabbed the ball and gave Tjark Ernst no chance from the penalty spot.

Ernst had made good saves from former AZ Alkmaar striker Troy Parrott and Marc Batra to keep Feyenoord in the game in the first half, but Feyenoord had the best chance of the opening period when Gjivai Zechiël shot over the bar from close range.

The visitors had a claim for a penalty of their own turned down in the 68th minute when Givairo Read claimed he had been pushed by Ezzalzouli, but referee Simone Sozza waved the appeals away.

The result leaves Giovanni van Bronckhorst’s side in 26th place in the Champions League table, with Internazionale up next in De Kuip on November 3.

World.title: Some important websites remain down after emergency shutdowns
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Websites in the Netherlands are coming back online following emergency shutdowns. This follows the discovery of vulnerabilities in the programming language on which many government, hospital and news sites are built, including Dutch News.

The organisation behind PHP, one of the world’s most widely used programming languages, said on Tuesday it would patch two flaws in its code.

The announcement prompted hackers to search for the holes and begin trying to attack sites, which US cyber security firm Cloudflare said on Wednesday it was noticing and defending against.

Sites were then swiftly taken down, including the government’s digital ID system DigiD and its online services portal MijnOverheid, the website of parliament, the umbrella organisation for the water boards, and a tool used by local councils for storing documents and scheduling meetings.

Some important sites, like anonymous crime reporting site Meld Misdaad Anoniem and domestic safety reporting network Veilig Thuis, were still offline on Thursday morning.

Disruptions

Dutch media companies were hit – RTL’s news website and app went down, and broadcaster NPO shut down the system used to upload content to its streaming services.

Several hospitals also took their websites down, as well as charities such as KWF cancer fund and the Dutch Heart Foundation.

Schiphol airport’s app stopped showing live flight information, and benefits agency UWV took a tool people use to report sick or recovered offline.

The problem was not limited to the Netherlands – the Flemish, German, French and Finnish governments all took websites offline.

What happened

Two critical flaws in PHP’s programming language were discovered in August using AI models from OpenAI and Google.

Google-owned cybersecurity firm Wiz, one of the firms that reported the flaws to PHP, said that the vulnerabilities in PHP had existed for over a decade, and said they ranked “among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history”.

PHP built fixes for the vulnerabilities into an update and said all companies using its code should install the update immediately. Prime minister Rob Jetten reiterated this call on social media.

Justice minister David van Weel said the fact that so many websites had been taken offline as a precaution “has an impact on our digital society”.

“Fortunately, there are currently no indications that the vulnerabilities are being actively exploited,” Van Weel stated through his spokesperson.

The National Cyber Security Centre said it had not seen any active hacks, and the PHP Foundation told news agency ANP it also had no indication of breaches.

World.title: How will recent scandals affect Polish politics?
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Aleks Szczerbiak Political scandals generate intense media attention and public outrage but rarely produce dramatic shifts in party support that they once did. They are now more likely to affect electoral outcomes indirectly by demobilising softer, less committed voters and influencing turnout, particularly among supporters of the government disappointed by its apparent underperformance and broken election promises. The hospital scandal Two high-profile political scandals dominated the Polish news agenda for much of this summer. The first centred on irregularities at Warsaw’s Southern Hospital (Szpital Południowy) and involved a young and relatively inexperienced doctor, Dawid Kacprzyk. In spite of his lack of a specialist qualification, Kacprzyk coordinated the hospital’s emergency department and reportedly earned a staggering 1.6 million złoty (€366,000) in the previous year alone. He also served as a Warsaw district councilor for the liberal-centrist Civic Coalition (KO) grouping, Poland’s main governing party led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. Public outrage intensified following reports that the hospital had operated a dedicated “VIP path” or special lounge where ruling-party-linked politicians and their families were allowed faster access and medical examinations without the usual queues faced by ordinary patients. Further claims emerged, including a whistleblower surgeon alleging that supervisory failures contributed to patient deaths and of improper private business activity in the hospital morgue. Poland’s health minister has unveiled a set of reforms intended to “rebuild trust” in public hospitals following a series of reports about exorbitant pay for some doctors and that politically connected patients could skip queues and use a "VIP lounge" https://t.co/pidAHxohc4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 8, 2026 For its part, KO insisted that the scandal was the personal misconduct of one former party member rather than a general problem affecting the entire healthcare system. They noted that Kacprzyk quickly resigned his council seat and hospital role, and that party-aligned Warsaw mayor Rafał Trzaskowski had dismissed the hospital board and two of his deputy mayors overseeing the city’s health services. KO argued that no specific names of preferential VIP patients had been publicly confirmed, any irregularities were being fully investigated by prosecutors and independent bodies, and political and legal accountability would follow if ethical breaches or crimes were proven. The government also pledged systemic reforms including measures to curb excessive pay for doctors. Nonetheless, the scandal struck a deep chord with the Polish public, triggering massive negative media and political fallout that aligned perfectly with the right-wing opposition’s narrative painting KO as part of a “Warsaw elite” that enjoys special privileges at the expense of ordinary citizens. The cryptocurrency scandal The second major summer scandal centred on allegations of financial impropriety and political entanglement involving Zondacrypto, once Poland’s largest crypto trading platform, that claimed over a million users but earlier this year collapsed abruptly after thousands of retail investors were unable to access their funds. However, what began as a major financial scandal escalated into political warfare, providing the government with powerful ammunition to attack the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and currently the main opposition grouping, party-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, and the broader conservative political eco-system over payments and donations made by the crypto firm. Prosecutors are investigating possible criminal offences relating to financing by Zondacrypto, a collapsed crypto firm, of organisations and individuals linked to the right-wing opposition, including the Polish version of US conservative conference CPAC https://t.co/swceV864nA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 26, 2026 For example, Zondacrypto sponsored the 2025 Polish edition of the Conservative Political Action Committee (CPAC) conference attended by the then-presidential candidate Nawrocki, advertised heavily with conservative media outlets such as the TV Republika television network, and made donations to foundations linked to high-ranking PiS figures such as former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro. The government also tried to entangle Nawrocki, who repeatedly vetoed its cryptocurrency regulation laws, into the scandal, arguing that he was protecting the shady interests of the industry and its political beneficiaries at the expense of ordinary Poles (the Tusk administration lacks the three-fifths parliamentary majority required to overturn a presidential veto). For their part, PiS and the broader Polish right dismissed the government’s accusations as a smear campaign and sought to shift blame for the scandal onto the Tusk administration for inadequate oversight to protect investors. Figures on the right, including those connected to foundations that received money, framed these dealings as legitimate sponsorships common across the media and other organisations. The president of the Polish Olympic Committee has been detained as part of a criminal investigation into Zondacrypto, a crypto firm that collapsed earlier this year and was a major sponsor of Poland's Olympic team https://t.co/QPG7ejAImD — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 27, 2026 PiS rejected claims that the party or associated groups received funds from the firm and defended Nawrocki’s vetoes as necessary against flawed legislation. Nonetheless, opinion polls found that most respondents linked the scandal to PiS and the right-wing opposition, providing the government with numerous attack lines to force them onto the defensive. The diminishing impact of scandals It is worth recalling how an earlier era of post-communist politics scandals possessed much greater transformative, system-altering capacity and could act as catalysts for the restructuring of the electoral landscape. For example, at the beginning of the 2000s, the so-called “Rywin scandal” was widely seen as a decisive factor in the near-destruction as a political force of the previously powerful, and then-governing, communist-successor Democratic Left Alliance (SLD). The scandal erupted in late 2002 when film producer Lew Rywin allegedly solicited a large bribe from the Agora media group, publisher of the influential liberal-left Gazeta Wyborcza newspaper, in exchange for media legislation changes while claiming to act on behalf of a “group holding power” (grupa trzymająca władzę) linked to the ruling party. A high-profile parliamentary investigative commission, sustained media focus, and a series of follow-on scandals and accumulation of allegations of deep-seated influence peddling by post-communist networks created a powerful narrative of systemic bribery and corruption, completely discrediting the SLD as a competent governing force. Having won a substantial victory in the 2001 parliamentary election, securing 41% of the votes, its support collapsed to only 11% at the next 2005 poll. This helped clear the way for the rise of the KO (originally Civic Platform)-PiS duopoly that has structured the Polish party system ever since, thereby establishing a precedent that scandals were electorally fatal transgressions. The contrast with the recent hospital and cryptocurrency scandals is instructive and illustrates a broader transformation in the relationship between political misconduct and electoral politics in Poland. Whereas in the more fluid party system of the early post-communist period a cluster of major scandals or single-event shocks could rapidly destroy dominant parties and restructure competition, now – although they still generate intense, high-octane political and media outrage – such controversies appear to slide off the main political actors with remarkably little immediate consequence. Indeed, neither of these recent scandals produced the dramatic shift in headline polling numbers that some observers, drawing on historical precedent, might have anticipated given the intensity of the media coverage. Scandal-neutralising structural shifts This change stems from three interlocking shifts in the structural dynamics of Poland’s political system. Taken together, they have substantially diminished the capacity of scandals to move headline poll numbers and trigger the kind of large-scale systemic realignments seen in an earlier era of post-communist politics. Firstly, the sheer velocity of modern political communication prevents single-issue-based scandals from sustaining public focus. In the early 2000s, a major corruption scandal could dominate the news headlines for months through concentrated media attention. The Rywin scandal unfolded through prolonged televised parliamentary commission hearings, keeping the story alive and allowing public outrage to build into a sustained narrative that slowly drained the ruling party’s legitimacy. Today, digital algorithms and the 24-hour news cycle ensure that a major story, whether about healthcare management or cryptocurrency, moves at a breathtaking pace and is overtaken rapidly as public attention moves onto the next domestic controversy, international development, or strategic counter-narrative. Seven people have been charged in relation to alleged corruption in the issuing of Polish visas to foreign nationals The scandal has engulfed the government since last week, but officials say the opposition is exaggerating the scale and nature of the case https://t.co/iHnIShb1pQ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 15, 2023 This hyper-accelerated news cycle means that even a high-profile case that generates intense short-term media coverage does not remain the dominant story for long enough to produce cumulative, system-level damage by limiting the time window in which a scandal can convert temporary disapproval into lasting shifts in voting intentions. Scandals thereby become a form of ambient “background noise” in Polish public life rather than a singular focal point for popular outrage. Secondly, and perhaps most formidably, the protective shield of deep polarisation and socio-political division renders large segments of the electorate relatively impervious to allegations against “their” side. After 2005, the Polish party system crystallised around a durable “post-transition” socio-economic divide reinforced by cultural and geopolitical fault lines. In this deeply fractured and highly polarised landscape, with large segments of the electorate embedded within hostile camps, when a scandal like the hospital crisis or cryptocurrency controversy breaks, voters interpret allegations levelled against “their” party through a tribal filter as a politically motivated hit job or the work of hostile media. So even severe scandals are shaped by, and largely confirm, existing political loyalties and rarely trigger cross-camp voter defections. This is a sharp contrast with the early 2000s, when the party system was still fluid and electoral volatility high. Our essential guide to Poland's parliamentary elections, which will take place one year from now. How does voting work? What do polls suggest the outcome will be? Which issues may animate the campaign? And what role will President Nawrocki play? https://t.co/fmdoFpBaxz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2026 Thirdly, the parties themselves have become far more professional at message discipline and crisis management. Today’s parties are centralised media machines staffed by sophisticated public relations strategists who view a scandal not as a moral crisis but a communication problem requiring aggressive damage containment. Rather than allowing a controversy to fester, they immediately launch counterattacks, accusing their opponents of far greater historical or concurrent corruption, and ruthlessly enforce internal party discipline and message conformity. They also deploy well-rehearsed crisis management playbooks including: personnel sanctions; framing the problem as local or individual responsibility, or residual rather than systemic failure; ordering visible audits, investigations, or reforms to demonstrate “taking action”; and co-ordinated messaging that seeks to close the story quickly and shift the focus back onto the other side’s weaknesses or broader policy issues. Differential mobilisation, not voter persuasion Yet while polarisation and professional crisis management allow parties to survive the immediate news cycle, this does not mean that scandals have become irrelevant. Rather, their effects are more subtle and delayed through the “slow-burn” mechanism of differential turnout by selectively demobilising specific voter segments. Although in a highly polarised polity the most committed hard-core partisans are relatively immune to negative information about “their” side, soft or conditional supporters may become disillusioned, or simply less motivated, when repeated scandals reinforce a narrative of self-interest or incompetence. The net result is a gradual, cumulative, asymmetric demobilisation of one camp that does not fully register in standard inter-election voting intention surveys, which generally show expressed party preferences among those willing to answer but not necessarily the intensity of that preference or the probability that a respondent will actually turn out to vote. In Poland’s deeply polarised political landscape, the next parliamentary election, scheduled for autumn 2027, is unlikely to be determined by persuading voters to cross the ideological divide. Rather differential levels of electoral turnout and mobilisation are likely to be the key, specifically: whichever side’s core base is more motivated to – and peripheral, less ideologically committed “softer” supporters are demotivated from – showing up on polling day. Young Poles are bucking the international trend by turning out at a higher rate than the oldest voters in recent elections. We spoke with experts and young voters to find out more about the growing frustrations that are driving this political engagement https://t.co/y1JpYYmbjb — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2025 And in a context where the election is likely to be closely fought, and relatively small differences in participation rates could prove decisive, although they may not produce dramatic changes in headline party polling preferences, scandals can still play a significant role. However, we are only likely to see the full impact of any such scandals when voters eventually go to the polls and actual turnout patterns are revealed. Given the general disillusionment with the current government and growing narrative of its underperformance and failure to deliver on its electoral promises, scandals are more likely to contribute to the demobilisation of the governing camp. It is anyway inherently more difficult for incumbent parties to mobilise their disillusioned supporters to turn out and vote than it is for motivated oppositions to rally their base to oust them. Indeed, revealed voter preferences in the summer 2025 presidential election – when Nawrocki won an unexpected victory over Trzaskowski, the ruling party-backed favourite – and more recently the severe setback for KO in the Kraków mayoral by-election, suggest that government supporters are already showing greater reluctance to vote. So, while their effects are routinely neutralised by fast-moving news, tribal shielding and professional spin, scandals still matter in Polish politics, although the battleground has shifted from voter persuasion to differential mobilisation. A Polish soldier who accidentally shot a Syrian refugee who had entered Poland over the border from Belarus has been acquitted of negligent use of a weapon. The Syrian man had been seeking 50,000 zloty (€11,500) in compensation from the soldier. The verdict was welcomed by defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, whose ministry had supported the soldier’s legal defence. ❗Podporucznik Wojska Polskiego został dziś uniewinniony przez Wojskowy Sąd Garnizonowy w Warszawie. Nie udowodniono mu żadnych zaniedbań w czasie służby na granicy z Białorusią. W listopadzie 2023 r. przypadkowo postrzelił on migranta. Od początku zapewniliśmy mu pomoc prawną… pic.twitter.com/RS2p2WsQ7Z — Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) October 21, 2026 The incident in question took place in November 2023 in Poland’s northeastern Podlasie province. The soldier, named only as Adam Ł. under Polish privacy law and who holds the rank of second lieutenant, had only recently received his first posting to the border, reports legal news service Prawo.pl. Since 2021, Belarus has been encouraging, assisting and in some cases coercing tens of thousands of migrants, mainly from Asia and Africa, to try to cross into Poland. Among those who make it over the border, most head westwards to Germany, while some have sought to claim international protection in Poland. In response, Poland has posted thousands of soldiers to the border, where they provide support to the border guard and police. Officers have at times faced violence from migrants trying to cross. In one case, in June 2023, a Polish soldier died after being stabbed. Poland has named a Moroccan man, Mohamed Addamrou, as the suspect in the 2024 murder of a Polish soldier, Mateusz Sitek, who was fatally stabbed while trying to stop a group of migrants from forcing their way through the border from Belarus to Poland https://t.co/mw8JuOPwcE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 10, 2026 A few months after that tragedy, Adam Ł. took part in an operation to apprehend a group of migrants who had crossed from Belarus and were around 2 kilometres from the border. After the soldiers called on the migrants to stop, one of them, a 23-year-old Syrian man, began to flee. As Adam Ł. chased him, the soldier slipped and fell, resulting in his gun, a PM-98 Glauberyt submachine gun, accidentally discharging two rounds. One bullet hit the Syrian man in the back, close to his spine. The soldier immediately began providing him with first aid, before the Syrian was taken to hospital. He was discharged a few weeks later and, in May 2024, was granted asylum in Poland. Initially, when it appeared possible that the Syrian could suffer partial paralysis, military prosecutors considered charging Adam Ł. with negligent use of a weapon resulting in serious injury, a crime carrying a prison sentence of up to eight years. In the end, that was downgraded to a lower charge of negligent use of a weapon causing impairment or a health disorder, which is punishable by up to three years in prison. The defence ministry provided the soldier with legal counsel from a special team set up in 2024 to defend military personnel. They advised him not to plead guilty. Eventually, prosecutors asked only that the court impose an indemnity of 2,000 zloty on Adam Ł., to be paid to the Syrian. The Syrian’s lawyer, meanwhile, sought 50,000 zloty for his client. The president has signed into law new rules removing criminal liability from officers who use firearms while serving on the border. The measures were passed in response to a surge in aggression from some migrants seeking to cross the border from Belarus https://t.co/sBMaoYhoCw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 16, 2024 In a ruling announced on Wednesday, a military court in Warsaw fully acquitted Adam Ł. Judge Michał Żak said that it remained unclear how the incident unfolded. He also pointed to expert evidence commissioned by the court that found the soldier’s gun could have had defects that caused it to fire when it hit the ground. Those doubts, and a lack of convincing evidence to support the prosecutor’s version of events, meant the charge of negligence could not be proven, found Żak. The verdict can still be appealed. The Syrian’s lawyer said they would wait for the judge’s full written justification before deciding whether to appeal. Kosiniak-Kamysz, meanwhile, welcomed the ruling in a social media post. “From the very beginning, we provided him with legal assistance,” wrote the defence minister. “A soldier who carries out his duties cannot be left alone, even in a difficult situation.” In May this year, another soldier was acquitted over an incident in which he fired shots towards a group of migrants who had illegally crossed the Belarussian border. The judge found that, in fact, the soldier had been fulfilling his obligation to defend the Polish border. A Polish soldier who fired shots towards migrants who had illegally crossed the border from Belarus has been acquitted of abusing his powers and threatening the lives of others The military judge found he had been fulfilling his duty to protect the border https://t.co/ugxq5tkdFV — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 27, 2026 In 2024, Poland’s government introduced a new law making it easier for soldiers and other uniformed officers serving at the border to use firearms. They now no longer face criminal liability for employing their weapons in certain cases. Since then, the government has also further strengthened physical border barriers and banned asylum claims by migrants who cross irregularly from Belarus. That has been followed by a significant drop in attempted crossings by migrants from Belarus: in the first half of this year, only 250 attempts were recorded, down from 15,500 in the same period of 2025 – a 98% drop. Poland also now claims to have a 100% success rate in apprehending those who do manage to cross. World.title: Poland condemns Ukrainian region for honouring figures associated with WWII massacres of Poles
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has condemned a decision by the Lviv region in Ukraine to declare 2027 a year honouring the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which led the massacre of Poles during World War Two, and one of its leaders, Roman Shukhevych. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the decision “suicidal”, saying that it harms Ukraine by making it harder for the country’s friends to support it. Foreign minister Radosław Sikorski announced that the local official responsible for pushing through the commemorations in Lviv has been banned from entering Poland. Decyzja Lwowskiej Rady Obwodowej, by 2027 rok był rokiem UPA i Szuchewycza, jest nieakceptowalna. Taka decyzja nie buduje wzajemnego zaufania między narodami, lecz wzmacnia podziały. Konieczne jest odcięcie się władz Ukrainy od tego stanowiska. — Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) October 20, 2026 On Tuesday, the Lviv regional council adopted resolutions proclaiming 2027 the year of the UPA, of Shukhevych, and of Oleh Olzhych, a poet and leading figure in the Organisation of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN). Sviatoslav Sheremeta, chair of the region’s committee on culture, said the decisions will pave the way for “large-scale events” to commemorate the UPA, Shukhevych and Olzhych. “This is our history, our heroes, and we must duly honour their memory,” he added, quoted by local news service Sokal Voice. The OUN was a nationalist organisation that sought Ukrainian independence. The UPA, a partisan formation, emerged in 1942 from a more radical faction of the OUN, with Shukhevych serving as its military commander. While the UPA is still remembered positively by some in Ukraine for its role in fighting against Moscow-imposed Soviet rule, in Poland it is associated with the Volhynia massacres, in which the UPA led the slaughter of around 100,000 Poles, mostly women and children. Poland has previously condemned official commemorations in Ukraine of Shukhevych and other figures associated with the UPA. And the resolutions adopted by the Lviv region on Tuesday likewise prompted a swift response from Warsaw. “Glorifying the UPA and criminal figures is contrary to European values ​​and the strategic and good-neighbourly nature of relations between Poland and Ukraine,” foreign ministry spokesman Maciej Wewiór told news website Wirtualna Polska. “Shukhevych is a criminal stained with the blood of thousands of innocent victims, people who were murdered simply because they were Poles,” he added, also noting that the UPA’s victims included Jews, Czechs, Armenians and Ukrainians themselves. Wewiór warned that, while the Ukrainian and Polish governments have recently made progress towards reconciliation over historical issues, “irresponsible local activists are damaging these relations by honouring people clearly responsible for crimes and collaborating with the Nazis”. The European Parliament has criticised Ukraine's @ZelenskyyUa for naming a military unit after a group that massacred Poles during WWII, calling it an "unprovoked escalation" that is “not in line with European values” and "disregards Polish sensitivities" https://t.co/54rbPSrs9S — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 8, 2026 On Wednesday, Tusk said that such decisions “harm Ukraine” by “making the work of Ukraine’s friends and supporters of closer cooperation very difficult”. By contrast, the “Russians always rub their hands in glee in situations like these”, added Tusk, quoted by Polsat News. Meanwhile, Sikorski announced that he had signed a motion to place Sheremeta, who has led the efforts to commemorate the UPA and Shukhevych in Lviv, on Poland’s “list of undesirable persons”. Wirtualna Polska reports that Sheremeta was previously banned from entry in 2017, under Poland’s former government, for his actions in blocking the exhumation and commemoration of Polish massacre victims buried in Ukraine. Podpisałem wniosek o wpisanie na listę osób niepożądanych w RP radnego obwodu lwowskiego S. Szeremeta, rekonstruktora Galizien Waffen-SS, autora pomysłu ustanowienia 2027 rokiem R.Szuchewycza, dowódcy UPA, który wydawał rozkazy wysiedlania i mordowania Polaków.… — Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) October 21, 2026 Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) also condemned the resolutions. It called Shukhevych “an architect of the genocide in Volhynia” as well as the “co-founder of collaborationist units operating alongside Germany”. It quoted an order issued by Shukhevych in which he wrote: “Cut them down to the last man. Burn villages inhabited exclusively by Poles; in mixed villages, eliminate only the Polish population.” However, the IPN noted that Olzhych – whom Lviv is also honouring next year – was the head of a group that condemned the crimes committed by the more radical faction of the OUN. The Lviv Regional Council has designated 2027 in the Lviv region as the Year of Roman Shukhevych, an architect of the genocide in Volhynia, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), and Oleh Olzhych, a leader of the OUN-M. Among those being commemorated, Roman Shukhevych stands out as… pic.twitter.com/Bge2muwjHz — Institute of National Remembrance (@ipngovpl_eng) October 21, 2026 Polish leaders have previously warned that the honouring of the UPA and figures associated with it would harm Ukraine’s chances of joining the European Union. Poland, like all other member states, can veto accession. However, there have also been recent signs of progress on issues of historical memory. Last year, in a diplomatic breakthrough, Ukraine lifted a ban on exhuming the remains of Volhynia massacre victims on its territory. But this year, President Volodymyr Zelensky triggered a diplomatic crisis when he approved the naming of a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. Since then, tensions have calmed, with Zelensky setting out a five-point plan that includes approving more exhumations. This month, the head of the IPN and its Ukrainian counterpart held their first meeting since 2018. World.title: Parliament approves liberalisation of Poland’s abortion laws
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The government’s majority in parliament has approved two bills that would liberalise Poland’s strict abortion laws. One would reverse the 2020 constitutional court ruling introducing a near-total ban on abortion; the other would decriminalise providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions. However, it appears likely that both measures will be vetoed by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition. His chief of staff reiterated on Tuesday that Nawrocki “supports the protection of life from conception to natural death”. Mamy to! Sejm przyjął dwa projekty: dekryminalizujący pomocnictwo w aborcji i przywracający aborcyjny kompromis. To niezbędne minimum i pierwszy krok. Jesteśmy to winni kobietom. pic.twitter.com/1yLyfuFCQC — Aleksandra LEO (@AleksandraLeo) October 20, 2026 When Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, took power in December 2023 from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, it pledged to soften abortion laws. However, since then, it has failed to do so, largely due to disputes between more conservative and liberal elements within the coalition. But now, a year ahead of parliamentary elections, that has changed, with the more powerful lower-house Sejm pushing through two abortion bills on Tuesday. One would once again allow abortions to be carried out in cases where a severe foetal abnormality is diagnosed. That would reverse a ruling by the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in 2020 outlawing such abortions, which the TK found contravened various constitutional principles, including the right to life. That judgement, which went into force in January 2021, means that abortion is currently only allowed in two cases: when a pregnancy results from a crime (such as rape or incest) or when it threatens the mother’s life or health. In Europe, only Malta has a stricter abortion law. The ruling was issued when the TK was stacked with PiS-appointed judges – including three who had been illegitimately appointed – and regarded as being under the control of the then-ruling party. It prompted the largest protests Poland has witnessed since the communist era. In the Sejm vote on Tuesday, 233 MPs were in favour of the new bill, with 203 opposed. Support came from parties in Tusk’s coalition, as well as the small left-wing Together (Razem). Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and The Left (Lewica), one of its coalition partners, have previously expressed support for an even greater liberalisation of the law, allowing abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. However, all of their MPs voted in favour of the compromise option on the table. Meanwhile, five MPs from the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), the most conservative element of the coalition, joined with the right-wing and far-right opposition in voting against the bill. In a separate vote, the Sejm also approved a bill that would decriminalise the act of helping a woman obtain an unlawful abortion. Currently, that is an offence that carries a prison sentence of up to three years. A previous attempt to pass such a bill was defeated in 2024, after most PSL MPs joined with the opposition to block it. That prompted Tusk to declare that abortion reform would be impossible during the current parliamentary term. However, on Tuesday, 217 MPs voted in favour and 213 against, meaning the bill was approved. A total of 27 MPs failed to attend the vote, including 10 from PiS, among them party leader Jarosław Kaczyński. If they had participated, the bill would likely have been rejected. All MPs from KO, The Left and Razem voted in favour of the bill, as did almost all from the centrist Poland 2050. However, 14 PSL MPs joined with the opposition in voting against it, including PSL’s leader, deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz. Both the bills approved by the Sejm now pass to the upper-house Senate, which can propose amendments but not block the passage of legislation. Tusk’s coalition has an even larger majority in the Senate than the Sejm. Once final versions of the bills are approved by parliament, they pass to the president, who can sign them into law, veto them, or ask the TK to assess whether they comply with the constitution. Given that Nawrocki is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a record number of government bills, and has declared his opposition to abortion, it appears very unlikely that he will sign either bill into law. President Nawrocki joined thousands of people on the National March of Life, Poland’s largest annual anti-abortion event, which is held under the patronage of the Catholic church https://t.co/8BQEVUoMZn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 20, 2026 Speaking to broadcaster Polsat on Tuesday evening after the Sejm votes, the president’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, said that Nawrocki would wait to see what the legislation looked like by the time it reached him. However, Bogucki noted that, “during his campaign, the president said he supported the protection of life from conception to natural death”. Bogucki also pointed to the fact that the TK, even before PiS was in power, had been “very clear” on “protection of life”. He also suggested that abortion was now suddenly back on the table because Tusk wants to “rehash ideological issues in order to cover up his incompetence in matters he should actually be dealing with”. .@BoguckiZbigniew o stanowisku prezydenta ws. aborcji ⬇️ 🗨️ Pan prezydent w tej kampanii mówił, że jest za ochroną życia od poczęcia do naturalnej śmierci@GoscWydarzen 🎙️ @mtejchmanhttps://t.co/ZJ4gKAPywM — PolsatNews.pl (@PolsatNewsPL) October 20, 2026 A further complication is the fact that the TK is currently in crisis. The government does not recognise any of its rulings (including the 2020 abortion ruling) due to the continued presence of judges illegitimately appointed under PiS. Meanwhile, Nawrocki and the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, have refused to accept five new TK judges appointed by the Sejm this year. Opinion polling has consistently shown that a majority of Poles want to liberalise the abortion law.
