World.title: Polish leaders condemn Hegseth’s “scandalous” remarks downplaying role of US allies in Afghanistan
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Leading figures from Poland’s ruling coalition have hit back at US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth over his recent remarks downplaying the contribution of America’s allies during the war in Afghanistan. The speaker of parliament, Włodzimierz Czarzasty, called the comments “scandalous”, while Prime Minister Donald Tusk read out a message sent to him by a Polish army medic who was serving in Afghanistan when the last of 44 Polish soldiers who died there was declared dead. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Chciałbym, żeby te słowa dotarły do naszych sojuszników, żeby już nigdy więcej nikt nie lekceważył wysiłku naszych żołnierzy. pic.twitter.com/gGJkh4Gnft — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 20, 2026 The controversy stemmed from a speech the US defence secretary gave to US military cadets in Tennessee on Saturday. Hegseth referred to his time serving as a US Army officer in Afghanistan, where he recalled that the International Security Assistance Force (ISAF) headquarters had flags from over 50 countries. “Except,” Hegseth said, “there were maybe five [countries] that contributed. It was actually closer to one or two that actually, by the end, were involved in kinetic operations. In fact, the patch ‘ISAF’ – we joked that it meant ‘I Saw Americans Fighting.'” The comments earned quick reproach from Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski, who aimed a message at Hegseth on social media, saying: “Tell that to the families of 44 Polish soldiers who died securing the tough Ghazni province.” Tell that, Mr @SecWar, to the families of 44 Polish soldiers who died securing the tough Ghazni province. https://t.co/vm4TM0sMJO — Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) October 18, 2026 On Tuesday, the remarks earned even stronger reproach from Czarzasty, who is the speaker of the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, and the leader of The Left (Lewica), one of the groups that forms Poland’s ruling coalition. At a press conference, Czarzasty said that Hegseth’s “scandalous” comments are “harmful to the families of Polish soldiers and to Polish national pride”. He also criticised President Karol Nawrocki – an opponent of the government and conservative ally of Donald Trump – for not condemning Hegseth’s remarks. It is “an insult to Polish soldiers” that Nawrocki, who serves as commander-in-chief, “is unable to stand up for their dignity and the dignity of those who died”, declared Czarzasty. To skandaliczne, że prezydent Polski boi się potępić polityków amerykańskich za brak szacunku do polskich żołnierzy, którzy zginęli w Afganistanie. pic.twitter.com/uyv54yDvrI — Włodzimierz Czarzasty 📚📖 (@wlodekczarzasty) October 20, 2026 Later on Tuesday, Tusk read out to his cabinet a text message he said he had received from a former military medic, whom he did not name. “Please stand up for soldiers, I beg you,” wrote the medic. “During my tour in Afghanistan, we confirmed the death of the last Polish casualty, a platoon sergeant whose wife was pregnant in Poland at the time.” “I received a medal from the Americans for helping them, for treating Americans. I didn’t have to do that. We treated them with our own Polish medicines,” they added. Tusk then added his own remarks, stating: “I would like these words to reach our allies. So that no one will ever again downplay the efforts of our soldiers. Wherever our allies, including our closest ally, the Americans, have needed our participation, Polish soldiers stood shoulder to shoulder with them.” Tusk also referenced Nawrocki’s silence on the matter. “Frankly, I was also counting on the president speaking out on this matter. But it seems I miscalculated.” Tusk is the first European head of government to directly criticise Hegseth’s remarks, although a spokesperson for British Prime Minister Andy Burnham did say on Monday that it was “wrong to diminish the role” of British personnel, 457 of whom died in Afghanistan. Of the 3,621 coalition deaths during the war in Afghanistan, around two thirds were Americans (2,461). The rest came from 31 different countries, with Poland’s 44 fatalities the seventh most of any nation. Hegseth’s remarks are not the first time that the Trump administration has caused anger in Poland by downplaying allies’ role in Afghanistan. In January, Trump himself suggested that other countries had “stayed a little back, a little off the front lines”. That prompted General Roman Polko, who commanded Poland’s GROM special forces unit in Iraq and Afghanistan, to call the US president “a coward who has never been on the front lines”. The former commander of Poland's special forces in Iraq and Afghanistan has condemned Donald Trump for questioning the contribution of America's allies "This is the cynicism of a coward who hasn’t been on the front lines himself," said General @PolkoRoman https://t.co/kElkAO5qX4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 23, 2026 The Polish government has also clashed with the US on other issues. In January, Tusk joined other European leaders in calling for Greenland’s sovereignty to be respected, following Trump’s calls for the island to be brought under US control. The following month, Tusk declared that Poland would not be a “vassal” of the US and suggested that Nawrocki wanted Poland to be too subservient to Washington. Czarzasty has twice this year clashed with the US ambassador over critical remarks he made towards Trump. However, at the same time, the Polish government has sought to maintain positive relations with Washington, given the United States’ role as Poland’s most important security partner. In June, Poland formally requested that the US establish a new permanent military base on its territory. Hegseth himself has praised Poland, calling it a “model ally” last year. The US State Department this month also announced that it was pushing for Poland to be allowed to join the G20 “as soon as possible”, pointing to its “growing leadership position in the international arena”. World.title: Poland detains Polish-Ukrainian military reservist on suspicion of espionage
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A member of Poland’s military reserve force has been detained for alleged espionage. On Monday afternoon, following media reports of the arrest, a spokesman for the military police confirmed that they had detained a 31-year-old man of Polish and Ukrainian citizenship, who holds the rank of senior private reserve. The suspect, who had at the time been undertaking a course at the Military Medical Academy (WAM) in Łódź, is being held on suspicion of declaring readiness to act for the benefit of a foreign intelligence service against Poland. That crime is punishable by up to eight years in prison. W dniu 16 października 2026 r. żołnierze z Oddziału Żandarmerii Wojskowej w Łodzi, zgodnie z postanowieniem Prokuratora Działu do Spraw Wojskowych Prokuratury Rejonowej Łódź-Polesie w Łodzi, dokonali zatrzymania mężczyzny w wieku 31 lat, obywatelstwa polskiego i ukraińskiego, w… pic.twitter.com/MLpqzfT4iO — Żandarmeria Wojskowa (@Zandarmeria) October 19, 2026 The Polish authorities have not revealed which foreign intelligence service the suspect – who has been placed in detention for three months – is believed to be associated with. Speaking later to reporters, deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk said that the man had “clearly shown himself to be someone who is conducting reconnaissance of certain types of military installations belonging to the Polish armed forces”. He also revealed that the suspect had recently obtained Polish citizenship. While the authorities have not released further information, Rzeczpospolita, a leading newspaper, reported earlier on Monday that the suspect, whom it named as Vasiliy, had been found in possession of several different phones, documents, and a large amount of money and gold. Poland has recently seen a number of high-profile cases of individuals charged – and in some cases convicted – of spying on behalf of Russia and Belarus. Poland’s security services recently revealed that the number of espionage cases they launched last year was more than double the figure for 2024. Over those two years combined, there were more investigations than in the previous three decades. This month, a former Polish soldier was sentenced to five and a half years for spying on behalf of Russia. The tasks assigned to him included reconnaissance of Rzeszów-Jasionka airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he travelled through Poland. A Polish man has been sentenced to five and a half years in prison for spying on behalf of Russia. He was tasked with reconnaissance of Rzeszów-Jasionka airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate @ZelenskyyUa while he travelled through Poland https://t.co/WCmhyHG1Kp — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 8, 2026 In July, a Russian married couple who had been studying in Poland were jailed for spying on behalf of Moscow and involvement in a plot to send a parcel bomb. In April, prosecutors charged a soldier from Poland’s Territorial Defence Force (WOT) with seeking to spy on behalf of Russia. The following month, three Polish citizens were charged with working on behalf of Russian intelligence to spread disinformation and conduct reconnaissance of NATO troops. In December last year, a Russian national was charged with running an espionage and sabotage network in Poland on behalf of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB). The agents he oversaw were mainly Ukrainians and Belarusians, as have been many others convicted of conducting Russian hybrid activities in Poland. World.title: Poland expels 15 Russians and Belarusians who tried to take part in Karate World Championships
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has detained and expelled 15 Russians and Belarusians who tried to take part in youth world karate championships that were taking place in the Polish city of Bielsko-Biała. “Eleven Belarusian citizens and four Russians entered the country on tourist visas, which was inconsistent with the declared purpose of their stay in Poland,” said border guard spokesman Szymon Mościcki. After being detained, they received orders to leave the country within eight days, which is “the shortest possible deadline”, he added, quoted by broadcaster TVP. Piętnastu obywateli Rosji i Białorusi zostało zatrzymanych przez Straż Graniczną. Przyjechali do Polski na wizach turystycznych, choć prawdopodobnie zamierzali wziąć udział w mistrzostwach świata w karate. Otrzymali decyzje nakazujące opuszczenie kraju.https://t.co/czcjQKZ2kw — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) October 19, 2026 The announcement came one day after the karate world championships in the cadet, junior and U-21 categories had finished in Bielsko-Biała. In early October, Russia’s TASS news agency had reported that some of the country’s junior karatekas, as competitors are known, had planned to compete in the tournament. The World Karate Federation (WKF) allows Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete under a neutral banner. However, Poland has a strict policy of not allowing Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete in tournaments on its territory. This year, it banned them from taking part in a World Cup ski jumping event. It was also removed as host of two European junior weightlifting championships for banning Russian and Belarusian athletes. On 15 October, the day after the championships in Bielsko-Biała had started, TASS reported that none of the Russian athletes had been allowed to register by the Polish organisers. Paweł Połtorzecki, president of the Polish Karate Union (PUK), confirmed that, despite PUK warning them not to come, Russian and Belarusian athletes had sought to take part, prompting the organisers to ask the border guard to conduct an inspection. “The first sign was the appearance of a Russian at the refereeing course,” he revealed, quoted by TVP. “That’s when the first detention occurred.” Gazeta Wyborcza, a leading Polish daily, reports that the Russian karatekas had obtained tourist visas from other countries in the European Schengen area, of which Poland is part. Poland itself does not issue tourist visas to Russians. Poland has been removed as the host of two European junior weightlifting championships after refusing to allow Russian athletes to take part The European Weightlifting Federation says it "does not accept discrimination based on geopolitical circumstances" https://t.co/j7PfiTHZ1M — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 9, 2026 Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has been one of Kyiv’s closest allies, providing military and humanitarian support while also pressing for tougher international sanctions against Moscow. Meanwhile, Poland has become the primary target in Europe for sabotage operations carried out by operatives working on behalf of Russia, including arson attacks and an attempt to derail a train. Russia has also repeatedly violated Polish airspace with drones, missiles and, most recently, a helicopter. In response to Russia’s aggressive actions, Poland has successively shut down all Russian consulates on its territory. Moscow responded by likewise closing all Polish consulates that it previously hosted. In January, Russia warned its citizens against travelling to Poland due to “Russophobia”. World.title: Poland breaks up international criminal group accused of laundering €77 million
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland says it has broken up an international criminal group responsible for laundering an estimated 337 million zloty (€77 million) by using currency exchange offices to illegally process money obtained from internet scams. Nine suspects – eight Ukrainians and one Belarusian – have been detained in a series of raids, which also resulted in the seizure of gold and cash worth over 1 million zloty. Służby rozbiły międzynarodową grupę zajmującą się praniem pieniędzy z oszustw inwestycyjnych i kryptowalut. Zatrzymano 9 osób, a skala transakcji przekroczyła 337 mln zł. Zabezpieczono złoto i gotówkę wartą ponad 1 mln zł. @Straz_Graniczna @PolicjaCBZC @ABW_GOV_PL pic.twitter.com/g2NQoqaPvP — Marcin Kierwiński (@MKierwinski) October 19, 2026 The accused – four women and five men aged between 26 and 53 – were arrested in Łódź, Warsaw and Małopolska province, announced Krzysztof Kopania, spokesman for the Łódź regional prosecutor’s office, which is leading the investigation. The detainees are four female cashiers, three men running the exchange offices, and two couriers used to transport money. All have been charged with participating in an organised criminal group and money laundering. They could face up to 15 years in prison if convicted. Prosecutors say that the gang, which operated in the cities of Warsaw, Lublin, Wrocław, Katowice and Gdańsk, collected money that had been obtained through internet fraud and transported it to cryptocurrency exchanges. It was then processed without complying with anti-money laundering procedures. Proceeds were then transferred to bank accounts, sent abroad by car, or concealed in fictitious purchases of gold. Most money was ultimately invested in cryptocurrencies. “The scale of the operation was enormous,” said Kopania. “It is estimated that between February 2025 and July 2026, members of the group took steps to conceal the origins of approximately 337 million zloty.” The ringleader was a 34-year-old Ukrainian national who made the key decisions and oversaw the domestic and international channelling of funds obtained from illegal sources, according to the Internal Security Agency (ABW) and border guard, which were also involved in the operation. Seven of the accused have been placed in pre-trial detention for three (or in one case two) months, while two have been bailed and ordered not to leave Poland. World.title: Prague’s Indian Community to Celebrate Navratri With Music and Dance
World.content:
The Indian community in Prague will gather for an evening of traditional music, dancing and food on Saturday, October 24, as Navratri 2026 returns to Top Hotel Prague.

Organized by Bharatiya Gujarati Samaj, the event will celebrate the cultural traditions of Gujarat, a state in western India known for its distinctive music, colourful clothing and energetic folk dances.

The programme will start at 5 pm and is open to people interested in Indian culture and traditions.



The celebration will feature Garba and Dandiya Raas, two traditional dances closely associated with Navratri festivities in Gujarat.

Visitors will also have an opportunity to enjoy Indian food, see traditional clothing and learn more about Gujarati culture.

Garba will be one of the main attractions of the event. The traditional Gujarati folk dance is performed in circles, with participants moving rhythmically to music and following a series of coordinated steps. The dance is closely associated with Navratri, a Hindu festival celebrated over nine nights in honour of the goddess Durga and the feminine divine.

Dandiya Raas is another traditional dance associated with the festival. Participants dance in pairs or groups while striking decorated wooden sticks together in time with the music. The movements, rhythms and colourful outfits make it one of the most recognisable features of Gujarati Navratri celebrations.

Beyond the dancing, the event will offer visitors an opportunity to explore different aspects of Gujarati culture, including traditional clothing and Indian food.

Traditional clothing is also an important part of the festivities. Women often wear colourful chaniya cholis, while men may dress in traditional kediyu outfits. Embroidery, decorative patterns and bright colours are common features of clothing worn for Garba and Dandiya Raas.

Tickets and further information are available on the Bharatiya Gujarati Samaj website.

World.title: Czech Constitutional Court Rules Sex Workers Must Pay Taxes
World.content:
The Czech Constitutional Court has ruled that income from voluntary sex work is subject to taxation, placing it on the same footing as earnings from other self-employed professions.

The decision clarifies that collecting taxes from sex workers does not amount to state approval of the activity.

The case concerned a woman who was ordered to pay more than CZK 900,000 in back taxes for income earned from paid sexual services in 2013 and 2014.



She challenged the assessment in court, but lower courts upheld the decision of the Czech Financial Administration. She subsequently appealed to the Constitutional Court, Novinky reported.

The woman argued that taxing prostitution effectively turned the state into a pimp, pointing to the distinction in Czech law between providing sexual services voluntarily for payment and acting as an intermediary in such activities.

While the former is not a criminal offense, procuring or facilitating prostitution in certain circumstances can be punishable under the Criminal Code.

The Constitutional Court rejected her argument, ruling that taxation serves a different purpose. According to the judges, the state is not profiting from another person’s labor but ensuring that taxpayers contribute fairly to public finances.

The court added that taxation should not be interpreted as moral approval of sex work or as official state recognition of the activity.

Under the ruling, income from prostitution falls into the category of earnings from independent professions.

The same broad category includes income earned by entertainers, coaches, athletes and models, as well as people who publish sexually explicit material on subscription platforms such as OnlyFans.

The court warned that exempting income from sex work would undermine the fair distribution of the tax burden and discriminate against other taxpayers.

The ruling does not legalize every activity associated with prostitution. Instead, it establishes that income earned through voluntary sex work must be declared and taxed under the same general principles that apply to other forms of self-employment.

World.title: Prague’s First Film Screening Took Place 130 Years Ago
World.content:
Prague’s first public film screening took place on October 18, 1896, at the Hotel U Černého koně on Na Příkopě Street.

Organized by the French branch of Thomas Edison’s company, the presentation introduced audiences to moving pictures, a technology that would soon transform entertainment across Bohemia.

The screening marked another milestone in a period of rapid technological change that had begun five years earlier.

In 1891, Prague hosted the Jubilee Provincial Exhibition, celebrating a century of industrial progress. The event helped reshape the city, leaving behind landmarks including the Industrial Palace, Petřín Lookout Tower and mirror maze.



The Hotel That Brought New Technology to Prague

The Hotel U Černého koně, or At the Black Horse, was among Prague’s most luxurious establishments in the late 19th century. Its owners, brothers Jindřich and Karel Cífka, were quick to recognize the commercial potential of new inventions.

Later in 1896, the hotel introduced another technological novelty, the X-ray machine. The device had been developed by German physicist Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen, who announced his discovery in December 1895.

Initially presented as an attraction, the machine soon acquired medical significance. In January 1897, physician Rudolf Jedlička used it to examine a patient suspected of having swallowed a foreign object. The image revealed a nail lodged in the man’s stomach.

Edison and the Lumière Brothers Compete for Audiences

The first film screening was organized by Adolf Oppenheimer, an optician and mechanic who operated a cinematograph supplied by Edison’s French company.

According to a contemporary invitation reproduced by Czech Radio, screenings took place daily, beginning at 4 p.m. and continuing hourly until 8 p.m. Additional shows were held on Sundays and public holidays. Admission cost 40 kreutzers, with discounts for schools.

Competition arrived almost immediately. Just five days after the Edison presentation, the Lumière brothers’ cinematograph was shown at the Hotel U Saského dvora on Hybernská Street.

Both companies promoted their technology as the genuine article. Their s emphasized the quality of their moving pictures and their international reputations, reflecting the intense competition surrounding the new medium.

Czech filmmakers soon began producing their own material. In June 1898, Národní listy reported on a cinematograph pavilion at the Prague Exhibition Grounds where two young architects presented original films, including scenes from everyday life in Prague.

Viktor Ponrepo Opens a Permanent Cinema

For several years, traveling cinematographs brought films to audiences around the country. A permanent venue eventually followed.

In September 1907, Dismas Šlambor, better known as Viktor Ponrepo, opened what is widely regarded as the first permanent cinema in the Czech lands. It was located in the U Modré štiky building on Karlova Street.

Originally a magician and illusionist, Ponrepo had become interested in image-recording technology after encountering Edison’s phonograph at the 1891 exhibition. He later toured the country with a traveling cinema before establishing his Prague venue.

Ponrepo became famous for greeting audiences with a bow before every screening. He eventually filmed the gesture and projected it before his shows, turning it into his personal signature.

By then, moving pictures had evolved from a technological curiosity into a new form of mass entertainment, with Prague among the cities embracing the change.

World.title: Meet Paulo Dias, the Expat Behind Prague’s Pintz Beer App
World.content:
Finding a good beer in Prague is rarely a difficult task. Finding the right pub, knowing what a pint costs and deciding where to go next is a different question.

For Paulo Dias, that challenge became the idea behind Pintz, a web app built to help people navigate Prague’s rich beer scene.

Originally from Portugal, Paulo has spent almost 15 years living abroad, moving between Slovakia and the UK before eventually taking a job in the Czech Republic.



He first arrived in the Czech Republic in 2021, spending several months in Opava before moving to Prague in February 2022. Even after the move, he was cautious about settling in. “When I moved to Prague, I wasn’t buying many things for my apartment, because if I moved again, I’d have to pack everything,” Paulo recalls.

That changed once his new job became more stable. By the end of the year, he was already thinking about staying.

I think the quality of life in Prague is quite amazing. It’s one of the best, if not the best, of the cities I know. I feel good here, I feel at home. That’s why I decided to stay.”

Prague’s pub culture

Prague’s pub culture became one of the ways Paulo built a social life after moving to the city. He started with local pubs in Žižkov.

“I started to make friends there, and then I thought it was a good opportunity for me to become more social.”

What struck him was how different the culture was from Portugal. He describes drinking there as more centered around wine, home gatherings, watching football with friends or celebrating birthdays, rather than regularly meeting at pubs during the week.

“I know people who meet every Monday. It’s impossible in Portugal, this mindset. People just stay at home or go for a coffee after dinner. There’s no culture like going to a pub.”

In Prague, meeting for a beer could instead become part of an ordinary weekday. That was something Paulo gradually came to appreciate about his new home.

“I don’t need to wait for the weekend to have my social life active.”

From sneaker prices to Pintz

The idea for Pintz grew out of a sneaker-price platform “The Real Sneaker Index” Paulo had been working on in his spare time. The two projects are quite different, but the first gave him a way of thinking about how prices could be collected and compared.

The connection to beer came almost as an afterthought. Paulo was already spending time in Prague’s pubs, and the idea eventually brought his side project closer to something he was experiencing himself.

“I was thinking, maybe I could apply the same idea to something more connected to everyday life. And then I thought, why not use it to track beer prices?”

What started as a price tracker gradually expanded into a way of exploring pubs. Users can now add information about individual places, from terraces and beer gardens to the beers they serve, while ratings give people a way to share their own experiences. “It’s not only about finding the cheapest beer. It started that way, but it’s really about quality.”

Pintz is now present in the US, Mexico, Atlantic Islands and across many countries in Europe.

Building it alone with AI

Paulo has been building Pintz alongside his Lead AI Platforms job, developing the platform himself with the help of AI. He works on it in the evenings, at weekends and whenever he can find the time.

“I’m not a coder, I’m not a developer, but I know what I want to do.”

AI has allowed him to take those ideas further without having to build every part of the platform from scratch himself. He sets up processes, monitors how they work and keeps adding and improving features as the project develops.

The speed at which he can turn an idea into something functional has been one of the biggest surprises for him.

“What impressed me the most is the capability of building anything with AI, especially digital products.”

What’s next for Pintz?

For now, his focus is on getting more people to use Pintz and bringing more pubs, breweries and beer brands onto the platform. He is also looking at sponsorships and other ways of turning the project into a sustainable business.

At the same time, he is conscious of how easily monetisation could get in the way of the experience he is trying to create. He does not want users to feel like they are constantly being sold something while using the app.

“I don’t want this to become an advertising app that people are annoyed to use.”

World.title: Prague Light Park at Žluté Lázně Takes Visitors Back to the 14th Century
World.content:
Prague’s Žluté lázně has opened a new edition of the Story of Lights, a seasonal light park inspired by the city’s medieval history.

Running from October 16, 2026, to January 31, 2027, the event features illuminated sculptures, interactive installations and, from November, evening boat trips on the Vltava River.



The park takes visitors back to 14th-century Prague during the reign of Charles IV, the Bohemian king and Holy Roman Emperor whose rule helped shape the city’s development.

Thousands of LED lights illuminate the grounds after dark, forming a route through displays inspired by the architecture, symbols and history of medieval Prague.

Among the installations are illuminated representations of Charles Bridge, Gothic towers, church arches, royal crowns and coronation regalia. The displays reinterpret historical motifs using modern lighting technology.

Some installations are interactive, with the organizers targeting families with children as well as adults looking for an evening activity outdoors.

The historical theme focuses on a period when Prague underwent major urban development.

Charles IV initiated the construction of Charles Bridge, founded the New Town in 1348 and helped establish Prague as an important political, cultural and religious centre in medieval Europe.

From November 6, visitors will also be able to combine their visit with an illuminated boat trip along the Vltava. The evening cruises are scheduled for Fridays, Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays.

World.title: Prague Expands Tram Network With Five Projects Underway
World.content:
Prague is expanding its tram network, with five projects now under construction across the capital.

Two new projects began in October 2026, extending the network from Malovanka to Strahov and from Libuš to Nové Dvory.

Work is also progressing on the tram line across Wenceslas Square, where the tracks have been connected between Vinohradská Street and the junction of Jindřišská and Vodičkova streets.



The projects aim to improve public transport connections to developing residential areas and strengthen links with other transport services, including the future Metro Line D.

New tram line to connect Malovanka with Strahov

Construction of the new tram line from Malovanka to Strahov began on October 5, following preparatory work. The tracks will run along Vaníčkova Street, starting at Bělohorská Street and continuing toward Strahov Stadium.

The Malovanka stop will also be modified and moved to a position before the intersection, allowing it to serve trams heading toward Strahov.

The existing Stadion Strahov stop, currently used for passengers to disembark, will be renamed Strahov.

Tram extension to Nové Dvory will complement Metro Line D

Construction of the second new line, extending the tram network from Modřany through Libuš to Nové Dvory, began on October 7, 2026.

The extension will introduce two stops, Přírodní and Nové Dvory. At Nové Dvory, the line will end in a loop using Durychova, Libušská and Chýnovská streets.

The new connection is being developed alongside plans for Metro Line D and the wider expansion of the surrounding residential area. It will provide a direct tram connection to central Prague, including the Palackého náměstí area, with a future connection toward Smíchov also planned.

The extension will change operations on tram line 17. Once the project is completed, the temporary dead-end terminus in Libuš will be removed, allowing single-ended trams to return to longer routes. A second tram line is also planned for the new tracks after Metro Line D opens.

Hodkovičky gains a new tram stop

The new Hodkovičky stop, located between Belárie and Černý kůň, is another addition to Prague’s tram infrastructure in the south of the city.

The stop is intended to improve access to public transport for residents of the growing residential developments nearby. Further housing construction is also expected in Nové Dvory, where the planned tram extension will provide additional transport capacity.

Tram tracks connected across Wenceslas Square

Work on restoring tram services across Wenceslas Square is also progressing. In early autumn, construction crews connected the tracks running from Vinohradská Street, past the National Museum, across the square and toward the junction of Jindřišská and Vodičkova streets.

The track infrastructure in this section is complete. Remaining work includes finishing the surrounding surfaces and installing overhead power lines.

Once these works are finished, the new line will restore tram services across Wenceslas Square, strengthening public transport connections in central Prague.

World.title: Prague Christmas Markets 2026 Start in November – Dates and Locations
World.content:
Prague’s Christmas markets will return in November 2026, with the first stalls opening at Náměstí Míru on November 20.

The main markets in Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square will follow on November 28, bringing traditional Czech food, handmade decorations and a program of seasonal performances to the city center.

Náměstí Republiky follows on November 25, and Tylovo náměstí opens on November 26.



The main markets at Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square begin on November 28 and continue until January 6, 2027. The other markets close on Christmas Eve, December 24.

Here are the opening dates and hours for the main locations.

– náměstí Míru — November 20 to December 24, 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.

– náměstí Republiky — November 25 to December 24, 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.

– Tylovo náměsti — November 26 to December 24, 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.

– Old Town Square — November 28 to January 6, 2027, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m.

– Wenceslas Square — November 28 to January 6, 2027, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m.

Smaller Christmas Markets Across Prague

Several markets open before the main city-center venues and offer alternatives for visitors who want to explore different neighborhoods.

Further options include the market at Anděl and Lesser Town Christmas on Kampa Island.

náměstí Jiřího z Poděbrad will host farmers’ markets during Advent, with a design market joining them every Sunday during the season. These events offer opportunities to browse locally made products and find gifts beyond the usual Christmas-market stalls.

World.title: Modeselektor to Open Spectaculare Festival at Prague’s ROXY
World.content:
Berlin electronic duo Modeselektor will open the 14th edition of Spectaculare on 3 March 2027, bringing their live show to ROXY alongside new music from their latest album, MDSLKTR

Gernot Bronsert and Sebastian Szary will perform a set combining techno, electro, hip-hop and bass music, accompanied by visual projections and lighting.

The concert comes shortly after the release of MDSLKTR, an album that revisits the sound and influences that have shaped the duo’s nearly three-decade career.



The record follows Classics Vol. 01, a project that revisited material from their early albums Hello Mom! and Happy Birthday! and drew on years of studio recordings and unfinished ideas.

With MDSLKTR, Modeselektor return to the sounds that first defined their music, drawing on Berlin rave culture, techno, electro, IDM and hip-hop while continuing to move between genres.

Since emerging from Berlin’s underground electronic scene, the duo have built an international following through their studio albums, live performances and collaborations with artists including Radiohead frontman Thom Yorke, Tommy Cash, Flohio and Blixa Bargeld.

They also formed Moderat with producer Apparat and run the independent record label Monkeytown Records.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Festival Spectaculare (@spectaculare_music)

Berlin-based multi-instrumentalist Philipp Johann Thimm will open the evening. A longtime collaborator of Apparat, Thimm has worked across electronic and acoustic music as well as audiovisual projects. His work on Apparat’s album *LP5* contributed to a Grammy-nominated project, while his solo work explores the meeting point between electronic composition and live instrumentation.

World.title: Reuters: Hungary could drop Russia’s Rosatom from Paks nuclear project
World.content:
Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s government is considering replacing Russian state-owned Rosatom as the main contractor for the Paks II nuclear expansion, according to Reuters. A final decision is expected later this year or in early 2027, as the government reviews the project’s costs, viability and potential alternatives.

Hungary is considering a major change to its flagship nuclear power project, with the government reportedly sounding out alternative suppliers to replace Russia’s Rosatom at the Paks nuclear power plant expansion.

Two sources familiar with the review told Reuters that all options remain on the table, including changing the main contractor. The government is examining the legal, technical and financial implications of such a move, as well as its potential impact on the project’s timetable and overall viability.

A source close to the administration said the government was leaning towards the conclusion that the expansion itself was necessary, but that Rosatom should not be involved.

Decision expected by early 2027

The government of Prime Minister Péter Magyar is expected to make a final decision on the Paks II project later this year or early next year, according to Reuters.

The expansion was originally estimated to cost EUR 12.5 billion. By the time the first concrete was poured in February 2026, Hungary had already spent more than EUR 2 billion on the project.

The contract was awarded to Rosatom without a public tender in 2014, under former prime minister Viktor Orbán. It has since been amended five times, while a sixth amendment has reportedly been prepared but not signed.

Replacing the Russian company would not be straightforward. According to Reuters, Hungary could have to absorb the EUR 1.1 billion already paid to Rosatom, as well as potential penalties for terminating the contract. No alternative supplier has been publicly identified.

If you missed it: Hungary could lose EUR billions in compensation if Paks II project is cancelled, expert warns

Rosatom says it has received no termination notice

Rosatom told Reuters that it was continuing work according to the schedule agreed with the Hungarian state. The company also said production of the main equipment for the future reactor units was under way.

“We have received no formal notification from the customer of any intention to terminate the contract, nor do we see any legally justified grounds for such a decision,” a company spokesperson said.

The statement suggests that no formal termination process has been communicated to Rosatom, despite the reported review and discussions about alternative suppliers.

A European supplier could make the project easier to manage in terms of foreign policy and sanctions, one source told Reuters. However, changing the contractor would not eliminate the project’s technical and management challenges.

EU court ruling adds to Paks II uncertainty

The project has already faced legal and regulatory complications. In September 2025, the Court of Justice of the European Union annulled the European Commission’s 2017 approval of state aid for Paks II, adding another obstacle to the expansion.

The project is also politically sensitive because of Hungary’s close nuclear cooperation with Russia following Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. While EU countries have reduced their reliance on Russian oil and gas, Rosatom has so far avoided EU-wide sanctions.

Paks II is Rosatom’s most prominent nuclear power project within the European Union. Finland cancelled its contract with the Russian company in May 2022, and the two sides have since been involved in legal disputes.

Hungary still plans to rely on nuclear energy

Despite the possible change of contractor, the Magyar government remains committed to nuclear power, Reuters reported. Nuclear energy provides large amounts of low-carbon electricity around the clock, helping balance renewable sources whose output varies with the weather.

Hungary expects electricity demand to rise, making nuclear generation an important part of its future energy mix. Zsuzsa Beres, deputy state secretary for nuclear energy and international relations at the Ministry of Economy and Energy, recently said nuclear energy and its supply chain offered significant potential to strengthen Europe’s own capabilities.

As a possible interim measure while the future of Paks II is reviewed, the government is also exploring a 20-year extension of the operating licences for the four existing Russian-built reactors at Paks. Their current licences expire between 2032 and 2037.

World.title: Hungary shuts down government portals for 48 hours over critical cybersecurity risk
World.content:
Hungary has temporarily taken the magyarorszag.hu government portal and several other official websites offline due to a serious cybersecurity threat affecting systems worldwide. Zoltán Tanács, Minister for Science and Technology, said the precautionary measure was introduced after two critical vulnerabilities were discovered in PHP, a programming language widely used to run websites. Online administration through magyarorszag.hu is expected to remain unavailable for around 48 hours.

Why has Hungary’s government portal been taken offline?

In a Facebook post on Thursday, Zoltán Tanács announced that access to magyarorszag.hu and several other government websites had been temporarily suspended overnight due to an international cybersecurity risk.

The threat is linked to a vulnerability known as PHP2Shell. PHP is one of the world’s most widely used programming languages, powering a significant number of websites and online services. Security experts have identified two serious flaws that could allow attackers to execute programmes remotely on vulnerable servers, potentially without needing a password.

“We have found no signs of an attack, but administration through the portal is expected to be suspended for around 48 hours until the vulnerability is fixed,” the minister wrote.

He stressed that the decision was taken as a precaution to protect citizens’ data and ensure the safe operation of Hungary’s digital government services. At the time of writing this article, magyarorszag.hu was unavailable.

Millions of servers could be at risk

Hungary’s National Cyber Security Institute issued a critical alert on 21 October, assigning the vulnerabilities a severity score of 9.2. The institute urged system operators to install the available security patches immediately.

Where an immediate update is not possible, experts recommend temporarily disconnecting affected systems from the internet or shutting them down if necessary.

Exploiting the vulnerabilities could allow attackers to run malicious code on servers, access sensitive information, or modify and delete website content. As PHP is used extensively around the world, the flaws could potentially put millions of servers at risk.

PHP developers have already released security fixes, but website operators must install them to protect their systems. Experts have also warned that updating a WordPress website alone may not be enough: the PHP version running on the underlying server must also be checked and updated where necessary.

If you missed it: Cyberattack hits Hungary’s State Treasury as experts trace attack to Russian servers

Other European countries have also suspended services

Hungary is not the only country to have taken precautionary action. According to Tanács, several European countries have temporarily restricted access to government websites and public services in response to the same threat.

The Netherlands: Authorities reportedly took several systems offline, including government services, online systems associated with the Port of Rotterdam, hospital websites, websites belonging to major political parties and the national cybersecurity centre’s own website.

Authorities reportedly took several systems offline, including government services, online systems associated with the Port of Rotterdam, hospital websites, websites belonging to major political parties and the national cybersecurity centre’s own website. Finland: Several government online services were temporarily suspended.

Several government online services were temporarily suspended. Denmark: A nationwide system used for communication between schools and parents was taken offline.

A nationwide system used for communication between schools and parents was taken offline. France: The Interior Ministry temporarily shut down certain websites operated by local administrative authorities.

Some services operated by Wikipedia and the BBC were also reportedly affected.

The shutdowns were precautionary measures, and there were no confirmed reports that the affected government systems had been compromised. However, cybersecurity company Cloudflare detected attempts to exploit the vulnerabilities even before the security patches were released.

Artificial intelligence helped uncover the flaws

The vulnerabilities are particularly concerning because experts believe they may have been present in the affected software for more than a decade without being detected.

Wiz, a cybersecurity company owned by Google’s parent company Alphabet, was among the organisations involved in identifying the flaws. The company highlighted the role of artificial intelligence, describing the vulnerabilities as among the most serious security issues ever uncovered with the help of AI.

Tanács said advanced AI solutions had helped experts identify the long-hidden weaknesses. He also urged businesses to ask their IT and information security specialists to check whether their websites are affected and to implement the necessary fixes as soon as possible.

World.title: JD Vance refuses to endorse Benjamin Netanyahu, brings up Viktor Orbán’s election defeat as a reason
World.content:
US Vice President JD Vance has pointed to his unsuccessful endorsement of former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán as he explained why he would not publicly back Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of Israel’s elections.

JD Vance avoided answering a journalist’s question

“I have endorsed one foreign candidate for election in my entire life. First of all, it didn’t go particularly well, as much as I’m very much an admirer of the [now former] prime minister, Orbán,” Vance said on Wednesday, responding to a question about whether he supported Netanyahu’s re-election campaign, reports Anadolu Agency.

Orbán, whose Fidesz party lost power after 16 years in Hungary’s April election, received Vance’s public backing shortly before the vote. The US vice president travelled to Budapest during the campaign, voicing support for Orbán and criticising what he described as outside interference in Hungarian politics. Despite that endorsement, Orbán suffered a decisive defeat.

LOL — JD Vance says "I’ve endorsed one foreign candidate in my entire life, and it didn’t go particularly well, as much as I’m very much an admirer of Orban" https://t.co/pyRzXtnPyb — Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) October 21, 2026

Vance leaves Netanyahu endorsement to Trump

Speaking at a news conference in Cincinnati, Ohio, JD Vance said his immediate priority was the US political calendar rather than foreign elections. “We’re in the middle of an American election cycle where I’m very focused on getting candidates elected in the United States of America,” he said.

Vance stressed that declining to endorse Netanyahu did not mean he was attacking the Israeli leader. “I’m not attacking Bibi Netanyahu. I’m not endorsing Bibi Netanyahu,” he said, adding that the final decision rested with US President Donald Trump.

Trump endorsed Netanyahu on Sunday, declaring his “Complete and Total Endorsement” of the Israeli prime minister’s re-election bid ahead of the 27 October vote. He praised Netanyahu’s leadership and co-operation with Washington, particularly over confronting Iran.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Orbán defeat offers a political lesson

JD Vance’s reference to Orbán is notable because the Hungarian leader was a prominent ally of Trump’s political movement and a symbol of the nationalist right in Europe. His election defeat was therefore a setback for a political figure whom Vance had personally championed.

The vice president is also navigating domestic divisions over Israel. Critics of Netanyahu’s government have argued that its decisions contributed to the conflict with Iran, making an endorsement politically sensitive for some American voters.

By invoking Orbán’s defeat, Vance offered a pointed explanation for keeping his distance from Israel’s campaign while maintaining that he remains an admirer of the former Hungarian prime minister.

World.title: Hungary ranks among Europe’s worst for rule of law in new global index
World.content:
Hungary has fallen further in the 2026 World Justice Project Rule of Law Index, ranking 78th out of 143 countries worldwide and last among 31 countries in the EU, EFTA and North America. Its score declined slightly, with the report highlighting setbacks in fundamental freedoms and safeguards against authoritarian rule.

Hungary recorded an overall score of 0.50 in the 2026 WJP Rule of Law Index, published by the World Justice Project (WJP) on 21 October. Its score fell by less than 1% compared with the previous year.

The country ranked 31st out of 31 in its regional group, which covers the European Union, the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) and North America. Hungary also placed 49th out of 51 high-income countries.

The report’s findings come amid a broader global decline in the rule of law, with 62% of countries recording a deterioration in their scores.

Hungary scores poorly on government accountability and civil justice

Hungary’s weakest results came in several areas related to institutional checks, transparency and the functioning of the justice system.

The country ranked 121st globally for constraints on government powers, placing last in its regional group. It also ranked 86th for open government and 78th for fundamental rights.

Civil justice was another area of concern. Hungary came 100th out of 143 countries globally, placing last regionally and among the 51 high-income countries included in the index. The country also ranked last regionally for regulatory enforcement, at 106th worldwide.

Hungary’s other results were mixed. It ranked 66th globally for the absence of corruption and 77th for criminal justice, while its strongest performance came in order and security, where it placed 23rd worldwide and 15th in its regional group.

The index measures the rule of law through eight factors, including government accountability, fundamental rights, regulatory enforcement and the operation of civil and criminal justice systems.

FACTOR GLOBAL RANK REGIONAL RANK* INCOME RANK** Constraints on Government Powers 121/143 31/31 50/51 Absence of Corruption 66/143 30/31 47/51 Open Government 86/143 31/31 46/51 Fundamental Rights 78/143 31/31 47/51 Order and Security 23/143 15/31 22/51 Regulatory Enforcement 106/143 31/31 51/51 Civil Justice 100/143 31/31 51/51 Criminal Justice 77/143 31/31 47/51

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Freedom of expression and civic participation under pressure

The report identifies a continuing global decline in safeguards against authoritarian rule. More than 86% of countries have experienced a sustained five-year deterioration in at least one of three areas: constraints on government powers, open government or fundamental rights. Hungary is among them.

Freedoms that support public debate, civic engagement and government oversight have also come under pressure.

According to the WJP, freedom of opinion and expression declined in 64% of countries, including Hungary. Freedom of assembly and association deteriorated in 67% of countries, while civic participation weakened in 65%.

The report also points to problems in justice systems worldwide, identifying undue executive pressure and interference as leading drivers of institutional decline.

Civil justice weakened in 64% of countries and criminal justice in 58%. Meanwhile, the ability of judiciaries to limit government powers declined in 63% of countries, although Hungary was not included in that particular finding.

Access to civil justice and protection against discrimination improved in many countries, but Hungary did not record improvements in either area.

Denmark leads as global rule of law decline continues

Denmark topped the 2026 global rankings, followed by Norway, Finland, Sweden and Luxembourg. At the other end of the list, Venezuela ranked last, preceded by Afghanistan, Haiti, Cambodia and Nicaragua.

Within Hungary’s regional group, Denmark was the strongest performer, ranking first worldwide. Norway and Finland followed.

Greece and Bulgaria joined Hungary at the bottom of the regional rankings, with Hungary recording the lowest score of the three.

The overall picture remains concerning, although the WJP noted that fewer countries experienced declines this year than in the previous edition. Nevertheless, deterioration continued to outnumber improvements, with 62% of countries recording a decline.

Poland offers a contrasting example of recovery. It registered the world’s largest improvement over three years, with its score rising by 4.22% since 2023 as democratic checks and institutional safeguards began to recover. The WJP said it was too early to determine whether Hungary would follow a similar trajectory.

Rule of law linked to economic stability

The index also highlights a connection between strong rule-of-law performance and economic conditions.

Countries with above-average GDP per capita, lower-than-median inflation and investment-grade sovereign credit ratings generally achieved stronger scores in the index.

For countries and investors alike, the findings suggest that the rule of law is not only a question of democratic governance but also an important factor associated with economic prosperity and stability.

Hungary’s overall score of 0.50 places it well behind the strongest-performing countries and underscores the challenges identified in government accountability, civil justice and fundamental rights.

The full country results, including Hungary’s performance across all 44 sub-factors, are available on the World Justice Project’s official website.

World.title: Seven must-see museum highlights in Budapest this 23 October
World.content:
Among the museum highlights in Budapest this 23 October are a once-stolen Raphael, a medieval crown discovered on Margaret Island, and a chair said to reveal witches.

On 23 October 2026, Hungary will mark the 70th anniversary of the 1956 Revolution.

The national holiday is also an opportunity to explore Budapest’s museums, where centuries of Hungarian history come to life through art, historical objects, and exhibitions.

From photographs documenting the 1956 Revolution to a medieval crown discovered on Margaret Island and a Raphael painting stolen from a Budapest museum, these seven highlights give a closer look at the stories behind Hungary’s art, history, and traditions.



House of Terror Museum: Photographs of the 1956 Revolution

As Hungary marks the 70th anniversary of the 1956 Revolution, the House of Terror Museum is a good place to start. Its exhibition, We Made World History: 1956-2026, features historical photographs documenting the uprising against Soviet-backed communist rule.

One photograph shows young revolutionaries at Blaha Lujza Square, with the former National Theatre in the background. The theatre was demolished in 1964, making the photograph a reminder of how much Budapest has changed since the revolution.

Hungarian National Museum: A medieval crown discovered on Margaret Island

Margaret Island is known today for its gardens, running paths, and picnic spots. However, in 1838, a medieval crown was discovered in a royal tomb at the island’s former Dominican convent.

The Margaret Island Crown dates to the 13th century and features decorations of lilies and rosettes. It has been associated with King Stephen V, although historians have yet to establish with certainty who was buried with it.

Centuries before it became one of Budapest’s most popular recreational spaces, Margaret Island was closely connected to Hungary’s medieval royal family. The crown is a reminder of that lesser-known history.

Hungarian National Gallery: The painting that inspired City Park’s balloon

Anyone who has visited City Park may have noticed the red-and-white balloon rising above the trees, but did you know its design was inspired by a Hungarian painting?

The Balloon (Léghajó), painted in 1878 by Pál Szinyei Merse, depicts a small balloon floating across a vast sky above the countryside. The artwork was inspired by a balloon journey undertaken by the artist’s brother-in-law, Béla Probstner, at a time when balloon flights were still an unusual spectacle.

More than a century later, the painting’s distinctive striped balloon inspired the design of BalloonFly, the tethered balloon attraction in Budapest’s City Park.

Museum of Fine Arts: The Raphael masterpiece stolen from Budapest

One of the Museum of Fine Arts’ most famous paintings was once at the centre of an international art theft. Raphael’s Esterházy Madonna, painted around 1508, depicts the Virgin Mary with the infant Jesus and John the Baptist. It takes its name from the Hungarian Esterházy family, whose art collection played an important role in the museum’s history.

In 1983, thieves stole the painting alongside six other valuable artworks from the Budapest museum. The stolen paintings were recovered in 1984, with six discovered at a monastery in Greece. The Esterházy Madonna eventually returned to the Museum of Fine Arts, where it remains part of the collection.

Museum of Ethnography: The chair said to reveal witches

According to Hungarian folklore, a wooden chair could help reveal witches hiding among ordinary villagers.

The Museum of Ethnography includes a Lucaszéke (St. Lucy’s Chair) dating to 1867. Made from nine types of wood, the chair was associated with a tradition in which people believed they could identify witches by standing on it during Christmas Eve midnight Mass.

The chair was supposed to be destroyed after use. However, a priest in the village of Vál recognised its significance and preserved it. Today, it is among the museum’s ten highlighted objects.

Budapest History Museum: When Buda, Pest, and Óbuda became one city

Budapest wasn’t always one city. Until 1873, Buda, Pest, and Óbuda were separate settlements that eventually came together to form the Hungarian capital.

At the Budapest History Museum’s Castle Museum, the permanent exhibition Budapest – Light and Shadow: 1000 Years of History of the Capital traces the city’s development through historical objects, maps, and photographs.

The unification of the three settlements on 17 November 1873 marked a turning point in Budapest’s history. The late 19th century brought major developments, including Andrássy Avenue, the Parliament building, and the Millennium Underground Railway. For anyone familiar with Budapest today, the exhibition puts some of the city’s most recognisable landmarks into historical context.

Ludwig Museum: What will Hungarian art look like in 30 years?

After centuries of Hungarian history, the Ludwig Museum turns our attention to the present and what comes next. From 20 to 25 October, the museum will present The Next 30, a pop-up exhibition featuring works by contemporary Hungarian artists, particularly those created since 2000.

The exhibition marks 30 years since the museum reopened as the Museum of Contemporary Art in 1996. It also raises an interesting question: which artworks will future generations look back on to understand Hungary’s art scene today? With just six days to see the exhibition, the national holiday falls right in the middle of its run.

World.title: Hungary shuts down bank: What happens to customers’ money?
World.content:
Hungary’s central bank has revoked Trive Bank’s operating licence and ordered its liquidation after finding that the lender no longer has sufficient capital to continue operating. Depositors are set to receive compensation within seven working days, up to the statutory limit.

The Hungarian National Bank (MNB) announced the decision on Wednesday, adding that the move would not threaten the stability of the country’s financial system.

The bank had fewer than 100 depositors, while its outstanding household loans amounted to less than HUF 2 billion (EUR 5.3 million). According to the MNB, its lending portfolio represented well below 0.01% of Hungary’s total banking market.

Will customers get their money back?

The National Deposit Insurance Fund (OBA) will pay eligible depositors within seven working days, up to the statutory compensation limit of EUR 100,000 per depositor per credit institution.

At the current exchange rate, this is worth more than HUF 36 million. The actual amount paid will depend on each depositor’s eligible balance and the applicable rules.

Customers do not need to submit a separate application to the OBA. The compensation process will be based on information provided to the fund by Trive Bank.

The MNB has appointed Financial Stability and Liquidation Non-Profit Ltd. (PSFN) to oversee the liquidation, in accordance with the relevant legislation. The process officially begins on the date the central bank’s decision is communicated.

Why was Trive Bank shut down?

The MNB said its ongoing supervisory activities had revealed that Trive Bank’s capital position no longer allowed it to continue operating in the market. The lender primarily offered small-value online personal loans, advertising a process that could reportedly take as little as 15 minutes.

The central bank had previously ordered the bank to ensure continuous compliance with legal requirements concerning its own capital, and had also imposed a fine. However, the bank failed to meet those requirements, according to the MNB.

The regulator said the decision was intended to ensure an orderly and regulated withdrawal from the market while protecting customers and maintaining confidence in Hungary’s banking sector.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

What is Trive Bank?

Trive Bank, which has Turkish roots, entered the Hungarian market offering digital lending services. Its online model focused on providing personal loans through a streamlined application process. Despite the bank’s closure, the MNB stressed that its limited size meant the decision would have no meaningful impact on Hungary’s financial markets.

The priority is the orderly settlement of the bank’s affairs and the repayment of eligible deposits under the deposit guarantee scheme.

World.title: Hungarian university breaks into world’s Top 100 with international business master’s
World.content:
Corvinus University of Budapest has secured a place among the world’s top 100 institutions in the 2027 QS International Trade Rankings, with its International Economy and Business Master’s programme ranking 99th globally. The university also achieved an impressive 32nd place in the Executive MBA category, becoming the only institution from Central and Eastern Europe to feature in that list.

The rankings, published by international higher education ranking organisation Quacquarelli Symonds (QS) on 14 October, assess programmes that prepare students for careers in international business and trade.

Corvinus is the only Hungarian university represented in either of the two rankings.

Corvinus excels in graduate outcomes and career support

The university performed particularly well in several individual indicators in the 2027 rankings. In the Executive MBA category, Corvinus ranked 15th worldwide for graduate outcomes and career support. It also achieved joint 18th place for innovative teaching and 20th for research performance.

Its International Economy and Business Master’s programme performed strongly in graduate outcomes, ranking 58th globally in the Master’s and MBA category, despite placing 99th overall.

These indicators assess different aspects of the programmes, offering prospective students a more detailed picture of their strengths beyond their overall positions.

Bruno van Pottelsberghe, rector of Corvinus University of Budapest, said the rankings provided valuable feedback for students, employers and the university itself. He added that the institution aimed to equip graduates with knowledge and skills relevant to the global marketplace, enabling them to tackle real-world business challenges with confidence.

If you missed it: Hungary’s Corvinus University breaks into global business rankings with multiple top positions

How does QS assess international trade programmes?

The QS International Trade Rankings are produced in collaboration with the Hinrich Foundation, with separate lists for Executive MBA programmes designed for experienced professionals and Master’s and MBA programmes.

To qualify, institutions must hold internationally recognised accreditation or an appropriate QS Stars rating. Their programmes must meet specific international trade curriculum requirements, while universities must also demonstrate sufficient research performance and academic reputation. QS assesses a maximum of one programme per institution in each ranking.

The methodology evaluates six criteria: international trade curriculum content, institutional reputation, graduate outcomes, industry engagement, innovative teaching and research.

Curriculum content accounts for 30% of the overall score in both rankings. Graduate outcomes and industry engagement each contribute 15%, while institutional reputation carries greater weight in the Executive MBA category.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Which universities lead the 2027 rankings?

The top positions went to institutions in the United States and the United Kingdom. In the Master’s and MBA category, the Thunderbird School of Global Management at Arizona State University took first place with its Master of Global Management programme.

The University of Cambridge led the Executive MBA rankings with its Global Executive MBA programme.

Against this international competition, Corvinus’s 32nd-place finish in the Executive MBA category and its Master’s programme’s entry into the global top 100 mark notable results for Hungarian higher education.

World.title: BREAKING: International arrest warrant issued for György Matolcsy’s son
World.content:
Hungarian authorities have issued an international arrest warrant for Ádám Matolcsy, the son of former central bank governor György Matolcsy, in connection with suspected economic fraud. Another man, György Stofa, is also wanted.

Ádám Matolcsy wanted over suspected economic fraud

An arrest warrant has been issued for Ádám Matolcsy, son of former National Bank of Hungary (MNB) governor György Matolcsy, according to the Hungarian police website. The warrant was issued on Wednesday afternoon by the Central Investigative Prosecutor’s Office in connection with suspected economic fraud.

Authorities are also seeking György Stofa, with reports indicating that international arrest warrants have been issued for both men. Their names appeared on the police website shortly after prosecutors announced developments in the ongoing investigation involving the central bank and its foundations.

Read more about the Matolcsy case:

Former Hungarian central bank governor Matolcsy detained

Prosecutors seek to arrest former Hungarian central bank chief Matolcsy

Development follows former central bank chief’s detention

The move comes on the same day that prosecutors detained György Matolcsy and questioned him as a suspect in a case involving the management of assets linked to the central bank’s foundations.

Prosecutors allege that a securities-lending agreement signed in February 2025 was used in an attempt to transfer control over the PADME Foundation’s assets to people who would remain under Matolcsy’s influence after he left office. According to the prosecution, the alleged arrangement was intended to enable the former governor and his son to make investments for their own benefit.

The alleged transaction involved Optima and the Central European III Private Equity Fund, represented by Quartz Befektetési Alapkezelő Zrt. Prosecutors say the agreement transferred ownership control over an asset manager overseeing assets with a market value of nearly HUF 200 billion (approximately EUR 547 million). The precise financial damage has not yet been established.

Prosecutors seek Matolcsy’s pre-trial detention

György Matolcsy was questioned for several hours on Wednesday but did not make a statement about the allegations, according to his lawyer, Pál Bátki. He was transferred to a police detention facility after the interrogation.

The Central Investigative Prosecutor’s Office has requested his pre-trial detention, with a judge expected to decide whether to order it. Prosecutors have also detained two other people in connection with the case, while seeking international arrest warrants for two further individuals.

World.title: Berlin Process Needs to Level the Playing Field in Bilateral Disputes
World.content:
On October 22, Montenegro will host the Berlin Process Leaders’ Summit while itself dealing with a neighbouring EU member state’s power to halt its EU accession progress.

The country is widely considered a frontrunner for EU membership and has provisionally closed 21 of 33 negotiating chapters. Yet neighbouring Croatia is holding up progress over unresolved bilateral issues ranging from war crimes and missing persons to state property claims, maritime borders and the Jadran sailing ship.

Few would question the importance of investigating war crimes or settling state borders, which are legitimate matters that should not be pushed aside for the sake of enlargement. The real question is: is it acceptable for an EU member state to make the accession process conditional on its own demands without any scrutiny of the demands’ relevance, proportionality or prospects for resolution? When bilateral disagreements become EU accession vetoes, they cease to be a problem for just the two countries involved.

This issue has repeatedly arisen across the Western Balkans. In May 2024, Albania’s relations with Greece became strained after Albania imprisoned Fredis Beleris, the ethnic Greek mayor-elect of Himara, who was convicted of vote buying. Greece warned that the affair could affect Albania’s EU ambitions.

World.title: Held Together with Wire: Inside Romania’s Neglected Arms Industry
World.content:
Jobs for the boys

At Uzina Mecanica Bucuresti, Romania’s only tank manufacturer, the general manager Mihai Rafiu was detained over the summer by anti-corruption prosecutors. He is accused of taking bribes from a contractor in exchange for approving procurement deals. The case is still open.

UM Bucuresti declined to comment on the ongoing investigation itself. But the company confirmed to BIRN that its board has temporarily reassigned Rafiu’s duties to the company’s economic director. Rafiu did not respond to questions sent through the company.

At Carfil, one of Romania’s main ammunition makers, a similar story played out a decade earlier, although what followed was rather unusual. In 2015, Carfil’s general manager, Aurel Veltan, was arrested and later convicted of abuse of office for steering company contracts to a firm without following proper procurement rules. A court sentenced him to a suspended prison sentence and banned him from holding leadership roles at state-owned companies for five years. However, Veltan apparently never left Carfil. According to his resume, he stayed on as head of the marketing and sales unit, and in October 2024 he was promoted to commercial director.

Veltan told BIRN that Carfil restructured in 2024 and brought in experienced people for leadership roles, including himself. He pointed to his three decades working in the company’s commercial department. He declined to comment on the criminal case or the sentence he served.

Some of the men running these plants have both a political resume as well as a police file. Ioan Narcis Chisalita, interim director of Arsenal Resita, an artillery factory, spent years as a senator and worked as an adviser to former prime minister Viktor Ponta, who was forced out of office in 2015 after a nightclub fire that killed 65 people.

In 2019, prosecutors named Chisalita as a suspect in a wider corruption case involving a regional road authority, accusing him of using his position in a political party to help push through illegal job appointments. One part of that case against him was closed last year – not because he was cleared, but because the statute of limitations had expired. A separate related case is still active in court, but Chisalita told BIRN he is not a party to the proceedings.

He added that he was appointed interim director of Arsenal Resita because of his “personal experience in corporate governance and in running private companies as an administrator”.

Other figures raise political rather than legal questions. Razvan Marian Pircalabescu spent many years advising ministers before serving as an advisor in the prime minister’s office in late 2024 and 2025 – a period that spanned governments from both of Romania’s main parties, the Social Democratic Party (PSD) and the National Liberal Party (PNL). In August 2025, he was named general manager of Romarm. His own resume shows he simultaneously serves as board president of Carfil, one of the 15 companies Romarm oversees, meaning he effectively answers to himself.

Carfil told BIRN that Pircalabescu’s dual role is “outside the company’s scope of authority” and declined to comment further. Pircalabescu did not respond to enquiries.

At the Sadu munitions plant in the southwestern part of Romania, Viorel Salvador Caragea was, until recently, a special administrator, an Economy Ministry-appointed overseer of the company’s finances.

Caragea spent nearly three decades in the police force, rising to become the top police official in Gorj county before retiring. He was appointed to the job at Sadu with the backing of the Save Romania Union (USR) party. Since then, the national press have reported a string of legal disputes: courts have twice ordered him to pay damages over comments he made online about a prosecutor and a mayor.

Sadu confirmed that Caragea had received BIRN’s questions. The company later informed BIRN that on September 17, after the questions had been sent, he was dismissed as its special administrator. The company gave no further explanation.

These five are by no means anomalies. Several other Romarm subsidiaries have board members or directors with similar political backing, appointed under different governments and different parties.

But the problems extend well beyond those running the companies. Inside the factories themselves, the picture is even more troubling.

World.title: Acquittal Fuels Doubts over Transfer of Bosnian War Crimes Cases to Serbia
World.content:
Novakovic was acquitted in May this year but Karlica’s case was returned for a retrial on certain charges; in August, the Belgrade Court of Appeal upheld Novakovic’s acquittal, and this month, the Humanitarian Law Centre said Karlica was also found not guilty.

Alic said he was “disappointed” with the court proceedings in Belgrade, in which he said he testified.

“I wouldn’t say you get used to it, but as time passes and you follow these proceedings, you come to see that certain people are simply going through the motions,” he said.

Murat Tahirovic, president of the Association of Victims and Witnesses of Genocide in Bosnia, said the verdict fitted a pattern evident in Serbia. He cited the case of eight Bosnian Serb former police officers charged over the execution of more than 1,300 Bosniak civilians at a warehouse in the village of Kravica near Srebrenica in July 1995.

“There is a trial that is still ongoing, which has not been completed, and which started in 2015, involving eight police officers from Kravica,” said Tahirovic.

“That case has been dragging on for 11 years. There is always some reason to postpone it. However, the question is what to do, how to make it serious, so to speak.”

“Any case transferred there will not get its necessary epilogue. If there is a conviction, the sentences will be minimal or there will be acquittals.”

According to Cestic Jelovac, the indictment brought against Novakovic and Karlica by war crimes prosecutors in Serbia did not cover the same factual and legal framework as the indictment transferred from Bosnia, given that the prosecution in Serbia refuses to bring charges of crimes against humanity.

Cestic Jelovac said the prosecution failed to submit new evidence. The judge’s verdict was also “problematic”, she said, “as the court did not assess the presented evidence in an appropriate manner”.

“In the explanation, the judge states that women and children were transported by tractor to the settlement of Urije in order to be sheltered and protected, which is unacceptable because the court did not look at the broader context of the attack on Alici and Ekici and the forced relocation of the Bosniak population.”

“Even with the qualification of a war crime against the civilian population, nothing prevents the court from looking at the role of the accused through the broader context of the event, the way civilians were treated before the event covered by the indictment, and the connection of individual actions. Exactly what the High Court in Belgrade failed to do in the proceedings against Milenko Karlica.”
