World.title: Anbumani seeks demolition of retaining wall and walkway being built in Pallikaranai Marsh
World.content:
PMK president Anbumani Ramadoss on Thursday (October 22, 2026) demanded the demolition of a retaining wall and walkway being constructed in the Pallikaranai Marsh, alleging that the structures had obstructed rainwater flow and caused flooding at Pallikaranai and Jalladianpet.

In a statement, he said rainwater from the October 17 rainfall had accumulated in the two localities as it could not drain into the marsh because of the Forest Department’s ‘Neithal Restoration and Conservation Works’. He said a six-foot-high retaining wall was being built along a 3-km stretch of the marsh, along with a 2-km walkway, despite warnings that the structures would obstruct drainage. He added that an official’s assurance that pipes beneath the structures would facilitate water flow had proved incorrect.

Dr. Anbumani said he had voiced concern on September 4, while Pasumai Thaayagam president Sowmiya Anbumani and he inspected the site on September 6 and 12 respectively. He said that while rainwater drained within hours in several parts of Chennai that had received more than 30 cm of rain on October 17, the stagnant water at Pallikaranai and Jalladianpet had to be pumped into the marsh and had not yet drained completely.

He warned of flooding at Velachery and Perumbakkam if the heavy rain continued during the Northeast monsoon and demanded that the government halt the project, demolish the structures already built, and order an inquiry to identify those responsible for implementing it.

World.title: MoES Secretary Srinivasa Kumar to address ASTC annual convention on October 30
World.content:
Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES) Secretary T. Srinivasa Kumar will inaugurate the annual convention of the Academy for Science, Technology & Communication (ASTC) and also deliver the foundation day distinguished lecture at Balakrishna Hall, CSIR-National Geophysical Research Institute (CSIR-NGRI), Uppal Road in Hyderabad on October 30.

The programme will feature a special c on “Earth Sciences, Strategic Resources & Advanced Technologies for India’s Future” and the presentation of ASTC Annual Awards in five categories — Lifetime Achievement Awards, Excellence Awards in Science and Technology, Science Popularisation Awards, Best Academician Awards, and Best Startup Awards.

Among those expected to participate are Vice-Chancellor of Homi Bhabha National Institute, Mumbai, U. Kamachi Mudali; former MoES Secretary M. Ravichandran; and the Directors of the CSIR-National Institute of Oceanography, Goa, and the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology, Pune.

ASTC will also release two issues of ASTC Communications, a publication aimed at promoting public awareness of preventive healthcare. The publications are Healthy Kidneys for Life: Chronic Kidney Disease - Awareness, Screening and Prevention, authored by Sree Bhushan Raju, and Eye Health for Everyone: Awareness, Early Checks & Prevention, authored by Vipin Das Anthony, said ASTC secretary C.L. Narasimha Rao in a press release on Thursday (October 22, 2026).

World.title: Amit Shah slams Opposition, says protests will achieve nothing, NDA will form next government in Punjab
World.content:
Union Home Minister Amit Shah on Thursday (October 22, 2026) slammed Opposition parties, including the Congress and the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), saying protests and demonstrations would achieve nothing, and asserted that the NDA would form the next government in Punjab.

Inaugurating projects worth ₹8,941 crore aimed at cleaning the Yamuna in Delhi, Mr. Shah asserted that the BJP would seek a mandate from people in 2029 after rejuvenating the river.

In a blistering attack on the Congress and AAP, Shah said the Opposition parties had accused the ruling dispensation of EVM tampering and vote theft, but had been out of power in many States for decades.

Mr. Shah, detailing plans to clean the Yamuna, also accused the previous Congress and AAP governments in Delhi of allowing sewer water discharge into the river and said the BJP government had now managed to reduce the discharge.

Attacking AAP convenor Arvind Kejriwal, Mr. Shah said the "politics of excuse" would not save the AAP in the upcoming Punjab Assembly polls.

People in Punjab want an NDA government, he said, claiming that the AAP would be routed in the polls.

Mr. Shah also asserted that the prevailing drug trafficking menace would be ended after the formation of an NDA government in Punjab.

World.title: Session on personalised cancer treatment in Bengaluru on October 24
World.content:
Bengaluru-based Shobha Trust, in collaboration with Samprada Hospital, will organise a day-long session on ‘Individualised Drug Therapy in Cancer’ at Vivanta on Residency Road in Bengaluru, on October 24. The session will focus on the growing role of personalised approaches in cancer treatment.

Oncologists will participate in discussions on developments in cancer care and the importance of tailoring treatment to individual patients.

“As cancer treatment continues to evolve, understanding how therapies can be tailored to individual patients is becoming increasingly important,” said Dr. Radheshyam Naik, founder, medical director and head of Medical Oncology, Haematology and Bone Marrow Transplantation at Samprada Hospital.

Breast cancer among younger women

Highlighting the importance of breast cancer awareness during October, Dr. Naik said the disease is a significant concern among younger women in India, contrary to the common perception that it primarily affects older women.

Citing estimates from the National Cancer Registry Programme, he said breast cancer accounted for over 27% of all cancer cases among women aged 15–39 in 2022.

He stressed the need to dispel the misconception that younger women were largely protected from the disease. Ignoring a breast lump or other unusual changes because of age could delay diagnosis and treatment, he said.

Warning signs include a new or persistent lump, changes in breast shape or size, skin dimpling, nipple inversion, and unusual nipple discharge.

“Age alone should never be a reason to dismiss a possible symptom. While not every breast change indicates cancer, it is important to consult a doctor to establish the cause rather than ignore it,” Dr. Naik said.

Younger women might overlook symptoms because they consider themselves less vulnerable, attribute changes to hormonal fluctuations, or postpone consultations owing to work and family commitments, he said.

Dr. Naik emphasised the importance of breast awareness and timely medical evaluation. Women should familiarise themselves with what is normal for their breasts and seek medical advice if they notice unusual changes. However, breast awareness does not replace appropriate screening or diagnostic tests, he said. The choice of investigation depends on a woman’s age, symptoms, medical history, and risk factors.

He cautioned that the absence of a family history of breast cancer did not eliminate the risk. Although inherited genetic factors can increase susceptibility, the disease can also affect women without a known family history.

Emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI), could support breast cancer detection by helping radiologists identify suspicious abnormalities in mammograms, improve consistency in image interpretation, and prioritise cases requiring closer examination. Such tools could complement conventional diagnostic procedures and improve screening efficiency, he said.

World.title: Mysuru Dasara: Karnataka CM orders probe into Cabinet colleagues being stopped by police at pooja enclosure
World.content:
Karnataka’s Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar has directed Chief Secretary Shalini Rajneesh to conduct an inquiry and submit a report on police officers restricting some Ministers from entering the venue during the Nandidhwaja Pooja held near the North Gate of Mysuru palace on October 21.

“It is evident that the officials acted high-handedly by restricting the Ministers. I personally intervened immediately to facilitate the Ministers’ entry. However, such irresponsibility from officials cannot be tolerated. Therefore, I have ordered the Chief Secretary to conduct an inquiry into who is responsible for this, and submit a report,” the Chief Minister stated. H.C. Balakrishna, P.M. Narendraswamy, and K.S. Basavantappa were the Ministers who were stopped.

The incident had drawn criticism, with the opposition BJP alleging caste prejudice. P.M. Narendraswamy, and K.S. Basavantappa belong to the Dalit community. Yet another Minister Shivaraj Tangadagi, also a Dalit, was stopped, but was allowed to go in after the Chief Minister intervened.

‘Don’t give caste dimension’

Meanwhile, Deputy Chief Minister G. Parameshwara has said it is inappropriate to give a caste dimension to incidents arising during the enforcement of security and protocol.

He said the Chief Minister has a prescribed protocol that the police are required to enforce strictly, particularly during events involving huge crowds where security arrangements have to be closely followed.

“Although the Ministers were initially stopped while the Chief Minister moved ahead, the Chief Minister later returned and took them along. The police were performing their duty. There is no need to create an unnecessary controversy over the matter,” he said.

Objecting to the repeated use of the expression ‘Dalit Ministers’ in relation to the incident, Dr. Parameshwara asked why they could not simply be referred to as Ministers. “Should every individual be identified by their caste? Are Ministers belonging to other communities referred to by their caste?”

He further said, “I am not saying there were no lapses. Such mistakes can happen. But it is not appropriate to turn such minor lapses into a major controversy.”

Privilege motion

Meanwhile, irked by the police restrictions at the venue of Nandidhwaja Pooja, BJP MLA T.S. Srivatsa, who represents Krishnaraja assembly constituency under whose purview the Mysuru Palace falls, has threatened to initiate a privilege motion in the Legislative Assembly after he was denied entry to the enclosure created for the Nandidhwaja Pooja.

He said he would write to the Assembly Speaker G.S. Patil about the denial of his right to shower petals on the Nandidhwaja in his own constituency. The matter will be raised in the next Legislature session in Belagavi, he said.

When Mr. Srivatsa brought the matter to the notice of a senior police official present at the spot, IPS officer C.B. Ryshyant said the police had created different layers of security enclosures around the Nandidhwaja for the pooja. Instructions had been received to allow only the Chief Minister and the Minister in-charge of the district Yathindra Siddaramaiah into the inner-most ring while the subsequent layers of enclosure were reserved for Ministers and MLAs.

Most of the MLAs stood outside the innermost enclosure and watched Mr. Shivakumar carry out the rituals at the designated spot for Nandidhwaja pooja near the Kote Anjaneyaswamy Temple, situated just outside the North Gate of Mysuru Palace.

World.title: Karnataka plans 200 cochlear implants for children with hearing loss
World.content:
Karnataka has planned 200 additional cochlear implants for children with severe to profound hearing loss in 2026-27 under ‘Aalisu Kanda’, the cochlear implant programme being implemented as part of the Shravan Dosh Mukta Abhiyan.

The programme, implemented by the Health Department of Karnataka, is aimed at helping eligible children with hearing impairment develop speech, language, and communication skills through cochlear implant surgery and post-operative rehabilitation.

A total of 575 cochlear implant surgeries were performed under the programme during the financial year 2025-26, according to details provided by the department. For the current financial year, the department has planned the procurement and distribution of 200 additional implants to ensure that eligible children can undergo surgery without delay.

Two phases of procurement

Health Minister U. T. Khader said the planned procurement will be carried out in two phases. In the first phase, 75 cochlear implants will be supplied to empanelled hospitals. Surgery for these children is expected to be completed within the next one to two months.

Speaking after inaugurating a symposium on ‘Alisu Kanda’ in Bengaluru on October 22, the Minister said the department has planned to procure another 125 implants within the next three months. These will be supplied to empanelled hospitals based on the requirements of beneficiaries and their clinical needs.

The two phases will together provide 200 additional implants during 2026-27. The planned supply is intended to maintain the availability of devices in hospitals and support timely intervention for children who meet the eligibility criteria, he said.

Early intervention crucial

Severe to profound hearing loss can affect a child’s ability to develop speech and language, communicate with others, and participate in education. Early identification of hearing impairment, followed by timely treatment and rehabilitation, is important to improve outcomes.

Cochlear implants are electronic devices that help people with severe to profound hearing loss access sound. However, implantation is only one part of the process. Children need appropriate post-operative care and rehabilitation to learn to interpret sounds and develop communication skills.

Karnataka’s programme provides for screening of beneficiaries, audiological assessment, and verification of eligibility before surgery. After implantation, children undergo device activation and mapping, which help ensure that the device is appropriately programmed.

Rehabilitation and follow-up

The programme includes structured Auditory-Verbal Therapy (AVT), regular follow-up, and parental counselling. These services are intended to help children develop listening, speech, and language skills, and make the best use of their implants.

Rehabilitation requires sustained support after surgery. Regular follow-up helps monitor a child’s progress and address needs arising during the process of developing communication skills. Parental counselling is also part of the programme, enabling families to support the child’s learning and rehabilitation.

The department’s approach combines surgery with post-operative therapy and follow-up rather than treating implantation as a standalone intervention, the Minister said.

Aim to improve access and inclusion

The programme aims to improve access to cochlear implantation for eligible children across Karnataka, support early speech and language development, and strengthen their ability to communicate.

It also seeks to improve children’s educational and social inclusion, including their participation in mainstream education. Timely procurement and distribution of implants to empanelled hospitals are expected to help maintain service delivery and ensure that children receive treatment according to their needs.

World.title: Green Visakha seeks time-bound environmental commitments from poll candidates in Visakhapatnam
World.content:
Green Visakha, an environmental NGO in Visakhapatnam, has urged candidates contesting the Greater Visakhapatnam Municipal Corporation (GVMC) local body elections to make environmental protection and public health priorities in their election agendas.

In a statement issued on Thursday (October 22, 2026), Green Visakha president Raja Rama Mohan Roy called for measurable, time-bound commitments on air pollution, industrial wastewater, drinking water security, forest conservation and urban greening.

Green Visakha expressed concern over proposed artificial intelligence (AI) data centres, citing potential impacts on water availability, electricity demand, public health and local infrastructure. It urged the Andhra Pradesh government to halt further steps towards establishing the facilities until their resource requirements and environmental impacts were independently assessed and disclosed for public scrutiny.

The organisation said industrial emissions, vehicular pollution and construction dust were concerns in areas including Gajuwaka, Gangavaram and Parawada. It called for stricter pollution monitoring, enforcement of environmental standards and public disclosure of air-quality data.

It also urged candidates to protect Kambalakonda forest and Mudasarlova reservoir, prevent the release of untreated industrial wastewater, conserve groundwater recharge zones and ensure the long-term survival of trees planted under greening programmes.

Green Visakha called on political parties and candidates to publish their environmental commitments, set measurable targets and timelines and report progress transparently to the public.

World.title: Why are Andhra Pradesh’s civic poll nominations under the Supreme Court’s scrutiny? | Explained
World.content:
The story so far:

The YSR Congress Party (YSRCP)’s allegation of obstructions during the filing of nominations for elections to urban local bodies (ULBs) has landed the State Election Commission (SEC) in a tight spot, and the process has come under the Supreme Court’s scrutiny. The focus has now shifted from political claims to the SEC’s ability to establish a level playing field.

The question in Andhra Pradesh’s municipal elections is no longer only who will win the civic bodies. It is also whether every eligible candidate gets a fair opportunity to enter the contest. The Supreme Court’s intervention, following a petition by the YSRCP, has come at a critical stage of the electoral process.

By directing the Commission to examine complaints of alleged obstruction, consider extending nomination deadlines wherever it finds candidates were unable to file papers because of the law-and-order situation, and defer publication of the final candidates’ list till October 25, the court has made it clear that adherence to an election calendar cannot, by itself, settle concerns about electoral fairness.

The court’s directions do not establish the YSRCP’s allegations as true. They do, however, require the authorities to examine whether any candidate was denied the opportunity to contest because of a breakdown in law and order.

What does the YSRCP allege?

The YSRCP approached the Supreme Court after the Andhra Pradesh High Court declined, on October 18, to extend the nomination deadline. The party had first approached the High Court before the nomination process began, seeking preventive measures over its apprehensions of violence. A single judge declined omnibus relief on October 15 but gave individual candidates liberty to approach the election officers concerned for remedial action.

The opposition party alleged that its candidates had been assaulted, threatened, obstructed from reaching nomination centres and, in some instances, deprived of their nomination papers. Before the Supreme Court, the YSRCP’s counsel claimed that nearly two-thirds, or about 63%, of its candidates were prevented from filing nominations, a claim the State strongly contested. The nomination period for the ULB elections ran from October 16 to October 18.

The YSRCP’s petition cited alleged incidents in Punganur, Rayachoti, Kadapa and Tirupati, including the alleged snatching and tearing of a candidate’s nomination papers in Kadapa and the alleged prevention of nine candidates from entering Returning Officers’ offices in Tirupati. It also referred to an alleged attack on the convoy of YSRCP MP P.V. Midhun Reddy.

The political significance is considerable. In local elections, where a candidate’s personal network, caste equations, local influence and access to party machinery can be decisive, preventing a rival from entering the race can be more effective than defeating that rival at the polling booth.

An uncontested victory may be entirely legitimate when no opponent chooses to contest. It becomes a matter of serious concern if potential opponents were prevented from filing nominations. That distinction is central to the dispute.

The YSRCP’s allegations cannot be treated as proven merely because the Supreme Court entertained its petition. Equally, the complaints cannot be dismissed as political rhetoric without examining the evidence. The test is whether the alleged obstructions can be established through candidate representations, contemporaneous complaints, video recordings, police records and the accounts of election officials. The Supreme Court itself noted that the YSRCP had placed before it representations made physically and electronically, along with video clips purportedly evidencing obstruction.

What must the SEC do now?

The Supreme Court has placed the immediate responsibility for examining the complaints on the SEC. The Commission must consider the material submitted by the YSRCP and its candidates and decide whether the nomination deadline should be extended in places where it concludes that candidates were unable to file papers because of law-and-order problems.

The court directed the SEC to take a decision by October 22. If an extension is granted, the additional filing period must be at least 48 hours from the publication of the SEC’s decision. Late on October 21, the SEC ordered that the election process in all 100 ULBs be stopped forthwith, and said it would issue an order after obtaining reports from the Collectors and police chiefs on October 22.

The Director General of Police was directed to ensure necessary protection to candidates, police deployment and CCTV coverage at nomination centres. The matter was posted for further hearing on October 27, with the SEC and the State government required to file compliance affidavits.

These directions place the SEC at the centre of the controversy. Its credibility will depend not on whether its decisions favour the opposition or the ruling coalition, but on whether they follow the evidence and apply uniform standards.

A blanket extension across the State would not necessarily be the fairest solution. It could disrupt the schedule even in places where no credible obstruction has been reported. Conversely, a rigid refusal to reopen nominations despite substantiated evidence could turn procedural compliance into an instrument of exclusion.

The more defensible course is a transparent, ward-specific assessment, supported by recorded reasons. Candidates making similar claims should be treated according to the same evidentiary standards, irrespective of political affiliation.

Why did the court step in during an election?

The case also raises an important question about the limits of judicial intervention during elections. Courts generally exercise restraint once the electoral process begins, recognising the authority of election commissions and the need to prevent litigation from disrupting scheduled polls. But restraint does not mean that constitutional courts must remain powerless when the fairness of the process itself is challenged.

The Supreme Court observed that free and fair elections form part of the Constitution’s basic structure and that the right to participate by filing nominations is a facet of that principle. It said the YSRCP had made out a prima facie case for directions after considering the party’s representations and electronic evidence, including video clips.

That is a significant distinction. A prima facie assessment is not a final finding that violence occurred as alleged, nor is it a judicial endorsement of every claim made by the opposition. It means the material warranted further scrutiny and protective action.

The State government’s lawyers contested the YSRCP’s account, arguing that the situation was being misrepresented and alleging that the opposition itself contributed to the disturbances. These counter-allegations, too, require evidence. The dispute cannot be resolved merely on the basis of the rival parties’ credibility.

What is at stake for the parties?

For the YSRCP, the Supreme Court’s intervention offers an opportunity to substantiate its charge that its candidates were denied a fair chance to contest. But the party must demonstrate that its complaints are specific, verifiable and supported by evidence. A favourable interim order is not proof of a Statewide conspiracy against it.

For the ruling Telugu Desam Party-led National Democratic Alliance (NDA), the challenge is equally clear. It must ensure that the administration and police respond impartially to complaints, rather than allowing allegations of partisan conduct to undermine confidence in the elections. The responsibility of the government is not discharged merely by denying the opposition’s charges.

The SEC, meanwhile, must demonstrate that it can act independently of both sides. Transparent decisions, clear reasons for accepting or rejecting complaints, and effective security arrangements would be more convincing than public assurances of neutrality.

The consequences extend beyond the immediate municipal contest. Local bodies are the first point of contact between citizens and elected government. If voters begin to believe that political competition is determined by access to nomination centres rather than by public support, the damage will reach beyond individual wards.

What happens next?

The Supreme Court has not ordered a blanket reopening of nominations across the State. Rather, it required the SEC to determine where relief is warranted and to protect candidates’ ability to participate. That approach preserves the Commission’s primary responsibility while subjecting its decisions to judicial scrutiny.

The decisive question is whether the Commission’s examination produces credible, evidence-based remedies. If genuine obstruction is established, relief must be meaningful enough to restore the opportunity to contest. If claims are unsupported, the Commission must explain why they do not merit intervention.

The Supreme Court has placed that responsibility squarely on the SEC. Its decisions and compliance before the October 27 hearing will show whether the intervention has translated into effective safeguards, or whether doubts about the fairness of the nomination process will persist.

World.title: PM Shehbaz addresses provincial apex committee meeting in Peshawar
World.content:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif is addressing a meeting of the provincial apex committee to review the overall security situation in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

The premier arrived in Peshawar earlier in the day on his first visit to the province since the imposition of governor’s rule and the declaration of an emergency on Oct 11.

Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir and KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi, along with federal ministers and newly appointed provincial advisers, attended the meeting.

Addressing the meeting, PM Shehbaz reiterated that emergency and governor’s rule had to be imposed “under extreme compulsion”.

Describing the province as “very beautiful”, the premier expressed his hope that the government “work hard day and night and speedily make it progress towards development and prosperity”.

“This is the province that is the first extremely strong wall of the homeland,” he noted.

The prime minister went on to remark that the province was “shattered with wounds due to the circumstances created in the past several years”.

He highlighted the poor law and order situation over the past six years, recalling that security forces and law enforcement agencies had made sacrifices to establish peace in KP.

He added that “80,000 people were martyred and the [economy] suffered a loss of several hundred billion dollars. Only then, in 2018, was peace completely restored in this country”.

PM Shehbaz regretted that “terrorists were summoned back here” after peace had been established, “washing down all sacrifices down the drain”. “I believe there can be no greater injustice to this country than this,” he added.

“There can be no greater enmity with the country than not honouring and respecting such sacrifices, not holding them in esteem,” the premier remarked, highlighting that young soldiers left their homes and families to defend their country.

He called for an “all-encompassing analysis as to why this happened”, adding that there was “no worse insensitivity, criminal negligence, and hostility towards the national interest than this”.

The premier said: “All issues of the people were pushed aside — whether it is education, healthcare, or protecting the lives and property of the people — and [having] matters with terrorists instead.

State media had reported that the meeting was to review the overall security situation in KP and measures being taken to combat terrorism.

The Centre had imposed emergency and governor’s rule in KP citing the PTI-led provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism. The decisions were also endorsed by the Parliament last week amid protests by the opposition.

Governor Kundi, along with Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, had chaired a meeting of the provincial apex committee a day after governor’s rule was imposed.

In the meeting, the governor — who is now in charge of running the province — assured Naqvi he would enforce all policies of the federal government and work together with the security forces for peace and prosperity of the province.

Kundi asserted that under the new set-up, tackling terrorism would be the priority.

Later that day, Kundi, addressing a press conference, called for greater coordination between the Centre and the province, stressing that policies on counterterrorism will “come from Islamabad [..] not Kabul,” in an apparent jibe at the PTI-led KP government, which has been accused of maintaining a “nexus” with terrorist groups by federal ministers.

The Centre’s move to impose governor’s rule and emergency in KP also followed a mobilisation drive and protest march by the PTI and in opposition at the Centre, to demand the release of its jailed founder, Imran Khan.

Intense negotiations between the two sides a week before the imposition of governor’s rule had failed to yield any results, with counterterrorism policy being one of the main reasons behind the breakdown of their talks.

The PTI said it was being left out of security decisions concerning KP, which the Centre denied . It also called for reviewing the counterterrorism policy, while the latter criticised the KP government’s efforts to combat terrorism in the province and objected to its stance on dialogue with the Afghan Taliban.

Soon after, the Centre also authorised the deployment of Pakistan Army troops and assets in aid of civil power in KP.

World.title: President Zardari to visit Germany from Oct 22-24 to discuss bilateral ties
World.content:
President Asif Ali Zardari will undertake a visit to Germany from Oct 22 to 24 to discuss bilateral ties as the two countries are set to mark 75th anniversary of their diplomatic relations.

In a statement issued on Thursday, the Foreign Office (FO) said the president’s visit is “part of high-level exchanges between Pakistan and Germany”.

It “holds special significance in the context of the 75th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between the two countries being commemorated this year”.

It said the visit reflects the “deep commitment of both countries to further strengthening the partnership”.

During his visit, President Zardari will hold meetings with his German counterpart Frank-Walter Steinmeier, as well as senior leadership and business leaders, with a “particular focus оп economic and trade cooperation”, FO said.

Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah is also expected to accompany the president on his trip, with the matter being discussed in Murad’s meeting with German Consul General Mr Thomas E. Schultze.

In September, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar met German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.

During the meeting, Germany appreciated Pakistan’s mediation efforts in regional conflicts, especially in the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab while the two sides also agreed to “get negotiations on peace for Ukraine going”, according to the German foreign office.

Meanwhile, in June, a German delegation announced plans to bring about 30 German companies to Pakistan and link local businesses to European markets.

World.title: LHC summons Punjab home secretary, Kot Lakhpat jail superintendent in plea seeking release of Imran’s sisters
World.content:
LAHORE: The Lahore High Court (LHC) on Thursday summoned the Punjab home secretary and the superintendent of Kot Lakhpat jail in connection with a petition seeking the release of former prime minister Imran Khan’s three sisters.

Imran’s sisters — Aleema Khan, Noreen Niazi and Uzma Khan — were detained by authorities in September, under the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, 1960, as the PTI geared up for a planned protest march towards Islamabad. Their detention was ordered for 30 days.

A day earlier, Aleema’s son, Shahrez Khan, filed a fresh plea challenging their detention. It stated that Imran’s sisters remained at Lahore’s Kot Lakhpat jail despite the lapse of the 30-day period of their detention.

Justice Abher Gul Khan took up the petition on Thursday.

Advocate Rana Mudassar Umar appeared on behalf of the petitioner and submitted that the detention orders of the three sisters had expired on Oct 19 and 20, but they had not been released.

Justice Khan asked the counsel why he had not made the Lahore deputy commissioner a respondent in the petition.

The counsel replied that the deputy commissioner had not been impleaded because the detention notification issued by the official had expired.

Uzma’s husband, Ahad Khan, also approached the rostrum and requested the court to summon the deputy commissioner. The judge, however, observed that the official could not be summoned as he had not been made a party to the petition.

Subsequently, the court adjourned the hearing until Oct 28 and directed the home secretary and the jail superintendent to appear in person along with their reports on the matter.

In Wednesday’s petition, Shahrez contended that the detention period had expired, but the three sisters remained in custody. He asked the court to order their release.

It was argued that their detention was a consequence of their efforts for their brother’s release. It further contended that the preventive detention could not replace ordinary criminal law and that the order violated Article 10 as well as the safeguards of Section 3 of the MPO.

The petitioner requested the court to direct the jail superintendent to produce the detainees before the court and “set them at liberty, in the interest of justice, equity and fair play”.

The petitioner asked the court to declare the detention orders void and issue directives for the detainees’ release, while suspending the operation of the orders.

World.title: New Delhi steps up air pollution controls ahead of winter
World.content:
India began annual measures on Thursday to tackle toxic air pollution in New Delhi, a megacity of 30 million people regularly ranked among the world’s most polluted capitals.

Delhi’s air quality deteriorates in winter, when cooler air traps pollutants close to the ground. Major sources include coal-fired power plants, traffic, construction and farm stubble burning in neighbouring areas.

The Delhi government on Wednesday announced a ban on open rubbish burning and ordered food stalls to stop using coal or firewood.

In previous years, such measures have failed to curb pollution, which peaks from November to January, when levels of cancer-causing PM 2.5 microparticles often hit more than 300 micrograms per cubic metre, 20 times the World Health Organisation’s recommended daily maximum.

Monitors recorded 233 micrograms per cubic metre early on Thursday, about 15 times the limit.

The government’s Commission for Air Quality Management has predicted air quality to remain “poor” in the coming days.

A study in The Lancet Planetary Health in 2024 estimated that 3.8m deaths in India between 2009 and 2019 were linked to pollution that exceeded India’s own air quality guidelines.

Last year, pollution levels peaked at 846 micrograms per cubic metre, 56 times the WHO limit.

The UN children’s agency warns that polluted air puts children at heightened risk of acute respiratory infections.

Further restrictions take effect on November 1, including doubled parking fees and work-from-home arrangements for government office staff, aimed at reducing traffic emissions.

Tighter construction rules will also begin then, followed by a complete ban on construction and demolition from Dec 10 to Jan 20.

Last month, the authorities also imposed a construction ban that will run from Dec 10 to Jan 20 as part of a winter action plan to tackle pollution. It will include restrictions on vehicular traffic aimed at encouraging residents to use public transport.

World.title: IMF sees 1.3pc contraction in Pakistan this year due to Iran war
World.content:
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) on Thursday forecast a sharp drop in economic output in Pakistan, the Middle East and North Africa this year due to the US-Israeli-led war against Iran, followed by a rebound to 6.6 per cent growth in 2027, while warning that further energy production disruptions could worsen the outlook.

The IMF said the region’s output was expected to contract by 1.3pc as a result of the war’s impact on energy production, shipping, tourism, trade and confidence. Economic output would increase sharply in 2027, but output in those economies would generally stay below pre-war projections.

The war’s impact had been substantial, but uneven, with oil-exporting economies directly affected by disruptions to energy production and shipping hit harder, and oil importers proving to be more resilient, the IMF said in its regional outlook released Thursday in Dubai.

The IMF said its baseline assumed that the conflict would abate in early 2027 and that trade would gradually normalise during the year, but it said the outlook remained clouded by “exceptionally high uncertainty.”

“The main risks derive from further disruption to energy production and trade routes that could drive energy prices higher,” the IMF said in a statement outlining its key messages, noting external financial conditions could also tighten.

External financial conditions could also tighten if investors reassess AI-driven productivity gains and interest rates rise further amid heightened concerns about inflation and fiscal positions, it said.

Oil importers had proven more resilient, with domestic demand supported by remittances and tourism flows, favourable financial conditions, and prompt policy responses that safeguard consumers from higher commodity prices, the IMF said.

Growth in the Caucasus and Central Asia was moderating toward a more sustainable pace, the IMF said, forecasting a 5.2pc rise in economic output in 2026 and 5pc in 2027.

The IMF underscored the mantra it delivered during last week’s annual meetings, urging policymakers to prioritise maintaining price stability, while preserving fiscal sustainability, maintaining central bank independence and enacting structural reforms to boost productivity and create jobs.

World.title: Noor Zaman stuns defending champion Gawad to reach Silicon Valley Open quarters
World.content:
Pakistan’s Noor Zaman stunned defending champion and world No. 4 Karim Abdel Gawad of Egypt 3-1 on Wednesday to reach the quarter-finals of the PSA Gold Silicon Valley Open at the Redwood City in California.

The 22-year-old overcame the second seed 11-9, 11-7, 9-11, 11-6 in 52 minutes at Squash Zone, handing the Egyptian a shock defeat in the $143,500 men’s event.

“I was ready mentally and physically today, and I think now is the time for me to beat the top players,” Noor said after the match.

Noor, ranked among the world’s top 35 players, had earlier booked his place in the last 16 with a 3-1 victory over American wildcard Bransten Ming. After losing the opening game 3-11, he fought back to win 11-5, 11-8, 11-9 in 41 minutes.

The Peshawar-born player, grandson of former world champion Qamar Zaman and the 2025 U-23 world champion, has enjoyed a strong run of form in recent months, climbing into the world’s top 30 and collecting five PSA titles.

Meanwhile, Pakistan’s Mohammad Ashab Irfan bowed out in the last 16 after losing 3-0 to fifth seed Mohamed ElShorbagy of Egypt. Irfan had reached the round with a straight-games victory over Hungary’s Balazs Farkas, winning 11-6, 11-4, 11-5.

The PSA World Tour Gold event offers equal prize money for men and women as squash prepares for its Olympic debut at Los Angeles 2028.

World.title: Suspects in West Bank settler attacks put under house arrest
World.content:
All but one of the suspects arrested over recent settler attacks on an American photojournalist and a visiting French mayor in the West Bank have been released from detention and placed under house arrest, their lawyers said.

Israeli police had announced on Monday the arrests of 10 people implicated in the attacks in the occupied Palestinian territory, where violence by Israeli settlers is on the rise but perpetrators are seldom prosecuted.

Honenu, a legal aid organisation that often represents Israeli soldiers and settlers, said that all but one of the suspects had been released to house arrest.

Lawyer Assaf Gonen said in a statement that their arrests had only been “for show”, and were “intended to satisfy media pressure and foreign interests”.

The suspects have not been identified.

On Friday, photographer Heidi Levine, 65, who was on assignment for The Washington Post, was taken to hospital with broken vertebrae after being beaten by settlers while covering the West Bank’s annual olive harvest.

The incident comes 10 days after settlers beat an AFP photographer covering the West Bank olive harvest , Jaafar Ashtiyeh, leaving him also requiring hospital treatment.

A day later, settlers attacked a convoy of European diplomats and beat up Bernard Baudoux, 78, the mayor of the northern French town of Aulnoye-Aymeries who was on a goodwill visit.

The attacks drew international condemnation, but mixed messages from the Israeli government.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is facing a tight race for a new mandate, has tried to shore up his pro-settlement right-wing base and has cast doubt on the circumstances behind the recent settler attacks on Westerners.

His tone has drawn unusually strong criticism from the opposition, which has accused him of tarnishing Israel’s image.

Violence has flared in recent months in the West Bank, with near-daily attacks, thefts or vandalism by Israeli settlers against Palestinians.

Settlers have also been seizing olive groves owned by Palestinians, who see the trees as a cultural symbol.

Excluding east Jerusalem, around three million Palestinians live in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967, alongside more than 500,000 Israelis residing in settlements considered illegal under international law.

World.title: LHC issues notices to foreign secretary in contempt cases over detention of PTI-linked Pakistanis in UAE
World.content:
LAHORE: The Lahore High Court (LHC) on Thursday issued notices to Foreign Secretary Asim Iftikhar in two separate contempt petitions over alleged non-compliance with an earlier court order concerning two PTI-affiliated Pakistani citizens detained in the United Arab Emirates (UAE).

On September 14, the LHC had directed the foreign secretary to process and decide within 15 days representations concerning the detention of two citizens — Syed Salman Raza Zaidi and Muhammad Junaid Jahangir.

Justice Sadiq Mehmood Khurram heard the contempt petitions on Thursday. Barrister Abuzar Salman Niazi appeared on behalf of the petitioners and alleged that the two individuals remained deprived of consular, diplomatic, and legal access.

He recalled the court’s Sept 14 directive and contended that the petitioners had not been formally informed of any decision on their representations, even though a considerable amount of time had passed.

The counsel urged the court to initiate contempt proceedings against the foreign secretary for non-compliance.

After hearing initial arguments, Justice Khurram issued notices to the respondent secretary for submission of his reply by October 29.

In the main petitions, the counsel stated that Zaidi went missing from his residence in Sharjah on Sept 27, 2024, and was subsequently taken into custody by UAE authorities.

He said despite nearly two years having passed, the petitioner, Faryal Zainab, had still not been provided clear information regarding the charges against her husband Zaidi, the judicial proceedings, any sentence, or the complete court record.

Meanwhile, Advocate Niazi said Jahangir was allegedly detained on Sept 24, 2024, at Dubai airport on his return from Saudi Arabia.

Muhammad Ibrahim, Jahangir’s father, filed the petition challenging the alleged failure of the federal government and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) to provide effective consular protection and legal assistance.

The counsel for the petitioners submitted that despite representations having been filed regarding the detention of both citizens before the foreign secretary, the representations had not been processed.

Both petitioners had asked the court to direct that legal and consular assistance be provided to Zaidi and Jahangir, that their judicial records be obtained and that diplomatic-level steps be taken toward their return to Pakistan.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).

Seeing the address "Jorasanko" in that illustrated ad, I was immediately reminded of the Tagore family—specifically, their members who struggled with mental health. One was Birendranath Tagore, the fourth son of Maharshi Debendranath. He was brilliant at mathematics but suddenly fell victim to "wind-disease" (mental instability). The other was Somendranath, another brother of Rabindranath.

The Nobel laureate poet knew well which medicines helped the "insane." I learned of another —not for the ABD Pills of Dum Dum, but a special notice from "S.C. Roy & Co." at 167/3 Cornwallis Street. They advertised Dr. Umesh Chandra Roy’s world-famous "Great Cure for the Mad," priced at five rupees per bottle. The ad claimed that for over 70 years, this medicine had cured "millions of violent madmen and all kinds of nervous patients." This  would appear with a quote from the poet himself, saying: "...I have been aware of its efficacy for a long time." Was the "Great Cure for the Mad" then used on Birendranath or Somendranath? I know bringing up Rabindranath's name is somewhat irrelevant, but seeing these old drawings makes my mind wander in a thousand directions!

The illustrated  I mentioned was published in 1952—the day I saw the picture of the shackled madman in the paper. That drawing was made several years after legendary artists had already begun to dominate Bengali advertising. By then, Bengalis had seen hundreds of fantastic drawings for various products. A legend like O.C. Ganguly was earning forty rupees a month at Calcutta’s "Stronach Advertising" as early as 1937. An agency named "Paradise Advertising" existed in Calcutta in 1928. No one can really speak of agencies in East Bengal (now Bangladesh) before the Partition. We mostly know of the birth of agencies like Bitopi, East Asiatic, or Interspan in the 1960s. Clearly, advertising production in both Bengals (undivided India at the time) was centred in Calcutta. Be that as it may, an agency required an artist—someone to present the matter attractively to lure customers.

But not all sellers went to agencies. Instead, they took "ugly" creations (by today’s standards) made by local artists to make printing blocks for newspaper offices. The madman illustration is a classic example. The calligraphy in that ad was purely amateurish—something no professional agency would ever approve. Whether that ad ran before 1952 or if that was the first, I do not know.

It is undeniable that finding artists from the era before the establishment of agencies (pre-partition) is extremely difficult. Only a handful of artists signed their names on those ads, and even then, it was just a tiny first initial of their name and surname, usually in English. Pranabesh Maity, who drew ads in the 60s and 70s, had a more bitter experience. He claimed that even if artists signed, agency bosses would often erase the signature to imply that the agency was everything and the artist didn't matter.

This makes me think of the "Lost Tribes" and a piece by Premendra Mitra about the Patuas (traditional scroll painters). Premendra once had a great desire to find the lost Patuas of Kalighat. Briefly, the story goes like this—a young boy walking the streets of Kalighat would watch with wonder a specific style of indigenous painting. Ordinary men in dirty clothes sat cross-legged on mats in small roadside shops, painting those pictures. Yet, the walls of the shops were adorned with framed, colourful photographs of gods and goddesses. People coming to the temple preferred to buy the framed photos. Even so, the Patuas would sit down to paint whenever they found a moment’s respite between sales.

Then came a day when not only the scroll paintings but even the expensive printed pictures of deities vanished from those shops. The Patuas disappeared too. I don't know if that young boy was Premendra himself—since his childhood was spent in North India, having been born in Varanasi. But for a creative man like him to imagine that boy while thinking of the Patuas is not far-fetched. When a kind soul eventually went looking for those Patuas, he was utterly disappointed. He learned that they had been pushed out of the city. Their descendants had not become "useless" painters; some took jobs as labourers in jute mills or chose other professions. At most, unable to ignore the "blood connection," some practised their hand at painting the chalchitra (background canopy) of idols. Premendra tracked down a few of these "unfortunate" descendants and asked to see old scroll paintings. He was shocked to find they had almost nothing left. One or two pulled down a bundle of papers tucked into the thatch of their huts. Premendra saw the pathetic state of those soot-stained, discoloured papers—they were ready to crumble at any moment. Calling the insects "connoisseurs of art," a somber Premendra described how those paintings were being destroyed.

The author was accompanied by an art collector. His friend bought some paintings that were in good condition from the descendants for an unexpectedly high price. Later, he and others wrote about them. Premendra noted how his "self-satisfaction" was bruised. He commented that while many were becoming famous artists by adopting the Patua style, and those paintings were selling at major exhibitions to decorate drawing rooms—even impressing Pablo Picasso—the Patua sitting on a dirty mat in a narrow shop and the ordinary customer buying them for a pittance are nowhere to be found today.

Thinking of the early artists of Bengali advertising, I am reminded of Premendra Mitra's essay "Barbar Yuger Pore" (After the Barbaric Age), just as I was of The Lost Tribes of Israel. In it, I found no real difference between the forgotten Patuas and the nameless illustrators from the dawn of Bengali advertising.

The artists whose work I later came to know and appreciate were giants like Annada Munshi—whose ideas and illustrations revolutionised the look and feel of Bengali advertising. But I wanted to see what kind of "ugly and tasteless" creations (as labelled by later critics) Annada and his peers had replaced. Without seeing those, how could I understand the evolution of style?

Here, I must mention the artist Hemen Majumdar. He is never known to have drawn for s. Everyone knows that when art lovers discuss him, his paintings of "drip-wet Bengali women" inevitably come up. Who that woman was, was once a subject of intense speculation. A few know that he often painted while keeping a photograph by his side. Hemen had taken photos of his wife, Sudharani, in various poses as she returned from bathing in the family pond. His wife was his model. When giving the picture its final form, he would simply change Sudharani’s face and paint the face of a relative instead—much like modern-day Photoshop!

Essentially a romantic artist, Hemen Mazumdar never illustrated s himself. Yet, his signature style of depicting women was extensively adapted by other advertising artists.

Though Hemen was skilled at copying photographs, he knew the magic of glorifying them with colour. But that wasn't all. This was a man who was invited to design the gateway for King George V’s visit to India, who was a pioneer in publishing art journals, who painted the landscapes of Kashmir at the invitation of the Maharaja, who was the "Court Artist" of the Maharaja of Patiala, and who gave an artistic form to Mahatma Gandhi at the spinning wheel. He didn't just paint wet clothes!

At the same time, it is true that his skill at painting beautiful women was so popular that other artists, while drawing women for s, often mimicked Hemen’s postures—or those of the women painted by Raja Ravi Varma. Thus, even without drawing for ads himself, Hemen was "present" in this branch of art through the figures of women drawn in his style. Of course, bringing out the "wet-clothed" look or suggestive sensuality in black-and-white newspaper ads was a difficult task!

It’s worth mentioning that Hemen’s own work was occasionally used in advertising. An organisation called "Bengal Autotype" used to run ads featuring a sketch of Rabindranath Tagore by Hemen, accompanied by the Poet’s message. The advertisers even sold prints of that picture. The ad read: "A Wonderful Picture of Poet." Each print cost one rupee, with an additional 50 paise for postage. This ad appeared in the Visva-Bharati journal in the late 1930s, detailing the paper quality and dimensions.

In the eyes of some critics, the work of the "erotic painter" Hemen began to gain popularity in 1926 after a commercial firm in Mumbai bought his paintings to make calendars. The "forbidden" sword of the Hemen-style became a weapon for advertising illustrators too. One could easily call them followers of Hemen’s "voyeuristic" work. However, no matter how they were drawn, it's not as if the artists of the Battala press or the Patuas hadn't used such "swords" long before! Based on the consumer's mindset, this tradition seems never-ending—at home, abroad, and everywhere else.

Sandip Dasgupta has spent nearly three decades working in the editorial offices of newspapers and news portals. He has authored several history-based books, and a subject particularly close to his heart is the illustrations created by Bengali artists.
