World.title: Son of Aung San Suu Kyi Says He Has First Call With Her in 5 Years
World.content:
YANGON—The son of Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi said he spoke Thursday to the detained former democratic leader for the first time in more than five years.

“Today, I was finally able to speak with my mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, after more than five years. Hearing her voice again means more than words can express,” Kim Aris said in a post on Facebook.

Aung San Suu Kyi is detained at a “designated residence” in the capital, Naypyitaw, according to Myanmar authorities, where she has been sequestered since being unseated in a 2021 military coup.

AFP could not immediately reach Aris—who lives in the United Kingdom—and it was not clear how he spoke to his mother, who won the 1991 Nobel Peace Prize for efforts to bring democracy to Myanmar.

However, images accompanying his Facebook post appeared to show him standing outside the Myanmar Embassy in London.

“I am deeply grateful to everyone who has stood by my mother and me. I believe your voices helped make this moment possible,” Aris wrote.

“But my mother is 81 and remains unjustly detained. One conversation is not regular family access.”

Myanmar’s military held Aung San Suu Kyi in almost total seclusion for five years following the February 2021 coup, which ended a tentative decade-long experiment with democracy.

But in recent months authorities have increasingly advertised the loosening of her detention and published photographs of her taking private meetings, as supporters have demanded “proof of life” of the octogenarian.

On Monday, authorities in Myanmar said she received a package from Britain’s King Charles III, including two books about soil and a “sealed diplomatic communication” from the monarch.

Buckingham Palace did not comment on the contents of the communication.

Myanmar authorities said Aung San Suu Kyi was moved from a prison in Naypyitaw to house arrest in April, and in August they published images of her meeting the nation’s Red Cross representative.

After ruling Myanmar as military chief for five years, Min Aung Hlaing—who ousted Aung San Suu Kyi in the 2021 coup—was earlier this year installed as civilian president.

Analysts describe the election putting him in elected office as a charade, and say he may be loosening restrictions on Aung San Suu Kyi in a bid to court international legitimacy.

World.title: Japan’s Sasakawa Renews Myanmar Peace Pledge as Regime Battles Arakan Army
World.content:
Yohei Sasakawa, honorary chairman of Japan’s Nippon Foundation, met putschist president Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyitaw on Monday, pledging once again to assist Myanmar’s “internal peace process.”

Sasakawa made a similar promise during his last visit in August. This time, regime media said only that he offered to help strengthen Myanmar’s “human resources,” without elaborating on what that would entail. No details were released on what progress had been made since his earlier pledge to support peace efforts.

Sasakawa’s latest visit comes amid fierce fighting in Rakhine, where the regime is struggling to defend the state capital, Sittwe, from the ethnic Arakan Army (AA)’s attacks. Sasakawa previously mediated a ceasefire between the Myanmar military and the AA in 2021, though fighting resumed in late 2023 after Operation 1027. The regime has since lost 14 of 17 townships in Rakhine.

The regime claims to be open to peace talks with ethnic armed organizations (EAOs), but has excluded the AA from talks so far. It has demanded that the People’s Defense Force, the armed wing of the civilian National Unity Government, surrender.

Sasakawa’s latest meeting follows the regime’s self-styled “peace talks” with several EAOs that were not actively fighting the regime, having maintained earlier ceasefire deals with the Myanmar military even after the 2021 coup—an event that led other EAOs to resume fighting.

Separately, two EAOs that had been fighting the regime—the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army and the Ta’ang National Liberation Army—agreed to ceasefires with the regime under direct pressure from China.

The regime insists that EAOs, after signing ceasefires, must transform themselves into Border Guard Forces under the Myanmar military’s command or disarm.

The Nippon Foundation on Wednesday declined to comment on the details of Sasakawa’s latest meeting with Min Aung Hlaing. The organization believes the most useful contribution it can make in Myanmar is through “quiet, practical engagement rather than public commentary,” its executive director, Takashi Arikawa, told The Irrawaddy.

“It is not helpful to discuss the substance of ongoing efforts before there are results that can be shared publicly,” he said.

Political analyst Htin Kyaw Aye noted that multiple countries and organizations are currently exploring ways to address Myanmar’s crisis, including attempts to open dialogue between the regime and resistance forces.

“Japan and Sasakawa may be among those countries and organizations. But they haven’t released details about their plans, so it is hard to gauge what measures they will take and what impacts they could have,” he said.

In recent weeks, Japanese lawmakers Hiromichi Watanabe and Shunsuke Takei visited Naypyitaw and met with Lower House Speaker Khin Yi. Meanwhile, Tokyo hosted meetings between U.S. officials and Myanmar regime representatives this month, leading to speculation that Tokyo is considering a shift in its policy toward engagement.

Japan suspended official development assistance to Myanmar after the 2021 coup. Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi reiterated in July that relations would only improve if the junta halts violence, releases detainees including jailed civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi, and pursues genuine political dialogue.

Months ago, the regime publicly appealed for previously agreed aid to be restored.

World.title: Buying Gas or Buying Surveillance? Gas-Rich Myanmar’s Deal With Russia
World.content:
Anyone who still thinks Russia is simply bankrolling Myanmar has the direction of money backwards. In this arrangement, Myanmar is the customer. It is preparing to buy Russian gas and, in doing so, send money into a Russian economy still financing the war in Ukraine. Russia, meanwhile, is offering technology in return: satellite navigation, communications, Earth observation and aerospace cooperation. In other words, Myanmar is not being paid to stand with Russia. Myanmar is paying Russia, while Russia trades technology for access to a new market.

In August 2026, Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing traveled to Moscow for an official visit and met Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin. The visit produced 12 agreements and memoranda covering everything from energy and culture to competition policy and space technology. Four of them are particularly interesting because the technologies involved have obvious civilian applications, but equally obvious military ones.

The four were:

Memorandum Memorandum on information and communication technologies; Memorandum satellite navigation, human spaceflight Memorandum between the Myanmar Space Agency and Bauman Moscow State Technical University on technological and aerospace cooperation.

At roughly the same time, Russia and Myanmar were also negotiating something much less futuristic: liquefied natural gas.

The interesting part is that Myanmar was not discussed only as the final customer. According to the Myanmar President’s Office, the talks also covered onward supplies of Russian LNG to China and Thailand. That changes the scale of the arrangement considerably. Russia is not simply looking for another buyer. Myanmar is being considered as a possible regional distribution point for Russian LNG into Southeast Asia.

That is where the arrangement starts to look slightly extravagant.

Myanmar already has substantial natural-gas reserves and remains a major gas exporter. Recent estimates put its proven reserves at around 22.5 trillion cubic feet, while a large share of its production is exported. It certainly does not suffer from a geological shortage of natural gas.

So why import Russian LNG?

Part of the answer may simply be infrastructure, contracts and energy shortages. Having gas underground is not the same thing as having sufficient gas available in the right place, at the right time and in the right form. But the Russian side has another obvious problem: it needs markets.

Western sanctions and the war in Ukraine have placed sustained pressure on Russia’s traditional energy relationships. Russia’s finances are under considerably more pressure than before the war. The liquid part of the National Wealth Fund on September 1, 2026, was lower than ever, at 13,194.88 billion rubles (US$159.94 billion). Russia therefore has every reason to find new buyers for what it still has in abundance. And what Russia has in abundance is natural resources.

Myanmar offers access to the Southeast Asian market. Russia offers LNG. So far, fairly conventional.

The LNG story did not begin in August. In April, Russian Energy Minister Sergei Tsivilev and Myanmar Energy Minister Ko Ko Lwin were already discussing supplies of Russian LNG, petroleum products and crude oil. Myanmar’s Ministry of Electricity and Energy was quite specific about what it wanted: favorable prices, quality guarantees, secure transportation and long-term supply. The same visit produced a Memorandum of Cooperation between the Ministry of Electricity and Energy and RC-Investments. The framework was designed with Russia identifying suppliers and partners and Myanmar facilitating Russian hydrocarbon and petrochemical deliveries.

Myanmar’s LNG import system already exists. Imports resumed in late 2025 after a four-year break, with LNG loaded at the Bintulu LNG complex in Malaysia and delivered to the Thilawa floating storage unit near Yangon. So, Russia is effectively trying to insert itself into an existing supply chain. Kpler expected Myanmar to import around 0.4 million tonnes of LNG in 2026, mainly to supply the Thanlyin and Thaketa power plants. Myanmar’s own Ministry of Information confirms that LNG imports are now feeding around 500 MW of generation in Yangon.

What Russia appears prepared to provide alongside it is considerably more interesting.

The Roscosmos agreement includes satellite-navigation measurement stations, access to navigation data, a COSPAS-SARSAT ground station and an ASPOS opto-electronic telescope station. Russia will also help select and train Myanmar astronauts. According to the Myanmar Space Agency (which already took the announcement down from their website), the stated purposes include economic development, search and rescue, scientific research and monitoring hazardous objects in space. All very peaceful.

Then the cooperation expanded further. On August 19, Min Aung Hlaing met Roscosmos Director General Dmitry Bakanov. Their discussions included Earth-observation satellite imagery, a satellite-navigation measuring station, the Rassvet low-orbit communications system, nano-satellites and continued Russian assistance in developing Myanmar’s space capabilities.

None of these technologies is inherently military. That is precisely the point. They do not need to be. Remember the Chinese balloon incident in 2023? A Chinese high-altitude balloon crossed the United States before being shot down by an F-22 off the coast of South Carolina on February 4. Beijing insisted that it was a civilian airship used mainly for meteorological research which had simply been blown off course. The U.S. State Department had a rather different interpretation. A U-2 surveillance aircraft examined the balloon while it was still in the air and confirmed that it carried intelligence-collection capabilities. The U.S. government later described it as part of a broader Chinese military-linked aerial surveillance program.

Earth-observation technology works on exactly the same uncomfortable boundary between civilian and military use. The same satellite imagery that monitors forests, floods, agriculture or climate can also show roads, buildings, camps, vehicles and changes on the ground. Optical satellites provide detailed imagery; synthetic-aperture radar can observe through cloud and at night; repeated passes over the same area show what has moved, appeared or disappeared. Communications systems can connect remote communities. They can also support command and control. Radio-electronic technology can support industry. It can also support surveillance and electronic warfare. Calling the technology civilian therefore tells us very little about what it can actually be used for. A satellite looking for deforestation can look at a military base just as easily.

Below is the kind of imagery Russia can produce. These are examples from Russian Resurs-P and Canopus-V satellites:

Resurs-P4 and P5 can produce panchromatic imagery at about 1 m resolution and multispectral imagery at roughly 3-4 m. As for the Canopus-V imagery, you can clearly distinguish agricultural plots, settlements, roads and terrain. Russian Space Systems explicitly lists infrastructure monitoring among the applications of these Earth-observation systems.

And what about Rassvet? It is essentially Russia’s answer to Starlink, a low-Earth-orbit broadband communications network being built by Bureau 1440, part of Russia’s X Holding. Bureau 1440 describes the satellites themselves as “5G base stations in orbit”. The target orbit is around 800 km, with advertised speeds of up to 1 Gbit/s and latency below 70 milliseconds. The satellites communicate with each other through laser links, while user terminals can be installed on fixed sites as well as cars, ships, aircraft and trains.

Militarily, the potential is obvious. What it can potentially do is provide broadband communications in places where terrestrial networks are absent or unreliable. That could support communication between command posts, mobile units, aircraft or unmanned systems. It could also transmit satellite imagery and other intelligence quickly from one location to another.

Myanmar is an unusually important place to make that distinction.

Myanmar’s civil war is nearly as old as the country itself. Armed conflict between the central state and ethnic organizations began almost immediately after independence in 1948. The Karen conflict started in 1949, while other ethnic insurgencies developed across Kachin, Shan and other border regions. These were not temporary rebellions. They became long-running territorial conflicts over autonomy, federalism, political control and, in some cases, independence.

The Myanmar military has never been particularly effective in many of these areas. Geography is one reason. Ethnic armed organizations operate in mountains, jungles and forests along the borders with Thailand, China and India. They know the terrain, move in small units, use ambushes and landmines and often operate among populations with which they have close local connections. The Myanmar military has traditionally been much stronger in towns, on major roads and around fixed military positions.

The military is therefore not acquiring these capabilities in an abstract security environment. It is fighting an actual war.

Better Earth observation means better information about what is happening on the ground. Better satellite navigation means better positioning. Better communications mean better coordination. Better mapping means a clearer picture of roads, settlements, bases and infrastructure in territories that the military has historically struggled to control.

Russia does not need to sign a memorandum saying that it will help Myanmar locate ethnic armed organizations. No government writes agreements like that. It only needs to provide the infrastructure that makes locating them easier.

Ana Brown is a nuclear lawyer, academic and intelligence analyst specialising in defence economics, and an ALM candidate at Harvard University.

World.title: ‘They’re Definitely Afraid of Her’: Aung San Suu Kyi’s Son Speaks Out
World.content:
Kim Aris would much rather stay out of the spotlight. But when his mother Aung San Suu Kyi was once again imprisoned after Myanmar’s military coup in 2021, he realised he could no longer remain silent. As a part of his mission to draw attention to his mother’s plight and the continuing struggle of the people of Myanmar, he came to Prague last week.

There he attended the democratic Forum 2000 Conference to remind the world that wars raging closer to home have not brought an end to those that have been devastating countries thousands of miles away for years.

His mother is now 81 and her family do not know exactly where she is being held or in what conditions. In an interview with Chechia’s Seznam Zpravy daily, he asks: if he, as her own son, does not stand up for his mother, how can he expect anyone else to do so?

When you look at Myanmar today, more than five years after the coup, what kind of country do you see?

I see a country torn apart by civil war, with people on the ground facing a very, very desperate situation. The military continues to bomb civilians regularly and refuses to stop its brutality against the population despite international pressure.

And yet, despite all this, I don’t think the situation is quite as straightforward as the rest of the world tends to portray it.

The people of Burma have shown incredible strength over the past five years, and the military is nowhere near as strong as it would like the rest of the world to believe. In fact, I would say the country is more united today than it has been for decades. It’s just very difficult for the outside world to see that at the moment.

We are witnessing something of a diplomatic rehabilitation of regime leader Min Aung Hlaing. He was warmly received in Malaysia, and the United States has begun direct talks with his government. What do you think of these developments?

I think those who are now trying to negotiate with the military are going to be very disappointed when they realise that the military is making promises it simply cannot keep.

Are you referring, for example, to American efforts to gain access to Myanmar’s rare earth mineral deposits?

Yes. But those minerals are not being mined in areas controlled by the military. Many of the promises the military is making concern things it simply cannot deliver. And even if it could deliver them, we’ve known for decades that the military frequently breaks its promises.

When was the last time you heard from your mother directly?

I’ve received just one letter from her in the past five years. That must have been about three years ago now.

This summer, photographs finally emerged showing her meeting representatives of the Red Cross. When you first saw those pictures, did they reassure you, or did they raise even more questions?

At first, I wasn’t even sure whether to believe that the meeting had actually taken place. After all, over the past five years, the military has put out a great deal of false information about my mother’s health and whereabouts.

For example, they claimed she had been transferred to house arrest, and we know that isn’t true. But when I found out that the photograph was genuine—or at least that one of them was—it gave me some hope that she was, at least, still alive.

Do you think the military is afraid of Aung San Suu Kyi herself or of what she continues to represent?

They’re definitely afraid of her. Why else would they keep her locked up?

And she really is a symbol for the people. People in Burma recognise how much she has sacrificed for them over the past 30 or 40 years. They know that she has been willing to stay in Burma, to remain with them and go through the same hardships they’ve had to endure.

Your mother remains a symbol of democracy for many people. But is there anything from her time in government that you personally disagree with? I’m thinking, for example, of the Rohingya crisis.

No, I’ve never had a problem with any of her decisions. She was in an extremely difficult position, and the international community failed to understand just how delicate that situation was.

I think it’s much clearer now that she simply wasn’t able to do everything she might have wanted to do. But I believe she did more for the Rohingya than anyone else, and people don’t realise that.

They say she remained silent on the issue, even though what she actually said about it would fill entire volumes. They say she went to The Hague to defend the military. But they say that without ever having properly listened to what she actually said there. So my advice to people is this: go and listen to what she said. Find out exactly what she did to help the Rohingya.

She initiated the establishment of the Kofi Annan Commission the day after she came to power. That was before the issue had even become a major concern for the international community. She was taking steps to help the Rohingya, and representatives of the Rohingya community I’ve spoken to have told me that she did everything she could for them.

Most people associate Aung San Suu Kyi with politics or the Nobel Peace Prize. Was it difficult growing up with someone who was both a parent and such a prominent public figure?

I grew up with it, and I think that, when you’re a child, everything just seems normal. You don’t know any other way of life, so you don’t really know what’s normal and what isn’t. From a very early age, I was aware of what she represented, but I don’t think those two things are mutually exclusive. She can be my mother and, at the same time, a very prominent political figure.

You’ve said before that you never wanted to become involved in politics, and that your mother didn’t want that for you either. Yet here you are, travelling, campaigning and speaking publicly about Myanmar. When did you realise that staying out of the spotlight was no longer an option?

When they put her in prison five years ago, I realised I had to speak out. After all, I’m her son. And if I don’t do anything, how can I expect anyone else to stand up for her?

How much of what you’re doing today is about your mother personally, and how much is about Myanmar itself? If your mother were released tomorrow, would you continue campaigning for democracy in Myanmar?

I think my mother would do a pretty good job of that herself. If I manage to secure her release, then I can feel that I’ve done my job well too.

For much of her life, Aung San Suu Kyi was seen as the daughter of Aung San, the general who played a key role in Burma’s struggle for independence from British colonial rule. Do you sometimes feel that you, too, are defined by your mother’s name?

I suppose I do, to some extent. After all, it’s very difficult not to have that image hanging over you. But at the same time, I’m doing this because I want to. I think it’s important that we all try to do whatever we can. People often don’t realise that they’re capable of doing much more than they think.

As a child, did you understand why your mother chose to stay in Myanmar rather than live a safe life with her family in Britain?

Yes, I did. I was actually with her when she was first placed under house arrest, so I saw what was happening with my own eyes. In some ways, it felt like a natural continuation of what had been happening before, because we’d been watching the situation in Burma gradually deteriorate.

I can’t say it was easy, but I think that, because I was a child at the time, I was somehow able to accept it. It’s difficult to explain. I think adults often find it harder to deal with change. And if she’d been imprisoned five years ago without my having already spent decades living with our separation, I think it would have been much harder.

What was it actually like when your mother was first placed under house arrest? Can you describe what happened?

When they first came to arrest her, they arrived with several trucks to take away the student revolutionaries who were staying in the house as well. I remember watching them being taken away. Then they put barbed wire around the entire compound, set up guard posts, cut the telephone lines and stopped us from leaving the house.

But at least we were still in her own home, and her own doctor was allowed to visit her. Even after I returned to England, I could send her parcels, and sometimes we were able to communicate. The past five years have been completely different.

You mentioned the student movement earlier. Is the revolution still visible on the streets of Myanmar today?

Yes, it is. It may not be as visible as it once was, but there is still an enormous amount of resistance across the country. In some places, like Yangon, things might appear quite normal. Other journalists I’ve spoken to who have been there have told me that everything looks remarkably normal. But it certainly isn’t. There are still huge numbers of people doing everything they can to change the situation. They’ve simply gone underground, so they’re not as visible as they used to be.

Do you ever feel that the junta has forced you into a role you would never have chosen for yourself?

Yes. I wouldn’t be doing this otherwise.

And what would you be doing?

Spending time with my children and working. I’m a trained carpenter.

How do you explain to your children what’s happening to their grandmother, and what’s happening in Myanmar more generally?

We’ve been talking about it for years, and they’ve had to come to terms with it too. They understand what’s happening in Burma. I still try to protect them as much as I can. Being in the public eye isn’t easy, and I want to keep them as far away from all that as possible.

Do you believe you’ll ever see your mother again?

Yes, I do. She’s been released before, and the situation in Burma could change at any moment. Even if the resistance doesn’t achieve victory in the near future, I think there’s still a chance that she could be released.

The interview first appeared in Czech at Seznam Zpravy. Daniela Kucerova is the new outlet’s foreign news department editor. Her main area of focus is Asia, particularly China and neighboring regions.

World.title: China Moves to Cement Myanmar Influence After U.S. Talks With Regime
World.content:
As Washington resumes direct engagement with Myanmar’s military regime, Beijing moved to cement its overarching influence last week by meeting with nine political parties in Yangon to gauge public sentiment.

The Chinese delegation was led by Peng Xiubin, director‑general of the Chinese Communist Party’s International Liaison Department. Present at the meeting were representatives of the military’s proxy Union Solidarity and Development Party, the National Unity Party, People’s Party, People’s Pioneer Party, Shan and Nationalities Democratic Party, Arakan Front Party, Kayin People’s Party, Unity and Development Party, and New Chinland Congress Party.

Participants said the Chinese side raised five key points, including Myanmar public attitudes toward China and challenges in bilateral relations.

“The Chinese side asked how the Myanmar people view them,” one participant told The Irrawaddy. “Some parties noted that sections of the public hold negative or skeptical views. They urged China to do more to show how it is helping Myanmar so that people understand.”

Anti-China sentiment in Myanmar has surged since the 2021 coup, triggered by Beijing’s support for successive military regimes, supplying them with battlefield hardware, technology and diplomatic cover. China is a key arms supplier and the biggest investor in post-coup Myanmar, propping up an embattled regime shunned by much of the international community and sanctioned by the West.

Most of the parties present at the meeting took part in Jan.-Feb. regime elections that were widely dismissed as a fraud to cement military rule.

However, leaders of the National Democratic Force (NDF) and the Shan Nationalities League for Democracy (SNLD)—Htet Aung Kyaw and Sai Kyaw Nyunt—joined the talks despite their parties being dissolved for defying the regime’s electoral roadmap. One party leader said the duo attended in a personal capacity after being invited individually, rather than as representatives of their banned organizations.

The CCP delegation also asked about priority areas for cooperation, and parties’ views on peace, the economy, and domestic issues.

The meeting came as coup leader Min Aung Hlaing made progress in securing formal engagement with Washington. U.S. officials held their second round of talks with regime representatives in Tokyo earlier this month after Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance flew to Naypyitaw for talks with coup leader Min Aung Hlaing in September.

“The Chinese side made no mention of the recent U.S.-Myanmar talks, focusing instead on gauging our views,” said one participant. “Some parties stressed that they prefer engagement with China, a neighbor.”

Party leaders said they also discussed trade policy and technical support for agriculture while urging China to help reopen the Muse–Mandalay highway, a vital trade corridor. After losing control of major trade routes with China in northern Shan, the regime has imposed a near total blockade on Chinese imports to starve ethnic armed organizations of tax revenue.

Saw Han Aye, chair of the People’s Pioneer Party, said: “We asked the Chinese to increase investment and reopen trade routes as soon as possible, and Beijing affirmed it wants more frequent exchanges.”

While Beijing rejects accusations of interfering in Myanmar’s internal affairs, the belief that its investments prop up a military regime waging war on its own people is widespread within the country. Anti-China sentiment soared to new levels in 2024, when Beijing pressured ethnic armies to halt northern Shan offensives that were threatening the regime’s grip on power.

When China’s Asia envoy Deng Xijun called for ethnic autonomy during a Naypyitaw ceremony marking the Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement’s anniversary last week, critics pointed out that northern Shan State is already controlled by ethnic armies under Beijing’s thumb.

World.title: Migrants Urge Thai Gov’t to Let Them Work Free of Myanmar Regime Extortion
World.content:
Myanmar migrants are urging the Thai government to let them work legally without so-called Certificates of Identity (CI), which they say the military regime back home is weaponizing to extort money from them.

CI, issued by the regime under a quota system for overseas laborers hired in Myanmar, allow workers to register for work permits and renew their visas in Thailand.

Starved of hard currency, the regime has recently moved to harness CI issuance to grab the hard-earned money of migrant workers, saying it will not renew the papers unless workers remit a portion of their earnings back home through official channels and pay two percent income tax.

Under remittance rule introduced in late 2023, workers must send at least 25 percent of their monthly salaries home through regime-controlled banks, which means a fixed, artificially inflated exchange rate. Traditionally workers rely on the informal “hundi” system, which offers better exchange rates.

In response, the Myanmar Migrant Workers’ Representative Coordinating Committee in Thailand (MMWRCCT) has launched a campaign calling on Thai authorities to abolish the CI requirement for visas and work permits and instead allow employment solely based on the Pink Cards issued by the Thai government to regularize the status of migrants and refugees

Since Oct. 18, workers have staged an online photo campaign to press their demands.

Myanmar’s shadow National Unity Government (NUG) has expressed support for the campaign.

Workers say they are not willing to pay any form of tax to the regime which does little to protect and promote their rights.

“The regime does not even provide proper passport services, so why should we pay them any money?” said a Myanmar worker in Chonburi.

The campaign began after the regime opened new CI issuing centers on Oct. 14 in Samut Sakhon, Samut Prakan, Surat Thani, Chiang Mai and Chonburi in order to prey on migrant workers whose permit cycle expires in December. There they must show evidence that they have remitted their due share of their earnings through the regime’s banking channels.

Pouring oil on the flames, Labor Minister Maung Myint earlier this month told migrant workers in Thailand to “think of the money as a donation.”

“We are campaigning to live and work with Pink Cards only,” said Khaing Gyi of the Aid Alliance Committee. “The regime’s demand for 25 percent remittance and tax payments can only be stopped by the workers themselves.”

He insisted this is not a protest against Thailand, but “simply a request to be allowed to work legally with Pink Cards.”

Workers complain that the CI centers are expensive, Byzantine and riddled with corruption in the form of demands for unofficial fees. Many laborers, who may be barely literate and speak little official Burmese, have to reply on brokers, which makes them prone to overcharging and fraud.

Campaigners have petitioned both houses of the Thai Parliament to abolish the CI requirement and crack down on brokers profiting from migrants.

MP Sia Jampatong of the House of Representatives committee said the government “must seriously review the CI center system, because the labor registration process must exist to certify status and protect rights, not be left to become a channel for officials to make a living, or provide an opportunity for the military government to exercise power over the lives of working people,” according to news outlet The Reporters.

And Senator Thewarit Maneechai pledged to bring the demand to the consideration of the Senate Labor Committee “to consider further relevant actions,” it added.

Thai activists also expressed solidarity. The Thailand Migration Reform group warned that allowing Myanmar’s regime to control migrant registration “undermines Thai sovereignty and fuels corruption.” It urged Thai authorities to review the CI system and revert to the Pink Card framework used before 2009.

Until then, migrants lived and worked legally in Thailand with Pink Cards alone. “If workers could survive with Pink Cards before, why not improve that system and use it again?” said one migrant who has lived in the country for over 30 years.

According to Thailand’s Labor Ministry, there were nearly 3.5 million registered Myanmar workers with work permits in the country as of August this year, of whom only about 430,000 hold CI cards. The regime recently admitted that remittance has become a major source of foreign currency income for Myanmar.

World.title: Thousands Flee as Regime Troops Push Into Myanmar’s Oil Hub
World.content:
Regime troops backed by airstrikes are pouring into Magwe Region’s Myaing Township as the battle for Myanmar’s oilfields escalates, forcing thousands of residents to flee.

Reinforcements from the Light Infantry Division in Pakokku, an hour to the south, are bolstering the offensive to seize territory — nicknamed “Anyar Dubai” for its oil wealth — from resistance groups.

Resistance forces have controlled the area since 2022, repelling repeated efforts to choke off their crucial revenue stream. However, a regime offensive backed by 1,000 troops gained a foothold on May 24, seizing the Well-2 oil field in Tae Gyi village.

The latest push began on October 18, when regime reinforcements arrived in Kamma town, Pakokku Township while gyrocopters bombed the nearby village of Ohntaw, killing five people, including children, and injuring four others.

On Monday, the troops arrived in Myaing’s Twinma village, controlled by regime-aligned militia, and set up camp there. According to Sayar Htwe from the Anyar Myay Civil Society Organization, up to 5,000 residents fled neighboring villages as airstrikes and troops advanced.

“We have no information on where the troops are heading, but we can assume they are reinforcements for Tae Gyi village,” Sayar Htwe told The Irrawaddy.

Regime troops suffered heavy losses in the three-month battle for Tae Gyi, where they are now encircled and entirely reliant on airdrops for ammunition and supplies.

On September 28, the regime reported that troops had seized 131 small-scale oil rigs in the area, torching some to prevent them from falling back into resistance hands.

On Monday, the Magwe resistance’s Anyar Myay Coalition urged the public to remain on high alert for airstrikes and attacks, as regime troops were mobilizing in Pakokku, Myaing and Pauk townships. It warned that regime troops camped in Tae Gyi had killed around 50 civilians and torched 600 houses since May.

World.title: Regional Body Expels Myanmar Regime’s Human Rights Fig Leaf
World.content:
The South East Asia National Human Rights Institutions Forum (SEANF), a regional umbrella group, has expelled a fig-leaf human rights body controlled by Myanmar’s military regime after it refused to cooperate with a compliance review.

SEANF on Monday said it has terminated the membership of the Myanmar National Human Rights Commission (MNHRC) because it is not an independent institution promoting and protecting human rights.

Established in 2007, SEANF now consist of just five national human rights commissions aiming to strengthen regional cooperation, from Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, the Philippines and Timor-Leste.

The decision, made on Oct. 1 and put into effect immediately, came at the 11th hour before Myanmar was to assume the umbrella group’s rotating chairmanship in 2027.

It follows a review of whether the MNHRC still met the Paris Principles standards for independence, effectiveness, and integrity, which SEANF uses to define a national human rights institution.

SEANF told the MNHRC in early September to respond, but the MNHRC refused, saying the review “did not comply with” the network’s procedural rules—a frequent fallback by the putschist regime in dealing with regional organizations of which it has fallen foul.

SEANF then decided unilaterally that the MNHRC “no longer satisfies the definition of a national human rights institution under amended Article 1 of the SEANF Rules of Procedure,” namely being independent to promote and protect human rights, it said in Monday’s statement. The decision was made in “a fair, transparent and evidence-based manner,” it added.”

The MNHRC was also kicked out of the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions (GANHRI) and the Asia-Pacific Forum (AFP) in 2025.

SEANF added the MNHRC can reapply for membership if it can demonstrate efforts to comply with the Paris Principles.

Established under the quasi-civilian Thein Sein administration in 2011 and once recognized as a “partially independent” body, the MNHRC went rapidly downhill when its leadership was replaced with regime loyalists after the 2021 coup.

It has since remained conspicuously silent about the regime’s glaring human rights violations while offering it a veneer of respectability and protection from scrutiny. Anecdotal evidence suggests that anyone coming to the MNHRC with a complaint could expect a knock on the door from the regime’s enforcers soon after.

Rights groups in Myanmar and beyond have long called its removal from global networks.

Prominent activist Khin Ohmar of Progressive Voice told the Irrawaddy that SEANF’s decision was “a long-awaited principled action” and “strips the criminal military junta-controlled MNHRC of regional legitimacy.”

“This decision sends a clear message that this body can no longer hide behind a SEANF membership card,” she added.

World.title: Tokayev Meets Atletico Madrid CEO as Kazakhstan Seeks to Expand Football Cooperation
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev met with Atletico Madrid Chief Executive Officer Miguel Ángel Gil Marín to discuss expanding cooperation in football development, infrastructure and youth training in Kazakhstan, according to the presidential press service.

Tokayev praised the existing partnership with the Spanish football club, expressing confidence that Gil Marín’s visit would help take cooperation to a new level. Kazakhstan is investing in modern football infrastructure, training facilities and youth development programs while continuing the privatization of most domestic football clubs, Tokayev said.

He also highlighted ongoing work with FIFA to build more than 100 new football pitches for children across the country. During the meeting, Tokayev praised the achievements of Spain’s national team and its football development system, expressing interest in studying and applying Spanish expertise to train a new generation of Kazakh players.

Gil Marín thanked Tokayev for his attention to promoting football in Kazakhstan. He also spoke positively about Atletico Madrid’s academy infrastructure in the Almaty Region, saying it could eventually become one of the leading football training complexes.

Kazakhstan’s growing role in European football

Kazakhstan is also seeking to host UEFA Futsal EURO 2030, having joined six other bidders, such as Croatia, Finland, France, Georgia, Poland and Spain. According to UEFA, final bid dossiers must be submitted by June 8, 2027, with the host association scheduled to be appointed in September 2027.

Kazakhstan has already secured several major UEFA events. Astana will host the 51st UEFA Congress and the UEFA European Under-19 Futsal Championship in 2027. Astana Arena is also scheduled to host the UEFA Super Cup in 2028.

Kazakhstan has established itself as a competitive force in futsal as Almaty’s Kairat has won the UEFA Futsal Cup twice, while the national team reached the semifinals of the FIFA Futsal World Cup and won bronze at the European Championship. Kazakhstan currently ranks eighth in the world and is competing for qualification for the 2028 World Cup.

Kazakh football officials have also received UEFA appointments for matches in European club competitions during the 2026-2027 season. Olzhas Abraev will serve as a UEFA delegate for the Champions League match between Türkiye’s Fenerbahçe and the Czech Republic’s Slavia Prague. Alexander Keplin, deputy general secretary of the Kazakhstan Football Federation, will oversee the Europa League match between Armenia’s Ararat-Armenia and the Netherlands’ AZ Alkmaar.

Ayan Alzhanov, head of the federation’s international relations department, has been appointed delegate for the Conference League match between Georgia’s Iberia and Sweden’s Mjällby.

World.title: Kazakhstan, China Plan Pilot Autonomous Trucking Route Between Countries
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and China plan to launch a pilot project for autonomous freight transportation along an international route between the two countries, following an agreement to establish a joint center for intelligent transport systems and unmanned technologies.

The agreement was signed on Oct. 16 in Astana by Kazakhstan’s Road Research Institute and China TransInfo Group, according to Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Transport.

The new Joint Competence Center will focus on intelligent transport systems, autonomous driving and the digitalization of road infrastructure. It will combine China TransInfo Group’s expertise in artificial intelligence and autonomous technologies with the research institute’s experience in road research, standardization and technical regulation.

One of the center’s key priorities will be a pilot project for autonomous freight transportation along the China-Kazakhstan international route.

Other planned initiatives include automated vehicle weight and dimension control, including weigh-in-motion technology, and the establishment of a test site for autonomous driving. The parties will also explore the creation of a transport operations control center integrating industry information systems and data-sharing mechanisms.

The agreement provides for expert exchanges, professional training, joint seminars and reciprocal visits. The parties have identified initial activities and next steps for implementing joint projects.

“The center will serve as a platform for the scientific and technical assessment of advanced digital and unmanned technologies and their adaptation to Kazakhstan’s conditions,” said Kenzhebek Azatbekov, vice president of KazDorNII.

“Our goal is to ensure the implementation of pilot projects and prepare proposals to improve the regulatory and technical framework of the road sector,” he added.

The initiative aims to develop Kazakhstan’s intelligent transport infrastructure, strengthen the country’s scientific and technical capabilities, and introduce modern technologies along international transport corridors.

World.title: Kazakhstan Signs $4.8 Billion in Investment Documents at KGIR 2026 in Shymkent
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan signed 22 investment agreements and memorandums worth $4.8 billion at the ninth Kazakhstan Global Investment Roundtable (KGIR 2026), which brought together more than 500 investors and business representatives from over 40 countries in Shymkent, reported the prime minister’s press service on Oct. 22.

Speaking at the event, Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov highlighted the country’s investment opportunities and plans to attract foreign capital into manufacturing, energy, agriculture, transport, digital infrastructure and other priority sectors.

“Kazakhstan’s GDP exceeded $300 billion last year, growing by 6.5%. Since independence, the country has attracted nearly half a trillion dollars in foreign direct investment. More than $100 billion has been attracted over the past five years alone,” Bektenov said.

He emphasized the importance of modernizing the economy through advanced technologies, new production facilities and deeper processing of raw materials, adding that Kazakhstan remains open and predictable for long-term investment.

Bektenov also invited investors to participate in major projects, including a data center valley in Ekibastuz and the development of Alatau City, a planned high-tech city.

Major investment agreements

Among the documents signed were investment agreements for several large-scale projects, including a $730 million 1,000-megawatt wind power plant with an energy storage system in the Kostanai Region.

The package of signed agreements also includes a $249.6 million intelligent road monitoring system for Kazakhstan’s highways, signed between the Ministry of Transport and Freedom Lab.

Memorandums of understanding covered a range of additional projects, including a network of 20 regional inclusive schools valued at $1 billion, a $1 billion multifunctional terminal at Kuryk Port, and the $650 million Kazakhstan International Medical City project.

A framework agreement was also signed for a $74.3 million plant in Shymkent to produce PET preforms and recycle plastic.

Foreign investment and economic modernization

Before the plenary session, Bektenov reviewed projects being developed with international partners in manufacturing, agriculture and food production, and energy. These included Masdar’s wind power project in the Zhambyl Region, renewable energy projects by China Energy in the Karagandy and Turkistan regions, a Carlsberg Group beverage plant in the Almaty Region, and projects in Alatau City.

The prime minister noted that international companies continue to choose Kazakhstan for new investments. The government also highlighted measures intended to support investors, including services through Kazakhstan Investment House, a proposed special Altyn visa regime, access to English-law principles through the Astana International Financial Center, and mechanisms to protect investor rights and support investment projects.

World.title: C5+1 at Ten: How Central Asia Turned Diplomatic Dialogue Into Strategic Partnership
World.content:
The Samarkand meeting marks a decade of engagement between the United States and Central Asia, reflecting the region’s growing strategic importance, Kazakhstan’s role in advancing regional diplomacy, and a shift toward more ambitious economic cooperation.

In 2015, the United States and the five Central Asian countries established a diplomatic platform that reflected a relatively simple proposition: the region’s challenges and opportunities were better addressed through sustained regional dialogue than through five separate bilateral relationships.

A decade later, the C5+1 format has become one of the principal mechanisms for engagement between Washington and Central Asia. The ministerial meeting held in Samarkand on Oct. 19, 2026, marked its tenth anniversary at a time when transport connectivity, critical minerals, energy security, and resilient supply chains are reshaping the region’s international significance.

The platform’s evolution tells a broader story about Central Asia itself. Once frequently approached through the strategic priorities of its larger neighbors, the region is increasingly developing its own diplomatic agenda, seeking investment from multiple partners and positioning itself as a bridge between major markets.

From a regional initiative to a presidential-level platform

The origins of C5+1 are important to understanding its significance today. The format was formally established in 2015, when the foreign ministers of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan met U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry in Samarkand. The meeting followed an earlier gathering in New York and established a commitment to regular consultations.

Kazakhstan played a consequential role in advancing the concept of a regional mechanism for engagement with Washington. Policy discussions and proposals developed through Kazakh-American channels helped shape the idea that ultimately became C5+1. Its establishment, however, required the participation and support of all five Central Asian countries and the United States.

The underlying logic was straightforward but ambitious: Central Asia could strengthen its international standing by engaging major external partners collectively while preserving each country’s sovereignty and independent foreign policy.

For several years, C5+1 developed primarily through ministerial meetings, working groups, and cooperation on security, economic development, and environmental issues. Its institutional foundations gradually strengthened. A C5+1 Secretariat was established in 2022, while working groups expanded cooperation in the economy, energy and environment, and security.

The decisive political milestone came in September 2023, when then-U.S. President Joe Biden hosted the first-ever C5+1 presidential summit on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

The participation of all five Central Asian presidents elevated the platform to an entirely new level. It demonstrated that Washington was prepared to engage the region collectively at the highest political level and that Central Asian governments were willing to coordinate their priorities within a shared diplomatic framework.

The New York Declaration emphasized sovereignty, territorial integrity, regional connectivity, energy cooperation, and security. It also reflected a growing recognition that Central Asia’s economic potential and geopolitical position warranted sustained attention from the United States.

The significance of the 2023 summit was therefore not simply that six presidents sat around the same table. It was that a format originally built around ministerial consultations had developed into a platform capable of supporting strategic dialogue at the highest level.

Why the past few years have mattered most

Although C5+1 was established in 2015, its more recent development has been particularly consequential. The platform has increasingly moved beyond diplomatic declarations toward commercial engagement, infrastructure development, and cooperation on strategic resources.

The November 2025 C5+1 summit in Washington D.C., hosted by President Donald Trump, reinforced this shift. According to U.S. officials, the meetings generated more than $25 billion in commercial deals and commitments across sectors including transportation, energy, finance, and other industries. These figures represent announced agreements and commitments rather than completed investments.

The economic dimension is essential. For Central Asian governments, closer relations with the United States can support investment diversification, access to advanced technologies, industrial development, and the expansion of export markets. For Washington, the region offers opportunities to strengthen commercial ties, diversify supply chains, and develop partnerships in sectors increasingly important to economic and national security.

The latest meeting in Samarkand continued this trajectory.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with the foreign ministers of the five Central Asian countries to discuss economic cooperation, regional connectivity, energy, critical minerals, and security. The joint statement reaffirmed a vision of the United States and Central Asia as long-term partners.

One of the most consequential priorities was the development of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, commonly known as the Middle Corridor. By connecting Central Asia across the Caspian Sea to the South Caucasus and European markets, the route offers opportunities to diversify trade connections and strengthen the resilience of international supply chains.

For Kazakhstan, this agenda has direct strategic implications. As a major regional economy with extensive transport infrastructure and access to the Caspian Sea, the country has a strong interest in improving logistics, harmonizing customs procedures, and attracting investment into transport and industrial facilities.

The Samarkand discussions also highlighted critical minerals and their processing. Rather than focusing exclusively on the extraction of raw materials, the countries have an opportunity to develop higher-value production, establish industrial capacity, and integrate into international supply chains for advanced manufacturing and energy technologies.

These priorities connect regional diplomacy with tangible economic interests. The central question is increasingly not whether Central Asia attracts international attention, but how effectively the region can translate that attention into long-term development.

Kazakhstan and the value of regional diplomacy

For Kazakhstan, the development of C5+1 fits within a broader multivector foreign policy aimed at maintaining constructive relations with major powers while protecting national interests and expanding economic opportunities.

Regional engagement adds an important dimension to this approach. By working through C5+1, Kazakhstan can pursue bilateral priorities with Washington while also supporting initiatives that benefit Central Asia as a whole.

This is particularly relevant in transport connectivity, investment promotion, energy security, and the diversification of export routes. Infrastructure networks and supply chains rarely stop at national borders. Their commercial viability depends on coordination among neighboring countries, predictable regulations, and efficient cross-border procedures.

The same logic applies to security. Cooperation on counterterrorism, border management, cybersecurity, and transnational crime can be more effective when national efforts are complemented by regional dialogue and international partnerships.

Kazakhstan’s role in advancing the original concept of C5+1 also illustrates a broader point: regional countries do not need to remain passive recipients of great-power strategies. They can help shape the mechanisms through which external powers engage with them.

At the same time, the effectiveness of the platform depends on maintaining a balance between collective priorities and national interests. The five Central Asian countries have different economic structures, political priorities, and relationships with external partners. C5+1 is most useful when it accommodates those differences while identifying areas where cooperation produces clear mutual benefits.

A changing geopolitical landscape

The renewed attention to Central Asia is taking place amid intensifying competition over transport routes, energy resources, critical minerals, and technological supply chains.

The region’s geography gives it a distinctive position at the intersection of Europe and Asia. Its economic potential, natural resources, and proximity to major markets have become increasingly relevant as governments and businesses seek to diversify trade and reduce vulnerabilities.

Yet it would be misleading to interpret C5+1 simply as a geopolitical instrument directed against another power. Central Asian governments have consistently pursued diversified international partnerships, maintaining relations with Russia, China, Europe, the United States, and other partners.

Their objective is not necessarily to choose one external partner over another. It is to expand their room for maneuver, attract investment, and ensure that international engagement contributes to national development.

For Washington, sustained engagement offers an opportunity to become a more significant economic and strategic partner in a region that U.S. officials have acknowledged deserves greater attention. For Central Asia, the value of that engagement will ultimately depend on whether diplomatic commitments lead to new markets, productive investment, technology transfer, and better infrastructure.

The question is therefore one of implementation rather than diplomatic symbolism.

Looking toward 2027 and beyond

The prospect of further high-level U.S. engagement, including the prospect of a regional visit by President Donald Trump in 2027 as referenced in remarks attributed to Secretary of State Rubio, would reinforce the momentum generated by recent C5+1 meetings. The timing and details of any such visit would need to be confirmed through official announcements.

More important than any single visit, however, is whether the platform can maintain political attention between summits and ministerial meetings.

The tenth anniversary provides an opportunity to assess what C5+1 has achieved and what its next phase should deliver. The platform has moved from its founding ministerial meeting in Samarkand to a presidential summit in New York in 2023, another presidential-level gathering in Washington in 2025, and renewed ministerial engagement in Samarkand in 2026.

That progression is evidence of institutional continuity and growing political relevance. But longevity alone is not a measure of success.

The next stage should prioritize the implementation of existing agreements, stronger links between government dialogue and private-sector participation, and measurable progress on transport connectivity, investment, critical-mineral processing, and regional trade.

The relationship between C5+1 and the B5+1 business platform could also help turn diplomatic priorities into commercially viable projects by bringing companies and investors more directly into the process.

Ultimately, the significance of C5+1 lies in the gradual transformation of how Central Asia engages with the world. A mechanism conceived as a framework for regular consultations has evolved into a channel for high-level diplomacy and increasingly ambitious economic cooperation.

For Kazakhstan and its neighbors, the challenge is to ensure that this progress strengthens regional agency rather than merely reflecting the strategic priorities of external powers.

Ten years after its establishment, C5+1 has demonstrated that sustained diplomacy can create a platform with growing strategic weight. Its next decade will be judged by a more demanding standard: whether that platform can deliver lasting economic opportunities, stronger regional connectivity, and tangible benefits for the people of Central Asia.

The author is Sapargali Shalgimbayev, the president of the CFive Intellectual Platform.

World.title: Kazakhstan, ICAO Pledge to Strengthen Civil Aviation Cooperation
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakh Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov met with International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Secretary General Juan Carlos Salazar in Astana on Oct. 21 to discuss strengthening cooperation on aviation safety, infrastructure development and the country’s transit potential.

During the meeting, Bektenov highlighted the strategic importance of cooperation with ICAO as Kazakhstan seeks to strengthen its transport and logistics potential, develop aviation hubs and expand its role as a regional transit center.

Salazar praised Kazakhstan’s progress in aviation safety. According to him, the country ranks among the world’s top 20 states under ICAO’s aviation safety assessment, with a score of 95.7%. He also noted Kazakhstan’s efforts to develop airport and air navigation infrastructure, while domestic airlines are modernizing their fleets and expanding international routes.

Kazakhstan’s civil aviation sector has recorded significant growth in recent years. Over the past five years, the industry’s gross output increased 6.5 times to $2.9 billion. In 2025, the country’s airports handled 31.8 million passengers, while the international route network expanded to 161 destinations.

The officials attributed these results to the consistent implementation of international standards and the expertise of Kazakh aviation professionals. They also highlighted the importance of the Civil Aviation Development Master Plan through 2050, which is currently being developed. The document is expected to set strategic priorities for modernizing the sector, establishing aviation hubs and strengthening Kazakhstan’s international competitiveness.

Bektenov and Salazar reaffirmed their commitment to closer cooperation between Kazakhstan and ICAO to further improve aviation safety and support the sustainable development of civil aviation.

Salazar arrived in Kazakhstan to attend Aviation Safety Week 2026. His visit marks the first official visit by an ICAO secretary general to a Central Asian country, according to the prime minister’s press service.

World.title: Kazakhstan Approves Military Reform Plan to Modernize Armed Forces
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Security Council has approved a military reform plan aimed at modernizing the Armed Forces, restructuring military management and training, and establishing a new Unmanned Forces branch, according to the presidential press service.

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev chaired an Oct. 21 Security Council meeting, where he called for the creation of a modern, mobile and technologically advanced army in the shortest possible time.

“Special attention is required for service security, command culture, and the efficient use of public resources. The interaction between the army and society also needs to be changed. This is a matter of comprehensive reform. Half‑hearted solutions will not yield the necessary results,” Tokayev said.

Deputy Security Council Chair Aida Balayeva presented the main provisions of the plan, which was developed with consideration of international military experience, modern warfare and proposals from domestic specialists. Defense Minister Aidos Myrzakhmetov reported on the planned modernization of the Armed Forces.

The plan introduces a two-stage model of compulsory military service. Recruits will spend the first six months training at military training centers and the next six months serving in military units, focusing on combat training and carrying out tasks as part of their units.

The reform also includes measures to strengthen servicemen’s safety and protect their rights. Kazakhstan plans to establish military adviser positions and an authorized body for servicemen’s affairs to reinforce military discipline. Other initiatives include expanding the unified military-patriotic training system, increasing the number of specialized military schools and improving initial military training.

The Armed Forces will also adopt a new information and communications strategy and improve educational work based on the constitutional principle of Law and Order. Organizational measures under the plan are scheduled for completion by the end of 2026, while the main conceptual reforms are expected to be implemented in 2027.

Tokayev also instructed officials to complete by the end of the year the work of a commission conducting a comprehensive review of the Defense Ministry.

He stressed that military security is a national priority requiring coordinated efforts across relevant government bodies. The government and the Security Council will coordinate implementation of the reform plan.

World.title: Kazakhstan Ranks Among World’s Top 15 Gold Producers
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan ranked 15th among the world’s largest gold-producing countries in 2025, producing 82.4 tons of gold, according to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS). However, output declined 5.4% from 87.1 tons in 2024, while global gold production rose 2% to 3,800 tons.

China remained the world’s largest producer with 384.3 tons, followed by Russia (345 tons), Australia (293.2 tons), Canada (213.3 tons), and Peru (208.9 tons). The five countries accounted for 37.9% of global gold production, reported EnergyProm on Oct. 21, citing the World Gold Council.

Ghana ranked sixth with 187.3 tons, followed by the United States (157 tons), Uzbekistan (125.4 tons), Mexico (113.5 tons), and Indonesia (104.2 tons). Ghana recorded the largest increase among these countries, with production rising 21%, while Indonesia’s output fell 24.8%.

Kazakhstan accounted for approximately 2.2% of global gold production. Across the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), gold output reached 592.5 tons in 2025, up 1.2% year on year and 6.6% compared with 2020. Uzbekistan recorded the strongest five-year growth, increasing production by 25.2% and accounting for approximately 68.5% of the region’s total increase.

Kazakhstan’s national statistics show a different production measure. According to the Bureau of National Statistics, output of unwrought and semi-manufactured gold, or gold in powder form, fell 4% to 127 tons in 2025, from 132.3 tons a year earlier. Refined gold production declined 4.2% to 71.2 tons, from 74.3 tons. These figures differ from international estimates because of variations in methodology and product classifications.

The downward trend continued in January-September. Production of unwrought and semi-manufactured gold and gold powder fell 11% year on year to 84.7 tons, while refined gold output decreased 11% to 47.7 tons.

Meanwhile, Kazakhstan extracted 30.5 million tons of gold-bearing ore in January-September, up 9.4% from the same period in 2025. However, gold-bearing concentrate production fell 16.9% to 197,800 tons.

For full-year 2025, gold ore extraction declined 6.2% to 39.2 million tons, while concentrate output dropped 26.4% to 307,400 tons.

The divergence highlights a key factor in gold production: higher ore extraction does not necessarily translate into greater output of gold-bearing concentrates or refined gold, as results also depend on the gold content of the ore and the efficiency of processing.

According to the USGS, global gold reserves were estimated at 66,000 tons this year. Australia held the largest reserves at 13,000 tons, followed by Russia with 12,000 tons. Kazakhstan’s reserves were estimated at 2,300 tons, representing approximately 3.5% of the global total. These geological reserves differ from the gold central banks hold as financial assets.

World.title: Turkic World: From Shared History to Shared Future
World.content:
There are critical moments in the life of nations and states when shared history ceases to be merely a memory and becomes a force shaping the future. I believe the Turkic World is living through such a moment today.

Across a vast geography connecting East and West, the Turkic World brings together a population of around 180 million people, bound by deep historical and cultural ties and increasingly connected through trade, transport, investment, education, technology and people-to-people cooperation. What for centuries was sustained through common language, culture, traditions and collective memory is increasingly taking institutional and practical form under the umbrella of the family Organization of Turkic States (OTS).

The transformation has been remarkable. Since its establishment in 2009, the OTS has evolved from a platform focused primarily on political dialogue and cultural affinity into a comprehensive and action-oriented framework of cooperation.

As I approach the completion of my tenure as Secretary General, I see this moment not simply as an occasion to look back at what has been accomplished. More importantly, it is an opportunity to reflect on what makes our cooperation distinctive, what it can offer to our peoples, and what kind of Turkic World we wish to build together in the decades ahead.

A unity rooted in something deeper

The OTS possesses a quality that is rare among international organizations.

International institutions are often created in response to a particular political challenge, economic necessity or security concern. The foundation of the OTS is different. Our cooperation rests upon something that existed long before the establishment of the Organization itself: centuries of shared history, linguistic affinity, common cultural traditions, values and a profound sense of belonging to the same civilizational space.

Common history, language, identity and culture are not simply references to our past. They provide a foundation of trust upon which strong and sustainable cooperation can be built.

Few, if any, international organizations enjoy such a natural foundation. Yet heritage alone does not guarantee a shared future. The responsibility of our generation is to transform this historical closeness and affinity into opportunities, connectivity and cooperation that respond to the realities and challenges of the 21st century.

There is a simple expression that captures this idea particularly well: “Together, We Are Stronger.”

Remarkably, these words are understood across the Turkic World and require almost no translation, reflecting the deep linguistic and cultural bonds among our peoples. Today, “Together, We Are Stronger” is not merely an expression of solidarity, but a guiding principle for practical cooperation.

From shared identity to institutional strength

One of the most important transformations of recent years has been the gradual conversion of this natural affinity into institutional capacity.

Today, the OTS continues to make significant strides in strengthening cooperation among its Member States. Currently, 65 cooperation mechanisms exist under OTS umbrella, which range cover– from economy, trade, transport and customs to energy, digitalization, industry, science and technology, health, education, youth, agriculture, labour and social protection, intellectual property, space and many others. Since 2023 alone, 32 new mechanisms have been established – matching the total number created by the end of 2022. This reflects not only the expansion of our agenda but also the growing determination of our member states and observers to translate shared priorities into concrete institutional cooperation.

What matters even more than the numbers is a change in how we work together. Political consultations have become more frequent and substantive; ministries and specialized institutions are in closer contact; and our ability to think together, plan together and act together has grown. I would describe this stage of our development in three words: implementation, transformation and institutional deepening.

As chair of the coordination committee of the Turkic Cooperation Organizations, the OTS maintains close and structured cooperation with affiliated and related organizations, including the Parliamentary Assembly of Turkic States (TURKPA), the International Organization of Turkic Culture (TURKSOY), the Turkic Academy, the Turkic Culture and Heritage Foundation, the Turkic Investment Fund (TIF) and the Union of Turkic Chambers of Commerce and Industry (TCCI). Together, these institutions contribute to a multidimensional framework of cooperation, strengthening institutional ties and advancing shared priorities across the Turkic World.

The establishment and operationalization of the Turkic Investment Fund represent an important milestone in this evolution. For the first time, the Turkic States have created a joint financial institution designed to mobilize their economic potential, support investment and entrepreneurship, strengthen small and medium-sized enterprises and facilitate joint projects. The Council of Central Banks, the Turkic Green Finance Council and the Turkic Investment Promotion Network (TurkIPAnet) further reinforce this emerging financial and investment architecture.

Yet among the most encouraging developments I have witnessed during my tenure is the emergence of cooperation networks beyond governmental and formal institutions, including within the private sector and professional communities.

Notaries, auditors, engineers, trade unions and representatives of other professions are establishing contacts, creating networks and exploring institutional forms of cooperation within a broader Turkic framework. This growing cooperation is also reflected in initiatives such as the Union of International Road Transport Associations of the OTS, the Union of Turkic Ski Resorts and the Turkic Red Network, bringing together stakeholders across transport, tourism and humanitarian cooperation. Business communities, universities, young people, experts and professional associations are finding their own reasons – and increasingly their own ways – to connect.

When people and professional communities begin building connections on their own initiative, cooperation acquires a life beyond institutions. It becomes rooted in society itself.

For me, this is one of the clearest signs of the growing maturity of Turkic cooperation.

An emerging economic and strategic space

The growing importance of the Turkic World is shaped not only by our shared heritage, but also by the scale of our collective economic and strategic potential. According to figures reported for the end of 2025, the combined GDP of OTS Member States and Observers exceeded $2.4 trillion, their aggregate trade turnover reached approximately $1.27 trillion.

Together, the Turkic States would represent the world’s 11th largest economy and third-largest energy provider. With substantial reserves of oil, natural gas, coal and critical minerals, including over 40 percent of global uranium production, our countries possess significant energy potential while increasingly investing in renewable energy development.

In a time of rising demand and fast changes in global energy systems, working together is not optional – it is a necessary thing to do. Recent OTS Summits stress the importance of energy security which depends on connecting pipelines, power grids, storage, and transport routes to ensure stable supply, increase trade, and strengthen economic and geopolitical stability.

The Turkic States are strengthening regional and international energy connectivity through major infrastructure projects, including the Southern Gas Corridor, the Central Asia–Azerbaijan Green Energy Corridor, the Kambarata-1 Hydropower Plant and the Black Sea Submarine Cable. These initiatives reflect the growing role of the Turkic World in enhancing energy security, diversifying supply routes and advancing renewable energy cooperation.

In this regard, the Turkic World Vision-2040 provides an important strategic framework. It calls on us to deepen economic integration, improve connectivity, strengthen institutions, invest in knowledge-based industries, and promote sustainable and inclusive growth.

Perhaps nowhere is this logic more visible than in connectivity.

The Trans-Caspian International East-West Middle Corridor is becoming an increasingly important link between Asia and Europe, with freight volumes potentially reaching 11 million tons by 2030. The China–the Kyrgyz Republic–Uzbekistan railway, with a projected capacity of up to 15 million tons annually, will further strengthen regional connectivity and expand trade opportunities across Eurasia.

But a modern corridor is more than railway tracks, roads and ports. Goods must cross borders efficiently; information and documentation must move with them.

The OTS is complementing physical infrastructure with customs and digital solutions, including the Simplified Customs Corridor, e-Permit, e-CMR and digital TIR, to facilitate cross-border trade and reduce administrative barriers. The Digital Economy Partnership Agreement and ongoing efforts to conclude a free trade agreement in services and investment will further strengthen economic integration among our countries.

We also welcome the recently established cooperation among competition authorities, financial intelligence units, investment promotion agencies, supreme audit institutions and tax administrations. These partnerships strengthen institutional connectivity and improve economic governance across the Turkic World.

The digital economy remains at the center of this agenda. Digital trade platforms, interoperable e-customs systems, fintech cooperation, secure data exchange, and common approaches to digital regulation can make economic relations more efficient and accessible. Digital transformation is not simply a technical matter. It is one of the foundations of modern economic integration.

The objective is straightforward: to make connectivity work better for those who actually use it.

Taken together, these developments point towards the gradual emergence of a more connected Turkic economic space – one in which infrastructure is reinforced by efficient borders, trade is supported by investment, and the strengths of individual countries increasingly become sources of shared opportunity.

Towards a more connected Turkic World

For the younger generation, the Turkic World should be a living space of opportunity. The Turkic Universities Union (TURKUNIB) and Orhun Exchange Programme help bring students, academic staff and universities closer together. Youth initiatives, including the Youth Volunteering Educational Programme, the Multilateral Youth Exchange Programme and the International Youth Camp, further promote people-to-people contacts, mutual understanding and a sense of shared identity among young people across the Turkic World. Meanwhile, initiatives under discussion such as the Turkic ID and Common Museum Card aim to facilitate travel and access to our shared cultural heritage.

A transport corridor becomes more valuable when businesses use it. Business cooperation becomes stronger when supported by investment. Investment becomes more productive when connected with technology and human capital. And all of these become more sustainable when our societies participate in and benefit from the process.

The future of the OTS therefore lies not simply in expanding the number of areas in which we cooperate, but in bringing existing mechanisms together into a more coherent space of opportunity.

Our strength lies precisely in building upon our unique foundations while remaining open to the wider world.

Our long-term direction is set out in the Turkic World Vision-2040.
