Human rights defenders stressed that their monitoring covered only between a quarter and a third of the republic’s settlements, and even there, the documentation was incomplete.

A Crime Against Humanity

Russian criminal law contains no specific offence of enforced disappearance, meaning that there is no corresponding legal classification or penalty. Yet on December 18, 1992, Russia was among the states that approved United Nations General Assembly Resolution 47/133, adopting the Declaration on the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance. The declaration defines enforced disappearance as the deprivation of a person’s liberty by state agents or people acting with state authorisation, followed by a refusal to acknowledge the detention and the concealment of the person’s fate or whereabouts.

The declaration called on states to prevent such practices and to make enforced disappearance a separate criminal offence. When disappearances are widespread and systematic, and the state refuses to acknowledge them, investigate them or punish those responsible, they may constitute crimes against humanity, which are not subject to a statute of limitations. Article 7 states: “No circumstances whatsoever, whether a threat of war, a state of war, internal political instability or any other public emergency, may be invoked to justify enforced disappearances.”

In 2006, Russia reversed its position and refused to ratify the International Convention that had been developed on the basis of the declaration. By then, it had effectively become the second European country, after Bosnia and Herzegovina, in terms of the number of people who had been forcibly disappeared. Lawyers from the Legal Initiative organisation alone won more than 1,000 cases concerning disappearances in Chechnya before the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR).

In late August, Serbian general Ratko Mladić died while serving a life sentence imposed by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia for crimes against humanity. The tribunal found him guilty of the Srebrenica massacre, the largest mass killing in Europe since the Second World War. On Mladić’s orders, Bosnian Serb forces killed 8,372 men and boys from Bosniak Muslim families. Until their remains were found, exhumed and identified, the victims were considered forcibly disappeared. More than 40,000 people disappeared during the conflicts in the former Yugoslavia.

It is no coincidence that Russia has still not recognised the Srebrenica massacre as genocide, while its Foreign Ministry formally expressed condolences to Mladić’s family.

The “Health” Settlement

In early 2001, rumours spread across Chechnya about bodies found in the abandoned dacha settlement of Zdorovye, just over half a mile from Khankala, Russia’s main military base in the republic. Since January 2000, the headquarters of the Joint Group of Forces conducting the so-called counterterrorism operation had been based there. That was the official term used in Russia for the Second Chechen War. The settlement stood deserted, and people were afraid even to venture into it.

In early February, the family of Adam Chimaev, who had disappeared after being detained in December 2000, paid a Russian serviceman for information about the location of his body. Risking his life, Chimaev’s father found his son near a holiday cottage. The body bore signs of torture and three gunshot wounds to the chest. The father paid the military another $3,000 to retrieve the body and bury his son.

By the end of February, three more families had found the bodies of relatives who had disappeared during cleansing operations. The case then attracted widespread attention. Memorial and Human Rights Watch jointly produced a report titled The Dirty War: Disappearances, Torture and Extrajudicial Executions. The settlement was covered by Kommersant and Radio Liberty. Later, the Legal Initiative represented the victims’ relatives before the European Court of Human Rights after the state refused to investigate the crimes.

Technically, this was not a mass grave but a dumping ground, where the bodies of people tortured to death were discarded in place of rubbish. After the scandal broke, prosecutors opened an investigation and found around 60 bodies of men and women. Almost all were dressed in civilian clothes, and many had their hands and feet bound with wire. Most had gunshot wounds inflicted at close range to the abdomen, chest or head. The bodies were at different stages of decomposition, ranging from several weeks to a year. This meant the settlement had been used as a dumping ground for the dead for several months.

Immediately after the reports were published, the authorities cordoned off the settlement, claiming that militants had allegedly mined the area. The bodies were laid out for identification in a dilapidated hangar at an emergency services base in Grozny. Within two weeks, nearly 30 people had been identified. All had previously been detained by the military and then disappeared. Evidence indicated that at least five of them had been taken alive to the Khankala military base.

The last to be identified were three women: Nura Luluyeva, the wife of Chechen judge Said-Alvi Luluyev, and her cousins, Markha and Raisa Gakayev. According to the European Court of Human Rights judgment in Luluyev and Others v. Russia, on June 3, 2000, the women went to a market in Grozny and were caught up in a cleansing operation. Soldiers in camouflage uniforms and masks pulled sacks over the detainees’ heads and drove them away in a Ural military truck. The prosecutor’s office, Interior Ministry and FSB all claimed that the women did not appear on any list of detainees. When their bodies were found, sacks were still covering their heads — possibly the very ones used during their abduction.

The authorities then hurriedly buried the unidentified bodies in a mass grave on the outskirts of the cemetery in the village of Prigorodnoye.

The remains of Ilyas Gachayev and brothers Emedi and Adam Soltamuradov, who had been taken from Mesker-Yurt following the operational intelligence provided by Girkin, were identified by their relatives only after the mass burial, using photographs taken by forensic experts. The bodies were still clothed, with their hands bound behind their backs. Shamil Yashuyev was never identified, but one of the bodies gnawed by dogs was wearing a jacket resembling the one he had been wearing when he was taken from his home.

On August 21, 2001, Chechnya’s prosecutor, Vladimir Chernov, told the Interfax news agency: “There is no witness testimony confirming that federal forces were responsible for these killings. Therefore, the main theory pursued by investigators is that the mass grave was organised by Chechen militants.”

Mass Reburials

Chernov justified the hasty burials by citing the lack of facilities to store the bodies and claimed that the evidence collected would be sufficient for any future identification. Yet investigators failed to preserve the clothing or collect forensic evidence. They conducted no autopsies, established neither the causes of death nor injuries sustained before death, took no dental X-rays, recovered no bullets and collected no samples for DNA testing. The authorities did everything they could to ensure that the bodies would never be identified and the killers never found.

The remains of more than 30 people from the Zdorovye settlement still lie unidentified in a mass grave in Prigorodnoye.

The search for mass graves was long conducted by the General Lebed Peacekeeping Mission. According to its head, Alexander Mukomolov, who until recently was a member of the Human Rights Council under the Russian president, 119 mass burial sites were identified in Chechnya between 1999 and 2009. They may contain the remains of around 1,500 people: victims of enforced disappearances, Russian soldiers reported missing in action, and civilians killed in bombing raids and shelling.

Most of the burial sites remain unopened to this day. They are excavated only when they obstruct construction projects planned by the Chechen authorities. In such cases, the remains are dug up and reburied elsewhere. Reburial without identifying the victims of serious crimes has become standard practice in the republic.

For years, Russian and Chechen authorities have repeated the same explanation: Chechnya has no laboratory capable of identifying human remains, and Russia lacks the necessary specialists. In reality, Russia began building the infrastructure for identifying the dead, particularly soldiers, as early as 1995. American military personnel helped their counterparts in the Russian Defence Ministry master modern techniques and supplied equipment for DNA analysis.

The United States was a pioneer in this field. American anthropologists, forensic pathologists and criminal investigators played a crucial role in investigating crimes committed by military dictatorships in Latin America. FBI experts helped establish what became the world’s most advanced system for exhuming and identifying remains from mass graves in the former Yugoslavia. Mukomolov repeatedly cited the experience of Bosnia and Herzegovina as an international benchmark and urged the authorities to apply the same approach in Chechnya.

Russia itself drew on American expertise in 2008, immediately after the five-day war in Georgia. More than 100 Russian forensic specialists were deployed to South Ossetia, accompanied by a mobile laboratory. Russian authorities announced to the world that between 1,500 and 2,000 civilians had been killed in South Ossetia during the five-day war and attempted to accuse the Georgian authorities of genocide. In reality, the number of South Ossetian victims was ten times lower: 162 people. There was no need to deploy so many forensic specialists other than for propaganda purposes.

Two months before the war in Georgia, in June 2008, one of the largest burial sites in Chechnya was discovered in Grozny’s Leninsky district, near a Christian cemetery. It contained around 800 bodies. In July, another site containing several hundred bodies was found near the village of Goryacheistochnenskaya. But Viktor Ledenev, head of the Investigative Committee in Chechnya, refused to conduct exhumations, citing a shortage of specialists and inadequate infrastructure.

Even Nurdi Nukhazhiev, the former human rights ombudsman under the head of Chechnya, publicly identified what he saw as the real reason behind this policy of concealment:“It is precisely the Defence Ministry that is doing everything possible to obstruct the creation of an interagency commission to identify abducted and missing persons, as well as the establishment of a laboratory in the Chechen Republic to identify exhumed bodies…”

Freedom in Exchange for Danger

The official objective of the Second Chechen War was to combat terrorism. The authorities persistently referred to the campaign as a “counterterrorism operation,” rather than a war. This was largely a legal manoeuvre. Declaring martial law would have required the approval of a parliament that was still independent at the time and compliance with international obligations, above all the Geneva Conventions.

But in September 1999, public concern centred above all on security. Political scientists would later describe the social contract offered to citizens by the new prime minister, Vladimir Putin, as “freedom in exchange for security.” The public readily accepted it.

Initially, the West sharply criticised Russia’s methods. But those methods only drove more recruits into the militants’ ranks. The unrestrained brutality of the military and security services became one of the factors behind the emergence of shahidkas — women, often the widows and sisters of those killed, who were turned into “human bombs” after relatively rudimentary psychological and ideological conditioning.

After the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, Vladimir Putin was the first foreign leader to call US President George W. Bush to offer his condolences. Putin stressed that Russia had already spent two years defending the civilised world against Islamist terrorism in Chechnya. Western attitudes began to shift. Basayev, Khattab, Umarov and the Caucasus Emirate they led were placed on US terrorist lists. The West definitively abandoned the idea of an international tribunal for Chechnya.

When Putin opened Russian airspace to NATO aircraft and raised no objections to US military bases in Central Asia, the Second Chechen War came to be regarded as one front in the global war on terror.

In reality, the West and Russia shared a record of war crimes in this conflict. When confronted with accusations of human rights abuses in Chechnya, Russia pointed to Guantánamo Bay, Abu Ghraib, secret CIA prisons in Europe, and civilian casualties in Afghanistan and Iraq.

But a comparison of how the United States and Russia protected their citizens from terrorist attacks suggests that counterterrorism was never a priority for the Russian authorities. After September 11, the United States overhauled its security system. In the quarter-century since, no terrorist organisation has come close to repeating Osama bin Laden’s “success.” In Russia, by contrast, terrorist attacks became a recurring feature of life: the 2002 Moscow theatre siege, the 2004 attacks in Ingushetia and the Beslan school hostage-taking, the 2005 assault on Nalchik, and countless bombings targeting cars, buildings, hospitals, markets, aircraft and metro stations.

The authorities exploited every attack to concentrate presidential power and strengthen the security services. But the goal was not to fight terrorists; it was to suppress political opposition and civic dissent.

It was not until 2013, on the eve of the Sochi Winter Olympics, that the security services managed to stabilise the situation in the Caucasus. International developments played a significant role. When the Islamic State (ISIS), founded by former members of Saddam Hussein’s Iraqi security services, seized parts of Iraq and Syria and declared a caliphate, radicals from around the world, including the North Caucasus, flocked to join it. Russian security services simply opened the border to them.

In March 2024, Islamic State followers stormed the Crocus City Hall concert venue, opened fire and set the building ablaze. The attack killed 151 people and injured more than 600. Foreign intelligence agencies had warned the FSB of an impending terrorist attack. Yet on March 19, three days before the assault, Russia’s leadership publicly dismissed the warnings as “outright blackmail by Western countries” and an attempt to destabilise society. The FSB did nothing to prevent the attack.

Today, in Russia, Ukrainians are branded terrorists, while Islamic State militants are no longer the primary focus.

The terrorist attack took place in a climate of complete public silence. There is nowhere left to ask the authorities what became of the social contract of September 1999, and no one left to ask the question. This is what became of it: the methods of terror honed in Chechnya have become a central instrument of Russian state policy, both at home and abroad.

The practices of filtration — enforced disappearances, secret prisons, torture and extrajudicial executions — became a principal means of “bringing the population into line” after the annexation of Crimea, and later across all the regions of Ukraine occupied by Russian forces in the first months of the war. According to human rights defenders, the practice of so-called “short-term enforced disappearances” has also spread beyond Chechnya to regions across Russia itself.

▇ Replace Chechens with Ukrainians in Anna Politkovskaya’s articles, Novye Aldy and Khatuni with Bucha, Izium or Kherson, and Grozny, Komsomolskoye, Argun and Shali with Mariupol, Bakhmut, Kharkiv or, right now, Kyiv, and her reporting will read as entirely contemporary — and entirely prophetic.

This article was produced in collaboration with the Memory Project, a civic initiative comprising Russian lawyers, human rights defenders and researchers who investigate enforced disappearances and preserve historical memory.

World.title: Uzbekistan, South Korea discuss AI transport, Middle Corridor development
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 22. Uzbekistan and South Korea discussed cooperation on artificial intelligence-powered traffic management, road safety and railway transport, as well as opportunities to strengthen the Middle Corridor’s transit capacity at a meeting in South Korea on October 21.

This was reflected in the statement by the Uzbekistan Ministry of Transport, following a meeting between Uzbekistan’s Deputy Transport Minister Ilkhomjon Abdugafarov and South Korean Deputy Land, Infrastructure and Transport Minister Jeong Eui-gyeong on the sidelines of the World Congress on Intelligent Transport Systems (ITS) in Gangneung, South Korea.

The sides reviewed cooperation in highway management, road safety and real-time monitoring and analysis of traffic flows.

Particular attention was paid to the potential introduction of intelligent traffic lights and AI-based traffic management solutions. These technologies could help improve traffic flow, reduce congestion and enhance road safety.

Additionally, the officials discussed international cooperation in railway transport. South Korea thanked Uzbekistan for its support regarding the country's participation in the activities of the Organization for Cooperation between Railways (OSJD) and its accession to the organization.

Moreover, South Korea expressed readiness to work with Uzbekistan on developing the Middle Corridor, increasing its transit capacity, upgrading transport and logistics infrastructure, and implementing potential joint infrastructure projects along the route.

World.title: Apple commits up to $100M to U.S. titanium supplier for iPhone models
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 22. Apple will invest up to $100 million over the next three years in its partnership with U.S. titanium producer Perryman Company and expand cooperation with Qnity Electronics to manufacture key components for the iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro in the United States.

According to the company announcement, the agreements are part of Apple's American Manufacturing Program (AMP), launched last year to expand advanced manufacturing and the production of critical components in the country. The initiative forms part of the company's broader $600 billion, four-year commitment to U.S. manufacturing and innovation.

Perryman, a Pennsylvania-based family-owned company, will supply titanium for Apple products, including the iPhone Duo, the company's first foldable iPhone. At its facility in Houston, Pennsylvania, the company melts, forges and rolls specialty titanium containing at least 80% recycled material for the device's enclosure.

Apple said the Grade 5 titanium enclosure is designed to provide strength and durability for the foldable smartphone.

Apple is also expanding its partnership with Qnity Electronics, headquartered in Delaware, which joined AMP in March. Qnity will produce advanced films in the United States for the variable-aperture camera system in the iPhone 18 Pro.

The technology is central to the device's 48-megapixel Fusion Main camera, allowing it to adjust light intake and depth control. According to Apple, on-device intelligence automatically enables the camera to capture more light in darker conditions and preserve sharper detail in brighter settings.

"We're thrilled to expand our work with companies producing advanced materials and components for our newest iPhone lineup right here in America," Apple Chief Operating Officer Sabih Khan said.

He said American innovation was vital to Apple's products, from the titanium used in the iPhone Duo to camera technology in the iPhone 18 Pro. Khan added that the expanded partnerships would help the company grow AMP and support U.S. jobs.

Apple works with suppliers across all 50 U.S. states and supports more than 450,000 jobs in the country, according to the company. Through AMP, it aims to bring more advanced manufacturing and critical component production to the United States.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Libya aim to boost agricultural trade
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 22. Kazakhstan and Libya intend to expand trade in agricultural products, with a focus on supplies of Kazakh grain and meat, the Kazakh Ministry of Agriculture said.

Agriculture Minister Aidarbek Saparov and Libya’s Minister of Agriculture and Livestock Abdul Latif Al-Taher discussed prospects for bilateral cooperation.

Saparov noted that strengthening trade and economic ties with Libya and expanding the presence of Kazakh agricultural products on North African markets is a priority.

“We are ready to increase supplies of high-quality and competitive agricultural products to the Libyan market. First of all, we are talking about grain crops, beef and lamb. Our task is to move from existing potential to specific trade projects, expand business contacts and create sustainable supply channels that meet the needs of the Libyan market. Kazakhstan has significant resources to implement these plans,” the minister said, presenting the capabilities of the Kazakh agro-industrial complex.

Kazakhstan’s production potential provides a solid basis for expanding export geography. The grain harvest has exceeded 27 million tons for two years in a row. Oilseed production has reached 4.8 million tons, and legumes over 1 million tons. Over the past five years, agricultural exports have doubled and exceeded $7 billion.

In the last marketing year, 15.3 million tons of grain were exported, 70 percent more than in the previous comparable period.

Diversification of export destinations and development of new markets remain among the priorities for the agricultural sector.

Abdul Latif Al-Taher stressed the importance of strengthening international ties in agriculture. According to him, direct interaction between relevant agencies will help identify promising areas of cooperation and create additional opportunities for mutual supplies.

“We are interested in expanding cooperation, exchanging professional experience and creating additional opportunities for mutual supplies. I am confident that direct dialogue will help identify the most promising areas and give a new impetus to our trade and economic relations,” the minister said.

The sides also paid special attention to prospects for exporting Kazakh meat products. The country has 9.3 million head of cattle and 24.3 million head of sheep and goats. These figures form a substantial resource base for developing livestock farming and expanding supplies of domestic meat to foreign markets.

To realize the export potential in practice, the sides considered issues of veterinary and phytosanitary cooperation, product safety, and improving trade procedures. Agreeing on requirements for supplied products and conditions for their market access will be an important stage of further work.

World.title: Kazakhstan, CNPC may draft technology plan for 2027-2030
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 22. Kazakhstan and China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC) may develop a joint plan for implementing technologies in 2027-2030, the Kazakh Ministry of Energy said.

The proposal was made following the 4th Kazakhstan-CNPC Technical Seminar in Astana, which focused on introducing modern technologies and improving the efficiency of developing Kazakhstan’s oil and gas fields.

The document should specify particular fields and pilot sites, responsible executors, funding volumes, implementation timelines, and measurable performance indicators. It is also proposed to define criteria for the success of tests and conditions for the transition to industrial use of the technologies.

The seminar was attended by Deputy Minister of Energy Yerlan Akbarov. He said cooperation between Kazakhstan and China, based on friendship and strategic partnership, has significant potential for the further technological development of the oil and gas industry.

Interaction with CNPC has continued for almost 30 years. During this time, cumulative oil production at the assets of Aktobemunaigas, the PetroKazakhstan group and Mangistaumunaigas has exceeded 350 million tons. The accumulated experience of cooperation creates a basis for further introduction of advanced solutions aimed at improving production efficiency and rational use of subsoil resources, the deputy minister noted.

Akbarov stressed the importance of practical application of modern technologies, including in geological exploration, geological modeling, enhanced oil recovery, drilling, geophysical surveys and digital field management.

Special attention was paid to adapting advanced technologies to the conditions of Kazakh fields. In particular, the sides considered the possibility of applying the experience of point flooding at the Daqing field, the prospects for polymer flooding at the Kalamkas field, as well as gas injection, development of high-viscosity oil fields, hydraulic fracturing and gas lift technologies.

According to Akbarov, replenishing the resource base remains an important area of further work. In this regard, it is necessary to continue studying the prospects of the Pre-Caspian Basin and the South Turgay Basin, and to ensure sustainable development of operating production assets.

The deputy minister also emphasized the need for timely financing and high-quality implementation of planned measures. Shared responsibility for the rational use of subsoil resources, preservation of the fields’ production potential, and introduction of effective technological solutions is an important condition for the sustainable development of Kazakhstan’s oil and gas industry, he added.

World.title: Capital One offers up to $4,300 in travel value to Venture X Business users
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 22. Capital One has introduced a limited-time promotion for new Venture X Business credit cardholders, offering up to $4,300 in travel value through bonus miles and travel credits as the card marks its third anniversary.

According to the announcement of Capital One, the offer, which began on October 20, allows eligible new cardholders to earn 150,000 bonus miles, valued by the company at $1,500, after spending $40,000 within the first four months of opening an account. Those who spend $120,000 within the same period can earn an additional 150,000 miles, also valued at $1,500, along with a $1,000 credit for bookings through Capital One Business Travel.

The promotion comes on top of the card's standard $300 annual travel credit, bringing the total potential travel value to $4,300.

Eligible cardholders can also receive a fourth night free at select Premier and Lifestyle Collection hotels when booking stays of at least four nights through Capital One Business Travel, the company's travel booking platform for business owners.

"Travel plays an important role in how many businesses build relationships, pursue opportunities and drive growth," said Ami Vedak, Managing Vice President of Capital One Business. She said the rewards allow business owners to convert spending into travel benefits while retaining access to the card's premium features.

The Venture X Business card offers unlimited two miles per dollar on purchases, 10 miles per dollar on hotels and rental cars booked through Capital One Business Travel, and five miles per dollar on flights and vacation rentals booked through the platform. Other benefits include a 10,000-mile anniversary bonus, complimentary access to Capital One Lounges and Capital One Landings, and no preset spending limit. The card carries an annual fee of $395.

Capital One Business Travel is available to cardholders at no additional cost and provides booking and travel management tools for businesses.

The new-cardholder promotion follows a separate limited-time offer announced on September 30 for existing Venture X Business customers. Under that offer, eligible cardholders can receive a $500 Capital One Business Travel credit after spending $3,000 on bookings through the platform by December 15, 2026.

The new-cardholder offer is available for a limited period to eligible applicants approved during the promotional window. Applicants must meet the relevant spending requirements within the first four months after opening their accounts to qualify for the rewards.

World.title: Snowy 2.0 to cost 12 times more than initial budget with further delays
World.content:
The cost of delivering Australia's biggest renewable energy project has doubled since the last estimate and is now set to become fully operational a year later than expected, according to a major review.

Snowy Hydro has released its much-anticipated cost reassessment for the Snowy 2.0 hydropower project, revealing it could cost up to $25 billion, with first power expected in early 2029 and the project to be fully operational later that year.

While the Commonwealth-owned company has set a target cost of $22 billion, it is allowing for an additional $3 billion to be spent on the project if required.

Snowy 2.0, which started being built seven years ago, had an initial budget of $2 billion and was originally expected to start operating in 2021.

Those figures were revised as part of a "project reset" three years ago, which projected first power would be delivered in late 2027 and Snowy 2.0 would be fully operational a year later, at a cost of $12 billion.

Dennis Barnes was appointed Snowy Hydro CEO in 2023. (ABC News: Isla Evans)

Late last year it was announced that the project's contractor Future Generation Joint Venture (FGJV) would conduct a "line-by-line reassessment", which has now been released three months later than initially expected.

Snowy Hydro CEO Dennis Barnes said he was "incredibly disappointed" with the update.

"We had a project that was stalled and had billions of dollars of claims on the table in 2023," he said.

"I'm pleased we've got progress, progress doubled in the first year after the reset.

"What I'm disappointed about is obviously the resultant costs of the progress we're making."

Dennis Barnes says more people are now working on Snowy 2.0 than what was expected in 2023. (ABC News: Isla Evans)

Mr Barnes said the "design immaturity" that was faced before the 2023 reset had contributed to the latest cost blowouts.

"We've understood that we're going to need a lot more people for a lot longer to deliver this job," he said.

"This job is 80 per cent people costs, we've got 5,000 people on the job now working across multiple work fronts and that's obviously a lot more than we thought in 2023."

The review found 65 per cent of machine tunnelling and 90 per cent of cavern excavation had now been completed and work to build the underground power station was underway.

While Mr Barnes said the project was in its "strongest position yet", he could not rule out further cost blowouts beyond the most recent targets.

"There's never any guarantees with mega projects, we're doing a world first thing in many respects in really complex conditions," he said.

" But the project is hitting its milestones of late, we have a lot of the risks behind us. "

How did Snowy 2.0 get here?

Snowy 2.0 is designed to underpin Australia's electricity security and affordability over coming decades, as the country transitions away from fossil fuels.

Based in the New South Wales Snowy Mountains, it will link two dams through about 27 kilometres of tunnels and include an underground pumped hydro station the size of the Sydney Opera House.

The project will act like a giant battery, pumping water upstream when electricity is cheap and releasing it back downstream to generate power when demand is high.

Snowy 2.0 will store excess power from wind and solar and deliver it to the grid when needed. (Supplied: Snowy Hydro )

It has a total capacity of 2,200 MW and is expected to power three million homes for a week, the equivalent of about 26 million household batteries.

Unlike batteries, pumped hydro offers long-duration storage, meaning it is designed to be a renewable energy insurance policy during days when there is limited sun or wind.

But Snowy 2.0 has been embroiled in controversy since it was announced by former Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull in 2017, including cost blowouts, missed deadlines, scrutiny over safety issues and contractor disputes.

A major setback came after one of the initial three tunnel boring machines, Florence, got stuck in early 2023 for 11 months after hitting soft ground and creating a sinkhole.

The National Audit Office gave Snowy 2.0 a glowing review in 2022 but the most recent audit, released earlier this year, found "significant deficiencies" in the management of the hydropower project.

The project is billed as critical for the security of the national energy grid as coal-fired power stations continue to close. (ABC South East NSW: Isla Evans)

In a submission to a parliamentary inquiry examining the project's delivery, Snowy Hydro said initial "design immaturity" and the project's "inherent complexity" had been the primary drivers of additional costs.

"Productivity underperformance and cost escalation have also been significant factors," the submission read.

"Others have related to project-specific complexities that have developed during delivery.

" Snowy Hydro has learned and taken action in response to these challenges. "

A submission from Future Generation Joint Venture (FGJV), the group responsible for the project's construction, said "unprecedented geotechnical uncertainty" and "significant geopolitical upheaval" had contributed to cost escalations.

"Unlike metropolitan tunnelling projects, where initial ground investigations are typically well-developed, ground investigations within a national park are necessarily limited," the submission said.

"As a result, conditions only become fully apparent as excavation progresses."

Snowy 2.0 is being built in complex geological and remote conditions. (ABC News: Isla Evans)

Project benefits report released

Along with the cost reassessment, Snowy Hydro has also released an economic study conducted by engineering consultant GHD.

It found the project will contribute $18 billion to Australia's economy during the delivery phase and reduce wholesale electricity costs by more than $7b by 2075.

Mr Barnes said all technologies were needed for the energy transition, including batteries, pumped hydro and gas for firming.

"We issued a report earlier in the year to show what the grid looked like with and without Snowy 2.0 and on those periods, which are pretty common, where we get no wind and we get no sun for days on end, batteries run out of juice, they don't get recharged," he said.

"We actually saw that in January in South Australia, there was a period where the batteries run out of juice and prices went very high.

"So with Snowy 2.0 in the grid, we see that the prices in those periods were $7,000 a MWh lower."

Chris Bowen has previously criticised the former Coalition government's handling of the project prior to Labor taking over. (ABC South East NSW: Isla Evans)

A joint statement from Energy Minister Chris Bowen and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said abandoning the hydropower project would "undermine grid reliability", scrap 5,000 jobs and lead to higher electricity bills.

"Once completed, Snowy 2.0 will be an incredible national asset, supporting Australia's energy security, price stability and the transition to renewable energy," the statement said.

"The pumped hydro expansion of the Snowy Scheme will provide more than half of the total energy storage the grid needs by 2050, strengthening energy security and putting downwards pressure on energy prices."

World.title: NT government accused of politicising Kumanjayi Little Baby's death
World.content:
Emotions boiled over in Northern Territory parliament today, with the government accused of politicising the tragic death of a five-year-old girl through a parliamentary motion against an opposition member.

Country Liberal Party Child Protection Minister Robyn Cahill began the day by moving a motion condemning her Labor counterpart Chansey Paech over comments he made to the media on Tuesday.

Following the release of a damning report into the NT's Department of Children and Families and its failings relating to Kumanjayi Little Baby, Mr Paech referenced Jefferson Lewis, who has been charged with her murder and is yet to enter a plea or face trial.

Robyn Cahill says Mr Paech's comments cannot be justified by grief, politics or frustration. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

While speaking on the motion today, Ms Cahill used parliamentary privilege to repeat Mr Paech's comments, which were later aired by Channel 9 and the broadcast shared on the MLA's social media account.

During her speech, Ms Cahill told parliament "a man has been charged over the death of this little girl and that matter is before the courts".

"Every member of this house knows what that means," she said.

" We choose our words carefully because what matters most now is that justice is done for her and seen to be done. "

Ms Cahill said Mr Paech's comments were "offender-focused commentary" and "condemnable".

"There is no justification [Mr Paech] can offer for these comments — not grief, not politics and not frustration with the government," she said.

The report by Greg Shanahan and Karen Webb released on Tuesday found there were extensive failings by the department. (ABC News: Randi Dahnial)

"Kumanjayi Little Baby's family deserve better and so does our community."

Following the release of the report into the child protection system, Mr Paech and some child safety advocacy organisations criticised the government for only scrutinising the department while glossing over failures in other areas, including corrections, the justice system, domestic violence and housing.

They also said the report focused too much on the actions of Kumanjayi Little Baby's mother — a repeated victim of domestic violence.

Paech hits back

During Mr Paech's contribution to the debate, he said the government had politicised Kumanjayi Little Baby's death by moving the motion, which the government used its majority to pass.

A Central Australia-based MLA, Mr Paech said he had also supported the little girl's family throughout their ordeal in Alice Springs.

"I was there when Kumanjayi Little Baby's family needed someone," he said.

" I was there, I helped out with the sorry camps, I helped out with the family, I continue to help out with the family and I am not going to apologise for standing up and calling out the injustices. "

Mr Paech also said "everyone in [the] community" knew the "situation around the tragic loss of life of Kumanjayi Little Baby".

Chansey Paech accused Ms Cahill of "leaking to the media" following reports by News 24 and the NT News yesterday. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"To pretend or suggest I have said something that is not already out in the public domain, that my communities are not already talking about, is disrespectful to them," he said.

Mr Paech also accused Ms Cahill of "leaking to the media because that's where the stories" around Kumanjayi Little Baby "are coming from".

During question time, Labor backbencher Dheran Young asked Ms Cahill whether her department was investigating how "confidential information" identifying Mr Lewis as one of five "safe adults" in Kumanjayi Little Baby's life, had been leaked to News 24 and the NT News.

The outlets reported yesterday that a person referenced in the Webb-Shanahan report released on Tuesday as having been nominated by the department as "safe" was Mr Lewis.

In response, Ms Cahill did not address whether there was an investigation, instead saying "any information coming into the public arena that one would not expect" was "of concern".

"We are absolutely focused on not having information in the public arena that shouldn't be," she said.

"I am absolutely confident that nobody would have released information that they know that they shouldn't be releasing."

Ms Cahill said Mr Young should ask the "people who have actually put that information out into the public arena where they got it from".

"That's really the obvious place to start," she said.

World.title: Police investigating death of woman and child in Melbourne's east
World.content:
Detectives are investigating the circumstances around the death of a woman and a child in Melbourne's east tonight.

Victoria Police said they were called to Prospect Street in Box Hill just before 6:20pm, with reports a woman had been found unresponsive outside an apartment block.

An unresponsive child was discovered nearby a short time later.

"The woman and primary school-aged child could not be revived and sadly died at the scene," a police spokesperson said.

At this stage, police are not looking for anyone else in relation to the incident.

Anyone who witnessed the incident or has information has been urged to phone Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000.

World.title: Man charged over WA MP threats says weapon was musical instrument
World.content:
A man charged over an allegedly threatening incident at Labor MP Hannah Beazley's office has told a Perth court he was holding a musical instrument, not a weapon, as police allege.

John Lawrence Smart is accused of making threats at Ms Beazley's electorate office in inner-city Victoria Park on Wednesday while in the possession of an "improvised martial arts weapon".

The police prosecutor told Perth Magistrates Court he was armed with an "implement resembling nunchucks", and had a second, similar implement attached to his belt.

He said Mr Smart was "shouting and screaming at staff".

But Mr Smart said the items were claves, wooden percussion sticks, which he had been playing for years.

Loading...

Holding his head in his hands during the hearing, Mr Smart referenced "the holy grail", and made claims about people who he said had "destroyed" his head.

"They don't understand what I'm going through," he said at one point.

Mental health history

The 56-year-old has been charged with being armed to cause fear, making a threat and possessing cannabis.

The magistrate said she had been given a "multi-page mental health assessment".

She said Mr Smart had a diagnosis of schizophrenia and had been an involuntary mental health patient in the past.

The man allegedly visited Hannah Beazley's electorate office brandishing a pair of nunchucks. (ABC News: Madigan Landry)

The court heard he often played "drumsticks" in public and thought the government was "attempting to target or pursue him".

The magistrate refused bail and he will appear in court again on October 29.

The court heard he may be put on the wait list for the Frankland psychiatric facility.

'Menacing' threats

Speaking earlier today outside parliament, Ms Beazley said Wednesday's incident was not the first time she has faced "very menacing" threats.

Her comments came as WA Police released vision of Mr Smart's arrest, showing the wooden implements police allege he used.

It comes just days after federal independent MP Helen Haines was left fighting for her life after losing both of her legs when a man allegedly ran into her with his car outside her Victorian electorate office.

Ms Beazley said her staff had been "absolutely exemplary" in handling the incident and assisting police.

"I could not be prouder of them. I also could not be more worried about them," she told reporters.

Hannah Beazley's office remained closed on Thursday, although Ms Beazley said her staff were still working. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

Incident prompts rethink

Ms Beazley, the Disability Affairs and Local Government Minister, said this type of incident was "not new" for her staff, but it had prompted a rethink.

"Just a couple of weeks ago I instructed the police to drop an issue when I had been getting very menacing threats online," she said.

"But I dropped it because I just didn't have the time to deal with it.

" And really, I'll probably be picking that up again because it's also up to people like me to pursue these matters, to ensure that they aren't normalised and they aren't acceptable in the community. "

Hannah Beazley says she has received messages of support. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Ms Beazley said despite offering to close the office today, her staff had chosen to keep working, adding she was "heartened" by the messages of support she had received.

World.title: Affordable home scheme went from 'blessing' to 'disaster', buyers say
World.content:
It was spruiked as a scheme to allow low and middle-income earners to purchase their first home in Canberra, but almost five after signing on, some participants are yet to move in.

Instead, some buyers say they have been left stranded as they grapple with incomplete works while locked in contractual disputes with the builder.

"[I'm] just stuck in a no man's land, where I'm a home-owner but I have no home," Tash Lawther said.

"It's the sense of powerlessness — it's supposed to be a home, the place you feel safe and comfortable in, and this house is going to be a reminder of the years waiting.

"I do feel like ... maybe it wasn't possible within the price-capped contract."

The ACT Suburban Land Agency’s Affordable Home Purchase Scheme was set up to provide affordable properties in the fast-growing new suburbs of Whitlam and Taylor.

Canberra resident Tash Lawther has been locked in contractual disputes with the builder of her Whitlam property. (ABC News: Lily Nothling)

Ms Lawther was initially excited when she was selected, via a ballot, to purchase land and a three-bedroom one-bathroom townhouse in Whitlam for about $440,000 in December 2021.

"It was a little bit of good news to share after a couple of really hard years post-COVID and just a little bit of joy for everybody to get excited about," she said.

Participants were advised construction would start in 2022 and would be completed in 2023.

Instead, the project was overshadowed by lengthy delays before work finally began.

Suburban Land Agency chief executive Adam Davey says some of the homes are taking "extraordinarily long" to finish. (ABC News: Robert Baird)

Suburban Land Agency chief executive Adam Davey said the ACT government had been providing rent assistance to 11 buyers for about two years as works dragged on.

"I would have to say that the homes are taking an extraordinarily long time to finish," Mr Davey said.

"They are nearly finished, but they're not quite there from what I can see."

Independent assessors denied

Despite being advised their homes have reached practical completion, some buyers think the work is not yet finished.

They are refusing to sign their certificates of occupancy and have been issued with formal notices of breach of contract, with a threat of potential buyback action.

"In the last year, seeing action happening at first was exciting," Ms Lawther said.

" But now I'm looking and this house isn't what I thought I signed up for. "

The scheme works as a lottery for hopeful home-owners to enter the housing market. (ABC News: Lily Nothling)

Last month, Ms Lawther brought an independent assessor to her practical completion inspection, resulting in them both being told to leave the property due to unauthorised access.

In a subsequent email, the builder advised independent inspectors would not be allowed on site prior to handover because the homes had already been inspected and passed by the certifier.

"I just want someone who's on my side, on my team, looking at my contract and … supporting me in responding to the builder, saying, here are all the incomplete works, here are what the defects are," Ms Lawther said.

Buyers of townhouses in Whitlam say their properties have not been completed according to their contracts. (ABC News: Lily Nothling)

Earlier in the process, buyers said they were shocked to discover their homes had not been built from brick, despite it being the only external material on the inclusions list.

Instead, the Suburban Land Agency endorsed the use of foam cladding, but admitted the builder had failed to properly communicate the change with the buyers.

'Blessing' turned 'disaster'

Kathy Bai also purchased a home down the street from Ms Lawther as part of the scheme.

When she initially found out about the program, she thought it was a "blessing".

"I really want to settle in Canberra, but the housing market is so expensive," she said.

She was advised construction on her home was completed in late 2025.

But Ms Bai is yet to move in while she disputes issues with the property.

Kathy Bai was told her home was finished last year but is yet to move in. (ABC News: Lily Nothling)

She has described the experience as a "disaster" and said she felt let down by the scheme's operator, the Suburban Land Agency.

"It's kind of like you're talking to a wall," Ms Bai said.

"I don't feel like they're standing with us."

Call to 'redesign' scheme

Independent MLA Fiona Carrick has fielded multiple complaints and concerns from home buyers about the scheme.

She said the management of the program was causing huge levels of emotional and financial stress.

"I think the SLA needs to look after the people purchasing these affordable homes and they need to have a look at the program and redesign it," she said.

" They need to make sure that a delay of five years and the stress involved with that doesn't happen again. "

Independent MLA Fiona Carrick says she has been receiving complaints from buyers about townhouses in Whitlam bought through the scheme. (ABC News: Lily Nothling)

Chief Minister Andrew Barr told the ACT Legislative Assembly the Suburban Land Agency was working with the buyers and builders to avoid potential buyback action.

"The scheme itself … has generally been positive, but there are certainly lessons to be learnt and we appear to have one builder in particular who has been very difficult to deal with both for the SLA and the home purchasers," Mr Barr said in the Assembly.

"It isn't acceptable, the behaviour of the builders in this instance."

Mr Davey said the Affordable Home Purchase Scheme had worked, "broadly speaking".

"Of the 181 homes participating in that scheme, 170 people have moved into their homes," he said.

The affordable housing scheme has seen 170 people move into their ACT properties, according to the SLA. (ABC News: Lily Nothling)

The scheme started running in May 2021 and held its final ballot in March 2022.

Mr Davey said the agency had recently sent its own inspector to the properties in Whitlam to examine quality and completion issues.

"We've provided those reports to the builder and said 'you need to finish these things', and we're in the process now of providing the latest report to the buyers, because we want them to have confidence in what's being done out there," he said.

World.title: 'Reprehensible': The Trump money grab that disgusts former adviser
World.content:
Anthony Scaramucci may no longer be the shortest-tenured press secretary in the history of the White House but he is increasingly concerned about the direction of the United States under President Donald Trump.

Speaking to 7.30 after his record of 11 days in the job was broken, Mr Scaramucci highlighted issues of corruption and a Trump-led plutocracy.

"In our society now, there's a very large group of people that feel hopeless, they're despairing, and they look at the system and say, 'Oh my God, it's a two-tiered system and I'm not part of the tier that can take advantage of these things or get away with breaking the law'," Mr Scaramucci said.

"This is something that we really have to fix unless we want to further corrode society.

"This has been a phenomenal country and very heavy damage has been done to the country by the president and his family, and we have to call it out."

Katie Zacharia lasted just five days as White House press secretary. (Reuters: Kevin Lamarque)

Asked specifically what he thought Mr Trump had failed on, his former press secretary zeroed in on tariffs, his handling of the Epstein files and committing the US to war in the Middle East.

'Reprehensible': Mooch hits out at Trump

Australia's former ambassador to the United States Joe Hockey earlier issued a warning about corruption in Washington but on Thursday Mr Scaramucci took it further, accusing Mr Trump of lining his own pockets at the expense of his own supporters.

US President Donald Trump has made a significant amount of money during his second term in office. (Reuters: Umit Bektas)

"This is hard for me to admit ... but had he won the election in 2020, I think the world and America would've been better off because he had people around him that were running compliance and his general counsel was rock solid," Mr Scaramucci said.

"He had a group of Republicans that were more traditional in terms of the way they were handling things."

Mr Trump's personal wealth has increased significantly since his return to office.

It was revealed in his own financial disclosure in June that the president made $US1.4 billion ($2 billion) from several cryptocurrency ventures in the past year.

"The crypto thing is probably the most reprehensible," Mr Scaramucci said.

"And I expect him over the next two years to make billions and billions of dollars for himself."

Mr Trump and his administration have recently and repeatedly denied any corrupt dealings while he has been in office. Mr Trump said he donated his salary during his first term as president.

Anthony Scaramucci during his tenure as White House Communications Director. (Reuters: Joshua Roberts)

However Mr Scaramucci said making money was the primary driver for Mr Trump and he was using it to turn Washington DC to his financial advantage.

"He's surrounded now by plutocrats that are being very obsequious towards him," Mr Scaramucci told 7.30.

"He sees each of them as a potential money centre for him and his family.

"People say that Washington is a swamp, and I say that Donald Trump turned Washington into a gold-plated hot tub. It's no longer a swamp.

"He's figured out a way to get the gold plating in there and the bubbles going for everybody.

"And don't go by me, 87 per cent of Americans when they're polled now believe that their government is corrupt."

Anthony Scaramucci says Donald Trump has turned Washington DC into a "gold-plated hot tub". (Reuters: Al Drago)

Corruption concerns have been reported by several sources.

A Gallup poll in early September found that 89 per cent of constituents polled believed government corruption is widespread.

The figure represents a 20-year high.

A CNN poll released this week found 19 per cent of registered voters believe it it is the top issue before the US midterms, while a September Reuters/Ipsos poll put that figure at 12 per cent.

While Mr Scaramucci conceded that the Trump administration's tax cuts may have in a "small way" helped some of America's lowest earners he is of the belief voters will rail against Mr Trump at the upcoming midterm elections.

"I think these sorts of referendums are going to show you that his political power has been weakened," Mr Scaramucci told 7.30.

Witkoff, Putin and a warning

If those elections lead to the Democrats taking back control of the House and possibly the Senate, Mr Scaramucci said Democrats should not try to attack Mr Trump like they did during his last term, when the Democrat-controlled house voted to impeach him.

Russian President Vladimir Putin shakes hands with US special envoy Steve Witkoff during a meeting at the Constantine Palace in Saint Petersburg, Russia. (Sputnik: Kristina Solovyova/Pool via Reuters)

"I would implore them to try to come up with policies and ideas to fix the problems that the American people are after," he said.

"We know throughout history that when we go after our political adversaries, we try to jail them or we try to impeach them, we actually get the opposite effect.

"Adolf Hitler was made more powerful by his arrest. On the more positive side, Nelson Mandela was made more powerful by his 27-year imprisonment.

"I think we have to be very careful punishing our political adversaries, no matter how bad Donald Trump is.

"What happened here in the state of New York and in the city of New York in 2024 actually weirdly made [Trump] more powerful," Mr Scaramucci said, referring to Mr Trump's 2024 conviction by a New York jury for falsifying business documents.

"I'm really hoping that the Democrats do not go in that direction."

The Trump administration's recent openness to doing deals with Russian President Vladimir Putin is another source of concern for Mr Scaramucci.

Mr Trump recently did a deal with Russia for diesel and Mr Putin met with US envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg.

The meeting led to the Kremlin announcing that Mr Putin agreed to resume three-way negotiations next month with Washington and Kyiv, aimed at ending the war in Ukraine.

Russia is still terming the war a special military operation. Since it began in February 2022, hundreds of thousands of lives have been lost.

The Ukrainian capital of Kyiv has come under frequent attack from Russia. (Reuters: Gleb Garanich)

Despite that, Russian state media posted a clip of Mr Witkoff calling Mr Putin "a humanitarian".

Mr Scaramucci said the comments were a sign of the scale of sycophancy in Mr Trump's midst.

"That's how nuts these people are that are around Donald Trump. And that's what Donald Trump and people like Vladimir Putin expect people to do, is to say lies about them," Mr Scaramucci said.

" He couldn't be less of a humanitarian, if you look at the war crimes, and you look at what he's done to his own people and you look at the treachery over the 27 years that he's reigned in Russia. "

World.title: Relatives of Elizabeth Struhs speak at final day of inquest
World.content:
The sister of Elizabeth Struhs has told a coronial inquest she hopes her sister's death can provide learnings to save "the next quiet little girl who cannot speak for herself, before it's too late".

The inquiry has been examining whether various government agencies' responses to the eight-year-old's child protection case, before her death in 2022, were adequate.

Elizabeth Struhs had type 1 diabetes, and died in her Toowoomba home after her father, Jason Struhs, stopped providing her with her lifesaving insulin.

Elizabeth Struhs died in 2022. (Supplied)

He had recently converted to a fringe religious group, The Saints, which his wife was a member of.

The group holds anti-medical intervention views, and pressured Jason Struhs to stop treating his daughter, citing God would save her instead.

'Rare' opportunity to reconnect

The inquest in Brisbane ran for a week and a half and heard from nearly 30 witnesses.

Elizabeth's oldest sibling, Jayde Struhs, was emotional today as she shared several family statements about her "cheeky", "gentle", "clever, kind" little sister to the court.

She told the inquest Elizabeth had "never left my heart" when she chose to leave her family's Toowoomba home, and her mother's religion, at 16 when her sister was just two.

"I thought about her every day and kept every photo of her I could get," she said.

In mid-2019, Elizabeth's father Jason Struhs rushed her to hospital in a coma, against her mother Kerrie Struhs's wishes.

It was before she had been diagnosed with type 1 diabetes.

Kerrie Struhs was later imprisoned for several months for neglect over the incident.

Jason and Kerrie Struhs were members of The Saints religious sect. (ABC News: Sharon Gordon)

Jayde Struhs said she used the "rare" opportunity to reconnect with her younger sibling during her hospital stay in Brisbane.

"I watched her learn to do her own finger pricks [for her diabetes]. She was proud of it," she said.

"I'll always be grateful I was there."

Elizabeth's future 'taken from her'

The inquest heard Elizabeth Struhs died at home in the first week of January 2022, with Jayde Struhs learning about it days later when a journalist sent her a text.

"Asking if I knew the Struhs family in Toowoomba … I searched online and found a headline about an eight-year-old girl who was found dead, with a photograph of my parents' home underneath," she said.

"That was how I learned my little sister was gone."

Jayde Struhs has shared several family statements and memories about her younger sister Elizabeth. (ABC News: Scott Kyle )

She told the inquest about the heartbreaking experience of having to arrange a funeral for her young sister.

"We had to choose the flowers and the dress that she would wear, and the urn that now sits in my living room where I see it every day," she said.

"Elizabeth should have had everything that lies ahead of an eight-year-old girl, high school, best friends, a first job, falling in love, finding out who she was going to be," she said.

"That was taken from her.

" I think about the young woman she would become, and I grieve for her every single day. "

In 2025, Jason and Kerrie Struhs, as well as other members of The Saints, faced a weeks-long murder trial over Elizabeth's preventable death.

They were acquitted and instead found guilty of manslaughter.

Her parents were each sentenced to more than 14 years in prison, with the 11 other sect members sentenced to between six and nine years in prison.

Jayde Struhs says she found out about her sister's death through the media. (Supplied)

A statement from Elizabeth's aunt and uncle, Melissa and Adam Struhs, was also read to the court today.

"The very first time, and only time, we got to see and hold her was around four months of age, she was so sweet and peaceful that day," the statement said.

"The last time was when we were standing around her coffin and apologising, we couldn't do more to protect her.

"We have had almost five years to sit with that, and it hasn't gotten any easier to acknowledge."

Melissa and Adam Struhs said they grieved never getting to know their niece as she grew older due to the family becoming estranged, but "having Elizabeth in our lives would have been something we would have loved".

'So much more life to give'

Another older sibling of Elizabeth's, who cannot be named for legal reasons, said they often felt guilt about what had happened, knowing how vulnerable she was.

"Guilt that you didn't or couldn't do anything to prevent it," they said.

The statement described hopes of going back to simpler times — watching movies with Elizabeth and watching her laugh so hard she would cry, playing cricket on their driveway or dancing together to Don Spencer songs in the living room.

"I think about what future she would have had," they said.

"She had so much more life to give."

Coroner Ainslie Kirkegaard held back tears as she addressed Jayde Struhs, thanking her for sharing such "private and precious memories", and for keeping Elizabeth "alive in our hearts".

"It is also an opportunity for us all to reflect that Elizabeth was and remains infinitely more than the events that have brought us here over the past two weeks," she said.

The coroner will reserve her decision and will hand down her findings in 2027.

World.title: Live: Head notches fighting century as Aussies bat to save second Test
World.content:
(Getty Images)

In the history of Test cricket, just four sides have ever responded to the ignominy of being asked to follow on by coming back and winning the match.

Australia, in the 40 times they have been asked to do so, has never managed it.

They have, however, drawn 11 pf those matches and that surely is the only hope that the Aussies have on day five at St George's Park.

Hello everyone and welcome to the final day of the second Test from Gqeberha, as Australia stares down the barrel.

My name is Simon Smale, Dean Bilton and Henry Hanson are with me and it's safe to say that if we are to be still with you for the entirety of the next seven hours or so, we're going to need a fightback of epic proportions from an Australian team that has wilted in the face of South Africa's fast-bowling.

Travis Head is nearing a century but was streaky as Danish bacon at times, while Steve Smith has a literal pain in his neck and is likely to be under-strength as a result.

The Aussies still trail by 170 runs. The situation is bleak.

But stranger things than this have happened in Test cricket. I once saw Monty Panesar survive 35 balls alongside Jimmy Anderson in Cardiff save a Test.

And, with all the respect and love for Monty in the world, if he can survive that long, then Australia's far more accomplished lower order batters can do their part too.

World.title: ‘Incredibly disappointing’: Snowy 2.0 cost blows out to $25b in biggest setback yet
World.content:
BusinessThe economyRenewables ‘Incredibly disappointing’: Snowy 2.0 cost blows out to $25b in biggest setback yet Nick Toscano October 22, 2026 — 10:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The cost of the Commonwealth government’s troubled Snowy 2.0 pumped hydro scheme has exploded to potentially $25 billion – more than four times its original estimate – and its completion date has been pushed out to late 2029 as its builders grapple with severe geological challenges and soaring construction pressures. Updated advice released by Snowy Hydro Limited on Thursday night moves the estimated cost of the problem-plagued mega-project from $12 billion to $22.2 billion, with a contingency buffer bringing the potential price tag to $25 billion, marking the most severe setback yet for Australia’s largest renewable energy development. Snowy 2.0 involves digging 27 kilometres of tunnels beneath the Kosciuszko National Park. Alex Ellinghausen Snowy 2.0, a massive 2200-megawatt energy-storage project in the Snowy Mountains of NSW, is designed to act like a giant battery, storing vast amounts of energy by pumping water uphill when electricity is plentiful and then releasing it downhill through turbines when the grid needs a critical boost. Energy planners consider it a project of national significance in Australia’s shift away from ageing coal-fired power stations because of its ability to back up renewables during stretches of low wind and sunlight, with enough storage capacity to power 3 million homes for a week. When the project was first conceived in 2017, then-prime minister Malcolm Turnbull thought it could be built for $2 billion in just four years. But a year later, when the project received final investment approval in 2018, its estimated cost had already risen to nearly $6 billion. This week’s latest revision means the potential cost has quadrupled since construction began.



One of the largest and most challenging engineering projects undertaken in Australia, the project faced a succession of setbacks and delays, bogged down pandemic-related disruption, supply chain pressures and difficult tunnelling conditions deep beneath an alpine national park. The complexity of excavating extensive underground tunnels through unpredictable rock has compounded construction delays and added to costs. Related Article Electricity ‘Potentially catastrophic’: Leaked videos reveal severity of Snowy project’s blunders The latest cost revision, however, arrives at a sensitive time for the Albanese government, which is under pressure from the Coalition and One Nation over the cost of its ambitious renewable energy rollout plans. It also intensifies broader anxieties about Australia’s ability to build enough renewable energy and storage capacity in time to keep power supplies and prices steady as the majority of the nation’s ageing coal-fired power stations reach the end of their operational lives over the coming decade. Dennis Barnes, chief executive of Snowy Hydro, on Thursday acknowledged that the cost increase was “incredibly disappointing”, but insisted the long-term value of Snowy 2.0 to Australia’s energy reliability was stronger than ever.



“The scale of Snowy 2.0’s energy storage is world-leading – more than half of the total energy storage the grid needs by 2050 will come from Snowy 2.0 alone,” he said. “Snowy 2.0’s massive, long-duration storage will be the grid’s insurance policy against multi-day wind and solar droughts, helping to prevent blackouts and control price spikes that would otherwise flow through to household electricity bills,” he said. Related Article Renewables ‘Diabolic’: Massive cost pressures on $12 billion Snowy 2.0 revealed Barnes attributed the bulk of the cost blowout to “design immaturity”, saying underdeveloped planning work when the project was first conceived had obscured the true scale and geotechnical complexity. He said the decision to reset Snowy’s contract with its principal construction contractor, Future Generation Joint Venture, in 2023, had protected the project from the threat of an even larger cost overruns. “Moving from a fixed-price contract, which was never suitable for such scale, uniqueness and complexity, has protected the project from an even greater cost increase,” he said.



Federal Energy Minister Chris Bowen and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher pointed the finger at the previous Coalition government for signing off on underprepared plans. “This revised cost and delivery schedule has been driven by cost pressures in the construction sector and the significant geological challenges of the project, exacerbated by design immaturity when it was first announced by the former government,” they said. “The government remains transparent about the pressures facing this project and securing the best possible outcome for taxpayers, energy consumers and the grid. The former Coalition government left behind a project facing major delays, rising costs and serious delivery risks.” The ministers cited the findings of a new independent economic assessment of Snowy 2.0’s net benefits, which include improving the availability of low-cost renewable energy and limiting wholesale power price spikes by reducing the need to call on expensive gas-fired power generation during peak evening demand periods and ageing, failure-prone coal-fired power plants. “The Coalition itself said Snowy 2.0 was ‘critical to the security and stability’ of the national electricity market and will ‘put downward pressure on wholesale electricity prices’ – those facts have not changed,” they said.



However, opposition energy spokesman Dan Tehan called on Bowen to apologise to taxpayers for the extent to which “costs have blown out under his watch” and said Bowen should resign or be removed as energy minister. “If the CEO of a company oversaw such blowouts, the board would have no choice but to sack him – Anthony Albanese should do the same to Chris Bowen,” he said. Related Article Updated

Energy Tesla and power giants revolt against Australia’s ‘EV charger tax’ As Australia’s energy transition approaches a critical juncture, state and federal governments are relying on Snowy 2.0 to play a major role in the future make-up of the grid. More than half of the remaining coal-fired generators are scheduled to close by 2035 as their owners grapple with rising maintenance costs, declining reliability and competition from cheaper renewables, especially during daylight hours. The Australian Energy Market Operator and major electric companies insist that replacing those plants with wind and solar – backed up by gas-powered generation, large batteries, and pumped hydroelectric systems like Snowy 2.0 – is the cheapest way to maintain grid reliability, rather than forcing the extensions of coal-fired power plants that can break down with no notice and cause huge price rises. There are clear signs that the clean energy transition is having a positive impact on prices. New data from the market operator, to be released on Friday, reveals wholesale electricity costs – what retailers pay generators before selling power to customers – fell 27 per cent year-on-year across eastern Australia in the September quarter, the lowest average for that period since 2021, partly due to a boom in grid-scale batteries smoothing out price spikes by shifting greater volumes of lower-cost renewable energy from the daytime to the evening peaks.



“Electricity use continues to grow, but more solar and storage is changing when energy is produced, drawn from the grid and shifted across the day,” AEMO executive manager of policy Violette Mouchaileh said. World.title: ‘Stark reminder’: Racing boss emails horse owners over Caulfield Cup death
World.content:
SportRacingSpring racing carnival ‘Stark reminder’: Racing boss emails horse owners over Caulfield Cup death Danny Russell October 22, 2026 — 8:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The state’s racing boss has written a personal email to all Victorian thoroughbred owners to explain his organisation had not “closed the book” on its review of the Caulfield Cup horse tragedy. In the Thursday afternoon message, Racing Victoria CEO Aaron Morrison said the death of Chris Waller’s star mare Ohope Wins was a “tragic racing accident” that had been felt deeply across the industry. Racing Victoria CEO Aaron Morrison says the Caulfield Cup horse death has been felt across the industry. Alex Ellinghausen “The vision clearly showed that Ohope Wins was brought down by the fallen Half Yours, rather than suffering a spontaneous injury beforehand,” Morrison wrote. “However, we have not simply closed the book. Our veterinary team is separately overseeing a standard post-incident review, including a post-mortem, so that any relevant information can be used for research and education.





“Saturday was a stark reminder of the risks our jockeys accept every time they ride and their immense bravery,” Morrison said. “Like our horses, their safety is of paramount importance.” Morrison said Racing Victoria’s trackside vets had worked for an extended period “exploring every option to save Ohope Wins in consultation with her owners” after the mid-race carnage. “Tragically, despite those efforts, she could not be saved,” he said.



The email explained that stewards had reviewed all camera angles and interviewed Zahra and McNeil on Tuesday morning, as well as three other jockeys from the race – Jabez Johnstone, Rachel King and Ethan Brown – before clearing all riders of blame. “We’re blessed to have an outstanding stewards panel in Victoria, and they worked proactively and swiftly to conclude a thorough inquiry into the incident on Tuesday,” Morrison said. John Allen (left) rides Kingswood to win the Caulfield Cup. Getty Images “Our responsibility is to identify the risks we can reasonably foresee, put strong safeguards around them through the best available science, veterinary care and rules and respond openly and professionally when an incident occurs.” Morrison backed the industry’s ongoing approach to safety, and the efforts of Racing Victoria’s 35 vets, highlighting a 99.95 per cent safety record involving 40,000 starters in races each year.



“That’s a fatality rate of 0.05% in flat races, which is among the best globally,” he said. “In the Caulfield Cup, the last fatality was when Mummify sadly went amiss post-race 21 years ago. “As we approach Melbourne Cup week, I want to remind the industry of the veterinary measures in place to protect our horses. “Our most significant safety initiatives are focused on the Melbourne Cup and international horses. Why? Because they were overrepresented in our serious injury and fatality data.” The Melbourne Cup was brought to its knees in 2020 after seven deaths in seven years, many of them from soundness issues.



Related Article Spring racing carnival How a former Carlton coach used Patrick Cripps to crack an exclusive racing circle “The veterinary protocols introduced in 2021 have delivered five successive Melbourne Cups without a serious horse injury,” Morrison said. “Whilst that is a strong result, we are not complacent and know that not every incident can be prevented. “When it comes to raceday, we will have five vets on course each day of the Melbourne Cup carnival, supported by a team of veterinary nurses and sampling assistants. “On Caulfield Cup day, our vets, stewards, medical team and raceday staff responded with professionalism and compassion in the most difficult of circumstances, and I thank them for that.”



Morrison offered the industry’s condolences to Waller, Ohope Wins’ owners Yulong and Waller’s staff. “The loss of any horse is felt most profoundly by those who work with them,” he said. Morrison also congratulated trainer Gavin Bedggood and jockey John Allen for winning the Caulfield Cup, as well as host Melbourne Racing Club. World.title: One Nation MP says his party plans to govern in first speech
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsWAOne Nation One Nation MP says his party plans to govern in first speech Hamish Hastie October 22, 2026 — 7:46pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items.
