One Nation MP Luke Herdegen says his party intends to govern in Western Australia in a maiden parliamentary speech loaded with attacks on mainstream politics and the Labor Party. Herdegen’s 20-minute first speech delivered from the dispatch box in front of his parents and a group of about 30 supporters in the public gallery brimmed with platitudes about patriotism, the Australian spirit and culture alongside criticism of gender-identity politics and mass immigration. Luke Herdegen in Parliament earlier this year. Ross Swanborough He included a warning to Labor that harked back to leader Pauline Hanson’s infamous 1996 maiden speech where she said Australia was at risk of being “swamped by Asians.” “We will stand up against mass immigration - if you try to swamp our nation with migrants,” Herdegen said.



Much of his speech involved scolding Labor and warning that his byelection victory was not an anomaly. “I stand here alone, the sole One Nation member of this assembly, but I don’t feel lonely because I know my friends are coming,” he said. “I know members across the chamber and even some behind me don’t understand what’s happening, you don’t understand what happened in Secret Harbour, and you’re racking your brains trying to figure out how to stop it from happening again. “The truth is you can’t stop it “The people are ready to send an orange wave through this chamber and through every chamber in our nation, and no seat on either side will be safe.”



Herdegen said Labor had no labourers. “Too many of you have never held a real job in your life,” he said. South Perth MP Geoff Baker looked back at Scarborough MP Stuart Aubrey after that statement. Aubrey was a FIFO electrician before entering politics. Herdegen said his party was “fighting to win and intend to govern.”



“The outer southern suburbs are One Nation heartland now,” he said. Herdegen also took aim at Labor for its selection of Georgia Tree as his opponent during the campaign. Tree works as a Woodside lobbyist and lived in inner-city Perth which dogged her the entire campaign. He accused Labor of using safe electorates as: “job programs for party hacks” “We all know what happens in a safe government seat: nothing”



“The arrogance to attempt to parachute in yet another party apprentice - that fit your current agenda and factional alliances in the face of struggling families is truly astonishing.” Herdegen also rejected the claim his party was racist. “False accusations of bigotry and racism do not scare us and will not stop us,” he said. Herdegen’s speech was met with a standing ovation from his supporters. The One Nation MP staged a huge upset when he ousted Labor from the seat of Secret Harbour in a byelection triggered by the retirement of former Labor Minister Paul Papalia. Herdegen wrested the seat from Labor with a primary vote of 39.1 per cent - a swing of 30.7 per cent from the 2025 election 18 months earlier.

World.title: Unmasked: The far-left extremist suspected of burning down 143-year-old town hall
World.content:
WorldEuropeParis protests Unmasked: The far-left extremist suspected of burning down 143-year-old town hall Max Stephens and Neil Johnston October 22, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

London: Hodei Ciarra Docampo only had to turn to his father for advice on how to burn down the 143-year-old town hall in the French city of Limoges. The 34-year-old “ultra-left” agitator was arrested by French special forces at his parents’ home three days after allegedly setting the building alight. Wearing a black balaclava, ski goggles and a bucket hat, the suspect was filmed allegedly tending to the blaze as it spread from the ground floor to the belfry. Arson appears to be something of a family tradition in the Ciarra Docampo household. The act of arson in Limoges destroyed the town hall’s roof and neo-renaissance clock tower. AFP His father, Fernando Ciarra, a 70-year-old Basque separatist, was sentenced to three years in prison last April for arson attacks in Limoges, according to the French regional newspaper La Dépêche, and an investigation by The Objective, a Spanish online newspaper. He is said to have burnt eight vehicles belonging to Enedis, the national electricity distributor, in February 2020 and carried out attacks on a broadcast station and mobile phone tower.



The latest act of arson in Limoges caused the neo-renaissance clock tower to collapse in a ball of flames in front of a baying crowd, encapsulating the devastation unleashed by rioters during protests across France on Saturday. Related Article Protests France sends in troops as Paris simmers in aftermath of riots Limoges Mayor Guillaume Guérin quickly labelled Ciarra Docampo as the alleged “mastermind” of the attack. Prosecutors said Ciarra Docampo, who has links to the group Les Soulèvements de la Terre (The Uprise of the Earth), was on a terror watch list and convicted of assaulting a police officer two years ago during a protest at a wood pellet factory. At 6am on Tuesday, armed police from RAID, France’s elite tactical unit, broke down the door of his family home in the village of Bussière-Boffy, 40 kilometres from Limoges, and arrested him. Ciarra Docampo faces up to 20 years in prison if convicted.



Prosecutors do not believe the town hall’s destruction was the work of a single overzealous protester, but that it was deliberately targeted by an organised far-left group. “What happened is unacceptable,” Guérin said. “The involvement of the far-left has been clear from the start in this fire. You don’t destroy a 200-year-old building in a few hours with a box of matches and a lighter.” Loading He claimed they brought fireworks, mortars and battering rams to break down the building’s doors. “You don’t just carry such items around in a backpack,” he said. France’s intelligence agencies and counter-terror police are assessing to what degree the nationwide riots, which began as student protests weeks ago, were infiltrated by members of the “black bloc”, an umbrella term for far-left violent anarchists.



Its members are a loose assortment of extreme-left organisations without any leadership or hierarchy. They frequently clash with police and target symbols of wealth and capitalism, such as banks and insurance companies. Related Article Protests Just what do France’s angry youth want? It’s complicated Security experts have estimated that about 5000 black bloc or far-left violent actors were on the ground during the riots in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Limoges. Jean-Yves Camus, a political scientist and expert on extremism, stressed that the violence was planned and involved many non-French nationals. “It is not a political group; it is a bunch of anarchists clad in black who act together with the demonstration and with the intent of violently confronting the police,” he said. “They are really treated as a threat by the intelligence community.



“Apparently, on October 17 people were speaking English and German during the riots; it’s a very strong possibility people came from Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Switzerland to take part in what was a planned demonstration. “There was a plan, there was an exchange of information; those people did not simply get a train to Paris and join the demo [by chance].” A protester kicks a tear gas canister in Paris. Getty Images Questions have also been raised by commentators about whether hostile states were seeking to exploit the destabilisation and violence for political gain. “Russian and Iranian actors would gain from the chaos,” said Dr Elias Forneris, a French citizen and head of research editorial at the British defence think tank Rusi.



“Back in autumn 2018, there were already questions about whether Russian bots were amplifying the Yellow Vests movement on Twitter. Related Article Political unrest Macron attacks ‘stupid’ claims by Trump and others blaming migrants for riots “Social media amplification would be easy to execute. Direct interference is more difficult and would require a great scale to make any impact, in movements involving hundreds of thousands of protesters.” Determining which rioters were far-left agitators and which were opportunistic looters from the city’s outskirts is expected to prove an almost impossible task. French President Emmanuel Macron denounced comments that blamed “migrants, jihadists and communists” for the violence in a veiled swipe at US President Donald Trump.



Speaking during a visit to Qatar, Macron did not name anyone but said that the “manipulation of information” after Saturday’s riots had led to “comments that are as unacceptable as they are stupid, from many people, including foreign leaders”. On the streets of Paris, the clean-up continued, with rows of shops and cafes still boarded up. Glass littered pavements and burnt-out cars were still being removed four days after the violence. At Good Vibes cafe on Magenta Boulevard, owner Gregory Desfoux, 49, surveyed the damage to his bakery, which opened just two weeks ago. Baguettes and shattered glass were still strewn across the floor, with bricks from the building’s exterior having been removed and thrown at police. “They smashed the window with metal bars. They took the bakery items. They eat all they could eat and after, they break everything,” he said.



“When we arrive at 10, we saw them. There were still some people in the shop, and they are crazy.” Related Article Analysis

Protests Nothing left to loot: Parisians ponder the real cost of another night of riots Further up the boulevard, Aidons Hassan Rashadul, a mobile phone shop owner, said his insurer was refusing to pay out €90,000 ($144,000) in damages and stolen stock. He said rioters also stole 500 parcels and he was helpless as more and more descended on his shop. “They destroyed everything inside and they took absolutely everything,” he said. “There was nothing I could do to stop them.”



‘They came to destroy’ In nearby O’Fleurs de Magenta, Clemence Ramon, a florist, said masked men had used iron bars to break into the shop before destroying it and raiding the flowers. “They broke the glass of the shop; they took all the plants, all the flowers, the money, and the day after, when we came back in the shop, it was like war, war in the shop,” she said. “On the street, the flower pots were on the floor and there was glass everywhere. They came here to destroy, and they don’t care what they are destroying. Flower, phone shop, pharmacy, bakery, all destroyed. They even broke into people’s apartments.” Macron pledged to prevent a repeat of last weekend’s riots and looting, as the Yellow Vest movement filed plans for a Paris march on Saturday, presenting the government with its next big test.



“There must be no wavering at the top of the state,” he said. The Telegraph, London Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: We’ve been asked to ‘turn down the temperature’. Here’s how we start
World.content:
NationalHaines attack Opinion We’ve been asked to ‘turn down the temperature’. Here’s how we start Saul Eslake Economist October 22, 2026 — 7:30pm

October 22, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Like so many Australians, I am shocked, appalled and horrified by the dreadful attack on independent MP Dr Helen Haines on Monday, and my thoughts have often since been, and remain, with her, her family and friends, and her constituents in her electorate (especially those who saw what happened, and rushed to offer their assistance). I support the calls that have been made by Governor-General Sam Mostyn AC, by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, by opposition frontbencher Andrew Hastie, and others, for the temperature of public debate to be “turned down” and for Australians to find ways of disagreeing with each other more respectfully and civilly. The federal MP for Indi, Dr Helen Haines, was terribly injured during an incident outside her electorate office. Nine, the ABC, AFR/Ben Grubb One of the things – not the only one, to be sure, but an important one – that has contributed to the coarsening of public debate and personal discourse, in Australia as in other countries, has been the vastly greater scope people nowadays have to post derogatory, vile, obscene and abusive comments and content on social media platforms and traditional media websites from behind the veil of pusillanimous anonymity. Sadly, many people feel emboldened (if that’s the right word) to write or say things anonymously, or using pseudonyms, that they would never write or say if they knew they could be identified. Traditional newspapers stopped publishing Letters to the Editor from “concerned pensioner of Parramatta” or “Mother of three from Frankston” decades ago: those who want to express their opinions in that format have long been identified by their name and their locality.



So why do those same media organisations allow people to throw verbal rocks at others using made-up and false names on their websites? Why do social media platforms allow it? Why are they not accountable for what is said on their platforms, in the same way that publishers of newspapers and magazines, and proprietors of radio and TV stations, are potentially liable for things that appear in their pages, or are transmitted over their airwaves? Related Article Analysis

Haines attack The sinister meme that appeared just hours before the attack on Helen Haines Banks and other financial institutions are required to ascertain and verify who their customers are before allowing them to open accounts. Why shouldn’t the same be expected of people “opening accounts” on social and legacy media platforms? Yes, it might cost them some money – as it costs banks and other institutions – but they can afford it. The question should be, can we as a society afford to continue to allow them not to do it? This is not a “censorship” or “free speech” issue. I’m not suggesting that people should be prevented from expressing their opinions (beyond what is already proscribed by existing “hate speech” legislation). What I am suggesting is that people should be accountable for what they say, and how they say it, in public forums; and the operators of those forums, in particular, those who make money out of said forums (whether by taking paid subscriptions or through selling s) should be accountable for how they are used. Nor am I suggesting that requiring people who make comments on media platforms to do so using their real names will eliminate the risks of further attacks on public figures such as we have seen this week – after all, the alleged perpetrator of this appalling crime actually did put his real name to his social media posts.



Floral tributes outside Helen Haines’ office in Wangaratta this week. Jason Robins But I do think that if people knew their real names and localities (though not, of course, their residential addresses) would be published alongside their comments on social media or other platforms, they would be much more likely to “self-censor”. And that would, in turn, be a significant contribution to “turning the temperature down”, as the prime minister has asked all of us to do. Saul Eslake is former chief economist of ANZ Bank and of Bank of America Merrill Lynch in Australia, and is now principal of Corinna Economic Advisory based in Hobart. World.title: ‘Incredibly disappointing’: Snowy 2.0 cost blows out to $25b in biggest setback yet
World.content:
BusinessThe economyRenewables ‘Incredibly disappointing’: Snowy 2.0 cost blows out to $25b in biggest setback yet Nick Toscano October 22, 2026 — 10:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The cost of the Commonwealth government’s troubled Snowy 2.0 pumped hydro scheme has exploded to potentially $25 billion – more than four times its original estimate – and its completion date has been pushed out to late 2029 as its builders grapple with severe geological challenges and soaring construction pressures. Updated advice released by Snowy Hydro Limited on Thursday night moves the estimated cost of the problem-plagued mega-project from $12 billion to $22.2 billion, with a contingency buffer bringing the potential price tag to $25 billion, marking the most severe setback yet for Australia’s largest renewable energy development. Snowy 2.0 involves digging 27 kilometres of tunnels beneath the Kosciuszko National Park. Alex Ellinghausen Snowy 2.0, a massive 2200-megawatt energy-storage project in the Snowy Mountains of NSW, is designed to act like a giant battery, storing vast amounts of energy by pumping water uphill when electricity is plentiful and then releasing it downhill through turbines when the grid needs a critical boost. Energy planners consider it a project of national significance in Australia’s shift away from ageing coal-fired power stations because of its ability to back up renewables during stretches of low wind and sunlight, with enough storage capacity to power 3 million homes for a week. When the project was first conceived in 2017, then-prime minister Malcolm Turnbull thought it could be built for $2 billion in just four years. But a year later, when the project received final investment approval in 2018, its estimated cost had already risen to nearly $6 billion. This week’s latest revision means the potential cost has quadrupled since construction began.



One of the largest and most challenging engineering projects undertaken in Australia, the project faced a succession of setbacks and delays, bogged down pandemic-related disruption, supply chain pressures and difficult tunnelling conditions deep beneath an alpine national park. The complexity of excavating extensive underground tunnels through unpredictable rock has compounded construction delays and added to costs. Related Article Electricity ‘Potentially catastrophic’: Leaked videos reveal severity of Snowy project’s blunders The latest cost revision, however, arrives at a sensitive time for the Albanese government, which is under pressure from the Coalition and One Nation over the cost of its ambitious renewable energy rollout plans. It also intensifies broader anxieties about Australia’s ability to build enough renewable energy and storage capacity in time to keep power supplies and prices steady as the majority of the nation’s ageing coal-fired power stations reach the end of their operational lives over the coming decade. Dennis Barnes, chief executive of Snowy Hydro, on Thursday acknowledged that the cost increase was “incredibly disappointing”, but insisted the long-term value of Snowy 2.0 to Australia’s energy reliability was stronger than ever.



“The scale of Snowy 2.0’s energy storage is world-leading – more than half of the total energy storage the grid needs by 2050 will come from Snowy 2.0 alone,” he said. “Snowy 2.0’s massive, long-duration storage will be the grid’s insurance policy against multi-day wind and solar droughts, helping to prevent blackouts and control price spikes that would otherwise flow through to household electricity bills,” he said. Related Article Renewables ‘Diabolic’: Massive cost pressures on $12 billion Snowy 2.0 revealed Barnes attributed the bulk of the cost blowout to “design immaturity”, saying underdeveloped planning work when the project was first conceived had obscured the true scale and geotechnical complexity. He said the decision to reset Snowy’s contract with its principal construction contractor, Future Generation Joint Venture, in 2023, had protected the project from the threat of an even larger cost overruns. “Moving from a fixed-price contract, which was never suitable for such scale, uniqueness and complexity, has protected the project from an even greater cost increase,” he said.



Federal Energy Minister Chris Bowen and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher pointed the finger at the previous Coalition government for signing off on underprepared plans. “This revised cost and delivery schedule has been driven by cost pressures in the construction sector and the significant geological challenges of the project, exacerbated by design immaturity when it was first announced by the former government,” they said. “The government remains transparent about the pressures facing this project and securing the best possible outcome for taxpayers, energy consumers and the grid. The former Coalition government left behind a project facing major delays, rising costs and serious delivery risks.” The ministers cited the findings of a new independent economic assessment of Snowy 2.0’s net benefits, which include improving the availability of low-cost renewable energy and limiting wholesale power price spikes by reducing the need to call on expensive gas-fired power generation during peak evening demand periods and ageing, failure-prone coal-fired power plants. “The Coalition itself said Snowy 2.0 was ‘critical to the security and stability’ of the national electricity market and will ‘put downward pressure on wholesale electricity prices’ – those facts have not changed,” they said.



However, opposition energy spokesman Dan Tehan called on Bowen to apologise to taxpayers for the extent to which “costs have blown out under his watch” and said Bowen should resign or be removed as energy minister. “If the CEO of a company oversaw such blowouts, the board would have no choice but to sack him – Anthony Albanese should do the same to Chris Bowen,” he said. Related Article Updated

Energy Tesla and power giants revolt against Australia’s ‘EV charger tax’ As Australia’s energy transition approaches a critical juncture, state and federal governments are relying on Snowy 2.0 to play a major role in the future make-up of the grid. More than half of the remaining coal-fired generators are scheduled to close by 2035 as their owners grapple with rising maintenance costs, declining reliability and competition from cheaper renewables, especially during daylight hours. The Australian Energy Market Operator and major electric companies insist that replacing those plants with wind and solar – backed up by gas-powered generation, large batteries, and pumped hydroelectric systems like Snowy 2.0 – is the cheapest way to maintain grid reliability, rather than forcing the extensions of coal-fired power plants that can break down with no notice and cause huge price rises. There are clear signs that the clean energy transition is having a positive impact on prices. New data from the market operator, to be released on Friday, reveals wholesale electricity costs – what retailers pay generators before selling power to customers – fell 27 per cent year-on-year across eastern Australia in the September quarter, the lowest average for that period since 2021, partly due to a boom in grid-scale batteries smoothing out price spikes by shifting greater volumes of lower-cost renewable energy from the daytime to the evening peaks.



“Electricity use continues to grow, but more solar and storage is changing when energy is produced, drawn from the grid and shifted across the day,” AEMO executive manager of policy Violette Mouchaileh said. Malcolm McGregor of Balgowlah remembers using the logarithm tables book (C8) for maths in the 1950s. When he and a classmate were answering the same question, he used the logbook and had the answer in a few lines. His friend took many lines. Both had the correct answer. The teacher wrote at the top of his friend’s paper “Use logs, you log”.

“With our neighbours (PNG and NZ) playing in the NRL, isn’t it time to swap ‘National’ with ‘Oceanian’?” wonders Kerry Kyriacou of Strathfield. “Come to think of it, how does Australia take part in Eurovision? World.title: ‘Stark reminder’: Racing boss emails horse owners over Caulfield Cup death
World.content:
SportRacingSpring racing carnival ‘Stark reminder’: Racing boss emails horse owners over Caulfield Cup death Danny Russell October 22, 2026 — 8:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The state’s racing boss has written a personal email to all Victorian thoroughbred owners to explain his organisation had not “closed the book” on its review of the Caulfield Cup horse tragedy. In the Thursday afternoon message, Racing Victoria CEO Aaron Morrison said the death of Chris Waller’s star mare Ohope Wins was a “tragic racing accident” that had been felt deeply across the industry. Racing Victoria CEO Aaron Morrison says the Caulfield Cup horse death has been felt across the industry. Alex Ellinghausen “The vision clearly showed that Ohope Wins was brought down by the fallen Half Yours, rather than suffering a spontaneous injury beforehand,” Morrison wrote. “However, we have not simply closed the book. Our veterinary team is separately overseeing a standard post-incident review, including a post-mortem, so that any relevant information can be used for research and education.





“Saturday was a stark reminder of the risks our jockeys accept every time they ride and their immense bravery,” Morrison said. “Like our horses, their safety is of paramount importance.” Morrison said Racing Victoria’s trackside vets had worked for an extended period “exploring every option to save Ohope Wins in consultation with her owners” after the mid-race carnage. “Tragically, despite those efforts, she could not be saved,” he said.



The email explained that stewards had reviewed all camera angles and interviewed Zahra and McNeil on Tuesday morning, as well as three other jockeys from the race – Jabez Johnstone, Rachel King and Ethan Brown – before clearing all riders of blame. “We’re blessed to have an outstanding stewards panel in Victoria, and they worked proactively and swiftly to conclude a thorough inquiry into the incident on Tuesday,” Morrison said. John Allen (left) rides Kingswood to win the Caulfield Cup. Getty Images “Our responsibility is to identify the risks we can reasonably foresee, put strong safeguards around them through the best available science, veterinary care and rules and respond openly and professionally when an incident occurs.” Morrison backed the industry’s ongoing approach to safety, and the efforts of Racing Victoria’s 35 vets, highlighting a 99.95 per cent safety record involving 40,000 starters in races each year.



“That’s a fatality rate of 0.05% in flat races, which is among the best globally,” he said. “In the Caulfield Cup, the last fatality was when Mummify sadly went amiss post-race 21 years ago. “As we approach Melbourne Cup week, I want to remind the industry of the veterinary measures in place to protect our horses. “Our most significant safety initiatives are focused on the Melbourne Cup and international horses. Why? Because they were overrepresented in our serious injury and fatality data.” The Melbourne Cup was brought to its knees in 2020 after seven deaths in seven years, many of them from soundness issues.



Related Article Spring racing carnival How a former Carlton coach used Patrick Cripps to crack an exclusive racing circle “The veterinary protocols introduced in 2021 have delivered five successive Melbourne Cups without a serious horse injury,” Morrison said. “Whilst that is a strong result, we are not complacent and know that not every incident can be prevented. “When it comes to raceday, we will have five vets on course each day of the Melbourne Cup carnival, supported by a team of veterinary nurses and sampling assistants. “On Caulfield Cup day, our vets, stewards, medical team and raceday staff responded with professionalism and compassion in the most difficult of circumstances, and I thank them for that.”



Morrison offered the industry’s condolences to Waller, Ohope Wins’ owners Yulong and Waller’s staff. “The loss of any horse is felt most profoundly by those who work with them,” he said. Morrison also congratulated trainer Gavin Bedggood and jockey John Allen for winning the Caulfield Cup, as well as host Melbourne Racing Club. World.title: Insults and hostility in the chamber
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Insults and hostility in the chamber October 22, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Photo: Matt Davidson To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Australia is facing a crisis of character, driven by the erosion of mutual respect and constructive debate. One only has to listen to Question Time to witness the appalling behaviour of our elected representatives. Instead of robust, intellectual policy discourse, the chamber routinely devolves into a theatre of personal insults, selective hearing, and outright hostility. It is a profound failure of parliamentary dialogue. If the people who lead this country want to foster a more respectful and cohesive society, they must begin by leading by example. After all, when our highest leaders behave like children in a school playground, we cannot be surprised when the rest of the nation follows suit.

Miranda Lewis, Camberwell PM, take a stand on conduct

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese needs to make a definite statement about the need for the community to treat each other with common decency. Perhaps he could call a meeting of all members of parliament and facilitate an agreed process of how debate should occur in both houses such as personal attacks will not be tolerated, debates will be about the issues and members will refrain from personalising them, any members personalising debates will be removed from the chamber by the Speaker of the House with no exceptions.

We surely can’t be asking the public to ″⁣lower the temperature″⁣ of debate when our elected representatives aren’t being seen to do the same. It starts from the top.

Brendan Douglas, Alphington Extend a helping hand of kindness

Thanks to your correspondent (Letters, 22/10) for their call for all of us to be kind. After learning of the news about Helen Haines I boarded a plane in Italy and arrived home in Melbourne and wanted to see the best in people and have hope for a new wave of respect and consideration for each other. We are a great country, which collectively is richer then past generations, but the fast pace of our digital transformation is crowding out kindness and our natural co-operative instincts. We can, and need to, do more for those in our community who live on the margins. But feeling left out, having less than you feel you deserve or having mental health vulnerabilities is no excuse for violence. We cannot wait for others to tell us how to be kind and respectful. The story we tell ourselves is the story we become.

Julianna Green, West Footscray



Time for a little reflection

It is a bit hypocritical for the PM, and for that matter politicians of all persuasions, to claim the moral high in urging discussions to be more respectful and less heated. One only has to observe Question Time in Canberra and other capitals. The insults, catcalling and interruptions of speeches is considered a ″⁣treasured″⁣ piece of the Westminster parliamentary system. Time for MPs to look in the mirror at their own behaviour before they lecture morality to their constituents.

Stephen Saks, Glen Iris Assume the best in all? What if?

Our adversarial political system, our civic culture, our digital environment and, sadly, our psyche, all incline us to a Machiavellian approach to government where we suspect politicians, or at least most of those of the party with which we disagree, of being self-interested, cynical, wrong-headed malign opportunists who deserve contempt and combat. I do not claim to have been immune to this. What if, instead, we took a Pollyanna-ish view, where, naively, we assume that most politicians are basically concerned citizens with good intentions, who are subject to the same conflicts, temptations, and human frailties as the rest of us, and who deal, as best they can, with the challenges of putting their beliefs and values into play in a complex world of wicked problems that are almost impossible to understand and solve?

I suspect the undoubted risks of living in a naively forgiving society may well be less than those of today’s cynical, over-excited and conflict-riven one.

Michael Liffman, Middle Park THE FORUM Community first

The growth in data centres with their huge appetite for energy and water has occurred with minimal community consultation and apparently a lack of credible information (″⁣$3 billion power pole shock″⁣, 22/10). Community anger and distrust is believable and understandable. That these data centres are being courted by government as an economic advantage seems duplicitous when we still have insufficient information regarding their energy requirements and the potential hazards of co-location among housing and in inner-city suburbs.

It’s as though they’ve appeared overnight and now we just have to deal with them. Governments at all levels have to consider both the social and economic cost, otherwise all the benefits, again, go to the corporations and not to us, the community.

Denise Stevens, St Kilda Power to the people

The real fight against the AI industry building data centres in local communities around the world is being taken on not by submissive governments but by real people whose lives and amenities are actually impacted. Keep up the fight.

Peter Randles, Pascoe Vale South



City’s quality of life

As a social and urban planner of 50 years’ experience, I reject former New York mayor Bill de Blasio’s “solution” for Melbourne: build as many high-rise buildings as possible and “as tall as you can go” in inner Melbourne.

Do Melburnians want Melbourne to be Melbourne or somewhere else? I would hate to have to look back in 50 years and say “Ah, remember when we destroyed the essence and fabric of a beautiful city?“

Steve Bracks is right: Melbourne has outer suburbs. Accept them, stop punishing their residents and service them properly. Give them the equal of inner suburbs. Six major urban fringe hubs with top quality medical, educational, social and community services, retail, commerce, leisure and recreation, and jobs are what is needed (not to mention our dozen or so even more neglected regional cities and towns). Both sets of hubs are already well on their way: build on them.

Metro fringe hubs will make Melbourne even so much better at what it really does brilliantly: quality suburban living, as attested to by The Age’s own series penned by residents of suburban Melbourne.

Ken Marriott, Newport Housing solutions

Ben Carroll has lurched to the past (″⁣Labor bets on building homes for first buyers″⁣, 22/10). In the 1950s, Victoria built tens of thousands of homes, whole suburbs, of well-built, well-located public housing in places like Hampton, Heidelberg, Bellfield, Broadmeadows, Geelong, Ballarat, Bendigo and more. Quality rental housing for working Australians.

Victoria then spent the 1960s and early 1970s selling those same houses to sitting tenants. Great for the buyers who benefited from the subsequent capital gains, bad for the future generations of low-income families denied access to these affordable rental homes. Housing built on government-owned land should be used to house the tens of thousands of low-income families on public housing waiting lists desperate to access stable, well-located affordable accommodation.

Craig Horne, Fitzroy North Public assets gone

Unfortunately for Jess Wilson, preceding governments have sold off most of Victoria’s assets. She may actually have to provide stewardship of a responsible government, so that Jeffed is not replaced by Jessed.

Mike Pantzopoulos, Ashburton Misplaced faith

The Victorian Liberal Party’s faith in privatisation is touching. However, as a privatisation agnostic I have yet to see evidence that privatising services delivers better outcomes for anyone except those who profit from their initial purchase of government-built expertise.

Jenni Colwill, Preston Tax reform for the young

I love Ross Gittins. However, for the record I have never supported increasing the GST (Comment, 21/10). I admire Josh Frydenberg too; but why on earth should working people be paying more tax when they are struggling to pay their bills now?

The income tax compensation, like the last GST, is nearly always the tax reduction they should have had through indexation. It will be a mirage. I support real tax reform, indexation at the lower end and new top marginal tax rates that do not provide double or triple advantage to high-income earners.

That’s right. Just like the Keating tax reforms which were real.

Like Gittins, I don’t mind paying more tax but not for AUKUS and hundreds of billions of wasted dollars. Whether people like it or not, real tax reform is normally and rightfully connected with some level of fiscal discipline.

The best way to look after the young is to devise a tax system for them. Give them the advantages of a new system that those reaping the advantage of the old cannot access. Stop loading up the young with a burden that is both unfair and unprincipled. HECS-HELP now falls into that category.

Bill Kelty, Secretary, Australian Council of Trade Unions, 1983-2000, Eltham



Move on WA take

Kudos to Ross Gittins’ article on increasing GST, but surely another point to address in the GST redistribution would be to readjust the formula so that Western Australia’s politically motivated unfair GST carve-out is rectified.

Ron Townsend, Mount Eliza Other things on the mind

Not a month ago, for the first time, I ran my groceries through a self-service checkout. I packed them and walked away. As I was walking to the car, it struck me, I don’t think I paid for them. I returned to the store and apologised profusely. The attendee was gracious and said, well at least you came back. Many don’t. I can completely understand Ben Carroll’s lapse in memory, not paying for his petrol. For heaven’s sake, he must have a million things on his mind. He’s running the state. I’m retired and was concerned about the rain that day disrupting my walk on the beach.

Frank Flynn, Cape Paterson GST disadvantages

There are more disadvantages to increasing the GST than are being considered. It’s a discriminatory tax, just as a flat income tax would be. Low-income earners would pay the same as high-income earners on future purchases. The cost of housing would increase, at a time when house construction is in rapid decline. Far more productive would be to level a super profit tax on the banks and mining companies, ensure all big businesses pay the appropriate tax, and address transfer pricing engaged by many of our large organisations. These are measures that would be fairer, not inflationary and not add to the cost of living many are experiencing now.

Barry Buskens, Beaumaris Cost of security

Those of us concerned about the safety of the 226 federal and 599 state and territory politicians are living in la-la land if we think that 24-hour security can be provided for them. We should take into account that while there is no publicly available figure for the 24-hour security cost for all 226 federal MPs, in 2024-25 alone the Australian Federal Police spent $523 million on protection for politicians and government buildings.

Eric Palm, Gympie, Qld Trump’s strategy?

As the US mid-term elections draw closer, with the result leaning towards the Democrats after two years of Trump mismanagement and rule by decree, Donald Trump suddenly “discovers” trillions of dollars of misused funds by the Democrats. Could this be the pretext for Trump to invoke the Insurrection Act and claim a national emergency to cancel the election?

Peter Russo, Brunswick West



Levy the polluters

I’m no economist (“The growing cost of food inflation”, 22/10). But I know that the Make Polluters Pay Alliance says climate disasters are costing the equivalent of $3800 per Australian household per year. And economist Dr Timothy Neal has calculated that we have probably individually suffered a more-than $20,000 hit to our annual economic output thanks to global warming damage around the planet.

It must be time for a federal climate compensation fund levy on coal and gas exports. If not now, then when?

Lesley Walker, Northcote Change city voting

At the Melbourne Assembly, the Lord Mayor of Melbourne, Nick Reece, stated that “we need to return to good governance in Victoria”. I agree. Does that include addressing the inequality in the voting system for the City of Melbourne whereby businesses get two votes to residents one? This is not what democracy looks like. Sydney had this system but it was abolished in 2023 and apparently Sydney survived. So why do we still have it?

Jenny Macmillan, Clifton Hill Yeah, right, good point

Your correspondent (Letters, 21/10) commented that only in maths do two negatives make a positive. Spoken language can do what maths can’t: have two positives make a negative.

Yeh/yes. Right.

Yes/yeh + Right = a negative, especially with a raised eyebrow.

Bernadette Cheesman, Wendouree Village Take responsibility

It’s time for anonymity on social media to be abolished. It would be one step in making people take responsibility for what they say.

Vicki Serl, The Basin It’s so ‘crosstrating’

And so say all of us young lad (Letters, 22/10). The deteriorating state of society “crosstrates” me no end. I wish we could create a kinder world for your generation to inherit.

Jane Ross, San Remo



Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING Politics

It’s a good time for the whole country to stop watching the news, take a deep breath, go outside and smell the roses.

Eric Kopp, Flinders After listening to David Pocock’s address at The National Press Club, I want to live in the Australia that David Pocock wants to live in.

Ron Mather, Melbourne



In terms of social division and the fomenting of societal unrest, just remind me of which political party is advocating the jailing of former political leaders before Christmas.

Ross Corben, Knoxfield Furthermore

Donald Trump has been played by Vladimir Putin just as American voters have been played by Trump. Both Putin and Trump are hell bent on power at any cost.

Paul Chivers, Box Hill North Trump, always wanting to make a “deal” before the mid-terms, sells Zelensky and Ukraine down the river. Putin must be chuffed.

Greg Curtin, Nunawading I’m disappointed to note the recent announcement of the Nobel Prize for Literature. I thought Donald Trump would have been a certainty for his fiction.

Ronald Burnstein, Richmond Thanks to Elon Musk’s decision to slow down Starlink, Ukraine’s war with Russia was seriously compromised, resulting in the potential loss of lives and territory to an aggressive Russia.

Chris Burgess, Port Melbourne



If we are obliged to adjust the GST why can’t we extend it rather than increase it?

Bronwen Murdoch, South Melbourne If it’s a fait accompli that extra power is required via large poles for data centres, then let those who need the power pay for it to be put underground, along with power

for the community along that route.

Bruce Cormack, Kilsyth Finally

Maybe Premier Ben Carroll forgot to pay for his fuel because he was distracted by the potholes he had encountered as he drove (CBD, 22/10).

Matthew Hamilton, Kew

World.title: One Nation MP says his party plans to govern in first speech
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsWAOne Nation One Nation MP says his party plans to govern in first speech Hamish Hastie October 22, 2026 — 7:46pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

One Nation MP Luke Herdegen says his party intends to govern in Western Australia in a maiden parliamentary speech loaded with attacks on mainstream politics and the Labor Party. Herdegen’s 20-minute first speech delivered from the dispatch box in front of his parents and a group of about 30 supporters in the public gallery brimmed with platitudes about patriotism, the Australian spirit and culture alongside criticism of gender-identity politics and mass immigration. Luke Herdegen in Parliament earlier this year. Ross Swanborough He included a warning to Labor that harked back to leader Pauline Hanson’s infamous 1996 maiden speech where she said Australia was at risk of being “swamped by Asians.” “We will stand up against mass immigration - if you try to swamp our nation with migrants,” Herdegen said.



Much of his speech involved scolding Labor and warning that his byelection victory was not an anomaly. “I stand here alone, the sole One Nation member of this assembly, but I don’t feel lonely because I know my friends are coming,” he said. “I know members across the chamber and even some behind me don’t understand what’s happening, you don’t understand what happened in Secret Harbour, and you’re racking your brains trying to figure out how to stop it from happening again. “The truth is you can’t stop it “The people are ready to send an orange wave through this chamber and through every chamber in our nation, and no seat on either side will be safe.”



Herdegen said Labor had no labourers. “Too many of you have never held a real job in your life,” he said. South Perth MP Geoff Baker looked back at Scarborough MP Stuart Aubrey after that statement. Aubrey was a FIFO electrician before entering politics. Herdegen said his party was “fighting to win and intend to govern.”



“The outer southern suburbs are One Nation heartland now,” he said. Herdegen also took aim at Labor for its selection of Georgia Tree as his opponent during the campaign. Tree works as a Woodside lobbyist and lived in inner-city Perth which dogged her the entire campaign. He accused Labor of using safe electorates as: “job programs for party hacks” “We all know what happens in a safe government seat: nothing”



“The arrogance to attempt to parachute in yet another party apprentice - that fit your current agenda and factional alliances in the face of struggling families is truly astonishing.” Herdegen also rejected the claim his party was racist. “False accusations of bigotry and racism do not scare us and will not stop us,” he said. Herdegen’s speech was met with a standing ovation from his supporters. The One Nation MP staged a huge upset when he ousted Labor from the seat of Secret Harbour in a byelection triggered by the retirement of former Labor Minister Paul Papalia. Herdegen wrested the seat from Labor with a primary vote of 39.1 per cent - a swing of 30.7 per cent from the 2025 election 18 months earlier.

World.title: Unmasked: The far-left extremist suspected of burning down 143-year-old town hall
World.content:
WorldEuropeParis protests Unmasked: The far-left extremist suspected of burning down 143-year-old town hall Max Stephens and Neil Johnston October 22, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

London: Hodei Ciarra Docampo only had to turn to his father for advice on how to burn down the 143-year-old town hall in the French city of Limoges. The 34-year-old “ultra-left” agitator was arrested by French special forces at his parents’ home three days after allegedly setting the building alight. Wearing a black balaclava, ski goggles and a bucket hat, the suspect was filmed allegedly tending to the blaze as it spread from the ground floor to the belfry. Arson appears to be something of a family tradition in the Ciarra Docampo household. The act of arson in Limoges destroyed the town hall’s roof and neo-renaissance clock tower. AFP His father, Fernando Ciarra, a 70-year-old Basque separatist, was sentenced to three years in prison last April for arson attacks in Limoges, according to the French regional newspaper La Dépêche, and an investigation by The Objective, a Spanish online newspaper. He is said to have burnt eight vehicles belonging to Enedis, the national electricity distributor, in February 2020 and carried out attacks on a broadcast station and mobile phone tower.



The latest act of arson in Limoges caused the neo-renaissance clock tower to collapse in a ball of flames in front of a baying crowd, encapsulating the devastation unleashed by rioters during protests across France on Saturday. Related Article Protests France sends in troops as Paris simmers in aftermath of riots Limoges Mayor Guillaume Guérin quickly labelled Ciarra Docampo as the alleged “mastermind” of the attack. Prosecutors said Ciarra Docampo, who has links to the group Les Soulèvements de la Terre (The Uprise of the Earth), was on a terror watch list and convicted of assaulting a police officer two years ago during a protest at a wood pellet factory. At 6am on Tuesday, armed police from RAID, France’s elite tactical unit, broke down the door of his family home in the village of Bussière-Boffy, 40 kilometres from Limoges, and arrested him. Ciarra Docampo faces up to 20 years in prison if convicted.



Prosecutors do not believe the town hall’s destruction was the work of a single overzealous protester, but that it was deliberately targeted by an organised far-left group. “What happened is unacceptable,” Guérin said. “The involvement of the far-left has been clear from the start in this fire. You don’t destroy a 200-year-old building in a few hours with a box of matches and a lighter.” Loading He claimed they brought fireworks, mortars and battering rams to break down the building’s doors. “You don’t just carry such items around in a backpack,” he said. France’s intelligence agencies and counter-terror police are assessing to what degree the nationwide riots, which began as student protests weeks ago, were infiltrated by members of the “black bloc”, an umbrella term for far-left violent anarchists.



Its members are a loose assortment of extreme-left organisations without any leadership or hierarchy. They frequently clash with police and target symbols of wealth and capitalism, such as banks and insurance companies. Related Article Protests Just what do France’s angry youth want? It’s complicated Security experts have estimated that about 5000 black bloc or far-left violent actors were on the ground during the riots in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Limoges. Jean-Yves Camus, a political scientist and expert on extremism, stressed that the violence was planned and involved many non-French nationals. “It is not a political group; it is a bunch of anarchists clad in black who act together with the demonstration and with the intent of violently confronting the police,” he said. “They are really treated as a threat by the intelligence community.



“Apparently, on October 17 people were speaking English and German during the riots; it’s a very strong possibility people came from Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Switzerland to take part in what was a planned demonstration. “There was a plan, there was an exchange of information; those people did not simply get a train to Paris and join the demo [by chance].” A protester kicks a tear gas canister in Paris. Getty Images Questions have also been raised by commentators about whether hostile states were seeking to exploit the destabilisation and violence for political gain. “Russian and Iranian actors would gain from the chaos,” said Dr Elias Forneris, a French citizen and head of research editorial at the British defence think tank Rusi.



“Back in autumn 2018, there were already questions about whether Russian bots were amplifying the Yellow Vests movement on Twitter. Related Article Political unrest Macron attacks ‘stupid’ claims by Trump and others blaming migrants for riots “Social media amplification would be easy to execute. Direct interference is more difficult and would require a great scale to make any impact, in movements involving hundreds of thousands of protesters.” Determining which rioters were far-left agitators and which were opportunistic looters from the city’s outskirts is expected to prove an almost impossible task. French President Emmanuel Macron denounced comments that blamed “migrants, jihadists and communists” for the violence in a veiled swipe at US President Donald Trump.



Speaking during a visit to Qatar, Macron did not name anyone but said that the “manipulation of information” after Saturday’s riots had led to “comments that are as unacceptable as they are stupid, from many people, including foreign leaders”. On the streets of Paris, the clean-up continued, with rows of shops and cafes still boarded up. Glass littered pavements and burnt-out cars were still being removed four days after the violence. At Good Vibes cafe on Magenta Boulevard, owner Gregory Desfoux, 49, surveyed the damage to his bakery, which opened just two weeks ago. Baguettes and shattered glass were still strewn across the floor, with bricks from the building’s exterior having been removed and thrown at police. “They smashed the window with metal bars. They took the bakery items. They eat all they could eat and after, they break everything,” he said.



“When we arrive at 10, we saw them. There were still some people in the shop, and they are crazy.” Related Article Analysis

Protests Nothing left to loot: Parisians ponder the real cost of another night of riots Further up the boulevard, Aidons Hassan Rashadul, a mobile phone shop owner, said his insurer was refusing to pay out €90,000 ($144,000) in damages and stolen stock. He said rioters also stole 500 parcels and he was helpless as more and more descended on his shop. “They destroyed everything inside and they took absolutely everything,” he said. “There was nothing I could do to stop them.”



‘They came to destroy’ In nearby O’Fleurs de Magenta, Clemence Ramon, a florist, said masked men had used iron bars to break into the shop before destroying it and raiding the flowers. “They broke the glass of the shop; they took all the plants, all the flowers, the money, and the day after, when we came back in the shop, it was like war, war in the shop,” she said. “On the street, the flower pots were on the floor and there was glass everywhere. They came here to destroy, and they don’t care what they are destroying. Flower, phone shop, pharmacy, bakery, all destroyed. They even broke into people’s apartments.” Macron pledged to prevent a repeat of last weekend’s riots and looting, as the Yellow Vest movement filed plans for a Paris march on Saturday, presenting the government with its next big test.



“There must be no wavering at the top of the state,” he said. The Telegraph, London Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Firefighters battle bushfire at Christchurch's Bottle Lake
World.content:
Firefighters are responding to a vegetation fire at Bottle Lake in north-east Christchurch.

Fire and Emergency (FENZ) received multiple calls around 8.30pm on Thursday about a fire on the perimeter of Bottle Lake.

FENZ said three fire engines, two water tankers and a rural pump were at the scene, with the first arriving appliance describing the blaze as the size of a bus.

It said the fire may have started on the beach.

The blaze was not close to any structures, FENZ said.

Earlier this year, both Civil Defence and FENZ warned Christchurch City Council that Bottle Lake Forest Park could be problematic in a fire.

FENZ Canterbury district commander Dave Stackhouse told the August meeting people may have trouble escaping.

World.title: Destiny Church leader Brian Tamaki says he's been denied entry to Australia
World.content:
Destiny Church leader Brian Tamaki says he has been denied entry into Australia over "inflammatory and concerning" statements online.

Tamaki took to social media saying he had flown to Brisbane for a church conference, when he was detained by the border force.

In the video, the religious leader says he was interrogated for 12 hours, before his visa was cancelled.

"It was a whole day spent on Tuesday being interrogated by different border control officers in a tiny cell-like room, shut doors, and it was a very intense time," Tamaki said.

Tamaki said he had been detained in Australia under Section 116 of Australia's Migration Act.

He claimed Australian Border Force documents said his presence in Australia "may risk the good order of the Australian community, or a segment of the Australian community, namely the Sikh and Muslim communities".

The documents also described his social media statements as "inflammatory and concerning", Tamaki claimed.

Tamaki had earlier this week appeared in Manukau District Court, where he denied claims he incited rational disharmony.

In June, he accused Modi of purging Christians in the South Asian nation.

"He [Modi] is currently purging India of all Christians and burning church buildings down," Tamaki had said in a video posted on social media.

"I think we should reciprocate in kind. Let's purge New Zealand of Hindus, Sikhs and Muslims. And, while we're at it, if they're burning churches down, why don't we burn mosques and their temples down? Tit for tat."

Tamaki told media outside court that he had challenged religion, not race.

"They're trying to say it's racial, and I'm saying to them it never has been. I don't dislike or hate anybody," he said.

"In all my 35, 40 years of ministry, it's about acceptance, it's about love, it's hope and faith."

Tamaki denied intentionally picking 31 October for a rally of his Destiny Church supporters in central Auckland to coincide with the city's annual Diwali Festival.

In June, police seized Tamaki's firearms after temporarily suspending his licence. They revoked his licence in August.

He had announced on social media that police had decided he was no longer a "fit and proper person".

A spokesperson from the Australian Department of Home Affairs said they couldn't comment on individual cases, but said the Australian Government was committed to protecting the community from the risk of harm posed by non-citizens who engage in criminal conduct or behaviour of concern.

"The Australian government will continue to act decisively to protect the community from the risk of harm posed by individuals who choose to engage in criminal activity or behaviour of concern, including visa cancellation or refusal where appropriate."

World.title: Enrolled but not that interested: Three first time voters on why they are or aren't engaged with politics
World.content:
Audio player for " The race to enrol NZ’s youth " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2088411%2Fenrolled-but-not-that-interested-three-first-time-voters-on-why-they-are-or-aren-t-engaged-with-politics

The race to enrol NZ’s youth Checkpoint Download MP3 27m

Over 100,000 young people may miss the chance to vote, with enrolment numbers still drastically low and the deadline to sign up just days away.

With the last chance to register to vote fast approaching this Sunday, still less than 69 percent of 18-24 year olds have signed up to cast their vote.

In many electorates, youth enrolments are even lower, sitting between 50 and 60 percent.

South Auckland's Ōtāhuhu has the lowest numbers of all, with only 50.6 percent of rangatahi enrolled to vote.

The main street of Ōtāhuhu. (File photo) RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

By contrast, the Banks Peninsula has nearly 94 percent of young voters signed up.

Unlike the sparsely populated area most people know, the Banks Peninsula electorate consists of rural areas like Little River, Akaroa and Mount Herbert, but also includes the suburban edges of Christchurch, like Halswell and Cashmere.

But what exactly is causing the drastic difference, and why are so many young people not enrolling?

Checkpoint brought together three first time voters to find out what is on the minds of rangatahi as voting day fast approaches.

Enrolled, but 'not that interested in politics'

Eighteen-year-old Gordon Shapiro lives in Little River, a tiny rural town on the Banks Peninsula, where he enrolled to vote last month, a few weeks after his 18th birthday.

He's about to graduate from Akaroa Area School, where he's one of less than 130 students from Year 1 to 13.

Gordon Shapiro is one of less than 130 students at Akaroa Area School. (File photo) RNZ / Dan Dalgety

Shapiro said he has never really been interested in politics, and only started engaging in the past year.

With his first chance to vote only weeks away he's not feeling too confident about where his vote will land.

"I feel like it's pretty harsh on us because this year is a pretty interesting one... because what I've seen from looking at all the parties, I reckon it's going to be quite a close one."

Meliame Mafoa is also 18, and about to finish her last year at South Auckland's Ōtāhuhu College, where she is head girl.

Coming from an electorate with the lowest enrolment rate for youth in the country, she's also feeling unsure about who she will cast her vote for.

While her school encouraged her to enrol, Mafoa said she feels like there's a lack of information for young people in her community.

"This group came over and they gave this whole presentation about voting and they even gave us a presentation about how we have the lowest enrolment rates... we were surprised to see that.

"My information either [comes] from a few of my friends who keep up with the news, with the politics, because I'm not interested in politics as well."

She said she wants to access more information about the election, but doesn't always know how.

Toreakore Ford-Takiri, 19, is in her first year of a law degree at Victoria University in Wellington, where she moved from her hometown of Tokoroa.

Tokoroa town centre. (File photo) RNZ / Evie Richardson

She's enrolled in the Māori electorate of Te Tai Hauauru on the West Coast of the North Island which takes in Tokoroa.

It's been two years since she pre-enroled at 17, and now that she's finally able to, she said it's incredibly important to her to vote.

"Being a Pacific Islander, but also being of Māori descent, it's technically in our blood. You know, it's everything around us is political and it may not look like it, but it does impact us quite a lot.

"I want to vote on behalf of my siblings that cannot, and on behalf the mokopuna or the teina that may come after me. So for me, I'm thinking for the future and not just my present."

What issues are young people worried about?

Checkpoint asked all three what they thought the biggest issues currently affecting rangatahi were.

Shapiro said living in a rural community, natural disasters and weather events were becoming a bigger issue.

"It's certainly a major concern for a lot of the people who live here and a lot of the businesses out here, because a lot of the businesses are around the centre area, which is in the low ground, which is where all the water will go."

Little River has been hit by floods multiple times in recent years. (File photo) Nathan Mckinnon/RNZ

As a first year university student living away from home, Ford-Takiri said she worried about the fact the fees free programme had been scrapped.

"I am so privileged to have been received a scholarship... from when I was a school leaver and that goes through three years of my studies, so that's accommodation, taken off of my plate.

"But also the tuition fees just go up... I just see it go up and up each year and I just feel like next year, what is going to happen to our fees? Am I going to be needing to have an extra loan?"

Dreams to give back to the community

With record numbers of young kiwis leaving the country, politicians have been pushing to convince youth to remain in the country this election campaign.

But Mafoa, Ford-Takiri and Shapiro all said they don't need any convincing, and have no plans to leave any time soon.

Shapiro, who aims to join the Defence Force as an army officer after finishing school, said he feels loyal to New Zealand.

"I don't see myself really moving away, at least not just yet. Currently, I think I have a pretty good chance at staying in the country and doing well.

"What my friends usually do is they either go to uni or start traveling, and I feel like I don't really want that big burden of debt initially. So what I want to do is I want to join the military who can pay for my education, teach me skills, let me lead people and help people overseas and in the country, I think it's just a great way to start my adult life."

After Mafoa finishes school at the end of this year, she plans to study to be a doctor. Specifically, a heart surgeon.

She said she wanted to stay and work in New Zealand to give back to her community.

With close to a decade of study in front of her though, she's worried about the cost it will take to get there.

"The tuition fees, the debt that comes with that is very big, and that's what pushes us to think, do we really, really want to go through this path, knowing that after this we have so much money to pay off."

But she said her reasons for pursuing medicine were driving her forward.

"The reason why I want to become a doctor is because of my grandmother. She couldn't go to any healthcare, any hospitals, no clinics because of that barrier with healthcare, because you don't see many of our people there in that department, in that field.

"She didn't feel like she would be understood, she couldn't speak English very well.

"For me... getting into that medical field, I'm representing many, many cultures, many Pacifica families, not only my Tongan culture. Because seeing that familiarity in a place you don't have much knowledge of - I mean, it's healthcare, it's medical stuff, you don't know all these words, you don't know where to go - but seeing that familiar face, it just brings that warmth in you, in you thinking, I'll be understood because I see somebody I know, I see somebody that might understand me."

After she finished her degree, Ford-Takiri hoped to work as a criminal and family lawyer.

She didn't always see herself staying in the country after finishing high school, a few years ago she envisioned herself leaving to earn a higher salary, before bringing her skills back home.

But since beginning study, she said she's realised what an impact she can have on her community.

"Having looked at this current coalition and what's been going on, it just made me realise that I could be here for better things and I'd rather be serving my people from where I am than going away and coming back trying to serve them with knowledge that is so not relevant to them."

'It's just the financial barrier stopping us'

With student loans looming, the cost of living was something all three rangatahi brought up.

Mafoa lives in an eight person household, with five siblings. Her father is the only income for the family.

"Sometimes we need a ration on some things to pay the bills, to pay rent, but then also send money back to the islands, help our family there, because they too are struggling.

"I know that my family has a lot of potential to do great things, me and my siblings, we have a lot of potential, it's just that financial barrier that's really stopping us."

Ford-Takiri said she's worried about the rising cost of petrol and how it's impacting her whānau .

With 10 siblings, her family already have a lot on their plate.

"I also have little brothers who want to pursue rugby league, and for them to pursue rugby league, it's very essential for them to be in clubs and be in rep teams and etcetera, so drive.

"My mum and dad, they drive to Auckland and back, to Rotorua and back."

'A lot of them are there just to show face'

The young people Checkpoint spoke to weren't all that confident that politicians really knew what it felt like to be a young person today.

Ford-Takiri said studying in Wellington meant she often saw politicians out on the street, and at university events, but she said there presence alone didn't feel like enough.

"Usually at our open days there will be like Labour Party, National, Greens and there will always be a few politicians there if not just their leaders. From what I have experienced a lot of them are there just to show face, just to be like yeah I'm in the community but they're not, they're not in the community, they're not participating, they're not taking part in any of the community events.

"They haven't really... talked one-on-one or within a group or participating in an event that youth will be at or that youth will thrive in."

Ford-Takiri threw a "special mention" to the Green Party's Tamatha Paul, who also comes from Tokoroa, something she said was "mind-boggling."

Tamatha Paul. (File photo) RNZ / Mark Papalii

She said it mattered to her that she was able to see herself reflected in those sitting in parliament.

"What matters to me most is seeing people like her in our communities, not only in our universities or workplaces, but at DJing parties or having fun with youth for youth and coming up with bright ideas."

Shapiro said the local candidates for Banks Peninsula had recently come into his school to answer their questions.

"My first initial reaction from meeting them was that most of them, I feel like most of them are from the outskirts of Christchurch... but I feel like it takes a real local to fully grasp things that are needed and what can be fixed."

He said he'd like to see the candidates getting out in the community more often, particularly in between election cycles, to keep young people informed as they reach voting age.

"I feel like they should do a regular thing where they go to a school every, I don't know, half a year or a year just to keep in contact with that younger community."

World.title: Labour candidate Kerrin Leoni clarifies whānau function with gang members
World.content:
A video seen by RNZ shows Labour candidate Kerrin Leoni, wearing her Labour Party jacket, speaking with Mongrel Mob members about enrolling to vote and changing the government.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins has heavily criticised Green and Te Pāti Māori candidates for their recent election campaign visit to a Mongrel Mob pad.

He said it was unacceptable for politicians to "go out and celebrate with gangs", and that it was "really, really ill considered, they made a real error of judgement."

Leoni acknowledged she has whānau in gangs and said she attended a whānau function earlier this month, with some gang members present - but it was not a gang pad.

One of the candidates Hipkins criticised was Te Pāti Māori's Oriini Kaipara, who told a Whakaata Māori debate this week her Tāmaki Makaurau opponent Kerrin Leoni had recently been campaigning with gang members.

Kaipara said Leoni had since deleted a social media post about it.

Leoni denied that during the debate, and sought to clarify the situation in a Facebook post on Thursday evening.

"To be clear, I have not attended a gang pad, at all during this campaign. I said at the debate I have close whānau who are gang members. In early October, I attended a whānau function where some of those present were whānau gang members."

Leoni - a former Auckland councillor - said her whānau supported her political career.

"I will not turn my back on them or pretend they are not my whānau because of their associations. I've always tried to be a role model for my whānau," she wrote.

She said she was disappointed it had become the main focus following the debate, and she wanted to focus on the issues that matter to voters.

RNZ has seen a video of Leoni at a whare with Mongrel Mob members, wearing her Labour jacket, holding a sign depicting her and Hipkins and handing out flyers.

"Some of them you might know, that aren't enrolled to vote, and they can have the power to change this government," she said in the video.

RNZ sought comment from Hipkins and his office referred to his statements earlier in the day.

He said Leoni has been open that she has whānau in gangs.

"I have not asked her for a detailed breakdown of every interaction that she's had with members of her own family, but she did say yesterday that she had not visited a gang pad as part of her election campaigning, and I have absolutely accepted that," he said.

World.title: 'I want a revolutionary': Tauranga councillor seeks new CEO
World.content:
Tauranga City Council has approved a six-figure budget to find a new chief executive, who councillors say will need to lead significant organisational change.

Marty Grenfell resigned suddenly on September 29 after eight years in the role. He left three days later.

The council appointed Gareth Green, who managed the mayor's office, as acting chief executive.

Today, it confirmed he would continue as interim chief executive from Tuesday.

The appointment was made at Wednesday's council meeting, at which the council also set a budget of up to $100,000 (excluding GST) to recruit a permanent replacement.

Tauranga City Council acting chief executive Gareth Green. LDR/Kelly O'Hara

It could be used for executive search fees, advertising, assessment, due diligence, candidate travel, legal and independent remuneration advice and other recruitment and appointment costs.

A subcommittee will oversee the recruitment process, made up of Mayor Mahé Drysdale, Deputy Mayor Jen Scoular, Tauriko councillor Martin Rozeboom and Pāpāmoa councillor Steve Morris.

Tauranga mayor Mahé Drysdale. LDR/Alyse Wright

This committee would recommend a shortlist of candidates for interview. The full council will make the final appointment.

Drysdale told the meeting that finding a new chief executive needed to be treated as a priority and was expected to run until March.

He said Tauranga was grappling with growth, a difficult financial situation and significant reform, while the council also needed to drive change from the Davison review.

The review into January's Mount Maunganui landslide tragedy criticised how the organisation managed risk.

"It's about finding someone that has the ability to implement change within the organisation," Drysdale said.

The council needed a leader who could take staff through that change, improve organisational culture, manage risk and strengthen the council's service to the community.

Local government experience was not vital, but would help, given the complexity of the sector.

Appointing a new chief executive was "probably the most important role that we will do through our term".

Scoular said the council needed an experienced, independent person involved in the recruitment process.

She said transformational leadership would be critical, pointing to major infrastructure delivery, cultural change and what she described as a period of instability and continuing change.

Rozeboom said the successful candidate would need to quickly assess whether the organisation had the expertise and capacity to meet the demands of Tauranga's growth.

Arataki councillor Rick Curach said understanding public service and the relationship between the chief executive and elected members would be critical.

Welcome Bay councillor Hautapu Baker said he did not want "another CEO that's just rewrapped, but the same archetype".

Tauranga City Council Welcome Bay ward councillor Hautapu Baker. LDR/Kelly O'Hara

"I want a revolutionary, I want a disruptor, but I also want someone who can weave people, weave opportunities, weave outcomes together."

Matua Ōtūmoetai councillor Glen Crowther said the council needed to find a "sweet spot" between experience, an understanding of local government and innovative thinking.

Te Papa councillor Rod Taylor said he was looking for someone who could "bring the organisation back together" after years of change.

Te Awanui councillor Hemi Rolleston said the council also needed to consider what would attract strong candidates, given the organisation's highly public challenges.

"It's become an extraordinarily big job and extraordinarily big challenge."

The council needed someone courageous enough to challenge elected members.

"We don't want somebody that's just coming in to execute what this council wants. We want a healthy tension at the table."

The permanent chief executive may be appointed for a term of up to five years.

A report presented to the meeting identified desired capabilities including organisational transformation, risk leadership, major infrastructure delivery, financial management, political acumen, relationship-building with iwi and hapū, and the ability to provide elected members with "free, frank and high-quality advice".

The council plans to appoint an independent executive search partner after a selective closed-tender process. Proposals were received on October 14.

Under the indicative timetable, the position description, candidate brief and selection criteria would be finalised next month before advertising and the executive search begin.

The report indicated the recruitment process was expected to run until about March.

Former Tauranga City Council chief executive Marty Grenfell. LDR/Alyse Wright

Grenfell resigned amid fallout from the Davison report.

Former judge Paul Davison's report criticised the council's risk management over four decades before January's deadly Mauao landslide, which killed six holidaymakers at a council-owned holiday park.

He recommended ways the council could improve, which it has committed to completing.

In a statement today announcing Green's interim appointment, Drysdale said he had the council's "full support and a clear mandate to lead the organisation with the authority of the chief executive".

This included making whatever changes Green considered necessary to "strengthen the organisation and its performance".
