World.title: Waikato ecosanctuary welcomes more kākāpō and Mahoenui giant wētā
World.content:
Two kākāpō and more than 100 Mahoenui giant wētā have been released at the country's largest ecosanctuary, after 25 years of ecological restoration.

The new additions mean there are now five kākāpō at Sanctuary Mountain Maungatautari in Waikato, as part of a mainland habitat trial that began in 2023.

The trial is a partnership between the Department of Conservation's Kākāpō Recovery Programme, Te Rūnanga o Ngāi Tahu and mana whenua, in a bid to protect one of the world's rarest parrots.

Sanctuary chief executive Helen Hughes said when the reserve was formed 25 years ago, it was hard to imagine native wildlife thriving on Maungatautari.

"The arrival of these new kākāpō and Mahoenui giant wētā taonga is a reminder that this is not a finished story. It's continuing to evolve, and we're excited about what comes next."

One of the Mahoenui giant wētā. SANCTUARY MOUNTAIN / SUPPLIED

The sanctuary covers more than 3363 hectares of native forest behind a 47-kilometre pest and predator-proof fence, protecting 730 native species, including the 15 native species returned to Maungatautari through iwi-to-iwi tono tikanga.

Since its inception, several birds including North Island Brown Kiwi, tuatara, kōkako, tīeke, hihi and toutouwai have been released into the sanctuary.

Hughes said its mana whenua and iwi partners, the Department of Conservation, recovery and breeding programmes, staff, volunteers and supporters, had worked together to help threatened species to recover and thrive.

DOC's acting operations manager for kākāpō Annie Wallace said one of the biggest challenges in the bird's recovery was finding suitable predator-free habitat for a growing population.

"The two males joining today will join the three who have lived at the site since 2023, helping build our understanding of how kākāpō use fenced mainland habitat."

The new additions come after a bumper breeding season that saw the national kākāpō population reach 325 birds.

Ngāi Tahu representative on the Kākāpō Recovery Group Tāne Davis said Ngāi Tahu felt a strong sense of responsibility towards the kākāpō as a taonga.

Sanctuary Mountain. SANCTUARY MOUNTAIN / SUPPLIED

"With the urgent need to find new homes for the manu, it is important that we continue to try new things working alongside our mana whenua partners."

The Mahoenui giant wētā were bred through a programme at Ōtorohanga Kiwi House in partnership with Ngāti Maniapoto, mana whenua and DOC.

The release of 122 wētā at Maungatautari on Thursday, came just over a year after the translocation of 192 of the native insects last August.

Ōtorohanga Kiwi House marketing manager Tyler Lloyd said it was an honour to have bred and raised the remarkable wētā.

"Seeing them take their place in the forest at Maungatautari is an incredibly rewarding moment for everyone who has cared for them. It is the moment that patient, daily work becomes part of something much bigger."

Ngāti Koroki Kahukura along with Ngāti Hauā, Raukawa and Waikato, maintain deep and enduring connections with Maungatautari as a treasured tūpuna, and help to guide the sanctuary's direction.

Sanctuary Mountain Maungatautari co-chair and Ngāti Koroki Kahukura representative Norma Taute said for mana whenua, Maungatautari was a tūpuna (ancestor).

"The restoration of this maunga has always been about restoring the health and mauri of the maunga, strengthening our connection to place, honouring our responsibilities as kaitiaki and working together through kotahitanga.

World.title: 'Not a consideration': Who picks up the phone on election night?
World.content:
Analysis: It's one of the defining questions of Election 2026 - will Opportunity get the opportunity to help form a government for the next three years?

The fledgling party has left its mark on the political landscape, regardless of how it polls on election day, ushering in seldom-heard conversations about bipartisanship and long-term planning.

We know from the past month of intense campaigning that Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong, should her party cross the five percent threshold and hold the balance of power, promises to talk first to the party with the most seats.

Audio player for " The rise of AI politics, who gets on the phone November 8, & National's front bench risk " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2087485%2Fnot-a-consideration-who-picks-up-the-phone-on-election-night

The rise of AI politics, who gets on the phone November 8, & National's front bench risk Caucus Download MP3 47m

We know Labour leader Chris Hipkins is happy to take that call and that National leader Christopher Luxon is not, but if that remains everyone's position on 8 November, what happens then?

Wong rings Luxon "and it goes straight to voicemail", deputy political editor Craig McCulloch jokes in this week's episode of RNZ's politics podcast, Caucus.

The great question is whether Luxon actually does pick up the phone and negotiate, or not.

On this week's Stuff Leaders' Debate, Luxon made the Mitre 10 Mega of all rulings-out - or at least, he appeared to.

He said he had ruled out joining a coalition with Opportunity in the same vein as having ruled out a coalition with Labour or Te Pati Maori.

He listed all the parties he wouldn't work with.

"I don't know how much clearer I can be," he has taken to saying over and again.

"I am serious about it," Luxon told debate moderator Paddy Gower. "It's not a consideration."

It's unusual for a prime minister to be so definitive, because if he was to U-turn on that position after the election, he would be a laughing stock, but McCulloch says Luxon immediately undermined his tough line by refusing to promise to quit, rather than pick up the phone.

"If he really meant what he's saying, he would have no issue staking his job on it."

The political reality is that, if Luxon refused to make that call, his caucus would decide for him by rolling him.

As RNZ political editor Jo Moir says: "The National Party base is not going to accept that as the conclusion at the end of all of this."

It highlights the fact that if these leaders hold fast, coalition negotiations could be incredibly unstable and jobs could be lost.

For Wong, there are no set rules, but she has suggested she won't run parallel negotiations with both major parties, as New Zealand First has done in the past.

Moir says that's inexperience showing and McCulloch says, "In a negotiation, surely you want to see all the options available to you" - but it may be Wong's way.

"We'll genuinely try and do good-faith negotiating with the largest party first," she told Newstalk ZB. "I think that's the fair thing to do, but if we feel like we have to walk away because we're compromising too much, then we would go to the other side and see what they've got."

There's wriggle room, however, a willingness to see what the other side has to offer and Labour will almost certainly be willing to offer more.

As Wong faces questions about the negotiations and bottom-lines, you can't help but notice she seems less comfortable with the core policies being pitched by the existing coalition parties.

Moir has asked her about this on the campaign trail.

"She pointed out ACT's policy to freeze the minimum wage, New Zealand First's and ACT's policies to abolish the Waitangi Tribunal, National's policy to drug testing beneficiaries... all the examples she used were from centre-right parties. She didn't put up anything from the centre-left that she fundamentally disagrees with."

"Qiulae Wong is having to walk quite a fine line in her messaging to court both that left and right vote," says McCulloch. arguing that if Opportunity went with the centre-right, it would represent the change within government without needing to change the prime minister.

Going right, "she sees the party's role as being very much a handbrake".

Then there's Labour. There's no rule saying it has to play the wallflower.

"Labour definitely picks up the phone," Moir says. "They've never said, 'we're not picking up the phone'.

In the final two weeks of the campaign, expect more questions about phone calls and what might transpire from 8 November.

World.title: Schutt banned for two matches after prescription medication failure
World.content:
Australian women's fast bowler Megan Schutt has been banned for two matches for failing to meet guidelines on the use of prescription medication.

Cricket Australia confirmed Schutt's suspension in a release on Thursday afternoon.

"The breach was a failure to adhere to requirements under the Sports Science and Sports Medicine guidelines with regard to prescription medication," Cricket Australia said.



"This relates to a single incidence which occurred while out of competition and was not for performance-enhancing purposes."



The two-match ban applies to all international and domestic cricket.

Schutt starred in the recent three-match ODI series against Bangladesh. She had series figures of 10-71.

She has not played in a three-match T20 international series against New Zealand, which wraps up tonight at North Sydney.

Schutt released a statement acknowledging the breach and accepting the penalty.

"I fully accept the penalty handed down and apologise for failing to meet the standards expected of me," Schutt said in her statement.

"I'm sorry for the attention this has caused and appreciate the support I've received.

"While this occurred out of competition and was not performance related, I understand that I am responsible for following the Sports Science and Sports Medicine Guidelines, which players receive regular education on, and I should have adhered to these guidelines."



Cricket Australia said it would continue to provide "appropriate support" to Schutt and to reinforce standards and responsibilities expected of all involved in the game.

World.title: Aussie Borlase on winning side as Atlanta Dream leads WNBA Finals
World.content:
Angel Reese recorded 21 points and 12 rebounds to help the Atlanta Dream secure a 97-71 home victory over the Golden State Valkyries, giving the Dream a 2-1 lead in the WNBA Finals after Game 3.

Rhyne Howard added 16 points, and Naz Hillmon had 15 for the Dream, who also host Game 4 on Sunday (AEDT).

Australian guard Izzy Borlase played a solid role for the Dream on Wednesday night, local time. She played 26 minutes, finishing with 12 points, including one three-pointer, plus five rebounds, two assists and a block.

Another Australian Opals star, Miela Sowah, sat on the bench for the Valkyries and will remain there throughout the finals due to her restricted status as a development player.

The Dream highlighted one of Borlase's drives to the basket on its social media.

It was the second straight strong game for Reese, who had 30 points and 16 rebounds in Game 2, which the Dream also won for its first-ever victory in the Finals. She now has a double-double in each game of the Finals.

"It feels good when you're in the finals. It's a long season, and you play against everybody and go through and push through, but when you can do it at the highest level, this is what you live for, this is what the off-season is for," Reese said.

"I put the work in for this moment, and I'm just happy I could lead the team to a win. We're feeling good going into Saturday."

With the game tied at 49 in the third quarter, Atlanta scored eight straight, including four by Reese. Golden State got within 59-55 on Tiffany Hayes's lay-up, but could get no closer as Atlanta closed the quarter, scoring 12 of the final 14 points.

With Atlanta up 17 in the fourth quarter, Jordin Canada overthrew Reese on the break, but she saved the ball by throwing it over her head underneath the basket to Howard, who got fouled.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

Golden State could never recover. Gabby Williams scored 15 points, and Hayes added 14 for the Valkyries.

"Protect home court," Howard said of the team's focus. "Giving our fans a show. We fought for this arena so we had to protect it. It's big. We went and stole one, but we can't let them come in and do the same thing."

The game was moved from the Dream's home Gateway Center Arena to the NBA's Atlanta Hawks home arena. Wednesday night's game was sold out, with more than 17,000 fans attending, as is Game 4 on Saturday at the same venue.

The game got off to a slow start as Atlanta led 9-1 after the first five minutes. Golden State missed its first eight shots before Aminata Gueye scored the first basket with 4:39 left.

They got within 13-10 before Naz Hillmon hit consecutive 3-pointers and then Reese hit one. The Dream led 23-15 after the opening quarter.

Atlanta built its lead to 37-26 midway through the period. Golden State was able to hang around and only trailed 46-40 at the break as the teams combined to shoot 15-for-31 (48 per cent) from behind the arc.

That was more completed 3-pointers in the first 20 minutes than in either Game 1 or Game 2.

Game 1 and 2 had huge ratings, with the opener on NBC averaging 2.1 million, the most ever for a first game of the Finals. Game 2, which was broadcast on USA Network, averaged 1.33 million viewers.

AP/ABC

World.title: Amid the hunt for World Cup glory one of Tonga's greats is not done yet
World.content:
As Tonga's World Cup campaign prepares to hit fever pitch, Tui Lolohea cannot stop smiling even when the young bulls give him stick.

After a training session in the lead-up to Friday's match against Lebanon it is rising prop Demetric Vaimauga, who is the kind of guy you hear before you see, that gees Lolohea up.

"Awwww yeah, it's Mr I Ain't Done Yet!" Vaimauga crows as he grabs Lolohea by the shoulders.

That's what they called Lolohea in an Instagram post after he came off the bench for an injured Latu Fainu to set up a try in Tonga's 30-12 win over England last week and he's been copping it ever since.

It was a cameo Lolohea, at 31 and with Tonga enjoying more depth and talent in the halves than ever before, thought would never come.

But once it did it added to an already sterling legacy in the red jersey, tacking an extra chapter on a story that, against all odds, is still being written.

Lolohea has already played for Tonga more times than any other player in history and against the Cedars he'll extend his own record with his 23rd cap.

Along with Jason Taumalolo, Lolohea is the only player to have appeared in each of Tonga's five wins over Tier 1 nations, making them the only two constant faces in every image of Tonga's greatest days.

Loading Instagram content

Lolohea has been wearing these colours when those days were still just a dream. When he debuted for Tonga back in 2015, Fainu, the man he replaced last week and will partner in the halves on Friday, was only nine years old.

Vaimauga himself had just turned 11 and as the giant youngster runs away cackling, Lolohea fires back in Tongan through a grin and shakes his head.

"I knew I'd get stick for this. Mr I Ain't Done Yet — they're always taking the piss out of me," Lolohea said.

"I hope he gets banged next time he goes off the back fence, so I can go laugh at him.

"They joke around, but I am one of the oldest in the team and it's good to show you can run around with the young bucks."

Jason Taumalolo and Tui Lolohea have played in every one of Tonga's wins over Tier 1 nations. (Getty Images: Anthony Au-Yueng)

Lolohea and Taumalolo are the elders this time around as the two longest-serving players in the team by a mile and while Taumalolo dragged Tonga into a new world, Lolohea is very much a product of the old.

Watching his debut from 11 years ago against Samoa on the Gold Coast is a measure of how far things have come.

When the two meet again next week it will be in front of a sold-out crowd at Parramatta Stadium, which they probably could have filled twice over, and both sides will boast some of the best players in the world.

Back on Lolohea's first day, a little over 12,000 came through the gates and both nations had to choose between grey beards, who wanted to give back to their community, journeymen who knew this would be as good as it got, or youngsters before their big futures came for them.

International rugby league has come a long way since Tui Lolohea's Test debut. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

Lolohea was one of the latter and at the time he was counted as one of rugby league's brightest prospects, with feet so fast tackling him was like trying to grab a handful of smoke.

So much has transformed since those times but according to Lolohea, the most important things have stayed the same.

"Why you're doing it, what you're representing, that never changes," Lolohea said.

"We're a little dot on the map and there's always talk about financial stuff but the pride of our island nation, the proud culture we put out to the people, we've built that over the years and the support from the people is massive.

Why Jason Taumalolo is still more than just a man for Tonga In the NRL, we only talk about what Jason Taumalolo can't do anymore. But when he pulls on the red of Tonga it's a reminder of what he still is and always will be for the island nation and for Test rugby league.

"That's what we want to represent, our people and our family names, where we come from.

"I was just a little kid back then. I remember the passion, for Tonga and Samoa, and we're on the big stage now but the passion is still there even though it was a long time ago."

Plenty of familiar faces from that night are still around. Kristian Woolf is still the coach, Sika Manu, Lolohea's first captain, is in camp as an assistant and Konrad Hurrell is the team's media manager.

But only Lolohea is still playing, making him the last son of the olden days before the heroes came back home.

He remembers frantically messaging Taumalolo in 2017, asking if he really was going to come back to Tonga and marvelling at what followed.

He cannot forget his intercept try in the win over New Zealand, head cocked back and laughing as he went over, or his late score in the semi-final against England that gave Tonga hope of a miracle, or of the trip back to the islands that followed, where the team was given medals of honour at the royal palace.

Amid a good NRL career for the Warriors and Wests Tigers before a lengthy stint in Super League, where he's spent the last eight seasons, including the last five with Huddersfield, Lolohea might never have fulfilled the club expectations he carried into his Tongan debut.

Instead, his finest hours have come for Tonga itself, for whom he is both pioneer and icon.

They've never won a big game without him and his reward has been honours that are usually bestowed on heroes of ancient wars.

His people have named trophies after him and he has been granted lands outside the family village of Lapaha by King Tupou VI.

The team's official nickname is Mate Ma' Tonga, which translates to "die for Tonga" but the memories Lolohea has helped create for his nation are immortal, like the win over Great Britain in 2019 or the breakthrough victory over Australia the following week.

Tui Lolohea has carved out a fine legacy in Tongan red. (Getty Images: Kai Schwoerer)

On the back of those glories a whole new generation of stars chose Tonga and players like Isaiya Katoa, Robert Toia, Leka Halasima and Tolu Koula have not just become part of the cause, they have taken it further.

They beat New Zealand again in the Pacific Championships two years ago and pushed Australia to the limit in the final. Lolohea, of course, played in both and set up a try in the latter.

Tonga are not here to compete anymore, they are here to win — against Australia, New Zealand, England, Samoa or anybody else who wants some.

Taking the World Cup itself back to Nuku'alofa is not an idle fantasy. It's a dream Tonga can hammer into reality as part of a new world order Lolohea and his generation helped create and somehow, he is still part of it.

Apart from Taumalolo, his only fellow survivor from 2017, the other legends from the old days are done.

Tui Lolohea has played in England for close to a decade now. (Getty Images via PA Images: Martin Rickett)

Between Katoa, Fainu and Junior Amone, Tonga have more class and options in the halves and the nation had every right to move on from Lolohea years ago.

But Lolohea himself is still here, refusing to be swept away, a lot older and a bit slower but as he showed against England, still capable of making a difference for the better.

"To still be here after all this time, I'm fortunate to be here again and running around with the young guys and some of the superstars of our game," Lolohea said.

"It's an honour, every time.

Rugby League World Cup quick hits From Kalyn Ponga's magnificent Test debut to a mighty Tongan victory years in the making here are the quick hits from week one of the Rugby League World Cup.

"It's crazy to think, because I watch these guys every week and now I'm playing alongside them and I remember when we didn't really have any halfbacks at all.

"The depth we have now, it's such a big positive not just for now but for the years to come."

Lolohea knows this World Cup might be his last. He's finished up at Huddersfield and is still sorting out where he'll play next.

He is expected to drop back to the extended bench for next week's clash against Samoa and barring injury, it will be the same for the knockout stages.

This game against Lebanon could be it, the last time the legend of Tui Lolohea as a Tongan hero happens in front of us and not in our memories and that makes it worth savouring.

Tui Lolohea is hoping to build on his cameo appearance against England. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

He played rugby league for Tonga more times than any other person who has ever lived but it is still a privilege to him, a prize beyond what he can ever say.

Even after all these years it still makes his father, Paul, smile and get as emotional as he ever does.

Growing up it was just the two of them. Lolohea's mother died when he was just one year old due a heart condition and if Friday is the end, father and son will be together for it.

But there might be a truth in the jokes the young fellas tell: Lolohea isn't done yet.

"He [Lolohea's father] flew in Tuesday morning, he'll be here for the next couple of weeks to enjoy the last ride, no matter what happens," Lolohea said.

"But we never know these days, do we? I'm just buzzing I got on the field again. I'm glad I got to play my part."

World.title: Potential PNG signing helping to heal Cooper Bai's family rift
World.content:
Marcus Bai has explained how he and son Cooper moved past the rift that fractured their family, as the Gold Coast forward edges closer to signing a deal with the PNG Chiefs.

Cooper was warmly greeted by his father at Port Moresby's Jacksons International airport yesterday after being granted permission to explore his options ahead of the opening of the November 1 contracting window.

The 19-year-old has been high on the Chiefs' list of targets since the club got the green light to enter the NRL in the 2028 season, with the forward proving a hit with local crowds in Papua New Guinea across his two-Test international career.

PNG Chiefs unveil new logo ahead of 2028 NRL entry The PNG Chiefs logo brings together elements representative of the country ahead of its NRL debut in 2028.

But Cooper's journey hasn't always been smooth, and last year he invoked the ire of his legendary Kumul father when he turned down a deal with Melbourne Storm to remain at the Titans.

"He promised one thing … and then he went and did the other thing, and I was cranky with him," Marcus told AAP.

"I said you've got to be fair and square, that's not how you treat the clubs and people.

"It's not good for us as a family, I was really pissed off with him for that, and I was really angry at him.

"Now [with the chance to join the Chiefs], I said go and have a look and you and your girlfriend sit down and [think through] before making a decision."

Cooper Bai angered his father Marcus (pictured) by going back on his word with regards to signing for the Storm. (Getty Images: Shannon Morris)

Marcus said Cooper had shown maturity by speaking to the Gold Coast to ask permission to visit the Chiefs.

Cooper was due to visit PNG on a family holiday after he was ruled out of the Kumuls' World Cup campaign with a hamstring injury.

"He's only young. He's still finding his feet, and if he comes here there will be a lot of pressure on him," Marcus said.

"The crowd here are tough, they tell you straight up [if they're not happy]."

The chance for Cooper to join the Chiefs would represent a full circle moment for the Bai family.

Marcus left Papua New Guinea in the 1990s to pursue a career as a professional rugby league player, going on to win titles in the NRL and Super League.

He would likely stand down from the Chiefs board if Cooper was to sign a deal to join the club for its inaugural season in 2028.

"I'm proud of his achievements, it is hard to do what he's done and to be able to have an interest from many clubs, it's pleasing for me as a father," Marcus Bai said.

AAP

World.title: Man United captain branded 'disgrace' for comments following latest loss
World.content:
Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes has been labelled a "disgrace" after questioning manager Michael Carrick's tactics following a Champions League defeat to Como.

Fernandes said his side failed to apply enough pressure and adopted a "mood of defeat" after conceding early in Thursday morning's 4-1 loss, a result that increased scrutiny on Carrick.

Como opened the scoring in the second minute and United collapsed, with only a stoppage‑time consolation goal from Joshua Zirkzee making the scoreline slightly less severe.

"We started on the wrong foot and they scored very early," Fernandes told TNT Sports. "There was not enough pressure on the ball and not many good movements off the ball. There were many things not going our way.

"It's a decision from the [coaching] staff not to press man-to-man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence.

Asked if his comments amounted to criticism of Carrick's tactics, Fernandes said: "That's on the manager and staff to see, not me.

"Sometimes you have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable."

The Manchester United captain was heavily criticised by former Liverpool defender Jamie Carragher for his comments.

Carrick raised his arms up in an apology as he approached Manchester United's travelling supporters after the full-time whistle. (Getty Images: Marco Luzzani)

"For Bruno Fernandes to do that, it's a disgrace really," he said on CBS Sports Golazo.

"Last season he got Player of the Year, that was on the back of Michael Carrick becoming the manager, he wouldn't have got that award without Michael Carrick.

"When you think of him as a footballer, he's a talent, but in terms of attitude and the way he goes about things, it's not right at all.

"He's reacted like that because he's been brought off and he's embarrassed tonight by the manager.

"When he talks about pressing … for years, Bruno Fernandes has meant Manchester United can't press because he does things for the crowd.

"I commentate on games watching Man United, and he runs all over the place like a kid in the schoolyard, for the supporters.

"They all think he's working hard, he's not, he's killing the rest of the team.

"Watching him play every week, throwing his arms up at the other players constantly in the game is an absolute disgrace what he's done there, considering how he's performed this season.

"Awful attitude and not what a Manchester United captain should be."

Carrick's position has come under increasing pressure with United now winless in seven matches, and he responded by questioning the players' lack of willingness to run.

"There's a little bit on whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don't run and you don't run forward and you don't run back, you ain't gonna win," he said in his press conference when notified of Fernandes's criticism.

"It was more than disappointing," the 45-year-old manager said in a separate interview for TNT Sports. "I think everybody's got to take responsibility for that. I'll take responsibility for the overall team and performance, it stops with me and I'm fine with that.

"But as a supporter of this football club, to see a performance like that is unacceptable, I have to say."

Carrick said his side had failed to show the required intensity.

"It's the motivation and the purpose and the intensity of a game of football that you have to bring. We didn't bring that today," he said. "I've got to apologise for the performance."

Fernandes also questioned United's mentality after the early setback.

"Conceding early makes us go into the game with a mood of defeat," he said.

United have three points from their opening three Champions League matches and host AS Roma in their next fixture in the competition.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: Diamonds looking lost and panicked as Constellation Cup woes continue
World.content:
We are halfway through the Constellation Cup and it is hard to know whether to panic about the state of the Diamonds.

Australia finds itself in a 0-2 hole after losing in Auckland 56-50 and in Christchurch 62-50, with two Tests still left to come in Sydney and Melbourne.

This is the last opportunity the Diamonds have to prepare against international opposition without another series scheduled between now and the 2027 home Netball World Cup.

The Diamonds are hoping to defend their Netball World Cup title in Sydney next year. (Getty: Steve Christo)

The Diamonds have looked uncharacteristically lost and panicked, while the coaches have struggled tactically. Some of Australia's greatest ever players are out of form but still getting a starting position, and fans are questioning why more hasn't been done to develop the next generation of talent.

The recent events at the Commonwealth Games probably feed into the worry, seeing the side fall short of the gold medal match for the first time in August.

If the Diamonds concede all four Tests to New Zealand, they are also expected to be knocked off their number one world ranking, a status they've held since 2013.

So, is the series a lost cause? Are injuries to blame? Or should we hold our breath and hope home-crowd advantage swings momentum? Here are the main talking points at the midway point of the Constellation Cup.

Missing key players

Jo Weston's (right) work out front makes it easier for the goal keeper to win ball. (AAP: James Ross)

Australia is dearly missing defenders Sunday Aryang and Jo Weston.

25-year-old Aryang ruptured her ACL in the last Constellation Cup series and is yet to make it back on court. Veteran Weston made herself unavailable for selection to give her body a much-needed break and focus on her Masters studies.

Their work rate at goal defence and wing defence make a huge difference. Weston is a relentless tagger, wearing down the opposition and slowing play outside the circle.

Could she be coaxed into changing her mind? After all, a similar situation happened in 2022, when Weston was originally rested from the series but received an SOS call to cover injury with Australia trailing 2-0. Her team went on to win the final two games at home.

Kate Moloney was ruled out of game one due to a nasty finger injury. (Getty: Ross MacDonald)

The team has also had to rejig its midcourt following injuries to Kate Moloney and Jamie-Lee Price. Moloney was ruled out of the game on Sunday after suffering a finger laceration while trying to catch a ball at training. She returned to play on Wednesday with stitches.

Price appeared in the first match but sustained a calf injury that prevented her from playing in the second. In both instances, head coach Stacey Marinkovich decided to play Liz Watson out of position at centre before subbing her off in the third quarter. It hasn't been the captain's best performance.

Jamie-Lee Price may not be able to return for the rest of the series. (Getty Images: Graham Denholm)

Whether Price will be able to make it back by Sunday is unclear, but the Diamonds desperately need to do something different defensively. They've been unable to consistently hold up New Zealand's ball speed and the feed into target Grace Nweke.

In Auckland, they were behind on the gain stat 13-6 and in Christchurch it was just as bad, 9-2.

Home-crowd advantage

Silver Ferns smash the Diamonds 3-0 to clinch Constellation Cup The Diamonds were swept aside in Perth by 18 goals, as New Zealand clinch the 2024 Constellation Cup with one game to go.

Since 2014, the Constellation Cup has been played as a four-Test series, granting each country equal hosting rights, and that home-crowd advantage is no joke.

Over the past five series, the team hosting has emerged victorious in 18 of the 20 Tests played.

Because of this, we're unlikely to see either national body agree to hold an uneven number of Tests in the future. Even if it'd be more exciting for fans to see a team win outright than by goal aggregate.

It's certainly been tough going in New Zealand again this year. The Silver Ferns have been the better side in six of the eight quarters and have forced the opposition to make 29 changes, scrambling to find answers.

It's been five years since the Diamonds last won a Test across the ditch. That outing was Marinkovich's second in charge and Watson's first as captain.

In fact, Marinkovich's winning record in New Zealand only sits at seven per cent. But does that really matter if the team wins the overall series, you may ask? Well, in the 10 series preceding her appointment in August 2020, Australia only lost it once.

Australian coaches Stacey Marinkovich and Nicole Richardson were left scratching their heads after the loss. (Getty: Fiona Goodall)

In the five completed under her tenure, Australia has conceded it twice. A loss in 2026 would give Marinkovich a 50 per cent Constellation Cup success rate. Although she is contracted through to the end of 2027, there is a lot hinging on these results.

New Zealand last beat the Diamonds in Australia two years ago in Perth to claim the 2024 trophy. It was the first time in history they'd won three consecutive games within the series.

Now there's a real chance it could happen again.

However, if we're to borrow a cricket analogy, it's important to wait till both teams bat before we place our final judgement. Home-crowd advantage tells us there's a possibility we could be sitting here in a week's time in a very different state of mind, with two wins on the board.

High penalties

Umpire Gary Burgess officiates a match at the Netball World Cup. (Twitter: Gary Burgess)

A key area holding the Diamonds back has been the lopsided penalty count.

New Zealand has conceded 100 penalties so far, while Australia has conceded 145. That's a lot of time standing beside your player, unable to contribute to play.

What didn't help in the second game was the repeated offensive contacts called against the shooters, as they pushed off the body of Kiwi defender Kelly Jackson, trying to get free.

Donnell Wallam was called four times in 11 minutes of play. Sophie Garbin was called three times across 50 minutes. Kiera Austin tallied up to 12 penalties to finish as the third-most penalised Diamonds player on the night.

As per the typical etiquette in international netball, two neutral umpires have been appointed to officiate the series: Welsh umpire Alison Harrison and English umpire Gary Burgess.

"We had some offensive contacts, so we've just got to seek some clarification from the umpires as to what it is they're seeing so we can adjust for that in the future," Marinkovich said post-play.

"The fact that we also rotated our whole defence line from wing defence to the keeper, I don't think that we're that ill-disciplined throughout the entire unit and we've got to understand what it is that we're doing so we can adjust.

"In history, for the last four years, we've been penalised in New Zealand and it kind of shifts when we're in Australia … But I don't think our game plan changes too differently."

Silver Ferns captain Karin Burger and Diamonds captain Liz Watson. (AAP: James Ross)

That's an interesting observation as the umpires' calls should be consistent no matter where a game is played. But Silver Ferns captain Karin Burger had a similar thought.

"Obviously, knowing that Australia has the home crowd next and 50/50 calls always tend to go in the home side's way, it means the scrap is going to be even harder," Burger said.

"Later in the series there's going to be more tired bodies and defenders are going to need to be really smart about their line to the ball … so that we're contesting clean ball."

How much it means

The scary part is how much New Zealand is gunning for the trophy.

The Silver Ferns have already been brimming with confidence and head coach Noeline Taurua said they believed the Constellation Cup was just as big a pinnacle as the Commonwealth Games gold they won in August.

"You always have that trans-Tasman rivalry, and you've got to back up four straight outings against the one team," Taurua said.

"It is definitely the battle of the minds and the hearts and the bodies."

ABC Sport will live blog game three of the Constellation Cup in Sydney, starting at 4pm AEDT.

World.title: Scatterbrained Australian approach opens door to South African victory
World.content:
Among those who fret over the ongoing primacy of Test cricket in the face of the T20 onslaught, Australia's tour of South Africa had long shaped as an enticing proposition: the two best sides in the world squaring off, a clutch of veteran tourists confronting ghosts of controversies past, and Australia commencing a year-long run of battles its aging superstars see as legacy-shaping.

Some of that probably distracted us from what a bittersweet prospect it was, too. For how, as anyone glued to this contest in the past two weeks will have asked themselves at some point or other, can a game so awash with money have conspired to deny us regular helpings of this fun and fascinating South African outfit? Of real cricket that matters?

Twenty-four hours ago, it was centurion Temba Bavuma reminding the world not only of his life-affirming resurgence as a batsman, but of the great shame that in the last two years, he's only had eight other opportunities to strut his stuff at Test level.

Quick hits: Sore Smith doesn't return as Marnus throws it away on horror day Steve Smith reaches a major milestone but doesn't return and Marnus Labuschagne makes a mockery of an enormous reprieve on a disastrous fourth day for the Aussies in Gqeberha. Here are the quick hits from South Africa.

Early on day four at Gqeberha, the focus shifted to beanpole all-rounder Marco Jansen, fresh from his swashbuckling 85 with the bat, now tearing through the Australian batting order like the Grim Reaper. Lurking not so much in the shadows as slightly off to the side of the stage, stirring up drama and intrigue, there was also the imposing figure of Proteas attack leader Kagiso Rabada.

That and a few subtler problems added up to an unmitigated disaster for Australia. Replying to South Africa's declared total of 425, the scatterbrained and frankly embarrassing tourists were skittled for 99 in their first innings and asked to follow on.

By default, Australia fared a little better in the afternoon, finishing the day at 4-156 with Travis Head undefeated on 87. But with its deficit of 170, and a neck injury to Steve Smith — who hasn't appeared to bat yet in the second innings — it will take something truly remarkable for Australia to pull this game out of the fire on the fifth and final day.

The main impression Australia's performance left was of the sheer needlessness of the entire debacle. What was the first innings batting plan, if any? Why were so many batsmen in such a hurry in a scenario from which Australia was never going to win?

Travis Head was the only Australian batter to show a bit of fight in the face of South Africa's onslaught on day four. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Richard Huggard)

Which is not to take the focus of South Africa's unstinting excellence. Another emblematic figure in that sense was off-spinner Simon Harmer, who many thought should have been dropped for this game.

Instead, he's made big runs, caught everything that has come his way, and chipped in with two key wickets. Australia has had no such unassuming star.

Jansen, with 5-33 from 11 overs in the first innings chaos, was the chief destroyer, but there were wheels within wheels. The mere presence of Rabada, who was missing from the first Test, seems to have transformed South Africa's collective energy from a little too amiable in Durban to ruthless and faintly menacing here.

Jansen was the most visible example of this phenomenon. In Durban, he'd bowled with pace and incision to spark Australia's initial collapse. But as his influence waned and Matt Renshaw got going, he silently brooded away in his own world, looking a little like Alain Delon's expressionless assassin in Le Samourai.

Today he was an entirely different man — gregarious, energetic, fired up. To his usual bouncers he added fist-pumps and fiery send-offs. Like Rabada in the memorably testy corresponding game eight years ago, he got up in Australia's grill and wouldn't go away.

Marco Jansen was back to his menacing best as Australia crumbled under his pressure on day four. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard/Gallo Images)

A brief catalogue of Australia's worst misdemeanours in the first innings bears mentioning. Marnus Labuschagne again drove with hard hands, slightly off balance, with his bat plane all wrong, therefore couldn't complain about the bad luck of departing to a one-handed screamer by Harmer in the cordon. Alex Carey, Beau Webster, Mitchell Starc and Pat Cummins each either walloped or wafted at deliveries they should have respected, especially given the dire state their team was in at the time.

In the second innings, Nic Maddinson again nudged lamely at Rabada to be caught behind the wicket. As in Durban, Labuschagne again squandered a promising start when a break in sight, heedlessly thrashing Harmer into the deep to hole out for 39 when drinks were about to be brought on. And Webster, again neither looking comfortable nor batting with due caution, was dismissed cheaply at the worst possible time. Renshaw, who had looked relatively comfortable, shouldered arms to be bowled by Rabada.

And for all that, and Australia's loss of 13 wickets for the day, South Africa's attack was a man down for most of the day after lionhearted quick Anrich Nortje suffered a groin injury in his fourth over. Things could actually have been worse.

Only a day ago, one felt the confluence of luck, momentum and a single special innings had changed the game's course without any great culpability on Australia's behalf. The feeling is very different now. South Africa will arrive for the final day with victory in its mind — in this game, foremost, but also perhaps in a series that is now thrillingly alive.

World.title: Quick hits: Sore Smith doesn't return as Marnus throws it away on horror day
World.content:
Steve Smith doesn't return after reaching a major milestone and Marnus Labuschagne makes a mockery of an enormous reprieve as Australia is sent barrelling towards a chastening defeat in Gqeberha.

Here are the quick hits from day four of the second Test between Australia and South Africa.

1. Fiery Marco tears through the Aussies

Fresh from his swashbuckling 85 on day three, the towering Marco Jansen continued to terrorise the Australians on day four.

The left-arm seamer was at his fiery, probing best, with his aggression and accuracy proving all too much for the tourists in their first innings.

Jansen dismissed both Scott Boland and Travis Head early in the day, before a few tense exchanges with Marnus Labuschagne appeared to light a fuse somewhere deep in the big man.

Labuschagne and Jansen had a few tense exchanges on day four. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard/Gallo Images)

He proceeded to treat Matt Renshaw to a send-off — seemingly in Afrikaans — upon having the Yorkshire-born Queenslander caught at gully, before sending Alex Carey packing in a double breakthrough in the shadows of lunch.

Unfortunately for the Aussies, Jansen wasn't done there, with the South African having Beau Webster caught in the cordon to claim his fifth wicket and continue Australia's horror day.

2. Sore Smith reaches 11,000 and doesn't return

Amid the carnage up the other end, Steve Smith was just about hanging in there.

Struggling with a neck issue, the Australian received running repairs at multiple points during his innings and never quite looked his usual self.

Smith received multiple rounds of treatment for a stiff neck. (AP Photos)

Even so, Smith was at the crease long enough to become just the 12th batter to score 11,000 Test match runs, joining Ricky Ponting and Allan Border as the only Australians in that rare air.

But the Australia vice-captain was in serious discomfort throughout his innings, and departed promptly after joining that exclusive club.

The stiff-necked Smith was bowled through the gate by Wiaan Mulder for 28 as Australia was asked to follow on after being skittled for just 99, their fourth-lowest Test total against the Proteas.

And in a massive blow for his team, the Australia vice-captain did not recover in time to return to the crease as wickets started falling in the tourists' second dig, remaining in training gear in the dugout as Australia limped towards stumps.

3. Two remarkable grabs, two very different reactions

We have been treated to some seriously sensational slip catching in Gqeberha.

Following in the footsteps of Renshaw — who made a stunning low catch late on day two — Simon Harmer produced his own moment of magic early on day four.

With Australia 3-45 in its first innings and already beginning to teeter, the desperately out-of-touch Labuschagne drove unconvincingly, sending his thick edge flying low and hard towards the cordon.

Harmer dived dramatically to his left, using his sizeable left hand to pluck the quickly dropping ball from the air in front of second slip.

It was a stunning reflex grab from Harmer. (Fox Cricket)

And the off-spinner was absolutely pumped with his effort, throwing his head back and roaring as he got to his feet.

It provided quite some contrast to Renshaw's bewilderment after pouching his similarly excellent catch earlier in the Test.

Harmer and Renshaw had very different reactions to their similarly excellent catches. (Fox Cricket)

4. Marnus throws it away after enormous reprieve

With Australia beginning its second innings needing 326 runs to just make South Africa bat again, Labuschagne had a golden opportunity to revive his sputtering Test career and make up for his rash dismissal earlier in the day.

Coming in after the early departure of Nic Maddinson, the signs were good for the Queenslander, who knuckled down with Head to push Australia towards 100.

And it was beginning to feel like Labuschagne might have finally been on for a score when he was the beneficiary of a huge reprieve in the 28th over.

Given out LBW to a Harmer off break, Labuschagne reviewed the decision in a blink and it was high drama as both camps waited for ball tracking to take an unusually long time to build.

Eventually, the technology projected the ball to be missing leg stump by what surely wasn't much more than a coat of paint.

Labuschagne survived by the skin of his teeth. (Fox Cricket)

Helmet off and head back, Labuschagne was making no secret of his relief.

But only moments later, he threw it all away, mistiming his slog and holing out to long-on for 39.

Labuschagne's relief was short-lived. (Fox Cricket)

It was an ugly, ugly dismissal and one that left Australia once again on the rack with shadows lengthening in St George's.

5. Consecutive night shifts for Boland

With Australia proceeding to lose both Renshaw and Webster late on, Boland once again found himself batting in the dying embers of a day.

It was the second consecutive evening the Victorian had been called on as nightwatchman, and for the second consecutive evening, he made his way through to stumps.

Again, he betrayed no hint of annoyance with his sacrificial role, instead digging in and bravely finding his way through a couple of overs of twilight finger spin.

It was another committed shift from Boland — but boy, it's some reward for taking a five-wicket haul on his return to the team.

He'll begin day five alongside Head (87*) with Australia 4-156 and still 170 runs away from making South Africa bat again.

Tech.title: YouTube says it isn’t testing hiding the dislike button
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

On Tuesday, I published a story about how YouTube appeared to be testing hiding the dislike button on videos, with at least two users on X sharing screenshots of the dislike button moved into the three-dot menu. But a YouTube spokesperson, in a Wednesday statement to The Verge, confirmed that YouTube is “not testing hiding the dislike button on YouTube for users.”

However, YouTube is introducing a new UI for creators on their uploaded videos where the dislike button will be moved.

Here’s the full statement, from spokesperson Kimberly Taylor:

We are not testing hiding the dislike button on YouTube for users. We’re introducing a new UI for creators on their own uploaded videos, where dislike is behind the three-dot menu, and as always, they can find their full dislike counts in Studio, alongside other analytics.

The new UI is rolling out to creators in “the coming weeks,” Taylor says.

The change for creators follows past adjustments to the dislike button on the platform. YouTube hid the public dislike count on videos starting in 2021 as a way to prevent harassment, and it removed the dislike button video from Shorts earlier this year.

Update, October 21st: Added context about the UI rollout timing from Taylor.

Tech.title: Tesla says customers can add their own vehicles to the robotaxi fleet next year — will it happen?
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

For years, Elon Musk has been making big promises to Tesla owners about unsupervised autonomous driving and the ability to add their own vehicles to the company’s robotaxi fleet. During today’s third-quarter earnings call, the company finally gave itself a deadline.

According to Tesla VP for Autonomous Driving Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla owners will be able to add their own vehicles to the company’s robotaxi fleet in the second quarter of 2027. Here’s his exact quote (emphasis ours):

Like I mentioned earlier, the software for Cybercabs and Model Y is the same. And pretty soon we’ll be able to release the same software as part of the V15 release to customers. The only additional requirement is to make sure that, for example, the customer Model Y can be part of the geofences and the fleet management that Tesla has for it to be fully autonomous. We suspect somewhere around Q2 next year is when we can turn on some of the first customer vehicles to be part of the robotaxi fleet.

It’s important to mark this deadline because it’s likely that Tesla will sail right past it. When it comes to autonomous driving and robotaxis, Musk has a pretty clear pattern: he sets bold, short-term deadlines that end up slipping by years — or never happening at all. Still, Tesla has made steady, incremental strides in the tech behind its consumer driver-assistance features. But the long-promised goal of “unsupervised” Full Self-Driving remains unfulfilled.

In 2019, Musk stood on stage at the company’s first AI Day and vowed that customer-owned vehicles could be used as part of a “Tesla Network” of robotaxis, earning their owners passive income while driving around autonomously, looking for fares. He likened it to Uber or Airbnb. Musk also said that by 2020, a “million” Tesla robotaxis would be out on the road.

As of yet, neither promise has come true. Tesla has a few hundred Robotaxis in Texas and Florida, some of which still have human safety monitors. It also has several dozen fully driverless Cybercabs in Austin.

Still, FSD growth was a bright spot in Tesla’s earnings this quarter. More people buying new Teslas in North America are choosing to add Full Self-Driving (Supervised), the company reported. Over 75 percent of new buyers picked the feature this quarter — a big jump of almost 20 percentage points compared to last quarter. Still, Tesla’s vehicle sales were down this quarter, as revenue flatlined and profits dipped.

Tesla also revealed a new Robotaxi safety website, in which the company says it has driven 3.3 million miles autonomously. That’s up from 380,000 unsupervised miles driven the company reported in July.

But even if Tesla opens up its robotaxi fleet to customer-owned vehicles, major regulatory hurdles remain. Unsupervised autonomous ride-hailing requires specific local and state regulatory permits. Insurance may be difficult to obtain. And in most places, it’s still illegal for individuals or outside companies to use their own self-driving cars as driverless taxis or passenger rides.

There’s also the tension between different types of Tesla owners. Older Model 3 and Y vehicles without the latest full-self-driving hardware suites (or AI compute infrastructure) are constrained by hardware capability. Dedicated vehicles like the Cybercab are built specifically for driverless passenger service, whereas consumer vehicles require additional software layers to guarantee safety without human intervention.

Tesla might be confident it can clear every technical and legal hurdle by Q2 2027. But history says this could easily become just another deadline that quietly slips by.

Tech.title: Data centers could erase decades of air quality gains
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

A rush of new data centers could bring air pollution roaring back to levels not seen since the 2000s in Texas, which has become ground zero for the physical infrastructure behind generative AI.

New and proposed data centers are demanding a tremendous amount of electricity. How developers and utilities meet that demand — with gas turbines or renewable energy — will determine just how dirty things will get. So far, though, things are looking grim.

Tech companies and data center developers are devising new ways to get enough electricity, including building out their own power sources. But if all planned data center projects were to plug into the electricity grid in Texas and be powered by the anticipated grid mix, soot and smog-forming pollutants would skyrocket, according to a new report from the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC). In just five years, it would be enough pollution to wipe out decades of gains in air quality.

“There is a good chance that our children and grandchildren will breathe dirtier air than we did.”

In that scenario, fine particle pollution or soot from the power sector would more than triple, reaching its highest level since 2006. Smog-forming NOx emissions would increase 136 percent, approaching pollution levels from 2004. Planet-heating carbon dioxide pollution would climb 90 percent above what they were in 2025.

That’s not set in stone, of course. HARC modeled different outcomes based on three different projections for data center energy demand. Many proposed data center projects are speculative and could fall by the wayside. And developers can limit the environmental impact of a data center by building solar and wind farms onsite.

NOx emissions could be up to 10 times lower if data centers pair grid power with renewable electricity generated onsite. But if developers decide to build gas engines on site to power their data centers as a way to avoid long wait times to connect to the grid, the opposite could also play out, resulting in the highest pollution levels possible.

Data center capacity is typically measured by how much power they draw, and Texas has become the leading data center market in this measure with 26 gigawatts of existing and under-construction capacity. Texas is also bracing for four times more proposed data center capacity running on power generated onsite than any other state, according to a separate Wood Mackenzie report published in March. And in many cases, developers are turning to less efficient gas turbine technology in order to speed construction — another trend that’s making the data center boom more polluting than it needs to be.

“There is a good chance that our children and grandchildren will breathe dirtier air than we did,” John Hall, HARC CEO, said in a press release. “The transportation sector, the state, and other stakeholders have been working for decades to successfully bring these [emissions] numbers down, and that progress is now at risk.”

Tech.title: Meta to create a new class of shares to fund AI push
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Meta says it’s issuing a new class of shares to fund its AI initiatives. As part of its third-quarter earnings report released on Wednesday, the company says the non-voting stock will also go toward potential acquisitions and employee compensation, with trading beginning in 2027.

“The scale of investment required to compete, sustain growth, expand infrastructure, and pursue new strategic initiatives amidst the AI transformation taking place in the industry is significant,” Meta says in the press release. Susan Li, Meta’s chief financial officer, added during an earnings call that the new class of shares will “expand our funding tools and give us flexibility to invest behind the unprecedented momentum we’re seeing across every part of our business driven by AI.”

Meta has poured billions of dollars into the AI race as it builds (and promotes) sprawling data centers, poaches top talent from other companies like OpenAI, and builds AI models capable of rivaling those from other tech giants. The company expects capital expenditures between $135 billion and $145 billion this year, up from the previous $130 billion and $145 billion estimate.

It’s been a busy past few weeks for Meta, which launched its AI agent, Muse, in September. Like other AI agents, Muse can do things like clean out your email inbox, book restaurant reservations, and plan trips. The Muse app shot to the top of app stores shortly after its rollout, and hit 10 million downloads in the US this week. Meta also rolled out its Muse Wonder model this week.

Muse’s launch hasn’t come without some snags. Amid concerns about user privacy, a tech YouTuber reported that the agent gave out his address to a stranger on Facebook Marketplace. The company has also had to pause Muse’s conversation-sharing feature after researchers discovered chats publicly available on the web.

Tech.title: New York’s first microdrama film festival searches for its audience
Tech.content:
is a reporter focusing on film, TV, and pop culture. Before The Verge, he wrote about comic books, labor, race, and more at io9 and Gizmodo for almost five years.

It remains to be seen if people really want to watch vertical content on horizontal TV screens, but many filmmakers and creators were confident that their latest projects would play well at Alza — New York City’s first microdrama film festival. Founded by former Tribeca Festival chief operating officer Pete Torres, Alza, which took place October 16th through 18th, was billed as a showcase for the “the creativity, innovation, and growing cultural impact of stories made for the vertical screen.” The festival featured a selection of microdrama and film premieres as well as industry-focused panels with executives who all seemed to genuinely believe that vertical entertainment is going to be an integral part of the future.

Most fans of vertical videos and microdramas consume them through their mobile devices, but platforms like Instagram and Vurt have been rolling out dedicated smart TV apps that are designed to keep vertical video viewers glued to their couches. The popularity of YouTube — which you can access in so many different ways — has spooked major streaming services like Disney Plus, Netflix, and HBO Max into experimenting with feeds of vertical clips. Alza was filled with people who were confident that they were leading the charge to legitimize vertical content as an art form that’s going to revolutionize the entertainment industry. There’s no denying that some microdramas have been wildly successful, but Alza’s programming left me doubtful that the future is vertical.

The Alza red carpet. Image: The Verge / Alex Parkin

As odd as I personally found much of what was playing at Alza, it did seem to entertain some of the festival’s other attendees, many of whom were middle-aged women. None of the screenings were packed, but while watching a few steamy, romance-forward dramas, I was surprised to hear peals of laughter and gasps coming from the front of the theater, where festival staffers encouraged people to sit in order to have the best viewing experience.

“We’re making content that speaks to mainstream women who are part of this mobile-first movement.”

Appealing to female viewers has been one of the primary goals of GammaTime, the microdrama platform founded by former Miramax CEO Bill Block. When I spoke with Block and GammaTime’s head of development, Amy Sullivan, they told me the platform’s library of content has been designed to appeal to viewers and their general moods at different points throughout the entire day.

“We’re making content that speaks to mainstream women who are part of this mobile-first movement, who are on their phones in the mornings, the afternoons, at night,” Sullivan explained. “We have easy watches, we have rom-coms, and we have stuff that’s a little spicier — but not too salacious — for perhaps later at night. We’re trying to meet everyone where they are at every time of day.”

Block pointed to daytime TV watchers as one demographic that GammaTime has been especially interested in bringing into the fold. Though soap operas are still very popular in the US, their overall ratings have been declining in recent years as people’s attention has been pulled elsewhere. Block insisted that rather than disappearing, traditional daytime TV viewers have been migrating to other sources of entertainment, like on-demand streaming services and social media platforms.

“They’re still here, but they’re watching this while they’re pretending to work a little bit at the office,” Block said, referring to people who fire up microdrama apps for a quick hit of fun. “They’re at home, too, but this is the new daytime, the new 5–6PM, and the new 10PM plus.”

Block and Sullivan noted how, even when overall production costs are kept low, operating as a successful studio is still very expensive. It takes a lot of money to reach different demographics of potential viewers while maintaining various ad partnerships, which is why GammaTime has outsourced much of its marketing efforts overseas.

“We’ve got an edge in Tel Aviv, and I would honestly say the brains of the operation is our partner Slava Mudrykh and his customer acquisition, AI, and marketing teams,” Block said. “Because this is all Instagram and TikTok — that’s where you’re acquiring [new users.]”

“There’s so much nebulosity in this space, and it just seems like a lot of times, nobody actually watches the stuff they’re making.”

“Companies like ReelShort and DramaBox were kind of the first wave of these newer verticals, but because they’ve gone so crazy with AI, I think of them like cruise ships that have run themselves aground,” Paskowitz told me. “Now there are a lot of American companies that smell an opportunity, but there’s so much nebulosity in this space, and it just seems like a lot of times, nobody actually watches the stuff they’re making.”

Paskowitz believes that filmmakers owe it to their audiences and the brands that they work with to put out projects that actually look good. He also thinks that because studios that want to become the “HBO of verticals” now have an “AI slop button to press,” they’re losing sight of what people really want to watch. Paskowitz was adamant that using gen AI in any capacity for film production is a slippery slope that can quickly lead to the erasure of the human element. That, he said, is why Layover was produced traditionally.

Image: Andru Marino

“I’m even against doing hybrid productions because it’s easy to start cutting corners, and the public is going to see,” Paskowitz explained. “That idea sends chills through my body because it starts with ‘Let’s replace that tree, let’s replace all these buildings, let’s replace all the background work.’ And then at some point, it’s ‘Look, we’ve come so far. Let’s just replace all the actors.”

Something that struck me as the festival continued was how — while some projects featured AI elements — the vast majority of them starred human actors who all seemed very proud of their work and excited to share it with the public. These microdramas might not win any awards outside of Alza, but there are real people making them. That might also be why I was so surprised to hear Block jokingly say that the rise of vertical content “is all part of the decline of the West.”

After our interview, Block and Sullivan repeatedly stressed that he wasn’t being serious, which may be true given the line of work they’re in. But even if Block was just kidding, his words stuck with me because it feels like there may be some truth to the idea of decline. Verticals / microdrama production has become a multibillion-dollar industry because we live in a society that encourages us to engage with almost every aspect of our lives through the tiny screens that stay in our pockets. It’s no surprise that Hollywood sees vertical microdramas as the next big thing. But their cheesiness, lackluster production values, and formulaic stories don’t exactly make them feel ready for the red carpet treatment.

Additional reporting by Andru Marino.

Tech.title: Meta says it would’ve made over $22 billion if it didn’t have to pay a child safety settlement
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Meta had to shell out $9.89 billion to pay for a chunk of the child safety settlement it reached with US attorneys general. That’s according to the company’s third-quarter earnings report released on Wednesday, which says Meta’s income from operations would have been $22.89 billion without the settlement.

In August, Meta agreed to pay $17.1 billion to settle a massive nationwide lawsuit that claimed the company harmed children by making its social media platforms “addictive” by design. It will also only pay $5.3 billion of this amount if YouTube and TikTok implement stricter settings and safeguards for kids, which Meta also agreed to as part of the settlement.

Meta’s total costs and expenses amounted to $51.61 billion, including the amount it agreed to pay as part of the settlement. The company may have even bigger litigation costs in its future, as a New Mexico court ordered Meta to pay $25 billion over the Cambridge Analytica scandal on Wednesday.

Even with the fees associated with its legal battles, Meta reported earning $64.60 billion in revenue, marking a 26 percent increase from the same time last year. “We hit major milestones this quarter toward delivering personal superintelligence for everyone,” Meta CEO Zuckerberg says in the press release. “Our investments are paying off, the core business is strong, and we’re seeing velocity across the board.”
