Tech.title: Meta says Muse has over 10M users, with shopping a top activity
Tech.content:
Meta said during its third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday that its AI app Muse has been adopted by more than 10 million users, confirming estimates released earlier this week by market intelligence firm Sensor Tower.

But it is how people are using it and how much they’re spending that has caught CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s attention. Zuckerberg said about 25% of people who set up Muse now use it daily, helping improve retention.

He also shared that over a quarter of Muse’s engaged users who were shopping via the AI agent had an average purchase size of over $200, which was surprising even to industry insiders.

“Plaid told us that they hadn’t seen activity like they’re seeing with their connector on any other service before,” Zuckerberg said, referring to the financial technology company that connects payment apps to customers’ bank accounts. Muse uses Plaid’s connector to enable agentic shopping.

Beyond shopping, Zuckerberg said other popular uses for Muse include personal productivity tasks, such as connecting the AI agent to users’ email or calendars. The exec stressed that this indicates users trusted Muse’s security setup, which includes a feature called “Muse Secure VM” designed to protect their data and privacy. He also mentioned that the forthcoming “Muse Confidential VM” will prevent even Meta from seeing users’ content.

Now that Muse has achieved “product-market fit,” Zuckerberg said Meta’s focus will shift to scaling the AI agent, increasing revenue, and optimizing its compute costs. Remarkably, the tech company is forecasting that Muse will eventually bring in more revenue per user than its “family of apps” users do today — meaning its users on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Messenger. Currently, that figure is around “several hundreds of dollars annually,” Zuckerberg said.

Meta has said it ultimately intends to monetize Muse by keeping it free for most users but keeping a percentage of the commerce taking place on the platform. Power users who want access to the most advanced AI models or more tokens will also have to pay.

Zuckerberg also noted that Meta believes Muse will be profitable after it scales.

“On the compute side, we are building out the capacity to serve more than a billion people over the next few years,” he told bankers and analysts on the Q3 earnings call. “In the near term, Muse is very compute-intensive to run, but we expect to improve its cost efficiency by more than 10x in the next year, which will enable it to be profitable once the revenue lines are at scale.”

Muse will also play a central role in Meta’s smart glasses strategy. Reality Labs, the division responsible for smart glasses, VR, and the metaverse, is still losing billions. However, the division’s losses are expected to improve from $19.1 billion in 2025 to $15 billion this year.

Beyond scaling and supporting its hardware strategy, Zuckerberg teased the company’s plans for something he called the “Muse network.” He described this as taking Muse from a “single-player game” to one where “your Muses can work with your friends’ and your families’ [Muses].”

“And if you want to buy something, it’s not just navigating to that business’s website; it’s talking to their agent,” he added.

Tech.title: Year-old AI lab Flapping Airplanes raises $1B at a $6B valuation
Tech.content:
Year-old startup Flapping Airplanes has wowed Silicon Valley with an impressive founding team and a mission to find ways to train large models with less data. On Wednesday, the company announced it had raised a $1 billion Series A round, co-led by Index and Lux, reportedly at a $6 billion valuation.

The round comes just nine months after the company launched with a $180 million seed round from GV, Sequoia, and Index. That seed round had valued the company at $1.5 billion, so its valuation just quadrupled.

Other participants in the new round included earlier backers Sequoia, GV, and Kleiner Perkins. Valor, Atreides, Kleiner Perkins, A*, and Nvidia are also investors in the company.

Flapping Airplanes was founded by Aidan Smith and brothers Asher and Ben Spector. Smith is a former founder and Thiel fellow who worked at the brain implant company Neuralink during college. Asher Spector was a statistics PhD at Stanford, while Ben Spector was a computer science PhD student at Stanford and founded Prod while at MIT.

Prod is an almost secret-society, five-year-old student-run startup accelerator that has “become one of the most powerful talent incubators in Silicon Valley,” wrote Sequoia partner David Cahn, a Flapping Planes investor, in a post earlier this year explaining why he invested. Together, the founders “are building the ‘young person’s AGI lab,’” as Cahn described it.

The founders describe their work as “the world’s most complete megakernel framework. It can perform entire training runs, serve inference, play video games, and even do all three simultaneously in a single kernel.” (A kernel is a program that runs on a GPU, and a megakernel bundles many tasks into one program.)

The founders claim the framework “can overlap memory-bound inference with compute-bound training,” meaning it can run a task that spends most of its time waiting for data to be fetched alongside one that spends most of its time doing math, so the chip is rarely sitting idle. The premise is that AI has barely scratched the surface of what GPUs can do, and they believe it can create intelligent systems “without ingesting half the internet.”

The goal is systems that cost less to train and run. “A model that’s a million times more data efficient is probably a million times easier to put into the economy,” Asher Spector told TechCrunch shortly after the startup launched.

They now have a fresh $1 billion to hire and attempt to turn that goal into reality.

Tech.title: Tesla starts Optimus robot production in California as profit falls 43%
Tech.content:
Tesla has started production of its Optimus humanoid robot at its factory in Fremont, California, in a manufacturing space once dedicated to making electric vehicles, the company announced Wednesday.

“The bots coming off this line are the first production-quality bots that we have manufactured,” Tesla wrote in its third-quarter letter to shareholders. “While we will continue to iterate on the hardware and manufacturing process, we have proven that the current manufacturing process for Optimus is suitable for a commercial product.”

Tesla CEO Elon Musk said on a conference call that he considers this “early production” and that the ramp will be slow and “somewhat bumpy because it is such a radically new product.” He nonetheless claimed Tesla will be able to make 20,000 of them per week by the end of 2027.

“There’s still some things we need to tweak about the design, because you need to deliver a robot that is safe and reliable and has long duration, so it can’t, like, wear out after a month,” he said. “And there’s still quite a lot of work to do with regard to the AI and the robot for it to be truly useful for open-ended tasks.”

That forward-looking development wasn’t enough to lift the company’s otherwise middling third-quarter earnings, results that typify a company in the midst of a major bet. Tesla’s revenue was flat and its expenses skyrocketed as it pressed the accelerator on its Optimus robots, AI, and autonomous driving. The end result was a 43% drop in profits.

The company’s revenue was largely driven by EV sales, which were flat year-over-year at $20 billion. Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles in the third quarter, about 6,000 more than the previous quarter, but fewer than in the same period last year.

Tesla’s total third-quarter revenue was $28.04 billion, a skosh below the $28.09 billion it generated in the third quarter of 2025. Tesla’s third-quarter revenue was also about $200 million lower than the previous quarter’s haul of $28.23 billion.

Tesla saw a 16% year-over-year decline in revenue from its solar and energy storage business to $2.8 billion, which it blamed on tariff-related customer refunds. There was some positive revenue growth in its services business, a category that includes customer subscriptions to its Full Self-Driving advanced driver-assistance software. Tesla’s services business grew 33% year-over-year, bringing in $4.6 billion and accounting for a record $734 million in gross profit for the quarter.

None of this was enough to outpace Tesla’s spending on artificial intelligence projects and its Optimus robot, which took a big bite out of profits.

The company reported $787 million in net income, a 43% drop from the same period in 2025, when it earned $1.37 billion. Lower regulatory credit sales also put pressure on its profitability.

Tesla executives on the earnings call, including Musk, CFO Vaibhav Taneja, and Ashok Elluswamy, vice president of AI software at Tesla, all took bullish positions on the company’s FSD product, even as the timeline to give consumers the “unsupervised” version was delayed yet again. Today, Tesla owners can subscribe to a supervised version of the software that requires the driver to pay attention and be ready to take over at any time. The unsupervised version would be the equivalent of Level 4 autonomous driving capabilities similar to those used in robotaxis.

“We suspect somewhere around Q2 next year is when we can turn on some of the first customer vehicles to be part of the robotaxi fleet,” Elluswamy said, referring to when privately owned Tesla vehicles equipped with FSD (Supervised) would receive a software update enabling unsupervised driving.

Musk said during the company’s earnings call in April that the unsupervised version would “probably” be released in the fourth quarter of this year.

This story has been updated with information from Tesla’s quarterly conference call.

Tech.title: Meta’s Ad Sales Are Suffering Now That Europeans Can Pick Less Personalization
Tech.content:
Meta’s advertising growth in Europe is slowing now that residents have the option for less of their personal data to influence what s they see.

Advertising revenue in Europe continued to decelerate in the three months through September, the company said on Wednesday, underperforming its global figures. In the region, advertising revenue grew 18 percent year-on-year, slowing from the previous two quarters and lagging the 33 percent growth seen in the US and Canada.

Though Meta did not explicitly blame the introduction of the Less Personalized Ads model on Wednesday, chief financial officer Susan Li had previously warned “we’re seeing the impact of less personalized ads offering in Europe now that it’s fully rolled out, and that may be an additional headwind,” in July’s second quarter results follow-up call. The preceding two quarters had seen advertising growth fall from around 40 percent to 24 percent; in the US and Canada, it had accelerated from 31 percent to 33 percent, according to Ball.

“We believe the EU’s free, personalized advertising option is contributing to the European slowdown,” Dominic Ball, equity research director at market analysis firm Rothschild & Co Redburn, told WIRED.

Meta began to offer Instagram and Facebook users the LPA option at the beginning of this year, after EU regulators ruled that it was breaching its Digital Markets Act obligation to give consumers the choice of an equivalent service that uses less of their personal data and hit the firm with a €200 million fine. Sales growth has slowed in the region since the start of the year, when Meta rolled out the option. The European Commission said that charging EU users who did not want their personal data used for personalized advertising for an ad-free service, a measure Meta introduced in the EU in November 2023, did not satisfy this. Meta does not disclose how many people have chosen each option.

Tech.title: I Worked for a Whole Day Using Only the iPhone Duo. Here’s How It Went
Tech.content:
An iPhone 18 Pro is $1,199. An iPad is $449. If you want both—the iPhone as your primary device and the iPad to handle some work when you’re away from your desk—you'll be spending a total dollar amount that’s pretty close to the $1,999 price of Apple’s first folding smartphone, the iPhone Duo.

So can the Duo’s 7.6-inch screen pull double duty as a phone and a workstation? Does it make sense to shell out a few hundred more dollars for a single gadget that can theoretically handle the workload of two devices?

I wrote my entire iPhone Duo review on Apple’s new handset. I used a note-taking app called Bear, which was mercifully optimized for the Duo’s larger screen. (Read my review and you’ll hear about how most apps aren’t optimized; it could take weeks or months for everything to look right.) But surprisingly, I didn’t hate the experience.

I have run this experiment before on Android foldables and even smart glasses with virtual workspaces, but iOS has its own unique hurdles. Notably, iOS doesn’t recognize a Bluetooth mouse or trackpad by default. Instead, you have to go to the phone’s accessibility settings and enable AssistiveTouch—then you’ll get an iPad-like cursor that lets you navigate the Duo’s interface and select text without constantly reaching for the touchscreen.

Even with the cursor, small tasks like pasting hyperlinks into a written piece or quickly Googling topics for additional research are slower and more cumbersome, so I left those for the end when I moved everything into WIRED’s content management system. Even then, I had to switch over to my desktop for the final touches.

Apple also imposes arbitrary multitasking restrictions in iOS because, well, Apple likes to control how people use its devices. For example, if you open two apps in split-screen mode, you can only view them in an equal 50-50 split. Unlike most operating systems that let you adjust how much of each app you can see by dragging the border in between the windows, iOS leaves you stuck with a view that gives both apps equal screen space. If you want to use the iPhone in portrait orientation and stack two apps vertically, one on the top part of the screen and the other on the bottom, you’re out of luck. In portrait mode, you can only pin video apps to the top with another app below.

One thing Apple did get right is app pairs. You can “pin” two apps together, and they will live in your Recents, ready when you need them. Say you always want to look at your email and calendar together; you can pair them and find them in Recents whenever you need them. (Tap the bar in the middle to lock and save the pair.)

Tech.title: They Believe 2020 Was Stolen. They Could Be in Charge of Elections in 2028
Tech.content:
One was central to facilitating the bogus Cyber Ninjas audit of the 2020 vote in Maricopa County that found no evidence of voter fraud but cost taxpayers $4 million. Another is friends with a Covid-denying former boxer turned MAGA influencer who was filmed on the steps of the Capitol on January 6, 2021 shouting “1776.” Another was set to headline a rally with MyPillow founder and election denial funder Mike Lindell.

This is not a list of edgy MAGA influencers sharing hot takes on X, or podcast hosts on Rumble boosting wild conspiracy theories. No, this is a list of some of the Republican candidates running for attorney general in states across the US.

A WIRED review has identified a slate of GOP attorney general candidates in more than half a dozen states, including key swing states, who have repeatedly expressed their belief that the 2020 election was stolen. If elected, several have said, they are willing to relitigate 2020 once again—and all will potentially play a key role in the 2028 presidential election.

“Any attorney general should be dedicated to upholding the rule of law,” Christina Beeler, senior counsel for the Chicago Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights, tells WIRED. “The office of attorney general is a powerful office, and it is deeply important that anyone in that role is dedicated to upholding the rule of law and the results of elections.”

The role of attorney general in the administration and protection of elections differs from state to state, but in general, as their state’s chief legal officer they are required to be a check on both the governor and the federal government. The functions of the role have been highlighted in recent months, as attorneys general across the country have repeatedly stood up to President Donald Trump and his administration's efforts to take control of elections, seize ballots, and obtain voter rolls containing sensitive information on US citizens.

Here, WIRED has looked at GOP candidates for attorney general in Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, Nevada, and Kansas, where some have openly espoused baseless allegations about the 2020 election.

Arizona

Warren Petersen, an Arizona state senator, was one of the most vocal supporters of Trump’s baseless claim that the 2020 election was stolen. In 2020, he signed a document that asked Congress to accept 11 alternate electoral votes for Trump, and later signed another demanding the US Senate reject Arizona’s slate of electors.

Petersen was also central to getting the bogus audit in Maricopa County approved, a process run by a firm called Cyber Ninjas. The audit ultimately showed that Joe Biden had won by more votes than originally thought. The whole process cost Arizona taxpayers millions.

Tech.title: Greenlight Family Hub (2026): Finally, a Digital Wall Calendar With a Voice Assistant
Tech.content:
I set up a digital wall calendar at a friend’s house a couple of months ago. Her first question was one I’ve constantly asked myself as I test these devices in my own home: “Does it have a voice assistant?”

It feels like the one thing missing from these devices. Digital wall calendars have been on the rise in popularity this year, driven by the popularity of the Skylight Calendar. After testing multiple models in my own home, I can see why. These devices take any and all of the digital calendars you already have (Google Calendar, iCalendar, Outlook Calendar—you name it) and put them onto a single device in your home.

It’s great if you’re like my husband and me, who live by our Google Calendars but don’t want to be tied to our phones when discussing plans. These devices can also double as household management tools with meal planning, chore trackers, to-do lists, photo screen savers that double as a digital photo frame, and even financial management for your kids if you go with the Greenlight Family Hub.

The Greenlight Family Hub has been an interesting device in the world of digital calendars because of how many features it offers. It not only adds financial management, as the company was originally a banking tool for parents and their teens, but family location tracking, which uses the Greenlight app on a family member’s phone to show their location, or a GPS tracker that you can separately purchase for younger children.

But there’s one feature behind the paywall (a $10-a-month membership) that finally satisfies the thing I’ve always wanted: a voice assistant.

Greenlight’s proprietary voice assistant has been both easy to use and has given smart, thoughtful answers. So why isn’t there a voice assistant in every digital wall calendar? And conversely, why haven’t smart displays that do have smart voice assistants gained features like full-page calendars and chore charts?

Not Just a Calendar

Video: Nena Farrell

Part of what makes Greenlight’s hub different from other digital calendars is that the company is using the calendar as a starting point for the offerings it already has. That’s also why it’s called the Family Hub instead of just a calendar like most other devices I’ve tested. Greenlight grew from a banking tool to a way to manage chores and money for kids and teens, and has now become a full family management platform where you can track your family’s calendars, chores, kids’ spending, and even family locations.

Greenlight says it noticed the lack of voice support among competitors’ offerings and baked that into its hub intentionally. “Voice assistants have been around for over a decade, yet when building the specs for Family Hub, we noticed that voice support was absent in the digital calendar market," says Sushil Sharma, chief product officer at Greenlight. "Our goal with Hub was to create an all-in-one command center for busy families to engage with technology in a way that feels natural and seamless. By combining a voice assistant feature with a centralized home display, we are able to limit the number of devices families need in their home.”

It’s also smart for families with younger children—Sharma pointed out that not all kids can read and type fluently, and voice support makes it more accessible for them and the rest of the family. But it’s also a way people are expecting to interact with their home devices after years of smart speakers and smartphones offering voice support.

Voice Report

Photograph: Nena Farrell

Greenlight’s assistant reminds me of the modern, AI-powered iterations of Alexa and Google because it’s also powered by AI. Greenlight says its family AI assistant uses frontier large language models with Greenlight’s own proprietary safety tools that it designed with family safety in mind. That means the assistant shouldn’t get into sensitive or inappropriate topics (or accidentally tell your child Santa isn’t real) but will both schedule a timer and answer day-to-day questions. You’ll also see a conversation appear on the right-hand side, reminding me a lot of the Alexa+ experience on an Echo Show device.

Tech.title: Hugging Face’s New AI Biology Model Lets You Chat With DNA
Tech.content:
The AI platform Hugging Face on Thursday released a new open-source model for understanding DNA that can run locally on a laptop.

Developed in collaboration with researchers at Zhongguancun Academy in China and the University of Naples Federico II in Italy, the model is trained on genomic sequences and natural language so that people can ask questions about the effects of DNA changes on gene activity and health and get conversational answers in return.

Lewis Tunstall, a senior research scientist at Hugging Face, says the tool is meant to help researchers design new drugs and genetic therapies, and it could potentially aid patients in interpreting their own genomes.

“We've unlocked a new capability in language models, which is fundamentally about being able to chat with DNA,” he says of the new model, dubbed Carbon-X. Using natural language means even nontechnical users “can actually ask questions about DNA that wouldn't be accessible through any other tool.”

Known as essentially GitHub for AI models, Hugging Face provides a library of readymade AI tools and a platform for running primarily open-weight and open-source AI applications for developers, researchers, businesses, and people who want to experiment with AI without building everything from scratch. In September, Nvidia agreed to acquire the company for nearly $13 billion. (Hugging Face was also at the center of a major hack by OpenAI’s models earlier this year.)

Tech.title: This Preamp Costs More Than a Fancy Sports Car
Tech.content:
In the world of hi-fi, there’s “high end,” and then there’s Goldmund. Since 1978, the Swiss manufacturer has produced exquisitely designed, astonishingly high-performance and staggeringly expensive audio equipment. As it nears half a century of proudly uncompromised engineering, its determination to position its products as credible alternatives to jewellery, art, or other pricey indulgences for the superrich shows no sign of abating—quite the opposite.

I was recently invited to Goldmund's headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland, to experience the new Mimesis Statement, the company’s flagship analog preamplifier. Goldmund's HQ, incidentally, features the sort of high ceilings, generous use of concrete and glass, and fanatical tidiness that puts me in mind of a Bond villain who's decided to devote their time to audio gratification rather than global tyranny.

In a traditional stereo chain, a preamplifier takes the low-level signals from your source gear, handles volume and input selection, and feeds that clean signal to a power amp to drive your speakers. Most people use an integrated amplifier, one that combines pre-amplification and power amplification in the same box.

Those who want to take things to the next level often separate pre-amplification and power amplification into two boxes—to keep the precious audio signal away from any electrical activity that might compromise its integrity. Goldmund, naturally, is convinced that a preamplifier alone needs to occupy three separate boxes.

Tech.title: Hackers Exploited the PHP Vulnerabilities Days Before They Were Patched
Tech.content:
The internet’s mad scramble on Wednesday to patch a pair of critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a widely used web scripting language, was already too late to stop every attack, newly released details reveal.

Wednesday’s release of fixes for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP caused administrators and security staff to race to identify and patch vulnerable websites and apps, while attackers inevitably reverse engineered the fixes to learn how to exploit the flaws. Some governments and other groups even proactively took key websites down in anticipation of the release, so they wouldn't be targeted before they could apply the patches.

But in addition to detecting such active exploitation on Wednesday, research published Wednesday evening by Amazon Web Services indicates that at least one actor had started attempting to exploit the bugs—known collectively as PHP2Shell—on October 17, four days before Wednesday's public revelations.

AWS analysts spotted the October 17 exploitation on Wednesday while looking back at activity on one of their so-called honeypots, or intentionally vulnerable web servers or other digital lures that help researchers study attack methods and trends. The attempt came from an IP address that AWS says is linked to a “commercial anonymization network,” in other words a proxy network or VPN.

“While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure,” CJ Moses, AWS's chief information security officer, wrote in the research post.

Tech.title: Mark Zuckerberg Agrees to Stay in California Despite Billionaires’ Tax Ballot Measure
Tech.content:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has agreed to keep living in Silicon Valley for eight years, potentially exposing himself to billions of dollars in one-time taxes if California voters approve a contentious ballot measure next month, according to a company regulatory filing released Wednesday.

During a dinner with Meta board members on September 9, Zuckerberg informed them that he was considering leaving California because of the measure, known as Proposition 40, and that he planned to list his Palo Alto, California, home for sale four days later, the 109-page filing stated. The ballot proposal, which could be subject to lawsuits even if voters approve it, calls for a one-time 5 percent tax on stock and other assets held by billionaires in the state as of January 2026.

Many wealthy individuals, including Zuckerberg, currently avoid significant tax payments by borrowing against their shares and taking low salaries—$1 annually in the Meta CEO’s case. Zuckerberg purchased a home in Florida this past February, The Wall Street Journal reported at the time.

His potential cross-country move concerned a special committee of the board, whose members included attorney Robert Kimmitt, venture capitalist Charlie Songhurst, and DoorDash CEO Tony Xu. “The special committee was mindful about the difficulties the company faced during the COVID-19 pandemic when Zuckerberg could not be physically present with the company’s management team and did not want the company to face similar challenges going forward,” according to Wednesday’s filing.

Within days of the Meta board dinner, the special committee and Zuckerberg reached an agreement that links his ability to sell special company shares to his continued residence in California. It was finalized a week ago, and on Wednesday, Meta announced the details. It plans to create a new class of shares that hold no voting power. Selling these shares could potentially help raise funds for Meta’s expensive investments in AI data centers, without diluting Zuckerberg’s existing voting control.

All existing shareholders will receive the new nonvoting shares automatically in proportion to their existing holdings. Under what Meta called a “Founder Alignment Agreement” with Zuckerberg, he can sell 20 percent of those new shares to help pay any taxes he may owe. The remaining 80 percent would be available for sale in chunks over the next eight years as long as he remains in California. Any attempt to sell them early would require offloading some of his voting shares “unless there are material unforeseen circumstances that would render it prudent or advisable for Zuckerberg to reside elsewhere.”

Notably, the agreement specifies that Zuckerberg merely has to remain wherever Meta maintains its headquarters, so it’s possible that both he and the company could move together to another state. A number of California companies have left for Texas, Nevada, and other states in recent years. Google cofounders Sergey Brin and Larry Page are among the handful of billionaires widely believed to have exited California over the potential tax.

But with much of the most pioneering AI development happening in Silicon Valley, leaving the city of Menlo Park could be a difficult proposition for the Meta board to stomach. “The goal is to keep Zuckerberg continuing to lead the company from California and in close proximity to Meta Superintelligence Labs,” the filing stated, referring to the company unit behind its recent Muse AI models.

In the end, the exercise may have been for naught. Recent polling in California suggests that with about $129 million spent campaigning against Prop 40, it will fail to muster enough votes.

Tech.title: Apple Limitis iPhone Duo Purchases to 2 Foldable Phones Per Person
Tech.content:
If you were hoping to score multiple iPhone Duo devices from Apple when the new foldable becomes available on Friday, we have some bad news for you: The tech giant is limiting sales of the phone to two per person.

As reported earlier this week by MacRumors, when we attempted to add more than two to our bag on the Apple Store, we got the following message: “A maximum of 2 iPhone Duo can be purchased per customer. Please adjust the total quantity of iPhone Duo in your order before checking out.”

Screenshot by Corinne Reichert/CNET

The limit of two foldables per purchase will presumably also apply to those shopping in-store when the phone finally launches on Friday.

More from CNET

While preorders are backed up until the end of January — our estimated delivery when adding two to our bag is Jan. 25, as of the time of publication — Apple will have limited stock of the iPhone Duo in stores, though you may have to wait in line overnight to be one of the few people able to get their hands on one (or two).

While companies may limit the number of devices in each order, especially for stock-scarce products like game consoles, it’s been a while since Apple has restricted how many phones people can buy at once. Nearly two decades ago, the company launched the original iPhone to great fanfare in September 2007, but limited buyers to two per order (later easing it to five by the holidays). The restriction returned in 2012, when Apple limited orders to two iPhone 5 preorders per customer.

If you do want to buy more than one iPhone Duo, we found that we could add multiple to our carts while shopping at Verizon, AT&T, T-Mobile and Best Buy, though all of those purchases require you to 

The iPhone Duo is Apple’s first foldable phone, entering the mobile niche that Samsung and Motorola have been fighting over since 2020, with Google entering the fray with the first Pixel Fold in 2023. Chinese phonemakers like Huawei and Xiaomi have also released their own foldables, though none have been sold widely in the US.

Despite refined devices like the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, Motorola Razr Ultra 2026 and Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold releasing earlier this year, analysts predict that Apple’s new device will carve out a significant chunk of the market: The International Data Corporation expects the Duo to amount to 31% of the foldable share of the phones market by the end of the year, growing to 40% in 2027.

Customer preorders seem to have followed those predictions, though we’ll have to wait and see whether that appetite continues throughout the holidays and into the new year. Early reviews have been positive, with CNET Senior Reporter Abrar Al-Heeti noting that despite some downsides attributable to a first-generation device, the Apple foldable’s finer details make the experience feel fluid and cohesive.

“Personally, I have no plans of switching back to a slab phone anytime soon,” Al-Heeti said in her review.

Tech.title: A Privacy Company Just Saved the Clearest Flock Surveillance Map I’ve Seen
Tech.content:
A powerful, free Flock surveillance-tracking platform is now hosted by Proton, the creator of Proton Mail and Proton VPN. The move provides extra technical and legal protection for the interactive mapping tool, which Flock has repeatedly attempted to shut down through legal threats.

The deal, announced on Wednesday, gives the public access to a free database of Flock Safety’s automated license plate readers and AI surveillance cameras across the US.

Security researcher Joshua Michael first published the interactive map in September before facing a swift trademark complaint from Flock. Despite Flock’s demands for its removal, the map remains publicly accessible.

More from CNET

Flock’s surveillance networks capture license plates, vehicle details, human physical characteristics, and audio signals such as gunshots or shouting. While law enforcement agencies use this data to track and search suspects, privacy advocates warn that the technology enables widespread, unchecked tracking.

Proton also says the map shows far more Flock cameras are active than Flock currently says it has. Flock said this summer that it operates more than 120,000 cameras nationwide, but the tool says there are more than 214,000 Flock devices in service, with more than 80,000 in the planning stages.

A representative from Flock Safety didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

The map is one of the most usable Flock tools I’ve seen. Proton’s Flock tool has better visual clarity, faster search responses and a more intuitive interface than other sites I’ve tried and is available without a subscription to other Proton services.

I searched my own city, which canceled its Flock contact over a year ago. The map accurately reported that no active Flock cameras are currently present, but correctly located decommissioned Flock cams. Since the data is based on Flock’s own reporting, I place more trust in it than in crowdsourced tools like the Deflock app, which are subject to errors or misrepresentation.

Proton’s tool is striking to look at and simple to use. Proton

“My research on FlockSurveillance.org documents cybersecurity failures with national-security consequences,” map creator Joshua Michael told CNET. “My research argued that Flock Safety could not detect exports of their data and that because they hold data on nearly every American and their pattern of life, they are a national security threat to our country and people.”

Michael said Flock has “promised to take every measure possible to take my research offline,” he said, offering that as one reason why Proton moved to preserve the map in its Swiss servers. Switzerland enforces some of the world’s strongest privacy laws. Proton’s site notes that under Swiss data protection regulations, the company isn’t required to comply with requests that are not supported by a Swiss court order. Flock is a US-based company.

Camera locations are constantly changing, meaning a surveillance map could rapidly become dated.

“If new and reliable data becomes available, then we will update the map,” a Proton spokesperson told me. “We’re committed to keeping the public informed of all forms of surveillance where reliable data can be sourced.”

Another surveillance mapping option

While Proton’s map provides a specialized, point-in-time look at Flock Safety’s network, the Atlas of Surveillance offers a broader, historical catalog of the sweeping technologies US law enforcement agencies have quietly adopted over the years.

Powered by a network of volunteers who analyze public data and official government records, the Atlas database tracks everything from automated license plate readers to cell-site simulators and body-worn cameras. The project continuously updates its findings.

Tech.title: EA Shutters BioWare, Creator of Mass Effect, Dragon Age, KOTOR and More
Tech.content:
Video game publisher Electronic Arts is closing the venerable studio BioWare, maker of legendary series like Mass Effect and Dragon Age, it announced on Wednesday.

Recent years have seen record layoffs across the gaming industry as companies scaled back expansion during the COVID-19 pandemic, disrupting tens of thousands of careers and closing many studios. The shuttering of BioWare is a symbolic and substantial blow, presumably ending multiple fervently adored game series and carrying implications for the industry at large. The closure reportedly involves around 400 layoffs, about 50 of which were at BioWare, according to Bloomberg.

EA confirmed in a blog post Wednesday that the closure of BioWare accompanies the choice to stop development on the next game in the Mass Effect series, which BioWare first teased on Nov. 7, 2020 — otherwise known as N7 Day to fans, an in-universe reference that has become an annual day to share appreciation for the sci-fi roleplaying series.

More from CNET

It hasn’t been lost on fans that the shuttering of the 31-year-old studio comes just weeks before N7 Day, and social media has been awash with mourning for the many franchises that came out of BioWare.

The studio made a name for itself with Baldur’s Gate in 1998, its sequel Baldur’s Gate 2 and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic before branching into original game series with Jade Empire in 2005, the first Mass Effect in 2007 and Dragon Age: Origins in 2009.

BioWare found its niche in roleplaying games with well-written narratives and deeply detailed characters. The studio was lauded for developing rich arcs for “companion” characters with varied sexualities, some of whom the player could romance. Its queer representation earned the studio a devoted fanbase.

It’s worth noting that BioWare was shuttered shortly after EA closed a deal in August to be acquired by a business consortium that includes Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund. Saudi Arabia has criminalized homosexuality and transgender expression, imprisoning people and reportedly sentencing them to punishments including fines, flogging and death. The oil-rich country has also invested heavily in real-world sports, including boxing, golf and soccer, and EA’s blog post mentions “deepening” its core of sports games, which include the annual EA Sports FC and Madden NFL games.

“We believe we can use our experience building interactive entertainment, together with our relationships in sports, to create entirely new ways for fans to engage with the teams, athletes and sports they love,” the company said. “These will be disciplined investments that only scale when they demonstrate real potential.”

The business consortium that acquired EA for $55 billion also included the equity company Silver Lake and investment firm Affinity Partners, which is headed by Jared Kushner, son-in-law of President Donald Trump.

BioWare’s rocky recent years amid a changing industry

After a lengthy development, Dragon Age: The Veilguard launched in 2024 to favorable reviews, but its sales were far below expectations. EA

As the news went out, BioWare fans took to social media to remember the studio’s formative games, but few of its recent ones.

Backlash over the controversial ending of 2012’s Mass Effect 3 led the studio to develop a new trajectory for the series with Mass Effect: Andromeda in 2017, which got a lukewarm reception from fans. While Dragon Age: Inquisition was a hit in 2014, its sequel was reportedly mired in development difficulties and was reworked into the 2024 title Dragon Age: The Veilguard, which met with favorable reviews but a poor reception from fans, and fell short of EA’s sales expectations, IGN reported. Between those, the studio’s attempt at an action-adventure live-service game, 2019’s Anthem, launched in a flawed state, and its road to recovery of updates was cut short in 2021 when the studio stopped development.

BioWare’s last decade saw departures of people who had headlined the games that fans grew up playing, and the more recent missteps led to a cooling of the studio’s beloved reputation. But plenty of things changed in the larger games industry over that span, too, with development time extending from a few years to five or even longer, increasing the costs of making every game. That puts more pressure on new games to be big hits, selling millions of copies to float ever-longer development cycles. When they don’t, it has increasingly led to studio closures.

EA’s blog post announcing the BioWare departure reflects this new era of gaming, and perhaps changing tastes. It’s no surprise to hear the publisher is refocusing on “core areas” and thinning out existing teams, as any business does during an industry contraction. These seem to be shooters like Battlefield 6, action-adventure games like the upcoming Marvel’s Iron Man and the next Star Wars Jedi game (presumably referring to Respawn’s sequel to Jedi Survivor), EA’s sports franchises, The Sims and its skateboarding series, Skate. BioWare’s closure is nestled between those updates, and notably absent is any mention of other RPGs.

But amid recent years of gaming layoffs and shuttered studios, it’s hard to see BioWare’s closure as anything but a swan song for an era of gaming long passed on a new road paved by more laid-off developers and headed toward uncertainty. It’s not as much of a surprise, as analysts confided their worries about the future of EA-owned franchises to Polygon when the business consortium first announced its intent to acquire in September 2025.

There’s a dim hope that private ownership will liberate EA from shareholder pressure to try new risky gaming ideas, but the loss of BioWare is deeply felt among gamers who grew up playing risks that paid off for a time — and ensconced stories and characters in their hearts.

Tech.title: Tons of People Are Apparently Asking Meta’s Muse AI Agent to Shop for Them
Tech.content:
We’re about to be immersed in the busiest shopping season of the year, and if Mark Zuckerberg has his way, people will completely hand over the responsibility of buying stuff to their own personal AI agent. In fact, according to the Meta CEO, that is already happening.

During the company’s third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday, Zuckerberg said that over a quarter of Meta Muse‘s engaged users — now totaling more than 10 million — were using the AI agent for shopping, with an “average purchase size of over $200.”

“Plaid told us that they hadn’t seen activity like they’re seeing with their connector on any other service before,” Zuckerberg said, referring to financial services company Plaid, which facilitates payments between stores and buyers. He added that, due to higher-than-expected volumes, Meta had to work with payment app Stripe to raise credit limits to meet the shopping demand by Muse users.

More from CNET

Now that the AI agent has achieved what Zuckerberg referred to as a “product-market fit,” the name of the game for Muse in the long term is that we may be living in a reality where you have your own personal AI agent communicating with a business’s AI agent to complete transactions without you ever needing to speak with someone directly.

“Billions of Muses in a network at scale will be able to get more done for people and businesses by working together,” Zuckerberg said, painting a picture of what a large-scale Muse network could look like.

One of the goals is to get Muse to scale up its revenue, which he believes will eventually surpass the earnings of Meta’s combined existing family of apps: Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, Threads and Messenger.

‘The Muse network’

Then there’s the coming integration of Muse into Meta’s smart glasses, which will launch next month. Soon, you’ll be able to access Muse on the go, without having to pull out your smartphone to use it.

“Having your personal superintelligence with you throughout the day will be the most important part of the experience,” Zuckerberg said.

How will all this work together? That remains to be seen, but during the call, Zuckerberg referenced something called “the Muse network,” which he said is Meta’s plan to, if I understand things right, gamify the whole personal AI agent experience.

A Meta spokesperson didn’t immediately respond to CNET’s request for comment.

“It’s not just a kind of single-player game where you have your Muse, but making it so that your Muses can work with your friends’ and your families’ [Muses],” Zuckerberg said, before bringing the conversation back to shopping, “And if you want to buy something, it’s not just navigating to that business’s website; it’s talking to their agent.”

Meta announced third-quarter revenue of $64.6 billion, a 26% jump from the $51.2 billion announced this time last year. Costs were significantly higher, however, up by 68% to $51.6 billion due in large part to the company’s “agreement with 52 attorneys general to resolve litigation related to teen mental health and social media, which provides for payments of up to approximately $18.59 billion.” Net income was up by 264% year-over-year to $9.9 billion for the quarter.

Tech.title: AI and Data Centers Will Impact Midterm Voting, According to Experts
Tech.content:
As far as public opinion goes, artificial intelligence is not a bed of roses. With the Nov. 3 elections looming nationwide, an issue that was barely a blip a year ago has become a full-blown backlash and a likely spoiler in the midterm elections.

A new poll from ABC News, the Washington Post and Ipsos found that a majority of Americans (57%) believe AI is bad for society, with many more pointing to its dangers than the potential benefits the tech could bring. An even larger number of those polled (66%) are opposed to the construction of new data centers in the US, and more (72%) would be opposed if it were in their community.

Opposition to AI crosses party lines. The technology has faced a surge in public disapproval this year, putting political candidates on blast and potentially affecting outcomes in key races, political and polling experts told CNET.

More from CNET

Ambivalence about AI also feeds into negativity toward data centers, which have, in a short time, become a rare bipartisan issue everyone’s talking about, according to Christopher Lee, partner and senior political strategist for Foresight Strategic Advisors.

Lee, who has closely followed election trends in southwestern states such as Nevada and Arizona, said the issue of data centers — massive AI server and compute farms that consume vast electricity and water resources — is going to “hammer” some candidates, especially those who weren’t transparent with constituents in the past about the cost to communities. If a politician voted for the construction of a data center earlier this year, their “political career is going to run into a stone wall,” he said.

Reading the room

The ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos survey asked a wide range of questions about how Americans will vote in the midterms and what they think of the political parties. Alongside the economy, immigration and the war against Iran, the AI rollout is a critical issue.

As noted by CNET reporter Katelyn Chedraoui, AI regulation and data center construction have been the subject of controversy, protests and increased legal action in communities.

The poll confirmed as much: 67% of respondents felt the government isn’t doing enough to regulate AI, with risks including widespread job losses, psychological dependency, economic inequality and even human extinction. Fears and negativity toward AI also extend to the election process itself, with AI election interference among Americans’ top 10 fears for 2026.

A national PR campaign funded by tech leaders and supported by the Trump administration, meant to tout the alleged benefits of data centers, such as job creation and technological advancements, doesn’t seem to be having the intended effect. Some politicians, especially those running for congressional seats, seem to be better at reading the room.

According to Lindsey Cormack, an associate professor of political science at Stevens Institute of Technology and co-host of the podcast Government That Doesn’t Suck, many candidates are paying close attention to how they communicate about AI developments, with a particular focus on the problems they present rather than the benefits they provide.

“It’s difficult to persuade people with promises of economic development when they’re worried about their electricity bills or water supply,” she said.

Cormack, creator of the congressional newsletter archive DCinbox, has tracked a sharp rise in lawmakers linking data centers to consumer energy costs. In an email to CNET, she noted that between January and September 2025, just 5% of Republican newsletters discussing data centers mentioned electricity bills or ratepayers (4 of 76). Over the same period in 2026, that figure surged to 54% (97 of 180). Democrats showed a similar focus, with 40% of their data center newsletters (71 of 176) raising the issue in 2026.

The midterms won’t be the end of the battle. AI and data centers are “going to be an issue in 2028 and 2030 and way beyond that,” Lee said.

Tech.title: Google Chrome Will Notify You If You’re on a Scam Website
Tech.content:
Google’s Chrome will start showing alerts for suspicious or dangerous websites when Enhanced Protection mode is on.

Google’s Chrome browser is adding several new features to help guide people away from websites known for scamming visitors, including sites that try to trick people into opening their computers to vulnerabilities.

In a Tuesday blog post, Google outlined a series of new features that can kick in as long as Enhanced Protection mode is enabled.

If the browser detects you’re on a suspicious website, Chrome displays a clear, “This site doesn’t seem right” pop-up warning. That warning will show as an overlay over the content, with the option to instead mark the site as safe. But that’s just if the site is suspicious. For websites that Google deems as dangerous, meaning that they’re commonly associated with causing harm, a full red page showing the warning will appear. It will direct the user away from continuing.

More from CNET

The new feature focuses on helping users avoid fake antivirus and browser update scams, even creating a scam likelihood score.

Chrome will also fight against ClickFix scams, in which a website tricks someone into copying and pasting code into their computer, often under the pretense of fixing a fake vulnerability. When Chrome detects that someone is being tricked into copying code on such a site, it will clear the clipboard and display a warning message. This is meant to help stop the practice in real time since, if successful, it could allow a scammer to gain full access to one’s device.

To use these features, users must opt into Chrome’s Enhanced Protection mode via the browser’s privacy and security settings.

The security suite provides real-time defenses—such as blocking “ClickFix” social-engineering attacks—in exchange for sharing additional browsing data with Google. Users should weigh this enhanced protection against the expanded data collection before enabling the feature.

Tech.title: Lawsuits Allege Delivery Robots Recorded Biometric Data Without Permission
Tech.content:
Food delivery robots might not just be carrying burritos. They could be taking a measurement of your face.

Two proposed class action lawsuits in Chicago accuse Coco Robotics and Serve Robotics of collecting biometric information without consent and using it to train their artificial intelligence systems. The Cook County residents allege that the companies violated Illinois’ Biometric Information Privacy Act, which requires companies to provide written notice of the types and purposes of data collection, obtain prior written consent, and maintain set retention and deletion schedules.

Plaintiff Mitchell Breidinger said that even though he hadn’t chosen robot delivery for his DoorDash groceries, a Coco robot showed up at his home in September 2025. Breidinger said that while he was entering a pickup code, the robot’s cameras captured his face, head and hands and that lidar — a type of 3D imaging technology — measured the geometry of those body parts. Breidinger also alleged that a Coco remote operator watched the delivery on video and that the company didn’t notify him in writing of its intent to collect his biometric data or how long it would retain it.

More from CNET

The other plaintiff, Barry Schain, said he received three Serve Robotics deliveries with his Uber Eats orders even though he hadn’t selected robot delivery.

The lawsuits seek statutory damages of $1,000 per negligent violation or $5,000 per intentional or reckless violation, plus other unspecified relief. Both companies have denied the claims, saying they don’t record the biometric data of customers or people who walk by the robots on the street.

A Serve Robotics spokesperson said in a statement to CNET that its robots “use cameras and sensors to navigate the sidewalks of Chicago safely. Serve does not use that data to identify individuals, and our systems are not designed to identify individuals or create biometric profiles.”

Coco Robotics didn’t respond to a request for comment, but a company spokesperson told the Associated Press that the company collects only navigational data “to make sidewalks safer for all users” and that it does “not share data from the beginning or end of delivery trips under our data sharing partnerships.”

The robot privacy pitfall

Robotic deliveries have expanded significantly since Starship Technologies’ inaugural package delivery nearly a decade ago. Starship said it surpassed 10 million deliveries globally by midyear.

Coco Robotics now operates about 1,000 robots for deliveries in Chicago, Los Angeles, Washington, DC and Miami. Serve Robotics has more than 2,000 in Los Angeles, Atlanta, Dallas-Fort Worth, Miami, Chicago and Alexandria, Virginia. Both companies primarily deliver food for DoorDash, Uber Eats and Grubhub.

According to most projections, global robotic delivery will expand rapidly over the next several years. One forecast estimates that the US market will grow from $252 million in 2025 to $3.1 billion by 2035. And it won’t just be food and groceries. Deliverables could include medicine, industrial parts and a wide variety of retail goods, and there could also be a rise in delivery by drone and boat.

As fear and anger mount over technology increasingly encroaching on people’s everyday lives, delivery robots — which use AI, cameras and lidar to navigate sidewalks — are advancing rapidly. Just as the backlash against other AI surveillance tools and Flock Safety cameras has cropped up all across the US, there’s a growing pushback against potential privacy violations from delivery robots, which have been punched, kicked, tipped over and defaced, according to a recent story by The New York Times.

Privacy experts and digital rights activists also raise concerns that autonomous courier technology will eliminate delivery jobs and be used by the government or corporations to track people’s activities.

Tech.title: The 3-in-1 Alloop Wearable Could Replace Both Your Wellness Wristband and Ring
Tech.content:
This wearables industry has become increasingly saturated with smart rings and wrist-based fitness trackers, so any company that wants to compete in the space has to get creative. Enter Alloop, a modular, AI-native health wearable announced on Wednesday.

According to a press release, Alloop can be worn in three ways. The company calls this the Trio.

As part of the Trio, there are four pieces of hardware. There’s a wristband, a ring, the Cube — a compact sensor system that collects your health data — and Halo, which offers tap-to-speak, light, color patterns and haptic feedback to communicate reminders, device information, your wellness status and more.

More from CNET

You can wear the wristband with both the Cube and Halo for extra feedback and to log with your voice; the wristband with just the Cube for a lighter, more discreet wrist-based design; or snap the Cube into the ring for the most compact version of the wearable, ideal for sleep.

From top to bottom: Halo, the wristband and the Cube sensor system. Alloop

What Alloop measures

The Cube’s sensors measure resting heart rate, heart rate variability, blood oxygen, breathing rate and temperature. You can also log your meals and supplements using photos, voice or text. Collectively, this allows Alloop to provide a sleep score and information about nutrition, activity, strain, recovery and health trends.

Compatible with iOS and Android, the Alloop app’s health dashboard brings key data into a unified view.

There’s also Bio Age, which uses 18 measurements across six health categories, including nutrition, bodily signals and lifestyle, to determine your biological age and show the factors contributing to it. As opposed to one’s chronological age, biological age estimates how you’re supposedly aging at the cellular level.

Even after removing the Halo hardware, you’re still left with the Cube to track your health metrics. Alloop

Alloop AI

The Alloop Trio was built around a personal AI health agent. You can log your meals, symptoms, feelings and more using text, voice and images, while Alloop AI connects that information to the health data collected by the Cube’s sensors and then uses it to offer guidance, proactive insights, personalized plans and more.

This is similar to how AI agents created by other wearable companies work.

It uses Google Gemini and ChatGPT, an Alloop spokesperson said.

Subscription-free

Alloop described the Trio in its press release as an open health platform, as, unlike other fitness trackers, its app doesn’t require a subscription. However, there will also be an optional Pro plan with usage-based access levels, costing about $5 per month.

While the free plan will serve the vast majority of people for everyday health management and light conversational AI use, the Pro plan will provide more in-depth health-related research and enhanced personal agent capabilities.

“By drawing on a user’s longer-term data, health goals, daily behaviors and interaction context, Pro will support deeper insights and more personalized planning,” the Alloop spokesperson said.

Supported integrations include the ability to import data from medical records, lab tests, continuous glucose monitors and third-party wearables and health apps, including Apple Health and Google Health.

The Alloop ring is lighter and easier to use during sleep. Alloop

Privacy

According to the press release, Alloop “specifies health data protection across collection, transfer, storage and management, with controls that let users review, delete and export their data.” The company’s privacy policy adds that it doesn’t sell personal information and that health and wellness information isn’t used for advertising or marketing.

“Our policy is to keep US users’ data within the United States, without transferring it overseas,” said the Alloop spokesperson.

The company is developing its privacy and security practices to meet the requirements of the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation and the California Consumer Privacy Act, with the goal of completing a SOC 2 examination and obtaining ISO/IEC 27001 certification. SOC 2 is a voluntary compliance standard for safeguarding customer data, while ISO/IEC 27001 is a global standard for information security management systems.

However, you should always exercise caution and read the fine print before sharing your health data with any company or AI agent.

Community

There will be a community feature that allows you to share your progress and see others’ across workouts, meals, daily life and health routines and protocols. You can also create groups, take part in shared challenges and chat with each other in the Alloop app.

Alloop’s privacy policy states that when you use the community features, the company collects profile information, follows, posts, images, comments, reactions, feed activity and messages, which can help it respond to reports, enforce community rules and protect you from spam, abuse and security threats. Depending on the feature and visibility settings, the information you publish may be visible to others.

A look at Alloop’s community feature in the App Store. Alloop/App Store

Price and availability

The Alloop Trio will launch on Nov. 10 as a crowdfunding campaign on Kickstarter. Subject to change, the crowdfunding price is $299.

Shipping is estimated for late December 2026 to early January 2027.
